en: The Original Preface to the *Record of Pointing at the Moon* (Zhuyuelu) of the Shuiyuezhai Collection:

Ji Shuye delighted in forging; Ruan Yaoji delighted in waxed sandals. When their minds were in such states of ease, they regarded all other worldly pleasures arrayed before them as things unworthy of diverting them.
This did not require them to be particularly sagacious or wise; it simply required that they lacked [the attachments] of those two [other men].
Those who were biased all understood that forging metal and making sandals are not worth admiring; they collectively ridiculed him for his misplaced preferences.

Yet, because of the talent and excellence of his two sons, even when compared to those who carelessly roam amidst the bellows and crucibles or loiter among the fire and wax, though one might exhaustively explain the subtle essentials to them so they would cease their fondness [for such things], they would only laugh heartily and ultimately would not be moved by it.
Once they have been so enlightened, then the heavens and earth are this furnace and bellows; the myriad things are the wax within this fire. Who is sufficient to grasp them?
Who is sufficient to linger among them? Cheng Bozi regarded the achievements of Yao and Shun as floating clouds, claiming that such engagement with external objects leads to the loss of one’s will.
Is it not the intention of one who compiles excerpts from the Five Classics that it should be thus? Human preferences are not uniform;
some may revere metalworkers while disparaging cobbler-makers, or revere cobbler-makers while treating metalworkers as slaves—is this not an excess?

Since my hair was tied in two braids, I have loved reading the Buddhist scriptures (*zhufén*), and I have especially loved the words of the Chan school (*zōngmén*). In the summer of the year Yihai, I attended upon Master Guǎn Dōngmíng at...
At Zhutang Temple in the commandery, I was fortunate enough to have my withered sprouts moistened by the nectar of the Dharma; my ignorance was dispelled to a great extent.

Soon thereafter, the Master attained transcendence at dawn and cast off his mortal shell, while the five schools of Chan closed their ears, unwilling to hear him speak again. I, however, remained submerged in the dregs of worldly learning.
Thus, I often said to my peers: "The subtle essence of the Six Arts of the sages and all their commentaries cannot be understood without reading the Buddhist scriptures (Zhufun)."
One attains the truth. Born among the myriad things, one becomes a human being; as a human, one is male; as a male, one knows how to read books;
in books, one comes to know the *Zhufeng* (Buddhist scriptures); and within the *Zhufeng*, one comes to know the School of the Lineage (the Chan/Zen tradition).

This is like obtaining a cow from the Snowy Mountains after searching through oxen, and further being able to obtain curd from milk, fresh butter (*sarpis*) from curd, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) from fresh butter, and finally the finest essence (*amṛta*) from clarified butter.
"Though there be other attractions, I shall not shift from this. This was precisely my talk at a time when I was carefree amidst the furnace and bellows, idling by the fire and wax.
Consequently, the books upon my shelves were mostly the words of the Chan (Zen) school.

Whenever I read them, it was as if I were carrying a single flask and a single bowl, following various venerable elders through long forests and deep ravines, even though the waves of the human world reached the heavens and the dust [of the mundane]—
Dust obscures the sun; yet when I sit or rest my head upon this [mat], it is as if I were holding a *lingxi* horn, attaining the subtle power to ward off dust and part the flowing mist.

Though the winds swirl and the earth is stirred up by the surging waves, they cannot invade me. Whenever my mind finds its ease, I immediately record these things by hand; I shall do so whenever my spirit is inclined toward the brush.
Though pressed by the insignia of rank, he would surely decline them; though pulled and tugged by his young children, he would surely decline them.

When cold and heat thin his flesh and bones, and hunger and thirst press upon his viscera, he has no leisure to look back; how could he possibly shift his attention to the miscellaneous array of other worldly pleasures?

To reach such an extreme of detachment—why must it necessarily provoke the ridicule of others? I have long been my own object of ridicule. In the year Yiwu (1655), the accumulated records [of his life] were compiled.
It consists of thirty-two fascicles. When my friend Chen Mengqi saw it, he mistakenly praised it; Mengqi subsequently transcribed two copies.
Coincidentally, while on official business in Huangzhou, I passed through my hometown and visited Yan Daoche at his residence;
he too mistakenly praised it and presented me with Mengqi’s copy. Daoche immediately wished to have it carved into printing blocks, whereupon I laughed and said, "This is my *Ji*..."
The hammers of the Shi family and the clogs of the Ruan family—whatever is called "fitting for one's intent" is in fact a lethal poison.
This is why the Way is blocked. I have already explained its perversity; do you then wish to cause those with eyes to join in mocking its perversity?
Jian stopped him. By the year Xinchou, I had requested leave from Shaowu to return home. Daochen then wished to carve it into woodblocks for printing.
This intention became even more firm. He said, "You claim this is eccentric; you may say so. However, it can serve to eliminate many other eccentricities.
Did not the ancients say, 'Only with a wedge can one extract a wedge'? He then composed a verse of aspiration and led his younger brothers, nephews, and disciples to practice it.
Since I could not stop him, I did not dare conceal my own eccentricity, and thus have set down these sequential conditions.
I have initiated this at its very beginning and titled it *The Record of Pointing at the Moon from the Water-Moon Studio*. The water-moon is an illusion, yet it is called "pointing at the moon.
Is there truly such a thing as that which Panshan described—a solitary moon of mind suspended aloft, its light swallowing the ten thousand phenomena?
I cannot know for certain. Its substance must be tested in the furnace and the fire.
Written on the day of Wuyi in the fifth month of summer in the Renyin year of the Wanli era by the student of the Nalanda Cave,
Ju Rují, as a preface to the *Discourse on the Record of the Finger-Moon* (with a descriptive account).
He records his vow for the carving of the *Record of the Finger-Moon*.

Although the Buddhist scriptures contain both the paths of doctrine (*jiao*) and the school (*zong*), the World-Honored One said: "In my forty-nine years of dwelling in this world, I have never spoken a single word.

If so, how could there be any teaching that is not the school? However, the school-gate must rely upon genuine realization; it admits not even a hair’s breadth of falsehood. Observe the venerable masters of old:
for several decades they would point to their chests and claim self-assurance, yet only at the very end did they become those seen by the clear-eyed.
Only after a person has undergone refinement do they begin to achieve awakening; thus, how easy is it to speak of such realization?

Once awakened, their observance of the precepts becomes ever more refined and their examination of faults ever more meticulous, even to the point of entering the mountains for further tempering beneath a broken-legged cauldron.

Such is the demeanor of one with true realization—surely this is not what is meant by "one who knows the Dharma fears"? As for those nowadays who merely look upon the gateways and doorways [of the monasteries]...

They then claim to have realized and attained [enlightenment], proceeding from there to revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs. Licentious and unrestrained, they remain no different from ordinary people regarding sound, form, wealth, and profit;
yet they engage in lofty discourse and grandiloquent talk, openly deceiving the world. Alas! Is this deceiving the world, or is it deceiving oneself?
There are days when one's beard and eyebrows fall out and one vomits blood; there is no time left for regrets. Why then should you cast the blame upon the lineage? The verse says:
The world at large repents its sins and cultivates merit; I too cultivate merit to extinguish my sins.
Only the transmission of the Dharma-treasure Is supreme for continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
May I, in birth after birth, never lose my way on the correct path,
but practice directly to attain the supreme fruit of Bodhi; may I universally deliver all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm,
and in turn cause those beings to awaken, practicing without losing their way on the correct path.
Relying briefly on the finger pointing at the moon, one clearly perceives the cloudless moon revealed within the vast,
unimpeded ocean of nature; realizing that one's own essence is entirely identical to that of the Buddha,
one gradually eliminates long-standing habitual tendencies, proceeding step by step until reaching the shore and ascending the peak.
Be careful not to deny cause and effect; If you wander aimlessly and recklessly, you will invite calamity.
Unless you eliminate killing, stealing, lust, and falsehood, How can you hope to avoid falling into hell?
Yet there is a word that points beyond this: Right above your head is the blue sky.
Autumn moon, the wutong tree drips with dew; spring breeze, the willow trees hold mist.
Written on the third day of the eighth month in the year of Xinchou, the Wanli era, by Yan Cheng of Wu Prefecture, with greetings.

The Seven Buddhas:
Vipaśyin Buddha (the 998th of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*). The verse says: "The body is born from within the signless (*animitta*)."
It is like various forms produced by illusion; the mind-consciousness of the one who creates the illusion is fundamentally non-existent. Both sin and merit are empty and have no place of abiding.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world; he was born into the Kṣatriya caste. His clan name was...

Kulika: father Paṇḍu, mother Paṇḍuvāstī; residing in the city of Paṇḍuvāstī, he sat beneath a Pāpala tree and preached the Dharma at three assemblies, delivering three hundred and forty-eight thousand people. He possessed two supernormal powers.
The first was named Khaṇḍa; the second was named Tiṣya. His attendant was Aśoka; his son was Bhadraṃkara.
Śikhin Buddha (the 999th Buddha of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*) spoke in verse: "All wholesome dharmas that arise are fundamentally illusory; All evil karma one creates is likewise illusory.
The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind. Illusion produces that which has no root and no real nature."
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was seventy thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was of the Kṣatriya caste and the Kauṇḍinya clan;
his father was named Mingxiang (Vimalaprabha) and his mother Guangyao (Prabhāvatī). He resided in the city of Guangxiang (Prabhāsa) and sat beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree.
He held three assemblies for preaching the Dharma, delivering two hundred and fifty thousand people. He had two disciples with supernormal powers:
the first was named Abhibhū and the second was named Vāsa. His attendant was Kṣāntivādin, and his son was Ananta.
▲The verse of Vipaśyin Buddha (the first of the thousand Buddhas of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*) says: "By borrowing the four great elements, one forms a body;
the mind is originally unborn, arising only due to objects. If the external object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist; sin and merit are like illusions—they arise and then perish."
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was sixty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Kṣatriya caste, with the clan name Koliya.
His father was Sudīpa and his mother was named Śīlā. He resided in the city of Anupama and sat beneath a Pāla tree.
He preached the Dharma on two occasions, delivering one hundred and thirty thousand people. He had two disciples of supernatural power: first, Upasena; second, Uttara.
Attendant: Jiumie; Disciple: Miaojue.
Verse by Krakucchanda Buddha (the first honored one of the present Bhadrakalpa): To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha-body;
To realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha-illusion. When one realizes that the nature of both body and mind is empty, How can such a person differ from the Buddha?
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world. He was born into the Brahmin caste, with the clan name Kāśyapa;
his father was named Riddha and his mother Suśobhanā. He resided in the city of Sāṃkāśya and sat beneath a Śirīṣa tree.
In a single assembly for preaching the Dharma, he delivered four ten-thousand people across. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Sani and Vīra.
His attendant was Sujāta, and his chief disciple was Jayasena.
▲ The verse of Kanakamuni Buddha (the second honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) says: The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha;

If there were truly a knowing subject, there would be no Buddha distinct from it. The wise are able to know that the nature of sin is empty; They remain serene and are not terrified by birth and death.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was thirty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.
He was of the Brahmin caste, with the clan name Kāśyapa; his father was Mahāguṇa and his mother was Sujayā. He resided in the city of Śuddhavatī and sat beneath an Udumbara tree as a Brahmin.
In a single assembly, he preached the Dharma and delivered thirty thousand people. His two disciples with supernormal powers were Śūrpaka and Uruvilvākāśyapa.

Tathāgata Bahulokadhātupradīpa (Multitudinous World-Light), with the attendant Ananda and the son Śāstṛ, [and] Kāśyapa Buddha (the third honored one of the Bhadrakalpa), spoke in verse: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure;
from the beginning, there is neither birth nor extinction. This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit."
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states: When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, this Buddha appeared in the world.
He was of the Brahmin caste, with the family name Kāśyapa; his father was Brahmadeva and his mother was Vasudharā.

Residing in the city of Vārāṇasī, he sat beneath a nyagrodha tree and delivered a single assembly of teachings, delivering twenty thousand people. His two disciples of supernormal powers were Tiṣya and Bharadvāja.

The attendant Shanyou gathered his troops. Huankui said: "When I first compiled the *Record of Pointing at the Moon*, I recorded the verses of the Seven Buddhas but excised all accounts of their traces in the world as found in the *Āgamas*.

Later, seeing that people who had heard only a superficial account of 'mind is Buddha' mostly dismissed the existence of the retribution and transformation bodies, I realized why the ancients had recorded these [traces] with such subtle and profound care."
In essence, the *Gāthās* elucidate the ultimate realization of the Dharmakāya, while the *Āgamas* demonstrate the general outline of the traces of transformation.

It may be said that they together dispel both [the views of] annihilation and permanence, and harmonize both phenomena and principle. The *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) was completed by Daoxuan and finalized by Yang Dainian;
its purport is not to be taken lightly. Therefore, I have recorded it here in full. This record also briefly includes accounts of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
For this reason:
Śākyamuni Buddha (the fourth honored one of the Bhadrakalpa) was of the Kṣatriya caste. His father was King Śuddhodana; his mother was Māyā of the Kṣatriya clan.
Since the renewal of heaven and earth and the initial opening of Jambudvīpa, his family has served as kings for generations. Throughout the Buddha’s successive kalpas...
While practicing the path, he encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha, who bestowed upon him the prophecy that he would become a Buddha in this kalpa.

Subsequently, during the era of Kāśyapa Buddha, he attained the Way as a bodhisattva and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he was known as the Great Being Mahāmañjuśrī (Huming Dashi). When the time for his manifestation arrived...

He then descended his spirit into Māyā. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year (the *Zhengzong* edition reads "ninth") of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, in the year Jia-yin, he was born from the right side of Māyā.
At the time of his birth, he emitted the radiance of great wisdom, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
From the earth, golden lotus flowers surged forth, spontaneously supporting his two feet. With one hand he pointed toward heaven, and with the other...
He pointed to the ground, walked seven steps, and looking around in the four directions, said, "In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am honored.
Yunmen said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow and fed him to the dogs, just to ensure peace throughout the world.
Yunfeng Yue said, "Although Yunmen possessed a strategy for settling turmoil, he lacked the means to emerge from it."
The Path of the Body. Jueyun of Langya said: "Yunmen may truly be said to have 'taken this profound mind to serve the dust-motes and lands';
this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. A monk asked Jiufeng Qian: "I have heard that you, Master, have said:
'The various sages who appear from time to time are merely messengers. Is this so? He replied: "It is. [The monk asked: "What about the World-Honored One’s single hand? [Jiufeng] said: "It is."
[Zhaozhou] pointed at the sky. Then, pointing with one finger at the ground, he said, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
Why, then, is he called a "messenger"? Feng said, "Precisely because he pointed with one finger at the sky and one finger at the ground, he is therefore called a messenger."

From the time of his birth, various miraculous events occurred, as fully described in the sutras. When he reached the age of forty-two (the *Zhengzong* edition reads twenty-seven), at nineteen years of age, on the eighth day of the second month, he desired to seek renunciation. He thought to himself, "What further encounter shall I have?
Thereupon, he went out for excursions through the four gates and beheld the four conditions of birth, old age, sickness, and death; moved by both sorrow and joy in his heart, he reflected:
"Alas! This old age, sickness, and death are ultimately to be loathed and departed from.
Then, at the hour of midnight, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, with palms joined in reverence within the window, spoke, saying: "The time for renunciation has arrived; you may depart.

Thereupon, the various devas supported the hooves of the horse he rode, and he leaped through the air, transcending the city walls and departing. He said: "Until the eight sufferings are severed, the Unsurpassed will not be attained."

"Bodhi! Without turning the wheel of Dharma, I shall never return. King Śuddhodana pondered this deeply and dispatched his ministers by the tens of thousands to persuade him to return to the palace, but he remained resolute and did not turn back. He entered Mount Taṇḍula to practice the Way;
first, at the place of Ārāḍa Kālāma, he studied the concentration of non-perception for three years, but realizing it was not the path, he abandoned it. He then went to the place of Udraka Rāmaputra.
For three years, he practiced the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; realizing it was not [the final goal], he abandoned it as well.

He then went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where he joined with various non-Buddhists and subsisted on a daily diet of hemp and wheat for six years. The World-Honored One thought to himself: "This asceticism is not the correct liberation.
I shall accept food and thereafter attain Buddhahood. He then bathed in the Nairañjanā River, and the heavens caused the river to flow backward for him.
The World-Honored One pulled him out from beneath the tree and accepted the milk-gruel offered by the daughter of the cowherd.

He then proceeded to the foot of the Piṇḍapātra tree, where the Lord of Devas manifested a man who gathered auspicious grass to serve as his seat. Auspicious clouds and propitious winds arose on all sides, swirling and billowing about.

The celestial Māra thought: "The World-Honored One has attained the Way and has temporarily been subjected to suppression. Leading his hosts, he shall create difficulties. He manifested all manner of terrifying and desirable objects to the limit of possibility.
Yet the World-Honored One remained unmoved and unperturbed. He pressed the earth with his finger, and the great earth shook violently; the Māras were all cast down and prostrated.
Thereupon, he subdued them. Thus the Sūtra says: "By means of no-thought and no-mind, and without any grasping or practice, he completely overcomes all non-Buddhists.
Having first tested them through heterodox methods and demonstrated various skillful means, he awakened their diverse views and led them to Bodhi.
Then, on the evening of the seventh day of the second month in the third year of King Mu (the *Zhengzong* edition reads the thirty-third year of King Zhao, the year Wuyin), he entered [Nirvāṇa].
In right samādhi, by the time the morning star appeared on the eighth day, he attained great enlightenment and realized equal and perfect awakening.
He then sighed, saying: "How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of a Tathāgata; yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they are unable to realize it.

At that time, he was thirty years of age (some say he attained the Way on the eighth day of the twelfth month; according to the Zhou calendar, this corresponds to the second month, which is the twelfth month of the Xia calendar).

Six years after his attainment of enlightenment, he returned to preach the Dharma for King Śuddhodana. The King was greatly delighted and dispatched five hundred noble sons of his clan to follow him and leave the household life.
One day, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and the great assembly had gathered, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said:
"Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat.
Bazhao Che said: "In a state of frantic bustle, it pervades the earth and fills the heavens. Xuedou’s verse says: "Among the assembly of sages, only the true author knows;
the Dharma-king’s decree is not like this. If there were a *śrāmaṇera* guest within the congregation, why would Mañjuśrī need to strike once?
Huanji said: "If you can realize this, then [it accords with] what is stated in the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra*..."
That is to say: without having left Tuṣita Heaven, he has already descended into the royal palace; without having emerged from his mother’s womb, he has already finished delivering sentient beings.
Throughout ten ages of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present thought-moment. Boundless lands and realms—self and other—are not separated by even the tip of a hair.
This is like Gu Kaizhi painting a human figure: though he captured its spirit, it remains, after all, just a painting. (From the *Xiangyan Chanshi Yulu*)
The story of the tree. Xuefeng said, "At the Wangzhou Pavilion, I have already met you. The story of Xuansha’s three types of sick people.
Facing a deceased monk, awakening is before one's eyes. The Buddha-dharma on deep mountains and rocky cliffs. Gaofeng seeing Xueyan.
Yan asked, "Are you asleep or dreaming? Who is the master? All of these are like painting a cat based on a model. *Ei!* These are all [merely imitations].
"This is a painting. How can it be the real? *Duh!* Did you not hear Yunmen say: 'Tell me, how many people in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception have now lost their positions?
Even after passing this, you must practice for another thirty years.'"
One day the World-Honored One ascended the seat and sat in silence. Ānanda struck the gavel and said, "We request the World-Honored One to preach the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said, "In this assembly there are two bhikṣus who have violated the Vinaya; therefore, I shall not preach the Dharma.
Using his power of penetrating others' minds, Ānanda examined the assembly and subsequently expelled those bhikṣus. The World-Honored One remained silent once more. Ānanda again...
He said, "Just now, because two bhikṣus had violated the precepts, those two bhikṣus have already been expelled. World-Honored One, why do you not preach the Dharma?
The World-Honored One replied, "I vow never to preach the Dharma for those of the Two Vehicles, such as the śrāvakas. Having said this, he descended from his seat.
Nantang Jing said: "The first arrow was still light; the second arrow was deep.
One day, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Kāśyapa struck the gavel and said, "The World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma," and he immediately descended from the seat.
While the World-Honored One was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma for his mother, King Udayana missed the Buddha and commanded a craftsman to carve an image of him out of sandalwood.

When the World-Honored One descended from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the image likewise came out to welcome him. The World-Honored One called out three times, and the image responded three times, whereupon he said:
"The true Buddha of non-action truly resides within my body."

"Eh? At that very body. While the World-Honored One was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for ninety days, and upon his departure from the celestial realm and descent, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all went to the empty space to welcome him.
There was the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, who thought to herself: 'I am a woman of the nunhood; I must surely remain [behind].'"

The Great Sangha saw the Buddha later than [the nun]; it would have been better for her to use her supernormal powers to transform herself into a Wheel-Turning Sage King surrounded by a thousand sons so as to see the Buddha first.
Thus her wish was fulfilled. As soon as the World-Honored One saw her, he rebuked her, saying: "Lotus-colored Bhikṣuṇī!"
"How is it that you have bypassed the great assembly to see me? Although you see my physical body (rūpakāya), you do not yet see my Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Subhūti, sitting in meditative seclusion within his cave, beheld my Dharma-body."
Jianfu Huiyun said: "The bhikṣu Padmavarṇa was deceived by hot words; do you still know that the life of this old man Gautama is in the hands of another?"
The World-Honored One displayed a *cintāmaṇi* jewel that reflected the colors of its surroundings and asked the Kings of the Five Directions, "What color does this jewel produce?

At that time, the Kings of the Five Directions each described it as having a different color. The World-Honored One then hid the jewel and raised his hand, saying, "What color does this jewel produce?
The Kings replied, "There is no jewel in the Buddha's hand; how can there be any color? The World-Honored One said, "Why are you so deluded?"
[The man] was extremely [attached]. I took a worldly pearl and showed it to him; he immediately insisted that it had blue, yellow, red, or white colors.
I took a genuine pearl and showed it to him, yet he knew nothing of it at all. At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions all realized the Way for themselves.
Because of the Brahmin Kāla, who offered a *saṃpuṣpita* *aśvattha* flower, the World-Honored One summoned the immortal and told him, "Let go. The Brahmin let go.
The Buddha called to the rishi again: "Put it down. The Brahmin then put down a flower from his left hand.
The Buddha called to the rishi again: "Put it down. The Brahmin said, "Now both my hands are empty;
what more do you want me to put down? The Buddha said, "I am not asking you to put down these flowers; you should..."
Relinquish the six external objects, the six internal sense organs, and the six consciousnesses within them all at once;
when there is nowhere left to relinquish, that is the place where you lay down your body and life. At these words, the Brahmin realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The World-Honored One, because the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (*Samantacakṣus*) wished to see Samantabhadra but could not find him, entered into meditative absorption three times in succession to survey the trichiliocosm in its entirety.
Throughout the great trichiliocosm, he searched for Samantabhadra but could not find or see him.
He then returned to inform the Buddha, who said, "You need only give rise to a single thought within the stillness of samādhi, and you will immediately see Samantabhadra.
Thereupon, as soon as Wubian gave rise to a single thought, he saw Samantabhadra in the sky, riding upon a six-tusked white elephant.
Yunju Shun said: "O worthy ones, how do you understand this? Yunju says: 'Puyan topples the World-Honored One;
the World-Honored One topples Puyan. You tell me, where is Samantabhadra?'"
The World-Honored One was questioned by a seer possessing the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā). "The World-Honored One possesses six supernormal powers, whereas I possess only five.
What is that one power? The Buddha summoned the seer, who responded, "Yes. The Buddha said, "That one power—ask me about it."
Xuedou Xian said: "The Old Barbarian originally did not know that there was this one penetration; instead, he struck the orthodox because of the heterodox.
Langye Jue said: "The World-Honored One did not know it; this can be called striking the heterodox because of the orthodox. The Five Supernatural Powers did not know it."
"Striking the upright because of the crooked. Yunfeng Yue said, "The Great Gautama was completely exposed by the non-Buddhists.
There was one who came forward, unwilling to concede, and I asked him: 'What is that one penetration?
Cuiyan Zhi said, "'The Five Penetrations'—when asked thus, the World-Honored One answered thus; yet, fundamentally, he did not understand."
Regarding that "One Passage," the *Baoye Yuansong* (Verses on the Source of the Precious Leaves) says: "One passage—do you ask me? The mouth is the gate of calamity.
Bringing forth causes and carrying their fruits, The Great Dharma King of Shame and Compassion.
Regarding the "Bridge-Breaking" verse by Liren (Lun): "One passage—do you ask me? The mysterious pivot has its bolt reversed; A hairless lock."
With a single pull, he pulls it open. Three wives sit facing one another. Miaoxi said:
"In these times, there is a certain kind of 'clay-mold manipulator' who often, at a single point, mistakenly fixes upon the zero mark on the scale."
One day the World-Honored One commanded Ānanda: "The time for the meal is approaching; you should enter the city with your alms bowl.
Ānanda responded with assent. The World-Honored One said: "Since you are carrying the bowl, you must follow the ritual protocol of the seven Buddhas of the past. Ānanda then asked:
"What is the ritual of the Seven Buddhas? The World-Honored One called to Ānanda, and Ānanda responded.
The World-Honored One said, "Take this bowl and go. Because of this, a bhikṣu asked: "In the Dharma of the World-Honored One, wherever I look, there is [the Buddha]."
“The place of realization is not yet [fixed]. World-Honored One, what should you point out? The World-Honored One said, “Bhikṣu So-and-so, what should I point out?
This question of yours is just like this. Because Jīvaka was skilled at distinguishing sounds, the World-Honored One went to a cemetery and saw five skulls.
He struck one skull and asked Jīvaka, “Where was this person born? Jīvaka replied, “This person was born into the human realm.”
Again, he struck the bell once and asked, "Where was this life born? He replied, "This life was born in the heavenly realm.
Again, striking the bell once, he questioned Jīvaka, "Where was this life born? Jīvaka was ignorant of where it had been born.

The World-Honored One, while the Seven Virtuous Daughters were wandering in the Śītavana cemetery, one daughter pointed to a corpse and said, "The corpse is here; where has the person gone? Another daughter asked, "How so?"
"What do you say? The sisters observed closely, and each attained realization. Moved by this, Śakra devānām indra scattered flowers and said, "I pray that you, Holy Sisters, tell me what you require;
I shall provide for you for the rest of my life. The women replied, "In our home, the four requisites and the seven treasures are all fully provided.
We require only three things: first, a single tree without roots; second, a place where neither sun nor moon shines."
"A single piece. A place where three shouts would not echo through the mountains and valleys. Indra said, "I possess everything that is required;
however, as for these three things, I truly have none. The woman said, "If you do not have these, how can you possibly save others?"
Śakra was at a loss for what to do, so he went together with him to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Kauśika, even my great disciples, the Arhats, do not understand this meaning;
only the great Bodhisattvas can understand it. When the World-Honored One was on the path to enlightenment, he spread his hair to cover the mud and offered flowers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
When Dīpaṃkara saw the place where the hair had been spread, he then signaled for [the assembly] to withdraw."
The assembly then pointed to the ground and said, "On this plot of land, it is fitting to establish a Brahma-shrine.

At that time, there was among the assembly a wise elder who took a banner-staff and planted it at the spot where they had pointed, saying, "The establishment of the Brahma-shrine is complete. Then the various devas scattered flowers and praised him.
Once, while walking with Ānanda, the World-Honored One saw an ancient stupa of a Buddha and immediately paid his respects.
Ānanda asked, "Whose stūpa is this? The World-Honored One replied, "It is the stūpa of the Buddhas of the past.
Ānanda asked, "Of whom were the Buddhas of the past disciples? The World-Honored One replied, "They were my disciples. Ānanda said:
It should be understood thus: On the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, Mañjuśrī had spent the summer retreats in three places.
When Kāśyapa intended to strike the gong to expel him, as soon as he raised the gong, he saw hundreds of thousands of millions of Mañjuśrīs.
Although Kāśyapa exerted all his supernatural powers, he could not lift the gong. The World-Honored One then asked Kāśyapa, "Which Mañjuśrī do you intend to expel? Kāśyapa...
[Zhaojue] Qinqun said:
"It is a pity he let this one move pass. Had he waited until Śākyamuni the Old Man said, 'Which Mañjuśrī do you wish to expel?
and then struck him once with his staff, let us see what he would have done to settle the matter. Yunju Yuan said: [He missed the point].
"When one family has business, a hundred families are busy.
To the east of the city there was an old woman who had been born at the same time as the Buddha; she did not wish to see him and would always avoid him whenever he approached.
Nevertheless, wherever she looked toward the east or west, everywhere she saw only the Buddha. She then covered her face with her hands, but—
"Extending even to the ten fingers and palms, they are all entirely Buddhas.
Xuedou Xian said: "Although he is but an old woman, she truly possesses the deeds of a man of honor.
Since she knows that evasion is somewhat difficult, she cannot help but swallow her words and suppress her breath. If you now do not wish to see the Buddha, I grant you this; however, be careful!"
It is forbidden to cover one's face with the hands. Why? Because it is clearly visible at the bottom of the eyes. One might think that under Xuedou, you are being taught "old lady Chan.
Once, when Mañjuśrī went to the place where the Buddhas had gathered, he found that the Buddhas had each returned to their own abodes, leaving behind only one...
A woman sat near the Buddha and entered into samādhi. Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying, "Why is it that this person has been able to approach the Buddha, while I have not?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "You need only awaken this woman and cause her to arise from her samādhi."
“You should ask her yourself. Mañjuśrī circumambulated the woman three times and snapped his fingers once; he then supported her and carried her up to the Brahma Heaven.

Yet, despite exhausting all his supernatural powers, he was unable to bring her out. The World-Honored One said, “Even if there were hundreds of thousands of Mañjuśrīs, they too would not be able to emerge from this woman’s samādhi.
Below here, past lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is the Bodhisattva Wangming (Vimalakīrti).”

“Sā. She was able to bring this woman out of her samādhi. At that moment, the Great Being Wuming (Vimalā) emerged from the earth, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One commanded Vimalā to come forth. Vimalā returned to the woman’s side, snapped her fingers once, and the woman thereupon emerged from her samādhi.
Wuyun Feng said: "Not only was Mañjuśrī unable to emerge from this samādhi, but I fear that even the Tathāgata could not have emerged from it.
As for the intent of the teaching, how do you understand it? Cuiyan truly loved to question the monks:
"Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi? Wangming [emerged] from below."
Fanglai asked, "For what reason was it possible for a woman to emerge from meditative absorption? No one was able to answer.

Only Ying Shao Wu, at the moment of the question, pinched his own knee with his hand and departed. Zhen laughed and said, "The customer who sells spoons and chopsticks has not yet arrived. Hong Juefan remarked:
"In the Teachings there is the causal account of a woman emerging from meditative absorption; this has been discussed in the monastic communities."
This is extremely numerous. Were it not for those whose Dharma-eye is clear and who have personally encountered a true master, one could not understand this clearly.
Zen Master Dayu Zhi used to ask the monks: "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas; why was he unable to bring the woman out of her samādhi?
Yet the Bodhisattva Wuming came from the lower regions and, with but a single snap of his fingers, was able to bring her out of samādhi?"
No one could respond, so he spoke on his own behalf: "The monk goes to the temple to stay; the thief strikes when the house is unguarded.
I, Zizhi, loved these words and composed a verse to record them, saying: "A single snap of the fingers suffices to emerge from samādhi;
How could the Buddha-dharma require effort? I use it whenever I need to use it; I do not care whether Manjushri is clearly manifest or not. When Master Yun’an saw this, he remarked: [He approved.]
The next day, he ascended the seat and, employing the previous anecdote, said: "As for Mañjuśrī and Wǎngmíng, was there any distinction of superiority or inferiority in their realization?
If you say there was none, why was it that Mañjuśrī could not emerge from the woman’s samādhi? Consider this very day:
when the ritual master strikes the Dharma drum and the great assembly together arrives before the seat, who will emerge from the woman [for you]?"

The Master settled the matter. "Are they the same or different? After a long silence, he said: "Have you not heard it said: 'If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the conditions of time and season'?
The entire assembly are guests under the gate of the Patriarch. You who are superior practitioners seeking the profound—try to observe this with careful attention.
If you can see it, your work as a renunciant will be finished; you will attain liberation and peace, and there will be no need for worldly toil."
Observing with leisure, he gave a shout and descended from his seat. Yun’an also had a verse that said: "The Buddha-nature is a matter of natural truth;
who says there is another teacher? Where Wangming snapped his fingers, the woman emerged from meditation. Not a single iota of effort was expended."
How could that which is contemplated ever move? Sentient beings are all equally so. Yet in daily life, one naturally harbors many doubts. Miaoxi said:
"There is a certain kind of deliberation regarding the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients, which is called the 'work of needle and thread,' or the 'Chan of the young gentlemen.
For instance, when deliberating on the words of the woman emerging from samādhi, it is said: 'Mañjuśrī is the [seventh] Buddha of the seven Buddhas...'"
The Master said: "Why was Mañjuśrī unable to emerge from the woman's samādhi? He replied: "Mañjuśrī had no karmic affinity with the woman.
[The Master asked: "Wangming is a Bodhisattva of the First Ground; why was he able to emerge from the woman's samādhi? He replied: "He had a karmic affinity with the woman.
The Master added: "An enemy has a head, and a debt has an owner. Furthermore, there is a discussion that says Mañjuśrī acted improperly.
Wumen had a mind; therefore, he could not emerge from the woman’s samādhi. Wangming was without mind; therefore, he was able to emerge. The verse says:
“When the mind has a place of application, it becomes an error; When there is no intention in seeking, it is perfectly as it is. Furthermore, some have deliberated:
“Why was it that Manjusri could not emerge from the woman’s samādhi? The handle of the ladle was in the woman’s hand.”

[This is] the inner [meaning]. Why was it that Wǎngmíng could emerge? It is like a worm gnawing through wood. Again, it is said: "It is because of the wind blowing upon the fire. And again: "What can one do about the woman?

Those with the most extreme erroneous interpretations go so far as to perform the gestures of a woman entering meditative absorption and emerging from it, pushing [the image], snapping their fingers once, and crying out to Heaven several times. [They conclude with]: "We humbly pray you will still enjoy [this offering]. [Then they] sweep away [the offerings].
Regarding such matters as the "sleeves," when viewed with a cool mind, they are enough to put one to shame. Miaoxi’s verse says:
"Attaining or not attaining—this is fixed, yet not the true fixation. Wangming and Mañjuśrī have lost their very lives.
Yuánwù Qín’s verse says: "The Great Samādhi is equal to empty space; In its vastness, who can discern it? The Woman and Gautama, based on..."
What could possibly be made straight? The lion’s springing forth shakes the very heavens and earth; the elephant king’s circling turns requires no external effort.
Who wins and who loses? Who emerges and who enters? The rain disperses and the clouds vanish; it is a clear blue sky and a bright sun.
"Do you not see? The colt tramples people underfoot throughout the world; Linji was not yet a 'white-thief' (a master thief). The nun Miaozong composed a verse:
"Gold cannot purchase gold; water cannot wash water. Since duality is not established, how can there be a single [oneness]?
To fail to clarify Mañjuśrī is like playing with one's fingers inside a boot. Tianyi Huai composed a verse: "Mañjuśrī is entrusted above."
Brahmā was unenlightened; with a light snap of his fingers, the woman [awakened] Huangmian Gautama.
Watch him fall once and rise again. Baofeng’s Illuminating Verse says: "Brushing the jade zither, he plays beneath the moon; The melody is so lofty that a response is hard to find.
Though the Five Marquises exhaust their lifelong ambitions, From now on, they will grow weary of looking at the Odes and Documents. Shimen.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) verse says: Sitting amidst a multitude of peaks shrouded in white clouds, Cuckoos cry in deep valleys, unaware of spring.

Pei Xiu wrote a preface for the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), in which he said: "Those who are in a state of complete enlightenment all day long yet have never realized complete enlightenment are ordinary beings (*pǔfán*).
Those who are fully endowed with complete enlightenment and abide in the maintenance of complete enlightenment are the Tathāgatas."

Chan Master Cibian Baoyin of Mount Jingshan in the Song dynasty distinguished their words as follows: "To be fully endowed with perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) is the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
To abide in perfect enlightenment while throughout the day never having experienced perfect enlightenment is the state of a Tathāgata. — *Congrong lu* (Record of Ease and Composure).

Ten Verses in Praise of the Mahāyāna The Great Way is ever present before one’s eyes; though it is ever-present, it is difficult to behold.
If you wish to awaken to the true essence of the Way, do not attempt to eliminate sound, form, or speech. Speech itself is the Great Way; there is no need to rely on severing afflictions (*kleśa*).
Afflictions are fundamentally empty and quiescent; it is only deluded sentiments that entangle one another. All things are like shadows and echoes.
One does not know what is evil or what is good. To have a mind that grasps at signs as being real is certainly to fail to realize the nature of seeing.

If one wishes to perform deeds to seek Buddhahood, the Buddha is but a great omen within birth and death; the karma of birth and death constantly follows one, and one has not yet awakened from within the dark prison.

The wisdom-mind of sentient beings is small; they can merely refrain from giving rise to the notion of "self. They are constantly satiated by the Dharma-food of *nirvāṇa*.
