When movement and stillness are both forgotten, there is eternal quiescence; one naturally accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*). If one says that sentient beings are different from the Buddha, they remain far removed and perpetually distant from the Buddha.
Since the Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual, they are naturally and ultimately without remainder. (2) The Dharma-nature is primordial.
Eternally quiescent, vast and boundless, one settles the mind amidst acceptance and rejection, yet is turned about by the two opposing realms.

Restraining the countenance to enter meditative absorption and sitting in dhyāna, one gathers the objects of perception to settle the mind through contemplation; practicing the Way like a wooden puppet moved by a mechanism, when will one reach the other shore?
All phenomena are fundamentally empty and without attachment; objects are like floating clouds that must eventually disperse. Suddenly, one awakens to one's original nature.
Empty from the start. It is like a feverish illness breaking into a sweat. Do not speak of this before those lacking wisdom; it would scatter your physical body to the stars.

(3) I report to you sentient beings the direct path: it is neither existent nor non-existent. Since it is neither existent nor non-existent, there is no duality. Why need one debate emptiness in opposition to existence?
Existence and non-existence are names established by the deluded mind. Break through one and do not dwell in the other; these two names arise from...

Your emotions are active; when emotions are absent, that is precisely Suchness (*tathatā*). If you wish to seek the Buddha while clinging to emotions, it is like setting a net on a mountain to catch fish—it merely wastes effort and is of no benefit.
How much labor have you wasted in vain! You do not understand that "the mind itself is the Buddha," which is truly like riding a donkey while searching for a donkey.
Do not harbor hatred toward anything, nor do you love anything; these afflictions (*kleśa*) must be eliminated. If they are eliminated, then—
One must eliminate the body. When the body is eliminated, there is no Buddha and no cause; when there is no Buddha and no cause, nothing can be attained.

Spontaneously, there is neither dharma nor person. (4) The Great Way is not attained through practice; the teaching of practice is a provisional means for the sake of the foolish and ignorant. Having attained the Principle, one turns back to observe practice.

Only now do you realize that your efforts were in vain; you have not yet awakened to the Great Principle of Perfect Penetration. You must ensure that your words and deeds support one another, and you must not cling to the intellectual understandings of others.
When the light is turned back toward the source, there is absolutely nothing at all—who can truly comprehend this teaching?

I instruct you to seek it within yourself; therein you shall see your own past transgressions. Cast off the sores and tumors of the five desires, and you will attain liberation, carefree and autonomous.
Wandering through various directions to sell one's elegance for a low price—who is there to give rise to the resolve to buy? Such a person may also attain a state like mine, free from sorrow.

(5) Internal views and external views are both evil; the path of the Buddha and the path of Māra are equally mistaken. Harassed by these two great Pāpīyas, one then perceives weariness with suffering and seeks happiness.
Upon awakening to the fact that the essence of birth and death is empty, where can Buddha or Māra find any foothold? It is solely due to deluded sentiment that they are distinguished.
Separate. Previous and subsequent bodies are solitary and meager; one wanders through the six realms of rebirth without ceasing.

That karmic bonds cannot be eliminated, and that one drifts through birth and death, is entirely due to the superficiality of adventitious arising. The body is fundamentally empty and unreal; who is it that returns to the source?

Whether existence or non-existence, I myself am capable of this; there is no need for the deluded mind to engage in speculative calculation. The bodies of sentient beings are identical to the Great [Void].
Empty. Where can afflictions take root? Simply by being free from all seeking, afflictions naturally dissolve and fall away.

(6) How pitiable are these bustling sentient beings, each clinging to their own particular divergent views; they only wish to seek cakes upon the griddle, yet do not understand how to return to the source and observe the flour.
Flour is the very basis of both the correct and the deviant; through human effort it is transformed into a hundred variations, and whatever is required may be made at will.
Transcending all constraints, one need not rely on partial attachments or cravings; non-attachment is itself liberation. To have seeking is to encounter the snare.

With a heart of compassion toward all equally, True Suchness and Bodhi manifest of themselves. If one harbors the dualistic mind of "self" and "other," one will not see the Buddha’s face even when facing him directly.
(7) How many deluded people are there in the world who, while already possessing the Way, seek the Way once more, searching extensively through various [teachings]?

Their interpretations are in such confusion that they cannot even save themselves; they merely seek out the texts of others to speak in disorder, claiming their own views to be the ultimate truth and most exquisite.

They labor in vain throughout their lives, passing them away in emptiness, sinking into the cycle of birth and old age for eternal kalpas. Turbid attachments entangle their minds and refuse to let go;
their pure, wise mind brings them only self-affliction. The forest of the *tathatā* dharma-realm is, conversely, turned into thorns and wild weeds by those who cling only to the yellow [scriptures].
The leaves are gold; failing to realize this, one discards the gold to seek the jewels, thereby losing mindfulness and wandering in madness.

Though one forcefully maintains the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), reciting sutras and treatises within the mouth, the mind remains constantly withered. Once one awakens to the emptiness of the fundamental mind, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is fully present without deficiency.
(8) The Śrāvaka severs delusions mind after mind; yet the very mind capable of severing them is itself a thief—a thief that steals the thief.

They eliminate one another in succession. When will they ever realize the fundamental silence of words? Though they recite a thousand scrolls of sutras from their mouths, they do not recognize the sutras within their own bodies;

failing to understand the perfect penetration of the Buddha-dharma, they labor in vain over the lines and characters. Such are the ascetic practices of the dhūtas and the arduous austerities of the āraṇyakas.
To hope for merit in future lives is to distance oneself from the Sage; how then can the Great Way be attained?

It is like dreaming of crossing a river: once the ferryman has carried one across to the north bank, one suddenly awakens to find oneself sleeping peacefully in bed, having lost the means of the crossing—the ferry and its rules.
The ferryman and the person being ferried were originally strangers to one another; yet sentient beings remain deluded and entangled.
Coming and going through the three realms, one becomes utterly exhausted. Awakening to birth and death as being like a dream, all seeking of the mind naturally ceases.

(9) To realize this is itself bodhi; to understand it fundamentally, there are no rungs on a ladder. One can only sigh for the common person, bent over and hunched, unable to take even a single step at eighty years of age.
They have spent their entire life in vain toil, unaware that the days and months have slipped away. Look up and observe your teacher.
Mouth: Like a nursing infant who has lost its mother, clergy and laity alike gather in profusion, listening all day long to his dead words while failing to observe their own impermanence.
Their mental conduct is as greedy as wolves and tigers; one must lament the narrowness and inferiority of the Two Vehicles.

One must surely subdue the six sense-faculties, abstaining from wine, meat, and the five pungent roots. With eyes of perversion, they look upon others drinking and eating, yet they themselves engage in further perverse and frantic conduct.
Madness. In his cultivation, he abstained from salt and vinegar. Had he awakened to the Supreme Vehicle of Ultimate Truth, he would not have needed to differentiate between male and female.
(10) Fourteen Verses on the Fourteen Topics: Enlightenment and affliction are non-dual; yet sentient beings do not understand the Way of cultivation.
They wish to sever and eliminate afflictions, yet afflictions are originally empty and quiescent. Taking the Way, they further seek the Way.
The single thought-moment is it; why must one seek it elsewhere? The Great Way is right before one’s eyes, yet the foolish and deluded fail to realize it.
Buddha-nature is heavenly, true, and spontaneous; it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor created through cultivation.

Failing to recognize that the three poisons are illusory, they falsely cling to the floating and sinking of birth and death. They regarded the past as a time of lost opportunity, yet today they finally realize it is not too late.

Observance and transgression are non-dual; the man of great capacity applies them without obstruction. He is not constrained by the rules of the precepts, for observance and transgression are fundamentally unborn from the beginning.
The foolish person is bound by external prohibitions, while the wise person finds all conditioned activity to be empty.

The Śrāvaka encounters obstructions at every turn, whereas the Mahāsattva’s physical eye is perfectly penetrating. The divine eye of the Two Vehicles is clouded with cataracts; they falsely cling to existence and non-existence within the void.
Failing to realize that form and mind are unimpeded, the Bodhisattva dwells together with worldly beings yet remains pure, never defiled by the world.

The foolish crave attachment to *nirvāṇa*, while the wise find the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) within birth and death. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is empty and beyond verbal expression; its dependent origination is rarely understood by anyone.
A hundred-year-old child who lacks wisdom is but a child, whereas a child who possesses wisdom is a hundred years old. Thus, there is no distinction between the Buddha and sentient beings.
2. Sentient beings and Buddhas are no different; great wisdom is not distinct from folly. Why seek the jewel elsewhere?
Within the field of one’s own body, there is naturally a bright pearl. The right path and the deviant path are non-dual; understand that ordinary people and sages share the same way.

Delusion and awakening are fundamentally without distinction; nirvana and birth-and-death are as one. Ultimately, all objects of攀缘 (pān-yuán) [clinging/conditions] are empty and still; seek only within the realm of thought.
Pure and void; not a single dharma can be apprehended. Spontaneously entering the realm of no-remainder, phenomena and principle are non-dual, and the mind-king is sovereign and carefree.

In the fundamental nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*), there are originally no ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*); everything is nothing other than the Buddha-work. Why need one restrain the thoughts and practice seated meditation?
Delusive thoughts are originally empty and still; there is no need to sever or eliminate objective conditions (*ālambana*). The wise have no [discursive] mind.
It can be attained. It is naturally free from contention and clamor. If one does not recognize the unconditioned Great Way, when will one realize its profound mystery?

Buddhas and sentient beings are of one kind; sentient beings are themselves the World-Honored One. Ordinary people deludedly give rise to discrimination, clinging to existence within non-existence and rushing headlong into confusion.
Once one thoroughly understands that greed and anger are empty and quiescent, where would there not be the Gate of Truth? Whether in stillness or turmoil, it is no different.
2. Śrāvakas weary of clamor and seek stillness, much like one who discards flour in search of bread. Yet the bread has always been flour; its transformation follows the person’s efforts.
Afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves awakening (*bodhi*); the absence of mind is itself the absence of objects.
Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa. Greed and anger are like flames and shadows. The wise have no mind to seek a Buddha; the foolish cling to what is false.
To cling to what is "correct" is merely to labor in vain throughout one's entire life, failing to behold the wondrous crown of the Tathāgata.
When one thoroughly realizes that the nature of lust is empty, the cauldrons and furnaces of hell cool of their own accord. Good and evil are non-dual; my own body and mind are joyful.

Transcending both good and evil, the Dharma-body is sovereign and without fixed location. Whatever meets the eye is nothing other than perfect awakening. The six sense-objects are, from the very beginning, [the Dharma-realm].

Emptiness and stillness—ordinary beings deludedly give rise to attachment. Nirvana and birth-and-death are fundamentally equal; throughout the four seas, who is superior or inferior? The unconditioned Great Way is spontaneous;
there is no need to employ the mind to calculate or measure it. Bodhisattvas are carefree and spiritually penetrating; all they do naturally contains wondrous enlightenment.
Śrāvakas cling to the dharmas and sit in meditation, like silkworms spinning silk to bind themselves. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is originally...

Perfectly luminous. Once the illness has been cured, why persist in clinging to the medicine? To fully realize that all phenomena are equal is to dwell in a state of carefree purity, emptiness, and joy where form and space are non-dual.
The nature of phenomena is fundamentally devoid of blue or yellow; sentient beings merely fabricate literary compositions.

To speak of self and other, or of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, is for one's own mind to be agitated and deranged. Failing to recognize the wondrous principle of perfect penetration, when will you ever attain realization?
Truly eternal, yet unable to treat one's own illness, one instead teaches others medicinal prescriptions;
outwardly appearing to be virtuous, yet inwardly remaining like a jackal or a wolf. To the fool, hell is feared; to the wise, it is no different from heaven.

When the mind does not arise in response to external objects, every step taken is a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Buddhas and sentient beings are non-dual; sentient beings create [their own conditions] themselves.
To divide and distribute [the mind]. If one wishes to eliminate the three poisons, yet remains far removed from them, one will not escape calamity.

The wise know that the mind is Buddha; the ignorant delight in going to the Western Land. Birth and death are non-dual; all phenomena in the world are like illusions. Birth and death are like lightning;
the Dharma-body is sovereign and universally penetrating, entering and exiting mountains and rivers without interval. This is due to inverted deluded thoughts.

The fundamental nature is empty. Prajñā is without delusion or confusion; the three poisons are inherently liberated from the very beginning. Why then is it necessary to restrain the mind through meditative contemplation?
It is only because fools do not understand that they must rely on the precepts and rules for decisive judgment.

Failing to recognize quiescent *tathatā*, when will they ever reach the other shore? For the wise, there is no evil to be severed; their functioning follows the mind, whether in union or dispersion. The *dharmatā* is originally thus.
Emptiness and stillness are not bound by birth and death. If one wishes to sever afflictions, such a person is a deluded fool of ignorance.
Afflictions are themselves bodhi; what need is there to seek meditation and contemplation elsewhere? In the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), there is neither Buddha nor Māra.
The substance of the mind is formless and undivided. Severing duality, the Great Man acts with majestic dignity, carefree and autonomous.
There is no hindrance. Nothing can cause harm; it is as firm and solid as vajra. It does not cling to the two extremes but dwells in the Middle Way—serene, neither annihilated nor eternal.
The five desires, greed, and anger are themselves the Buddha; hell is no different from heaven.
Fools give rise to false discriminations and wander wildly through the cycle of birth and death. The wise realize that form is without obstruction; for the śrāvakas, there is nothing that is not...
How distressing! The Dharma-nature is fundamentally free of blemish or obscuration, yet sentient beings delusively cling to colors such as blue and yellow.
The Tathāgata guides the ignorant and deluded, sometimes speaking of hells and heavens; these exist inherently within the body of Maitreya—why must one seek them elsewhere through conceptualization?
To cast aside the Buddha-image of True Suchness, such a person is truly insane. Within the minds of the Śrāvakas, this remains uncomprehended; they merely pursue after external forms.

Regarding the "Chapter on Words": The Chapter on Words is fundamentally not the True Way. It only serves to increase contention and rigidity; within the mind there are vipers, snakes, and scorpions that inflict wounds as soon as they sting.
Failing to grasp the meaning from within the words, when will one ever realize the true and eternal?
Upon death, one enters the Avīci Hell, where the consciousness suffers calamities in vain. "The True and the Conventional are Non-dual. Thus the Dharma Master preaches the Dharma.
Excellent! Yet within the mind, one is not free from afflictions (*kleśa*). While speaking of words and texts to transform others, one instead increases their birth and old age.

Truth and falsehood are fundamentally non-dual; yet ordinary people discard the false in search of the Way. The fourfold assembly gathers like clouds to listen to lectures; on the high seat, the debates are grand and vast.
Those sitting south and north contend with one another, and the fourfold assembly speaks of this as being "excellent" (or perhaps "doubtful and resentful"). Although [the mouth] speaks thus...
Speaking of the Ambrosia (Amṛta), one’s mind remains habitually parched and withered. Having not a single coin oneself, one spends day and night counting the treasures of others;

this is exactly like a foolish person of no wisdom who discards true gold to carry grass upon their shoulders. With the three poisons unabandoned within the heart, I do not know when one will attain the Way.
To "unravel the bonds" is non-duality: the Vinaya Master, while upholding the precepts, binds himself; yet even this self-binding is [non-dual].
He was able to bind others. Outwardly, he maintained a demeanor of tranquility, yet inwardly his mind was like a surging wave.
Without boarding the raft of birth and death, how could he cross the river of craving? Not understanding the true principle of the orthodox teaching, his heterodox speech was profuse.
There were two bhikṣus who had violated the precepts; they went to consult Upāli, who explained their offenses according to the Vinaya. This only caused their [transgressions] to increase further.
Within the square-zhang chamber, the layman Vimalakīrti immediately came to rebuke Śāriputra, who remained silent and without reply.
Vimalakīrti’s preaching of the Dharma was beyond reproach; his nature of precepts was like space, abiding neither within nor without this Sahā world.
When urged to abandon birth and extinction, he refused; suddenly awakening, he became one with Śākyamuni. The Chan Master embodies the non-duality of the object and its illumination.
Free from ignorance, from where could afflictions arise? Hell and heaven are of one single mark; nirvana and birth-and-death are empty names.
There is neither greed nor anger to be severed, nor is there any Buddha-way to be accomplished. Sentient beings and Buddhas are equal;
natural, sagely wisdom is ever-awake and unsullied by the six sense objects. Every word uniquely accords with non-arising; this is the single, perfect enlightenment.
Contemplating profound liberation, the three periods of time are all serene and level. Neither dharma nor vinaya, one self-restrains; carefree and transcendent, one truly enters perfect realization.
Severing these four propositions and hundred negations, like space, there is no action and no reliance. In its functioning, it is unimpeded;

I am now flowing freely and at ease, envying neither princes, kings, ministers, nor officials. The four seasons remain as indestructible as adamant; whether in suffering or joy, the mind remains unmoved.
Constantly unchanging, the Dharma-treasure exceeds Mount Sumeru; wisdom is vaster than the rivers and seas.
It is not led astray by the eight winds, nor does it possess either diligence or indolence. It floats and sinks according to its nature as if in a state of madness, wandering freely and unrestrained.
Even if a sword were to fall upon one's head, I would remain serene and unperturbed—delusion and enlightenment are non-dual.
In delusion, one takes emptiness to be form; upon awakening, one takes form to be emptiness. Delusion and awakening are fundamentally without distinction;
form and emptiness ultimately remain identical. The fool calls south north, while the wise person realizes there is neither east nor west.
If you wish to seek the wondrous principle of the Tathāgata, it is ever present within a single thought-moment. A mirage is not water by nature, yet the thirsty deer chases it in frantic haste.
[Commentary: How deluded! One's own body is empty, false, and insubstantial; yet one seeks emptiness within emptiness. The confusion of worldly people has reached an extreme.
It is like a dog barking at the roar of thunder. **Verses on the Twelve Hours:** *Ting (3–5 AM):* Within the frantic mechanism [of the mind] lies the person of the Way.

Having endured suffering and hardship through immeasurable kalpas, they still do not believe in the ever-present wish-fulfilling jewel. If one grasps at external objects, one enters further into delusion.

The Ford: To have even a hair’s breadth [of conceptualization] is already dust; do not dwell upon the old appearances of formlessness. Seeking a teacher externally is not the truth. Sunrise at the Hour of the Rabbit (Mao):
In its functioning, there is no need for clever artifice. Even if the divine light illuminates existence and non-existence, it remains as it is.

As soon as a thought arises, one is beset by the disturbances of Māra; even if one exerts effort, one will never reach completion. Day and night, one is twisted by others and by the notions of self and other.
Without contrivance, simply follow along as it is. When has affliction ever arisen in the mind? At the hour of eating, ignorance is fundamentally the body of Śākyamuni.
Sitting or lying down, one does not know that this is originally the Way; thus one busily undergoes suffering and toil. To recognize [it as such]—

Seeking intimacy or distance within sounds and forms is merely the way of one defiled by the world. If you intend to seek the Buddha-way with the mind, ask the empty sky to begin your departure from the dust.
From the hour of Youzhong (9–11 a.m. until Si (11 a.m.–1 p.m.): For those who have not yet attained realization, do not let teachings reach you.

Even if you thoroughly master the words of the Patriarchs, do not settle upon "ultimate meaning" within the heart. Merely maintain the profound mystery that is beyond words; do not rely on conceptual recognition.
The former was not it; for a moment, one spontaneously consents and ceases to pursue. For kalpas on end, one will not be driven by demonic realms.
At noon, within the body of the four elements, lies a priceless jewel. One refuses to cast away the mirage and the empty flowers. To practice with deliberate effort only leads to increasing hardship.
There has never been delusion, so do not seek enlightenment. Let the morning sun set as many times as it may; within this body of form...
The formless body; on the road of ignorance is the path of non-arising. Before noon has passed, how could the mind-ground ever have attained the definitive meaning?
The texts of others contain no distinction between kin and stranger; there is no need to employ the mind to seek a conceptual intent. Let it run free and unrestrained, beyond all taboos.

It dwells eternally among humanity yet does not belong to this world. Its functioning never departs from the midst of sound and form; throughout kalpas, when has it ever been absent for even a moment?
Cast it aside at the hour of *bùshí* (the seventh watch). To study the Way, one must first not loathe poverty. Manifest forms are originally but provisional accumulations;
since they have no fixed shape, what use is there in seeking the "Real"? To strive for purity is merely to weary the spirit;
recognize that all things are but neighbors to ignorance. Do not seek a dwelling place beneath words; for a brief moment, one is called a renunciant. At the hour of *mùrù* (the eighth watch).
Illusory sounds do not endure; even the delicacies of dhyāna-joy are not consumed. Who could further drink the wine of ignorance?

It is neither to be cast away nor to be guarded. Vast and carefree, it has never existed. Though you may possess great learning and mastery of past and present, you are merely a madman wandering outside.
At the hour of dusk, the deluded child exerts effort and enters a dark room. Provisionally...

If the mind were to penetrate through immeasurable time, how could it have ever been different from today throughout the passing kalpas? To attempt to deliberate upon it is merely to chatter; this only serves to make the heart as black as lacquer.
Day and night, the radiance of the sun shines upon both existence and non-existence; yet people harbor doubts and call it "pāramitā.

When one is fixed in the hour of *hai*, even their courageous diligence turns into indolence, and not even a hair’s breadth of a mind for cultivation arises. This is the sign of formlessness (*animitta*).

Always sovereign within the light, he transcends Śākyamuni and surpasses his ancestral lineage. When the mind harbors even a speck of dust, it becomes obstructed; its dissipation remains like that of a dull-witted person.
His own house naturally possesses the love of those who have attained penetration. At the midnight hour, when the mind abides in non-arising, that is birth-and-death.
How could birth-and-death ever belong to existence or non-existence? When it is employed, it is employed without words. This is the Patriarch.
The Master says: "Matters outside are recognized; yet when they arise, they are not it. One searches with deliberate intent, but truly there is no trace.
When the demons of birth and death come to test you, let them try. At the hour of the Rooster (1–3 a.m.): A single round light has shone for a long time.

Searching within and without, nothing at all can be found. Yet its functioning within the realm of objects is perfectly complete. No head is seen, nor are there hands. Though heaven and earth may collapse...
The time has not yet passed; those who have not yet attained realization, listen to a single word: "Right here, right now—who moves their mouth? Hong Juefan said:
"Master Zhi’s *Song of the Twelve Hours* brilliantly clarifies the essential subtlety of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

However, as the years have long passed, many who are ignorant have altered its words to suit their own private interests. Among these, the most harmful distortions of the original intent are as follows:"
It is said: "At midnight, at the hour of Zi, when the mind abides in non-arising, that is itself birth-and-death. How could the dharmas of the mind ever belong to existence or non-existence?

When they are employed, they are employed; they vanish beyond words. Thus, even as they constitute birth-and-death, how could they ever belong to existence or non-existence? These words are indeed skillful.

However, the logical connection between the preceding and following lines is not coherent. Since it is said that birth and death do not belong to existence or non-existence, yet it is also said that they are employed when the time comes—how can this be?
Huanji said: "Juefan seeks the lineage of Master Zhigong’s words at the points where the text shifts;
however, he pursues the flowers without reaching the fruit. If birth and death do not belong to existence or non-existence, then they cannot be employed."

If one employs [the mind] at the very moment it is used, then mental phenomena do not belong to either existence or non-existence. Furthermore, how could there be such a thing as "employing it at the moment of use"?
Know, moreover, that birth has never truly been born and death has never truly died; they come with effortless ease and depart with effortless ease.
It is not that birth and death do not belong to existence or non-existence, yet one employs them at the moment of use—is this so? To perceive birth and death is to possess a mind.

Regarding the Dharma: if one sees that there is no birth-and-death, then there is no mind-dharma. One does not see the ancients' saying, "If there is no Buddha within birth-and-death, then there is no birth-and-death"?
Birth-and-death and the mind-dharma are one and the same illusory bubble; one must not make such distinctions.
As for Master Zhi’s various hymns of praise, they extract the thorns of good and evil and tear asunder the net of ordinary and sagehood. If you can truly comprehend their essential meaning, then...
Trampling upon the crown of Vairocana, one ascends to the highest realm. If one seeks it through emotional attachments, one enters hell as swiftly as an arrow shot.
This is the treading of a true dragon or elephant; it is not something a donkey can endure.

In the winter of the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era, as he was about to pass away, he suddenly informed the assembly of monks to move the statue of the Vajrapāṇi deity from the temple and place it outside.
He then spoke privately to someone, saying, "The Bodhisattva is about to depart. Less than ten days later, he passed away without illness.
His entire body was fragrant. As he approached death, he lit a single candle and entrusted it to Wu Qing, an attendant of the Rear Palace. Qing reported this matter to the Emperor.
The Emperor sighed and said, "The Great Master will not remain with us any longer. This candle must have been his way of entrusting me with his final affairs.
Consequently, he provided a grand funeral at Zhongshan Dulongfu and ordered Lu Chui to compose an inscription for the Kaishan Vihāra.
Within the tomb, Wang Jun erected a stele at the temple gate, and his portrait was circulated everywhere. Huanki said:
"What a pity that this single branch of candlelight cannot be entrusted to the right person; instead, it becomes a matter for future funeral rites. Heh!"
If one were to hold a Buddhist assembly, it would be best to bury it all in a single pit along with Emperor Wu of Liang.

Thus, he composed a verse: Dharma’s single sandal was carried back to Xiangling; Zhizong’s single candle cast its shadow within the Liang palace. The green spring has already faded and the traveler is far away;
Falling flowers fill the steps, the moonlight is cold. The Silver River stretches across, the jade water-clock nears its end; The dream is shattered.
The well-wheel creaks in the dew.
As for the Great Being Shanhui, he was a native of Yiwu County in Wuzhou.

On the eighth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty (the Dingchou year), he descended into the home of Fu Xuanci in Shuanglin Township. His original name was Xi. At the age of sixteen, he married Liu...
The woman’s name was Miaoguang. She gave birth to two sons, Pujian and Pucheng. At the age of twenty-four, she went with her fellow villagers to the Jiting Bay to dredge for fish.
Having caught some, she submerged the basket in the water and said, "Those that leave may go; those that stay may remain. Some people called her foolish.
It happened that a monk from India named Sengtoutuo arrived and said, "I and you both made a vow together at the time of Vipaśyin Buddha."
"The robes and alms bowl are currently in the Tuṣita Heaven palace; on what day shall they return? He then ordered [Huisong] to look at his reflection in the water.
[Huisong] saw a halo and a jeweled canopy. The Great Being smiled and said to him, "In a forge, there is much dull iron; at the door of a skilled physician, there are many patients.
Saving sentient beings is the urgent priority—why do you contemplate that pleasure? Huisong pointed to the summit of Mount Song and said, "This may be..."

He settled there. The Great Being lived by personally tilling the soil. When someone stole beans, wheat, melons, or pears, the Great Being saw them and immediately gave them away, placing the items in a basket for them to take.
By day he engaged in manual labor, and by night he practiced the Way. He beheld the three Tathāgatas—Śākyamuni, Suvarṇapuṣpa, and Dīpaṃkara—emitting light that enveloped his body.

From the very beginning, it has been eternally abiding and pure; its awakened substance is perfect and complete, for the single principle is uniformly level.

(Those who cling to names and marks do not believe that the mind itself is Buddha; they develop faith upon seeing this. Second, "the name itself is Buddha" means that although the rational nature is broad and level, yet in accordance with...

Regarding "those who flow [with the mundane]," they are unaware in their daily lives and must rely on the external influence of verbal teachings to hear the names [of the Buddhas], thereby giving rise to faith and developing understanding.

(The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because there is a mind of deluded thought, one is able to know the meanings of names. From this point downward, those who possess dark realization are excluded. Regarding "the practice of the three contemplations is itself Buddhahood":

having heard the names and attained understanding, one must rely on the aforementioned three contemplations to return to the source. (This refers to the outer ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). They take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the inconceivable object of contemplation.)

This refers to the five stages of practice (*pañca-vinaya-sthāna*). The Great Master [Zhiyi] indicated that he resided in this stage. In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra-śāsana*), the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), as well as in the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and Shared Teachings, these are all termed the "Stage of Provisions" (*sambhāra-mārga*).

Regarding the fourth, "resembling Buddhahood": because the merit of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is profound, a semblance of its function is manifested. (This is the level of the inner ordinary person [*antar-pṛthagjana*]. One subdues ignorance internally and enters the iron-wheel stage of the ten levels of faith.

Without yet severing the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), from the seventh level of faith onward, these afflictions fall away naturally, and one attains the purity of the six sense faculties. As the Sūtra says: "The eyes born of one's parents see the entire trichiliocosm," and so forth. Zen Master Zhiyi indicated that he resided in this stage. In the Separate Teaching, this corresponds to the thirty minds prior to the [first] bhūmi. In the *Āgama* and Shared Teachings...)

All these are termed the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*). Although the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* establish four distinct stages of application following the "thirty minds," their designations and positions are identical while their expressed meanings differ vastly; only those with penetrating realization can skillfully harmonize them. Regarding the claim that the five parts are truly the Buddha:

through the development of the three minds, one attains the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and because this excellence increases at each successive stage, one awakens to the Perfect [Teaching] at the first *bhūmi*, which is the stage of the Copper Wheel.

This is like the Dragon Girl who attained Buddhahood in a single thought and manifested bodies throughout the hundred worlds; from this point on, it becomes increasingly superior until reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddha*). These involve forty-one minds in total, exhausting the ultimate cause. Although the specific stages differ, the Perfect Principle is without distinction. As for the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*):

This is precisely what is called the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Both the *Zang* (Tripiṭaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings state that this is the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*). As for "the sixth being ultimate and thus being a Buddha": it means that ignorance is forever exhausted and the awakened mind is perfectly fulfilled.

Because there is nothing to be realized in what is realized (this is wondrous enlightenment). The *Awakening of Faith* states: "When the initial and the fundamental are non-dual, it is called ultimate enlightenment. In the *Renwang jing*, this is termed the "supreme patience of quiescence" (*śānti-kṣānti*).

It is subsumed under the provisional Buddha of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) and corresponds to the second stage of the Perfect Practice (*yuanxing*). The Buddhas of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings (*zangtong erjiao*) may be understood accordingly. Since all six aforementioned stages are already identical to the Buddha (neither constricted nor confused), they universally possess the three bodies—Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya—as the primary reality.

The Three Jewels and the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*) correspond and interlace with one another; even the ten kinds of triple dharmas are inclusively subsumed without omission. As the verse says: "The Way, consciousness, nature, and prajñā; bodhi and the Mahāyāna body."

The virtues of the Three Jewels of Nirvāṇa each consist of three dharmas, which serve as the basis for the four lands. As for the four lands: first is the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light (the Dharma-nature land).

The Dharma-body resides therein; body and land correspond to one another. Second is the Real Reward Unobstructed [Land], which subsumes the two types of Enjoyment Lands: the Self-Enjoyment Land, where the Reward Buddha himself resides, and the Other-Enjoyment Land, where Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages reside.

Third is the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, and fourth is the Land of Shared Residence of Pure and Impure [Realms]. These are both lands of response and transformation, inhabited by Bodhisattvas prior to the stages, followers of the Two Vehicles, and ordinary beings.

In reality, however, there is neither body nor land, neither superior nor inferior. It is only for the sake of responding to the capacities of sentient beings that bodies and lands are provisionally taught. Thus it is said:
He distinguished between the superior and the inferior. The Master attained the mutual fusion of body and land, and the unimpeded harmony of the provisional and the real.

Thus, for over thirty years, he expounded the teachings day and night, producing four kinds of benefit and embodying the four *siddhāntas* (*siddha* meaning "pervasive"; *siddhānta* translated as "bestowal," for the Dharma of the Chan Master is bestowed universally upon sentient beings, who receive benefits according to their faculties like clouds).
Regarding the *loka-siddhānta*, it produces the benefit of joy, and so forth. His disciple Guanding recorded ten thousand words daily and compiled them; this is the general title.

Regarding the Tiantai teachings: On the seventeenth day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the Emperor dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree for the Master.
As he was about to depart, he addressed his disciples, saying, "I am now going and shall not return.
You must complete the construction of Nan Temple at Fulong; follow my plans exactly. An attendant said, "Were it not for the Master's power, how could this ever be accomplished? The Master—
He said, "This was prepared by the royal house; you all have seen it, but I did not. (The Master initially wished to establish a temple at Shiqiao.

While in meditative seclusion, he saw three divine beings wearing *fuzhan* turbans and crimson robes who said to him, "The temple you wish to build is not yet the right time. Once the Three Kingdoms are unified, there shall be a great patron to establish it. When the temple is built, the state will be clear and pure; it should be named Guoqing.

In the eighteenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict was issued to Sima Wang Hong to construct Guoqing Temple according to the Master's plans. On the twenty-first day, they arrived at Shicheng Temple in eastern Shan. 100 [characters].
At the image before the one-chi stone altar, he did not advance. On the twenty-fourth day, he said to his attendant, "Avalokiteśvara has come to welcome me; I shall depart before long.
At that time, his disciple Zhilang asked, "I do not know what rank or rebirth you will attain. The Master replied, "I have not led a community, so I shall surely purify my six sense faculties.
By sacrificing myself to benefit others, I shall obtain entry into the stage of the five ranks" (the five ranks of disciples refer to the preliminary expedients for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*).

His position [in the Dharma] was in perfect accord with the words spoken by Zen Master Sita in the past. He took up his brush and composed the *Gāthā on Contemplating the Mind*, completing the essential outline of the various Dharma gates.
He then sat in the lotus posture and passed away at the age of sixty, with forty years of ordination seniority. His disciples escorted him back to the Fulong Rock.

In the first year of the Daye era, an imperial envoy was sent to deliver the disciple Zhizao and the temple plaque into the mountains for the memorial feast on the anniversary of the Master’s death. Upon their arrival...
He assembled the Sangha and opened the stone chamber; there he beheld only an empty couch. At that time, a thousand monks were gathered, yet at the mealtime, suddenly one person was in excess.

Everyone said that the Master had manifested a transformation body to receive the offerings. From the time he first received the teachings of Chan until his final passing, he always wore a single tattered robe, never removing it in either winter or summer.
He resided at Mount Tiantai for twenty-two years and established twelve great sites of practice.
The sites included Guoqing Temple, which was the last of them, as well as Yuyuan Temple in Jingzhou and others, totaling thirty-six locations.
He ordained fifteen thousand monks, transcribed fifteen sets of the Buddhist canon, and fashioned eight hundred thousand images of gold, copper, clay, and painting;
his achievements were extensive, as detailed in his original biography.
▲ During the reign of Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty, the Great Master Sengqie of Sizhou arrived in Chang’an and Luoyang to propagate the Dharma.

From his youth, he lived with a carefree and unconventional air, as if mad. One day, he ordered his family to sweep and clean the house, saying, "A distinguished guest is coming.
On that very day, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang returned from the Western Regions and visited him. The Master asked the Master about the customs and landscapes of India.
He understood exactly what he saw. Zang paid his respects, circumambulated him, and proclaimed, "This is a bodhisattva.

His elder brother, Wanian, had been campaigning in Liaozuo for a long time, and his mother, Lady Cheng, was longing for news of him. The Master said, "This is very easy," and having informed his mother, he departed.

By evening he returned, bringing back a letter. Because he brought back [news] from ten thousand *li* away, people called him "Wanhui" (Ten-Thousand-Li Returner). Other miraculous traces of his were likewise numerous.
It was exceedingly much; it cannot be recorded in full.
▲ Chan Master Fenggan of Tiantai was a man of unknown origins. He resided at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai.

He cut his hair even with his eyebrows and wore garments of coarse cloth. He would often chant and sing songs of the Way while riding a tiger into the pine gate of the monastery, causing the monks to be struck with fear and awe. This was his original nature.

Yue said, "This is not illuminating. He requested the Master to speak further. The Master said, "Since you have not brought forth the myriad virtues, what can I teach you?
Han and Shi both prostrated themselves. The Master wished to travel to Mount Wutai.

(When a novice monk raised this matter, Zhaozhou spoke on his behalf, saying: "Mañjuśrī, Mañjuśrī. Later, he returned to Mount Tiantai and manifested parinirvāṇa.

Initially, when Lü Qiu Yin was departing to serve as the governor of Danqiu, he suddenly suffered from a headache that no physician could cure. The Master visited Qiu and sprayed him with consecrated water; he was immediately healed.

Behind the Sūtra Repository, it was now silent and deserted. The two, Hanzhu and Shishi, were currently performing manual labor in the monastic kitchen.
When Dao Yin entered the Master’s quarters, he saw nothing but tiger tracks. He again asked Master Qiao, "What practice do you perform here?

Qiao replied, "I merely attend to the spring grain to provide for the monks; when I am free, I recite and chant. Thereupon, he entered the kitchen to visit Hanzhu and Shishi, as described in the following chapter.
▲ Hanshanzi had no family lineage. To the west of Shifeng County, there were two cliffs known as Han and Ming;

he was named after his dwelling within the Han Cliff. His appearance was withered and emaciated; his coarse cloth tunic was tattered, and he wore a crown made of birch bark and dragged large wooden clogs.

He contracted his body and entered a fissure in a rock, saying only, "Each of you must exert yourselves. Suddenly, the rock fissure closed.
Lǚqiū, filled with grief and longing, ordered the monk Dàoqiáo to search for the traces of his departure.

As for Shi-de, his name and lineage were not recorded; he was so named because when Chan Master Fenggan was walking through the mountains, he came upon the side of a path at Chicheng and saw a child crying alone, so he picked him up and brought him back to Guoqing Temple. Later, the śramaṇa Lingyi took him under his care and...

One day, while sweeping the ground, the Abbot asked him, "Your name is Shide. Since Fenggan picked you up and brought you back here, what is your actual surname?
Shide dropped his broom and stood with his hands joined in a gesture of reverence. The Abbot questioned him again;
Shide simply took up the broom, finished sweeping the ground, and walked away. The Abbot could not fathom this. Hanshan beat his breast and cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! Shide.
He asked, "What are you doing? Shanshan replied, "I see that when a member of the eastern household dies, those of the western household offer their condolences.

Then the two danced, laughing and crying, and departed. When the assembly gathered at Guoqing Temple for the fortnightly recitation of the precepts, Shide clapped his hands and said, "You all huddle together with such thoughts;
what is that business about? The *vinaya* master (Weina) scolded him. Shide said, "Virtuous ones, wait a moment!"
Absence of anger is itself the precepts; purity of mind is itself renunciation. My nature and yours are in harmony. All dharmas are without distinction.

When food from the monastery kitchen was pecked by crows, Shi-de picked it up and struck the temple guardian deity with his staff, saying, "If you cannot protect your own food, how can you protect the monastery?
That night, the deity appeared in a dream to the monks of the entire monastery and said, "Shi-de has rebuked me."
Because of this, he was regarded as extraordinary and addressed as "Worthy Sir. Not long after, he disappeared while dwelling in seclusion at Stone Cliff with Hanshan.
Daqiao compiled the poems of Hanshan, and he also appended the gāthās he had obtained to that collection.
▲ The monk Pudu of Fenghua County in Mingzhou was of unknown clan and lineage. He called himself Qici. His physical form was stout and fleshy;
he had a furrowed brow and a protruding belly. His speech was inconsistent, and he would sleep wherever the ground lay.

The Master was standing on a street when a monk asked, "What are you doing here, Preceptor?

The Master said, "I am waiting for someone. The monk said, "He has come! He has come! (Master Niu-tou Huo added: "Go back! Go back! The Master said, "You are not that person. The monk asked, "Who is this person?
The Master said, "Beg me for a single coin. The Master had a song which says: "Just this..."

Mind, mind, mind is the Buddha; it is the most spiritual thing in the worlds of the ten directions. Its wondrous functioning, whether horizontal or vertical, is truly pitiable—nothing compares to the reality of the mind.
Soaring freely and at ease, there is nothing to be done; in this state of leisure lies the ultimate goal of the renunciant.
If one beholds the true Great Way before one’s eyes, not seeing even a hair’s breadth of it is truly marvelous. How could the myriad dharmas differ, and how could the mind be otherwise?
Why labor further to seek the meaning of the scriptures? The King of Mind is fundamentally beyond manifold knowledge; the wise simply clarify the stage of no-learning.
Is it anything other than being neither sage nor ordinary person? Not forcing conceptual discrimination, the sagely sentiment is solitary—the priceless pearl of the mind.
Fundamentally perfect and pure, ordinary names are but delusive emptiness of differing appearances. If a person can propagate the Way, the Way becomes clear;
its immeasurable purity and loftiness accord with the nature of the Way. Carrying your staff as you walk the roads of your former country, do not worry that the sound will not be heard in all places.

Furthermore, there is a verse that says: "In this world, likes and dislikes, praise and blame, are exceedingly common; reflect carefully upon this—what can you do about it? Simply broaden your stomach."
The intestines must endure; open up the ground of the mind and let things take their course.

If you meet a true friend, follow the natural measure; even if you encounter an enemy, harmonize with them. If you can resolve these matters within the heart, you will naturally realize the six *pāramitās*.

(This should be one verse; the following chapter should be another. The *Denglu* combines them into one, which is likely incorrect. I have a cloth bag; it is as empty as space, without hindrance. Unfold—
Opening wide throughout the ten directions, when entering, one contemplates Avalokiteśvara. I have a Hall of the Three Jewels; within it is empty, devoid of form or appearance.
It is neither high nor low, neither obstructed nor hindered. Those who study find no likeness to its essence; those who come find it impossible to grasp its model.
Only through wisdom can it be understood; among a thousand, there is not a single craftsman. From its four gates, the four fruits arise; throughout the ten directions, all offer worship. I—
There is a Buddha-body that the people of the world do not recognize. It is neither molded nor adorned; it is neither carved nor engraved.
There is not a single drop of plaster, nor a speck of color. Artists cannot paint it, and thieves cannot steal it.
Its physical form is inherently natural; its purity requires no wiping away. Although it is but a single body, it manifests as hundreds of thousands of millions of emanations.
Furthermore, a verse says: "One bowl for food from a thousand households; A solitary body wandering ten thousand *li*. With green eyes, I see few people; I ask the way at the head of white clouds.
In the third month of the Bingzi year, the third year of the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty (916 CE), the Master was about to manifest his passing.
At the eastern corridor of Yuelin Temple, he sat upright upon a flat rock and spoke this verse: "Maitreya, the true Maitreya, Manifests a thousand bodies..."

A hundred times ten billion times. From time to time he appeared to the people of his era, yet the people of that time did not recognize him. When his verses were finished, he passed away peacefully through transformation.
Thereafter, he again manifested in other regions, likewise carrying a cloth bag. The fourfold assembly vied with one another to paint his likeness.
▲ Fahua Zhiyan was the son of Xu of Shouchun. In his early twenties, he traveled to the Eastern Capital, where he subsequently received ordination at Qijuzhi Monastery.
He remained at the lecture hall for a long time. One day, while reading the *Record of Yunmen*, he suddenly attained awakening.

Before long, his knowledge of past lives became fully realized; he would speak and laugh to himself alone, his lips moving incessantly throughout the day. This was widely known as his recitation of the Dharma.
Huā named him accordingly. When Prime Minister Lü Xǔgōng asked about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, the Master said:
"Originally there is not a single thing; a single flavor, however, becomes true. When Jíxiān Wángzhèn asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
the Master said: "A surge of deep blue rises within the shadows of the green mountains; a precious pagoda chants aloud, shaking the morning breeze. He also said:
[Someone] requested the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and burned incense. The Master said: "Do not seek it by means of fasting and precepts; do not seek it from the Buddha.
Xu Yue, Assistant Instructor of the National Academy, asked about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. The Master said: "The one on the eastern side of the street.
Xu said: "I do not yet understand. The Master said: "Three kinds of people do not understand. A monk asked: "Does the world have a Buddha? The Master said: "The temple."
In the inner biography of Mañjuśrī, a questioner asked the Master, "Are you an ordinary person or a sage? He then raised his hand and said, "I do not dwell here.

On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of the *wuzi* year of the Qingli era (*848 CE*), as he was about to pass away, he said to those around him, "Since immeasurable kalpas past, I have perfected the Jetavana land and manifested my body to propagate the teachings. Now I am returning to the South. Having finished speaking, he turned to the right...
He passed away by the side [of the Emperor].

Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty had begun to suffer from illness, yet no heir to the throne had been established. The high ministers requested that a worthy member of the imperial clan be selected to reside in the capital.
That night, Renzong burned incense and prayed in silence, saying: "Tomorrow, I shall prepare a vegetarian feast in the Huacheng Hall and reverently invite [the deity]."
The Dharma Flower Great Being (Fahua Dashi) looked down upon them with no sign of turning back; those to his left and right could not hear him speak.

In the morning, he molded a statue with his own hands, completing it on the ninth day. He asked his disciple Huiyun, "To whom does this resemble? Yun replied, "It is no different from the Master himself.

In the seventy-second year [of his life], he resided in this land for approximately four hundred years.

The Provincial Inspector was about to sacrifice at the shrine of Mount Yue and was repairing the stone steps when, in the middle of the night, wind and thunder struck and a massive boulder fell from a peak, lying crosswise across the path.

The Master laughed and said, "There is no need for such great effort. He then stepped upon the rock; it spun and shifted with a sound like a thunderclap.
Thunder crashed; the path suddenly opened up as if by divine power. Outside the temple gate, tigers and leopards had suddenly gathered in a pack.
The Master said to the monks, "I shall drive them away for you all. Give me my staff. The assembly handed him the staff.

As soon as the Master stepped out of the temple, a tiger suddenly seized him and carried him off, while the other tigers and leopards vanished without a trace. The Master had a song that went: "Utterly still, without affairs."
There is no changing or altering. When there is nothing, what need is there to discuss a single segment? With a direct mind free from distraction, there is no need to sever other matters.
The past has already passed; the future is not yet to be reckoned. Sitting upright and doing nothing, who has ever called out to you?
To seek the method of practice outwardly is the mark of a fool or a stubborn man. Not storing a single grain of rice, he knows only to eat his fill whenever he encounters food.
(Shè lì qiè) Most people in the world are preoccupied with affairs and cannot keep pace with one another. I do not delight in being born in the heavens, nor do I cherish the fields of merit.
When hungry, I eat; when weary, I sleep. Fools laugh at me, but the wise understand. This is not because I am dull-witted; my fundamental nature is simply thus.
If I wish to go, I go; if I wish to stay, I stay. Upon my body I wear a single tattered robe. My feet...

Within, there is no change. Since there is no phenomenon, fundamentally there is no phenomenon. Why must one read written words? Erase the root of self and other, and darkly merge with the meaning within this.

All manner of toil and strain of body and sinew is not as good as sleeping beneath the forest trees. Staring blankly, one looks up and sees: the sun is high, and one eats rice from the very beginning.

To understand this for oneself: I have a single word—sever all discursive thought and forget all conditions. It cannot be obtained through clever speech; it can only be transmitted through the mind. Furthermore, there is another phrase:

Worldly affairs are wearying; they are not as good as the mountain peaks. Green pines obscure the sun; azure ravines flow on forever. Mountain clouds...

Having no anxieties regarding birth and death, what more need I worry about? Water and moon have no fixed form;
I am always simply at peace. All phenomena are thus: they are fundamentally unborn. Sitting upright and doing nothing, spring comes and the grass turns green of its own accord.

▲ National Teacher Qingliang Chengguan’s surname was Xiahou. He was a native of Shanyin. Possessing the intellectual capacity of two scribes, he composed the *Huayan shuchao*, which exhaustively elucidates the principles of the Perfect and Sudden teachings.
His spiritual manifestations were manifold, and all who possessed discernment revered him. After his passing, his disciples saw a deity clad in golden armor soaring westward through the air.

The Master composed a letter in response to the Prince’s inquiry on the Essentials of the Mind, which is recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu* (The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), as well as in the *Zheng Fa Yan Zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye) by Miaoxi.

It is neither existent nor empty, neither arising nor ceasing, without end and without beginning. One may seek it, yet it cannot be found."

Abandon them, yet do not depart from them. If one is deluded regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then confusion and suffering will arise in profusion; if one awakens to the true nature, then emptiness and luminosity will be vast and penetrating.

Although it is said that "the mind itself is Buddha," only those who have realized it know this for themselves. Yet, if there is realization and knowing, the sun of wisdom sinks into the realm of existence (*bhūmi*);
if there is neither illumination nor awakening, the dark clouds obscure the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If, in a single thought-moment...
When there is no arising, the limits of the past and future are severed; the luminous essence stands alone, and both things and self are all suchness (*tathatā*).

One directly reaches the source of the mind, where there is neither wisdom nor attainment, neither grasping nor rejecting, neither opposition nor cultivation. Yet, delusion and awakening remain mutually dependent, and truth and falsehood stand in relation to one another.

If one seeks the true while abandoning the false, it is like discarding one's shadow while toiling the body. If one realizes that the false is itself the true, it is like remaining within the shade until the shadow vanishes.
If one is without mind and forgets all illumination, then ten thousand anxieties are entirely cast aside. If one allows spontaneous, tranquil knowing to proceed, then all practices arise from this.

Leisurely and expansive, one allows for coming and going as they may; through quiet discernment, one awakens to their source and flow. Whether speaking or remaining silent, one does not lose the profound mystery;

whether moving or still, one never departs from the *dharmadhātu*. When speech ceases, both knowing and stillness are forgotten; when discussing contemplation, both stillness and knowing are illuminated. To speak of realization is to find it impossible to show to others;
to explain the principle is to find it incomprehensible without realization. Therefore, awakening to stillness means there is no stillness—this is true knowing.
There is no knowing. By means of knowing the non-dual single mind of quiescence, one accords with the Middle Way in which emptiness and existence are fused as one.
Without abiding and without attachment, there is nothing to grasp and nothing to collect. Right and wrong are both forgotten; subject and object are both severed.

When even this severance is quiescent, then Prajñā manifests before one. Prajñā does not newly arise outside of the mind; the nature of wisdom is inherently complete from the beginning. Thus, it is fundamentally quiescent.
That one cannot manifest it oneself is truly due to the power of *prajñā*. *Prajñā* and the nature of wisdom (*jñatā*) are mutually constitutive through their reciprocal transformation.
Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and initial cultivation are in reality not two distinct entities. When both are transcended in realization, then wondrous enlightenment is perfectly luminous;

when the beginning and end are encompassed and fused, then cause and effect penetrate one another. Every thought-moment acts as a Buddha; there is not a single mind that is not the Buddha-mind. Abiding in...
In the place where one attains enlightenment, there is not a single speck of dust that is not a Buddha-land. Thus, truth and falsehood, things and self—take up any one, and all are fully encompassed.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are seamlessly and uniformly identical in their essence. Know, therefore, that in delusion, the person follows the phenomena;

phenomena differ in ten thousand ways, yet people are not the same. In awakening, the phenomena follow the person; every person possesses the same single wisdom, thereby fusing with the myriad environments. Words reach their limit and thought ceases.
Severed from all extremes, what fruit and what cause can there be? Its essence is fundamentally quiescent and solitary; who could say it is the same or different?

Only by forgetting the self does one become empty and luminous, where the flow of phenomena is profound and harmonious. It is like the reflection of the moon upon water: empty yet visible. With no-mind, one mirrors images; though illuminating, it remains eternally empty.

they subsequently attained the two fruits [of the Path].
Huanji said: "Ānanda’s realization was old and dim; this monk did not fall into his trap, yet he ingested his poisonous medicine. If one were to..."
When the floodwaters subside, the crane takes flight; one may then tread upon the crown of Vairocana and ascend. Why then would there be two fruits?
To instead accept the instructions of a lesser sage and remain buried in obscurity for a lifetime!
As the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he sat cross-legged in the middle of the Ganges River.
King Ajātaśatru and the King of Vaiśālī were both on the riverbank; they spoke verses to entreat him, saying, "Do not enter parinirvāṇa.
He answered them in verse: "O two kings, dwell well-composed; do not grieve or lament in sorrow. My nirvāṇa shall be in tranquility, for I am free from all states of existence (bhava). Furthermore...
He reflected: "If I were to go to a single country, the other countries might dispute it; I should instead deliver all sentient beings through impartiality.
He then proceeded to the middle of the Ganges River to enter parinirvāṇa. At that moment, the mountains, rivers, and great earth shook in six ways.
Five hundred rishis from the Snowy Mountains, beholding this auspicious omen, flew through the air and arrived there. They prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet and said:
He said, "I shall bear witness to the Buddha-dharma for you, Venerable One. I pray that you will bestow great compassion and deliver us. The Venerable One accepted the request in silence.
He immediately transformed the Ganges River so that it became entirely golden ground. For the assembly of sages, he preached various Great Dharmas.
Then he thought, "The disciples I previously delivered should now gather here. In a brief moment, five hundred arhats arrived from—
He descended from the sky and ordained those sages, granting them full admission into the monastic order. Among that assembly of sages were two arhats:
one named Śāṇakavāsin and the other named Madhyāntika. The Venerable One, knowing them to be vessels for the Dharma, addressed them, saying:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa, having entered meditative absorption, entrusted it to me. Now, I..."
As it is about to perish, I entrust it further to you. Receive my teaching and listen to these verses: "The Dharma originally entrusted exists;
once entrusted, it is said to be non-existent. Each must awaken for themselves; having awakened, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
Having spoken these verses, he further committed the True Dharma Eye to Śāṇakavāsin and addressed Madhyāntika, saying: "In the past, the Buddha prophesied: 'The Buddha...'"
"After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, you shall propagate the Great Dharma in the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
Having spoken these words, he leaped into the air and manifested eighteen transformations; entering the *vāyu-cakra-vega-samādhi*, he divided his body into four parts.
One portion was bestowed upon the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; one portion was bestowed upon the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara; one portion was bestowed upon King Ajātaśatru;
and one portion was bestowed upon the King of Vaiśālī. Each constructed a jeweled stūpa to enshrine and make offerings to them.
This was during the twelfth year of King Zhou Li, the *guisi* year.
▲ The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śaṇakavāsin (also known as Śāṇakavāsa), was surnamed Viśākha. His father was Vanavāsin and his mother was Kauśeya.
He was a native of the kingdom of Mathurā. He remained in the womb for six years before being born. In Sanskrit, he is called Śaṇaka.
This is called the "spontaneously growing robe," which is the name for a species of nine-branched exquisite grass found in the Western Regions. It emerges whenever a sage is born;

when the Venerable One was born, this grass appeared. Formerly, when the Tathāgata traveled to teach and transform beings in the kingdom of Mathurā, he saw a grove of green trees with lush branches and leaves and said to Ānanda: "The name of this grove is Uruvilvā. One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa..."
A hundred years later, there was a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who turned the sublime wheel of Dharma here. A hundred years after that, Śāṇakavāsin was born;
he left the household life, realized the Way, and received the Dharma-eye of the Venerable Ānanda. Arriving at this grove, he subsequently subdued two fire-dragons.
The dragons took the Three Refuges and offered him the land, upon which he established a Brahma-palace. After the Venerable One’s work of transformation had lasted for a long time, [he passed away].
While reflecting on the Dharma, he traveled to the kingdom of Ṭhāṇa and found Upagupta, whom he took as his attendant. He then asked Upagupta, "How old are you?
He replied, "I am seventeen years old. [Upagupta] said, "Is it your body that is seventeen, or your nature that is seventeen?
He replied, "When your hair has turned white, is it your hair that is white, or your mind that is white? [Upagupta] said, "I only..."
"The hair is white; it is not the mind that is white. Kumāralāta said, "My body is seventeen [years old], but my nature is not seventeen. The Venerable One knew he was a vessel for the Dharma.
Three years later, he finally shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him, entrusting him with the Dharma-eye.
The verse of Dharma-transmission says: "Neither non-Dharma nor mind, Neither no-mind nor no-Dharma. When these mind-and-Dharma are spoken of, This Dharma is not..."
After the Venerable Cittaka had transmitted the Dharma, he immediately withdrew into the Śveta-hasti-parvata (White Elephant Mountain) in the south of Kaśmīra.
Later, while in samādhi, he perceived that the followers of Guptaka had become indolent and arrogant; he therefore went there to correct them.
When Guptaka saw the Master arrive and prostrated himself, the Venerable pointed his right hand upward, whereupon fragrant milk poured down from the sky.
He asked Guptaka, "Do you recognize this? Guptaka could not discern it; he then entered *samādhi* to observe it, yet still could not discern it.
He then inquired, "What kind of *samādhi* is this? The Venerable One replied, "This is called the Dragon’s Impetuous Display (*nāga-vikrīḍita*) *samādhi*.
You do not know even five hundred such *samādhis*. Furthermore, [you do not know] the *tathāgata-samādhi* or the *pratyekabuddha-..."*
"I do not know it. The *pratyekabuddha*s do not know this samādhi; the Arhats do not know it; even my teacher Ānanda’s samādhi, I do not know.
Now, how could you possibly know my samādhi? This samādhi is such that the mind neither arises nor ceases.
It abides in the power of great compassion and mutual reverence. Only those who reach this state can truly know it. Thereupon, all of Guptaka’s disciples...

They prostrated themselves in repentance and apology. The Venerable One again spoke a verse for them, saying: "Thoroughly penetrating that there is neither self nor other, the Most Holy have neither long nor short.
If you cast away thoughts of contempt and arrogance, you shall swiftly attain Arhatship. Upon hearing this verse, the five hundred bhikṣus followed the teaching and practiced accordingly;

they all attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*). The Venerable One then manifested the eighteen transformations and the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) to consume their [bodies].
Kumārajīva’s body was collected by Kumārabuddhi, who erected a stupa on Mount Vaṅgala; this was in the year Yiwu, the twenty-third year of King Zhou Xuan of the Western Zhou dynasty.
▲ The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the kingdom of Tāla (also named Upagupta, or alternatively Utpagupta). His clan name was Śūdra; his father was Kalyāṇamati.

He left home at the age of seventeen and attained the fruit [of Arhatship] at twenty. When he traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā to propagate the teachings, those who received ordination were exceedingly numerous.
Consequently, the palace of Māra shook violently, and Pāpīyān became distressed and fearful, eventually exhausting all his demonic powers.

He sought to harm the True Dharma. The Venerable One immediately entered *samādhi* to observe its origins. Māra, the Evil One, again watched for an opportunity and took a jeweled necklace to entwine around the Venerable One’s neck.
When the Venerable One emerged from concentration, he took three corpses—a human, a dog, and a snake—and transformed them into flower garlands.
He then addressed Māra with these words: "I shall repay you for this necklace with these flower garlands of mine. Māra was greatly delighted and led [the Venerable One away].
He received it upon his neck; it immediately became three corpses, infested with maggots and putrid with decay. Although he exhausted all his supernatural powers, he could not remove them.
He then ascended to the Six Heavens of Desire and informed the various lords of those heavens, and further went to the Brahmā King to seek deliverance. Each of them replied to him:
"The supernatural transformations performed by the disciples of the One Possessing Ten Powers—how could we common and lowly beings be able to dispel them? Pāpīyas said, "If that is so, what then?
The Brahmā King replied, "You should direct your mind toward the Venerable One; then you will be able to sever [these powers]. He further spoke a verse, saying:
"If one falls upon the ground, one must rise from the ground; to seek to rise apart from the ground is ultimately impossible.

Having heard this, Pāpīyas immediately descended from his celestial palace and went to the Venerable One's presence. He prostrated at the Venerable One's feet and offered a sorrowful confession. The Venerable One said: "From this day forward..."
"Will you no longer cause further disturbance to the Buddha-dharma? Pāpīyān replied, "I vow to turn toward the path of the Buddha.
The Venerable One said, "You may personally chant the refuge in the Triple Gem yourself. Pāpīyān joined his palms and chanted it three times; thereupon, the three corpses were entirely removed.
He leaped for joy, prostrated himself, and departed. He then went to visit an elderly bhikṣuṇī. Upon entering the door, he happened to brush against her alms bowl. The nun said:
"When the Buddha was in the world, the group of six bhikṣus were extremely coarse in their conduct; they did not come to my house even as often as this.
That a venerable one who succeeds to the ancestral position should behave with such coarseness—enough, let it be!"
Fenyang Shanzhao remarked, "I already know this is an error.
When the Venerable One was in the world teaching and guiding others, there were many who attained realization. For every person he liberated, he would place a tally-stick in a stone chamber.
That chamber was eighteen cubits long and twelve cubits wide; it became completely filled with them. Finally, there was one [tally] of great length..."

"O son, one named Gandharvasena has come to pay homage to the Venerable One and seeks to go forth from the household life. The Venerable One asked: 'Do you go forth with your body, or do you go forth with your mind?
He replied: 'I have come to go forth; it is not for the sake of body or mind. The Venerable One said: 'If it is not for the sake of body or mind, then who is it that goes forth? He replied:
'As for one who goes forth, because there is no self and no "mine," and because there is no self and no "mine," [that is what it means to go forth].'"

"The mind is neither born nor extinguished; that the mind is neither born nor extinguished is itself the eternal Way. The Buddhas are likewise eternal. The mind has no form or appearance, and its essence is the same.
The Venerable One said, "You shall attain great enlightenment and the mind will naturally become fully realized. You should rely upon the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha to perpetuate the noble lineage.
He then shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts (upasampadā), further telling him: "In your father's dream, there was gold..."
"Born on this day, you shall be named Tiṭṭhaka. The Tathāgata transmitted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye in succession until it reached me;
now I, in turn, entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: 'The mind is itself the original mind; the original mind is not a dharma.
If there were dharmas, there would be an original mind; but since it is neither mind nor dharma, it is the fundamental reality. Having thus entrusted the Dharma, he leaped into the void."

He manifested eighteen transformations, then returned to his original seat and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. Dhitika used the tally-sticks from within the room to cremate the Master’s body.
He collected the relics and constructed a stupa for offerings; this was the gengzi year, the thirty-first year of King Ping’s reign.

At that time, he was titled the Buddha Without Physical Marks (Amalakṣaṇa). Prior to this, those who transmitted the Dharma were all masters of the Tripitaka—comprising the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
Thereafter, the Vinaya teachings branched off separately into five schools; those who transmitted the Dharma thereafter transmitted only the Chan gate as well as the Sūtras and Śāstras.
▲ The Venerable Diṭṭhika, the Fifth Patriarch, was a native of Magadha. His original name was Gandhamukha.
At the time of his birth, his father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, its radiance illuminating heaven and earth; before it stood a great mountain, adorned with all manner of jewels.
A spring gushed forth from the mountain peak, flowing in torrents in all four directions. Later, he encountered the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra, who explained it for him, saying:
"The jewel mountain is my own body; the gushing spring is the inexhaustibility of the Dharma. The sun rising from the house is the sign of your current entry into the Path.
Its illuminating of heaven and earth signifies that your wisdom is transcendent. Because of this, his name was changed to [Vasu]bandhu (梵).
"Kundopadhānīya," which means "One Who Penetrates True Measure. Upon hearing this, the Venerable One leaped for joy and spoke this verse:
"The towering mountain of the seven treasures Constantly wells forth the spring of wisdom; Transformed into the flavor of the true Dharma, It can deliver all who possess the karmic affinity.
Venerable Upagupta also spoke a verse, saying: "I transmit my Dharma to you; You shall manifest great wisdom. The golden sun rises from the house..."
It emerged, illuminating heaven and earth. When the Venerable One heard the verse, he performed a prostration and took it up for preservation. Later, he traveled to Central India.
In that country, there were eight thousand great seers, with Mucilinda at their head; hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they led their assembly to pay him homage.
He said to the Venerable One: "In the past, we were born together in the Brahma Heaven. I encountered the Seer Asita, who bestowed the methods of the seers upon me;
you met a disciple of the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha), under whom you practiced *dhyāna*. Since then, our karmic destinies have followed divergent paths for six kalpas.
