The Venerable One replied: "To be separated by such accumulated kalpas is indeed not in vain. Now you may abandon the heterodox and return to the orthodox, so that you may enter the Buddha's path."

[The Buddha] mounted [the chariot]. Mīḍhika said, "In the past, the seer Asita gave me this prediction: 'Six kalpas hence, you shall encounter a fellow student and attain the fruit of outflowlessness.
That we have met now—is this not due to our karmic affinity from former lives? I pray that the Master will show us compassion."

“May I be liberated. [The Buddha] then ordained him and led him forth from the household life, commanding the noble ones to bestow the precepts upon him. As for the rest of the assembly of seers, they first gave rise to pride;
the Venerable One then displayed great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), whereupon they all simultaneously conceived the bodhicitta and were ordained at once.
He then addressed Mucilinda, saying: “In the past, the Tathāgata secretly entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma Eye (*mahādharmanetra-kośa*) to Kāśyapa, and it was passed down in succession...”
It was transmitted from master to disciple until it reached me; I now entrust it to you. You must protect and cherish it. Then he spoke this verse:
"The mind that penetrates the fundamental Dharma Is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Awakening is the same as non-awakening; Without mind, there is also no dharma.

Having spoken the verse, he leaped into the air and performed the eighteen transformations. Entering the fire-light samādhi (*tejo-dhātu-samādhi*), he spontaneously cremated his own body. Thus ended Mucilinda.
Together with eight thousand bhikṣus, he collected the śarīra relics and erected a stūpa on Mount Paṇḍaka to offer them worship;
this was the year Jichou (489 CE), the seventh year of King Zhuang’s reign.
▲ The Venerable Sixth Patriarch Mīzhējiā was a native of Central India. Having transmitted the Dharma, he traveled to North India to propagate his teachings.
There, he beheld auspicious golden clouds above the city walls and sighed, saying, "This is the breath of a person of the Way."

"There must be a Great Being who shall be my successor. He then entered the city. Amidst the bustling marketplace, there was a man holding a wine vessel who went up to him and asked, "From where do you come, Master?
Where do you intend to go? The Patriarch said, "I come from my own mind; I intend to go nowhere.
The man asked, "Do you recognize the object in my hand? The Patriarch replied, "This is a vessel for contact, yet it carries purity."
[The monk] asked, "Does my teacher recognize me? The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize you; if I were to recognize you, it would not be the true self.
He further said to him, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall subsequently reveal your original cause. The monk replied with a verse:
"From immeasurable kalpas past, until my birth in this land, My original surname was Bharadvāja, and my given name was Vāsukīta. The Patriarch said, "My teacher..."
Tidūka said: "In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through North India, he spoke to Ānanda, saying:
'In this country, three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be a holy man of the Bharadvāja clan named Vasumitra. He shall become the seventh in the lineage of the Dhyāna patriarchs.
The World-Honored One has predicted you; you ought to leave the household life. Thereupon, [Vasumitra] set down his vessel and paid homage at the side of the Master.
He stood up and said, "I recall that in a past kalpa, I once acted as a dānapati and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha bestowed a prediction upon me, saying:
'In the Śākya Dharma of this Bhadrakalpa, you shall propagate the ultimate teaching. This now accords with the Master’s words; I pray that you grant me deliverance.
The Patriarch immediately shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him, then told him: "The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye..."
"I now entrust this to you; do not let it be severed. He then spoke a verse, saying: "No mind exists that can be attained; That which is spoken of cannot be called a dharma.

If one realizes that the mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and its dharmas. Having spoken the verse, the Patriarch entered the Lion’s Vigorous Stride Samādhi (*siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*).
His body leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees, then returned to his original seat and transformed into fire to consume himself.
Vasumitra collected the sacred relics and enshrined them within a casket made of the seven precious gems; he then erected a stupa and placed them upon its upper tier.
This was in the seventeenth year of King Xiang’s reign, the year of Jiashen.
▲ The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, was a native of Northern India. He habitually wore pure garments and wandered through the streets carrying a vessel for wine;
sometimes he would chant or whistle, and people regarded him as mad. Upon meeting the Venerable Mīdhaka, he was informed of the Tathāgata’s past prophecy.
Recognizing his own prior karmic connection, he cast away his vessel and entered the monastic life. Having received the Dharma, he traveled to propagate the teachings as far as Kāmala.
In that country, Buddhist activities flourished extensively. Before the Dharma seat, there was suddenly a man of wisdom who declared, "My name is Buddhānandi;
I shall now debate the meaning of the Dharma with you, Master. The Patriarch said, "O benevolent one, where there is debate, there is no meaning; where there is meaning, there is no debate.

If you intend to debate the meaning, it will ultimately not be a discussion of meaning. Buddhānandi realized that the Master’s principle was superior and submitted with deep respect, saying, "I wish to seek [the Way]."
The Way moistened him with its sweet and numinous flavor, and the Patriarch subsequently granted him the tonsure and conferred the full precepts.
He further addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you; you must protect and uphold it. Thereupon he spoke this verse:

"The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When emptiness is realized, There is neither 'is' nor 'non-is. He then entered into a state of loving-kindness.
At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and the assembly of devas all came together to pay homage and spoke in verse:
"O Patriarch of the sages of this Bhadrakalpa, you shall occupy the seventh rank. Venerable One, have compassion for us and please proclaim the Buddha-ground.
The Venerable One arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma I have attained is not something that exists; if one realizes the Buddha-ground..."
Having departed from existence and non-existence, he spoke and returned once more to samādhi, manifesting the signs of nirvana.
Nandi immediately erected a stūpa made of the seven precious gems upon his original seat to enshrine his entire body; this was the year of Xīnwèi, the nineteenth year of King Ding’s reign.

Following the verse on the transmission of the Dharma by the Seventh Patriarch, there is a passage stating that [the Sixth Patriarch] manifested eighteen transformations beyond his physical body and entered the *maitrī-samādhi* to proceed toward the concentration of quiescence.
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, was a native of the country of Kāmala. His clan name was Gautama (the *Zhengzong* edition reads "Gou").

Dharmasubhūti had a *uṣṇīṣa* upon his head and possessed swift, unimpeded eloquence. Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Vasumitra, he traveled to the kingdom of Kāśī to convert others and arrived at the home of Viśāla.
Seeing a white light ascending from the roof of the house, he said to his disciples:
"There is a holy person in this house who speaks no words; they are a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. They do not walk the four crossroads, for they know that contact is defiling."
The elder came out to pay his respects and asked what he required. Bodhidharma said, "I am seeking an attendant.
The elder replied, "I have a son named Buddhabhadra; he is already fifty years old, yet his mouth has never spoken and his feet have never trodden the ground.
Bodhidharma said, "If it is as you describe, he is truly my disciple. Upon hearing this, Buddhabhadra rose immediately to prostrate himself and spoke a verse:
He asked: "If my parents are not my kin, who is the most intimate kin? If the Buddhas are not my Way, who is the ultimate Way?
The Patriarch answered with a verse: "What you say is intimate with the mind; parents cannot be compared to it. What you practice accords with the Way;
the minds of all Buddhas are identical to it. Seeking outwardly for a Buddha with form is unlike you. If you wish to recognize your own original nature..."
"The mind is neither conjoined nor disjoined. Having heard this verse, Bodhidharma took seven steps. The Patriarch said, "This child encountered a Buddha in the past;
his compassionate vows are vast and great. Fearing that his parents' affection would make it difficult for him to renounce the world, he remained silent and did not walk."
The elder then relinquished him, allowing him to leave the household life. The Patriarch subsequently conferred full ordination upon him and entrusted him with the Dharma, speaking this verse:
"Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of the mind is likewise so. If one realizes the nature of space, One penetrates the principle of True Suchness.

Vovada, receiving the Patriarch’s entrustment, immediately leaped into the void of space, scattered various precious flowers, and spoke this verse in praise: "My Teacher, the Patriarch of Meditation..."
In the middle [of his life], he was destined to become the eighth patriarch. His Dharma transformation of the multitude was immeasurable, and all attained the state of Arhat.
At that time, the Patriarch suddenly rose from his seat, manifested great supernatural transformations, and then returned to his original seat, remaining solemnly in nirvana.
The assembly went to that place and erected a stupa, enshrining his entire body within it. This was the year of Bingyin, the twelfth year of Emperor Jing’s reign.
▲ The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of the country of Ti-ga. His secular surname was Viśāla.
While traveling to propagate the Dharma in Central India, he encountered an elder named Gandhacchattra, who brought his son to pay him homage and said:

"This child has been in the womb for sixty years (the *Zhengzong* edition reads sixteen). Once, a seer remarked that this boy’s physical characteristics were extraordinary. Now he has met the Honored One."

[The Master] said, "You may leave the household life and become a monk. The Patriarch then shaved his head. At the moment of the *karmavācanā* ceremony, auspicious light illuminated the seat, and thirty-seven *śarīras* appeared before them.
From then on, he practiced with such diligence that he forgot all fatigue. Before long, the Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to him, speaking this verse:
"The True Principle is fundamentally nameless; It is through names that the True Principle is revealed. Having received the true and real Dharma, That which is not true..."
This is not false. Having finished the verses, he immediately entered the samādhi of cessation and attained parinirvāṇa. His body was cremated and the śarīras were collected;
a stūpa was erected at Nālandā Monastery. This was the thirty-fifth year of King Jing, the Jia-yin year.

Guifeng said: "His power of virtue was profoundly deep and his wisdom vast and great. The king believed in heterodox teachings and personally carried a crimson banner, inviting various masters of treatises to debate.
All the masters were defeated, and even when the king debated himself, he too was defeated; thereupon, he changed his heterodox mind."
▲ The Tenth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of Central India; his clan name is unknown. He remained in the womb for sixty years.
On the eve of his birth, his mother dreamed that a white elephant carried a precious throne, upon which rested a bright pearl, as it entered her chamber; thereupon he was born.
From birth, his divine radiance illuminated the room and his body was imbued with a wondrous fragrance. Although he grew up eating grain-based food, he never produced any waste or impurities.
His original name was Duṣprasaha (Difficult to Conquer). Later, while serving as an attendant to the Ninth Patriarch, he never slept;

it was said that his ribs never touched the mat, and thus he was given the title "The Venerable Flank" (Pārśva). When he first arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he rested beneath a tree and pointed to the ground with his right hand.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "This ground has turned golden; a sage shall enter this assembly. As soon as he had finished speaking, it immediately turned golden.
At that time, there was a son of a householder named Pūrṇaśa, who stood before him with palms joined. The Patriarch asked him, "Whence have you come?"
He said, "My mind does not go. The Patriarch asked, "Where do you dwell? He said, "My mind does not stop. The Patriarch said, "Then your mind is not settled?

He said, "The Buddhas are also thus. The Patriarch said, "You are not the Buddhas. He said, "The Buddhas are also not [the Buddhas]. (Dagui Zhi said: [Note: The dialogue continues with the Patriarch asking, "What is your name? and the monk replying, "My name is not fixed. The Patriarch then asks, "Who is it that is not fixed? The monk replies, "It is precisely this which is not fixed."]

The Patriarch asked one question; the youth gave one answer. Both were lacking in understanding. How do you all understand this now? Miaoxi said: "Even if you were to understand it right now, you would still have to practice for sixty kalpas over three lifetimes.

The Patriarch then spoke a verse: "This ground turns to gold; I knew beforehand that a sage was coming. He shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, And complete his realization through the Flower of Enlightenment.
Yaśas then spoke a verse in reply: "The Master sits upon the golden ground, Constantly expounding the true meaning. [He] turns..."

A light shone upon me. "Now enter into samādhi," [the Master] said. The Patriarch then ordained him as a monk, conferred the full precepts upon him, and entrusted him with the Dharma, speaking this verse:
"The true essence is naturally true; Because it is true, there is the principle of explanation. Having realized the Dharma of true truth, There is neither practice nor cessation.
After the Patriarch had entrusted the Dharma, he manifested supernatural transformations and entered nirvana, consuming himself by means of a self-igniting fire.
The śarīra fell from the sky in numbers beyond counting. The fourfold assembly gathered them in their robes and constructed stupas at various locations to make offerings.
This was the twenty-second year of King Jeong, the Jihai year.
▲ The eleventh patriarch, Venerable Pūrṇāśa, was a native of the country of Puṣpapura. His clan name was Gautama; his father was Ratnagātra.
He had seven sons, and the patriarch was the youngest. From his youth, his inclinations differed from those of his elder brothers.

He once said, "If I encounter a Great Being seated in the place of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I shall go there to attend upon him and rejoice in his merit. Subsequently, he encountered the Venerable Pārśva and was [thereby] ordained.
The Dharma. His ancestral teachings spread throughout immeasurable lands, and those who attained the fruit numbered five hundred.
Later, he arrived at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. There was an elder who came to his assembly. The Patriarch said to the multitude, "Do you recognize this person who has come?
The Buddha prophesied that the noble Aśvaghoṣa shall succeed to my Dharma. Thereupon, Aśvaghoṣa paid his respects and asked, "I wish to know..."

"Buddha. "Which one is it? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, that which you do not recognize is it. He asked, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is him?
The Patriarch said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is not him? [The other] said, "This is the meaning of the saw."
The Patriarch said, "That is the meaning of wood. The Patriarch asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? He replied, "It emerges together with you, Master.
Vasubandhu (Ma-ming) then asked, "What is the meaning of wood? The Patriarch said, "You have been cut by me. Vasubandhu was suddenly enlightened; he then requested ordination.
The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This Great Being was formerly King Viśākhā. Because his kingdom..."
There was a class of naked people who were as bare as horses. The King then exercised his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and divided his body into silkworms to clothe them.
Later, they were born in Central India. The horse-like men, moved by longing and affection, neighed piteously; thus he was named Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigh).
The Tathāgata had made a prophetic declaration that six hundred years after his parinirvāṇa, Aśvaghoṣa would, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, subdue heterodox paths and deliver countless beings.

[The Master] said, "This very moment is precisely wisdom. He then transmitted the Dharma, saying in verse: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; Brightness and darkness are never separate from one another.

I now transmit this dharma of concealment and manifestation, Which is neither one nor two. Having transmitted the Dharma, he immediately manifested supernatural transformations and entered a state of profound, perfect quiescence.
The assembly erected a precious stupa to enshrine his entire body. This occurred during the year Wuxu of King Zhou'an of this land.
Guifeng said: "With a mind of arrogance, Aśvaghoṣa vowed to cut out his tongue to challenge the Patriarch.

When the Patriarch established the doctrine of the Two Truths, Aśvaghoṣa immediately surrendered and took refuge in him. The *Zongjing Lu* states: "In Mount Vindhya in India, there was an arhat named Pūrṇa.
Aśvaghoṣa went to visit him; he was sitting upright in the forest, his spirit vast and profound, as if unfathomable. Aśvaghoṣa...
He said to him, "I am a śramaṇa who speaks with the intent to clarify what I understand; you must certainly yield to me.
If I do not prevail, I shall cut my own throat to apologize. The Arhat remained silent, his expression showing neither defeat nor triumph.
Though he was questioned four or five times, there was never any response from him. The monk withdrew and reflected to himself: "I have lost; he has won. How peaceful he is!"

He said, "Therefore, there is nothing by which I can be defeated. I have spoken thus because, although I know that a speaker may be defeated, as long as I myself cannot avoid speaking, I am truly ashamed.
He then renounced the world and became a monk. These two accounts differ from those in the *Chuan deng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp); I have recorded them both for clarity.
▲The Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
He was also named Guṅśeng (Victorious in Merit), as he was preeminent in all conditioned and unconditioned merits; thus he was so named.

Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Vasubandhu, he later turned the wonderful wheel of the Dharma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Suddenly, an old man prostrated himself on the ground before him. The Patriarch—
He addressed the assembly, saying, "This is no ordinary person; there shall surely be extraordinary signs. Having finished speaking, he vanished.
Suddenly, a golden man emerged from the earth, who then transformed into a woman. With her right hand she pointed toward the Patriarch and spoke this verse:

"I prostrate to the Venerable Elder, Who shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata. Now, upon this very ground, You proclaim and disseminate the Ultimate Truth. Having spoken the verse, she disappeared.
In an instant, they vanished. The Patriarch said, "Demons are coming to contend with me for power. After a short while, wind and rain arrived violently, and heaven and earth grew dark and murky.
The Patriarch said, "It is indeed true that demons have come; I shall eliminate them.

He then pointed toward the air, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting its majestic spiritual power and shaking the mountains and peaks. The Patriarch remained solemn upon his seat, and the demonic disturbances subsided accordingly.
After seven days had passed, a small insect, as large as a mayfly, hid its form beneath the Master’s seat.

The Master took it up with his hand and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This is a transformation produced by a māra, coming to eavesdrop upon my Dharma. He released it to let it go, but the māra could not move.
The Master addressed it, saying, "If you simply take refuge in the Triple Gem, you shall immediately attain supernatural powers. Thereupon, it returned to its original form.
He assumed a physical form and performed a rite of repentance. The Patriarch asked him, "What is your name?

How large is your retinue? He replied, "My name is Kambala; I have three thousand followers. The Patriarch said, "Exerting your supernatural powers to the full, what kind of transformations can you perform?
He replied, "I could transform a vast ocean; that would be but a minor feat. The Patriarch asked, "Can you transform the Sea of Nature? He asked, "What is the Sea of Nature?"
"I have never known this. The Patriarch then explained the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*) to him, saying: "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it;

the three samādhis and the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are manifested thereby. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra gave rise to faith and, together with his three thousand followers, sought ordination.
The Patriarch then summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*) upon them, further instructing them as follows:
He said, "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury shall now be entrusted to you. Listen to these verses: 'Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma;

light and darkness have never been two. Now I entrust this Dharma of realization, which is neither grasped nor abandoned. Having finished the entrustment, he immediately entered the Dragon-Sprint Samādhi.
He rose upright into the air, appearing like the orb of the sun, and then manifested his parinirvāṇa. The fourfold assembly grieved."
The True Body [of the Master] was at Longkan (Dragon Cave) in the thirty-seventh year of King [Gaozong], the Jia-wu year.
A non-Buddhist seeker challenged the Patriarch to a debate on doctrine. The king, his ministers, and the fourfold assembly were assembled together at the site of the debate.
The Patriarch asked, "What is the core tenet of your doctrine? He replied, "I am able to refute any statement whatsoever.

The Patriarch then pointed to the king and said, "The kingdom is currently peaceful and prosperous, and the Great King enjoys long life; I request that you refute this. The non-Buddhist was thus subdued.
According to the *Zongjing*, the non-Buddhist was Aśvaghoṣa, while the author of the treatise was Pārśva; Aśvaghoṣa [was the one defeated].

Therefore, [the claim] that he left home under the Venerable Pārśva contradicts both the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) and the *Zheng zong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage).
Furthermore, since the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Source Mirror) also records his words on Mount Yuntai, this would be self-contradictory. Master Song’s investigation is extremely detailed;
the record in the *Zongjing lu* is erroneous. Guifeng said: "He performed exquisite music and brought down various musicians; amidst the sounds of the music..."

Within [the assembly], he expounded upon the dharmas as suffering, empty, and non-self. Whether of noble or humble birth, those who left the household life encountered foreign troops surrounding them at that time;

they demanded nine hundred million gold coins. The King gave Aśvaghoṣa to them, and only then did they withdraw. He composed the *Ikṣu-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses, and also composed treatises such as the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
He was exceptionally skilled at guiding and inspiring others. Furthermore, the commentary on the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* refers to him as "Mahāsattva."
When he played the lute, the horses neighed; thus he was called Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigh).
The thirteenth patriarch, Venerable Kambalāmbara, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra.

Initially, he was a non-Buddhist teacher with three thousand disciples who were well-versed in various heterodox doctrines. Later, he received the Dharma from the venerable Aśvaghoṣa and led his followers to Western India.
The Elder crossed over. He had a crown prince named Meghasvāmin, who, hearing the Elder’s reputation, invited him to the palace to receive offerings.
The Elder said, “The Tathāgata has given this instruction: ‘A śramaṇa must not draw near to kings, ministers, or families of great power.
The prince said, “To the north of my capital city there is a great mountain. On that mountain is a stone cave where you may practice meditative seclusion.”
"Is this so? The Master replied, "Yes," and immediately entered that mountain. After traveling several *li*, he encountered a large python.
The Master walked straight ahead without looking back; the serpent coiled itself around his body. The Master then conferred the Three Refuges upon it, and having heard them, the serpent departed.
As the Master was about to reach a stone cave, an old man dressed in plain white robes came out, joined his palms in greeting, and asked, "Who are you? The Master said, "I am..."
"Where do you dwell? He replied, "In the past, I was once a bhikṣu who greatly delighted in solitude. There was a novice bhikṣu who frequently came to seek instruction;
however, I grew weary of responding to him and conceived thoughts of resentment. When my life ended, I fell into the body of a python and have dwelt in this cave for a thousand years.
Having just encountered the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the precepts, I have come to express my gratitude."—The Patriarch.
Question: Who else dwells upon this mountain? Answer: Ten *li* from here, there is a great tree that provides shade for five hundred great nāgas.
This king of trees is named Nāgārjuna, who constantly preaches the Dharma for the assembly of nāgas; I too have listened to and received it.

The Master (the Patriarch) then proceeded with his disciples to that place. Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said, "This deep mountain is solitary and remote, a place frequented by nāgas and pythons."
"Noble One, you are most supreme; why do you trouble your divine feet [to come here]? The Patriarch said, "I am not supreme; I have come to visit a worthy one.
Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself, "Has this Master attained the nature of certainty? Is he clear-sighted regarding the Way? Is he a great sage who continues the True Vehicle?
The Patriarch said, "Though you speak with your mind, I already know it with my own mind. Simply prepare for your renunciation; what need is there to worry that I will not [grant it]?"
The Sage Nāgārjuna, having heard this, repented and apologized. The Patriarch immediately granted him ordination, and together with five hundred dragon followers, they all received full precepts.
He further addressed them, saying: "I now entrust to you the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury of the Tathāgata. Listen attentively to these verses: 'The Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest;
it is called the True Limit (Bhūtakoṭi). One who awakens to this Dharma of hiding and manifesting is neither a fool nor...'"

After transmitting the Dharma, Jñānagupta manifested supernatural transformations; he transformed into fire to cremate his own body. Nāgārjuna collected the five-colored śarīra relics and erected a stūpa.
This was the renchen year, the forty-first year of Emperor Han.
Guifeng said: "He composed the *Treatise on Non-Self* (*Anātman-śāstra*) in one hundred verses. Wherever this treatise reached, it did not fail to subdue demons.
▲ The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was also named Nāgasena. In his youth, he was able to recite the four Vedas; as he grew, he became proficient in all arts.
His talent and eloquence were as brilliant as a deity. He left the household life and entered a stone cave, where he dwelt beneath a dragon tree (nāga-vṛkṣa), serving the dragon.
He was honored by all who encountered him. Having received the transmission of the Dharma from Venerable Māra, he later traveled to South India.

The people of that country largely believed in the efficacy of meritorious deeds. The Patriarch preached the Dharma for them, whereupon they said to one another, "If a person possesses meritorious deeds, they are foremost in the world;
as for speaking of Buddha-nature in vain, who can actually perceive it? The Patriarch replied, "If you wish to see Buddha-nature, you must first eliminate your *asmimāna* (self-conceit). They...

A person asked, "Is the Buddha-nature large or small? The Patriarch replied, "It is neither large nor small; neither broad nor narrow; it has neither merit nor retribution; it neither dies nor is born.

Upon hearing these words, which were superior in principle, they all returned to their original resolve. The Patriarch then manifested a body of sovereign mastery from his seat, appearing like a full moon disk;
the entire assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma but could not see the Patriarch's form. Among that assembly was...
The son of the elder, named Kanadeva, addressed the assembly, saying, "Do you recognize this sign? The assembly replied, "We have never seen such a thing before; how could we identify it?
Kanadeva said, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essential form of the Buddha-nature to show us. How do we know this?
It is because, through the samādhi of formlessness, his form is like the full moon; the meaning of the Buddha-nature is vast and expansive."
However, it was empty and luminous. Having finished speaking, the wheel-marked image immediately vanished. He returned to his original seat and spoke a verse:
"The body manifests the form of the full moon, To represent the essence of all Buddhas. The preaching of Dharma has no fixed shape, Employing means that transcend sound and color.

When the assembly heard this verse, they suddenly realized the state of non-arising. They all wished to leave the household life in order to seek liberation. The Patriarch then shaved their hair and commanded the others...
The Biography of Āryadeva: In South India there were five thousand non-Buddhist heretics who employed great magical illusions.

The king and the people of the land followed them in droves, unaware of the Buddha. The Venerable One was moved by compassion; he changed his appearance, dressing in white robes and carrying a ceremonial banner.
Every time he waited for the king to emerge, he would hasten before him, sometimes concealing himself and sometimes appearing. This continued for seven years.
One day, the king suddenly took notice of him and asked, "Who are you that precedes my procession? I pursue you but cannot catch you; I let you go but you do not leave."
The man said, "I am a wise person who knows all phenomena. The king asked, "Do you know what the various devas are doing now?
The man replied, "The devas are currently engaged in battle with the asuras. The king asked, "How can this be verified? The man said, "It shall be evident shortly.
A moment later, spears, halberds, hands, and feet fell from the sky in a chaotic swirl. The king was then filled with great reverence and faith, and he commanded his...
The non-Buddhists all came to pay homage to the Venerable One, who transformed them all and led them to take refuge in the Triple Gem.

He further composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, which he bequeathed to the world. Later, he transmitted the Dharma to Kāṇadeva, with the verse of transmission saying:
"To clarify the principle of the hidden and the manifest, one speaks of the logic of liberation; when the mind does not grasp at phenomena, there is no anger."

He was also without joy. Having entrusted the Dharma, he entered the Moon-Disk Samādhi (*candramaṇḍala-samādhi*) and extensively manifested miraculous transformations. He returned to his seat and, remaining motionless, entered into stillness.
When seven days had passed and it rained śarīra relics from the sky, the Venerable One again pointed toward the void from his seat and said to the assembly:
"In the past, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, a disciple of the Buddha Kanakamuni, made three vows. The first was that when he became a Buddha, all who were holy..."
First, when the noble ones transform and deliver beings, Heaven sends down rain; their very bodies become *śarīra*.

Second, all that is produced by the great earth may serve as medicine to cure the illnesses of sentient beings. Third, all who possess wisdom attain subtle knowledge and, through it, penetrate their past lives.
That the *śarīra* have now rained down is due to the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of Mahākāśyapa. Having spoken thus, he again became silent. This was Kāṇadeva.
He built a stupa together with the multitude and enshrined his entire body within it; this was the year Jichou, the thirty-fifth year of the First Emperor of Qin.

Guifeng said: "Born into a family of great wealth and nobility, he mastered the four Vedas and the celestial charts and prophecies. Consequently, he practiced sorcery with three companions until they were defeated.
He then left the household life and recited all the sutras and treatises of Jambudvīpa, claiming himself to be an omniscient person."
The Great Dragon took pity on him and led him into the dragon palace. Once he had attained awakening, he returned and converted the king, Brahmins, and non-Buddhists in countless numbers.
He composed several dozen treatises.
▲ The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśrāva.
Initially, he sought to cultivate meritorious deeds while also delighting in dialectical debate. Later, he went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.

As he approached the gate, Nāgārjuna, recognizing him as a man of wisdom, first sent his attendant to place a bowl filled with water before the seat. Upon seeing this, the Venerable [Kanadeva] immediately...
He cast a single needle into it and it went straight through;
they met with joyful accord. Langye Huijue’s verse says: "The water in Nāgārjuna’s bowl, The needle on Deva’s hair-fiber.
Everyone vies over gain and loss; Each person speaks of floating and sinking. If you do not see the wild geese in the clouds, How can you know the depth of the desert sands? The farmer moved...
At the corner foundation pillar, gold was found beneath the pillar-base.
Nāgārjuna immediately preached the Dharma for him; without rising from his seat, he manifested the form of a lunar disc. This is recorded in detail in the *Nāgārjuna Chapter*.
Having received the Dharma, the Patriarch later traveled to the kingdom of Kapilavastu. There lived an elder named Brahmāśrī. One day...
Mushrooms grew upon the trees in the garden like fungi; they were exceedingly delicious. Only the elder and his second son, Rāhula-bhadra, could see them and eat them.
As soon as they took them, the mushrooms would grow back again, and though they were consumed, they would reappear. None of the other relatives were able to see them.

The Patriarch knew there was a karmic cause from a previous life and went to the man’s house. The elder then asked the reason for his visit. The Patriarch said, “In the past, your family once made offerings to a bhikṣu.
However, that bhikṣu’s insight into the Way was not yet clear; he had received the faithful offerings in vain and was thus reborn as a wooden fungus.
Only you and your son have been diligent in your offerings, and so you are able to enjoy this fruit. He then asked the elder:

"How old are you? he asked. "I am seventy-nine," the elder replied. The Patriarch then spoke this verse: "If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, they must return their body to the offerings of the faithful.

When you reach eighty-one, this tree shall no longer grow. Having heard the verse, the elder was filled with even greater admiration and reverence, saying, "I, your disciple, am worn out by age and cannot serve as your master's attendant.
I pray that you grant me your youngest son so that he may follow you and leave the household life. The Patriarch [consented].
He said, "In the past, the Tathāgata prophesied that this son would become a great teacher during the second five-hundred-year period. Our meeting today surely accords with our past causes.
He immediately shaved his hair [and ordained him]. Upon reaching the city of Pāṭaliputra, he heard that various non-Buddhists intended to obstruct the Buddha-dharma.
After deliberating for some time, the Patriarch took up a long banner and entered among their assembly. They questioned the Patriarch, saying:"
"Why do you not come forward? the Patriarch asked. He replied, "Why do you not stay behind? The other said, "You seem like a lowly person.
The Patriarch said, "You seem like a man of noble status. He asked, "What Dharma do you understand? The Patriarch said, "You do not understand anything at all. He said, "I wish to attain Buddhahood."

The Patriarch said, "I have clearly attained Buddhahood. The other replied, "It is not fitting for you to have attained it. The Patriarch said, "I originally claimed that I attained it; you truly have not attained it.
The other said, "Since you have not attained it, why do you say you have? The Patriarch said, "Because you harbor a self, you do not attain it;
I am without self or the notion of self, and therefore I naturally attain it. When the other was thus defeated in argument, he asked the Patriarch, "You..."
"What is your name? the Master asked. He replied, "My name is Kanadeva. Having previously heard of the Master's reputation, he repented his errors and offered his apologies.

At that time, those in the assembly were still raising questions and objections against one another; the Master refuted them with unimpeded eloquence, whereupon they all submitted and took refuge in him.
The *Zhengfayan zang* states: In the Western Heaven (India), the bells and drums were prohibited, which was termed a "purification" (*sha'tai*).

After seven days had passed, the Patriarch, employing his supernatural powers, ascended the tower and struck the bell. The assembly of non-Buddhists gathered all at once and arrived at the bell tower.
The gate was locked. He then asked the one striking the bell, "Who are you? The master replied, "Heaven. He asked, "Who is Heaven? The master replied, "I. He asked, "Who is I?
The master replied, "You. He asked, "Who is You? The master replied, "A dog. He asked, "Who is the dog? The master remained silent.
The Patriarch said, "You. The outsider asked, "Who are you? The Patriarch said, "I. He asked, "Who am I? The Patriarch said, "Heaven. Thus they exchanged questions and answers seven times.

The assembly of outsiders realized they had been defeated by their own conceit. They reported this to the King, who again sounded the bells and drums to cause the Buddha-Dharma to flourish greatly once more.
He addressed his senior disciple Rāhula and entrusted him with the Dharma-eye, saying in verse: "To those who transmit the Dharma, I have explained the principle of liberation.
Regarding the Dharma, there is truly nothing realized; it has neither end nor beginning. Having thus transmitted the Dharma, he entered the Samādhi of Vigorous Prowess (Vaiśāradya).
He emitted eight rays of light from his body and returned to nirvana. His disciples erected a stupa to make offerings. This was the gengchen year, the nineteenth year of the Han Wendi reign.
The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, was a native of Kapilavastu. He traveled to Śibi to propagate the Dharma.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a river named Suvarṇavālukā (Golden Water), whose taste was exceptionally fine. In its midstream, the reflections of five Buddhas appeared.
The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "The source of this river is five hundred *li* away; there dwells the holy one Saṃghanandin.
One thousand years after the Buddha’s passing, he shall succeed to the sacred position. Having spoken thus, he led the assembly of disciples upstream.

They traveled upstream until they reached the place where Saṃghanandin was sitting peacefully in meditative absorption. The Patriarch and the assembly waited for him for three weeks before he finally arose from his concentration.
The Patriarch asked, "Is it your mind that is fixed, or is it your body? Saṃghanandin replied, "Both body and mind are fixed.
The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind are fixed, how can there be entering and exiting [of concentration]? Saṃghanandin replied, "Although there is entering and exiting, it does not..."

[He] lost the characteristic of meditative concentration. It was like gold in a well; the essence of the gold is eternally quiescent. The Patriarch said, "Whether the gold is in the well or the gold has come out of the well, the gold itself has neither motion nor stillness.
What is it that enters and exits? Daiten said, "If one speaks of the motion and stillness of the gold, what is it that enters and exits?
If one speaks of the entering and exiting of the gold, the gold is not motion or stillness. The Patriarch said, "If the gold is in the well, what is the gold that comes out? If the gold comes out..."
“Wellspring. What is that which remains? Daitetsu said, “If gold were to come out of the wellspring, what remains would not be gold.
If gold were in the wellspring, that which comes out would not be the object. The Patriarch said, “This principle is not so. Daitetsu said, “That meaning is not fixed.

The Patriarch said, “This meaning must fall away. Daitetsu said, “That meaning is not established. The Patriarch said, “Since that meaning is not established, my meaning is established. Daitetsu said, “My...”
[Upagupta said: "Although your meaning is established, the Dharma is not-self. The Master said: "My meaning is already established, because I am without self. Upagupta said:
"If you are without self, what meaning is further established? The Master said: "Because I am without self, your meaning is thereby established. Upagupta said:
"Whom did you, O Virtuous One, take as your teacher to attain this non-self? The Master said: "My teacher was Kāṇadeva; he realized this non-self. [Upagupta] raised an objection.
He praised him with a verse, saying: "I bow my head to the Teacher, Deva, who has emerged from you, O Benevolent One.
Because you, O Benevolent One, are without self, I wish to take you as my teacher. The Patriarch replied in verse: "Since I am already without self, you must perceive my self."

"If you take me as your teacher," [the Master said], "you must know that I am neither 'I' nor 'mine. At these words, Nandi’s mind was suddenly opened wide, and he immediately sought liberation. The Patriarch said, "Your mind is sovereign; it is not bound by me.

Having spoken, he took his golden bowl in his right hand and raised it up to the Brahma Heaven to fetch fragrant food, intending to serve it to the great assembly. However, the members of the assembly suddenly felt a sense of revulsion.
The Patriarch said, "This is not my fault; it is the result of your own karma. He then commanded Nandī to share his seat and eat with him.

The assembly again marveled at this, and the Patriarch said, "That you were unable to eat was entirely due to this reason. You should know that he who shared his seat with me is none other than the Tathāgata Śālarāja of the past.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he has manifested his traces here. You all, too, belong to the *Kṛta-yuga* (Adorned) Kalpa."
They had already attained the third fruit [of the path], yet they had not yet realized the untainted (*anāsrava*) state. The assembly said, "The spiritual power of our teacher is indeed credible.
However, regarding his claim that he was a Buddha of the past, they harbored secret doubts. Nandika, perceiving the arrogance of these beings, said:
"When the World-Honored One was in the world, the earth was level and even; there were no hills or mounds, nor rivers, streams, ditches, or canals. All the water was sweet and pure, and the grass..."

The trees flourished and the land was abundant; there were no eight sufferings, and the people practiced the ten wholesome deeds. Since his parinirvāṇa beneath the twin trees, more than eight hundred years have passed.

The world has become a desolate ruin, and the vegetation is withered and parched. People lack profound faith, their right mindfulness is slight, and they do not believe in *tathatā* (suchness), caring only for supernatural powers.
Having finished speaking, he gradually extended his right hand into the earth until it reached the limit of the *vajra*-wheel.

He took the nectar-water in a lapis lazuli vessel and carried it to the assembly hall. When the great multitude saw it, they immediately felt deep admiration, repented their transgressions, and prostrated themselves.
Thereupon, the Patriarch charged Saṃghanandin with the transmission of the Dharma-eye, speaking this verse:

"In the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be realized; It is neither grasped nor abandoned. The Dharma has no marks of existence or non-existence; How could it arise from within or without? Saṃghanandin...
Having heard the command, he respectfully received it with diligent devotion. He further spoke a verse of praise, saying: "Excellent, O Great Sage! Your heart’s clarity surpasses the sun and moon;
a single ray of light illuminates the world, and no darkness or Māra remains unvanquished. After transmitting the Dharma to his successor, he sat peacefully and returned to stillness.
The fourfold assembly erected a stupa for him in the twenty-eighth year of Emperor Wu, the Wuchen (戊辰) year.
▲ The seventeenth patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the son of King Ratnavyuha of Śrāvastī.
He was able to speak from birth and constantly praised the Buddha’s deeds. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and addressed his parents with a verse, saying:
"I prostrate to my Greatly Compassionate Father; I bow my head to my Flesh-and-Blood Mother. I now wish to leave the home-life; I pray you will have pity on me."

Out of compassion, his parents firmly tried to dissuade him; he consequently fasted for an entire day. They finally permitted him to leave the household life while remaining at home, bestowing upon him the name Saṃghanandin.
They further commanded the śramaṇa Śāṇakavāsin to serve as his teacher. For nineteen years, he never once grew weary or indolent.
He would often reflect to himself: "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life? One night, a divine light descended from above.
Seeing a path that was level and smooth, he walked on unconsciously for about ten *li* until he reached a great cliff. There was a stone cave there, and he took up residence in seclusion within it.
When the father lost his son, he banished Śrīlāta from the country and went abroad in search of him, but did not know where he was.
Ten years passed; after the Patriarch had attained the Dharma and received the prediction, he traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā to propagate the teaching.
Suddenly, a cool breeze swept over the assembly, bringing an extraordinary sense of physical and mental well-being, though they did not know its cause.
The Patriarch said, "This is the wind of the Way and Virtue. A sage shall soon appear in the world to continue the ancestral lamp.

Having spoken, he used his supernatural power to lead the great multitude on a journey through mountains and valleys. Within the time it takes to eat a meal, they arrived at the foot of a peak. He said to the assembly, "This peak..."

Above his head was a purple cloud shaped like a canopy; it was here that a sage resided. The Master lingered with the great assembly for a long time before seeing a young boy at a mountain hut holding a round mirror.
The boy walked straight up to the Master, who asked, "How old are you? The boy replied, "One hundred years.
The Master said, "You are still quite young; why do you say you are a hundred? The boy said, "I do not understand the principle of age; I am truly a hundred years old."
The Patriarch said, "Are you skilled in the pivotal point? The boy said, "The Buddha said:

'If a person lives for a hundred years without understanding the pivotal point of all Buddhas, it is not as good as living for a single day and attaining decisive realization. The Patriarch said, "What does that which is in your hand represent?
The boy said, "It is the great perfect mirror of all Buddhas; inside and out there is no flaw or obscuration. Two people may see it together, yet it is the eye of the mind."

They were all similar. When his parents heard their son’s words, they immediately let him go forth into homelessness. His grandfather took him back to his original home, and once he had received full ordination, he was named Gayāśīrṣa.
On another occasion, hearing the sound of wind blowing through the palace bells, his grandfather asked, "Are the bells ringing, or is it the wind?
Śīrṣa replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells that are ringing; it is my own mind that is ringing. His grandfather said, "As for the mind..."
"Who is it? Śātavāhana replied, "Because all are equally tranquil. The Patriarch said, "Excellent, excellent! Who else but you could continue my Way?
I now entrust the Dharma-eye to you. He spoke this verse: "The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth; The ground arises from conditions.
Condition and seed do not obstruct one another; Flower and fruit are likewise so. Having transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch leaned on a tree with his right hand and passed away. Great...
The assembly deliberated, saying, "The Venerable One has entered parinirvāṇa beneath this tree; shall it provide shade for his descendants?

We intend to enshrine his entire body on the high plateau and erect a stūpa there," but they were unable to lift him due to the collective effort required. Thus, they erected the stūpa directly beneath the tree. This was the Dingwei year, the thirteenth year of Emperor Zhao of the Former Han.
Guifeng said: "When the Venerable One passed away while clinging to a tree, the other arhats wished to move his body but could not;
even when they pulled it with the strength of many elephants, it would not budge. They then cremated him beneath the tree; once his body was consumed, the tree became even more lush and verdant."
▲The Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayāsata, was a native of the country of Mathurā. His surname was Udraka;
his father was Devaśaya, and his mother was Bhadra. She once dreamed that a great deity held up a mirror, and consequently she became pregnant. He was born after exactly seven days.
His body was as translucent as lapis lazuli; he never bathed, yet remained naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood, he delighted in solitude and his speech was unlike that of ordinary children.
While holding a mirror and wandering abroad, he encountered the Venerable Nandī and received ordination. Later, leading his disciples, he arrived at the kingdom of Mahācīna.
There he perceived an extraordinary fragrance emanating from the house of a certain Brāhmaṇa. As the Master was about to enter the house, the host, Kumāra—
Daowu asked, "Who are these followers? The Patriarch replied, "They are disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, Luoyun’s spirit was suddenly stirred;
he immediately closed his door. After a long while, the Patriarch knocked on the door. Luoyun said, "There is no one in this house. The Patriarch said:

The answer was, "Who is it that does not exist? (Fenyang Zhao, speaking on behalf [of the Master], said: "It is simply a matter of forgetting. Hearing these words, Puṇyatrāta realized he was an extraordinary person. He hurriedly opened the gate to welcome him.

The Patriarch said, "In the past, the World-Honored One made this prophecy: 'One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna) to propagate and flourish the profound transformation.
Now you have encountered me; you truly correspond to this auspicious destiny. Thereupon, Kumāra...
Rādhagupta developed the knowledge of past lives and, with sincere devotion, left the household life. Once he had received full ordination, the Dharma was entrusted to him. A verse says:
"When there is the seed and the ground of the mind, The causes and conditions can cause it to sprout. If there is no obstruction to these conditions, Birth will surely arise; otherwise, it will not.

Having thus entrusted the Dharma, the Patriarch leaped into the void and manifested eighteen miraculous transformations. Entering the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (the fire-transformation samādhi), he spontaneously cremated his own body. The assembly then [built a stupa]...
The construction of the stupa was completed during the twentieth year of Emperor Cheng of the Han dynasty, the year Wushen.
[This concludes the account of] the Nineteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kumāralāta, who was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi.
In the past, as a sovereign deva, he beheld the bodhisattva’s jeweled necklace and suddenly conceived a heart of attachment, whereby he fell and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
There, hearing Kauśika preach the Prajñāpāramitā, he ascended to the Brahma Heaven by virtue of that Dharma.

Because his faculties were sharp, he skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma, and the various devas honored him as their teacher. When the time arrived to succeed his lineage, he descended to the Yuezhi, and subsequently arrived at...
In the kingdom of Central India, there was a Mahāsattva named Jayata who asked:
"The parents of my household have long been faithful to the Triple Gem, yet they are constantly afflicted by chronic illness, and whatever they undertake never turns out as they wish.

On the other hand, my neighbors have long followed the occupation of caṇḍālas, yet their bodies are always vigorous and healthy, and everything they do succeeds. Why are they so fortunate while I am so guilty?"
The Patriarch said, "What is there to doubt? Furthermore, regarding the retribution for good and evil, there are three periods.

Ordinary people see only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long, or that the rebellious meet with fortune while the righteous suffer misfortune; they then claim that cause and effect do not exist and that sin and merit are empty.

Little do they realize that shadow and echo follow one another without the slightest discrepancy. Even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they shall never perish. At that time, Śāṇakavāsin—

Having heard these words, his doubts were suddenly dispelled. The Patriarch said: "Although you have already gained faith in the three karmas, you have not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion, delusion exists dependent upon consciousness, and consciousness depends upon non-awakening (avidyā). Non-awakening depends upon the mind. The mind is fundamentally pure;
it is without birth or extinction, without creation or action, without retribution or response, and without victory or defeat. It is profoundly still and luminously aware. If you enter into this..."
"This Dharma-gate may be equal to that of all Buddhas. All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions.

When Śāṇakavāsin received these words and grasped their meaning, his latent wisdom was awakened, and he earnestly sought ordination. (The *Zhengzong ji* records: The Patriarch asked, "Where are you from? You must inform your parents before you may become a monk.

Śāṇakavāsin replied, "My country is North India, three thousand li from here. However, I possess a minor art by which travel back and forth is easy. He then performed this art, and in an instant, he and the Patriarch arrived at that place.)

When Yato heard this from his parents, his grandfather subsequently conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon him. Once he had received the full precepts, the grandfather told him: "The time for my parinirvāṇa has now arrived.

You shall succeed me in carrying forward the legacy of my transformative teachings. He then entrusted him with the verse of the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*), which says: "By nature, there is originally no arising; It is spoken only in response to those who seek it.
Since nothing can be attained within the Dharma, Why harbor doubts about what is or is not resolved? He further said: "This is the purity of the realization of nature by the Tathāgata Subhavyūha."

"This is a phrase of purity; you should propagate it for future students. Having spoken these words, he immediately, while seated upon his cushion, used his fingernails to cleave his face until it was like a blooming red lotus.
A great radiance issued forth, illuminating the fourfold assembly, as he entered parinirvāṇa.
Śāṇakavāsa erected a stūpa to enshrine his entire body. This occurred in the fourteenth year of the Xinshi era, the Renwu year.
▲The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and vast, and he transformed and guided immeasurable beings.
Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and propagated the teachings of the Sudden Vehicle (*tun-jiao*). There, the assembly of students there valued only dialectical debate.
The leader among them was named Vaśu-bandhu (translated as "Pervasive Practice"). He always ate only once a day and did not lie down to sleep;

he prostrated to the Buddha during the six periods of the day, remained pure and free from desire, and was a refuge for the multitude. When the Patriarch was about to deliver him, he first asked the assembly:
"This ascetic Vaśu-bandhu is able to cultivate the Brahma-faring; can he attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied: "Our teacher is diligent; why [should there be any doubt]?"

"This is not possible. The Patriarch said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice asceticism for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it would all be the root of falsehood.
The assembly asked, "What virtues and conduct do you, Venerable Sir, possess that you should disparage our teacher? The Patriarch replied, "I do not seek the Way, nor am I inverted.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, nor do I treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, nor am I indolent."
"I have been negligent; I did not eat but one meal, nor did I eat mixed food. I was neither discontented nor greedy, and my mind harbored no expectations—this is what is called the Way.
When Pūrvavāsī heard this, he gave rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and joyfully praised him.
The Elder then said to the assembly, "Do you understand my words? It is because his resolve for the Way is so earnest that I acted in this manner."
"If the strings are too tight, they will snap; therefore, I did not encourage it. I have caused him to dwell in the ground of peace and happiness and enter the wisdom of all Buddhas.
He then addressed Viśvāmitra, saying, "When I just now rebuked and suppressed you before the assembly, was it not distressing to your heart? Viśvāmitra replied:
I recall that seven kalpas ago, I was born in the Land of Constant Peace and Bliss as a disciple of the Wise One Moon-Purity (Candraprabha).
He prophesied that before long I would realize the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin. At that time, a Bodhisattva named Great Radiance appeared in the world;
because I was old, I leaned on a staff to pay my respects to him. My teacher rebuked me, saying, "You honor the son and slight the father; how can you be so base? At that moment, I thought to myself:

"It was no fault. I request that the Master instruct me on this. The Master said, "You prostrated before the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha and leaned your staff against the wall, painting it over the face of the Buddha.

Because of this arrogance, you lost the two fruits [of the path]. Since I have been reproaching myself and repenting my errors, even when hearing various evil words, they have been like the wind or an echo;
how much more so now that you have heard the unsurpassed nectar—would you instead give rise to feverish affliction? Only..."
"I pray that you, in your great compassion, will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said, "You have long planted many virtues; you shall succeed to my lineage.

Listen to this verse of mine: 'If, upon hearing these words, one accords with the non-arising [of phenomena], being identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm—if one can understand it thus, one will fully penetrate both phenomena and principle.
Having transmitted the Dharma, the Patriarch sat upon his seat and inverted his head, planting it into the ground like the branch of a śāla tree."
Suddenly, he passed away. The multitude wished to cremate him, but even hundreds and thousands of people could not lift his body.

When the arhats used their supernatural powers to lift it, they likewise could not move it. The assembly then offered incense and made prayers; thereupon, the body collapsed and lay prostrate upon the ground.
The cremation and collection of the śarīra for the construction of a stūpa took place in the seventeenth year of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, the Jiaxu year.

At that time, the King of Yuezhi, having heard of the Master’s reputation for virtue, came in person to inquire about the Dharma. After he had paid his respects and requested an exposition, the Patriarch said:
"The Great King’s coming was by way of the Path; his departure now is likewise as when he came. The King sighed in admiration.

Yuanwu Qin’s verse says: "Most simple, most easy; most honored, most noble. Coming and going, it rests upon the crowns of a thousand sages. In the mundane and supramundane worlds, it is inconceivable.
A snap of the fingers, and the eighty-four thousand gates are perfectly accomplished; With a single leap, one enters directly."
The Stage of the Tathāgata.
▲ The twenty-first patriarch, Vasiṣṭha (婆修盤頭), was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Viśākha;

his father was Prabhācchada (光葢) and his mother was Gaurī (嚴一). Although his family was wealthy, they had no son. They prayed at a Buddhist stūpa, and the mother dreamed that she swallowed light and darkness.

Two months after the conception, seven days had passed when an arhat named Xianzhong (Worthy Multitude) arrived at their home. Guanggai (Radiant Canopy) prepared offerings and performed a prostration;
Xianzhong sat upright and accepted them. When Yan (Austere) came out to bow, Xianzhong rose from his seat and said, "Return this greeting to the Mahasattva of the Dharma-body.
Guanggai was suspicious of this, but Xianzhong said, "Your wife is carrying a holy child; when born, he shall become a lamp of wisdom for the world."
Therefore, I avoid it. However, from a single lactation, two children were born: one named Vaśiṣṭha (Poxu pantou), whom I revere;
the second named Cūḍapanthaka (Chuní—this means "Wild Magpie Child"). Long ago, when the Tathāgata was practicing the Way on Mount Himavat, Cūḍapanthaka nested upon his head.
Once the Buddha had attained enlightenment, Cūḍapanthaka received the retribution of becoming the King of Nadi. The Buddha prophesied this.
The Buddha said, "In the second five-hundred-year period, you will be born into the family of Viśākhā in the city of Rājagṛha as a sibling of a noble one;
now there is no discrepancy. One month later, she indeed gave birth to two sons. When the Venerable Vāṣpa was fifteen years old, [he attained realization].
The Arhat Liangdu ordained [the king’s sons]. Moved by this, the Bodhisattva Vibhāṣa conferred the precepts upon them.
They traveled to the country of Nādi to spread the teachings. The king there was named Nityeśvara and had two sons: the elder was named Mahāla and the younger was named Mañjuṣaka.
The king asked his grandfather, "How does the local custom of Rājagṛha differ from that of this place? The grandfather replied, "There, [the people] have formerly thrice..."
"A Buddha has appeared in the world. Currently, there are two masters guiding and transforming within Your Majesty’s kingdom. The King asked, "Who are these two masters?

The Patriarch said, "The Buddha prophesied that in the second five-hundred-year period, there would be two Great Beings of supernatural power who would leave the household life to continue the work of the Sage.
One is Your Majesty’s second son, Maṇiratha; as for me, though my virtue is meager, I shall be the other. Formerly, in the kingdom of Nādi, there was a wicked elephant.
It was harmful. Since Nala was born and the elephant ceased its depredations, thirty years had passed; yet people still did not know why it had ceased.
While the King was conversing with his kinsmen, a messenger suddenly reported that a massive elephant was approaching the city. The King was filled with anxiety.

The Patriarch said, "Narada has emerged; the affliction is resolved. The King then commanded Narada to come forth. Narada immediately went out south of the city and, facing the elephant, struck his belly and let out a great roar.
The city shook violently, and the herd of elephants fell prostrate. In a moment, they all fled in dispersal.
At this, people finally realized that their thirty years of peace were due to Narada. The King developed great reverence and faith, and commanded Narada to remain.

When the Patriarch [Bodhidharma] was about to leave the household life, the Master immediately conferred upon him the full ordination (*upasampadā*). He entrusted him with the verse of the Dharma-transmission, saying:

"The bubble and the illusion are equally unimpeded; why do you not awaken to this? To penetrate the Dharma within it—neither now nor of old. Having completed the transmission of the Dharma, he leaped into the air to a height of half a *yojana* and remained suspended there motionless.
The fourfold assembly cried out, "We pray that the Venerable One will cease his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); we wish to receive [his remains]."
Śarīra then returned to his seat and entered meditative stillness. His remains were cremated and a stupa was erected; this was the ding-si year, the twelfth year of Emperor Shang of the Han dynasty.
Guifeng said: "He thoroughly mastered the meaning of all the sūtras, expounding them with discernment, and extensively transformed sentient beings."
I suspect this may be Vasubandhu, yet I do not dare to be certain.
▲ The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Manoratha, was of the Kṣatriya caste. His father was King Nityodyata.

Having received the command of Venerable Paṇḍu, the patriarch subsequently left the household life. He transmitted the Dharma to Western India, where the king’s name was Śrī... (The text here is incomplete).
Dudu, of the Gautama clan, served the Buddha with diligent devotion. One day, while at his place of practice, a stupa suddenly appeared, four chi high.

He wished to lift it up for worship, but despite exhausting the strength of the multitude, they were unable to move it. The King convened a great assembly of the fourfold community and inquired as to its origin, yet none among them could know.
Zuo said, "This is a stupa of King Aśoka; it has manifested because it was moved by the King’s diligent devotion."
The King said, "I venture to ask for the essentials of the Dharma. The Patriarch said, "The Buddha-dharma can be mastered by possessing seven things and removing three substances;
only then can one study it. The King asked, "What are these three substances and seven things? The Patriarch replied, "The three substances to be removed are greed, anger, and delusion.
The seven things to be possessed are great compassion, joy, non-self, valor, benefiting others, subduing demons, and non-attainment. It is because people possess these that they attain clarity."
"I am not clear about this. Because of this, the King, having heard it, said: "A Most Holy One is difficult to encounter, and worldly pleasures are not lasting.

He immediately transmitted the throne to his crown prince and left the household life. After seven days, he realized the four fruits of arhatship. The Patriarch deeply comforted and instructed him, saying:

"While you reside in this country, skillfully deliver others. Now there is a person of great Dharma-capacity in a foreign land; I shall go there to transform them. When [the disciple] asked to be delivered, the Master said: [Note: The source text provided ends abruptly with "得度曰。師" (When [the disciple] asked to be delivered, the Master said). As the prompt requests a translation of the provided text, I have translated the portion available.]
"Your traces should extend throughout the ten directions; with a single thought, you should arrive here. Why trouble yourself to travel? The Patriarch replied, "Indeed.
Thereupon, he burned incense and spoke from afar to the Bhikṣu Huike (Hegelena) of the Kingdom of Mozhī: "You have instructed the flock of cranes;
as the fruit of the Way is about to be realized, you should know this for yourself. At that time, Huike was expounding Sūtra verses for King Baoyin. Suddenly, he beheld—
A strange fragrance formed into clusters. The King asked, "What omen is this? He replied, "The Venerable Mañjuśrī of South India is about to arrive;

this is the fragrant sign of his arrival. The King and Huike both turned westward and paid their respects. The Patriarch also responded by touching the ground three times with his hand toward the east.
They then took their leave and received ordination. Together with the assembly, they ascended into the void and proceeded toward the moon.
In the kingdom of Chi (Cīna), Hele-na and Baoyin welcomed the Patriarch to the royal palace to provide him with offerings.
On another day, Hele-na asked the Patriarch, "I have resided in these forest groves for nine *bái* (the land of India reckons one year as one *bái*).
I have a disciple named Longzi who was intelligent from his youth; though I have investigated through the three periods of time, I cannot discern his origin. The Patriarch said, "This boy..."
In the fifth kalpa, he was born into a Brahmin family in the Land of Wondrous Joy (Abhirati). He once offered sandalwood to a Buddhist temple to serve as a mallet for striking the bell;

as a result of this merit, he received the retribution of being exceptionally intelligent and wise, and was held in high esteem by the multitude. He asked again, "By what conditions did I attract this flock of cranes?
The Patriarch said, "During the fourth kalpa, you were once a bhikṣu. When you were about to attend a gathering at the Dragon Palace, you [and your companions]..."
The disciples all wished to follow him. You observed that among the five hundred followers, not a single person was worthy of such a sublime offering.

At that time, the disciples said, "Our teacher once preached the Dharma, saying that those who are equal in regard to food are also equal in regard to the Dharma. Now, since this is not the case, what sanctity can there be?
You then ordered them to attend the assembly; because they sat there and consumed the food indiscriminately, they were reborn as winged creatures—both master and disciples.
"Due to our past affinities, we have now followed you. Heilunna asked, "By what skillful means can you cause them to attain liberation?
The Patriarch replied, "I possess the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure; you should listen and receive it to transform beings throughout the bounds of the future.

He then spoke this verse: "The mind turns following the myriad objects; in the place where it turns, there is profound mystery. If one recognizes one's nature while following the flow, there will be neither joy nor sorrow. The flock of cranes...
Upon hearing the verse, the crane flew away with a cry. The Patriarch immediately leaped into the air and displayed the eighteen transformations.
Returning to his seat, he pointed to the ground, causing a divine spring to gush forth. He then spoke another verse: "The spring of the pure mind-ground Can moisten all things;

Surging up from the earth, It universally relieves the worlds of the ten directions. (The *Zongjing* edition reads "universally fills the limits of the ten directions. Having finished the verse, he became still and entered nirvana. The crane... [perished]. (Note: The character "勒" here likely indicates the end of the narrative or a scribal mark.)
Then, for King Baoyin, a stupa was built to enshrine his entire body; this was the year Yisi, the nineteenth year of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty.
The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Helena, was a native of the country of Yuezhi. His surname was Brahmin; his father was Qiansheng and his mother was Jinguang.
Having prayed to the golden pillar of the Seven Buddhas for a son, she dreamed that atop Mount Sumeru there was a divine child.
Holding a golden ring, he said, "I have come. At his birth, the heavens rained down flowers. Because there were such divine omens, the king nursed him within the palace;
the palace ladies raised him, and he immediately manifested as many sons, numbering about a thousand.
The king said, "I have no heir. I shall raise you all as crown princes. Now that there are a thousand bodies, which one shall be the true son? Having spoken, he—
One son emitted a light, and suddenly they could no longer see him; instead, he was seen at his parents' home. The King could do nothing about it.

At the age of seven, he saw a vulgar shrine among the common people and loathed the slaughter there; he entered the temple and shouted at them, whereupon the shrine’s images were subsequently destroyed.
The local community hailed him as a "holy child. When he reached the age of twenty-two, he left the household life and dwelt alone in a forest for nine years, reciting [the scriptures].

During the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* assembly, he was moved by the appearance of a flock of cranes following him. At thirty years of age, he attained the Dharma and traveled to Central India to propagate his teachings.

There, he preached the Dharma for King Abhayasāgara, moving the Sun and Moon Devas (Sūrya and Candradeva) to prostrate before him. When the King saw this with his own eyes, he questioned the Patriarch:
"How many lands do the sun and moon encompass? The Patriarch replied: "The worlds transformed by the thousand Śākyamunis each..."
There are ten billion Mount Merus, suns, and moons; if I were to explain them in detail, I could not finish. When the King heard this, he was filled with joy.
At that time, [the Master] propagated the unsurpassed Way and delivered those with karmic affinity. He had an eminent disciple, the Dragon Prince, who died young; his elder brother was Siṃha.

He was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory. He served a Brahmin, who was about to bury his son. When the multitude attempted to lift the coffin, they were unable to move it. Zu said to Shizi:
"In the past, when your younger brother wished to provide you with merit for the afterlife, he fashioned a Buddhist image;
you then believed in the Brahmins and cast it to the ground. Now, though your brother has passed away, he still wishes to awaken and transform you; therefore, he has manifested this."
"This is extraordinary. You must quickly make offerings to the image; then the coffin shall be lifted. Siṃha followed the command, and the coffin was raised.
Not long after, the Brahmin teacher died, and Siṃha then took refuge with the Venerable One. He asked, "I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind?
The Patriarch said, "If you wish to seek the Way, do not apply the mind to anything. Siṃha asked, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the work of a Buddha?"
The Patriarch said, "If you have something to employ, it is not merit; if you have nothing to do, that is itself the work of the Buddha. As the sutra says:
"Regarding the merits I have performed, there is no sense of 'mine'. Upon hearing these words, Śiṃha immediately entered the wisdom of the Buddha.
At that time, the Patriarch suddenly pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of phenomenon is this?

Shenxiu replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through heaven and earth, with five black streaks of vapor stretching across its center. The Patriarch asked, "What does this omen portend?
He replied, "It cannot be known. The Patriarch said, "Fifty years after my passing, there shall be [a king] in the kingdom of Northern India."
"It is difficult to arise. An infant dwells within your body; I am about to pass away. I now entrust the Dharma-eye to you; guard and uphold it well. He then spoke a verse:
"When the nature of mind is recognized, It may be called inconceivable. When it is clearly understood, nothing is to be obtained;
At the moment of attainment, one does not speak of knowing. Upon hearing this verse, Bhikṣu Siṃha was joyful and satisfied, yet he did not yet understand what calamity he was about to encounter.
Nan asked. The Patriarch then secretly revealed [the answer] to him. Having finished speaking, he manifested eighteen transformations and returned to stillness.

After the cremation was completed, they divided the *śarīra* relics, each wishing to erect a stupa. The Patriarch again manifested his form in mid-air and spoke this verse: "One dharma is all dharmas."
"All things are subsumed within this single Dharma; my own body is neither existent nor non-existent. Why then divide all these stupas?

When the great assembly heard this verse, they ceased their division and constructed the stupa at the site of the *dhātu* (relics) ceremony. This was the twenty-second year of Emperor Xian of the Later Han, the Jichou year.
▲ The twenty-fourth patriarch, the Venerable Siṃhabhadra Bhikṣu, was a native of Central India. His family name was Brahmin.

Having attained the Dharma, he traveled abroad and arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra. There was a śramaṇa named Parika (alternatively called Pārika), who had originally practiced the dhyāna-contemplation of the Hīnayāna.
He had five disciples, namely: Chan-ding (Dhyāna-sthiti), Zhi-jian (Jñāna-darśana), Zhi-xiang (Lakṣaṇa-grāha), She-xiang (Lakṣaṇa-tyāga), and [the fifth].
He did not speak. To the one who maintained silence, the Patriarch said: "The Buddha’s teaching diligently propagates Prajñā; who is it that maintains silence and thus contradicts the Buddha’s words?
To the one who advocated abandoning appearances, he said: "The Buddha’s teaching is complete in its dignified deportment and pure in its holy life;
how could it advocate abandoning appearances? To the one who clung to appearances, he said: "The Buddha-lands are pure, sovereign, and unattached; why do you cling to appearances?"
