The Master said to those who claimed to possess knowledge and vision: "The knowledge and vision of all Buddhas is characterized by non-attainment. This Dharma is subtle and wondrous; it is beyond the reach of awakening through hearing.
It is unconditioned and signless. What, then, is there to know or see? The fourfold assembly was all moved to submission.

Only the meditation master Dharmadatta, hearing that the fourfold assembly had been defeated in argument, came forward in indignation and frustration. The Master asked: "Virtuous one, you practice meditative concentration; why have you come here?"

[The Master said: "It is here. Since you have arrived here, why do you say you are practicing concentration (*samādhi*)? He replied, "Although I have come here, my mind is not distracted. Concentration follows the person who practices it; how could it depend on a location?
The Master said, "Since you, O worthy one, have arrived here, your practice has also arrived. Since there is no fixed location, how can it depend on the person practicing it?
He replied, "Because concentration is practiced by the person, it is not that the person practices concentration. When I was about to come here, its..."

[The monk] said, "I constantly practice concentration (*samādhi*). The Patriarch said, "It is not that the person practices concentration; rather, it is concentration that practices the person. When you first came here, who was practicing that concentration?
He replied, "It is like a pure, bright pearl with no obscurations inside or out. If concentration were fully realized, it would surely be like this.
The Patriarch said, "If concentration were fully realized, it would indeed resemble a bright pearl. But looking at you now, you are not of the class of pearls. He replied, "That..."
"The pearl is transparent and brilliant; both inside and out it is entirely settled. My mind is not distracted, just as this [pearl] is pure.
The Patriarch said, "That pearl has neither inside nor outside; how can you, O worthy one, speak of 'settling'? Impurities do not cause agitation; this 'settling' is not purity.
Upon hearing this, Dharmadatta prostrated himself and said, "In my study of the Way, I have been nothing but laboring in vain. May the Venerable One deign to instruct me."
I earnestly and piteously entreated him. The Patriarch said: "The dhyāna-concentration of all Buddhas has nothing that is attained;

the awakening path of all Buddhas has nothing that is realized. To have neither attainment nor realization is true liberation. Rewarding causes and answering effects—the karmic retributions of the world—are entirely not like this within this Dharma.
Having received the Patriarch’s instruction, Bodhidharma was awakened; his mind-ground became brilliantly clear. Once the Patriarch...

He gathered a community of five disciples, and his fame spread far and wide. As he was seeking a Dharma heir, he encountered an elder who led his son before him and asked the Patriarch, "This boy's name is Sthavira;
from the moment of his birth, his left hand remained clenched, and even now, at the age of twenty, he has still been unable to open it."
"May the Venerable One reveal its past cause. As the Patriarch looked at him, he reached out his hand and said, "Return my pearl to me.
The boy immediately opened his hand and offered the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder. The Patriarch said, "In a previous life, I was a monk named Po-sha.
Once, when I went to a vegetarian feast by the Western Sea, I received this pearl as an offering and entrusted it to him. Now he returns my pearl; the principle is indeed settled."
"So be it. The elder then permitted him to leave the household life. The Patriarch assembled the holy multitude and conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon him.
Because of his prior karmic conditions, he was named Vasiṣṭha. The Patriarch then said to him: "My teacher had a secret prophecy that you would encounter hardship before long.
The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye shall now be entrusted to you; you must protect it and universally moisten all beings until the end of time. He spoke in verse: The Right...
When he spoke of "knowing and seeing," both knowing and seeing are the mind; when the mind is present, there is knowing and seeing; knowing and seeing are right here and now.
Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch secretly entrusted his *saṃghāṭī* robe to Suta, instructing him to go to another country to transform beings according to their capacities.
Suta received the teaching and traveled directly to South India. The Patriarch, however, felt that he could not evade the difficult circumstances and remained alone in Kaśmīra at that time.
In this country, there were two non-Buddhists, one named Māmuta and the other named Durlabha. Having studied various magical arts, they plotted together to cause a rebellion;
disguised as Śākyaputrīyas, they secretly entered the royal palace. Consequently, King Milarek (Mīlaka) destroyed the Buddhist teachings.
Wielding a sword, he went to the Venerable One and asked, "Has the Master attained the emptiness of the aggregates? The Patriarch replied, "I have."
"The aggregates are empty. The King asked, "Are you free from birth and death? The Patriarch replied, "I am already free from birth and death.
The King said, "Since you are free from birth and death, you may give me your head. The Patriarch said, "This body is not mine; why should I begrudge my head?
The King then brandished his blade and severed the Venerable’s head. White milk gushed forth several feet high. The King’s right arm then fell to the ground, and he died seven days later.
Prince Prabhāśiras sighed and said, "Why has my father brought this calamity upon himself? He then led the assembly in repentance.
At that time, there was a rishi on Mount Śveta who had a profound understanding of cause and effect. He declared, "In a previous life, Siṃha and Rāhula were both laymen.
Because Siṃha envied Rāhula’s excellence in the Dharma, he secretly murdered him; thus, he now reaps the retribution. The assembly consequently understood that this was the result of ancestral karma.
The pagoda was constructed in the twenty-second year of Emperor Feidi of the Northern Wei, the year of Jīmōu (the Year of the Rabbit).
Xuansha Bao said: "Whether it be the Great or the Small Lion Venerable, they do not even know how to act as the master themselves.
Xuanjue asked: "Tell me, did he strike the mark or not? Fenyang Wuye Zhaō gave a different response: "He knew the Master would not [strike the mark]."
Regarding "Reluctance," Xuedou Xian said: "The masterful sovereign has his natural place. Cuiyan Zhi said:
"At that moment, the Venerable One extended his neck, and the King raised his blade. At such a time, could anyone have come forward and succeeded in remonstrating with him?
To this day, no one has resolved this public case. How would you monks of today resolve it?"
Tiantong Hua took up the words of various masters and said: Xuansha said, "Whether great or small, this venerable one does not even know how to take charge for himself;
he merely follows along with the coarse woolen cloth. Xuangjue questioned him, saying, "Tell me, did it strike home or not? This is using a shrimp to fish for a turtle.
Fenyang offered a different version, saying, "Knowing that you would not begrudge [the truth], he takes the wrong for the right. Xuedou said, "He acts..."

The King of the House is naturally present. Drawing water and setting fire—Cuiyan Zhi said, "At that time, when the King raised his sword and the Lion stretched its neck, if someone had been able to offer counsel at such a moment, would they have succeeded?
To this day, no one has resolved this public case. How will you monks resolve it now? Do not try to tell dreams. Bajiao said:
Selling jewels and bumping into a blind Persian; this is the crime of slandering others. Langya said:
"Kashmir possesses a fine sword, but alas, the sword has no eyes. The Venerable One possesses a fine lion, yet it cannot even turn back to look."
"Drawing the bow after the bandits have passed. He further said, "This group of fellows has been completely exterminated by this mountain monk.
Do you still see the Honored One Siṃha? Suddenly he picked up his staff, struck once, and said, "One cultivates the person and is careful in conduct for fear of bringing shame upon one's ancestors.
Huanglong Xin said, "I, Huanglong, wish to question Xuedou: since you are an adept, [how do you explain this]?"
The King asked, "For what reason did his arm fall off? Jingshan Hongdao said, "Alas, Master Meng, you have gone off in such a manner!
Gufeng’s profound verse says: Originally a man of the mountains, I love to speak of mountain talk. In the fifth month, I sell the pine breeze.
"Among humans, there is likely no one of such price. Yongming’s verse says: "The Venerable One’s principle is not erroneous;
Xuansha’s words are most extraordinary. His head fell following the blade’s edge; both sides differ by no more than a hair’s breadth. Huankan said: "How great and small is Yongming!
He has formed the views of a scholastic master (zaizhu) and has rashly intruded upon Prajñā."
▲ The twenty-fifth patriarch, Varsaganya (婆舍斯多), was a native of Kaśmīra. His family name was Brahmin; his father was named Śāntacaryā (寂行) and his mother, Nityasukha (常安樂).
Initially, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword and subsequently became pregnant. Upon his birth, her left hand remained in a fist.

He encountered the Venerable Siṃha (師子尊者), who transmitted the Dharma to him (the account of which is found in the "Chapter on Siṃha"). Later, he traveled to Central India, where King Kaniṣka (迦勝) offered him formal worship.

He made offerings. There was a non-Buddhist teacher who venerated the Selfless One (*anātman*). Previously, he had also been honored and respected by the king. Now, he sought to debate before the king in hopes of prevailing.
The Patriarch held himself in high esteem and said to him, "I understand silent debate; it does not rely on verbal expression. The other asked, "Who shall know who wins or loses?
The Patriarch replied, "We do not contend over winning or losing; we seek only the truth of the meaning. The other asked, "What do you take to be the meaning? The Patriarch—

[The monk] said, "I take 'no-mind' (wúxīn) to be the meaning. The Patriarch said, "Since you have no mind, how can you attain the meaning? The monk replied, "When I speak of 'no-mind,' it is a name, not the meaning.
The Patriarch said, "When you speak of 'no-mind,' it is a name, not the meaning; when I speak of 'non-mind' (fēixīn), it is the meaning, not the name.
The monk asked, "If it is the meaning, not the name, who is able to discern the meaning? The Patriarch said, "Your name is not the meaning; this..."

"What is the name of this name? he asked. The outsider replied, "It is called 'the nameless' for the purpose of distinguishing what is not a meaning. The Patriarch said, "Since the name is not a name, the meaning is also not a meaning.
That which distinguishes is itself a name; what, then, would it distinguish? Thus they exchanged questions and answers fifty-nine times.

The outsider was left speechless and submitted in faith. Miaoxi said: "Vasishtha, why such distress? At that time, had you seen him say, 'I request the Master to discuss in silence without relying on words,' you should have immediately said, 'The meaning has fallen.'"

"Is there now anyone who can engage in debate with Miaoxi in silence? Or perhaps a monk might come forward and say, 'The meaning has fallen into error. I know you are making your living inside a ghost cave!
At that moment, the Master suddenly turned his face north, joined his palms, and sighed deeply, saying, "My teacher, the Venerable Siṃha, meets with hardship today; this is truly lamentable.
He then took leave of the King and traveled south, eventually hiding in the mountains and valleys of Southern India. There, King Tiande welcomed him and provided for him with offerings.
The king had two sons. The elder was named Deśeṇa (德勝); he was fierce and violent, yet his physical vigor was abundant. The younger was named Amṛtodana (不如蜜多);

he was gentle and mild, yet constantly afflicted by illness and suffering. The king questioned a venerable elder, who explained the matter in terms of cause and effect; the king received this with reverence and faith.

There was a master of incantations who harbored resentment toward the grandfather; he placed poison in the grandfather’s food. The grandfather knew of it but ate it nonetheless, whereupon the sorcerer himself instead suffered the effects of the poison.
He then went forth under the Patriarch. Sixty years later, Emperor De-sheng ascended the throne;

deluded by the teachings of non-Buddhist paths, he interrogated the Patriarch, saying, "The Venerable Siṃha was already subjected to the persecution of the King of Kaśmīra; for what reason did he transmit the Dharma?

The Patriarch brought out the *saṃghāṭī* robe transmitted from the Venerable Siṃha and showed it to Sheng. Sheng ordered it to be burned; as the firewood was consumed, the robe emitted light of five colors.
It remained as before. Only then did Śūra repent and pay his respects. Initially, Śūra had wished to suppress the Venerable One; thus, he imprisoned Maitrī who went to offer counsel.
Now, having released Maitrī, she subsequently requested ordination. The Patriarch asked, "If you wish to leave the household life, for what purpose do you do so?
Maitrī replied, "If I were to leave the household life, I would not act for that purpose. The Patriarch said, "Not so."
"For what purpose? Maitreya replied, "Not for worldly affairs. The Patriarch asked, "Then for what purpose? Maitreya replied, "For the sake of Buddha-affairs.
The Patriarch said, "The Prince’s wisdom has reached the heavens; surely it is the descent of various sages. You must ordain him and lead him forth from the household life."
He attended the Patriarch for six years. Later, he received full ordination within the royal palace; at the moment of the *karmavācanā*, the earth shook violently.
Thereupon, the Patriarch bestowed upon him the verse of the transmission of the Dharma, saying: "The Sage spoke of knowledge and vision; within the objective realm, there is neither right nor wrong.

I have now realized true nature; there is neither the Path nor principle. After Rāhulamitra had received the verse, he asked, "May this robe be transmitted as well? The Patriarch said, "This robe is for..."

Because it was difficult [to transmit otherwise], he provisionally used the robe as a seal of verification. Your body, however, encountered no such difficulties; your transformative influence spread throughout the ten directions—why then rely on the transmission of a robe?
It is better to pay homage to the *Amṛtā* (Nirvāṇa). The Patriarch manifested spiritual transformations and burned himself with the fire of samādhi.

The śarīra remained level with the ground, reaching a height of one chi. King De-sheng built a stupa to enshrine them. This was the year of Yǒu (the 3rd year of Tàining, during the reign of Emperor Míng of the Eastern Jin).

This was the year [of his passing]. The *Chuanfa ji* (Record of the Transmission of the Dharma) states: The Patriarch leaped into the void and manifested eighteen transformations. He emitted a great radiance that illuminated heaven and earth.
Then, amidst the air, he transformed into fire and consumed himself. A rain of śarīra fell, yet they did not touch the ground. The assembly used their robes...
He received him with his robe-sleeve. Furthermore, it is said that the Master was also named Bharadvāja, and also named Bharadvala.
These two names, translated into Chinese, mean "Separate Industry Spring Assembly. Initially, in a royal garden in India, there was a spring whose water was so hot it could not be touched.
King Kṛkin asked the Master about this, and the Master replied: "The heat of the spring arises from three causes: first, there are hot stones beneath it; second..."

There are three types of karmic spirits. This is a case of such a spirit. Because [the practitioner] burned incense and performed repentance by a spring, a spirit appeared after a short while to express gratitude for his deliverance. After seven days, the spring became clear and cool as it was before.
For this reason, it is called by two names in Central India and Northern India.
▲ The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulamitra, was of the Kṣatriya caste and a prince of South India.
After attaining the Dharma, he traveled to East India. Its king, Drḍha, followed the non-Buddhist teacher Dīrghanakha the Brāhmaṇa.

When the Patriarch arrived, the king asked, "For what purpose have you come, Master? He replied, "To deliver sentient beings. The king asked, "By what Dharma do you deliver them? He replied, "Each..."
Inferring by analogy with his own kind, the Brahmin immediately manifested a great mountain atop the Patriarch’s head, its momentum pressing down.

The Patriarch pointed at it, and the mountain suddenly shifted to rest upon the heads of the assembly. Again, he pressed the ground with his hand; the earth shook, and the five hundred non-Buddhists were all unable to remain standing.
The Brahmin was struck with fear and prostrated himself in repentance. The Patriarch again pressed the ground, and the earth became still; he then pointed at the mountain.
Shanmei. On another day, the King prepared a great vegetarian feast and assembled various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas). He earnestly invited the Patriarch to attend the gathering.

Initially, the Patriarch was unwilling to go, but knowing that the site of the assembly was about to collapse, he went nonetheless. The King said, "Master, were you willing to come? The Patriarch replied, "I did not come for the sake of receiving offerings;
I came to save those from death. This place has already become a dragon’s lair; it will collapse in an instant. The King was terrified. And so...
The multitude was like a high plateau; when they looked back at the ground where they had stood, it had already become a deep, bottomless pool. The King’s reverence and faith increased further.
The Master expounded the Dharma for him, saying, "In your kingdom there shall be a sage who will succeed to my Dharma.

Previously, in East India, there was the son of a Brahmin, twenty years of age, who had lost both parents in childhood and whose name and lineage were unknown; he sometimes called himself "Adorned with Necklaces" (Yingluo), and others addressed him as such.
He was thus named Yingluo (Girdle) Boy. He went about begging from house to house in the villages. When someone asked him why he walked so hurriedly, he would say, "Why do you walk so slowly?
When asked what his surname was, he would say, "It is the same as yours. No one could fathom this. One day, the King and the Patriarch were traveling out together in the same carriage.
Yingluo prostrated himself before them, and the Patriarch said, "Do you remember past events? Yingluo replied:
"I recall that in a past kalpa, I lived together with my teacher. My teacher expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, while I expounded the profound *Sūtras*.
Today’s events are surely in accord with our past causes. The Patriarch looked at the King and said, "This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Hereafter, two more shall appear: one will transform the southern region of India, and the other will have his karmic affinity in China for nine years."
He returned once more to this region. Because of his past causes, he was named Prajñātāra.

The verse of entrusting the Dharma says: "The treasury of the true nature of the mind has neither beginning nor end; responding to conditions to transform sentient beings, it is expediently called 'wisdom'.
Having entrusted the Dharma, he took leave of the king, saying: "My work of transformation is finished; I shall now return to nirvana. I pray that you, O King, [abide] in the Supreme Vehicle."
Without forgetting his external protectors, he returned to his original seat. His manifested form was like the sun; after a short while, he again displayed eighteen miraculous transformations.
He emitted the fire of samādhi to self-immolate, raining down golden śarīra relics. The King enshrined them within a golden stupa.
This was the year Wuzi, the thirteenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
▲ The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India.
After attaining the Dharma, he traveled to Southern India, where the king, named Gandhāra, honored and made offerings to him with the utmost reverence.

Prajñātāra’s realization surpassed that of his contemporaries, and the king further bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. At that time, the king had three sons: Candravairocana, Guṇavairocana, and Bodhi.
Rāma was a bodhisattva of the later period. His grandfather, wishing to test what he had attained, took the pearls he had been given as an offering and asked the three princes:
"These pearls are perfectly round and luminous; is there anything that can equal them? Candracchāya and Guṇaprabha both replied, "Among the seven treasures, these are the most honored;
truly, nothing surpasses them. Bodhi, however, said, "These are merely worldly treasures; they are not sufficient to be considered supreme among all treasures."
The Dharma-jewel within is supreme. This is the light of the world, yet it is not sufficient to be supreme. Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is the illumination of the world, yet it is not sufficient to be supreme. Among all illuminations, the illumination of the mind is supreme.
This radiance of the jewel cannot illuminate itself; it must rely upon the light of wisdom to discern it. Once this has been discerned, one immediately knows it to be such.
A jewel. Once one knows it is a jewel, one then clarifies its preciousness. If one clarifies its preciousness, the treasure is not precious in itself;
if one discerns the jewel, the jewel is not a jewel in itself. That a jewel is not a jewel in itself means that it must rely upon the "jewel of wisdom" to discern the worldly jewel.
That a treasure is not precious in itself means that it must rely upon the "treasure of wisdom" to clarify the Dharma-treasure. Thus, when the teacher possesses the Way, that treasure is...
[The Master] manifested [himself]. "Sentient beings possess the Way; the jewel of the mind is likewise so. The Patriarch praised his eloquence and wisdom, and then asked again:
"Among all things, what thing is without marks? He replied: "Among all things, non-arising is without marks. He asked again:
"Among all things, what thing is the highest? He replied: "Among all things, the self of man is the highest. He asked again: "Among all things..."
"What is the greatest of all things? He replied, "Among all things, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the greatest.

The Patriarch knew he was a vessel for the Dharma, but as the time had not yet arrived, he remained silent and mingled with the crowd. (Miaoxi said: "Your reasoning is excellent. I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
When King Xiangzhi grew weary of the world and passed away, the multitude wailed and lamented; only Bodhidhara entered meditative absorption before the coffin and emerged after seven days.
He then followed his patriarch to seek ordination. Once he had received full precepts, the patriarch told him:

"The Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa; thus it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: 'In the mind-ground, all seeds are born;
through conditions, they again give rise to principles. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; when the flower blooms, the world arises. The patriarch then transmitted [the dharma] to him.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he immediately rose from his seat and extended his left and right hands, each emitting twenty-seven rays of light that shone brilliantly in five colors.
He then leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and consumed himself with fire.

Śarīra relics fell like rain from the sky, and the great assembly erected a stupa to collect and make offerings to them. This was in the first year of the Daming era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, the Dingyou year.
It was also thus.
Once, while Master Nanyue was attending a vegetarian feast at the invitation of the King of East India, the King asked, "Everyone here is reciting sutras; why is it that you alone do not recite?
The Master replied, "When this poor monk exhales, he does not follow external conditions; when he inhales, he does not dwell within the aggregates or realms."
Constantly turning such sutras as these, numbering hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of scrolls—not merely one or two scrolls.

Sù (to go upstream against the current); Shèn (the second tone, zhèn; a woman’s pregnancy); Zhài (the second tone, zhài; consumption/disease);
Qū (the first tone, qū; same as 祛); Suì (the fourth tone, ruì; the awn of grain); Chēng (an ancient form of the character 稱); Lǚ and Tàn (the first tone, dōu; and the fourth tone, sōu).
*The Record of Pointing at the Moon*, Scroll Four.
Regarding the Patriarch of the Eastern Land, the First Patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma: he was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
His clan was Kṣatriya, and his original name was Bodhitāra. Later, from the Venerable Prajñātāra, he...

The Venerable One said to him, "Regarding the various dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery (*pramāṇa*). Since *dharma* carries the meaning of 'thorough penetration,' you should be named Dharmatrata. Consequently, he changed his name to that of the present.

The Patriarch asked the Venerable One, "To which country shall you go to perform the Buddha-work? The Venerable One replied, "Although you have attained the Dharma, you must not yet travel far. Stay for now in South India.

Seventy-six years after my passing, you should go to China (*Zhendan*) and administer the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of superior capacity. Be careful not to travel too far; you would decline under the sun there. The Patriarch further remarked, "There is a Great Being there who is capable of being a vessel for the Dharma."

"No. Will there be obstacles for a thousand years to come? The Master replied: "In the regions you shall convert, those who attain Bodhi will be beyond counting. More than sixty years after my parinirvāṇa, that land will face a calamity;

the waters will surge and spread, but you shall subdue them through your own virtue. When you reach the South, do not remain there. They value only worldly achievements and do not perceive the principles of the Buddha. Even if you go there, you must not stay long. He then spoke this verse: "Traveling along the road, one crosses water and again encounters sheep;

Alone and weary, one silently traverses the river. At sunset, how pitiable are the pair of elephants and horses! Two young cassia trees flourish for a long time to come. He was asked again: "What further events will occur after this? The Master replied: "From now on, after one hundred and fifty years, there will be minor difficulties. Listen..."

My prophecy is as follows. A verse says: "Though auspicious within the mind, it is ominous without; the name of the monastery below the stream is not appropriate. Because of encountering a venomous dragon, a martial son shall be born; suddenly meeting a small mouse, there will be eternal stillness. He asked again, "What will happen after this? The man replied, "Two hundred and twenty years hence, one shall see a person beneath the forest who shall attain the fruit of the Way.

Listen to my prophecy: 'Though China is vast, there is no other path; it must rely on the feet of descendants to travel. The golden rooster knows how to hold a single grain of millet, offering sustenance to the Arhat monks of the ten directions.

He further expounded various verses, all of which were premonitions regarding the flourishing and decline of the Buddhist teachings, as recorded in detail in the *Baolin Zhuan* and the *Shengzhou Ji*. The Patriarch respectfully received these teachings and served diligently for four [years].
Ten years passed until the Venerable One passed away, whereupon [Buddhabhadra] proceeded to propagate the teachings in his own country. At that time, there were two masters:
the first named Buddhadasa and the second named Buddhasanta. Originally, they had studied together with their teacher, Buddhabhadra, in the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) meditative contemplations.
Having encountered the Venerable Prajñāpāramitā, Buddhadasa abandoned the Hinayana for the Mahayana and propagated the teachings alongside his master;

they were then known as the "Two Gateways of Ambrosia. Yet Buddhadasa was more preeminent, further dividing his followers into six schools: first, the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇavāda); second, the School of Non-characteristics (Alakṣaṇavāda);
third, the School of Samādhi and Wisdom (Samādhiprajñāvāda); fourth, the School of Preceptual Practice (Śīlacaryāvāda)... [fifth and sixth schools omitted].
The five schools of the Non-Attainment (Anupalabdhi) and the sixth school of Quiescence (Śānti) each clung to their own interpretations and separately developed their sources of transformation.
The Patriarch sighed deeply and said, "If even one of those teachers has already fallen into the tracks of an ox, how much more so for those who have fragmented [the truth] into six schools?

If I do not eliminate this, they will remain forever entangled in false views. Having spoken, he subtly manifested his supernatural power and went to the place of the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa), where he asked: "One..."

"What is the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena? Among the assembly, there was an elder named Sarabha who replied, "That which does not mutually interchange among all characteristics is called the true nature.

The Patriarch said, "If that which does not mutually interchange among all characteristics is called the true nature, by what means would it be determined? He replied, "Among all characteristics, there is truly no fixed determination. If...

[The monk] said, "If all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not fixed, what is it that is called 'real'? The Patriarch said, "All characteristics are not fixed; this is precisely what is called the 'characteristic of reality' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

You yourself are not fixed right now—how then could you attain it? The monk said, "My statement that they are 'not fixed' does not refer to characteristics themselves; rather, it refers to the meaning of those characteristics, which is likewise so.
The Patriarch said, "Your statement that they are 'not fixed' should be the characteristic of reality. Because it is fixed by means of non-fixation, it is not [merely] the characteristic of reality."

[The Master] asked about the mark (*lakṣaṇa*). He replied, "Since concentration is not fixed, it is not the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Because it is known that 'I' am not [the self], it is unfixed and unchanging.

The Patriarch said, "If you are now unchanging, how can it be called the true mark? That which has already changed and passed away—the same principle applies to its meaning. He replied, "Unchanging must exist;
because of whether it exists or does not exist, the true mark changes, thereby establishing its meaning. The Patriarch said, "The true mark is not..."
"Transformation. Transformation is not reality. Within existence and non-existence, what can be called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?

Śāvala knew that the Holy Master had attained profound liberation and reached the depths of understanding; he then pointed his finger at the void and said, "This is a mark of existence in the world, yet it is also capable of being empty.
Can this body of mine become like this? The Patriarch replied, "If you understand the true mark, you will see that there is no mark. If...
"Having realized that it is not a mark, its form is likewise so. Within form, one does not lose the essence of form; within the absence of marks, one is not obstructed by existence.

If one can understand it thus, this is called the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). When the assembly heard this, their minds became clear and bright; they paid homage with reverence and accepted it in faith.
The Patriarch suddenly vanished from sight and went to the school of the School of Formlessness (Nirābhāsa), where he asked: "You speak of 'formlessness'."
"How do you verify this? Among the assembly was one named Pratītya, who replied, "I clarify formlessness because the mind does not manifest.
The Patriarch said, "If your mind does not manifest, how can you clarify it? He replied, "I clarify formlessness because the mind neither grasps nor rejects.
At the very time of clarification, there is no one who clarifies. The Patriarch said, "Regarding all that exists and does not exist, your mind neither grasps nor rejects."
Furthermore, there is no "that which is to be attained," because all clarity is absent. He said, "Even when entering the Buddha-samādhi, there is nothing to be attained;

how much more so for one who seeks to know that which is signless? The Patriarch said, "Since you do not even know the signs, who speaks of existence or non-existence? There is still nothing to be attained."
"What do you call samādhi? He replied, "I speak of non-realization. Since there is nothing to be realized in realization, it is not samādhi; therefore, I speak of samādhi.
The Patriarch said, "If it is not samādhi, what should it be called? Since you have not realized anything, what is there to realize in non-realization?"
When Boluoti heard the Patriarch’s analysis, he immediately awakened to his original mind. He prostrated in gratitude to the Patriarch and repented for his past errors.
The Patriarch prophesied, saying: "You shall attain the fruit; you will realize it before long. There is a demon in this country; you shall subdue him before long.
Having spoken, he suddenly vanished. Boluoti went to the abode of Dinghui Zong and asked: "In your study of concentration and wisdom, are they one or two? He—
Among the assembly was one named Brahmadatta, who replied, "This concentration and wisdom of mine are neither one nor two.

The Patriarch asked, "Since they are neither one nor two, why are they called 'concentration' and 'wisdom'? He replied, "In concentration it is not concentration; in wisdom it is not wisdom. One is not one, and two is also not two.
The Patriarch said, "If in oneness there is no oneness, and in duality there is no duality, and since they are neither concentration nor wisdom, then by what..."
"What are concentration and wisdom? He replied, "They are neither one nor two. Concentration and wisdom can know; that which is neither concentration nor wisdom is likewise so.
The Patriarch said, "Since wisdom is not concentration, how then can it know? As for 'neither one nor two,' who is concentrated and who is wise?
When Pu-lan-tuo heard this, his doubts were dissolved like ice. He went to the fourth master, Jie-xing-zong, and asked, "What is called..."
"Precepts. What is meant by 'practice'? Regarding these precepts and practice, are they one or two? A worthy man among that assembly replied, "One is two, and two are one;
both are produced from them. Relying on the teaching without defilement—this is called the practice of the precepts. The Patriarch said:
You say that you rely on the teachings, yet this is precisely what constitutes defilement. Since both [the internal and external] are refuted, how can you claim to rely on the teachings?

These two are contradictory; they fall short of actual practice and are neither clear internally nor externally. How, then, can they be called precepts? He replied: "I possess both the internal and the external.
Once he has fully understood this and attained thorough penetration, it is itself the practice of the precepts. If one speaks of contradiction, then both are both right and wrong. Thus it is said:

"Pure! This is precisely precept; this is precisely practice. The Patriarch said: "Both 'is' and 'is not'—how can you speak of purity? Since you have attained penetration, why discuss 'internal' and 'external'?
Upon hearing this, the worthy man felt ashamed and submitted. He went to the school of Wudeng (No-Attainment) and asked:
"You speak of 'no-attainment. In no-attainment, what is there to attain? Since there is nothing to be attained, there is also no attainment of attainment. Among that assembly was one named Bao.
Jing said, "I say there is no attainment; it is not that non-attainment is attained. I shall speak of the attainment of attainment: non-attainment is itself attainment.

The Patriarch said, "If attainment is already non-attainment, then attainment is also non-attainment. Since you speak of the attainment of attainment, what is attained by this attainment of attainment?

He replied, "To see attainment as non-attainment—this non-attainment is itself attainment. If one sees non-attainment, it is called the attainment of attainment. The Patriarch said, "Since attainment..."

"It is non-attainment. To attain attainment is to have no attainment. Since there is nothing to be attained, what could possibly be attained? Upon hearing this, Baojing was instantly freed from the net of doubt.
He went to the abode of Jijing and asked, "What is meant by 'quiescence' (jijing)? Within this Dharma, what is it that is still and what is it that is quiescent?
Among the assembly, a venerable elder replied, "This mind is unmoving; this is called 'quiescence. Regarding all phenomena, there is—"
[The opponent] said, "Defilement is what we call 'quiescence'. The Patriarch said, "If the fundamental mind were not inherently still, one would need to rely upon quiescence.

Since it is fundamentally still from the beginning, what use is there for quiescence? He replied, "All phenomena are fundamentally empty; because they are empty of emptiness, within that emptiness of emptiness, we therefore name it 'quiescence'.

The Patriarch said, "If even emptiness is already empty, then all phenomena are likewise so. Quiescence is without mark; what is there to be stilled, and what is there to be quieted? He [the opponent]—
Upon hearing the instructions of his teacher, the Venerable One attained sudden and complete enlightenment. Thereupon, the six groups of disciples all vowed to take refuge in him.

His transformation spread throughout Southern India, and his fame resounded across the five regions of the Indian subcontinent. For sixty years, he delivered immeasurable multitudes. Later, he encountered King Vikramāditya, who intended to destroy the Buddha-dharma;
this king was actually the nephew of [the Venerable’s] grandfather. Out of compassion for him, the Venerable wished to dispel his ignorance, and the six groups of disciples likewise...
Each thought to himself, "The Buddha-Dharma is in peril; what means will our Master employ to rescue it? The Patriarch perceived their thoughts from afar and responded by snapping his fingers.

The six disciples all heard it and said, "This is the sound of our Master’s seal of faith. They all went to where the Patriarch was. The Patriarch said, "A single film obscures the sky; who shall cut it away?
Xiangzong Zongsheng stepped forward, intending to act. The Patriarch said, "Though you possess eloquence and wisdom,"

"Your power of the Way is not yet complete; for the time being, you have no affinity with the King. Zongsheng took his leave of the Patriarch and eventually arrived at the King's palace, where he expounded the essentials of the Dharma at length.
The King asked, "Regarding what you now understand, where does that Dharma reside? Zongsheng replied, "Just as Your Majesty governs and transforms the people, it should accord with the Way.
As for the Way possessed by Your Majesty, where does that Way reside? The King said, "The Way I possess is intended to eliminate heterodox teachings. You..."

"Regarding all dharmas, whom do you intend to subdue? The Patriarch did not rise from his seat; he knew in advance that the proponent’s thesis was superior and that the opponent would fall into error.

He summoned Prajñākaragupta and said, "Since your thesis is superior and you have not followed my instructions, you shall be defeated in debate with the King. Go quickly to rescue him! Prajñākaragupta said, "I pray you lend me your supernatural power.
As soon as he had spoken, clouds rose from beneath his feet, and he mounted them to appear before the King. Just then, the King was questioning the proponent.
Śaṅghabhadra was suddenly startled upon seeing him and forgot what he had intended to ask. He looked at Upagupta and said, "Is he who comes through the air right or wrong?
Upagupta replied, "I am neither wrong nor right; rather, I come as both right and wrong. If the King’s mind were right, I would be neither wrong nor right.
Although the King was struck with wonder and amazement, his arrogance was still burning fiercely, and he immediately banished Śaṅghabhadra. Upagupta said:
"Since Your Majesty possesses the Way, why do you banish śramaṇas? Although I have no understanding, I pray that Your Majesty will put me a question.
The King asked angrily, "What is this Buddha? Dazhu replied, "To see one's nature is to be the Buddha. The King asked, "Does the Master see your own nature?
Dazhu replied, "I see my Buddha-nature. The King asked, "Where does this nature reside? Dazhu replied, "The nature resides in its functioning. The King asked, "What is this functioning?"
[The King] said, "I do not see it now. Vimalakīrti said, "It is manifesting its activity right now; it is simply that you yourself do not see it. The King asked, "Is it present within me?
Vimalakīrti said, "If you were to employ it, there would be nothing that is not it. If you were not to employ it, its essence would be difficult to perceive.
The King asked, "When it is being employed, in how many places does it appear? Vimalakīrti said, "When it appears, it has eight locations. Your Majesty..."
He said, "The eight manifestations—please speak of them for me. Pāṭaliputra then spoke in verse: "In the womb, it is the body; in the world, it is the person.
In the eye, it is called seeing; in the ear, it is called hearing. In the nose, it discerns fragrance; in the mouth, it engages in discourse."
Held in the hand, it grasps; moved by the foot, it runs. It manifests everywhere, encompassing all buddha-fields, yet when withdrawn, it is contained within a single minute atom.
Those who recognize it know it to be Buddha-nature; those who do not recognize it call it the vital spirit (*prāṇa*). Upon hearing this verse, the King’s mind was immediately awakened.
He repented his former errors and inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. (Miaoxi said: "I now dare to ask everyone: which is the Buddha-nature? Which is the vital spirit?
The King further asked Bodhidharma, "Who is your teacher? Bodhidharma replied, "The Great King’s uncle, Bodhidharma.

Upon hearing this, the King immediately commanded his attendants to welcome the Patriarch to the royal palace. The Patriarch performed repentance for the King’s past transgressions; when the King heard this, he wept.
He declined. Following the imperial decree, Zongsheng was sent back to his country. A close attendant remarked, "When Zongsheng was banished, he already cast himself from a cliff.

The Master said, "Sheng is still alive; if we summon him, he will surely come. When Sheng was first subjected to the banishment, he felt ashamed that he could not rectify the King, and so he threw himself from a perilous precipice.
Suddenly, a divine being caught him with his hands and placed him upon a rock. Sheng said, "I am unworthy..."
"Śramaṇa, you ought to take the True Dharma as your master. You were unable to suppress the king’s transgressions; for this reason, you have cast away your body and reproached yourself.
What aid can the spirit provide? We pray that you will reveal the reason. Thereupon, the divine being spoke a verse, saying:

"The Master lived for a hundred years, yet at eighty he committed a transgression. Because he drew near to the Most Honored One, he cultivated his practice and entered the Way. Although he possessed but little wisdom,"
O Wisdom! You have harbored much self and other; toward the various worthies you have encountered, you have never once given rise to reverence.
For twenty years your merit has been such that your mind has not attained tranquility. Because of your cleverness and arrogance, you have come to this state.

That you have received the King’s lack of respect is a constant reminder that such is the fruit of your actions. From now on, do not be negligent; before long you shall achieve wondrous wisdom. May all the sages remain present.
The mind is like this; the Tathāgata is also thus. When Śrīśruta heard the verse, he was delighted and subsequently sat in quiet meditation within a mountain cave.
At that time, the King sent a messenger into the mountains to summon Śrīśruta. The Patriarch asked the King, "Do you know that Śrīśruta has come? The King replied, "I do not yet know.

The Patriarch said, "He will come only upon being summoned a second time. When the messenger reached the mountain, Śrīśruta took his leave; indeed, it was only after being summoned a second time that he arrived. The Patriarch then turned his thoughts toward the East.
Regarding the land of China: the Buddha prophesied that during the final five hundred years, the lamp of Prajñā-wisdom would spread its light there.
He consequently entrusted his disciple Amoghavajra to remain in India to transmit the Dharma, while he himself traveled to China. Thereupon, he took leave of the Patriarch’s stupa.
Parting from his fellow students, he said to the King, "Diligently cultivate pure deeds; I shall return in nineteen years.

The Patriarch sailed across the vast ocean for three full cycles of winter and summer before reaching the South Sea. This was indeed the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, the *gengzi* year, on the twenty-first day of the ninth month.
Xiao Ang, the Prefectural Governor of Guangzhou, received him with full ceremony and provided offerings, subsequently submitting a memorial to Emperor Wu.
The Emperor dispatched an envoy with a formal decree to invite him. On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived in Jinling.

The Emperor asked, "Since I ascended the throne, I have built temples, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond count. What merit do these deeds possess? The Master replied, "None at all. The Emperor asked, "Why is there no merit?
The Master said, "These are merely the minor fruits of the realms of humans and devas; they are tainted (*sāsrava*)."
...the cause [of this]. Like a shadow following a form, though it exists, it is not real. The Emperor asked, "What is true merit? The Patriarch said, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect;
its essence is inherently empty and still. Such merit is not sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked again, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?
The Patriarch said, "Vast emptiness—there is no 'sage' here. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? The Patriarch—
He replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not understand. Xuedou’s verse says:
"The Noble Truths are vast and open; how can one distinguish the mark? When asked, 'Who is this facing me? he still said, 'I do not know.
From this, he crossed the river in secret; how could he avoid the thorns that grew? The whole nation pursued him, but he would not return; for a thousand..."
"Empty for all eternity, yet we remember each other. Cease this remembering! When the pure wind pervades the earth, what limit can there be?
Looking left and right, he said, "Is there a patriarch here? Call him forth to wash the old monk’s feet.
Another record states that the Emperor later raised this question to Master Zhigong. The Master replied, "Your Majesty, do you recognize this man? The Emperor said, "No."
[When Emperor Wu asked about his own consciousness,] the Master said, "This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara who transmits the Buddha’s mind-seal.

The Emperor regretted his words and wished to dispatch an envoy to invite him back. The Master said, "Do not speak of sending one envoy; even if the entire nation went, he would not deign to take notice.
Yuanwu Keqin said: "Emperor Wu said, 'I do not recognize it. Now tell me, is this the same as what Bodhidharma spoke of, or is it different?"

It seems so, yet it is not so. Many people misunderstand this, saying that Dharma’s previous response was his own Zen teaching, while Emperor Wu’s subsequent question was directed toward Master Zhigong;
this is merely the "recognition of the known," which has no connection to the matter at hand.
At that time, when Master Zhigong asked such a question, tell me: how would you have answered? Why not?
"A single blow of the staff kills him; thus he is spared from being smeared with delusion. Master Zhigong’s transformation took place in the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era.
A considerable time has passed since then, so this must be a mistaken tradition. I have recorded it here because of Master Qin’s comment.
The Patriarch, knowing that his timing was not yet ripe for harmony, secretly returned north of the Yangtze River on the nineteenth day of this month.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived at Luoyang and took up residence at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. He sat facing a wall, remaining silent throughout the entire day;

no one could fathom him, and thus he was called the "Wall-Gazing Brahmin. There was a monk named Shen Guang who had long resided in the region of Yi and Luo and had extensively studied the scriptures.
He was well-versed in a multitude of texts and excelled at discussing the profound principles of the mysteries (*xuanli*). He often sighed, saying:

"The teachings of Confucius and Laozi, with their rituals, arts, customs, and regulations, as well as the books of Zhuangzi and the *Yijing*, do not exhaust the wondrous truth. Recently, he heard that the Great Being Bodhidharma was residing at Shaolin.

Thinking that the Ultimate Man was not far off and that he should attain the profound realm, he went to visit the Patriarch to seek his guidance. The Patriarch sat constantly in a meditative posture facing a wall; no instructions were heard. Huike [Guang] himself—

I reflect: In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow, pierce their flesh to provide blood for the hungry, spread their hair to cover the mud, and cast themselves from cliffs to feed tigers.
If the ancients were already like this, what person am I? When the snow fell heavily, Dazhu stood in attendance throughout the night;

by dawn, the accumulated snow had reached his knees, yet he stood with even greater reverence. The Patriarch looked at him and took pity on him, asking: "You have stood in the snow for a long time; what do you seek?"
"What is it? Huiguo asked, weeping with compassion. "I only pray that the Master, out of his great kindness, will open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all classes of beings.

The Patriarch said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort through vast eons; one must be able to perform what is difficult to do and endure what is difficult to endure."
"How can you, with such meager virtue and limited wisdom, harbor such a frivolous and arrogant mind while hoping to attain the True Vehicle? Your diligent toil is in vain.

Upon hearing these words from the Patriarch, Huiguo was inspired; he secretly took a sharp blade, severed his own left arm, and placed it before the Patriarch. The Patriarch knew that he was a vessel for the Dharma.
He then said, "The Buddhas, when first seeking the Way, forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma. You have now severed your arm before me; your request may indeed be granted.
The Patriarch subsequently changed his name to Huìkě and said, "Have you heard the Dharma-seal of the Buddhas?
Huìkě replied, "The Dharma-seal of the Buddhas is not obtained from another person. Huìkě said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to grant it to me."
Huineng said, "I will pacify your mind for you. After a long silence, [the monk] said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unattainable.
Huineng said, "I have finished pacifying your mind for you."
Bazhao Qingyuan said: "When a diamond man rubs the back of a clay man, where is the dharmakāya at that very moment? Yuanwu Keqin said:
"At such a time as this, where is the dharmakāya?"
After nine years had passed, he wished to return to India. He addressed his disciples, saying, "The time has come. You should each speak of what you have attained.
Daofu replied, "As I see it, one does not cling to words and letters, yet does not depart from words and letters, taking them as the functioning of the Way.
The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my skin. Nitzongchi replied, "What I now understand is like that of Ānanda."
He saw the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya; having seen it once, he did not see it again. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my flesh.
Daoyu said, "The four elements are fundamentally empty, and the five aggregates do not exist. In the place where I see, there is not a single dharma to be obtained.
The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my bones. Finally, Huikě prostrated himself and stood in his place. The Patriarch said, "You have obtained my marrow. Thus it was.
Looking toward Huìkě, he told him: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to the Great Being Kāśyapa;
it was passed down through successive entrustments until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and uphold it. I also confer upon you this robe as a token of the Dharma.
Each has its own symbolic significance, which you should understand. Huìkě said, "I beg the Master to explain this further. The Patriarch said:
The inner transmission of the Dharma-seal is used to verify and realize the mind; the outer entrustment of the *kāṣāya* robe is used to establish the fundamental tenets.

Yet in later generations, when times became degenerate, doubts and suspicions arose in competition: "I am a man from the Western Heaven," they would say, while others would say, "You are a native of this land—on what basis did you obtain the Dharma?"

By what means shall this be verified? You shall now receive this robe-transmission dharma. Hereafter, when it is difficult for people to arise [in faith], simply produce this robe along with my dharma-verses to serve as proof;
thus your transformation will be unimpeded. Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, the robe will cease its transmission, while the Dharma will pervade the entire realm of saṃsāra.
At that time, those who clarify the Way will be many, but those who practice the Way will be few; those who expound the principles will be many, but those who penetrate the principles...
Few indeed. There have been more than ten million who have secretly conformed to and secretly realized [the truth]. You must propagate this; do not disparage those who have not yet awakened.
A single thought that turns the faculty [toward the source] is identical to original attainment. Listen to my verse: I originally came to this land To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings.
One flower opens into five petals; The fruiting occurs naturally. The Patriarch further said: "I also have the four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*."
I entrust this to you; it is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground, intended to cause all sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter it.
Since I first arrived here, I have been poisoned five times in total. I once personally went out to test it by placing a stone upon it, and the stone split asunder.

This was because I originally left South India to come to this Eastern Land, where I beheld the land of Zhōngguó (the Red County, Divine State) and saw that it possessed the grand atmosphere of the Mahāyāna. Thus...

"Crossing the seas and traversing the deserts, I have sought a person for the sake of the Dharma. Our meeting has not been harmonious; I was as if dull-witted and taciturn. Now that I have obtained your transmission, my purpose is fulfilled. (A separate record states:

When the Patriarch first resided at Shaolin Temple for nine years, he preached the Dharma for the Second Patriarch, teaching only: "Cease all external conditions; let the internal mind be without breath. Let the mind be like a wall or a screen, and you may enter the Way.

Although Huike explained various aspects of the nature and mind, he never once realized the principle. The Patriarch merely refuted his errors and did not explain the essence of the mind of non-thought. Huike said abruptly, "I have already ceased all conditions. The Patriarch said, "Do not fall into annihilationism.")
