▲The Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, was surnamed Sima. His family had resided for generations in Henei, later migrating to Guangji County in Qizhou.

From birth he was exceptionally gifted; in his youth he admired the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the various gates of liberation appeared to him as if they were the result of past cultivation.
Having inherited the ancestral tradition, he restrained his mind and did not sleep; for sixty years, his side never touched the mat.

In the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he led his disciples to Jizhou. There they encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city, which remained besieged for seventy days without resolution.

As the multitude was filled with terror, the Master took pity on them and instructed them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, the rebels gazed toward the battlements and saw as if there were—
The divine soldiers then said to one another, "There must be an extraordinary person within the city," and they gradually withdrew.
In the year Jia-shen of the Tang Wu-de era, Master Huineng returned to Qichun and resided at Mount Poutou, where disciples gathered like clouds.

One day, he went to Huangmei County and encountered a young boy on the road whose physical features were remarkably refined and unusual for a common child. The Master asked him, "What is your surname?"
The Master replied, "He has a surname, but it is not a permanent surname. The Patriarch asked, "What is his surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Patriarch asked, "Does he have no surname?

He replied, "Because nature is empty, there is none. The Patriarch silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma and immediately dispatched an attendant to his mother’s quarters to request that she allow him to leave the household life.
Because of past karmic conditions, the mother showed no sign of reluctance and eventually consented.
He became a disciple, eventually receiving the transmission of the Dharma and the vestment. A verse says: "The nature of the lotus seed exists; With soil as its cause, the lotus grows.
When the great conditions unite with this nature, That which is born is, in truth, unborn.

In the *Guimao* year of the Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong, drawn to the flavor of the Master’s Way and desiring to behold his dignified bearing, issued an imperial decree for him to come to the capital. The Patriarch submitted a memorial declining the summons three times in succession. However—

On four occasions, the Emperor issued a command through a messenger, saying: "If he does not arise, bring his head here. When the messenger arrived at the mountain and delivered the imperial decree, the Master extended his neck toward the blade;
his countenance remained solemn and composed. The messenger returned and reported these circumstances to the Emperor, who thereafter held him in even greater reverence.
On the fourth day of the intercalary ninth month in the *Xin-hai* year of the Yonghui era of Gaozong, the Master suddenly addressed his disciples with a final admonition, saying: "All dharmas..."

"All have attained liberation. You all must each protect and cherish [this teaching], spreading it into the future. Having spoken these words, he sat peacefully and passed away at the age of seventy-two.
His stūpa was erected at his native mountain. On the eighth day of the fourth month of the following year, the door of the stūpa opened of its own accord;
his physical features remained as they were when alive. Thereafter, his disciples did not dare to close the door again.
▲The Great Master Wuzu Hongren was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. Previously, he had been a "pine-planting practitioner" at Mount Poutou.
He once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, saying, “May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, “You are already old;
even if you were to hear it, would you be able to propagate it widely? If you were to come again, I might yet wait for you. Thereupon, he departed.
He went to the water's edge and saw a young woman washing clothes. He bowed to her and asked, "May I stay the night?
The woman said, "I have parents and brothers; you may go and ask them. He replied, "Very well, I shall do so immediately. The woman nodded her head in agreement, and he turned his horse and departed.
The woman, surnamed Zhou, was the younger daughter of the family. Upon her marriage, she immediately became pregnant. Her parents detested her greatly and cast her out.

Having nowhere else to go, she spent her days spinning for hire in the village and stayed at night beneath a public shelter. After some time, she gave birth to a son; her parents considered this an ill omen.

He was consequently cast into a turbid harbor. When he was seen the following day, he had swum upstream; his physical appearance was bright and clear. Greatly astonished, [the fisherman] lifted him up.
Having reached the age of a young boy, he followed his mother to beg for food, and the villagers called him "The Child Without Surname.

He encountered a wise man who sighed and said, "This child lacks seven marks; he does not equal the Tathāgata. Later, he met Master Xìn and attained the Dharma, succeeding him in spreading the transformation.
At Mount Póutóu, during the Xiánhéng era, there was a lay practitioner surnamed Lú and named Huínéng who came from Xīnzhōu to pay his respects.
The Patriarch asked him, "Where have you come from? Lú replied, "From south of the Ling Mountains. The Patriarch said, "What do you seek? Lú said, "I only seek to become a Buddha.
The Patriarch said, "People of south of the Ling Mountains have no Buddha-nature; how can they become Buddhas? Lú said, "People..."
"In that case, there would be north and south. How could it be so with Buddha-nature? The Master ordered him to join the assembly in manual labor.
Lu said, "My own mind constantly gives rise to wisdom; not departing from its own nature, it is itself the field of merit. I do not know what kind of labor the Master intends for me to perform."
The Patriarch said, "This barbarian has an exceptionally sharp root-nature. Go to the fodder shed.

Lu prostrated himself and withdrew, then entered the rice-hulling workshop and applied himself to labor at the pestle and mortar, working day and night without ceasing for eight months. The Patriarch knew that the time for the transmission had arrived.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The True Dharma is difficult to understand; it must not be taken as a mere matter of recording my words. You should take this as your own responsibility. Each of you, according to your own inclination, compose a verse.
If the meaning of your words accords with the profound essence, then both the robe and the Dharma shall be entrusted to you. At that time, there were more than seven hundred monks in the assembly.
Among them was the Elder Shenxiu, whose learning encompassed both the inner and outer teachings, and whom the multitude revered and looked up to. They all recommended him, saying:
"If it were not for one as venerable and eminent as you, who would dare to face him? Shenxiu, having heard the widespread acclaim of the assembly, no longer reflected further;
he then inscribed a verse upon the wall of the corridor, saying: "The body is a Bodhi tree; / The mind is a stand for a bright mirror.
/ At all times diligently wipe and polish it, / And do not let it gather dust. The Patriarch, while walking about, suddenly saw this verse and knew it was composed by Shenxiu.
He then offered praise, saying: "Those of future generations who rely on this for practice shall likewise attain supreme fruits.

Originally, he had intended for the scholar Lu Chen to paint the *Lengqie* transformation scenes upon the wall; however, upon seeing the inscribed verses, he desisted from painting and instead instructed everyone to recite them.
While Lu was at the millhouse, he suddenly heard the chanting of the verses and asked his fellow students, "What are these passages? His fellow students...
He said, "You do not know. The Master was seeking a successor to the Dharma and had each of you compose a verse expressing your realization. This is the one composed by the Venerable Xiu;
the Master has praised it with deep admiration and will certainly transmit the Dharma and the robe to him. Lu asked, "What does that verse say?"
His fellow student recited it for him. After a long while, Lu said, "It is beautiful indeed, yet it is not yet fully realized.
The fellow student rebuked him, saying, "How could a mediocre person like you know this? Do not utter such delirious words. Lu replied, "Do you not believe me? I wish to respond with a verse."
The fellow student did not answer; they merely looked at each other and laughed. That night, Lu secretly informed a young boy and led him to the corridor.
Holding a candle himself, Lu invited Zhang Riyong, the Regional Inspector, to the side of Xiu’s verse and had him write another verse, which read:
"Bodhi originally has no tree, And the bright mirror is likewise not a stand. From the beginning, there is not a single thing— Where, then, could dust and grime settle? —The Patriarch.
Later, seeing this verse, [Nanquan] asked, "Who composed this? It does not yet reveal the nature. When the assembly heard the Patriarch’s words, they paid it no further heed.
That night, the Patriarch went secretly to the rice-hulling shed and asked, "Is the rice white yet? Lu said, "It is white, but it has not yet been sifted.
The Patriarch struck the pestle three times with his staff; Lu immediately struck the drum three times and entered the room. The Patriarch told him, "The Buddhas..."
He appeared in the world for the sake of one great matter: to guide beings according to their varying capacities.
Thus, there arose the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the teachings of sudden and gradual enlightenment as the gateways of instruction.

Nevertheless, he entrusted the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true *dharmaparyāya*—the Eye-Treasury of the True Dharma—to the preeminent Venerable Mahākāśyapa, who transmitted it in succession for twenty generations.
The eighth generation reached Bodhidharma, who resided in this land. He obtained Master Ke, and the lineage has been inherited down to the present day.
I entrust these Dharma-treasures and the robe transmitted to you; protect them well yourself and do not let them be severed. Listen to my verse:
"When sentient beings come to plant seeds, The fruit arises again according to the ground. Since insentient things have no seeds, they lack nature."

There is also no further birth. Having received [the transmission] while kneeling, Lu asked, "The Dharma rules have now been received; to whom shall the robe be given? The Patriarch said, "In the past, when Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet believe him.
Therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest that he had attained the Dharma. Now that faith has matured, the robe is merely a source of contention.

It shall stop with your person and will not be transmitted further. For the time being, you should remain hidden in seclusion and wait for the right time to go forth and transform others. Thus it was said.
This refers to the person receiving the robe, whose life was like a thread hanging from a string. Lu asked, "Where should I hide? The Patriarch said, "When you meet Hui, stop;
when you encounter Hui, conceal yourself. After Lu had prostrated at his feet, he took the robe and departed. That night he traveled south, and the assembly knew nothing of it.
Thereafter, the Fifth Patriarch no longer ascended the hall to teach. The assembly, filled with doubt and wonder, questioned him. The Patriarch said, "My Way..."
"Go! Why inquire further? He asked again, "Who shall receive the robe and the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "He who is capable shall receive them.

Thereupon, the assembly deliberated that the name of Practitioner Lu was "Neng" (Capable), and they immediately pursued him together. After the Patriarch had transmitted the robe and the Dharma, another four years passed.
In the second year of the Shangyuan era, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "My work is now complete; it is time to depart.
He then entered his room, sat upright, and passed away at the age of seventy-four. His stupa was erected on East Mountain in Huangmei.
Emperor Daizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Daman (Great Fulfillment), and his stupa was named Fayu (Dharma Rain).

Later, when the Song dynasty dispatched its armies to subjugate the region south of the Yangtze River, blood flowed from the Master’s flesh like teardrops; those who understood this sign knew that the Li clan would surely perish.
▲The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was surnamed Lu. His father’s name was Xing, and his mother was Li.
She experienced a wondrous dream, and upon waking, a rare fragrance filled the room. Consequently, she became pregnant and gave birth after six years.

A ray of light ascended into the sky at dawn, and a monk arrived to speak with the Patriarch’s father, saying, "This child should be named Huineng. The father asked, "What does this mean? The monk replied, "Wisdom..."
He bestowed the Dharma as a gift to rescue and aid sentient beings; being capable, he was able to perform the Buddha’s work.

Having finished speaking, he was lost to sight. The Patriarch did not drink his mother’s breast milk; at night, a divine being met him and poured nectar upon him. At the age of three, his father passed away.

His mother lived as a widow, and their family was in extreme poverty. From his youth, he gathered firewood and sold it to support his mother. One day, while carrying firewood through the marketplace, he heard a guest—

While reading the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he reached the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere," and was moved to a profound realization. He asked a guest, "What dharma is this?
The guest replied, "This is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Fifth Patriarch, Master Ren of Mount Dongshan at Huangmei, constantly taught people to recite this sūtra.
Upon hearing these words, the Patriarch was suddenly stirred and resolved to leave home to seek the Dharma; he then begged for it from the guest.

He prepared a year’s worth of provisions for his mother and then took his leave. He traveled directly to Shaoyang Prefecture, where he met the man of noble conduct Liu Zhilüe and formed a friendship with him.
There was also a nun named Wujinzang, who was Zhilüe’s paternal aunt; she had frequently studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The Master listened for a moment and immediately explained its meaning to her. The nun then took up the scroll and asked about the characters. The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize the characters, but I ask you about the meaning.
The nun said, "If you do not even recognize the characters, how can you comprehend the meaning? The Patriarch replied, "The wondrous principle of all Buddhas has nothing to do with written words.
The nun was struck with wonder and amazement; she informed the elders of her village and requested that he reside at Baolin Monastery.
The temple had been abandoned for a long time, yet the fourfold assembly had been repairing it, with people flocking there morning and night until it was suddenly restored as a precious monastery.

Huineng said, "I seek the Great Dharma; what is the use of staying here? He then left it behind and traveled to Huangmei to pay his respects to the Fifth Patriarch. The account of this is found in the chapter on the Fifth Patriarch.
After presenting his verse, he entered the Fifth Patriarch’s quarters at the third watch. The Fifth Patriarch again questioned him regarding his initial realization, saying, "It should be without..."
Upon hearing the words, "The mind arises wherever it dwells," the Patriarch attained great enlightenment. He then addressed the Fifth Patriarch, saying: "All phenomena do not depart from self-nature.
How unexpected that self-nature is fundamentally pure! How unexpected that self-nature is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing!
How unexpected that self-nature is fundamentally complete! How unexpected that self-nature is fundamentally unmoving! How unexpected...

"Performance gives rise to the myriad dharmas. The Fifth Patriarch, knowing that [Huineng] had awakened to his original nature, said to him: "If you do not recognize your own original mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit.
If you recognize your original mind and see your own original nature, you shall be called a Great Man, a Teacher of Gods and Humans, and a Buddha.

He then transmitted the robe and the Dharma to him. (Chan Master Huanglong Xin’s verse says: "The Sixth Patriarch was no great man back then; he asked another to write on the wall while he himself plastered over it. Clearly there was a verse saying 'nothing exists,' yet he accepted from that other family a single alms bowl. Subtle!")

Xì said: "Tell me, is the almsbowl an object or not an object? If you say it is an object, then Old Sīxīn is no true man. If you say it is not an object, what can you do about the almsbowl? Regarding the *Awakening to the Conditions of the Diamond Sūtra*:

In the initial preface to the *Platform Sūtra* by the Lu family, it is stated that the Sixth Patriarch attained awakening upon hearing the sūtra, yet it does not say he reached full realization (*dàchè*) at the point "should abide nowhere" (*yīng wú suǒ zhù*). It merely says he had a realization (*shěng*) upon hearing the sūtra. When he entered the room at the third watch, the Fifth Patriarch wrapped him in his *kāṣāya* so that no one would see him and preached the *Diamond Sūtra* for him;

it was at the passage "should abide nowhere" that he attained great penetration. This is according to the *Zàngběn* (Cang edition) of the *Platform Sūtra*. As for the third watch entry and the Fifth Patriarch’s interrogation on the *Diamond Sūtra*, these words are not recorded in the *Chuándēng lù*. The Fifth Patriarch then sent him away.

When the Patriarch arrived at the Jiuyang Ferry, he ordered the Fifth Patriarch to board the boat. As soon as the Fifth Patriarch did so, the Patriarch took up the oar. The Fifth Patriarch said, "It is I who should ferry you across.

The Patriarch replied, "When one is deluded, the teacher ferries one across; when one has attained awakening, one ferries oneself across. Although 'ferrying' is but a single name, its application differs.

Having been fortunate enough to receive the transmission of the Dharma from my teacher, I have now attained awakening; it is only fitting that I ferry myself across by means of my own nature. The Fifth Patriarch said, "Just so."
"It is so. Hereafter, the Buddha-dharma shall be propagated by you. After paying his respects and taking his leave, the Patriarch traveled south for two months until he reached Mount Dayu.
There, the monk Huiming—formerly a general—accompanied by several hundred men, came seeking to seize the robe and bowl. Huiming was the first to catch up with him;
the Patriarch cast the robe and bowl onto a rock, saying, "This robe is a token of faith; can it be won by force? Huiming attempted to lift it.
The robe and bowl could not move them. He then said, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of robes.

The Patriarch said, "Since you have come for the sake of the Dharma, you should set aside all external conditions and do not give rise to a single thought; I shall speak for you. After a long silence, the Patriarch said:
"Do not think of good; do not think of evil. At this very moment, what is the original face of Elder Ming?
Hearing these words, Huiming attained great enlightenment. He asked again, "Beyond the secret words and secret meanings you have spoken thus far, is there still another secret intent?
The Patriarch said, "That which I have told you is not secret. If you turn back and reflect, the secret is within you."
The border. Huiming said, "Although I was at Huangmei, I truly had not yet realized my own true face.
Now that I have received your instruction, it is like a person drinking water who knows its coldness or warmth for themselves. The practitioner here is now my teacher.
The Patriarch said, "If you are thus, we shall both study under the same master at Huangmei. Guard and uphold this well yourself. Huiming asked again, "Where is Huiming headed now?"
"Where have you gone? The Patriarch replied, "When you meet Yuan, stop; when you encounter Meng, dwell.

Mingli took his leave and returned to the foot of the pass, where he said to the assembly, "We have just traversed steep heights, yet there is no trace of him. We should seek him by another path. Thereupon, the assembly dispersed.
Later, he resided at Mount Meng in Yuanzhou. To avoid his master’s taboo name, he changed his name to Daoming.

After his master arrived at Caoxi, those who were searching for him gradually heard of his whereabouts. He subsequently took refuge among a hunting party in Sihui, where he remained for fifteen years.
From time to time, he preached the Dharma to the hunters as appropriate; the hunters then had him guard their nets.

If anyone captured them, he would release them all. At every mealtime, he would habitually place vegetables into the cauldron where meat was boiling. When questioned about this, he would reply, "I simply eat the vegetables from the edge of the meat.
On the eighth day of the first month in the first year of the Yifeng era, he suddenly felt that the time had come to preach the Dharma.
He accordingly traveled to Faxon Temple in Guangzhou, where he encountered Master Yinzong lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. He took up residence in the temple corridors.
One evening at night, as the wind blew the temple banners, two monks were heard debating. One said, "The banner moves. The other said, "The wind moves.

They argued back and forth without end. The Master said, "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves. It is your mind, O worthy one, that moves. The entire assembly was struck with awe.
Xuefeng said, "The great patriarchs have a dragon's head but a snake's tail; they deserve twenty blows.
As the Venerable Fu was attending him, he gnashed his teeth. Xuefeng said, "Even for me speaking thus, they deserve twenty blows. Miaoxi said:
Do you wish to recognize Elder Fu? When the rhinoceros gazes at the moon, patterns form upon its horns.
Do you wish to recognize Xuefeng? When the elephant is startled by thunder, flowers enter its tusks. Xuedou cites Baoling’s address to the assembly, which says:
"The Patriarch said, 'It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. Since it is neither the banner nor the wind, where does it reside? Someone [asked]: ...
"Act as the host for the Patriarch; come forth and meet with Baling. Xuedou said, "The wind moves, the banner moves.
Since it is wind and banner, where do you place them? If there is anyone who acts as the host for Baling, they too should come forth and meet with Xuedou.
He further composed a verse: "It is not the banner, nor is it the wind. Herein, the patch-robed monk..."
To circulate [this teaching]: crossing a river using a raft is an ordinary matter; charcoal burns on the southern mountain while the northern mountain glows red.
Furthermore: "It is not the wind, nor the banner—where else could it be? This has been picked up and cast aside by those who have newly begun their practice.
Nowadays, these deluded and ignorant Chan practitioners vainly claim that the "mysterious and profound" is the "single foot. Yuwang Puchong’s verse says: "Neither wind, nor banner."

There is no place for attachment. This wind and this banner have no place to cling. A soaring, noble falcon loses its tracks; a golden-maned lion crouching on the ground is thrown into confusion. A-he-he!
Whether you awaken or not, it makes one recall Xie Sanlang, fishing alone with a single line in the rain of the cold river.
Tiantai Shaoyun said: "The skillful means of the ancient sages are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The Patriarch said: "It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is your mind, O virtuous one, that moves. This is the Dharma-gate of the Unsurpassed Mind-Seal.
We are disciples under the Patriarch’s gate; how should we understand the Patriarch’s intent?

Do not say that the wind and banner do not move while your mind moves falsely. Do not say that you do not strike at the wind and banner, but rather grasp the meaning by way of the wind and banner themselves. Do not...
Regarding the phrase "What is it that moves when the wind blows upon the banner? some say: "To clarify the mind by means of objects; one need not recognize the objects themselves.
Others say: "Form is itself emptiness. Still others say: "It is neither the wind nor the banner that moves; one must realize this through wondrous understanding. Such are their interpretations.
What connection does this have with the intent of the Patriarchs? Since such an interpretation is not permitted, how, O Venerable Elders, should you understand it?
If you attain thorough awakening here, what dharma-gate will not be clear?
The skillful means of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas will be fully realized all at once; what further doubt could there be? Therefore, the ancients said:

The Way: one realization brings clarity to a thousand things; one delusion brings confusion to ten thousand. Does the Venerable Master realize this one principle today and yet fail to realize it tomorrow?
The *Chizhengchuan* (Record of Wisdom Realization) quotes a verse from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:

"Due to the attachments of one's own mind, The mind manifests as external objects. What is perceived therein does not exist; Therefore, it is said that 'mind-only' exists. The *Chuan* (Record) says: Cao... [text fragment]
When the Sixth Patriarch was living in seclusion by the creek, he was known as Layman Lu.

He once stayed at a monastery in Guangzhou and was walking in meditation at night when he heard two monks debating whether it was the wind or the banner that moved. One said it was the wind moving; the other said it was the banner moving.

The Sixth Patriarch stepped forward and asked, "How can you allow such common folk to engage in lofty discourse? It is not the wind or the banner that moves; rather, it is the minds of the venerable ones that move."
Chan Master Fākō lived in seclusion on Mount Wutai. Every night he invariably heard a voice calling out, "Fākō! Fākō was troubled by this.
After a long time, he attained self-awakening and said, "All these are the objects of my own mind; how could there be external sounds?
He dispelled them through the Dharma, and thereafter they ceased entirely. As for saying that what one perceives does not exist, it is because of the wind.
Banners depend upon one another; there is no fixed attachment. Because there is no fixed attachment, that which arises through conditions is called "non-arising.
Since the Sixth Patriarch’s teaching on perceiving objects is thus, so too is the realization of the auditory dust (śabda-dhātu) attained in the meditation on emptiness. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says:

"Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the sense-roots are removed, the dust of phenomena vanishes and awakening becomes perfectly pure.
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in silent illumination, it encompasses the void.
Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream-event"—this, he would not believe! Huanki said: "When I was young, I read the poetry of the Song people. 'The wheat waves—how could they..."
The winds swirl and roll; the dewdrops upon the lotus leaves do not form even a single drop. I was filled with joy, thinking this would serve as an excellent commentary on the "Wind and Banner" kōan.
However, upon reading the remarks and expositions of the great masters Xuefeng and Xuedou, I was suddenly disheartened and lost.
Master Hong’s present biography cannot yet be said to have crossed the threshold of these elders.
Yinzong invited the Master to the seat of honor and interrogated him on the profound meanings [of the Dharma].

Seeing that the Patriarch’s words were concise yet logically sound, and did not rely on written texts, Yinzong said, "I have long heard that the robe and the Dharma have come south from Huangmei; could you be the practitioner? The Patriarch replied, "Yes.
Yinzong prostrated himself and requested that the robe and bowl be displayed for the assembly to behold and pay homage to. Yinzong then asked again, "Regarding the entrustment at Huangmei..."
"How do you instruct others? the Patriarch said, "There is no instruction; we only discuss the realization of nature, not meditative concentration or liberation.
Huizong asked, "Why do you not discuss meditative concentration and liberation? The Patriarch said, "Because these two are dualistic dharmas and are not the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha-dharma is the dharma of non-duality. Huizong asked again, "What is the dharma of non-duality of the Buddha-dharma? The Patriarch said:
The Dharma Master expounds the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to clarify Buddha-nature. This is the non-dual dharma of the Buddhas.

As the Bodhisattva Mahāgovinda addressed the Buddha, saying: "Regarding those who have committed the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, or the icchantikas—do they sever their roots of goodness and their Buddha-nature?
The Buddha said: "Roots of goodness are of two kinds: first, the permanent; second, the impermanent. The Buddha...
The nature is neither eternal nor impermanent; therefore, it is not subject to interruption. This is called non-duality. First is the wholesome, and second is the unwholesome;
the Buddha-nature is neither wholesome nor unwholesome—this is called non-duality. As for the aggregates (*skandha*) and the elements (*dhātu*), ordinary beings perceive them as two.
The wise understand that its nature is non-dual; this non-dual nature is itself Buddha-nature. Upon hearing these words, Master Yin Zong joyfully joined his palms.
Master Zhenjing then raised the question of the non-dual Dharma asked by Yin Zong of the Patriarch. The Patriarch replied: "All Zen..."
Virtue. At that time, the small-scale Chan path was already at its midpoint.
In the monastic communities today, most merely discuss meditative concentration, liberation, non-thought, and non-action. Now tell me: which is it—the Sixth Patriarch’s or the present day’s?
If you distinguish them, there will be opposition and compliance; there will be right and wrong. If you do not distinguish them, what then?
If one does not distinguish them, nor discern the heterodox from the orthodox, the Dharma-vehicle of our school will be buried and lost. It is like the roads of the world:
some are direct, some are circuitous; some are perilous, some are easy. Those who travel these paths proceed when they may and stop when they must.
Does the great assembly still recognize the old monk of Letan? After a long silence, he said: "With this profound mind, offer it to the dust."
This is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, Yinzong gathered various eminent and virtuous monks to shave the Patriarch’s hair.
On the eighth day of the second month, he received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Zhiguang at Faxon Temple; the ordination platform there was originally that of the Song dynasty’s Guṇabhadra.
This was established by the Tripitaka Master. The *Record of the Three Baskets* states: "In the future, there shall be an incarnate Bodhisattva who will receive the precepts upon this altar.
Furthermore, at the end of the Liang dynasty, the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha personally planted two Bodhi trees beside the altar and said to the assembly:
"One hundred and twenty years hence, a great Mahāsattva shall expound the Unsurpassed [Dharma] beneath these trees."

He mounted [his vehicle] and delivered immeasurable multitudes. After the Patriarch had received the precepts, he opened the Dharma-gate of Dongshan beneath this tree, as if fulfilling a long-standing covenant.
On the following day, Magistrate Wei requested further instruction. The Master ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying:
"All of you, with pure minds, recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, O good friends, the wisdom of Bodhi and Prajñā..."
Worldly people originally possess this [Buddha-nature] of their own accord; it is only because their minds are deluded that they cannot awaken to it themselves.

They must rely on the guidance of a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to see their nature. You should know that between the foolish person and the wise person, there is originally no difference in Buddha-nature;
it is only because their states of delusion and awakening differ that there are the "foolish" and the "wise. I shall now expound for you the Dharma of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
I shall cause each of you to attain wisdom. Listen with a sincere mind; I will speak for you.

Good friends, worldly people spend their entire days reciting *prajñā* with their mouths, yet they do not recognize the *prajñā* of their own nature. It is like speaking of food without being satiated;
though their mouths only speak of emptiness, they will not see their nature for ten thousand kalpas, and it will ultimately be of no benefit. Good friends, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*...
*Pāramitā* is a Sanskrit term. This means "Great Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore. This must be practiced through the mind; it does not reside in verbal recitation.

If one recites with the mouth but does not practice with the mind, it is like an illusion, a transformation, a dewdrop, or a flash of lightning. If one recites with the mouth and practices with the mind, then mind and mouth correspond.
One's original nature is the Buddha; apart from this nature, there is no separate Buddha. What is meant by *mahā*? *Mahā* means "great."
The measure of the mind is vast and great, like empty space; it has no boundaries, nor does it possess squareness, roundness, largeness, or smallness.

It is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; it has no above or below, no long or short. It is without anger and without joy, without right and without wrong, without good and without evil, and it has neither beginning nor end.
All Buddha-lands are entirely identical to empty space. The wondrous nature of worldly people is fundamentally...

Emptiness. There is not a single dharma that can be apprehended; the self-nature of emptiness is likewise so. Good friend, do not hear my teaching of emptiness and immediately become attached to emptiness.
Above all, do not be attached to emptiness. If you sit in meditation with an empty mind, you will be attached to a state of indeterminate emptiness.
Good friend, the world’s empty space is able to contain the myriad things, their forms and images, the sun, moon, stars, and mountains.
The great earth, rivers, springs, streams, and brooks; grasses, trees, thickets, and forests; evil people and good people; unwholesome dharmas and wholesome dharmas; heavens and hells;
all the great oceans and Mount Sumerus—all these exist within space. The emptiness of the human nature of worldly beings is likewise thus.
Good friend, the self-nature is able to contain the myriad dharmas; it is great. The myriad dharmas reside within the nature of all people.

In the midst [of all things], if one sees both the evil and the good of all people and neither grasps nor rejects them, remaining unstained and unattached with a mind like empty space, this is called "Great";
therefore it is termed *mahā*. Good friend, the deluded speak of this with their mouths, while the wise practice it with their minds.
Furthermore, there are deluded people who sit in meditation with an empty mind, thinking of nothing at all, and claim for themselves that they are "Great. This...
There is a class of people with whom one cannot speak, because of their false views. Good friend, the scope of the mind is vast and great, pervading and encompassing the entire Dharma-realm.
When it functions, it is clearly and distinctly manifest; through its application, one immediately knows all. All is one, and one is all.
Coming and going are free and easy, for the essence of the mind is without obstruction—this is precisely *prajñā*. Good friend, all *prajñā*...
If wisdom arises entirely from one's own nature and does not enter from without, do not mistakenly apply your mind; this is called the true nature functioning spontaneously.
When the One is True, all is True. This is the great matter of the scope of the mind; do not practice the small path.

Though one may speak of emptiness all day long with the mouth, if one does not cultivate this practice within the heart, it is just like an ordinary person claiming to be a king—it can never be attained. This is not so.
My disciples, good friends, what is called *prajñā*? *Prajñā* is translated into the language of Tang as "wisdom.
At all places and at all times, to be free from delusion in every thought-moment and to constantly practice wisdom—this is *prajñā*.
To act with even a single moment of delusion is for *prajñā* to cease; a single moment of wisdom is for *prajñā* to arise. Worldly people are deluded and do not perceive *prajñā*.

If one speaks of Prajñā with the mouth while the mind remains constantly deluded, constantly saying to oneself, "I am practicing Prajñā," and though speaking of emptiness at every thought-moment, fails to recognize true emptiness—knowing that Prajñā has no form or characteristics and that wisdom is the very mind itself—if one interprets it in such a way, it is merely called the wisdom of Prajñā;
how can it be called a Pāramitā? This is a term from Western India (Sindh); in the language of Tang, it means "reaching the other shore. Thus it is explained.

The ultimate meaning is free from arising and ceasing; when one clings to objects, arising and ceasing occur, just as water has waves—this is called "this shore. When one is free from clinging to objects, there is no arising or ceasing;
it is like water constantly flowing through—this is called "the other shore," and is therefore named *pāramitā*.

Good friends, those who are deluded merely recite these words with their mouths; at the time of such recitation, they are thinking only of what is false and what is wrong. If every thought-moment were put into practice, this would be called...
This is the true nature. One who awakens to this Dharma is practicing Prajñā; one who cultivates this practice is performing Prajñā. Without cultivation, one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
with a single thought of cultivation, one’s own body is equal to the Buddha. Good friends, the ordinary person is the Buddha; afflictions (*kleśa*) are Bodhi.
If the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary person; if the succeeding thought is awakened, one is a Buddha. If the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction.
The subsequent thought that is detached from objects is itself Bodhi. O Good Spiritual Friend, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā is the most honored, the most supreme, and the foremost.
It is without dwelling, without going, and without coming; all Buddhas of the three periods of time emerge from within it.
You should employ great wisdom to shatter the five aggregates, afflictions, and worldly toil. By practicing in this manner, you will certainly attain the Way of Buddhahood and undergo transformation.

The three poisons become precept, concentration, and wisdom. Good friend, this dharma-gate of mine arises from one prajñā and gives birth to eighty-four thousand forms of wisdom. Why is this? Because sentient beings have eighty-four thousand afflictions;
if there were no afflictions, wisdom would constantly manifest, never departing from its own nature. One who awakens to this dharma is one of non-thought, non-recollection, and non-remembrance.

Be steadfast. Do not give rise to deception or delusion. By employing one’s own *tathāgatagarbha* nature and observing with wisdom, neither grasping nor rejecting any phenomena—this is precisely seeing the nature and attaining the Buddha-way.

Good friends, if you wish to enter the profound *dharmadhātu* and the *prajñā-samādhi*, you must cultivate the practice of *prajñā* and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; then you will immediately attain it.

Regarding the realization of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), you should know that these merits are immeasurable and boundless. They are clearly praised in the sūtras, such that they cannot be fully described.
This Dharma-gate is the Supreme Vehicle; it is taught for those of great wisdom and for those of superior faculties.
If people of small faculties and small wisdom hear it, they will give rise to disbelief. Why is this? It is like a great dragon sending down rain upon Jambudvīpa.
Cities and villages are all swept away, like jujube leaves carried off by a torrent; yet when it rains upon the great ocean, it neither increases nor decreases.
So it is with those of the Mahāyāna or the Supreme Vehicle: upon hearing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, their minds open and they attain awakening.

Thus one knows that the original nature inherently possesses the wisdom of *prajñā*; because one constantly employs this wisdom for contemplation and illumination, there is no need for external words.

For example, the rainwater does not originate from the heavens; it is originally the dragon that is able to bring it forth, causing all sentient beings, all grasses and trees, and everything animate and inanimate, to receive its moisture. The hundred rivers and myriad streams then flow back into the great ocean.
They merge into a single entity. The *prajñā*-wisdom of the original nature of sentient beings is also like this.
Good friends, when people of small capacity hear this sudden teaching, it is like plants and trees with small root-natures:
if they encounter a great rain, they all collapse on their own and cannot grow. People of small capacity are also like this; they originally possess *prajñā*—
Wisdom is no different from that of a person of great wisdom. For what reason, upon hearing the Dharma, do you not attain self-awakening?

It is because the obstacles of false views are heavy and the roots of affliction are deep. It is like a great cloud covering the sun; if it is not blown away by the wind, the sunlight will not appear.
The wisdom of *prajñā* has neither large nor small dimensions; it depends on whether the minds of all sentient beings are deluded or awakened.
It is the same. To see outwardly with a deluded mind and practice in search of a Buddha, without yet awakening to one’s own nature, constitutes having inferior faculties.

If, however, one awakens to the Sudden Teaching, does not cling to external cultivation, and constantly gives rise to right view within one's own mind, such that afflictions and worldly toil can never defile it, this is seeing one's nature.
O Good Friends, when one dwells neither within nor without and comes and goes with freedom, one is able to eliminate attachment.
The mind penetrates all without obstruction; one who can practice this way is no different from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* itself.
Good friend, all sūtras and all written words are established because of people; they can only be instituted by virtue of the nature of wisdom.
If there were no people in the world, all phenomena would fundamentally not exist. Therefore, know that all phenomena fundamentally depend on people.
It arises. All scriptures exist because they are spoken by people. Depending on those people, there are the foolish and the wise.
The foolish are called small persons; the wise are called great persons. When the foolish inquire of the wise, the wise expound the Dharma for the foolish.
Suddenly the foolish awaken, their minds open, and they are no different from the wise. O Good Friends, if one does not awaken, even a Buddha is merely a member of the multitude.
Birth. At the moment of a single thought of awakening, sentient beings are Buddhas. Thus, one knows that all phenomena are entirely within one's own mind.
Why not, from within one's own mind, suddenly perceive the true nature of *tathatā*? The Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra says: "My original fundamental nature is inherently pure;
if one recognizes one's own mind and sees one's nature, one attains the Buddha-way. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "At that very moment, there was a sudden breakthrough..."
I have attained my original mind, O virtuous friend. Under the guidance of Master Ren, upon hearing his words but once, I immediately awakened and suddenly perceived the true nature of *tathatā*.
Therefore, I shall circulate this teaching so that those who study the Way may suddenly awaken to Bodhi.

Each should observe their own mind and personally perceive its original nature. If one does not awaken to it oneself, one must seek a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who understands the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle and can directly point out the correct path.
Such a spiritual friend possesses great causal conditions; that is to say, they transform and guide others so that they may realize their nature.
This is because all wholesome dharmas are initiated through the influence of a spiritual friend. Thus it was with the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The twelve divisions of the sūtras exist within human nature; they are inherently possessed from the beginning.
If one cannot awaken to them oneself, one must seek the guidance of a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) before they can be seen. If one awakens to them oneself, there is no need to seek them externally.
If one persistently clings to the view that liberation can only be attained through another virtuous friend, this is impossible. Why? Because they are already within one's own mind.
Knowledge awakens itself. If one gives rise to deviant delusions, false thoughts, and inverted views, even if external spiritual friends provide instruction, salvation cannot be obtained.
However, if one gives rise to the correct and true contemplation of *prajñā*, in a single instant all false thoughts are extinguished.

Recognize the original nature of consciousness; upon a single awakening, one immediately reaches the stage of Buddhahood. Good friend, when wisdom contemplates and illuminates, it is transparently clear both internally and externally.
Recognize your own original mind. If you recognize your original mind, that is original liberation. If you attain liberation, that is precisely the *prajñā-samādhi*.
*Prajñā-samādhi* is precisely non-thought (*amanasikāra*). What is meant by non-thought? It is when, in perceiving all phenomena...
When the mind is free from defiled attachment, this is called non-thought (*amanasikāra*). Its function then pervades all places, yet it does not cling to any place.
It merely purifies the fundamental mind so that the six consciousnesses emerge through the six gates; amidst the six sense objects, they are neither defiled nor confused.
Coming and going with freedom, its universal application is unhindered—this is precisely the *prajñā-samādhi* of sovereign liberation, termed the practice of non-thought.

If one does not think of anything for even a hundred moments, constantly causing the stream of thought to cease, this is itself the bondage of dharmas; it is called an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Good friend, those who awaken to the dharma of non-thought penetrate all phenomena. Those who awaken to the dharma of non-thought perceive the realm of all Buddhas.
Those who awaken to the dharma of non-thought reach the stage of Buddhahood. Good friend, those in future generations who obtain my Dharma shall take this sudden teaching...

Regarding this Dharma-gate, if one makes a vow to receive and uphold it with those of identical view and practice—as if serving the Buddha—and does not regress for the rest of their life, they will certainly enter the ranks of the noble ones (*ārya*).
However, it must be transmitted; from antiquity until now, it has been handed down through silent transmission. One must not conceal the True Dharma.
If the views and practices are not identical and the person belongs to a different teaching, it must not be transmitted to them, as it would cause harm to them.

In the end, it will be of no benefit. I fear that ignorant people, failing to understand, will slander this Dharma-gate; for a hundred kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, they will sever the Buddha-nature.
Good friend, I have a verse on formlessness (*animitta*) which you must each commit to memory. Whether lay or ordained, simply practice according to this.
If you do not practice for yourself, merely memorizing my words will be of no benefit. Listen as I recite this verse: [Recitation follows]
Penetrating wisdom and the penetration of the mind are like the sun dwelling in the void; they transmit only the Dharma of seeing one's nature.

This world-transcending teaching shatters heterodox schools. In the Dharma, there is neither sudden nor gradual; there are only differences in the speed of delusion and awakening. Yet this very gate of seeing one's nature cannot be fully grasped by the foolish.

Though explanations may be manifold, when brought into accord with principle, they return to the One. Within the dark abode of affliction, one must constantly give rise to the sun of wisdom. [Heterodoxy...]
When afflictions arise, they are eliminated as they come. Use neither the false nor the true; when purity reaches its ultimate limit, there is nothing remaining.

Awakening has no inherent nature from the beginning; to give rise to a mind is itself delusion. When the pure mind dwells within delusion, simply remain correct and the three obstacles will not exist.
If people of the world cultivate the Way, nothing whatsoever shall hinder them. Constantly seeing one's own faults is what accords with the Way. Form...
All things have their own way; each does not obstruct or vex the other. To leave the Way and seek the Way elsewhere, one will not see the Way for the rest of one’s life.
Wandering from one place to another throughout a lifetime, one ends up regretting it at the end. If you wish to perceive the True Way, practicing what is right is itself the Way.
If you yourself lack the mind of the Way, you will walk in darkness and not see the Way. If one is a true cultivator of the Way, they do not see the faults of the world. If...
To see the faults of others while not rectifying one’s own is perverse. When another is at fault, I am not; when I am at fault, I have my own transgression.
Simply by rectifying the mind that seeks out faults, one strikes down and destroys afflictions. If monastic affairs do not concern you, stretch out both legs and lie down.
If you wish to transform others, you must first possess skillful means; do not cause them to harbor doubt, for this is the manifestation of your own nature. —The Buddha.
The Dharma exists within the world; awakening is not separate from the world. To seek Bodhi apart from the world is like searching for a rabbit’s horn.
Right view is called "transcending the world," while wrong view belongs to the world. When both wrong and right are completely cast aside, the nature of Bodhi is manifest as it is.

This verse represents the Sudden Teaching and is also called the Great Dharma Ship. Those who are deluded may hear the sutras for countless eons, yet for those who awaken, it occurs in a single instant.
Prefect Wei asked, "I have often seen monks and laypeople recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, wishing to be reborn in the Western Land.
I request that the Master explain whether it is possible to be born there. I pray you will dispel my doubts. The Patriarch said, "Governor, listen well; I, Huineng, shall explain it for you.
When the World-Honored One was in the city of Śrāvastī, he spoke of the West as a means of guidance. The scriptural text clearly states that [the land] is distant."

This is not far away. If one speaks in terms of its characteristics, the distance is said to be one hundred and eight thousand *li*. However, this refers to the ten evils and eight perversions within one's own body;

thus it is described as being far. To speak of it as far is for those of inferior capacity; to speak of it as near is for those of superior wisdom. There are two kinds of people, but the Dharma is not of two kinds.
There is a difference between delusion and awakening, and there is a disparity in the speed of insight. For the deluded person, reciting the Buddha’s name leads to seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
That person awakens to the fact that one purifies one's own mind. Thus the Buddha said: "According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure.
Your Excellency, for a person of the East, if the mind is pure, there is no fault; even for a person of the West, if the mind is not pure, there is transgression.
Those in the East who commit offenses yet recite the Buddha’s name seek rebirth in the West; those in the West who commit offenses yet recite the Buddha’s name—where would they seek rebirth?
The ignorant and foolish do not understand their own nature and fail to recognize the pure land within their own bodies; thus they pray for the East and pray for the West.
To one who has attained awakening, every place is the same. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Wherever you dwell, you shall always be at peace and happy. My Lord, as for the ground of the mind, simply...
There is no unwholesomeness. The Western Land is not far from here. If one harbors an unwholesome mind, it will be difficult to reach rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha.
Now I exhort you, O Good Friend: first eliminate the ten evils, and you have already traveled a hundred thousand leagues; next eliminate the eight deviant paths, and you have passed eight thousand.
If you see your true nature in every thought and always practice with equanimity and integrity, you will arrive as if in the snap of a finger and behold Amitābha. My Lord.

If you simply practice the ten wholesome deeds, why must you further contemplate rebirth in the Pure Land? If you do not sever the mind of the ten unwholesome deeds, what Buddha will come to welcome and invite you?
If you awaken to the sudden teaching of non-arising, you will see that the Western Land is but a mere instant away.

If you do not awaken to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and seeking rebirth, how can you reach it when the path is so remote? I, Huineng, shall move the Western Land within a single instant before your very eyes.
"Did you see it just now? Would each of you like to see it? The assembly all prostrated themselves and said, "If we can see it here, why must we further aspire for rebirth there?
We pray that the Master, out of compassion, will manifest the Western Land so that everyone may see it. The Patriarch said, "O Great Assembly! For worldly people, their physical body is a city;
the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are its gates. On the outside there are five gates, and within there is the gate of the mind."
The mind is the ground; nature is the sovereign. The sovereign dwells upon the ground of the mind. When nature is present, the sovereign is present; when nature departs, the sovereign is gone.
When nature is present, body and mind endure; when nature departs, body and mind perish. The Buddha acts within nature; do not seek him outside the body.
Delusion regarding one’s own nature is the sentient being; awakening to one’s own nature is the Buddha. Compassion is Avalokiteśvara; joy and relinquishment...
"Śrīghoṣa" (Potthapāda) refers to Śākyamuni; "Pure" refers to Śākyamuni; "Level and Straight" refers to Amitābha. The self and others are Mount Sumeru; the deviant mind is the ocean water;
afflictions are the waves; poisonous harm is the evil dragons; falsehood is the ghosts and spirits; worldly toil is the fish and turtles;
greed and anger are the hells; ignorance is the realm of animals. Good friend, constantly practice the ten...
Excellent! Heaven is then attained. When the human ego is removed, Mount Sumeru collapses; when the deviant mind is eliminated, the ocean dries up; when afflictions cease, the waves subside;
when poison and harm are forgotten, fish and dragons vanish. Within the ground of one’s own mind, the Tathāgata of enlightened nature emits a great radiance.

Externally, it illuminates the six sense-gates, purifying them and enabling one to transcend the various heavens of the six desires. Internally, it illuminates the three poisons of one’s own nature. Thus...
"The sins of the hells and other realms are all extinguished at once; one becomes transparently clear within and without, no different from the Western Land.

Without practicing this cultivation, how can one reach that place? When the great assembly heard these words, they clearly perceived their own nature; they all prostrated themselves and together exclaimed, "Excellent!
They cried out, "May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm hear this and simultaneously attain awakening and understanding. The Patriarch said, "If you wish to practice..."

"Practice can be undertaken by those living at home as well; it does not depend on being in a monastery. One who lives at home and is able to practice is like those in the East whose minds are virtuous.

One who dwells in a monastery but does not cultivate [the path] is like those in the West whose minds are evil. It is simply that when the mind is pure, that is itself the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Master Wei asked again, "How should one who lives at home practice? I pray you will instruct me. The Patriarch said, "I shall act as the leader for the great assembly..."
The Verses on Signlessness: Practice solely according to this; you will always dwell with me without distinction.
If you do not practice in this way, what benefit is there for the Path in shaving your head and leaving the household life? The verses say: If the mind is level, why toil to maintain the precepts?

If conduct is straight, what need is there to cultivate meditation? In terms of kindness, one nurtures one's parents; In terms of righteousness, those above and below show mutual compassion. In yielding, the honorable and the humble live in harmony; In patience, [the harsh and the gentle]...
Then all evils will not clamor. If one can drill wood to produce fire, red lotuses will surely grow from the mud. That which is bitter to the mouth is a potent medicine;

that which is harsh to the ear is surely loyal counsel. To reform one’s faults gives rise to wisdom; to protect one’s shortcomings is unvirtuous within the heart. Daily conduct should always be beneficial;
the realization of the Way does not depend on the giving of money. Bodhi is sought only within the mind—how [could it be found elsewhere]?
Toiling outwardly in search of the profound, you have heard and understood that by practicing according to this, paradise lies right before your eyes. The Patriarch spoke again, saying:
"Good friends, you must all practice according to these verses; by perceiving the self-nature within yourselves, you will directly attain the Buddha-way. The Dharma does not wait for anyone."
Huanji said: "The Patriarch taught people to eliminate the self and others and to remove the deviant mind.
Is this the same as Master Xiu’s practice of 'constantly and diligently wiping away' [the dust], or is it different? If you say they are different, in what respect do they differ?
If you say they are the same, why did Master Xiu not attain realization at Huangmei? If you say this is a statement from the 'second head,' the Patriarch also said:"

Practice according to the verse and you will directly attain the Buddha-way; this is not for the sake of secondary words. Only when one has realized this through and through does one truly have a share in study and inquiry.
Otherwise, one is merely a person who recites words. Even if the Patriarchs were present before one’s eyes every day, [one would still be lost].
"What can one do about it? Furthermore, one must employ great wisdom to shatter the afflictions and defilements of the five aggregates;

this is the Patriarch’s word. "No thought, no recollection, no attachment"—this is the Patriarch’s instruction. Yet, when addressing Xue Jian, he dismissed [the notion of stillness] by asserting that one must use wisdom to illuminate and break through afflictions;
when addressing Wo-lun, he said, "Do not cut off a hundred thoughts. How inconsistent is the path of the Dharma!
They are equal. Therefore, if you call it a bamboo whisk, you contradict it; if you do not call it a bamboo whisk, you deny it.

One cannot say there is speech, nor can one say there is no speech. Whether it be Mount Sumeru, a dried piece of dung, the "Cantonese monk’s robe," or the "price of rice in Luling"—all these are used to lead students of the Way onto the wondrous raft of the *Platform Sūtra*. Only after one has necessarily realized this can one be said to have attained it.
One is able to read the *Platform Sūtra*. Nowadays, those who read it generally claim it is clear and simple, and that they have no doubts in their minds;
yet, regarding the dynamic responses that move like wind and flash like lightning across various regions, they remain as bewildered as ever. Such people have not even dreamed of the *Platform Sūtra*.
If one were truly able to harmonize with the *Platform Sūtra*, those wind-like and lightning-like movements would be seen as nothing more than ordinary daily affairs.
"It is merely tea and rice; why do you harbor further doubts? He addressed the assembly, saying:
"Good friends, this Dharma-gate of mine takes concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā) as its foundation. The assembly must not be deluded by thinking that concentration and wisdom are separate.
Concentration and wisdom are one entity; they are not two. Concentration is the essence of wisdom, and wisdom is the function of concentration. That is, wisdom..."

When concentration is present, wisdom is established within it; when wisdom is present, concentration is established within it. If one understands this meaning, this is the training in the equality of concentration and wisdom.
Those who practice the path should not say that concentration gives rise to wisdom first, or that wisdom gives rise to concentration first, as if they were separate.

To hold such a view is to see phenomena as having dual characteristics: the mouth speaks of wholesome characteristics, yet the mind is unwholesome. Though there may be concentration and wisdom in name, there is no true union of concentration and wisdom.

They are not equal. If both mind and speech are wholesome, then internal and external are of one kind, and concentration and wisdom are equal. Self-awakening and cultivation do not depend on contention.

If you contend over which comes first or last, you are the same as those who are deluded. If you do not cease this competition for victory and defeat, you will instead increase the notions of self and dharma, remaining inseparable from the four marks.
Good friends, how are concentration and wisdom related? They are like a lamp and its light: where there is a lamp, there is light.
Without a lamp there is darkness; the lamp is the substance of light, and light is the function of the lamp. Although their names are two, their substance is fundamentally one.
This Dharma of concentration and wisdom is also like this. Furthermore, it is said: "Good friend, why do you establish 'non-thought' as the fundamental principle?
It is simply because people speak of 'seeing nature' with their mouths, while deluded people harbor thoughts regarding external objects; from these thoughts, [delusion] immediately arises."
From false views, all afflictions and deluded thoughts arise. In its own nature, there is originally not a single dharma to be obtained.
If one perceives anything as obtainable and falsely speaks of calamity or fortune, this is itself affliction and false view. Therefore, this Dharma-gate establishes non-thought as its central tenet.
Good friends, what is it that is "non-existent"? What is it that is "thought"? "Non-existent" means the absence of duality.
Characteristics. One is free from all thoughts of worldly affliction (*kleśa*). As for "mindfulness," it is mindfulness of the original nature of *tathatā*.

*Tathatā* is the essence of mindfulness; mindfulness is the function of *tathatā*. It is the self-nature of *tathatā* that gives rise to mindfulness. It is not the eyes, ears, nose, or tongue that can practice mindfulness.
Because *tathatā* possesses this nature, it gives rise to mindfulness. If *tathatā* were non-existent, then at that very moment, the eyes, ears, forms, and sounds would simply cease to exist.

[The Master] said, "It is destroyed. Good friend, when the self-nature of True Suchness gives rise to thought, although the six sense organs possess seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they remain unstained by the myriad objects, and the true nature is ever-sovereign.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'One can skillfully discern the characteristics of all phenomena, yet remains unmoved within the ultimate truth.
It also says: 'In this gate of sitting meditation, one fundamentally does not cling to the mind, nor does one cling to purity.'"
Nor is it non-movement. If one says there is attachment to the mind, the mind is fundamentally illusory; knowing the mind to be like a phantom, there is nothing to which one can be attached.

If one says there is attachment to purity, human nature is inherently pure; it is only because of deluded thoughts that True Suchness (Tathatā) is covered over. If one simply lacks deluded thoughts, the nature is naturally clear and pure.
To give rise to a thought and become attached to purity, however, is to produce the delusion of purity. Since delusion has no location, what is there for the one who clings to be attached to?
This is delusion. Purity has no form or characteristics; yet you set up the appearance of purity and claim it is your spiritual practice.
One who forms such a view obstructs their own original nature and becomes bound by purity. Good friends, if you would cultivate immovability, simply look upon all people when you see them.
Not perceiving the right or wrong, good or evil, or the faults and afflictions of others is itself the immovability of one’s own nature.
Good friend, when a person is deluded, although their body remains unmoving, as soon as they open their mouth they speak of the right and wrong, long and short, or good and evil of others;
this is to turn away from the Way. If one becomes attached to the mind or to purity, it obstructs the Way. A Verse on Formlessness says: "The deluded person cultivates merit..."

Cultivating the Way: To say that merely cultivating merit is itself the Way is a mistake. While the merit of giving and making offerings is boundless, the three evil karmas have been created within the mind from the very beginning.
If one intends to extinguish these sins by cultivating merit, one may gain blessings in future lives, yet the sins will remain. One should simply eliminate the conditions for sin within the mind;
each person must perform true repentance within their own nature. If one suddenly awakens to the true repentance of the Mahāyāna, all deviance is removed.
Practicing correctly, one is without fault. In studying the Way, one should constantly contemplate one's own nature; thus, one is of the same category as all Buddhas.
My Patriarch transmitted only this Sudden Dharma, universally wishing that all may see their nature and become of one essence. If you wish to seek the Dharmakāya in the future, [you must do so now].
Wash away all mental traces of the characteristics of phenomena; strive with diligence to see for yourself, do not be indolent. If the subsequent thought suddenly ceases, this life comes to an end.
If you awaken to the Mahāyāna and attain the vision of your nature, then with reverent palms joined, seek it with a sincere heart.
This verse was recorded by one who denied cause and effect.
Zen Master Huairang of Nanyue paid his respects to the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Song.
The Patriarch asked, "What kind of thing is it that comes like this? He replied, "To describe it as a single thing is not correct. The Patriarch asked, "Can it be cultivated or realized? He replied:
Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, defilement is not permitted. The Patriarch said:
"This very state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind. Since you are thus, I am also thus. The Indian Prajñātāra prophesied of you:
'From beneath your feet shall emerge a colt that will trample the people of the world to death. This destiny rests within your own heart; there is no need to speak of it in haste."
In the *Transmission of the Lamp*, it is recorded that the Patriarch asked, "What thing comes in such a manner? Huairang was speechless.
He then spent eight years until he suddenly attained realization. He then said to the Patriarch, "I have reached an understanding. The Patriarch asked, "How so? Huairang replied as follows.
It is the same as this. Zen Master Xingxiu of Qingyuan went to visit the Patriarch and asked, "What should one attend to so that one does not fall into stages?
The Patriarch said, "What have you been doing? He replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch said, "In what stage do you fall? He replied:
"If one does not even practice the Noble Truths, what hierarchy could there possibly be? His ancestors held him in high esteem and appointed him as the head of the assembly.
Chan Master Xuanjue of Yongjia had studied the sutras and treatises since his youth and mastered the Dharma-gate of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Upon reading the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, he realized the ground of the mind. Later, inspired by Chan Master Zuoxi Lang, he traveled together with Chan Master Ce of Dongyang to [visit the patriarch].
When Caoqi first arrived, he shook his mendicant’s staff and circumambulated the Patriarch three times, then stood there upright.

The Patriarch said, “A śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices. From what direction have you come, Venerable Sir, that you give rise to such great arrogance?
Caoqi replied, “The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch asked, “Why do you not realize non-arising and understand that there is no swiftness?”

He said, "The essence is itself non-arising; one realizes that it is fundamentally without haste. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment.
Huairang then assumed his full dignified demeanor to pay his respects, and after a short while, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Are you returning too soon?"
He said, "Fundamentally, it is not moving; how could there be speed? The Patriarch asked, "Who knows it is not moving? He replied, "You, O Benevolent One, yourself give rise to discrimination.
The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly grasped the meaning of non-arising. He asked, "If there is no arising, how can there be 'meaning'? The Patriarch said:
"If there is no mind, who is it that performs discernment? He replied, "Discernment, too, is not the mind. The Patriarch sighed and said, "Excellent! Stay for one night.
At that time, he was called "The One-Night Awakening" (Yi-su-jiao). Monk Fahai came to visit and asked, "Regarding 'this very mind is Buddha,' I pray you will grant me instruction.
The Patriarch said, "When the preceding thought does not arise, that is the mind; when the succeeding thought does not cease, that is the Buddha. To manifest all phenomena..."
The mind: to be free from all marks is itself Buddhahood. Were I to explain it in full detail, even an entire kalpa would not suffice.

Listen to my verse: "The very mind is called wisdom; The very Buddha is samādhi. When samādhi and wisdom are equal— (under the lamp, the character for 'equal' is read as 'maintain')— the mind becomes pure within.

To awaken to this Dharma-gate, rely on your own habitual nature; employing that which is fundamentally unborn, cultivating both together is the correct path. At these words, Fahai attained great enlightenment.
He praised him with a verse, saying: "The mind itself is originally the Buddha; Failing to awaken to this, one remains self-subdued. I know the causes of Samādhi and Prajñā;
Cultivating them both, one is free from all phenomena. Seng Zhitong had read the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* more than a thousand times, yet he could not comprehend the Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms.
He prostrated himself before the Patriarch to seek an explanation of their meaning. The Patriarch said: "As for the Three Bodies: the Pure Dharmakāya is your own nature."
The Perfect Reward Body is your wisdom; the thousands of billions of Transformation Bodies are your practice.

If one were to speak of the three bodies apart from the fundamental nature, it would mean having a body but lacking wisdom. If one realizes that the three bodies have no inherent self-nature, [then they are truly realized].

This is precisely what is called the Bodhi of the Four Wisdoms. Listen to my verse: "The self-nature inherently possesses the three bodies; Through its manifestation, it accomplishes the four wisdoms.
Without departing from the conditions of seeing and hearing, It transcends to the stage of Buddhahood. I now speak this for you; Believe it with clarity and you shall forever be free from delusion."

"Do not emulate those who run about in pursuit; they spend their whole day speaking of Bodhi. Tong said, "May I hear the meaning of the four wisdoms? The Patriarch said, "Since you have already realized the three bodies (trikāya), you must clearly understand the four wisdoms. Why ask again?
