It is said: The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure; the Mind of the Equality Wisdom is free from ailment. The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation sees without effort;
the Wisdom of Accomplishing Action is identical to the Perfect Mirror. The five, eight, six, and seven consciousnesses transform as fruit and cause;

they exist only through conventional designations and possess no real nature. If one leaves no attachment at the point of transformation, then amidst profuse activity, one forever dwells in the *nāga*-samādhi. (This refers to the teaching on transforming consciousness into wisdom.)

The middle [section] states: "The first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done; the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality; and the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

Although the sixth and seventh are transformed during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth are transformed at the level of fruition, this is merely a transformation of their names, not a transformation of their essence. Having offered universal prostrations and thanks, he praised them with a verse: "The three bodies are originally my own substance; The four wisdoms are fundamentally the clarity of the mind.
Body and wisdom merge without obstruction, Responding to things according to their forms. All arising cultivation is but delusion."
Movement. To dwell upon it is not the true essence. The wondrous principle is understood through the teacher; ultimately, there is no name for defilement.

The monk Zhidao, while reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, reached the passage: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are laws of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss.
Doubt arose within him, and he prostrated before the Patriarch to seek clarification. The Patriarch asked, "In what way do you doubt? He replied, "All..."

All sentient beings possess two bodies: namely, the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The physical body is impermanent; it has birth and it has extinction. The dharma-body is permanent;
it is without cognition and without awareness. As the Sūtra says, "When birth and extinction have ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss.
I do not yet understand which body attains this cessation and which body experiences this bliss. If it is the physical body, then when the physical body perishes, the four great elements...

They are dispersed; they are entirely suffering and cannot be called pleasure. If the Dharma-body were quiescent extinction, it would be identical to grass, trees, tiles, and stones—who then would experience pleasure?
Furthermore, the Dharma-nature is the essence of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates are the function of arising and ceasing.
One essence with five functions: birth and extinction are eternal. Birth means arising from the essence to manifest function; extinction means withdrawing function back into the essence.
If rebirth were permitted, then the categories of sentient beings would neither be severed nor extinguished.
If rebirth were not permitted, they would eternally return to quiescent extinction, becoming identical to insentient things. Thus, all dharmas would be [subsumed] by nirvana.
"Since that which is suppressed and subdued cannot even arise, what joy could there be? The Patriarch said, "You are a son of the Śākya;

why do you practice the heterodox views of permanence and annihilation and discuss the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle? According to your understanding, you hold that the Dharma-body exists separately outside of the physical body, and that one seeks quiescence apart from birth and death.
Furthermore, you infer the permanence and bliss of Nirvāṇa, claiming there is a body that experiences it."
This is precisely because you cling to birth and death and are addicted to worldly pleasures.

You should now know that for all deluded beings, the Buddha teaches that they mistake the combination of the five aggregates for their own self-nature, and differentiate all phenomena as external objects.

Thus, they love life and hate death, drifting through the flow of every thought-moment; unaware that these are like dreams and illusions, they falsely undergo the cycle of rebirth, taking what is impermanent to be eternal bliss.
Nirvāṇa is translated as the "characteristic of suffering. Throughout one's life, beings rush about in pursuit [of it]. Out of compassion for them, the Buddha revealed the true bliss of nirvāṇa:
in each moment there is no characteristic of arising, and in each moment there is no characteristic of ceasing; furthermore, there is no further arising or ceasing to be extinguished.
This is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (śamatha). At the very moment of its manifestation, there is no measure of that manifestation; this is what is called "eternal bliss. This...
In bliss, there is no one who receives it, nor is there anyone who does not receive it. How could there be such a thing as the designation of "one essence with five functions"?

How much more so when you further claim that Nirvāṇa suppresses and restrains all phenomena, causing them never to arise again? This is to slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma. Listen to my verse:
The Unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa Is perfectly luminous, eternally tranquil, and illuminating. The ignorant and foolish call it death; The non-Buddhists cling to it...
To sever [delusions], for those seeking the two vehicles, this is termed "non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra*). All such views belong to the domain of emotional conceptualization;

they are fundamentally the sixty-two views, established through false and provisional names. What, then, is the true meaning? Only those of transcendent capacity (*atimātra-pudgala*) penetrate it without grasping or rejection.

By knowing the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the self within the aggregates, as well as the various external forms and appearances—each and every sound—[they realize the truth].
The characteristics of sound are equal, like a dream or an illusion. Do not give rise to views of ordinary beings or sages; do not form a conceptual understanding of nirvana.

Cut off the two extremes and the three temporal limits. Constantly employ the functions of the sense faculties, yet do not give rise to the thought of "functioning. Discern all phenomena, yet do not give rise to the thought of "discernment.
Even when the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and winds strike mountains together in collision, there remains the bliss of true permanence and quiescence—the characteristic of nirvana.
"So it is. I shall now speak forcefully so as to cause you to abandon your false views. Do not seek understanding through mere words; I grant you a small portion of knowledge.

Upon hearing this, Daowen leaped for joy, prostrated himself, and withdrew. Seng Zhiche, whose original name was Xingchang and whose surname was Zhang, had been a man of the *renxie* (chivalrous) way in his youth.
Since the division between the Northern and Southern schools, although the two Patriarchs had forgotten distinctions of self and other, their disciples vied with one another.
Affection and hatred arose. Since the Northern School had established Master Xiu as the Sixth Patriarch, they resented that the transmission of the robe was known throughout the world;
they instructed Xingchang to assassinate the Patriarch. The Patriarch’s mind was enlightened such that he anticipated this event in advance and placed ten taels of gold between his cushions.
Changhuai brandished his blade and entered the room. Sengzu extended his neck toward him. Changhuai struck three times with the blade, yet it did not cause the slightest injury.
Sengzu said, "A righteous sword is not crooked; a crooked sword is not righteous. You owe me only gold, not your life. Startled, Changhuai collapsed.

After a long time, he finally regained consciousness. He sought mercy and repented his transgressions, expressing his wish to leave the household life. The Patriarch gave him gold and said, "Go for now; I fear the assembly might harm you.
Return on another day in a different guise, and I shall accept you. Chang received these instructions and fled under the cover of night.

He subsequently entered the monastic order and applied himself with diligence. One day, remembering the Patriarch’s previous command, he went to visit him. The Patriarch said, "I have been thinking of you for a long time."

"Why have you come so late? He replied, "I have received the Master’s pardon for my transgressions. Although I have now left the household life and practice asceticism, it is difficult to repay your profound kindness.

Is there any way to do so other than by transmitting the Dharma and delivering sentient beings? Your disciple has frequently read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, yet I have not yet understood the meaning of 'permanent' and 'impermanent.'"
"I beg the Master’s compassion to explain this briefly. The Patriarch said, "That which is impermanent is the Buddha-nature;
that which is permanent is the discriminating mind regarding all phenomena, both good and evil. [The monk] said, "What the Master has said greatly contradicts the scriptural texts.
The Patriarch said, "I transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal; how would I dare to contradict the Buddha’s scriptures? [The monk] said, "The scriptures state that the Buddha-nature is..."
[The Master said: "Permanence! Yet you, O Preceptor, say it is impermanent. All dharmas, whether good or evil, even including the bodhicitta, are all impermanent;
yet you, O Preceptor, say they are permanent. This is contradictory and causes students to become increasingly confused. The Patriarch said:

"Regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the past when I heard the nun Wujinzang recite it once, I immediately gave a lecture upon it. There was not a single word [of mine that was not in accord with the text]."
"One meaning does not accord with the scriptural texts... up to: 'For you, I have never had two teachings. [The student] said, "Your disciple’s capacity for understanding is shallow and dim.

Therefore, within the definitive teachings on *nirvāṇa*, these biased views are refuted, and true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity are clearly expounded.
You now rely on the words while turning your back on the meaning, taking the cessation of existence to be impermanence and the certainty of death to be permanence.
Yet, if one misunderstands the Buddha’s perfectly wondrous and final subtle words, what benefit is there even in reading them a thousand times?
Xingchang suddenly felt as if he had awakened from a drunken stupor and spoke this verse: "Because I guarded a mind of impermanence, The Buddha taught the nature of permanence.

The Master transmitted it to me, yet I too have nothing to attain. The Patriarch said, "You have now attained thorough penetration; you should be named Zhi Che. Later, the monk Zhi Chang visited the Patriarch.

Mao replied, "Your fundamental nature is like empty space. When you turn back to contemplate your own nature, you find there is not a single thing that can be seen;

Zhìhuáng first visited the Fifth Patriarch, believing that he had attained *samādhi*. He lived in a hermitage, sitting in meditation continuously for twenty years.

"Does the mind enter [samādhi], or does it not? If there is no entry of the mind, then all insentient things—grass, trees, tiles, and stones—should likewise be able to attain samādhi.

Huáng said, "When I am truly entering samādhi, I do not perceive the existence or non-existence of a mind. Cè said, "If you do not perceive the existence or non-existence of a mind..."

Huang had no further response. After a long while, he asked, "Whom does your master follow? Xuanze said, "My master is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi. Huang asked, "What does the Sixth Patriarch take to be meditative concentration?

Fundamentally empty; the six sense objects do not exist. There is no emerging and no entering; neither fixed nor distracted. The nature of dhyāna has no abiding; it is the stillness of dhyāna that is free from abiding.
The nature of dhyāna has no arising; it is the thought of dhyāna that is free from arising. The mind is like space, yet it lacks even the measure of space.

In movement and stillness there is no mind; the sentiments of ordinary and sage are extinguished; subject and object both vanish; nature and form are as they are (tathatā). There is no time when one is not in samādhi.

The Disciple’s Record: In the first year of the Shenlong era of the Tang Emperor Zhongzong, an imperial edict dispatched the envoy Bi Jian to welcome the Patriarch. The Patriarch declined on account of illness.
Bi Jian asked, "The virtuous practitioners of Chan in the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate samādhi."
"If one does not attain liberation through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), such a thing has never occurred. [The student] asked, "I do not yet understand how the Dharma taught by the Master is.
The Master said, "The Way is realized through the mind; how could it depend on sitting? A sutra says:
'If one says that the Tathāgata sits or lies down, this is practicing a deviant path. Why? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; there is neither arising nor ceasing."
"This is the Tathāgata’s pure meditation; all dharmas are empty and quiescent. This is the Tathāgata’s pure sitting;
it is ultimately without realization—how much more so regarding 'sitting' itself? Jian said, "When your disciple returns to the capital, His Majesty will surely question me.

I pray that you, Master, will compassionately point out the essentials of the mind so that they may be transmitted to the two palaces and to those in the capital who study the Way, like one lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps."
"What is dark is all made bright; this brightness is inexhaustible. The Master said, "The Way has neither light nor darkness. Light and darkness are merely the meaning of succession and alternation.
That 'brightness is inexhaustible' is also a name established through dependence upon its opposite, which is 'exhaustibility.

Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: 'Dharmas have no peer, because they do not depend on one another. Jian said, "Light is a metaphor for wisdom; darkness is a metaphor for affliction. For one who cultivates the Way..."
"If one does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter the afflictions, by what means can one escape from beginningless birth and death? The Patriarch said, "Afflictions are themselves bodhi;
they are non-dual and without distinction. To use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions is the view of the Two Vehicles—the capacity of those such as the sheep and the deer.
Those of superior wisdom and great root are not like this. Jian asked, "How is it so?"
"This is the perspective of the Mahāyāna. The Patriarch said, "Luminosity and ignorance—ordinary people see these as two. The wise, however, realize that their nature is non-dual.
This non-dual nature is the true nature. As for this true nature, it does not diminish when abiding within the foolish and ignorant."
Abiding among sages and worthies without increasing; dwelling amidst afflictions without becoming disordered; residing in meditative concentration without being stilled;
neither interrupted nor permanent; neither coming nor going; not existing in between, nor within, nor without; neither arising nor ceasing;

its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*); eternally abiding and never shifting—this is called the Way. Jian asked: "The Master speaks of 'neither arising nor ceasing. How does this differ [from other teachings]?"
The outsider asked, "Master, when you speak of 'neither arising nor ceasing,' you seem to use cessation to stop arising, and use arising to manifest cessation;
thus, while cessation is as if not ceased, you speak of arising as non-arising. As for what I call 'neither arising nor ceasing,' it is fundamentally without arising from the very beginning."

Now it is likewise not extinguished; thus it differs from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, simply do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever.
You will naturally enter the essence of the pure mind, which is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, yet possesses wondrous functions as vast as the sands of the Ganges.

If you grieve because you do not know my place of departure, know that I myself know my place of departure.

Abiding in the Truth: sentient beings are characterized by movement, while insentient things are unmoving. If one cultivates a practice of non-movement, one becomes like an insentient thing that does not move.
If one seeks true non-movement, one finds non-movement within movement; this non-movement is itself non-movement. Insentient things lack the seed of Buddhahood.
One who is well able to discern these characteristics realizes the non-movement of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). To hold such a view is itself the Truth.
As for its application, I respond to those who study the Way: "Exert yourselves and must apply your minds; do not, within the gateway of the Mahāyāna, instead cling to the wisdom of birth and death.
If you attain resonance upon hearing these words, then together we shall discuss the meaning of the Buddha. If you truly do not attain resonance, join your palms and let them be joyful.
This school is fundamentally without contention; to contend is to lose the intent of the Way. To cling to and contend with the gates of the Dharma is to enter into their own nature."
"Birth and death. Having heard this verse, the assembly all paid homage. Fahai bowed twice and asked, "When the Master enters nirvana, to whom should the robe and the Dharma be entrusted?

Externally there is not a single thing that can be established; all are the fundamental mind giving rise to the myriad dharmas. Thus the Sūtra says: "When the mind arises, the myriad dharmas arise;

Without giving rise to hatred or love, and without grasping or rejecting, one does not dwell on matters such as benefit or ruin, success or failure.

Serene, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and pure—this is called the Samādhi of One Mark. The second is samādhi. Just as when there are seeds in the earth, they are contained, nurtured, and brought to fruition; so too it is with a single characteristic and a single practice.
My preaching of the Dharma now is like seasonal rain that thoroughly moistens the great earth.
Your Buddha-nature is likened to the seed; encountering this soaking moisture, it shall all sprout and grow. Those who receive my intent will certainly attain Bodhi. Relying on...
"I, as a practitioner, have definitively realized the wondrous fruit. Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout.

The mind is likewise so. Its Way is pure and free from all marks. You must be careful not to contemplate stillness or to empty the mind;
this mind is fundamentally pure, with nothing to be grasped or rejected. Each of you must exert yourselves and go forth according to conditions as best you can.

The original mind. Behold your own nature: it is neither moving nor still; neither arising nor ceasing; neither going nor coming; neither right nor wrong; neither abiding nor departing.
Fearing that your minds may be deluded and fail to grasp my meaning, I now re-exhort you so that you may see your nature.

The forest trees turned white, and the birds and beasts wailed in grief. At that moment, a white light rose from the stupa and extended upward to the heavens; it did not dissipate until three days later.
The Patriarch was seventy-six years old. He had transmitted the robe at the age of twenty-four and tonsured himself at thirty-nine.
He preached the Dharma to benefit sentient beings for thirty-seven years.

The Master said, "The Dharma-power of the Monk is vast and great. When construction is undertaken in the future, I pray that you will preserve my ancestral graves;
as for the rest, I am willing to relinquish it all to become a precious monastery. However, this site was the vital artery of a "living dragon" and "white elephant";

thus, one may level the sky above it, but not the earth below. The temple was subsequently constructed behind [the graves], exactly according to his words. Previously, the Indian master Jñānabhadra...

The Tripitaka Master passed through this place, noting that its forests, peaks, and springs were like the Jewel Forest (Ratnavana) of India; he deemed it fitting to establish a Buddhist monastery there.
He prophesied that one hundred and seventy years hence, the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure would be propagated here, and those who attain the Way would be as numerous as the trees in a forest;
thus, it should be named "Jewel Forest" (Baolin). At that time, Hou Jingzhong, the Governor of Shaozhou, submitted a memorial to report the construction of the temple.
In the third year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, Zu’s arrival coincided exactly with that record. In front of the hall was a pond where dragons frequently appeared and disappeared.
One day, a form of immense size manifested; the waves surged violently, and clouds and mist shrouded the sky in darkness.
The assembly was filled with fear. Nanyue said, "You can manifest a large body, but you cannot manifest a small one.
If you are a divine dragon, you ought to be able to undergo transformations—manifesting the large through the small, and the small through the large. The dragon suddenly vanished;
a moment later, it reappeared in a small form, leaping out from the surface of the pool. Nanyue spread out his alms bowl and said, "You still do not dare enter this old man's [bowl]."
The Master held his almsbowl over the monk’s bowl; the dragon settled within the bowl and could not move. He carried it up to the hall and preached the essentials of the Dharma for him.
The dragon then shed its bones and departed; the bones were about seven inches long, complete with head, tail, horns, and feet, and were preserved at that temple.

Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of inhaling and exhaling. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you are inhaling and exhaling; if you do not understand, you are not inhaling and exhaling. The monk said, "What is inhaling and exhaling? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of breathing. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you are breathing; if you do not understand, you are not breathing. The monk said, "What is breathing? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of life. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you have life; if you do not understand, you are dead. The monk said, "I am alive now, but I do not know what life is. Zhaozhou said, "If you know what life is, you are already living; if you do not know what life is, you are already dead. The monk said, "What is living? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of being present. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you are present; if you do not understand, you are absent. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you are looking; if you do not understand, you are not looking. The monk said, "What is looking? The monk said, "What is seeing? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of perceiving. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you perceive; if you do not understand, you do not perceive. The monk said, "What is perceiving? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of cognition. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you cognize; if you do not understand, you do not cognize. The monk said, "What is cognition? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of consciousness. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you are conscious; if you do not understand, you are unconscious. The monk said, "What is consciousness? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of mind. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you have mind; if you do not understand, you are without mind. The monk said, "What is mind? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of thought. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you think; if you do not understand, you do not think. The monk said, "What is thinking? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of deliberation. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you deliberate; if you do not understand, you do not deliberate. The monk said, "What is relating? Zhaozhou said, "It is the very act of connection. The monk said, "I do not understand. The monk said, "I do not understand. Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, you continue; if you do not understand, you do not continue. The monk said, "What is continuing? Before Niutou had seen the Fourth Patriarch, how was it? The Master said, "Sufficient firewood, sufficient water. [The monk] asked, "After he saw him, how was it?
[The Master] said, "Sufficient firewood, sufficient water. An old master answered these two preceding questions by saying, "A thief does not strike the house of a poor man."

After he took up residence there, the grandeur of his Dharma assemblies rivaled those at Huangmei. During the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, when the community of disciples lacked provisions, the Master traveled to Danyang to seek alms.
Although it was eighty *li* from the mountain, he personally carried one *shí* eight *dǒu* of rice, going in the morning and returning by evening.

For three years, he provided for three hundred monks, never failing to provide for their two daily meals. The local magistrate, Xiao Yuanshan, invited him to the Jianchu Monastery to lecture on the sutras.
When the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was being recited, the listeners gathered like clouds. Upon reaching the "Chapter on Cessation and Tranquility," the earth shook. Prince Boling asked:

"When an object-condition gives rise to form, you do not say that the condition itself arises with the form. How, then, can one know the condition? It seems you wish to cause its arising to cease. The Master said:
"At the very moment the objective form first arises, both the nature of form and the nature of the object are empty. Fundamentally, there is no knower of the condition."

The measure of the mind is identical to cognition; it illuminates the source, yet its arising is non-arising. At that time, what arises subsides of itself; though one embraces darkness, the conditions for awakening arise.
When the mind is present, conditions do not pursue it, reaching back to the state prior to birth. Form and mind are neither nurtured nor sustained; from emptiness, there is fundamentally no thought.
Perception, sensation, speech, and thought arise; they initiate what has never before been initiated. How could one rely on the Buddha’s teachings for this? Question:
When the eyes are closed, one does not see forms, yet mental objects and deliberations are many. Since forms no longer engage the mind, from where do these objects arise? Master:

When the eyes are closed and one does not see forms, the inner mind moves and deliberations are many. These are the provisional functions of illusory consciousness; though they arise, they ultimately do not transcend [the mind]. Know this.
Form does not concern the mind, and the mind likewise does not concern form. As one acts, appearances arise and shift; like a bird flying through the sky, the reality remains.

Question: When an object arises, it has no fixed location; through conditions, cognition is produced. When the object passes away, awareness returns and shifts; that very awareness then transforms into an object.
If one uses the mind to drag the mind, it is still what is perceived by awareness. Following it, following it as it goes, one never leaves birth and cessation.

At this juncture, the Master said: "In the beginning, middle, and end of form and mind, there is truly no object of dependent origination. When one momentary thought forgets its own doubt, who can calculate movement or stillness?
This knowing is itself without knowing; the knower and the known do not meet. You should examine your own fundamental form for yourself;

why must you seek it beyond the realm? The preceding object does not change or pass away; the subsequent thought does not come from the present. To seek the moon by grasping its dark reflection is to pursue a mere trace."
Chasing after flying birds; wishing to know the nature of the mind is like looking at a dream. It is comparable to water in the sixth month—everywhere it is the same.
One cannot escape emptiness by avoiding it, nor can one achieve it by seeking it. I ask you about the image in a mirror: from where does the mind arise? He asked:
"When the mind is applied with exact precision, how can it be peaceful and secure? The Master said: "When applied with exact precision..."
At the moment of the mind, there is precisely no employment of the mind; to speak circuitously of names and characteristics is wearisome, while speaking directly is free from redundancy.

When there is no mind, there is precisely its employment; when it is constantly employed, there is precisely no [mind]. Now, I speak of the state of no-mind; it is not different from that which has a mind. A questioner asked: "The Wise One cites wondrous words, yet they should accord with the nature of the mind.

If the words and the path of the mind diverge, then even if they are joined, they will be a ten-thousandfold discrepancy. The Master said: [Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence regarding the Master's response.]

It is said: "The skillful means of speaking wondrous words are the Mahāyāna path for curing illnesses; they do not concern the discourse on the original nature. These arise from the transformations of emptiness.
Taking non-thought as the true permanence, one shall ultimately sever the path of the mind. When detached from thought, the nature is unmoving; birth and cessation are without contradiction.
Just as an echo possesses sound, a mirror-image can look back. Question: "If the practitioner perceives that objects exist, is this due to awakening?"

When one knows that objects have vanished, there are three minds: the preceding awareness, the subsequent awareness, and the objects themselves. The Master said: "The function of objects is not their essence;

once awareness has ceased, one should not engage in thought. Because one knows through awareness that objects have vanished, when awareness is present, objects do not arise—this applies to both the preceding and the subsequent awareness."

Furthermore, there are three types of delusion regarding the object. A question is asked: "If one abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) such that neither [subject nor object] arises, this is taken to be the true samādhi;

no karmic actions can pull one away. Yet, one does not realize subtle ignorance (*avidyā*), which slowly follows behind. The Master says: "I have further heard of others who falsely grasp at the arising of mental constructs (*cittamātra*).
Among these three, the goal is not accomplished; though they do not arise, they return to falsehood. The mind is bound by the state of formal reception (*samāpatti*). For...

This purifies karmic obstacles. A ten-thousandth part of the dust upon the mind is called ignorance when it is not understood; from subtle habitual causes they arise, and gradually the marks of phenomena appear.
When the wind comes, the waves roll; when one desires stillness, the water returns to its natural level. I wish further to speak of the path ahead, yet I fear that later minds might be startled.
The great beast of non-conceptualization roars; the emptiness of nature lets fall frost and hail. The stars scatter, the weeds of defilement are crushed, and though they may run—

Birds flying crosswise fall; the five paths are surely entangled. The four māras neither advance nor retreat. It is like a fierce fire blazing; it is also like a sharp sword cutting. A questioner asked:

"One relies on awakening to know the myriad dharmas, yet the myriad dharmas are originally thus. If one uses the mind by means of illumination, one only attains the use of the mind through illumination;
this should not be a matter within the mind. The Master said: "One relies on awakening to know the myriad dharmas; the myriad dharmas..."

In the end, it is of no avail. If one relies on the mind through artificial illumination, that mind should not exist apart from the [true] mind. Question: As one follows along, there is no discernment, and the luminous mind does not manifest before one.
Furthermore, fearing the mind may become obscured and dull, one applies effort within the mind; yet, the obstacles of ignorance remain difficult to eliminate.
The Master said: "That which exists should not exist; that which is sought should not be sought. Without discrimination, there is true discernment;

by attaining the dark, one brings forth the luminous mind. For the contemplative, the mind merges with its flavor; when the mind is maintained, it entrusts itself to meritorious practice. How could one discuss the difficulty of the 'obstruction of wisdom'?

It becomes a sickness only upon reaching Buddhahood. A question was asked: "In the midst of the process of resolving and communicating [the truth], it is indeed difficult to find a place of rest. Unless one employs practice..."
"O person, this difficulty is ultimately difficult to see. The Master said: "To seek a middle ground for inquiry, inquiry is neither difficult nor easy.
First, observe the mind within the mind; second, infer wisdom within wisdom. Third is the illumination of the inferrer; fourth is the penetration of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);

fifth is the name of liberation; sixth is the equalizing of the true and the false; seventh is the knowledge of the fundamental nature of phenomena; eighth is compassion that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); ninth..."
Pervading the void of the aggregates, the tenth stage is covered by clouds and rain. Reaching the ultimate limit, that which is without perception gives rise to fundamental wisdom from ignorance.

Like reflections appearing as the three karmas, it is like a phantom person manifesting at the crossroads. It does not abide in the limits of emptiness or existence; it should illuminate that which is non-existent within existence.

It does not emerge from within emptiness or existence, nor does it bring emptiness and existence together. This is named "The Middle Way" (Zhèzhōng). The Middle Way is beyond verbal expression; it is peaceful and settled.
There is no place for it to rest; how can its functioning be resolved? A question is asked: There is another kind of person who well understands emptiness and signlessness;

they say with their own mouths that concentration and distraction are one. Furthermore, they claim that within existence there is non-existence, and that both are equally realized as eternally quiescent in their functioning. They know that quiescence is the constant functioning.

To apply the mind is to realize the True Principle; yet it is further said that to employ it is to employ the "useless. Wisdom and skillful means are manifold; though words may seem chaotic, they accord with the Principle.
Suchness is the Principle as-it-is; it is not realized through the conscious mind. Since one knows that realization by the mind is erroneous, mind after mind is further extinguished.
Such a Dharma that is difficult to know cannot be understood even throughout eternal kalpas. Those who apply their minds in this same way cannot be transformed by the Dharma.

The Master said: "There are others who realize emptiness; it is still as discussed in the previous verse. Practicing emptiness and guarding quiescence, one’s consciousness and views may shift for a time.

Even if one realizes that true reality is the measure of the mind, in the end one will find that the original source has not been fully understood. He further spoke of the application of the cessation of the mind, which involves much wisdom and doubt.

This similarity arises precisely because one's nature is not clear. Having already labored in vain seeking emptiness, one dwells for eternal kalpas within obscure consciousness; clinging to marks, one is mostly ignorant.

When light is emitted, the earth immediately trembles—what could that possibly do for you? Question: Regarding the aforementioned practitioner who observes the mind, there is again the difficulty of the "gauze" (ro-huk).
Master: If observing the mind involves gauze, why wait to observe a delusory mind? Moreover, there is no such thing as a delusory mind.
[The Master] replied with composure: "It is difficult to speak of this. He asked: "For a long time there has been a great foundation;

yet when the paths of the mind diverge and intersect, one may perceive subtle obstacles and thereby reach the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). Were it not for a skillful teacher, no one could resolve this principle.
I look up to our Great Master to open the essential gate for us, to guide those who apply their minds so that they do not lose the right path. The Master said:

The fundamental basis of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the ground of karma; within the dream-like realm, differences arise. The subtle body of true reality (*tathatā*) is such that both form and mind are perpetually unaware of it.

Suddenly encountering a man of primordial chaos (*hundun*), who pities and takes compassion for all living beings, he entrusts his doubts to pose extensive questions; though he harbors the principle within, he remains ever luminous.

The dark paths of birth and death have been thoroughly penetrated; his mind is undisturbed by praise or blame. The rustic elder offers a clear response; the Master of Dharma feels humbled by his arrival.
Having received the medicine for all sentient beings, he returns as the very nature of form. In the first year of Xianqing, the local magistrate Xiao Yuanshan [presented this].

He requested that he remain at Jianchu, but the Master declined, saying it was not possible. He then commanded his chief disciple, Zhiran, to enter the room and entrusted him with the seal of the Dharma.

As he was about to descend the mountain, he said to the assembly, "I shall no longer set foot upon this mountain. At that time, the birds and beasts wailed in lamentation for over a month without ceasing.
In front of the hermitage were four large paulownia trees; in the middle month of summer, they suddenly withered and fell. The following year, in the first month...
On the twenty-third day of the month, he passed away without illness. He was interred at Mount Jilong. [Epitaph for] Zen Master Zhinan of Niuhead Mountain.
He was a native of the Hua clan from Qu’a. In his early twenties, his wisdom and courage surpassed those of others.

During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he served as a colonel (*langjiang*). He habitually hung a water-strainer from his bow; wherever he went, he would draw water from it for his own use. [He served] successively...
Having established military merit, at the age of forty, he requested to leave the household life. He entered Mount Wangong in Shuzhou to follow Chan Master Baoyue.
One day, while sitting in meditation, he beheld a strange monk over ten feet tall who said to him, "You have left the household life after eighty lifetimes;

you ought to increase your diligent practice. Having finished speaking, the monk vanished. Once, while the master was in meditative absorption within a valley, the mountain waters suddenly rose in a flood. The master—
He remained serene and unmoving, and the water receded of its own accord. A hunter encountered him there and subsequently reformed his ways to practice virtue.
Furthermore, two men who had previously served with him in the army, hearing that the Master had gone into seclusion, entered the mountains together to seek him out. Upon seeing him, they said:
"General, are you mad? Why do you stay here? The Master said, "I am mad and wish to wake up; you, however, are in the midst of a fit of madness.

"As for those who indulge in lustful sights and lewd sounds, and who covet glory and overstep their station, they wander through birth and death—by what means can they emerge from this on their own? The two men sighed in realization and departed.
Later, the Master went to see Master Rong, where he clarified the Great Matter. Master Rong once said to him, "I have received the seal of approval from Master Xinxin..."
The true instructions: that which has been attained is entirely lost. Even if there were a dharma superior to nirvana, I would say it is likewise like a dream or an illusion.
Now, a single speck of dust flying can obscure the sky, and a single mustard seed falling can cover the earth; you have now already transcended such views—what more need I say?
▲ Chan Master Zhìwéi of Niutou Mountain received the Dharma from Chan Master Fǎchí. Fǎchí was a Dharma grandson of Master Yán.
The Master once composed a verse for his disciple Huìzhōng, saying: "Do not fixate on thoughts; thoughts create the river of birth and death."

"In the ocean of the six realms of saṃsāra, there are no signs of emerging from the long waves. Zhong replied: "Thoughts and perceptions have always been illusory; their nature is itself without beginning or end.
If one realizes this meaning, the long waves shall naturally cease. The Master again showed him a verse, saying: "My original nature is empty and non-existent;
through conditions and delusions, 'self' and 'other' arise. How can one still these deluded sentiments? Return and sit in the place of emptiness. Zhong replied.
[The Master] said: "Emptiness and non-existence are the true substance; where do 'self' and 'other' exist? There is no need to suppress deluded sentiments; simply board the boat of Prajñā.
The Master, knowing that [Zhong] had attained realization, thereupon transmitted the Dharma to him. When Zhong first saw the Master, the Master immediately said, "The Mountain Master has arrived!
Later, when Zhong went out on a visit, the *lingxiao* vine in the Master’s courtyard had completely withered despite the height of summer. His attendants wished to—
They set out to attack him. The Master said, "It must not be done; if Zhong returns, [the trees] will flourish again. When Zhong returned, it was indeed as he had said.

Having received the Dharma, he went to live at Yanzuo Temple, where he served the Dharma with even greater rigor. Throughout his life, he never changed his single robe, and his only utensil was a single cauldron.
Once, there were two storehouses of grain offered for the monks; when thieves watched for an opportunity, tigers guarded them. County Magistrate Zhang Xun arrived at the mountain.
Xuefeng Zhong visited him and asked, "Are there any disciples here? Zhong replied, "There are three or five. Xuefeng said, "May I see them?
Zhong struck his meditation seat, and three tigers roared forth. Xuefeng was struck with terror and withdrew. His spiritual traces were numerous, but they are not recorded in full here.
He had a verse on settling the mind which says: "When person and phenomena are both purified, good and evil are forgotten. With a direct mind of true reality, Bodhi..."

At the Daochang Monastery, on the fifteenth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Dali era, after the assembly of monks had completed the *poṣadha* ceremony, he commanded his attendant to shave his hair and bathe his body.
That night, auspicious clouds covered his vihāra, and celestial music was heard from all four directions. At dawn the following day, he sat peacefully and passed away.
Suddenly, wind and rain arose, shaking and breaking the trees and vegetation, while a white rainbow pierced through the cliffs and valleys. This occurred in the fifth year.
In the spring, his body was cremated, and the resulting *śarīra* relics were beyond counting.

When Chan Master Xuanting of Anguo first visited Chan Master Wei, he was standing in attendance when a monk who lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* asked, "What is the meaning of the dependent origination of true nature?
After a long silence, Master Wei suddenly called out, "Virtuous One, you are currently..."
"At the moment of a single thought arising, this is dependent origination within true nature. Upon these words, the monk attained great enlightenment.
Miaoxi said, "When not even a single thought has arisen, it cannot be that there is no dependent origination.
Someone asked, "If not even a single thought has arisen, what do you call dependent origination? Miaoxi replied, "I simply want you to speak in such a manner."
▲ A monk asked Zen Master Tianzhu Chonghui, “Before Bodhidharma came to this land, was there still Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, “Setting aside for a moment whether it existed before he came, what is the matter right now? The monk said, “I do not understand; I beg the Master to instruct me.
The Master said, “The eternal void of ten thousand ages; the wind and moon of a single day. The monk was speechless. The Master spoke again: “O *śramaṇa*...”
"Understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "How is it from your own side? What does it have to do with whether Bodhidharma came or did not come?
His coming was much like a fortune-teller; seeing that you did not understand, he pierced through the lines of the divination for you.
Once the auspicious or inauspicious has arisen, everything is entirely within your own side—you must see it all yourself. The monk asked, "How so?"
This was Xie Budian. The Master said, "The moment you stepped out the gate, you were already off the mark. A monk asked, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go?
The Master replied, "The peaks of Mount Sheng are high and ever-accumulating emerald green; the bright moonlight of the River Shu shines with radiant splendor."
▲ When Mazu sent a messenger with a letter to Chan Master Daoqin of Jingshan, the letter contained a circle.
Upon opening the seal, the Master placed a dot within the circle and returned it sealed.
National Teacher Zhong said, "Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma. Jingshan Hongzhi said, "When Master Ma spoke, it was mid-winter, a time of severe cold;
when Master Qin spoke, it was early summer, a time of gradual heat. Although the cold and heat differ, both did not miss their respective seasons.
Why, then, did National Teacher Zhong say that Master Qin was still deluded by Master Ma? Do you understand?"
"Without wind, the lotus leaf moves; there must surely be a fish swimming. Xuedou said:
"Setting aside the fact that Jingshan was deluded, if he had presented this to National Teacher Huizhong, what other stratagem could he have employed to avoid being deluded?"
An elder of old said, "At that time, he simply sat down and left it at that. Another said, "He merely drew a line across it.

If it were like this, it would be nothing but a lack of shame. I dare ask: even if all the teachers of the world were each to possess the vajra-eye and perform vast displays of supernatural transformations, could they still avoid it? Xuedou’s insight is something I wish for everyone to know together.
Master Ma himself painted this scene at that time; even then, he was already deluding himself.
While the Master was in the palace of Emperor Daizong of the Tang Dynasty, he stood up when the Emperor approached. The Emperor asked, "Why do you rise, Master?
The Master replied, "How can you, O Patron (*dānapati*), perceive me, a poor monk, within the four modes of deportment?"
Miaoxi said, "If you do not seek it within the four modes of deportment, how can you see the single nation?
Duke Cui Zhao asked, "May I, your disciple, leave the household life to become a monk? The Master replied, "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man."
"This is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. At this, Cui attained a realization.
▲ Zen Master Zhizhe of Yunju on Mount Tiantai was once asked by the monk Jizong of Huayan Monastery:
"What is the meaning of 'seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood'? The Master said: "The pure nature is originally tranquil and still; it is without movement or fluctuation."

It does not belong to existence or non-existence, purity or defilement, long or short, grasping or rejecting; its essence is naturally *xiāorán* (serene and detached). To see clearly in this way is called "seeing one's nature.
Nature is itself Buddha; Buddha is itself nature. Therefore it is said: "Seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. [The questioner asks:

"Since nature is already pure and does not belong to existence or non-existence, how can there be 'seeing'? The Master said: "In seeing, there is nothing seen. [The questioner asks: "If there is nothing seen, why further..."

[The student] said, "There is seeing. The Master said, "Even the locus of seeing does not exist. [The student] asked, "When there is such seeing, who is it that sees? The Master said, "There is no one who can see.
[The student] asked, "Ultimately, what is the principle of this? The Master said, "Do you know? To falsely reckon that things exist is to have subject and object; this is what is called delusion.
Following seeing to give rise to conceptual understanding is to fall into birth and death. As for those who see clearly—"
"That is not so. To see all day long yet never having seen [it]—where one seeks its name, location, substance, or characteristics, they are unobtainable;
when both subject and object are utterly transcended, this is called seeing one's nature. [The student] asked, "Does this nature pervade all places?

The Master said, "There is nowhere it does not pervade. [The student] asked, "Do ordinary people possess it? The Master said, "Since I have just stated that there is nowhere it does not pervade, how could ordinary people not possess it? [The student] asked, "..."
For what reason are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not constrained by birth and death, while ordinary beings alone are entangled in this suffering?
When have they ever attained universality? The Master said: "Ordinary beings, within the nature of purity, calculate the existence of subject and object; thus they fall into birth and death."
The Buddhas and Great Beings well know that within the nature of purity, there is no attachment to existence or non-existence, and thus neither subject nor object is established. [A student] asked:

"If it is explained in this way, then there must be a person who can realize it or fail to realize it. The Master said: "Since even 'realization' itself cannot be apprehended, how could there be a person who realizes?
[The student] asked: "What is the ultimate principle? The Master said: "I shall state the essential point for you; you should reflect upon it immediately."
Within the nature of purity, there are neither ordinary beings nor sages, nor are there those who have attained realization or those who have not. "Ordinary" and "sage" are both merely names.
If one gives rise to understanding based on these names, one falls into birth and death. If one knows that provisional names are unreal, then there is no one who actually corresponds to those names.
It is further said: "This is the ultimate point of finality. If one says, 'I can realize this, but he cannot,' [one remains bound by duality]."

To perceive purity and impurity, or ordinary beings and sages, is a great illness. To form the understanding that there are no ordinary beings or sages is likewise a great illness, as it belongs to the category of denying cause and effect.
To perceive a pure nature in which one may dwell is a great illness; to form the understanding that there is no dwelling is also a great illness.
Nevertheless, although there is no movement within the pure nature, the application of skillful means is not destroyed.
When one gives rise to compassion and arouses pity, such a place of arousal is precisely the nature of total purity;
this may be called "seeing the nature and attaining Buddhahood. Jisong then bowed with great joy in gratitude and withdrew.
▲ Chan Master Niaoke Daolin saw that on Mount Qinwang there was a long pine tree whose branches curled and twisted like a canopy. He subsequently took up residence upon it;
thus he was called Chan Master Niaoke (Nest-of-Birds). Furthermore, a magpie built its nest beside him, becoming naturally tame and familiar with him.
He was also known as Master Quechao. He had an attendant named Huitong. One day, wishing to take his leave, the attendant said, "I have come forth from the household life for the sake of the Dharma.
Since the Master has not deigned to grant me compassionate instruction, I shall now go to various quarters to study the Buddha-Dharma.
The Master said, "As for the Buddha-Dharma, we have a little of it here too. [The attendant] replied:
"What is the Buddha-dharma of the Master? The Master picked up some cloth-hair from his body and blew upon it.
Tong thereupon realized the profound principle.
Daoyi of Dayuanshou said, "It is a pity that this monk took the sounds and colors of the Master’s words as his lifelong realization."
"Know that one's own radiance covers heaven and earth. Miaoxi said, "To critique it in such a manner, you have not yet dreamed of Niaoke.
When Laytan Zhun was about to take his leave, the Master wrote a verse and bestowed it upon him, saying:
"Niaoke blew on the cloth-hair; the old lady acted as attendant. Though the Way of the ancients and the present is the same, Baofeng does not [act as she did]."
It is so. In the second and third months, a gentle breeze fills the world; everywhere the hundred flowers bloom, and distant mountains appear like paintings.
On the crossroads, spring birds sing; from high crags, spring waters cascade. Every single thing is a gate of samādhi, its empty brilliance pervading the vast wilderness.
What a truly wonderful message! I write this to send you back to your home. This is the final word of the patch-robed monk.
"Alas! What words are these? Tonghou later resided at Zhaoxian Temple. Mauling served as the Superintendent of the Six Palaces and was held in high esteem by Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty.
During the spring, he visited the Zhaoyang Palace; while he was in the midst of admiring the flourishing flowers and plants, [the Emperor arrived].
Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air saying: "The marks of illusion arise and pass away without ceasing; they can destroy one's roots of goodness. How can you, O benevolent one, indulge in them?

Tong was thus moved to grief and earnestly petitioned Emperor Dezong for permission to leave the household life. The Emperor, though firmly intent on retaining him, could not refuse and granted his request.

Before long, he attained the Dharma. Later, due to Emperor Wuzong’s suppression of the teachings, he retreated deep into the mountains, and no one knew his whereabouts.
His secular surname was Wu, his given name was Yuanqing, and he was a native of Hangzhou.

At that time, both clergy and laity were holding a Dharma assembly. The Master entered while shaking his mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*). Dharma Master Taoguang asked him, "Why is there this sound at this Dharma assembly?
The Master replied, "If there were no sound, who would know this is an assembly? When Bai Juyi was serving as the governor of Hangzhou, he entered the mountain [to visit the Master].
He went to visit the Master and asked, "The place where the Chan Master resides is extremely dangerous. The Master said, "The Governor’s situation is even more dangerous.

Baizhang said, "My station secures the mountains and rivers; what danger could there be? The Master replied, "When fuel and fire intersect, the nature of consciousness does not rest—is this not dangerous?
He asked again, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Commit no evil."
"Practice all forms of goodness. Baizhang said, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say this.
The Master said, "Though a three-year-old child can say it, an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it. Baizhang bowed and withdrew.

A monk of eminent standing named Zhu Faxing requested that Jīvaka preach the Dharma. Jīvaka said, "The assembly must gather before it may be done.
Faxing then gathered the multitude. Jīvaka ascended the seat and said: "Guard your mouth and restrain your body and mind; Be careful not to commit any evils. Practice the one..."

"Excellent! In this way, one attains transcendence. Having said this, he fell silent. Dharmagupta (Faxing) requested again, saying, "I pray that the Venerable One will grant me instruction on the meaning of these verses, which I have not yet heard; even an eight-year-old boy has already memorized them by heart.

Kāśyapa (Yù) smiled and said, "Though an eight-year-old may recite them, a hundred-year-old who does not practice them gains nothing from the recitation. Everyone knows how to revere those who have attained the Way."
"Those who do not know that the Way is attained through practice—how tragic! Though my words are few, those who practice will benefit greatly.
On the tenth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Changqing era, he said to his attendant, "My life is now at its end. Having finished speaking, he sat and passed away.
Some say there was one named Yuanshou; perhaps this was a posthumous title for the Master.

From that time on, practitioners gathered like the spokes of a wheel. Two monks, Tanran and Huairang, arrived there.
"San. He asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? The Master said, "Why do you not ask about your own meaning?

The recorder said, "Why do you not record it? The Master replied, "The body of birth and death is like a revolving wheel;

From the initial consciousness until the cessation of the moving phase, it is exactly like this. How could years, months, or dates be recorded?"
The Emperor bowed his forehead to the ground and received [the teaching] with faith. After the Zhongzong ascended the throne, he honored him even more deeply.
In the third year of the Shenglong era, he took leave to return to Mount Song. On the third day of the third month, he addressed his disciples, saying:

"When I die, place my corpse in the forest to await the wild fire to consume it. Suddenly, Master Wanhui arrived; the Master was acting wildly, and they held hands and conversed. Those attending nearby listened intently.
He did not comprehend this at all. On the eighth day, he closed his door, lay down, and passed away peacefully. He was one hundred twenty-eight years of age.

In the second year of the Xiāntiān era, a stupa was constructed to enshrine them.
▲ Chan Master Shouzhuo obtained the Dharma from Xiu of the Northern School. He selected Mount Sanfeng in Shouzhou to build a thatched hut and reside there.
There was often a rustic man whose appearance was simple and plain, and whose speech was strange and unconventional.

At times, he would suddenly transform into the forms of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, celestial immortals, and the like; at other times, he would emit divine light or produce sounds. Such were the master’s studies.
Those who merely beheld him were all unable to fathom his nature. This continued for ten years, after which he suddenly vanished without a trace or shadow. The Master addressed the assembly, saying:
"The rustic has performed many-colored conjuring tricks to dazzle and delude people; it required nothing more than this old monk’s refusal to see or hear them."
Their skillful means are finite; I have not seen or heard of anything that is inexhaustible.
Master Puzao Duo of Mount Song did not disclose his name or lineage. His words and deeds were unfathomable, and he lived in seclusion on Mount Song.

In a mountain valley there was a shrine that was extremely efficacious. In the hall there was only a single hearth, yet offerings were made from near and far without ceasing, and many living beings were slaughtered for sacrifice.
One day, the Master led his attendant monks into the shrine and struck the hearth three times with his staff, saying: "Ho!"
"This stove is merely composed of clay and tiles. From where does the 'saint' come? From where does the 'spirit' arise? Yet you go on to slaughter living beings.
He struck it three more times, and the stove immediately collapsed and fell apart. In a moment, a man appeared wearing a green robe and a tall cap, prostrating himself before the Master.

"Karmic retribution! Today, having received the Master’s teaching on the Dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma*), we have been liberated from this place and reborn among the devas.
We have come specifically to express our gratitude. The Master said, "This is your own inherent nature; it is not something I have forcefully taught you. The spirit prostrated once more and vanished.
A short while later, an attendant monk asked, "We have served the Master for a long time, yet we have never received his instructions. What did the stove god receive?"
[The monk] directly grasped the essential meaning and immediately attained rebirth in heaven. The Master said, "I simply told him that it was composed of clay and tiles;
there was no other principle to explain to him. The attendant monk remained silent. The Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "Why do you not understand the nature that is inherently present? The attendant monks then bowed. The Master said, "Broken! Broken!"
"A fall! A fall!
Later, Zen Master Yifu recounted this to National Teacher An. National Teacher An sighed and said, "This man has realized that things and self are of one suchness;
he may be called like the bright moon in the sky—there is nowhere it does not reach. It is difficult to grasp the flow of his discourse. Yifu...

A question was asked: "I do not yet understand who it is that can grasp the thread of his discourse. Baizhang said, "It is those who do not know. A monk asked, "What is it like when every single thing is formless? The Master said, "If you prostrate, then it is only you and not I; if you do not prostrate, then it is only I and not you. The monk then bowed in thanks. The Master said, "That which is originally possessed is a thing that is not a thing. What is meant? It is this very principle. If you can see into this, then you will know that the Buddhas of the three times and all sentient beings are fundamentally one and the same. If you cannot see into this, then you will fall into the error of dualistic grasping and rejecting. Therefore, the Master said: "The nature of the Way is originally complete; there is no need for cultivation. If you seek through cultivation, you will only increase your delusion. This is why it is said that the Way is not something to be sought. If you can awaken to this, you will realize that the myriad phenomena are all the Buddha-nature. If you do not awaken to this, you will be lost in the confusion of the six paths. Therefore, the Master said: "When the mind is at rest, it is the Buddha; when the mind is active, it is a sentient being. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand dharmas are all the One Mind. If you do not see into this, then you will be caught in the net of the various views. Therefore, the Master said: "The Dharma is not something to be attained; it is only to be realized within oneself. If you can see into this, then you will know that the three realms are empty and still, and that the ten directions are originally tranquil. If you do not see into this, then you will be bound by the fetters of birth and death. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not far off; it is simply that people themselves create distance. If you can see into this, then you will know that the body is the Dharma-body and the mind is the Wisdom-mind. If you do not see into this, then you will be obscured by the clouds of ignorance. Therefore, the Master said: "To see the nature is to become a Buddha; to lose the nature is to become a sentient being. If you can see into this, then you will know that the myriad things are all the True Suchness. If you do not see into this, then you will be trapped in the cycle of samsara. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be grasped; it is only to be maintained in accordance with its nature. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand phenomena are all the Great Function. If you do not see into this, then you will be lost in the maze of the provisional teachings. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be spoken of; it is only to be transmitted from mind to mind. If you can see into this, then you will know that the three bodies are originally one and the four wisdoms are fundamentally non-dual. If you do not see into this, then you will be mired in the distinctions of names and forms. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be practiced; it is only to be lived in accord with reality. If you can see into this, then you will know that the six senses are the six paramitas and the five aggregates are the five wisdoms. If you do not see into this, then you will be entangled in the nets of the afflictions. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be sought; it is only to be found within the ordinary. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand dharmas are all the Unborn. If you do not see into this, then you will be caught in the snare of birth and extinction. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be attained; it is only to be realized in the present moment. If you can see into this, then you will know that the three worlds are empty and the eight consciousnesses are still. If you do not see into this, then you will be lost in the confusion of the twelve links of dependent origination. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be cultivated; it is only to be maintained in its natural state. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand things are all the Great Mirror Wisdom. If you do not see into this, then you will be obscured by the clouds of the five skandhas. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be analyzed; it is only to be experienced directly. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten directions are the Pure Land and the six paths are the Lotus Treasury. If you do not see into this, then you will be trapped in the cage of the three poisons. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be understood; it is only to be awakened to. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand phenomena are all the Tathagata-garbha. If you do not see into this, then you will be lost in the darkness of the four inversions. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be measured; it is only to be realized in the midst of activity. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand dharmas are all the Great Compassion. If you do not see into this, then you will be bound by the fetters of the eight winds. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be sought after; it is only to be found in the midst of the mundane. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand things are all the Great Emptiness. If you do not see into this, then you will be caught in the net of the two extremes. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be grasped; it is only to be let go of. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand phenomena are all the Great Stillness. If you do not see into this, then you will be lost in the confusion of the three times. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be attained; it is only to be realized in the present moment. If you can see into this, then you will know that the ten thousand dharmas are all the Unborn. If you do not see into this, then you will be caught in the snare of birth and extinction. Therefore, the Master said: "The Way is not something to be attained; it is only to be realized in the present moment. If you can see into this, then you will know that the three worlds are empty and the eight consciousnesses are still. If you do not see into this, then you will be lost in the confusion of the twelve links of dependent origination.
