By means of the Way, if the mind can transform things, one is identical to the Tathāgata.
▲ Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song was a native of Ique; his surname was Li. He received the Dharma from National Teacher An and lived in seclusion at Pangwu on the mountain.
One day, a divine being led a retinue to visit the Master. Upon seeing their appearance, the Master marveled at their extraordinary majesty.
He was greatly astonished. The Master then asked, "Welcome, virtuous one! Why have you come here? He replied, "Do you not recognize me, Master?
The Master said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; I view them all with a single eye. How could I make such distinctions?
He said, "I am the mountain deity of this peak; I can bring life and death upon people. How can you, Master, view me with a single eye? The Master said, "I am originally..."
"I am unborn; how could you cause me to die? I regard my body as equal to space, and I regard myself as equal to you.
Can you destroy space or yourself? If you could indeed destroy space and yourself, then I would be neither born nor extinguished.
Since you cannot even do this, how much less can you bring about my birth or death? The Spirit bowed his head and said, "I too am intelligent and upright."
"Regarding other deities, how could one know that the Teacher possesses such vast wisdom and eloquence? I pray that you grant me the true precepts so that I may cross over the world.
The Teacher said, "Since you have requested the precepts, you already possess them. Why is this? Because there are no precepts apart from the precepts themselves."
"What precepts are these? The deity said, "These are principles. I have heard them only vaguely; I seek only the Master’s precepts.
The Master then prepared a seat for him, held the incense burner, and straightened the desk, saying, "I confer upon you the five precepts.

If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can'; if you cannot, you should say 'No'. [The deity] said, "I respectfully receive the instruction. The Master said, "Can you refrain from sexual misconduct?"
[The Master asked: "Is it so? [He] replied, "I am also married. The Master said, "I do not mean this; I mean that you must be free from lustful desire.
[He] replied, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from stealing? [He] replied, "Why would I lack anything? How could I take what is not mine by theft? The Master said, "I do not mean this;
I mean that you must not bring blessings upon the licentious nor bring calamities upon the virtuous. [He] replied, "I can. The Master said, "Can you refrain from..."
“Do you kill? He replied, “I truly hold the handle of authority; how could I say I do not kill? The Master said, “I do not mean this.
I mean that there may be excesses, errors, doubts, or confusions. He replied, “I can [avoid these]. The Master said, “Can you avoid being arbitrary?

He replied, “I am upright; how could I be arbitrary? The Master said, “I do not mean this. I mean that your actions before and after may not accord with the Will of Heaven. He replied, “I can. The Master said, “You...”
"Are you not ruined by alcohol? He replied, "I am able. The Master said, "The above constitutes the Buddha's precepts.
He further said, "Maintain them with a conscious mind, yet do not cling to them with a constrained mind; act for the sake of others with a conscious mind, yet do not harbor thoughts of your own body.

If one can be thus, then though born before heaven and earth, one does not become a mere vital essence; though dying after heaven and earth, one does not become old. Throughout the day, one undergoes transformation."

Yet he does not move; he remains utterly silent and does not cease. To believe this means that though he marries, it is not for the sake of a wife; though he faces others, it is not for the sake of acquisition;
though he holds office, it is not for the sake of power; though he acts, it is not for the sake of past habit; and though he is intoxicated, it is not for the sake of delusion.

If one can be without mind regarding the myriad things, then indulging in desires will not constitute lust; if blessings fall upon the licentious and calamities upon the virtuous, it will not constitute theft;
if there is confusion, error, suspicion, or entanglement, it will not constitute killing; if one’s actions contradict the Way of Heaven in sequence, it will not constitute falsehood;

if one is muddled, deluded, or inverted, it will not constitute intoxication. This is called being without mind. Without mind, there are no precepts; without precepts, there is no mind. There is neither Buddha nor Sangha.
[The Master said: "There is no 'you' and there is no 'self. Who, then, would observe the precepts? The spirit said, "My supernatural powers are second only to those of the Buddha.
The Master said, "Of your ten supernatural powers, you possess five and lack five. Of the Buddha's ten, he possesses seven and lacks three.

The spirit drew back in hesitation, withdrew from his seat, and knelt to ask, "May I hear them? The Master said, "You can travel eastward through the heavens to the realm of the Supreme Lord (Shangdi)."
"And can you move the seven celestial bodies of the west? He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "Can you seize the terrestrial spirits, melt the Five Peaks, and bind the Four Seas?
He replied, "I cannot. The Master said, "This is called the 'five impossibilities.

A Buddha can empty all phenomena and realize the wisdom of the myriad dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma. A Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaust the span of billions of kalpas..."
There are three things that cannot be done: though one may possess the means, one cannot transform those with whom one lacks a karmic connection;

the Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, yet he cannot exhaust the realm of all sentient beings. Furthermore, fixed karma is not eternal, and the absence of a karmic connection is likewise but for a single lifetime.

The realm of sentient beings is fundamentally without increase or decrease; throughout it, not a single person can act as its master. Where there is a dharma but no master, this is called the "non-existence of dharma.
Where there is no dharma and no master, this is called the "mindless state. As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*);
he is simply able, through the mindless state, to penetrate all dharmas as they truly are. The Spirit said: "I am indeed shallow [in my understanding]."

[The disciple] said, "I am ignorant; I have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The precepts bestowed upon me by my teacher, I shall surely practice. Now I wish to repay your compassionate virtue, doing whatever I am capable of.
The teacher said, "I contemplate the body as having no substance and contemplate all phenomena (*dharma*) as impermanent (*anitya*). Being but a lump of flesh, what further desire could there be?"
The deity said, "Master, you must surely command me to perform a worldly task to display my minor divine powers, so that these five types of people—
those who have already resolved [to attain enlightenment], those who have first resolved, those who have not yet resolved, those who do not believe, and those who will certainly come to believe—

may behold my divine traces and know that there are Buddhas and deities, that there is capability and incapability, and that there is the spontaneous and the non-spontaneous. The Master said, "Do nothing."
"This is the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). This is right. The spirit said, "The Buddha also commanded spirits to protect the Dharma. How could you, Master, now violate and rebel against the Buddha?
I pray that you will grant me instruction according to your will. The Master, having no choice, spoke: "At Dongnyan Temple, the surrounding area is vast and treeless.

To the north there is a mountain with trees, yet it does not form a protective screen behind the temple. Can you move the trees from the northern ridge to the eastern slope? The spirit replied, "I have already done so."
"I have received your command. However, there will surely be clamor and commotion during the night; I pray that you, Master, do not be alarmed. Having spoken, he prostrated himself and departed.
The Master saw him off at the gate and watched him as he went, observing that his ceremonial retinue moved in a long, winding procession like those of a sovereign.

That very evening, a violent wind indeed arose with thundering peals of lightning, and the buildings shook and swayed. The Master said, "The words of the spirit have been verified. The assembly need have no fear. On the following day...
The weather cleared. Then the pines and cypresses of the northern cliff all shifted to the eastern ridge, standing there in dense, orderly rows.

The Master said to his disciples, "Do not let outsiders know of this; people will regard me as a sorcerer. In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the year of Bingchen, he instructed his followers, saying, "When I first resided at this temple, it was on the eastern ridge.
When I pass away, you must place my remains there. Having finished speaking, he appeared as if casting off a discarded shell.
▲ Chan Master Weizheng of Zhongnan Mountain received the Dharma from Pujì. He built a hermitage at Taìyì. Emperor Wénzōng of the Táng dynasty was fond of clams;
the coastal fishermen who supplied them in succession were greatly burdened by the labor. One day, among the imperial provisions, there was one that would not open despite being cracked.

The Emperor, finding it strange, immediately burned incense and prayed for it to open. It then opened, revealing the form and countenance of a Bodhisattva, complete with all the marks of sanctity. Thereupon...
It was stored in a casket made of *suvarṇa*, *śāli* rice, and *candana* sandalwood and bestowed upon Xingshan Temple for the monastic community to behold and venerate.

The Emperor asked his ministers, "What auspicious omen is this? Some reported that the Master should be prepared to provide counsel. Thereupon, the Master was summoned and questioned regarding the matter.
The Master replied, "Your servant has heard that things do not respond without cause; this is merely to inspire the Emperor’s faith. Thus, a sutra says: 'One should, by means of this...'"

"To those whose bodies are ready for deliverance, he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma for them. The Emperor said, "The Bodhisattva’s body has indeed appeared, but I have not yet heard him preach the Dharma.
The Master asked, "Does Your Majesty perceive this as permanent or impermanent? Do you believe it or not?
The Emperor replied, "This is a rare occurrence; I believe it deeply. The Master said, "Your Majesty has already heard the preaching of the Dharma."
The Emperor was greatly pleased. He issued an edict for all monasteries throughout the realm to establish statues of Avalokiteśvara, while retaining the Master in the inner palace chapel.

The Master repeatedly requested to return home, whereupon the Emperor decreed that he reside at Shengshou Temple. As soon as Emperor Wuzong ascended the throne, the Master suddenly retired to live in seclusion on Mount Zhongnan.
When people asked why, he replied, "I am avoiding my enemies. Later, his body was cremated; forty-nine *śarīras* were collected, and a stupa was erected for them.
A monk asked Master Jùngji of Mount Song: "What is one who practices the path of goodness? The Master said, "Carrying a cangue."
Daisō asked, "What is the practice of one who commits evil? The Master said, "Cultivate dhyāna and enter samādhi.

The monk said, "I am of shallow capacity; I beg the Master to point directly. The Master said, "If you ask me about evil, evil does not follow from good. If you ask me about good, good does not follow from evil.
After the monk had been silent for a long time, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "An evil person has no thoughts of goodness."
A good person has no evil mind. Thus it is said: "Good and evil are like floating clouds; neither has a place of arising or ceasing.
Upon these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Later, when Pokuo Duowen heard this account, he remarked, "This man has realized that all dharmas are non-arising."
Miaoxi said, "What can you do? You are merely creating deluded thoughts before your own skull.
▲ Chan Master Benjing of Sijingshan was a native of Jangzhou and the son of the Zhang family. He donned the monastic robes at a young age and received his dharma-transmission from Caoxi.
He resided at Sijingshan. Later, during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, the imperial envoy Yang Guangting went to gather *changchun* (evergreen) plants.

Feng went to the mountain and met the Master. Their discussion was profound and far-reaching. Upon his return, he reported this to the imperial court, and by imperial decree, the Master was summoned to the Inner Court (Neidaochang) to expound the principles of Buddhism alongside renowned monks and eminent scholars of the two streets.

A monk named Chan Master Yuan asked, "According to what you perceive, O Chan Master, what constitutes the Way? The Master replied, "A mindless state is the Way. Yuan said, "The Way arises because of the mind; how can you say it is non-existent?"
"The mind is the Way. The Master said, "The Way is fundamentally nameless; it is because of the mind that the Way is named. If the name 'mind' were real, then the Way would not be empty.
Since the mind, when investigated to its limit, is non-existent, upon what could the Way be established? Both are equally illusory; they are all merely provisional names.
Yuan said, "Does the Chan Master perceive body and mind as being the Way? The Master said, "The body and mind of this mountain monk have been the Way from the very beginning. Yuan—
[The student] said: "Just now you said that 'no-mind' is the Way, but now you say that body and mind are fundamentally the Way.

Are these not contradictory? The Master said: "'No-mind' is the Way. When the mind is extinguished, the Way is non-existent. Mind and the Way are one and the same; therefore, I say that 'no-mind' is the Way."
Body and mind are fundamentally the Way; the Way is also fundamentally body and mind. Since body and mind are fundamentally empty, the Way is likewise exhausted at its source and non-existent.
Yuan said, "Master Guan’s physical form is quite small, yet he understands this principle. The Master said, "Virtuous One, you see only my marks;
you do not see my marklessness. That which sees marks is what you, Virtuous One, perceive."
The Sūtra says: "All that has marks is entirely false and illusory. If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Way.
If one takes marks to be real, one will not be able to see the Way even after the exhaustion of kalpas. Yuan said: "I now request the Master to explain the markless within the realm of marks.
The Master said: "The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: 'The four great elements have no master; the body likewise has no self. It is without self..."

"What you have seen accords with the Way. Venerable sir, if you consider the four great elements to have a master who is the self, and if you harbor this view of a self, you shall not realize the Way even after an entire kalpa.
Upon hearing these words from afar, [Hui]yuan turned pale with alarm. The Master had a verse that said: "The four great elements have no master and are like water;
Encountering curves and meeting straightness, they know neither 'self' nor 'other. In both the pure and the defiled, no mind arises; Whether obstructed or released, what difference is there?"
Formerly, there were two points of contention. [The first was: "If touching objects is merely like water and devoid of mind, then what matters it whether one acts freely in the world?
Master Zhiming asked: "If you say that being without mind is the Way, then tiles and pebbles, which are also without mind, should also be the Way.

Furthermore, if you say that body and mind are fundamentally the Way, then since all four modes of birth and ten categories of beings possess body and mind, they too should be the Way. The Master said: "Great..."

If one interprets virtue through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it is worlds apart from the Way; such a person is merely seeking seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, rather than being a seeker of the Way.
As the Sūtra says: "There are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Since even the six sense faculties do not exist, upon what could seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing be established?
When traced to their source, they are non-existent; where, then, can the mind dwell? How could one not [realize this]?
He was like grass, trees, tiles, and rubble, clearly maintaining a vow of silence. The Master had a verse that said: "In seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing there is no obstruction;
In sounds, smells, tastes, and touches, one is always in samādhi. Like a bird flying through the air, simply so it goes— Without grasping or rejecting, without hatred or love."
"If one meets with the proper conditions while fundamentally having no mind, only then can one be called Avalokiteśvara.
Zen Master Zhen asked, "If the Way is without mind, does the Buddha have a mind? Are the Buddha and the Way one or two? The Master replied, "Neither one nor two."
[The interlocutor] said: "The Buddha saves sentient beings because he possesses a mind; the Way does not save people because it is without mind.

One saves and one does not save—how can there be no duality? The Master said: "If you say that the Buddha saves sentient beings while the Way has no such saving, this is for you, Great Virtue, to have falsely given rise to dualistic views.
As for a mountain monk like me, it is not so: 'Buddha' is a hollow name, and the 'Way' is also a false establishment."

Both are unreal; they are entirely provisional names. Within a single provisionality, how can one distinguish between two? [The questioner] says: "Buddha" and "the Way"—these arise from provisional names.
At the moment these names are established, who is it that establishes them? If there were an establisher, how could one say they do not exist?
The Master said: "Buddha" and "the Way" are established because of the mind. When one investigates the mind that establishes them, the mind, too, is non-existent. Mind...
Since both are non-existent, one realizes that neither is real; knowing them to be like dreams and illusions, one realizes their fundamental emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

To forcibly establish the two names "Buddha" and "Path" is the view and understanding of those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). The Master, on this account, spoke these verses on non-cultivation and non-action: "If one sees the Path, then one cultivates it;
if one does not see it, what is there to cultivate? The nature of the Path is like empty space; in empty space, what is there to cultivate? [The text continues: ...pervasive...
Those who contemplate the path of cultivation are like those who beat out fire to seek bubbles; they merely watch a puppet being manipulated, which stops all at once when the strings snap.
Chan Master Faka asked: "If both Buddha and the Way are but provisional names, then the twelve divisions of the teachings must also be unreal."
"Why have all the venerable masters of the past said that one cultivates the Way? The Master said, "Virtuous One, you have misunderstood the meaning of the scriptures.
The Way is fundamentally without cultivation, yet you, Virtuous One, cultivate it forcefully. The Way is fundamentally without action, yet you, Virtuous One, act forcefully.

The Way is fundamentally without affairs, yet you forcefully create many affairs. The Way is fundamentally without knowledge, yet within it you forcefully seek to know. Such a view is contrary to the Way. [He continued] from before...
"Venerable elders should not speak thus; it is simply that you, Great Virtue, do not understand. Please reflect upon this. The Master had a verse which said:

"The essence of the Way is fundamentally without cultivation; Without cultivating, one naturally accords with the Way. If one gives rise to a mind of 'cultivating the Way,' This person does not understand the Way.

They cast aside their single true nature And enter once more into a state of clamor and confusion. Should they suddenly encounter a person who cultivates the Way, The first thing is never to point toward the Way. An.

The Chan Master asked: "If the Way is a provisional name and the Buddha is said to be falsely established, and even the twelve divisions of the teachings are for the purpose of guiding beings and saving sentient beings—then all of these are false.
What, then, is true? The Master replied: "It is because there is falsehood that we employ the 'true' in contrast to it.

When one investigates the nature of falsehood to its root, it is found to be empty; how, then, could the 'true' ever have existed? Therefore, know that both the true and the false are entirely provisional names. (2)
Regarding the remedial treatment of phenomena: they possess no substantial reality whatsoever; when their fundamental source is investigated, all are entirely empty. [The student] asks:

"Since you say that all things are illusory, and illusion is identical to the Real, with no distinction between the Real and the illusory, what then is this? The Master said: "If one asks 'what is it,' [one has already fallen into conceptualization]."
All things are likewise illusory. As the Sūtra says: "There is nothing similar; there is no analogy. The path of language is cut off, like a bird flying through the sky.
How can one feel shame or submission? The Master has a verse that says: "Pushing toward the Real, the Real has no marks; Exhausting the illusory, the illusory has no form.

Turning back to observe the mind that pushes and exhausts, One knows that this mind, too, is but a provisional name. Realizing the Way is also like this: In the end, it is simply stillness. This is the Chan of penetrating one's nature.
The Master asked: "A Chan master reaches the most wondrous and the most subtle; true emptiness is where both extremes vanish, and the paths of Buddha and the world are both forgotten.

One cultivates the emptiness of nature, for names and forms are not real, and the world is like an illusion—all are but provisional designations. When one understands it thus, one must not sever the two roots of sentient beings:
good and evil. The Master said: "The two roots of good and evil both arise because of the mind. If you exhaustively investigate the mind and find that it exists..."

The sense-faculties (*indriya*) are likewise not empty. Since the mind, upon investigation, is found to be non-existent, by what cause could the faculties be established? A sutra says: "Wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are produced through transformation from the mind;

the causal conditions of good and evil karma are fundamentally without reality. The Master has a verse that says: "Since the wholesome arises from the mind, how could the unwholesome be separate from the mind?
Wholesomeness and unwholesomeness are external conditions; they do not truly exist within the mind. If one abandons evil, where would it be sent? If one takes [the wholesome],..."
"Who can be made to guard it well? Alas for those caught in dualistic views; they run back and forth, clinging to both ends.
If one awakens to the fact that there is fundamentally no mind, only then will one repent of former faults. Furthermore, an attendant asked: "From where does this body come?
After a hundred years, where does it return? The Master said: "It is like a person in a dream: from where does he come when dreaming, and from where does he go upon waking?"

[The student] departed. [The Master] said: "When one is dreaming, it cannot be said that it does not exist; once awakened, it cannot be said that it exists. Although there is existence and non-existence, their coming and going leave no trace.
The Master said: "This body of mine is also like a dream. He then presented this verse: "Viewing life as being like a dream,"

In a dream, there is truly turmoil; upon suddenly awakening, all things cease. It is just like the realization one has while still asleep: the wise understand that the dream is an illusion, while the deluded take the dream’s clamor as real.
To understand the dream is one thing, yet once awakened, there is no separate awakening—whether in wealth and honor or in poverty and low station.
There was no further path for conceptual discrimination. In the second year of the Shangyuan era, he passed into stillness (*nirvāṇa*).

He was posthumously titled Chan Master Daxiao. National Teacher Huizhong of Nanyang was the son of the Ran family of Zhuji. Having received the Dharma at Caoxi, he resided at Dangzi Valley on Mount Baitia in Nanyang.
For over forty years, he did not descend from the mountain. His spiritual practice became renowned, and Emperor Suzong [honored] the Master...

The Master was invited to reside at Qianfu Monastery. When the Tripitaka Master from Western Heaven, known as "Big-Ears," arrived in the capital, he claimed to have attained the supernormal power of reading others' minds.
The Emperor ordered the Master to test him. As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw the Master, he prostrated himself and stood to the right. The Master asked:
“Have you attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others? He replied, “I dare not say so. The Master said, “Tell me, where am I right now?
He said, “The Master is the teacher of this entire nation; how could you have gone off to West Shu to watch the boat races?
After a long silence, the Master asked again, “Tell me, where am I right now? He said, “The Master is the teacher of this entire nation.”
The Master said, "How is it that you are instead watching a monkey being entertained at Tianjin Bridge?
After a long silence, the Master asked again, "Tell me, where is this old monk right now? Zang was unable to fathom this. The Master rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit!
Where is your 'penetration of others' minds' (paracittajñāna)? Zang had no reply.
Later, a monk asked Xuansha, "Do you say that he was seen on the previous two occasions?
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "The Great-Eared Tripitaka Master did not see the National Teacher on his third attempt. I wonder where the National Teacher was?
Zhaozhou said, "He was on top of the Tripitaka Master's nostrils. Later, the monk asked Xuansha, "Since he was on the nostrils..."
[The Master] asked, "Why do you not see it? Sandou replied, "It is precisely because it is too close.

Baizhang Wenduan said, "If National Teacher [Huairang] were on the tip of the nose of Tripitaka Master [Xuanzang], how could it be difficult to see? One simply does not realize that the National Teacher was right upon Tripitaka’s eyes."
One day he called his attendant. The attendant responded. Thus he called him three times and was answered three times. The Master said, "I thought it was I who had failed you;
it turns out, rather, that you have failed me."
Miaoxi said: "In the Zen forests, this is called 'The National Teacher’s Three Calls to the Attendant' story.
From this point on, there has been a continuous string of complications. Only Xuedou saw through the very marrow of the ancients, saying: 'The National Teacher called the attendant three times.'"
"Pointing, yet not reaching. Xuefeng said, "It is clearly so. The attendant responded three times. "Reaching, yet not pointing.
Xuefeng said, "Yet it is not like that. I thought I was betraying you; who would have known you were betraying me?
You cannot deceive Xuedou. Xuefeng said, "Who says so? He then called to the assembly, saying, "What a fine 'you cannot deceive Xuedou. Nevertheless..."
Thus it is. Xuedou could not deceive Miaoxi; Miaoxi could not deceive the assembly; and the assembly could not deceive the pillar.
Xuansha said, "The attendant understands. Xuedou said, "Letting the prisoner go on parole only increases his cleverness.
Miaoxi said, "Two prizes for one wager. Yunmen asked, "What is the National Teacher’s betrayal?"
Regarding the passage on "the attendant's point": To understand it is itself groundless. Xuedou said, "In truth, he did not understand.
Xizong said, "This is what Xuefeng meant. Yunmen further asked, "What is the point where the attendant betrayed the National Teacher?
[Yunmen replied,] "Even if one were to grind one's bones to powder, one could never repay him. Xuedou said, "Groundless, groundless! Xizong said, "He drew the arrow by leaning against the target."
Fayan said, "Go for now; come back at another time. Xuedou said, "He cannot deceive me. Xiji said, "In fact, it was Fayan who understood.
Xinghua said, "One blind man leading a crowd of blind men. Xuedou said, "Truly blind. Xiji said, [and agreed].
These words came from the Master’s own mouth. Xuánjué questioned a monk, saying, “Where is the place where the attendant understands?
The monk said, “If he did not understand, how could he have been able to respond thus? Xuánjué said, “You have little understanding.
He further said, “If you can see into this, then you will recognize Xuánshā. [The monk] Xǐ said, “It puts me to shame! Cùyán Zhī said, “The State...”
The Master’s attendant lacked total understanding. Xueji said, “He is still somewhat better than that.
Touzi said, “Why do you press people so hard? Xuedou said, “A fellow who hides his roots. Xueji said, “When the principle is long, one follows it.
He added, “Only the talkative old master Zhaozhou could provide a footnote that leaves people in doubt. A monk asked, “Regarding the National Teacher’s three [questions]...”
He called to his attendant. "What was the meaning of this? Zhaozhou said, "It is like a person writing characters in the dark;

though the characters are not formed, the traces of the brushstrokes are already manifest. Xuedou then gave a shout. Xizong said, "Tell me, does this shout belong to the side of the National Teacher’s attendant, or does it belong to the side of Zhaozhou?
He followed this by giving another shout and then said, "If it were not for [Zhaozhou's] life-force..."
The five-colored cords of the roots are severed. How can one penetrate through this point? Xuedou said:
"If someone were to ask Xuedou, Xuedou would simply strike them. This too is for the sake of having the various quarters examine it.
Xiji said: "The heart of a thief is always suspicious. Xuedou further had a verse which says: "The meeting of teacher and disciple is no light matter. Xiji said: "These words..."

There are two ways of carrying [the burden]. When there is no business, they go together through the grass. Xixi said, "The people of Puzhou send off a thief; whether you carry it or I carry it, do not ask. Xixi said, "Let it go; wait until it cools, then look at it.
Let them compete for it head-to-head as they will under heaven. Xixi said, "If you rest right now, then rest;

if you seek the moment of realization, there is no time of realization. He spoke again: *Note: This passage is a dialogue from the *Wumen guan* (The Gateless Barrier), attributed to Wumen Huikai. It concerns the story of the monk Xixi (Xixi) and his master.*
If you seek a profound and subtle understanding, you will simply manage to interpret the story of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant.
Wherein lies the National Teacher’s betrayal of the attendant? And wherein lies the attendant’s betrayal of the National Teacher?
What connection could there be? The Goose King selects milk; he has never been of the same class as the duck.
This very point is the National Teacher’s work upon the edge of a sword. It is also said: "Does the National Teacher see the attendant? Does the attendant see the National Teacher?"
Nanquan arrived for an audience. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Jiangxi. The Master said, "Have you brought back the portrait of Master Ma?
He replied, "This very one here. The Master said, "What about the one behind it? Nanquan then fell silent.
Changqing said, "It is very much like not knowing. Baofu said, "He almost did not reach this place of yours, Master.
Yunju Xi said, "These two venerable elders both support him from behind; as for Nanquan’s 'resting,' does it support him in front or support him from behind?"
Emperor Suzong asked, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies? The Master stood up and said, "Do you understand?
The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Hand me the pure pitcher. He then asked, "What is the Samādhi of Non-contention?
The Master said, "The donor walks upon the crown of Vairocana’s head. The Emperor asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Do not mistake it for yourself."
The Pure Dharma-body of oneself. Miaoxi said:
"Do you all wish to see National Teacher Zhong? He is right within your own eyes. You miss him when opening your eyes;
you miss him when closing your eyes. Since he is already within your eyes, why do you miss him?"
When Miaoxi spoke thus, he too missed the mark by no small measure.
When Emperor Suzong arrived, the Master pointed to a stone lion and said, "Your Majesty, this stone lion is extraordinary;

please provide a turning word for it. The Emperor replied, "I am unable to provide a turning word; I request that you, Master, provide one. The Master said, "This mountain monk commits an offense. Later—
Danyuan asked, "Does the Emperor understand? The Master said, "Let us set aside whether the Emperor understands; how do you understand it?
Xuansha Bei remarked, "The Great National Teacher was exposed by his attendant."
Emperor Suzong invited him to watch a performance. The Master said, "Donor, what kind of mood do you have for watching a play?
Miaoxi raised this case and said: "Chan Master Fayun Yuan Tong asked, 'Tell me, where did the National Teacher land?
I, Miaoxi, dare to ask all of you: tell me, where did Chan Master Yuan Tong land? Upon this—
This was clearly seen. The Three Elders lived not far from one another.
When Master [Nanquan] came to visit Danxia, he happened to find him asleep. He then asked the attendant, Danyuan, saying, "Is the National Teacher in?"
The other said, "It is right here; it is simply that you do not see the guest. Xiangyun said, "You are going too far. The other said, "Do not say so;
even with Buddha-eyes one cannot see it. Xiangyun said, "Dragons give birth to dragon cubs; phoenixes give birth to phoenix chicks.
When the Master woke from his sleep, the attendant reported this to him. The Master struck him twenty blows and drove him out. Hearing of this, Danxia said, "He is truly no impostor."
Regarding the National Teacher of Nanyang, Tiantong Hua said: "The attendant was given a beating and sent out of the monastery; such an occasion occurs but once in a thousand years.
Yet how could Guizong avoid feeling his eyes burn with envy? Although Danxia was a master of the craft, what could he do? He fell right into the National Teacher’s net. You all—
Can you discern this yet? If not, it is like grasping a golden whip and asking a traveler returning home: "In the deep night, who walks with you along the Imperial Street?
Jingshan Ce said: "The National Teacher was fortunately sleeping soundly; it was the attendant who broadcasted his family's disgrace.
Had it not been for the many-mouthed Danxia, how could we have seen the National Teacher’s roar? I dare ask the assembly: What about the National Teacher?

Since he was already there, why did he not see the guest? If you can see through this point, you will not only know that Danyuan missed the mark, but you will also see for yourself the path by which one emerges.
Nevertheless, do not let your idle scholarly interpretations bury the mind of the Patriarch.
The Master asked Imperial Attendant Zilin, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From south of the city.
The Master said, "What color is the grass south of the city? He replied, "It is yellow. The Master then asked a young boy, "What color is the grass south of the city? He replied, "It is yellow."
The Master said, "This very boy could also be granted purple robes before the imperial curtain and discuss the profound mysteries before the Emperor.
Miaoxi said, "Do you think the National Teacher was preaching 'old woman’s Zen,' muddying the waters?"
The Master asked Imperial Attendant Zilin, "What is the meaning of 'Buddha'? He replied, "The meaning of awakening. The Master said, "Has a Buddha ever been deluded?
He replied, "Never. The Master said, "If so, what use is awakening?"
Miaoxi said, "If one does not enter the water, how can one see the tall man?
The Master, while commenting on the *Suyāma-sūtra*, said, "In general, when annotating a sūtra, one must first comprehend the Buddha’s meaning.

Miaoxi said, "If one does not comprehend the Buddha’s intent, how can one understand the task of annotating a sūtra? The Master then ordered his attendant to fill a bowl with water and place seven grains of rice within it.

A single chopstick was placed across the face of a bowl. [The monk] asked, "What is the meaning of 'offering' (feng)? Feng remained silent. The Master said, "I, this old monk, do not yet understand its intent;
how much less so the Buddha's intent!"
Guo of Mount Shishuang said: "The Palace Attendant had some achievement as a vanguard, but no merit in the rear.

At that time, as soon as he saw the National Teacher ask, 'What is the meaning of this? he should have simply replied, 'Grass and wood originally need not be brought forth,' and then kicked him over and walked away."
Even if the National Teacher possessed a mouth all over his body, there would still be no place for him to speak.
The Master asked a Zen guest, "From where have you come? The Zen guest replied, "I have come from the South. The Master asked, "What kind of teachers do you have in the South?
He replied, "There are quite a few. The Master asked, "How do they instruct people? He replied, "The teachers of that region [instruct] directly..."
I show this to the student: the mind itself is the Buddha. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*). You now fully possess the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
This nature is well able to raise the eyebrows, blink the eyes, move about, and function throughout the entire body.

When the head is touched, the head knows; when the foot is touched, the foot knows. Therefore, it is called the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (*Samyak-saṃbuddha*). Apart from this, there is no other Buddha. This very body...
Therein, there is arising and ceasing. Yet the nature of the mind has never arisen or ceased since beginningless time.

As for the body’s arising and ceasing, it is like a dragon shedding its bones, a snake sloughing its skin, or a person leaving an old house; thus, while the body is impermanent, its nature is eternal.
This is roughly what is taught in the South. The Master said: "If that were so, then there would be no difference between this and the non-Buddhist outsider, Śreṇika."
[The Master] said: "It is different. He says: 'Within this body of mine there is a spiritual essence (ātman). This essence is capable of knowing pain and itch.
When the body perishes, the spirit departs, just as when a house is burned, the master of the house departs; the house is impermanent, but the master of the house is eternal.
If one examines it in this way, neither the heterodox nor the orthodox can be distinguished. Which of these is correct? In my recent travels, I have seen many such [views]."

In the region of Sè, the situation has become even more grave. He has gathered three to five hundred followers and, looking up at the heavens, proclaims that this is the "Southern School's" fundamental tenet.
He has altered the *Platform Sūtra*, intermingling it with vulgar talk and excising the holy intent, thereby deluding and confusing his later disciples;

how can this constitute true teaching? Alas! Our school is being lost. If one were to claim that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are the Buddha-nature, then [the Buddha-nature] would be impure...

One should not say that the Dharma is free from seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. If one engages in seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, then that is indeed seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing;
it is not the seeking of the Dharma. The assembly asked again: "In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the definitive meaning opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;

how is this to be understood? The Master said: "When it says 'opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,' it does not even mention Bodhisattvas or those of the Two Vehicles, let alone ordinary sentient beings."
"If one were to fall into such delusion, would that not be identical to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? The monk asked again, "Which of these is the Buddha-mind?
The Master said, "The walls, the tiles, and the rubble are. The monk said, "This greatly contradicts the sutras. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
'Because it is apart from insentient things such as walls, it is called Buddha-nature. Now you say these are the Buddha. I do not yet understand whether mind and nature are different."

"They are not different. The Master said, "In delusion they are different; in awakening they are not different. [The student] asked, "The sutras state that Buddha-nature is permanent and the mind is impermanent.
Why do you now say they are not different? The Master said, "You rely merely on the words and not on the meaning.
It is like water freezing into ice during a cold month, yet when it becomes warm, the ice melts back into water. When sentient beings are deluded, they congeal their nature."
It is the mind that accomplishes [sentience]. When sentient beings awaken, they release the mind and it becomes nature.

If you insist that insentient things lack Buddha-nature, then the Sūtra should not say that "the triple world is but mind. This would clearly be you contradicting the Sūtra yourself; I do not contradict it. Question:
If insentient things possess Buddha-nature, do they also understand how to preach the Dharma? The Master said: They preach it incessantly and without interruption. [The questioner] asked: How so?
"Why do you not hear it? the Master asked. "You yourself do not hear," [the monk] replied. "Who is it that can hear it? he asked.

"The various sages can hear it," the Master said. "Then sentient beings must have no share in it? he asked. "I preach for the sake of sentient beings; I do not preach for the sake of the sages," the Master said.
"I am deaf and blind," [the monk] said. "I do not hear the insentient preaching the Dharma. You, Master, ought to hear it. The Master said:
“I have not heard it either,” [Nanquan] said. [The monk] asked, “Since you, Master, have not heard it, how do you know that insentient things preach the Dharma?
The Master said, “It is precisely because I have not heard it. Had I heard it, I would be equal to the various sages; then you would not hear me preaching the Dharma.

[The monk] asked, “Will sentient beings ultimately hear it? The Master said, “If sentient beings were to hear it, they would no longer be sentient beings. [The monk] asked, “As for insentient things preaching...”

"What scriptural authority is there for this? The Master said, "Have you not seen it stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: 'The lands speak, sentient beings speak; all things of the three periods of time speak'?
Are sentient beings not those possessed of feeling (*sattva*)? [The monk] replied, "Master, you only speak of insentient things having Buddha-nature; as for those with feeling, what of them?
The Master said, "If even insentient things are thus, how much more so those with feeling? [The monk] said, "If that is so, then the teachers of the South..."

[The student] asked: "If seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are the Buddha-nature, it should not be appropriate to judge them as being the same as those of the non-Buddhists. The Master said: "I do not say that they lack Buddha-nature.

Do the non-Buddhists not also possess Buddha-nature? It is simply because their perception is erroneous; within a single dharma, they give rise to two views, and for that reason, they are wrong. [The student] asked:
"If both [Buddhists and non-Buddhists] equally possess Buddha-nature, then when one kills a sentient being, the karma of retribution will inevitably be exchanged between them."

"Injuring insentient things, one hears not of retribution. The Master said: "Sentient beings are the primary retribution (*vipāka*). To conceive of 'self' and 'what belongs to self' and harbor resentment brings about sinful retribution.
Insentient things are their secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*); they lack a mind of resentment. Therefore, it is said that there is no retribution for them. [The interlocutor] asked:
"In the teachings, we see only sentient beings attaining Buddhahood; we do not see insentient things receiving the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Furthermore, O Worthy One..."
"Throughout the kalpas of the thousand Buddhas, which of these is the insentient Buddha? The Master said: "It is like a crown prince who, before receiving the throne, is but a single person.
After he has received the throne, the entire realm belongs to the king. How could there be a separate realm that receives the throne?
Now, when sentient beings receive the prediction of Buddhahood, the lands of the ten directions are all entirely the Buddha Vairocana."

[The questioner asks: "How could there be any further possibility of insentient things receiving the prediction of enlightenment? [Dongshan] said: "All sentient beings dwell entirely within the Buddha-body.

When they relieve themselves, defiling the Buddha-body with filth, or when they bore into it and trample upon it, do they not commit offenses? [The questioner asks: "The Master says that sentient beings are in their entirety the Buddha;
toward whom, then, would one commit an offense? [The questioner asks: "The sutras state that the Buddha-body is without obstruction. Yet now, because of [these actions],..."
To manifest the Buddha-body as something obstructive and material—does this not contradict the intent of the Sage? The Master said:
"The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that one cannot speak of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) apart from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Do you believe that form is emptiness? He replied:

"This is the sincere word of the Buddha; how could I dare not believe it? The Master said: "If form is indeed emptiness, how could there be any obstruction? He asked: "What about the Buddha-nature of sentient beings?"
If they were identical, then by means of a single Buddha’s practice alone, all sentient beings would be liberated simultaneously.

Since this is not the case now, where does the meaning of identity reside? The Master said: "Do you not see that the *Avataṃsaka*’s doctrine of the six characteristics states: 'within identity there is difference; within difference there is identity.

This applies equally to the categories of formation and destruction, as well as to the general and the particular. Although sentient beings and Buddhas share the same nature, it does not hinder [the distinction between them]."
Each must cultivate for themselves and attain it for themselves; one has never seen another eat and be satiated. The Master said:

"When a person of knowledge points this out to a student, they simply recognize their own nature and realize the time of impermanence. Casting aside the 'shell-and-leak' body to one side, the numinous platform of wisdom-nature departs in clarity;
this is called liberation. The student asked: "How is this further accomplished? The Master said: "I have already explained this previously; it is still [a matter of] duality."

They rely on the standards of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*). Those of the two vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) loathe and seek to escape birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), taking delight in *nirvāṇa*. Non-Buddhists likewise say:

"I have a great affliction, namely that I possess a body," and thus they proceed toward the ultimate principle (*paramārtha-tattva*). Those who have attained the stage of stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) remain in the concentration of emptiness for eighty thousand *kalpas*;

those in the remaining three fruits [of the path] remain for sixty, forty, and twenty thousand *kalpas* respectively; and *pratyekabuddhas* remain for ten thousand *kalpas*. Thus do the non-Buddhists [proceed].

[They] dwell within the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception for eighty thousand kalpas. When the kalpas of the Two Vehicles are exhausted, they are still able to turn their minds toward the Great [Vehicle].

The non-Buddhists, however, immediately return to saṃsāra. It is said that the Buddha-nature is of one kind; what is the distinction? The Master said: "It is not of one kind. [The student] asked: "Why?"
The Master said, "Some are entirely without arising or ceasing; some are half-arising, half-ceasing, and half-without-arising-or-ceasing. [The monk] asked, "Who provides this interpretation?

The Master said, "In my own tradition, the Buddha-nature is entirely without arising or ceasing. In your tradition of the South, the Buddha-nature is half-arising, half-ceasing, and half-without-arising-or-ceasing.
[The monk] asked, "How are these distinguished? The Master said, "This [tradition] holds that body and mind are one and the same. [He continued,] "Body..."
"Externally there is nothing else; therefore, it is entirely without arising or ceasing. Your body in the south is impermanent, while your spiritual nature (*dharmatā*) is permanent;
therefore, it is half-arising-and-ceasing and half-non-arising-and-non-ceasing. He asked, "How can the Master’s physical body be the same as the Dharma-body, which is non-arising-and-non-ceasing?
The Master said, "Why have you fallen into a heterodox path? He replied, "When did this student fall into one?"

[The monk] said, “A heterodox path. The Master said, “Have you not read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? ‘To see forms or seek sounds is to walk a heterodox path. Is what you have seen now not exactly like that?

Yunmen said, “Body and mind are as one; there is nothing beyond the body. Where, then, are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth? Shending Yin said, “When the National Teacher spoke thus, he was a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail.

Dongchan Jin said, “Did the National Teacher allow this monk to see him apart from the marks of form and sound, or did he allow him to see him within the marks of form and sound? If he allowed him to see him apart from the marks of form and sound, how would this differ from the teachers of the South who speak of half-arising and half-ceasing?”

This is seeing through the characteristics of form and sound. Furthermore, it is said that to seek sound by means of form is to walk a deviant path. Is there no one among this assembly who can act as the presiding master for the National Teacher? Let me ask you this:

since body and mind are of one suchness and there is nothing else outside the body, why is this illusory, bubble-like body not identical to the Dharma-body? He replied: "I have studied the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

I have seen places where it is said that one sees the nature within the Middle Way of neither arising nor ceasing; I have also seen places where it is said that when this aggregate perishes, another aggregate arises, and the body possesses [this continuity]."

This is a passage concerning the transformation [of phenomena] while the divine nature remains undestroyed. How can you utterly dismiss it as being the same as the two views of annihilationism and eternalism held by non-Buddhists?
The Master said: "You have studied the world-transcending, unsurpassed, correct, and true Way; do you study the worldly views of birth-and-death, annihilationism, and eternalism?
Have you not seen Master Zhao say: 'To discuss the Truth is to oppose the conventional; to follow the conventional is to deviate from the Truth'? Deviating...
Because it is the ultimate reality, people are deluded regarding its nature and fail to return to it. Because it runs counter to worldly conventions, it is said to be bland and tasteless.

To those in the middle stream, it seems as if it exists and yet as if it does not; the inferior practitioners clap their hands and laugh at it. Do you now wish to learn from these inferior practitioners who laugh at the Great Way?
[The Master] said: "I too say that 'the very mind is Buddha,' and the masters of the South say the same. How could there be any difference between us?"

"One should not consider oneself right and others wrong. The Master said: "Sometimes names differ while the substance is the same; sometimes names are the same while the substance differs. It is because of this that confusion arises.
For instance, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, *tathatā*, and *buddha-nature*—these have different names but the same substance.
The true mind and the deluded mind, or Buddha-wisdom and worldly wisdom—these have the same name but different substances. In the South, you mistakenly took the deluded mind to be the true mind."
"To mistake a thief for one's own son" refers to those who take worldly knowledge and claim it to be the Buddha-wisdom;
this is like confusing fish eyes with bright pearls—they must not be treated as the same, for they require careful discernment. [The student] asked, "How can one avoid falling into this error?

The Master said, "You should simply observe minutely the aggregates (skandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), investigating each one thoroughly. Is there even a hair’s breadth of anything to be found? [The student] replied, "I have observed them minutely."
[The Master] looked at him and saw not a single thing that could be apprehended. The Master asked, "Have you destroyed the characteristics of body and mind?

He replied, "Body and mind are by nature detached; what is there to destroy? The Master asked, "Is there anything further outside of body and mind? He replied, "Since body and mind have no exterior, how could there be any thing?
The Master asked, "Have you destroyed the characteristics of the world? He replied, "The characteristics of the world are themselves formless (animitta); why use [the term 'destruction']?"

[The Master] further refuted him. The Master said, "If that is so, then you have already departed from error. A monk named Lingjue of Changzhou asked, "I have set my mind on leaving the household life, originally intending to seek Buddhahood.
I do not know how one should apply the mind to achieve this. The Master said, "When there is no mind to be applied, one immediately attains Buddhahood.
The monk asked, "If there is no mind to be applied, who is it that becomes a Buddha? The Master said, "It is the non-mind itself that spontaneously becomes [the Buddha]."
"Buddha. Even when attaining Buddhahood, he has no mind. [The interlocutor] said: "A Buddha possesses great inconceivability because he is able to deliver sentient beings.

If he were without mind, who would deliver sentient beings? The Master said: "Being without mind is the true delivery of beings. If one perceives that there are sentient beings to be delivered, that is precisely having a mind;
it is nothing other than the cycle of arising and ceasing. [The interlocutor] said: "If he is now without mind, how was it that the Benevolent One appeared in the world?"
[The student] said: "You have spoken of many paths of teaching; how could these be empty words? The Master said: "Even when the Buddha speaks the teachings, he is without mind. [The student] said:
"If he speaks the Dharma without mind, then there must be no speaking. The Master said: "Speaking is itself non-existence; non-existence is itself speaking. [The student] said:

"If speaking the Dharma is without mind, does the creation of karma possess mind? The Master said: "Without mind, there is no karma. Since there is now karma, the mind is subject to arising and ceasing. How [can it be otherwise]?"
He attained the state of no-mind. [The Master] said, "One who has no-mind attains Buddhahood immediately. [The Master asked,] "Have you, Preceptor, already attained Buddhahood this very moment?

The Teacher replied, "Since mind itself does not exist, who would say that one attains Buddhahood? If there were a Buddha to be attained, that would still be having mind. To have mind is to be subject to outflows (*āsrava*)."
"Where can one find a mindless state? [The Master] said, "Since there is no Buddha to be realized, does the Preceptor still have the use of a Buddha?

The Master said, "If the mind itself does not exist, from where could its function arise? [The Preceptor] said, "If one is utterly blank and without anything at all, does this not fall into the view of nihilism? The Master said:
"Originally there is no seeing. Who says it is severed? [The student] said, "Originally there is no seeing. [The Master asked], "Do you not fall into emptiness?

The Master said, "There is no emptiness into which one can fall. [The student] said, "Is there anything that can be fallen into? The Master said, "Since emptiness is non-existent, from where could a fall be established?
[The student] said, "Both subject and object are absent. Suppose someone were to come with a sword to take one's life; would that be existent or non-existent? The Master said, "It is non-existent."
The monk asked, "Is it painful? The Master said, "There is no pain either. The monk asked, "If there is no pain, to what realm is one reborn after death?

The Master said, "There is neither death nor birth, nor is there any realm. The monk asked, "Since you have attained mastery over the absence of all things, how should one apply the mind when pressed by hunger and cold?
The Master said, "When hungry, eat; when cold, put on clothes. The monk asked, "To know hunger and know cold must be due to having a mind."
The Master said, "I ask you: does the mind have a form? Does the mind have a physical substance? He replied, "The mind has no physical substance.
The Master said, "Since you know it has no physical substance, this is precisely the original absence of mind. How can you say it exists?

He asked, "If one encounters tigers and wolves in the mountains, how should one apply the mind? The Master said, "Seeing is as if not seeing; coming is as if not coming. In that state, there is simply no mind."
"Evil beasts cannot harm him. [The student] asked, "He is described as being tranquil and without affairs, solitary and detached, and without mind.

What kind of thing is he called? The Master said, "He is called the Vajra Mahāsattva. [The student] asked, "What physical form does the Vajra Mahāsattva have? The Master said, "Originally, he has no form or segments.
[The student] asked, "Since he has no form or segments, what can be called the Vajra Mahāsattva? The Master said, "He is called 'formless'."

Duan Jingang Dashi asked, "What meritorious virtues does the Vajra Mahāsattva possess? The Master replied, "If one’s single thought accords with the Vajra, one can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and one shall attain the vision of as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges."
The merit of this Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva is immeasurable; it cannot be fully expressed by speech nor described by the mind.

Even if one were to remain in the world for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and speak of it, one could never reach its end. [The student] asked: "What is meant by 'correspondence with a single thought' (*ekakṣaṇasamāyoga*)?

The Master said: "When both memory and wisdom are forgotten, that is correspondence. [The student] asked: "If both memory and wisdom are forgotten, who sees the Buddhas? The Master said: [He who has forgotten them].
"Forgetfulness is non-existence; non-existence is the Buddha. [The student] asked, "If it is non-existence, one says 'non-existence. How can it be called the Buddha?
The Master said, "Non-existence is empty, and the Buddha is also empty. Therefore, it is said that non-existence is the Buddha, and the Buddha is non-existence.

[The student] asked, "Since not even a hair's breadth can be grasped, what thing is it named? The Master said, "It has no name from the very beginning. [The student] asked, "Is there anything similar to it? The Master said, "It is without marks (formless)."
As for "the Resembling One": he is renowned in the world as the Peerless and Sole Honored One. You should strive to practice in reliance upon him;

no one can destroy this [path]. There is no further need for questioning. Wander at will, liberated and fearless. You shall always be protected by sages and worthies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In whatever place you may be, you shall always receive the reverence of devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The river...
The sand-spirit deities (*vālukā-devatā*) come to protect him so that he is forever free from obstacles; where could he not travel freely?
Even if one were to spend as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River dwelling in this world to describe it, one could never reach the end. Furthermore, he said:
When Chasha heard this, he attained great enlightenment on the spot. It was like waking from a dream, like a lotus flower opening.
To be in such a state is precisely what constitutes the "diamond circle" and the "thorny jujube. If you cannot swallow it and cannot penetrate it, you will not see where the ancients walked;
you will surely give rise to slander. Only when you have penetrated this point without doubt can you become a great vessel for others. Not...
"Be attached neither to this shore, nor to the other shore, nor to the middle stream.
Good friend, only when you have attained such skillful means and entered such a hidden lair can you truly become a teacher of men.
If you do not possess these various eyes of discernment—such as finding a path of understanding and a point of entry within the nature of mind—you will certainly not delight in being struck."
"A spark from flint, a flash of lightning. Yet people cherish such talk; yet again, they mistakenly take it as a substantial dharma.
Those who have found an entrance through a single mechanism, a single situation, a single blow of the staff, or a single shout would certainly not cherish such talk;
yet they too have misunderstood. Truly, as it is said, "what is seen differs," and there are gains and losses among one another.
As it is said in the teachings: "The Bodhisattva sees water as nectar; devas and humans see water as lapis lazuli;
ordinary people see water as water; and hungry ghosts see water as pus and blood.
Suppose there were a monk who loves lofty Chan to come forward and say, "Does Miaoxi have such visions as these? You should immediately say to him:
Whenever you meet someone, simply speak in this manner.
A monk asked: "An ancient worthy said, 'The lush green bamboos are all the Dharmakāya; the dense yellow flowers are none other than Prajñā.
Some people do not accept this, calling it a heterodox teaching, while others believe it, calling it inconceivable. I do not know—"
The Master said: "This is the realm of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī; it is not something that ordinary beings can believe or accept.
It accords with the meaning of the definitive Mahāyāna sūtras. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: 'The Buddha-body fills the entire Dharma-realm.'"
He manifests universally before all living beings; responding to conditions and fulfilling their needs, there is nowhere he does not reach.
Yet he always remains upon this seat of Bodhi. Since the verdant bamboo does not transcend the Dharma-realm, is it not the Dharmakāya?
Furthermore, the Prajñā Sūtra says: "Because form is boundless, Prajñā is also boundless. Since the yellow flowers do not exceed the realm of form, are they not Prajñā?
"Profound and far-reaching words—those who do not comprehend them find it difficult to direct their attention toward them. Thereupon, the Chan guest paid his respects and departed.

Furthermore, the Master of the Avatamsaka Sutra asked Master Dazhu, "Why does the Chan Master not permit that 'the green bamboo is entirely the Dharmakaya' and 'the lush yellow flowers are none other than Prajna'? Dazhu replied, "The Dharmakaya has no form; it manifests as the green bamboo."

Bamboo takes form through its shape; Prajñā is without cognition. It manifests its characteristics in response to yellow flowers, yet it is not apart from those yellow flowers and green bamboos that the Dharmakāya of Prajñā exists.
Thus, a sutra says: "The Buddha’s true Dharmakāya is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things like the moon reflected in water.
If the yellow flowers were themselves Prajñā, then Prajñā would be identical to insentient matter. If the green bamboos were...
"This is the Dharmakāya. Can the green bamboo still function [as such]? Master of the Seat (Zuǒzhǔ), do you understand? He replied, "I do not.
Zhū said, "If one has seen their nature, to say it 'is' is permissible; to say it 'is not' is also permissible. One speaks according to function and does not stagnate in right or wrong.

If one has not seen their nature, speaking of the green bamboo, they are stuck on the green bamboo; speaking of the yellow flowers, they are stuck on the yellow flowers; speaking of the Dharmakāya, they stagnate."

Regarding the Dharma-body, some say it is Prajñā while others do not recognize it as Prajñā; for this reason, they all fall into contentious debate. The Head of the Monastery (Zuozhu) bowed in apology and departed.
Miaoxi said, "The National Teacher maintained that 'every green bamboo shoot is entirely the Dharma-body,' and he maintained this position to the very end."
Dazhu broke through the "green, green bamboo is not the Dharmakāya" to the very bottom.

This old fellow takes that which was asserted and that which was refuted and brings them together into one place; there is nothing further to be picked up or set down, and he dares not move them by even a hair’s breadth.
He wants you students to possess the eye to penetrate the Diamond Circle of National Teacher Huairang. Furthermore—
Swallowing the great pearl and the thorny *kṣīrikā* fruit—those with eyes can discern this; those without eyes may not necessarily laugh at it.
It is further said: among the assembly, they deliberate that when these two venerable masters thus refine one another, one attains its essence (*tǐ*) and the other attains its function (*yòng*).
He who attains the function establishes himself within phenomena (*shì*); he who attains the essence...

in the gate of Buddha-activities (*buddhakārya*), not a single dharma is abandoned. As I am the Dharma King, sovereign over all dharmas, whether suppressing or exalting, there is neither gain nor loss.
Such a view is called "a dwarf watching a play. I, Miaoxi, wish for all of you to know my own perspective;
have you not heard it said: "A swarm of flies on the back of a worn-out donkey"?
A monk asked, "How can one attain Buddhahood? The Master said, "Simultaneously cast off both Buddha and sentient beings; liberation occurs right where you are.
The monk asked, "How can one achieve resonance with this? The Master said, "Do not contemplate good or evil, and you will spontaneously see your own Buddha-nature."
[The student] asked, "How does one realize the Dharma-body? The Master said, "Transcend the realm of Vairocana.

[The student] asked, "How does one attain the pure Dharma-body? The Master said, "Do not seek it from the Buddha. [The student] asked, "Which one is the Buddha? The Master said, "This very mind is the Buddha.

[The student] asked, "Does the mind have afflictions? The Master said, "The nature of afflictions is inherently detached. [The student] asked, "Is it not then severed? The Master said, "It is not severed."
"Yes. The Master said, "One who cuts off afflictions is called a follower of the Two Vehicles. That afflictions do not arise is called Great Nirvana.

[The student] asked, "Regarding sitting in meditation to observe stillness, how should one proceed? The Master said, "It is neither defiled nor pure. Why should you give rise to a mind to observe the mark of purity?
[The student] asked, "Does the Chan Master see the empty space of the ten directions as the Dharmakāya? The Master said, "This is grasping with a conceptualizing mind."
This is a perverted view. [A questioner] asked: "If the mind itself is the Buddha, may one still cultivate the myriad practices?

The Master said: "All the Sages were endowed with the two types of adornment; how could they have denied cause and effect? When the Master was about to enter nirvana, he took his leave of Emperor Daizong.
Daizong said: "After you pass away, what shall I, your disciple, rely upon as a memorial? The Master said: "Tell the donor to build for me a single..."

The Seamless Stūpa. The Emperor said, "I request that you, Master, provide me with the model for this stūpa. After a long silence, the Master asked, "Do you understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not understand.
The Master said, "After I have passed away, my disciple Yingzhen will know this matter. I beg Your Majesty to issue an edict to question him.
On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month in the tenth year of the Dali era, he passed away lying on his right side. His stūpa was erected at Dangzi Valley. Later, an imperial edict [was issued].
Yingzhen asked about the previous words. After a long silence, Yingzhen said, "Does Your Majesty understand? The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. Yingzhen then recited a verse:

South of the Xiang River, North of the潭 (Tan) Lake, Within lies gold filling the entire land. Beneath the shadowless tree, the same boat; Upon the lapis lazuli palace, no one knows. (The mountain shape is like a staff. (The seas are calm and the rivers clear. (On the lapis lazuli palace, there is no knowing.)
"Consciousness.

Layer upon layer, falling leaves; shadows round and full. For ten thousand ages, through all eternity, it is shown to people.

he was thus titled Great Master Zhenjue. He composed the *Song of Realizing the Way* (*Zhengdao ge*) and the *Essential Principles of Enlightenment and Cultivation in the Chan School* (*Chanzong wuxiu yuanzhi*), which proceed from the shallow to the profound.
Wei Jing, the Prefectural Governor of Qingzhou, compiled and arranged these into ten chapters, entitled the *Yongjia Collection* (*Yongjia ji*), both of which were circulated together.
In the world, it is known in India as the *Mahāyāna-śāstra of the Eastern Land*.

Within the nature of profound stillness, follow along with eating and drinking. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and all are empty—this is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment. This is certain.
This speaks of manifesting the True Vehicle. Some people are unwilling to accept it, yet they investigate it according to their own whims.

Its six kinds of divine functions are both empty and non-empty; its single orb of light is neither color nor form. It purifies the five eyes and attains the five powers—this can only be realized through direct realization.
Thus one knows it is difficult to fathom. To see one’s form in a mirror is not hard; to grasp the moon in water, how can one succeed?
Always walking alone, always treading solitary paths, those who have attained wander together on the road to Nirvana. Their melodies are ancient and their spirits pure, their wind naturally lofty;

Here [in China], it is translated as "cultivation through contemplation" (*sīwéi xiū*) or "meditative concentration" (*jìnglù*). These are all general designations for meditative stabilization (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Source" (*yuán*) refers to the fundamental, awakened true nature of all sentient beings; it is also called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), and it is also called...

The mind-ground: awakening to it is called wisdom (*prajñā*), and cultivating it is called concentration (*samādhi*). When concentration and wisdom are both clear and penetrating, this is termed *dhyāna*.

This nature is the fundamental source of *dhyāna*; therefore, it is called the "Source of *Dhyāna*" (*chanyuan*). It is also termed *dhyāna* (or *dhyāna-na*). Regarding "principle and practice": this fundamental source is the principle of *dhyāna*, while forgetting emotions and acceding to it is the practice of *dhyāna*;
hence, it is called "principle and practice" (*lixing*). However, what is described here is based on the various treatises composed by the different schools.

I have discussed the principles of Chan extensively, while speaking little of Chan practice; therefore, I have provisionally titled this work "The Source of Chan" (Canyuan). Nowadays, there are those who identify true nature alone as Chan;
this shows they do not comprehend the essential meaning of principle and practice, nor do they distinguish between the linguistic traditions of China and India.

Nevertheless, it is not that there is a separate essence of Chan apart from true nature; rather, it is simply that sentient beings are deluded regarding the truth and conjoined with sensory dust, which is termed "scattered" (san).

Distraction and concentration: only when one turns away from the mundane dust and unites with the Truth is it called meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). If one discusses the fundamental nature directly, it is neither true nor false, neither turning away nor uniting, neither fixed nor distracted.
Who would speak of "meditation" in such a state? Furthermore, this True Nature is not only the source of the gate of meditation;
it is also the source of all phenomena, and is therefore termed *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). It is also the source of sentient beings' delusion and awakening.
Therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* or the *ālayavijñāna* (as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*). It is also the source of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas;

therefore, it is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) (as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other scriptures). It is also the source of the myriad practices of Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is called the "Ground of the Mind" (*cittabhūmi*). These myriad practices do not transcend the six *pāramitās*, and meditation (*dhyāna*) is merely one among these six, occupying its respective position.

(“Principle” [yi] refers here to fundamental truth, not to benevolence, righteousness, or favors. The intent is to clarify that in all one’s actions, one must first examine the benefits and harms; there must be a valid reason and it must accord with the Way before one acts. Within the Buddha-dharma, there are three kinds of "principles" (yi) for which one may act: 1. Matters that benefit the physical body—namely, clothing, food, medicine, and housing. These are worldly principles. 2. Matters that benefit the Dharma-body—namely, the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and the six pāramitās.)

[The first three items] are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The third is to propagate the sublime Dharma and benefit all sentient beings. Even for other incidental matters related to the Dharma, they pertain to both the mundane and the supramundane. To engage in meaningless activities is a state of deranged mind.

(That is to say, whatever one does, if it does not relate to the three aforementioned types of matters, it is called "meaningless. Now, since one makes no such distinctions here, what benefit or purpose is there? One merely indulges in deluded thoughts and acts impulsively; thus, it is like madness. The first four lines describe the causes of karma; the last four lines describe the experience of retribution.)

Driven by delusion, one follows the whims of discursive thoughts; at the moment of death, one is dragged away by karma. Having followed such deluded thoughts, one acts impulsively without using the wisdom that realizes the truth to discern right from wrong—just like a madman.

Therefore, at the time of death, one is pulled along the path of karma; led by karma, one undergoes retribution in the future. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Ignorance is the overlord, and craving is the Māra-king; they employ the body and mind as servants, driving them like slaves."

Awakening does not arise from emotional states. At the time of death, one is able to transform karma: if within the mind there is a desire to act, yet one examines the principle and finds it improper, one must immediately cease;

if within the mind there is no desire to act, yet one perceives that it accords with principle, one must immediately proceed. This depends solely on the principle of right and wrong, not on the emotions of attachment or aversion. Thus, at the moment of death, karma cannot bind you, and you will move freely at will between the heavens and the human realm.

Generally speaking, if what you do morning and evening is dragged by the dust of emotion, then at the time of death you will be dragged by karma and undergo rebirth. Fayan Daoyuan spoke in his stead: "The disciple locks it; the Great Master locks it. Fadeng spoke in his stead: "Give me back the key!
An old master also spoke in his stead: "The lock of Jizhou; the lock of Qianzhou."

Someone asked a monk, "I have heard that you, Venerable Sir, are able to lecture on the *Treatise by Zhaolun*; is this true? The monk replied, "I dare not say so. The man said, "The *Zhaolun* contains the principle of 'the non-transmigration of things'; is this true? The monk replied, "It is. Thereupon, the man smashed a tea bowl against the ground and said: [...]* *Note: The original Chinese text provided here is incomplete, ending with the phrase "撲破曰" (smashed [it] and said).

The following is a reconstruction of the well-known anecdote based on standard versions of the text.* The man continued, "If things do not transmigrate, then when I smash this bowl, it must remain right here. Why has it already fallen to pieces? The monk was speechless. The man then said, "The Venerable One says he does not dare claim to understand the *Zhaolun*, yet he still speaks of its principles. This is like a person who claims to be a master of archery but cannot hit a target even ten paces away—how can such a person be called a master? You are no different! He then departed. The monk was deeply ashamed and thereafter ceased lecturing on the *Zhaolun*. *Note: The final sentence of the provided text fragment is translated as follows:* The man then smashed a tea bowl against the ground and said: [The rest of the dialogue follows].
"This is shifting and non-shifting. [The Master] said, "There is no counterpart.
Fayuan took his place and clapped his hands three times.
▲ There was a practitioner who sat with his back turned toward the Buddha Hall. A monk said, "Daoist, do not turn your back on the Buddha. The practitioner said:

The monk had no reply.
