Furthermore, there was another practitioner who followed the Dharma Master into the Buddha hall. The practitioner spat toward the Buddha, and the Dharma Master said, "Practitioner, you lack propriety;
why do you spit at the Buddha? The practitioner replied, "I have come from where there is no Buddha, so I am spitting on someone else.
The Dharma Master had no reply.
Guishan said, "The benevolent person is not the non-benevolent person; the non-benevolent person is the benevolent person.
Yangshan, acting on behalf of the Dharma Master, said, "Just spit at the practitioner. He also said, "If the practitioner has anything to say, you should tell him:

▲ A monk from Liutong Monastery in Taizhou wished to cross by boat. Someone asked him, "Since you possess the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), why do you rely on a boat?
He was unable to answer.
Tiantai Shaodai said: "I did not wish to alarm the assembly.
When an image of a Holy Monk was dripping with leaks from the roof, someone asked: "Since he is a Holy Monk, why does he have leaks?"
Tiantai Shaodai said: "The 'no-leakage' (anāsrava) is not the holy monk.
[This is like] a dead fish floating on the surface of the water. Someone asked a monk, "Is it not the case that fish take water as their life?
He replied, "Yes. [The questioner] asked, "Why then do they die in the water? The monk was speechless.
Tianlong Ji said: "Why does this fellow not die on the bank?
Feng Yanshi, the Chancellor of Jiangnan, was traveling with several monks to Mount Zhong. Upon reaching the "One-Person Spring," he asked:
"When one person draws from it, how can so many people find it sufficient? A monk replied: "It is not made to be lacking. He then added: "Who would [not]?"
Deficiency. The *Fayan bieyun* (Separate Sayings of Fayan) asks: "Who is it that lacks?

[One part. A woman asked, "How old is the Holy Monk? There was no reply.
Fayan spoke on his behalf, saying: "When the heart's intention is fulfilled, you will know.

The Road. The Mountain Master argued that he had arrived;
there was no reply. Niu of Guizong spoke on his behalf, saying: "I did not expect to meet you again.
Once, a monk entered the underworld and saw Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Kṣitigarbha asked him: "What kind of practice have you cultivated throughout your life?"
The monk said, "Recite the Lotus Sutra. [The Master] said, "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive.
[The monk] asked, "Is this speaking or not speaking? There was no response.
Gui宗 Rouru spoke on his behalf, saying: "On this return journey, I venture to request that you circulate this.
A hawk chases a pigeon; it flies toward the balustrade of the Buddha Hall and trembles. Someone asks a monk:
"All sentient beings dwell in constant peace and joy within the shadow of the Buddha. Why does the pigeon tremble upon seeing the Buddha? [The answer: "There is none."
[The Master] replied, “Yes. Faideng spoke on his behalf, saying, “I fear the Buddha.
An official asked a monk, “What is your name? The monk said, “Wujian (No-Selection). The official said, “Suppose you suddenly take a bowl of sand...”
[The Master] said, "Give it to the Elder. [The monk] asked, "And how about this? [The Master] said, "Thank you for the official's offering.
Fayan remarked separately, "This is still merely picking and choosing.
In Guangnan there was a monk living in a hermitage. When the Prince went out hunting, someone informed the hermitage master, "The Great King is coming; please rise to greet him."
[The monk] said, "It is not only the Great King; even when the Buddha came, I did not rise. The King asked, "Is the Buddha not your teacher? [The monk] replied, "He is.
The King said, "Seeing your teacher, why do you not rise? [The monk] was speechless.
Fayan Daoyuan said in his stead: "This is not yet sufficient to repay your kindness.
A monk asked Master Yuan Tong: "When a single speck of dust arises, the entire earth is fully contained within it. Do you still see the meditation seat?"
Yuantong said, "What do you call 'dust'? He then asked Faldeng, who replied, "What do you call a 'meditation seat'?
Dongchan Qi remarked, "Do these words from the two venerable elders clarify the point of his question, or do they fail to clarify it?"

If you examine the point of Yanguan’s question, have you reached a state of ultimate perfection yet? Try to judge it for me. Suppose I were to suddenly say to him, "You have already pointed it out to me;
what more do you want me to answer? How would you understand this? Do not say that he simply gave another turn of words.
▲ Once, after a monk had finished reciting the sutra with a young boy, he instructed the boy to place the sutra inside a casket.
The boy asked, "Where should I put what I have recited?"
Fadeng said in his place: "What sutra are you reciting?
Formerly, Chan Master Jingzhao asked National Teacher Lengyan: "The sutra says that if one can turn things over, one is identical to the Tathāgata;
if one is turned by things, one is called an ordinary person. As for this Shengyuan Tower, how do you turn it? Yan said: [He did not answer.]
[The Master] was speechless. Fenyang spoke on his behalf, saying: "Both are old men.
A monk arrived at Caoxi. The monk who guards the robes and bowl held up the robe and said: "This is [the burden] from the top of Dayu Ridge."
[The monk] could not lift it up. Yunmen asked, "Why is it in the Senior Monk's hand? [The monk] had no reply.
Yunmen said, "Neither of us has reached a resolution. He further remarked, "I took you for a lion cub."
▲ Formerly, when people from the kingdom of Goryeo came to Qiantang, they carved a sacred image of Avalokiteśvara. When they attempted to carry it onto their ship, it would not budge.

"Why does the sacred image not go to the kingdom of Goryeo?
Changqing Lingmo said: "Although its manifestation is universal, the appearance perceived is partial. Fayan Yue asked:
"Have you recognized Guanyin yet?"
Someone asked a monk, "What kind of lamp do you light? The monk replied, "A perpetually burning lamp. [The man] asked, "When was it lit? [The monk] said, "It was lit last year.
[The man] asked, "Where is the perpetual burning? The monk was speechless.
Changqing Lingmo said, "If it were not so, I would know that you do not allow yourself to be deceived. Fayan spoke differently:
"A gentleman is moved by profit.

"What is his merit? [The Master] said, "He is the Heavenly King Who Protects the Nation. "He protects only this country," [the other] asked. "He protects all countries universally," [the Master] replied.
"He becomes a Qin when in Qin, and a Chu when in Chu," [the other] asked. "On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month, you broke down the city walls of Zhenzhou;
where did the Heavenly King go then? The Master had no reply.
▲ An old master has a verse that says: "A single expanse of emptiness atop the mountain of the five aggregates; Entering and exiting through the same gate, we do not meet.

An elder said: "Since you did not recognize him, whom did you ask when you first rented [the robe]?
Once, a monk carrying an alms bowl arrived at a householder’s home and was accidentally bitten by a dog. The householder pointed to the *kāṣāya* and said:

"If a dragon wears even a single thread of this, the Golden-Winged Bird will not swallow it. Why is it that the Great Master, wearing the Dharma robes in their entirety, has instead been bitten by a dog?"
▲ Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty visited Xiangguo Temple. He asked a monk who was reading a scripture, "What sutra is this?
The monk replied, "The *Benevolent Kings Sutra* (*Renwang jing*). The Emperor said, "Since this is my own sutra, why is it in your hands? The monk was unable to respond.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "The August Heaven has no partiality; it assists only virtue.
[The Emperor] then opened the precious stupa and asked a monk, "Who are you? The monk replied, "I am the stupa master. The Emperor said, "This is my stupa;
why do you act as its master? The monk was speechless.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "The entire nation knows.

The monk Chaozong asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Sleeping Clouds Hermitage on Mount Lu. The Emperor said, "I have heard that where the clouds sleep deeply, one does not face the court.
Why, then, have you come here? Chaozong was speechless.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf, saying, "It is difficult to escape the ultimate transformation.
Later, when the monk entered the imperial presence, he reported, "Your Majesty, do you still remember? The Emperor asked, "Where did we meet?
He replied, "Since our parting at Vulture Peak until this very day. The Emperor asked, "What serves as proof? The monk was speechless.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf, saying: "This poor monk has come specifically because the scriptures in the capital temples were destroyed by fire.
The monks have requested an imperial grant. [The Emperor] summoned him and asked: "In the past, Kāśyapa Matanga was not burned;
why then has he been burned now? He had no reply.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf: "Your Majesty has not forgotten the entrustment.

Zong once dreamed of a divine being who informed him, saying, "I request that Your Majesty give rise to the bodhicitta. Consequently, during the early court audience, the Emperor questioned those at the palace gates, "How does one give rise to the bodhicitta? No one could answer.
Xuedou spoke on his behalf, saying: "Truly, this is rarely heard of in antiquity or today.
The Layman Yushan of Chaling had never traveled as a wandering monk. Once, when a transformation-monk arrived from Mount Lu, they discussed matters concerning the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen).
[Yushan] was instructed to contemplate the question: "When a monk asked Fadeng, 'How does one advance further atop a hundred-foot pole? Deng replied, 'Ugh! (Deng said: *E*).
For three years he practiced in this manner. One day, while riding a donkey across a bridge, he stepped upon a plank and fell;
at that moment, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He then composed a verse, which says: "I possess a divine pearl, Long confined by the dust of worldly toil.

Today the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, Illuminating the myriad peaks of mountains and rivers. From then on, he no longer traveled to seek teachers elsewhere. This master was Baizhang Yuanwen Chan Master.
He obtained the Dharma from Master Du.
During the Tang Dynasty, there was the Chan Master Yin. While he was of humble status, once while he was transporting a mallet to strike at some earth, he saw a large clod of soil.
In jest, he struck it forcefully with the mallet, and it shattered upon contact with his hand. At that moment, he attained great enlightenment.
▲ Master Louzi was a man of unknown origins; neither his personal name nor his clan name were known.
One day, while wandering through the streets and markets, he happened to be adjusting his socks and sash beneath a wine tavern when he heard someone upstairs singing a song that went:
"Since you have no heart, I shall also cease. At this, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and was thus named Louzi (The Man from the Tower).
▲ Shenzhao Benru Dharma Master once sought instruction from the Venerable Siming regarding the *Sūtra King* (this character should likely be an error).
The Venerable roared with a thunderous voice, saying: "Your name is Benru. Upon hearing this, the Master immediately attained realization and composed a verse:
"Everywhere I encounter the path back; At every turn, I reach my native land. This matter has been manifest from the beginning; Why wait for deliberation?"
▲The Dharma Master Yuanzhi Zhengwu of Shangzhushan in Lin’an Prefecture was the son of the Lin family of Tāizhōu.

He relied upon the Dharma Master Xián of the Báilián Temple and inquired about the Way of "Possessing Transformation" (jùbiàn). Xián pointed to a walking lamp and said: "A lamp such as this is devoid of intrinsic nature and transcends all attributes;

it is fundamentally empty and still. In principle, it is 'possessed' [of all potentialities]. However, the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of sages perceive it differently; thus, 'transformation' resides therein."

His master did not approve. Later, while sweeping the floor and reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, he reached the passage: "Know that dharmas are eternally without nature; the Buddha-seed arises from conditions.
Only then did he grasp the essential meaning and inform Huiliang (Lian). Huiliang approved.

Since the Master arrived with his disciples, he had constantly lamented that students of his own school were mired in literal records, to the point that they regarded the transmission of Tiantai as merely a study of texts—a view held in contempt by the Southern School.
He then went to visit Chan Master Ci’an Yuan of Huguo. During their conversation at night, the Master cited the verse by Dongpo on staying at Donglin:
“The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue; The color of the mountains—is it not the pure body? Eighty-four thousand verses have come forth tonight;

How will he explain them to others in days to come? He added, “It is not easy to reach such a state. Ci’an said, “You have not yet seen the path; how can you speak of ‘reaching’ it? Dongpo replied, “The sound of the stream—”
“This is the broad and long tongue. Are these mountain colors not the pure body? If one does not reach this ground, how could there be such a message?
The Hermitage Master said, “This is merely a man from outside the gate. [The monk] said, “Venerable Sir, do not be stingy; you may explain it for me.”
The Hermit said, "Just from this very point, exert your full vigor and scrutinize him closely.
If you can catch him in his vulnerability, you will know where your own natal root and spirit (the *mūlādhāra*) are situated. The Master did not sleep all night.
When the dawn bell rang, he cast aside his secret reserves and offered a separate verse, saying: "The Layman Dongpo is far too talkative; Within the barrier of sound and form, he desires..."

Pervading the body: "If the stream is sound and the mountain is form, no mountain and no water—how sad for such a person! (This fellow pondered over it; all night long he muttered in his sleep. He is a man outside Dongpo’s gate;
this fellow has not even reached the gate. He took this to tell Chican. Chican said, "I told you before that he is a man outside the gate."

(Tell me, is this a reward for him or a punishment? Do not err! The Master bowed in thanks. Shortly thereafter, there was one who had repaired the roof tiles of Mazu’s hall and requested words to promote [the teaching].
The Master wrote: "Send word to the old adept of Jiangxi: Let him be scorched by the sun and fanned by the wind. It is not that his descendants lack the means to manage it;
One must see the moment the ice melts and the structure crumbles. When Ch'an-am saw this, he laughed and said, "This indeed must be..."
Only this *ācārya* has attained it.
When Master Gōngqī was traveling toward Luóhàn, he encountered a young gentleman riding an ox along the way.
The Master asked, "Which way does the road to Luóhàn go? The gentleman patted the ox and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master shouted, "You beast! The gentleman replied, [and remained silent].
"Where does the path of the Arhat lead? The Master then patted the ox and said, "Speak! Speak!
The official said, "Even if it were so, there is still something lacking—the hooves and horns. The Master then struck him. The official patted the ox and ran away.
▲ Master Yunzheng of Mount Song in Fuzhou. A lay practitioner asked, "Dongshan said, 'There is one thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth.

[The layman] said, "Heaven and earth turn black; mountains and rivers flee. The Master said, "One more ghost is added before the Hall of King Yama; he lies down beneath Mount Beimang."
For a thousand years, he would say, "Happy! Happy! The Master said, "This too is a wild fox swallowing a mouse.
Long ago, there was an elder who did not speak a word to the monks for an entire summer retreat. A monk sighed and said, "I have let this summer pass in vain;
I do not dare hope that you, Reverend, will preach the Buddha-dharma, but I only wish to hear two characters of the True Cause."
"That is so," he replied. Upon hearing this, the elder said, "Dharma-teacher, do not speak so hastily. If one speaks of the true cause, there is not even a single word.
Having finished speaking, he tapped his teeth and said, "Just now, I spoke without reason; it was not right to say such a thing.

Furthermore, there was an old master who kept a novice boy, and neither knew the proper rules of decorum. A traveling monk arrived, so the master instructed the boy in the rituals of greeting.

At twilight, he was driven out in the pouring rain.

Langye Jue said: "Since that is not so, tell me: what was the meaning of the Patriarch’s wall-gazing? After a long silence, he said:

Regarding Chan Master Shuangxi Bunuo, Chan Master Song composed a poem in jest to mourn him, saying: "Successing the Patriarchs, I have always acted on their behalf;

The brush is difficult to wield; my lofty sentiments no one in the world understands. Where shall the clouds of compassion spread? Only the solitary moon is naturally suited to me.
After the master finished reading, he took up his brush and replied: "Who else has a spiritual affinity with me throughout my life? You, Xianqing, know my heart better than anyone.

Had I not intended to part from you at this time, I feared it might have interfered with this poem for my fellow practitioner. He threw down his brush and sat in passing away. Sixty years [had passed since his birth].
Afterwards, the door of the stupa opened of its own accord, and the true likeness [of the Buddha] was solemnly present.
Chan Master Lì of Fǎhǎi in Chùzhōu, because Emperor Huīzōng had converted his monastery into a Shénxiāo Palace, ascended the seat and said to the assembly:
"It is solely because one has not yet attained thorough penetration that one speaks of right and wrong; it is because of a lack of truth that one acts thus."

To distinguish this from that—to say "my own body does not even exist"—is to speak of what is beyond the reach of words regarding that which lies outside the body. Viewed through the Eye of Rightness, it is all a source of laughter.

Now, as the Sage Ruler has issued his decree to convert monasteries into temples of the Shenxiao (Divine Empyrean), adding yet another crown to the Buddha’s head—when one calculates it, what could be wrong with that?
Today, this mountain monk cannot help but slung his staff across his shoulder and hang [his robe] high.
With his alms-bowl bag, he settled his life within the Seamless Stupa; beneath the Rootless Tree, he whistled at the moon and chanted with the wind.
He left it entirely to the cloud-riding immortals to come here to chant over water, write talismans, and perform rites by clacking their teeth, so that in years to come he might achieve the Way.
He ascended on a bright day. He was worthy of repaying the unrequited kindness [of his patrons] and thereby assisting in the transformation of non-action (*wuwei*).
One only fears it may not be jade; if it is jade, how marvelous! Nevertheless, tell me: what is the monk’s turning-phrase? How would you say it? Do you understand?
Having cast down his whisk, he suddenly passed into stillness. The Prefect submitted a memorial, and by imperial decree, he was... [restored].
The temple plaque was changed to read "True Body" (Zhenshen).

Furthermore, when Chan Master Ming of Tianning in Ruizhou changed his title from "Virtuous Practitioner" (Deshi) to "Chan Master," after he had finished ascending the seat to express his gratitude, he said:
The wooden tablet was taken up with ease; the sitting mat was set down at the opportune moment. As clouds disperse and waters flow away, all is silent and the heavens and earth are empty.
Thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away.

He then entered the interior of the pagoda and sat upright, saying, "One guest does not require two hosts. He then passed away.

in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; in drinking tea and eating meals; in speaking and conversing; and in all that one does and thinks. When the mind is stirred..."
"Your mindfulness is still not correct. He said again, "The times are now in decline; among people, there are few who reach sixty or seventy years of age.
You have entered my Dharma, yet before you have even steadied your footing, thirty or forty years have already passed.
In an instant, decay and illness will arrive. When decay and illness arrive, old age arrives; when old age arrives, death arrives. How much further do you have to go? Still...
Furthermore, he was unrestrained in his conduct. Why did he not remain in pure stillness throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night?
When Wen Lügong was stationed in Beiping, the Venerable Dong came to visit him before departing. Wen Lügong said, "The Dharma Master is old; where else will you go?

He replied, "I am going to enter parinirvāṇa. Wen Lügong laughed, taking it to be a joke. Upon returning home, he told his sons and younger brothers that the Master’s tone was profound and steady, and that his conversation possessed a rich flavor.

He was an extraordinary monk. The Lord sent someone to observe him, and indeed, he entered *parinirvāṇa*. The Lord marveled at this for a long time. When it came time for the cremation, he went in person to watch the fire.
He placed a lapis lazuli bottle before the seat and made this vow: "The Buddha-Dharma is truly efficacious; I pray that the *śarīra* will fill my bottle.
As soon as he finished speaking, smoke descended from the sky and entered the bottle. When the smoke subsided, it was exactly as he had wished. —From the Record of Lord Lu.
From then on, he devoted himself wholeheartedly to the inner scriptures, regretting only that his realization had come so late.

There was a monk from Shu named Tai Liu who, while living among the assembly, often lamented that the Buddha-dharma was becoming muddled and corrupted, with heterodox views arising like swarms of bees.
He said, "If I attain true and correct insight through Zen practice, I shall not spare my verbal karma. He then made a vow to pay homage at the stupa of Mazu.
He practiced without ceasing for many years. Suddenly, one day, the stupa emitted white light, which moved him to a profound realization.
Later, he traveled extensively through various monasteries to test and examine veteran masters. Passing before Mount Xuedou, he remarked, "This old fellow has his mouth dripping with water.
Upon hearing these words, Xuedou seemed displeased. When Tai eventually met Xuedou, Xuedou said, "You do not approve of me."
Nanta said, "This old fellow truly has water dripping from his mouth. He then struck his sitting mat once and departed.
The temple steward, feeling resentful, sent men to assault him on the road, injuring Nanta’s leg. Nanta said, "This was sent by the old man Xuedou;
one day he shall surely lose a leg to repay me. Later, it indeed came to pass as he had said. Subsequently, Nanta arrived at...
In the capital, he was unrestrained in the marketplace. An official invited him to his home to provide offerings, but Daifu repeatedly declined.

The official insisted firmly and treated him with even greater reverence, constantly sending a handmaid to serve him food. One day, seeing the official arrive, he intentionally flirted with the handmaid.
Because of this, the official changed his attitude toward him, and Daifu was finally able to take his leave. Not many days later, he was seen standing upright in the bustling market.
He sat and attained transformation.

▲ Regarding the Honorable Duke Ou-yang: Formerly, while serving as an official in Lo-chung, he once went sightseeing at Mount Sung. He dismissed his attendants and servants and proceeded with unrestrained freedom.
Upon reaching a mountain temple, he entered its gate; there, tall bamboos filled the courtyard, the frost was clear, birds were singing, and the scenery was fresh and vibrant.

Ming Wenzhong was resting on the palace steps when an old monk sat beside him, reading a sutra with complete composure. The monk did not pay much attention to Wenzhong’s conversation nor respond to him.
Wenzhong found this strange and asked, "How long has it been since you, O man of the Way, have lived in the mountains? He replied, "It has been a very long time.
Wenzhong asked again, "What sutra are you reciting? He replied, "The Lotus Sutra. Wenzhong said, "In the past, when eminent monks faced the moment of death..."
"In every case, they passed away with laughter and ease. By what path did they achieve this? He replied, "It was through the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) alone.

The Emperor asked again, "Why is it that nowadays there is such silence and nothingness [regarding death]? The old monk smiled and said, "The ancients were in concentration and wisdom at every moment of thought;

how could they have been disturbed at the time of death? People today are in a state of distraction at every moment of thought; how could they attain concentration at the time of death? Wen Zhong was greatly impressed.
Happiness! He was unaware that his knees had even bent.
Xie Hishen composed a literary record of these events.
At the assembly hall of Yanguan, there was a monk serving as an administrator who suddenly saw a ghost messenger come to summon him. The monk said to the messenger:
"I am a person of affairs and have not yet had the leisure to practice. May I request permission to be excused for seven days? The messenger said, "I shall wait to report this to the king;
if he grants permission, you may return after seven days; otherwise, you must return immediately. Having spoken, he vanished.
When the seven days had passed, the monk could not be found anywhere. Later, someone asked another monk about it, saying, "If you are sought out..."
At the moment of wearing it, how can one resist him?
Dongshan spoke on his behalf, saying, "He has found you.
▲ Long ago, there was an official who composed a "Treatise on the Non-existence of Ghosts. One night, while he was wielding his brush, he suddenly saw a ghost appear and say:
"You say there is none; I wonder about that.
Wuzu Yan said, "If I had been there at that time, I would simply have made the gesture of a magpie’s beak with my hand and said to him, 'The valley calls out.'"
▲ Once, there was an ancient master who one day did not go to the hall. An attendant invited him to attend, and the master said, "Today I have eaten my fill of oil-cakes at the manor.
The attendant said, "The Master has never gone out. The master said, "Go and ask the manor owner.
Just as the attendant was about to leave, he suddenly saw the manor owner coming to thank the Master for visiting the manor.
Jingshan Dahui’s verse says: "The Abbot did not go to the hall; the steward thanked him for his visit.

Once a word enters the gate of officialdom, even nine oxen cannot pull it out. The *Congrong Lu* identifies this ancient case as an event involving Nanquan, while the *Zongjing Yuan* lists it among the cases of Ehu Fuzhao.
▲ In the past, there was a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) who asked a monk who had entered meditative absorption: "The seed of a Wheel-Turning King’s being is neither a Buddha nor an Arhat;
it does not receive a future body. What is the meaning of this? The monk then entered absorption to consult Maitreya.
Upon emerging from meditation, he recounted Maitreya’s words and replied: "It is like a potter molding clay to form a vessel."
▲ The monk Wonhyo of Tang was a native of Haedong (Korea). Having first traveled by sea, he set out to seek the Way at famous mountains.
Walking alone across a desolate marsh, he stayed overnight among the graves. Being extremely thirsty, he reached into a hollow with his hands and found sweet, cool spring water.
At dawn, he saw it was a skull. He loathed it intensely and felt as though he were about to vomit it out. Suddenly, he had a profound realization and sighed deeply, saying:

"When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, the skull is no different [from my own nature]. The Great Master Tathāgata said, 'The three realms are but mind. How could he have deceived me?
Thereupon, he ceased seeking further teachers and returned to the East Sea (Korea), where he composed commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The *Línjiān lù* states: When Chan Master Xuánshā Bèi was gathering firewood in the mountains, a monk nearby called out, "Master, look out for the tiger!
Seeing the tiger, Xuánshā looked at the monk and said, "It is you. When Dharma Master Língrùn was walking in the mountains, a wild fire flew swiftly toward him;
his companions all fled, but Rún walked on with his usual composure and said, "There is nothing outside the mind."
Fire. Fire is, in truth, the mind. One may think fire can be escaped, yet there is no way to avoid it; when fire arrives, one is extinguished.
Venerable Yanyang lived alone on a mountain, where snakes and tigers came to his hand to eat. When Master Guizong Chang was cutting grass and saw a snake, he cut it down.
A monk nearby said, "I have long heard of Guizong, but today I see for the first time a śramaṇa of such coarse conduct."
Chang said: "Are you coarse, or am I coarse? I have heard that there are four ways to verify the mind through intimacy with Prajñā:

namely, according to principle, according to phenomena, according to entry, and according to exit. Beyond both phenomena and principle, the School of the Patriarchs further possesses the application of the 'concealed point' (zangfeng).
Intimacy is used for self-cultivation; the application of the concealed point is used for governing others."
▲ Dharma Master Tang Xiuya’s Song for Reciting the Lotus Sutra: The mountain colors are deep and somber; pine smoke mingles in dense layers.
Beneath the empty forest, upon a flat, rounded rock, sits a monk. With legs crossed and staff resting across his lap, he recites the White Lotus Sutra.
From dawn until dusk, moving from left to right, tiger tracks and wolf tracks—ten fragments here, five there—were strewn with various flowers in disarray.
Having encountered them by chance, though not yet having come to know them deeply, I recognized them as men of old or men of the present: they were Tan Yan and Tan Yi.
I have heard that this sutra contains profound purports; the Emperor has praised it as truly wondrous in meaning. Closing my eyes and darkening my mind, I entered into contemplation.
Listen closely! A drop of *amṛta* has entered your scorched intestines. This is the intent of the Buddhas and the marrow of the Patriarchs;
it is my own heart and the purport of the scriptures. Alas, though fingers are snapped and hands are raised, one fails to reach what is right before one’s eyes—right now is the very moment.
How great! How truly extraordinary! The King of Emptiness seeks to enable all living beings to attain this, its radiance illuminating eighteen thousand lands, land after land.
All were of golden hue; within a single ray of light, the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence appeared.

Even a madman would still inquire of Maitreya: "I too, in my youth, studied emptiness and stillness; once I attained the state of no-mind, I simply rested. Today, I have personally heard this sutra being recited."
I initially realized that the donkey vehicle is not the ultimate truth; even I, in my youth, did not venture beyond my door, unwilling to let the dust of the mundane world stain my footsteps.
Today, having personally heard this sutra being recited, I realize for the first time that every step is a place of treasure.

I too, in my youth, loved to compose poetry, believing that such dark investigations would disturb my meditative concentration. Today, having personally heard this sutra being recited, what hindrance can there be to the use of brush and inkstone?
Relying upon the true nature, I too was once in my youth addicted to childish play, believing that half of my life had been spent in vain.

Today, hearing this sutra recited in person, I have finally realized that piling up sand is no small matter. In the past, I traveled through mountains and waters, thinking that those distant peaks were not my native home.
Today, hearing this sutra recited in person, I have finally realized that within the rivers and mountains there is not a single inch of land that is not home. I...

In the past, the mind-monkey was not yet tamed; it was constantly bound in vain by golden chains. Today, having personally heard this sutra recited, I have finally realized that there is nothing to serve as shackles or manacles.
When the Master recites this sutra, he chews each and every word until its essence is fully digested—the flavor of clarified butter (amṛta).

This flavor of clarified butter is precious and exquisite; it does not reside in the lips, nor does it reside in the teeth. It dwells only within the square inch of the heart of those weary in their worldly lives.
The Master recited one line of this sutra after another; with every line, the white ox personally took its step. The step of the white ox was as swift as the wind;
it was not in the west, nor was it in the east—it resided solely within the daily activities of floating life. To be unaware of these daily activities—how bitter it is!

With a belly for wine and an interior for rice, when the Elder calls out in a loud voice, the ox does not turn back. How is this any different from being deaf? How is this any different from being mute?
Blind! It is not that the ears of worldly people lack acuity; it is only that their acute hearing is deaf to the scriptures. It is not that the eyes of worldly people lack clarity;
it is only that their clear vision is blind to the scriptures. Though they possess hearing, they do not hear; though they possess sight, they do not see.
Turning like a pulley up and down, they die in vain and live in emptiness. All worldly people recognize the Master’s voice, but who among them can recognize the Master’s mind? Worldly people...

Everyone recognizes the Master’s form; who among them can recognize the Master’s name? The Master is a King of Physicians who carries out the Buddha’s command, coming to treat the illnesses of sentient beings.
He can cause the deluded to awaken and the frantic to find peace; he can purify the defiled and rectify the deviant;
he can transform the ordinary into the sagely. Thus, it is not only fitting for humans to pay him homage, but also for dragons to offer praise and for spirits to sing his praises.
The Buddha praised this in verse: "How could those who turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust fail to prostrate themselves and take refuge?
There was a monk named Wéntōnghuì of Báiyún Monastery in Kāifēng Prefecture, Hénán. His master had him in charge of the washbasin.
Once, some market vendors washed fresh fish in the basin; Wén grew angry and struck them, whereupon they suddenly fell dead. He then fled secretly to Huá...
At Zongchi Temple in the prefecture, he served as an elder for a long time—indeed, for more than twenty years.
One day, he suddenly said to his disciples, "A case from twenty years ago must be settled today. When the assembly asked for the reason, he replied, "You shall know it for yourselves at noon.
He then sat in the lotus posture to await the appointed hour. Just as Zhang Jun arrived in Guanzhong leading his troops, a soldier carried...

The soldier took his bow and arrows and went to the Dharma Hall, where he stared fixedly at Master Wen. Just as he was about to shoot him, Wen laughed and said, "I have been waiting for you, old monk.
The soldier said, "We have never met before. Now that I see you, my anger cannot be restrained;
why do you wish to harm me? Wen spoke to him of their past connection. The soldier suddenly recited this verse: "Enmity begets enmity; when will it ever end? Kalpa after kalpa..."

"How could this entanglement be accidental? It would be better to resolve it together with the Master. As soon as he said, "Now I shall go to the Western Heaven," he was seen to have passed away on the spot.
Wén then took up his brush and wrote a verse: "Thirty-three years of wandering, Taking on various forms along the way.
Who would have thought that meeting today Would resolve the obstacles that stood before me? Having finished writing, he became serene and still.
*Hua* (Compendium of the Unified Gazetteer).

The Third Generation after the Sixth Patriarch:
Chan Master Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou. He was a native of Changle in Fuzhou and a son of the Wang family.

When he was a child, he accompanied his mother to a temple to pay homage to the Buddha. Pointing to the Buddha image, he asked his mother, "Who is this? His mother replied, "It is the Buddha. The Master—

He said, "My physical form is no different from that of others; I too shall become a Buddha in the future. Having left the secular world at the age of seven, he became thoroughly proficient in the three studies of the Bodhisattva.

He attended Great Master Ma as his attendant. Whenever a donor sent offerings of rice for the midday meal, as soon as the Master lifted the lid of the tray, Great Master Ma would pick up a piece of fried cake and show it to the assembly, asking, "What is this? He did this time and again.
This lasted for three years. One day, while attending Mazu as they were walking along, they saw a flock of wild ducks fly past.
Mazu asked, "What is that? The Master replied, "Wild ducks. Mazu asked, "Where have they gone? The Master replied, "They flew away."
The Patriarch then twisted the Master’s nose. In his agony, the Master let out a cry. The Patriarch said, “You said it flew away, did you not? At these words, the Master attained realization.

(Xuedou’s verse: “Wild duck! Where do you go? Mazu saw it coming and spoke with it. They exhausted their talk on the sentiment of clouds, mountains, water, and moon; yet still not understanding, it flew away again. But he seized it—speak, speak!
The Master then returned to the attendant’s quarters and wept bitterly. A colleague asked him, “Are you thinking of your parents?”
The Master said, "No. [The monk] asked, "Was it because you were scolded by someone? The Master said, "No. [The monk] asked, "Then why are you crying?

The Master said, "My nostrils were pinched so hard by the Great Master that the pain has not yet subsided. A fellow practitioner asked, "What circumstance was there that did not accord with him? The Master said:

"You should go ask the Preceptor. A fellow practitioner asked the Master, "What was the karmic connection for Attendant Hai that he is weeping in his quarters and telling the Preceptor to explain it for him? The Master said, "He understands it himself; you should go ask him directly.
The fellow practitioner returned to the quarters and said, "The Preceptor told me that you understand it, so he instructed me to ask you myself."
The Master then laughed heartily. A colleague said, "Just now you were weeping; why are you laughing now? The Master replied, "Just now I was weeping;
now I am laughing. The colleague was left bewildered. The following day, when Mazu ascended the seat and the assembly had just gathered, the Master stepped forward and rolled up the cushion.
Mazu immediately descended from the seat. The Master followed him to the abbot’s quarters, where Mazu said, "I have not yet..."
[The Master] spoke. "Why did you roll up your mat so quickly? The Master said, "Yesterday, I was pinched by the Abbot until my nose ached.
The Patriarch said, "Where did you apply your mind yesterday? The Master said, "Today my nose does not ache anymore.
The Patriarch said, "You have thoroughly understood what happened yesterday. The Master bowed and withdrew. He attended [the Patriarch] again, standing in service.
Next, the Patriarch looked at the whisk in the corner of the rope bed. The Master said, "Is it used as this, or apart from this?

The Patriarch said, "When you open your two flaps of skin [your mouth] hereafter, with what will you save people? The Master took up the whisk and held it upright. The Patriarch said, "Is it used as this, or apart from this?
The Master hung the whisk back in its original place. The Patriarch let out a thunderous shout, which caused the Master to fall straight down three times.
[Baizhang] was deaf for three days. Not long after, he resided at Mount Daxiong. Because the cliffs and peaks where he dwelt were so steep and lofty, it was named "Hundred Fathoms" (Bai Zhang).
Scholars from all directions flocked there like deer. One day he said to the assembly, "The Buddha-dharma is no small matter.
In the past, when I was struck by a shout from Master Ma, my ears were deaf for three full days. When Huangbo heard this being recounted, he involuntarily stuck out his tongue.
The Master said, "In the future, will you not take up the lineage of Mazu? Baizhang replied, "Not so.
Today, because the Master raised this matter, I have been able to see Mazu’s great functioning of the spiritual mechanism (*da-ji-yong*). However, I do not yet recognize Mazu.
If I were to succeed Mazu, my descendants would later lose their own selves. The Master said, "So it is, so it is. When one's insight is equal to the teacher's, one diminishes the teacher."
"Half-virtue. Only when one's insight surpasses that of the teacher is one fit to receive the transmission. You possess an insight that greatly transcends your teacher. Baizhang then prostrated.
Guishan asked Yangshan about the circumstances of Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu: "What was the intended meaning of these two venerable masters?"
"How is this? Yangzi said, "This is manifesting great capacity and great function.
Muzhou asked, "Among the eighty-four *kalyāṇamitras* that Mazu produced, how many attained great capacity? How many attained great function?
Yangzi said, "Baizhang attained great capacity; Huangbo attained great function; all the others were merely teachers of exhortation. Muzhou said, "So it is."
Thus, Fenzhou said: "Once you have awakened, let it be; what more need be said? For three days your ears were deaf. Shimen said:
"If your ears had not been deaf for three days, how could you have attained awakening? Fenzhou said: "I speak thus."
"More than half a month's journey from other stone gates," Donglin said in total. "One should speak without avoiding having one's tongue cut;
one should tend the furnace without avoiding sparks flying back. How could the Buddha-dharma be bent to suit people?
Today, Donglin goes into the lair of the blue dragon to contend for the pearl. Regarding Baizhang’s great wisdom, it was not without reason that others were deaf for three days. —Fenzhou.
Shimen said, "How can these two blind men avoid [retribution]? Have these three elders ever attained awakening?
After a long silence, he said, "The patriarchs failed to resolve it; the calamity now reaches their descendants. Furthermore, Fengyang’s verse says:

"Whenever there was nothing to do, I attended before the Master. The Master pointed to something hanging on the corner of the rope-bench. I picked it up and returned to my original position to stand."
"A single shout, clearly transmitted to this day. Xuedou took it up and said: "How extraordinary, O Zen practitioners!

Nowadays, there are many who list its lineages, yet those who investigate its source are extremely few. Everyone says that Baizhang attained great enlightenment under a shout; is this truly so or not?
Nevertheless, while the blades may look alike, the fish and the 'ru' (a homophone for 'deer') differ. If one is clear..."
O blind man! You cannot deceive him by even a hair’s breadth. Take, for instance, when Mazu said, "In the future, with these two flaps of skin you will open, what will you use to save people?
Baizhang then held up his whisk. Was this like a worm gnawing through wood? Or was it like the simultaneous pecking and hatching?
If you wish to understand why everyone’s ears were deaf for three days, know that in a great furnace, refined gold leaves nothing behind.
His complexion changed. Yuanwu Keqin said: "Xuedou says, 'If you all wish to see it, your ears will be deaf for three days.
Like refined gold from a great furnace, there is no changing of color. How many people have been drowned by these words?
Xuedou wanted to vent his breath and reveal a single mechanism and a single realm that cannot be shattered through all eternity. You people, do not yet..."
"You have understood it well, Daowei Gao. Having come from Master Leshan Zun at Litan, you are now about to visit Yuanwu Keqin. On your way, you passed by Zhang Wujin. One day, Wujin said to you:
'I have been reading Xuedou’s *Nian-gu* (Picking up the Ancients), and upon reaching the story of Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu, he said:

"Fine gold from a great furnace should not change its color. As he threw down the scroll, he sighed, saying: "Truly..."* *(Note: The original text ends with "投卷歎曰：審" [threw down the scroll and sighed, saying: Truly...]. The ellipsis indicates the sentence was left unfinished in the source.)*
"If it were so, how could there be a Linji today? He then composed a verse, saying:
"The Master of Ma’s single shout at Daxiong Peak Pierced deep into the skull, leaving three days of deafness. When Huangbo heard it, he was startled and stuck out his tongue;
From this, the House Style was established in Jiangxi. Later, Chan Master Ping sent a letter stating: "Last summer, I read the lineage of the Linji school..."
I then realized that the Layman had attained great capacity and great function. Furthermore, he requested a verse from me. I composed a verse and sent it to him, saying:
"The master has already understood the tongue-licking and deafness; Beating one’s breast can only bring cries to the blue heavens. In the assembly at Panshan, he performed a somersault;
Only upon reaching this point does one know the madness of Puhua. In various quarters, people often regard me as clever and widely learned.
"Few know me. Since you, Master, have come from the Dharma seat of Jiangxi, you must surely be able to discern the superior from the inferior;
please try to explain this for me. Daoyuan said, "Your realization accords with that of Zhenjing Sishi. Zhang asked, "In what way?"
Dahui recited a verse on true purity: "Guest emotions turn with every step one takes;
Great majestic light cannot manifest. Suddenly, one shout deafens both ears; Natha’s eyes open, and Huangbo’s face appears.
Sishan Nian said: "Yunyan wished to ask Xuedou: 'Since this is refined gold from a great furnace, it should not change its color. Why [is this so]...'"
"Mòquè was deaf for three days. Do you all wish to know why? "From before, no one has recognized his meritorious service with the sweat of horses;

he simply wishes to re-examine his epoch-making achievements. Zhang struck the table and said, "Were it not for your words, how could we have seen the point where Zhenjing and Sijian applied themselves?
Had it not been for these two great elders, it would have been difficult to manifest the essence of Xuedou and Mazu."
After [Baizhang] had settled in his quarters, the Master of Horses sent three jars of sauce as a gift. The Master assembled the community for the formal lecture hall session;

having finished opening the letter, he took up his staff, pointed at the jars, and said, "If you can speak, I shall not break them; if you cannot speak, I shall break them. The assembly was speechless.
The Master broke the jars and returned to his quarters. One day Mazu asked the Master, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From behind the mountain."
The Patriarch asked, "Did you encounter anyone? He replied, "I did not encounter anyone. The Patriarch said, "Why did you not encounter anyone?
He replied, "If I had encountered anyone, I would have reported it to the Master. The Patriarch said, "From where did you get this news? He replied, "It is my fault.
The Patriarch said, "Rather, it is the old monk’s fault. A monk entered the Dharma Hall weeping. The Master [asked him].

[The Master] asked, "What? [The monk] replied, "My parents have both passed away; I request that you, Master, choose an auspicious day. The Master said, "Come tomorrow, and we shall bury them all at once.
While Guishan, Wufeng, and Yunyan were standing in attendance, the Master asked Guishan, "When the throat, lips, and mouth are all set aside, how do you speak?
Guishan said, "In that case, please let the Master speak for me. The Master said, "I am not unwilling to speak to you, but I fear..."
"Later on, you will lose your children and grandchildren. He then asked Wufeng. Wufeng said, "The Master must also close it up [put it away].

The Master said, "In a place where there is no one, I shall raise my hand to my forehead and look toward you. He then asked Yunyan. Yunyan said, "Does the Master have it yet? The Master said, [He has it].
"Losing my children and grandchildren.
Xuedou’s verse says: "I ask the Master to speak further: A tiger’s head sprouts horns as it emerges from the wild weeds. When spring ends in the Ten Continents, the flowers wither;
the coral groves shine bright under the blazing sun. Master, you too must clear them all away—this battle array of dragons and snakes."
Looking up at their stratagems, one cannot help but long remember General Li. A solitary osprey soars through the autumn sky ten thousand miles away—does the Master have such a thing?
A golden-maned lion does not crouch upon the ground; two by two and three by three, they tread the old path.
Beneath Mount Daxiong, they snap their fingers in vain.
Whenever the Master ascended the hall, an old man would join the assembly to listen to the Dharma. One day, when the assembly had withdrawn, only the old man remained.
The Master asked him, "Who are you? The old man replied, "I am not a human being. During the time of the past Kāśyapa Buddha, I once dwelt on this mountain.
When a student asked me, 'Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect? I..."
He replied, "It does not fall within cause and effect. Consequently, he fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes.

Now he requests the Master to provide a turning phrase on his behalf, so that he may be released from this wild fox body. The Master said, "Ask me. The old man asked, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within cause and effect?
The Master said, "He does not obscure cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment. He prostrated himself and said:
"I have already been released from my wild fox body and reside behind the mountain. I venture to request that you follow the monastic rules for the funeral of a deceased monk.
The Master ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) to strike the gavel and announce to the assembly: "After the meal, we shall escort the deceased monk. The great assembly gathered to deliberate;
they all felt at ease, yet there was no one ill in the *nirvāṇa-hall*. "Why is this so? After the meal, the Master led the assembly to the base of a cliff behind the mountain. With [the fox], he...
Using his staff, he pulled out a dead wild fox and performed its cremation according to the Dharma. That evening, the Master ascended the hall and recounted the preceding circumstances.
Huangbo then asked, "The ancients fell into the body of a wild fox for five hundred lifetimes because they gave one erroneous response."
"Excellent, excellent! What shall we do together? The Master said, "Come closer and I will tell you. Baizhang stepped forward and struck the Master with his palm.
The Master laughed and said, "I thought the beard was red; it turns out there is a red-bearded barbarian as well.
At that time, Guishan was serving as the steward (dianzuo) in the assembly. Situ Tuo raised the story of the wild fox and asked, "How would the steward handle this?"
Dazhu shook the door panels three times. Sima said, "That was quite crude. Dazhu replied, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter of such things.
Zhenjing’s verse says: "Not falling into concealment, nor failing to discern; He intends for him to cast off his fox-body from this point on. People... [text ends]
Everyone says it is good to retire from office, yet one has never seen a single person living beneath the forest trees. Zhenru Zhe’s verse says:
"In the great smelting furnace, Buddhas and Patriarchs are forged; when the mold is completely melted away, those who understand are at a loss.
A monk asked Jingshan Daokai, "Does a great practitioner of the Way still fall within the realm of cause and effect? Baizhang of old said, "No."
[The monk] asked, "Why did he fall into the body of a wild fox? Jing said, "Whenever you meet someone, simply present it thus.
The monk asked, "As for Baizhang’s later statement, 'He did not obscure cause and effect,' why was he freed from the body of a wild fox?
Jing said, "Whenever you meet someone, simply present it thus. The monk said, "Suppose someone were to ask Mount Jing, 'For one who has practiced great cultivation...'"
"Does a person still fall within cause and effect or not? I do not know what the Master said to him. Jing replied, "I told you:
whenever you meet someone, simply bring it up like this. Gao then offered a verse: "Not falling, not obscuring— A stone, a clod of earth.
Meeting on the road, The silver mountain shatters to pieces. Clapping hands and laughing 'he-he'— One scene in Mingzhou."
There was a simpleton named Budai (Hán Bùdài), Zen Master Xuefeng Daoyuan. While he was sitting in formal meditation at Jicui, he heard two monks discussing the "Wild Fox" kōan.
One said, "Even if one does not obscure cause and effect, one has still not escaped the body of a wild fox.
The other said, "If one does not fall into cause and effect, how could one have ever fallen as a wild fox? Upon hearing this, the Master sat bolt upright.

However, as I went to visit Jicui Hermitage and crossed a mountain stream, I experienced a sudden and profound realization. When I later related this matter to Master Nan, my tears flowed down to my chin before he had even finished speaking.
Master Nan ordered me to go to the attendant’s bed and sleep soundly; upon waking, I suddenly rose and composed a verse, saying: [Verse omitted per instructions]
Neither falling into error nor remaining in ignorance—monks and laypeople alike have nothing to hide or fear. This man’s spirit and bearing are like those of a king;
how could he begrudge the covering of his body? With a single *zhilu* staff, he acts with great freedom and ease. A wild fox has leapt into the ranks of the golden-haired lions;
seeing this, Master Nan rejoiced at it.
A monk asked, "What is the extraordinary matter? The Master said, "Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak. The monk bowed; the Master then struck him.
While they were all being pressed into labor digging the earth, a monk suddenly heard the drum roll, raised his hoe, laughed loudly, and went back.

The Master said, "How brilliant! This is the gate through which Guanyin enters into principle. Upon returning to the monastery, the Master summoned the monk and asked, "What principle did you perceive just now that led you to act in this way?
The monk replied, "Just now I was hungry; hearing the drum, I went back to eat my meal.
The Master then laughed.
Jingqing said, "At that time, there was this monk at Mount Gui. Gushan said, "At that time, there was no such monk at Mount Gui.
Wenyuan Kewen said, "This monk’s voice resounded so powerfully that it caused the eyes of fifteen hundred great virtuous teachers to flicker.
Yet, when it came to the final examination and verification, he was struck down."
He performs a back-flip somersault. Were it not for Guishan, who would have seen the greatness of his meritorious achievements?
Later, it was said that if one says "this monk exists," one only captures half the truth; if one says "this monk does not exist," one also only captures half the truth.
Today, as the sounds of the wooden board, the bell, the fish-bell, and the drum vibrate in unison, perhaps there will be someone who claps their hands and laughs heartily. Directly!
He said to him: "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva has come! This chapter is sometimes listed under the section on Guishan;
thus, various masters all attribute it to Guishan. This [attribution] follows the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
A monk asked Xitang, "Setting aside for a moment the case where there is a question and an answer, what is it like when there is neither question nor answer?
Tang said, "I am afraid it will rot away. When the Master heard this being cited, he said, "From the beginning, I have had doubts about this old brother.

The monk said, "Please, Master, speak. The Master said, "The 'single integrated mark' (yīhéxiàng) cannot be apprehended. The Master addressed the assembly, saying, "There is a person who has never eaten since long ago."
One does not say that rice is hunger; there is one person who eats all day long yet does not say they are full.
Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "One person stands atop a solitary peak with no way to emerge;
another person stands at a crossroads with neither front nor back. Which one is in front? Which one is behind? Do not conceptualize.
"Vimalakīrti does not act as Master Fuda; take care! He further said: "There is one person who remains on the road for kalpas without leaving home;
there is another person who leaves home but is not on the road. Which of these two is worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans?
Miaoxi took up Linji’s words and remarked: "The thief has already revealed himself."
Yunyan asked, "For whom do you labor so busily every day? The Master said, "There is one person who needs it.
Yunyan said, "Why do you not let him do it himself? The Master said, "He has no means of livelihood."
While Yunyan was boiling tea, Daowu asked, "For whom are you boiling it? Yunyan replied, "There is someone who wants some.
Daowu said, "Why not let him boil it himself? Yunyan replied, "Fortunately, there is this humble self here. Later, Yaoshan asked Yunyan:
"What are you doing? Yan said, "Carrying dung. Shan asked, "Which one? Yan said, "The one on the mountain.
Shan asked, "For whom do you come and go? Yan said, "To carry his belongings for him. Shan said, "Why not have them walk side by side? Yan said, "Do not slander him, Master.
Shan said, "It is not appropriate to speak thus. Yan asked, "How should I speak? Shan said, "Return [to your original state]."
"Have you ever carried it?
The Master then sent a monk to Zhangjing. "When you see him ascending the hall to preach the Dharma, you should immediately spread out your sitting cloth and prostrate.
Then, rising, take one shoe, brush away the dust on top with your sleeve, and turn it upside down to cover [the other]. That monk arrived at Zhangjing...
Jingyi followed his teacher’s instruction. Changjing said, "This old monk is at fault.
Huanglong Xin remarked, "Bazhang exhausted all his spiritual powers, yet it was not as good as Changjing saying, 'This old monk is at fault.'"
A monk asked, "I bring this raw jade to seek the Master; I pray you, Master, examine it for me. The Master said, "Last night, a tiger on South Mountain bit a great beast.
The monk said, "The true teaching is not mistaken; why do you not employ skillful means? The Master said, "You are a fellow who covers his ears while stealing a bell.

The monk said, "If one does not meet the discernment of Cai Yong, one is no different from firewood in a wild hut. The Master then struck him. The monk cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! The Master [said], "..."
[The monk] said, "To have such a mouthful of words! [The Master] replied, "Rarely do we meet one who understands. He then shook his sleeves and departed.

The Master said, "Today Baizhang has lost half the battle" (Fujian said: "Though he won a victory, he has had both feet cut off"). That evening, an attendant asked, "Why did the Master let that monk leave after he refused to acknowledge you?
The Master then struck him. The attendant cried out, "Heaven! Heaven! The Master said, "Rarely do we meet one who understands."
Zhiyin bowed. The Master said, "I have received your report. Zhaozhou visited the Master, who asked, "Where have you recently come from?
He replied, "From Nanquan. The Master asked, "What sayings or phrases did Nanquan speak recently? He replied, "For those who have not yet attained it, one must simply remain silent.
The Master said, "Setting aside that 'silent' phrase for a moment, how would you express the 'bewildered' phrase? Zhaozhou—
He stepped forward three paces. The Master then gave a shout. Xiangzhou made a gesture of shrinking his body. The Master said, "Excellent, profound stillness.
Xiangzhou then went out.
Alternatively, Xiangzhou said, "One who has not yet attained must be profoundly still. The Master then gave a shout. Xiangzhou made a gesture of fear.
The Master said, "How wonderful, this profound stillness. Xiu rose and departed with a dance.

On another occasion, when the Master had finished preaching the Dharma and the assembly was descending from the hall, he called out to them. As the assembly turned their heads, the Master asked, "What is this?"
Yaoshan identified this as "the sentence from Baizhang’s descent from the hall. [Baizhang] ascended the hall and said:
"The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. Its essence reveals true permanence, unbound by words and letters.
The nature of mind is unstained; it is fundamentally perfected of itself. Simply leave behind delusive conditions, and you are the Buddha of Suchness. [A monk] asked: "What is the Great [Dharma]?"
Relying on the essential principles of sudden enlightenment, the Master said: "First, you must bring all conditions to rest and cease from all affairs.
Regarding all phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome, mundane or supramundane—do not recall them, do not give rise to thoughts of them. Relinquish body and mind so that they are free and at ease.
Let the mind be like wood or stone, without discrimination; let the mind have no activity. When the ground of the mind is empty, wisdom..."

The sun manifests of itself, like the sun rising when the clouds part. Simply by ceasing all攀緣 (pān-yuán, mental clinging/seeking), exhausting the defilements and purities of greed, anger, craving, and grasping, one remains unmoved by the five desires and the eight winds. One is not bound by seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor deluded by various objects.
Spontaneously endowed with supernatural powers and wondrous functions, such a person is one who has attained liberation. Facing all things...

Regarding objects, the mind is neither still nor distracted; it is neither gathered nor dispersed. Penetrating through all sounds and forms without obstruction, such a person is called a "Way-person" (*mārga-pudgala*).
Neither employing good, evil, right, nor wrong, nor loving any single dharma, nor abandoning any single dharma, such a person is called a "Mahāyāna person.
They are not affected by any good or evil, emptiness or existence, defilement or purity, conditioned or unconditioned phenomena.
That which is bound by the merit and wisdom of both the mundane and supramundane realms is called "Buddha-wisdom.

When all such perceptions and emotions—whether regarding what is good or bad, right or wrong—are entirely unable to bind one, and one attains mastery everywhere, this is called a "Bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain enlightenment," and one immediately ascends to the stage of Buddhahood.
Question: Facing all objects of perception, how does one cause the mind to become like wood?
Shiguo departed. The Master said: "All dharmas fundamentally do not themselves declare themselves empty, nor do they declare themselves form;
nor do they speak of right or wrong, or defilement or purity. Nor is there any mind that binds people.

It is only that people themselves engage in false conceptualization and attachment, forming various kinds of interpretations, giving rise to various kinds of knowledge and views, and producing various kinds of craving and fear. One need only realize that all dharmas..."
They arise spontaneously; all exist because of one's own single thought of deluded inversion and the grasping of signs. Know that the mind and its objects fundamentally do not reach one another;
they are liberated in their very place. Each and every dharma is quiescent in its own place; each and every dharma is a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in its own place.
Furthermore, the nature that is primordially present cannot be designated by names. From the beginning, it is neither ordinary nor holy; neither defiled nor pure; neither empty nor existent;
and neither good nor evil. When associated with various defiled phenomena, it is called the realm of humans, devas, and the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
If the mind of both defilement and purity is exhausted, one dwells neither in bondage nor in liberation, and there is no longer any conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
For those whose mind-only is bound or liberated, they abide within birth and death with their minds at ease.
Ultimately, they do not conjoin with the various delusive, illusory afflictions, the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases of birth and death;

they remain aloof and without dependence, unconfined by anything, unhindered in going or staying, and as they traverse birth and death, it is like the opening of a door. Now, if a practitioner encounters various [circumstances]...
Regarding matters of suffering or pleasure, or those that are agreeable or disagreeable, his mind never retreats or yields. He does not dwell upon fame, profit, gain, food, or clothing;
he does not crave merit or benefit, nor is he obstructed by any worldly phenomena. He has no kin and no attachment.

Maintain equanimity toward suffering and pleasure; wear coarse clothing to ward off the cold and take simple food to sustain life. Remain steadfast like one who is dull-witted or deaf, and you will possess a measure of resonance with the truth.

If, within the mind, you extensively pursue learning and intellectual understanding, seeking blessings or wisdom, all of this belongs to birth and death and is of no benefit to the ultimate principle.
Instead, you will be drifted and drowned by the winds of the realm of intellectual understanding, returning once more to the ocean of birth and death. Thus spoke the Buddha.

This is the principle of non-seeking; to seek it is to deviate from it. This is the principle of non-seeking; to seek it is to lose it. If one clings to non-seeking, one is again the same as those who seek.
If one clings to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one is again the same as those who engage in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, a sutra says:
"Do not grasp at dharmas, do not grasp at non-dharmas, and do not grasp at what is neither dharma nor non-dharma. It further says: "The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata—this Dharma..."

It is neither real nor false. If one can for a single lifetime make the mind resemble wood or stone, such that it is not swept away or drowned by the aggregates (*skandha*), the realms (*dhātu*), the five desires, or the eight winds, then the causes of birth and death are severed.

One will attain freedom in going and staying, remaining unbound by the causes and effects of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and unrestrained by outflows (*āsrava*). At another time, one will again take that which was previously boundless by causes as the very cause.
Benefiting others through shared practice: one responds to all things with a mind free from attachment and resolves all bonds with unimpeded wisdom;

this is also called "prescribing medicine according to the illness. Question: If, as now, one has received the precepts, body and speech are pure, and one has already perfected all virtues, why is this so?
"Have you attained liberation? The Master replied, "I have attained a small measure of liberation, but I have not yet attained liberation of mind, nor have I attained liberation in all places.
The monk asked, "What is liberation of mind and liberation in all places? The Master said, "To seek nothing—not even the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha—nor even merit, wisdom, knowledge, or understanding.
When the notions of defilement and purity are exhausted, one does not even cling to this state of non-attainment."
Seeking this is correct. Furthermore, one does not abide in the state of extinction (*kṣaya*), nor does one rejoice in heaven or fear hell.

Being unimpeded regarding both bondage and liberation, the body, mind, and all places are termed "liberation. You must not say that merely purifying a small portion of the precepts of body, speech, and mind constitutes full realization;
you do not yet know the gates of precept, concentration, and wisdom as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, nor have you at all entered into untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*).

A single hair remains. Exert yourself and press forward; you must investigate with fierce intensity. Do not wait until your ears are deaf, your eyes grow dim, your face is wrinkled, and your hair is white.

When the suffering of old age has overtaken your body, when you are entangled by the grief of attachment, tears flow from your eyes, and your heart is filled with terror—having no foundation and knowing no place of departure—at such a time as this, you will be unable to adjust your hands and feet, even if you possess merit.
Wisdom, reputation, profit, and offerings do not save one at all; this is because the eye of the mind has not yet opened.

One merely contemplates various objects and does not know how to reflect back upon oneself, nor does one see the Buddha-way. All the karmic conditions of good and evil from one’s entire life suddenly manifest before one.
One feels either joy or terror as the six realms and the five aggregates appear simultaneously, all arrayed in magnificent splendor—houses, boats, carriages, and so forth.
The palanquin was magnificent and radiant; all these were manifestations arising from the greed and attachment of one’s own mind.

All evil environments were transformed into sublime realms. Yet, wherever the weight of greed and attachment led, and wherever the karmic consciousness drew one, there one would take birth, having no freedom whatsoever.
Whether as dragons or beasts, noble or base, nothing at all was predetermined. [The student] asked: "How can one attain freedom? The Master said:
Now, when you attain it, you attain it immediately. Whether confronted by the five desires or the eight winds, your mind remains free from grasping or rejecting.

Stinginess, envy, greed, and attachment, as well as the sense of "mine," are exhausted; both defilement and purity vanish. Like the sun and moon in the sky, they illuminate without depending on external conditions.

Every thought is like wood or stone, yet every moment is like one rushing to extinguish a fire on one's head. It is also like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, cutting through the current and passing over—without further doubt.

Stuck. Such a person cannot be categorized as belonging either to heaven or to hell. Now, when reading scriptures or examining the teachings, all words and phrases must be turned back toward one’s own self.
However, all verbal instructions merely clarify the self-nature of present-time discernment;
it is simply that you must not be swayed by any circumstances of existence or non-existence. This is your guide, capable of illuminating and shattering all [delusions].
The existence or non-existence of all objects is Vajra-wisdom; it possesses a quality of autonomous independence.
If one cannot realize it in this way, then even if one can recite the twelve Vedas, it will only result in the arrogance of overestimation, which is in fact a slander against the Buddha.
This is not cultivation. Rather, to be free from all sounds and forms, yet not to dwell in that freedom, nor to dwell in intellectual understanding—this is cultivation.
Reading scriptures and studying the teachings may be considered a good thing according to worldly standards; however, to those who have realized the principle, these are counted as obstructions.
Even one at the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) cannot escape flowing into the river of birth and death if they merely [cling to such practices]. But...

These teachings of the Three Vehicles all treat the maladies of greed, anger, and so forth. If at this very moment, in every thought-moment, there are maladies such as greed or anger, you must first treat them.
There is no need to seek out meanings, phrases, or intellectual understanding; such understanding belongs to greed, and greed turns into a malady.
At this very moment, simply remain free from all dharmas of existence and non-existence, and even remain free from that freedom itself—thus penetrating beyond the three propositions.
Externally, it is naturally no different from the Buddha. Since you are yourself the Buddha, why worry that the Buddha does not understand your speech?

It is only to be feared that you are not the Buddha, being bound by the various dharmas of existence and non-existence so as to lack freedom; for while the Principle has not yet been established, you already possess merit and wisdom.
One is carried away by merit and wisdom, like a lowly person being elevated to nobility. It is better to first establish the underlying principle than to wait for merit and wisdom;
if one desires merit and wisdom, they can be produced at the moment of need—gathering soil to become gold, turning gold into soil, and transforming the waters of the ocean into ghee and curd.
Shatter Mount Sumeru into fine dust; gather the waters of the four great oceans into a single pore. Render infinite meanings from a single meaning;
render a single meaning from infinite meanings. I pray you, hold this in high esteem. Now, speech must distinguish between the black and the white.

One must recognize the distinction between general and specific terminology. One must recognize the distinction between teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and those of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*). Teachings of definitive meaning clarify and purify; teachings of non-definitive meaning clarify and purify through turbidity.
To speak of the defilements at the margins of impure phenomena is to distinguish the ordinary person; to speak of the defilements at the margins of pure phenomena is to distinguish the noble one.

Based on the ninefold division of the teachings (*navāṅga-śāsana*), it is said that sentient beings prior [to this] lack eyes and must rely upon the refinement of a person. This is like the case of a deaf commoner...
As previously stated, you must simply instruct them to leave the household life, uphold the precepts, cultivate meditation, and study wisdom.
Even if they are laypeople of exceptional capacity—such as Vimalakīrti or the Great Master Fatu—you still may not speak to them in such a manner.

However, if you speak before śramaṇas who have already completed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four motions) and are fully endowed with the entirety of the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, [you may do so].
Furthermore, to speak to others in such a manner is called untimely speech. To speak when it is not the proper time is also called frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).

If one is a śramaṇa, one must speak of the purity of the Dharma and its boundaries; one must speak of the Dharma that is free from existence and non-existence, and free from all cultivation and realization, as well as free even from "freedom" itself.
If one strips away habitual defilements within the state of a śramaṇa, the śramaṇa eliminates the diseases of greed and hatred.
Do not dismiss them; they are also called "deaf worldly people. You must also teach them to practice dhyāna and study wisdom.

If they are monks of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha), once they have exhausted the diseases of greed and anger and dwell in non-greed, they will consider that to be sufficient. Yet this is the Formless Realm;

it obstructs the light of the Buddha and constitutes shedding the blood of the Buddha. You must also teach them to practice dhyāna and study wisdom; you must distinguish between the clear and the turbid.
Regarding "speech": turbid dharmas refer to various names such as greed, hatred, craving, and grasping; pure dharmas refer to various names such as bodhi, nirvāṇa, and liberation.
It is simply within this present mirror-like awareness that there are these two streams of purity and turbidity, and these dharmas of ordinary beings and sages.
Regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane—one does not grasp at them with even the slightest bit of craving or attachment.
Since one neither craves nor grasps, one abides in that non-craving and non-grasping, taking it to be the truth. This is the beginning of goodness; this is abiding in a disciplined mind.
These are the śrāvakas; these are those who cling to the raft and do not let it go; this is the path of the two vehicles; this is the fruit of dhyāna.

Since they neither love nor grasp, yet still dwell in non-grasping, this is "skillful within" [the realm], yet it is the teaching of the half-syllables (*ardhakṣara*). It is still within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
though one may avoid falling into the path of the two vehicles and avoid falling into the path of the māras, it remains a sickness of dhyāna and a fetter for bodhisattvas.

Neither relying on nor dwelling in non-attachment and non-grasping, yet not forming a conceptual understanding of such non-reliance and non-dwelling—this is "good in the end. This is the teaching of the full letters (*pūrṇākṣara*).

It avoids falling into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), avoids falling into the sickness of *dhyāna*, avoids falling into the Bodhisattva vehicle, and avoids falling into the rank of the Māra kings.

Because it serves as an antidote to the obstacles of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the stages (*bhūmyāvaraṇa*), and conduct (*caryāvaraṇa*), one perceives one's own Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) as clearly as seeing forms at night. As...

It is said that at the stage of Buddhahood, two delusions are severed: first, the subtle delusion regarding objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*); second, the extremely subtle delusion regarding objects of knowledge. Therefore, it is said:
"The man of great wisdom breaks through the dust to reveal the scroll. If one can penetrate beyond these three phrases, one will not be governed by the three stages. The teachings provide an analogy:
like a deer leaping three times out of a net, such a person is called a Buddha outside the marketplace (*zhan-wai fo*), unrestrained by any thing.
He attains the channel. This belongs to the Buddha after Dīpaṃkara. It is the Supreme Vehicle; it is the highest wisdom.

It is established upon the path of the Buddhas. Such a person is a Buddha; they possess the Buddha-nature. They are a guide. They cause one to obtain the wind that is without obstruction. This is unimpeded wisdom.
Hereafter, it enables one to attain mastery over the merit and wisdom of cause and effect. It acts as a vehicle to transport cause and effect.
