Abiding in birth, one is not detained by birth; abiding in death, one is not obstructed by death.
Abiding amidst the five aggregates (*skandhas*), it is as if a door were open; one is not hindered by the five aggregates. Going and staying are free, and entering and exiting are without difficulty.
If one can be thus, regardless of whether one’s rank or stage is superior or inferior—even down to the body of an ant—so long as one can be thus, all such beings are [enlightened].
The Pure and Wondrous Land is inconceivable. This is merely a discourse for those still bound. That [Land] is naturally without wounds; do not wound it.
The Buddha’s wounds and the Bodhisattvas’ wounds consist solely in speaking of dharmas such as existence and non-existence—all of this is wounding.
Existence and non-existence govern all dharmas. The Ten Stages are a river of turbid flow; yet they speak of them as a clear stream, and they describe the vertical aspect of clarity as turbidity.

Regarding these faults and afflictions: among the ten great disciples mentioned previously—such as Śāriputra and Pūrṇa, who possessed right faith, and Ānanda and Sunakṣatra, who possessed wrong faith—each has his own precedent and each has his own pattern; every one of them was exposed by the Teacher.
This is not the four dhyānas or the eight samādhis. Arhats and others remain in meditative absorption for eighty thousand kalpas;

they rely on and cling to their practice and are intoxicated by the wine of pure dharmas. Therefore, when śrāvakas hear the Buddha-dharma, they are unable to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Therefore, those who have severed their roots of goodness lack the Buddha-nature. The teachings state that this is called a "deep pit of liberation," a place of dread.

If one's mind regresses for even a single thought-moment, one falls into hell as swiftly as an arrow shot. Yet, one must not say categorically that there is regression, nor must one say categorically that there is no regression.
It is just like Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who nevertheless returned to the stage of Srotāpanna.
In the stage of *srotāpanna*, one is led by those of the same class; it cannot be said that they have regressed. At such a time, they are simply called a *srotāpanna*.

It is simply a matter of present discernment and awareness, being uncontrolled by any phenomena of existence or non-existence, and passing beyond the three propositions as well as all circumstances of favor or opposition.
Even if one hears of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas appearing in the world, it is as if one has not heard them.
It is similar. Furthermore, not relying on what has not been heard, nor forming a conceptual understanding based on such non-reliance, one says of another person that they have regressed;

this cannot be measured or quantified, for one cannot grasp them. To say that the Buddha, who dwells eternally in the world yet is untainted by worldly dharmas, has regressed from turning the wheel of Dharma is likewise to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. To say that the Buddha does not turn the wheel of Dharma...
To regress is likewise to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Master Zhao said: "The Way of Bodhi cannot be schemed or measured.

It is so high that there is nothing above it; so vast that it cannot be exhausted. It is so deep that there is nothing below it; so profound that it cannot be fathomed. To speak thus is like setting up a target only to invite an arrow.

To say that "mirror-like awareness" (jianjue) is not yet the discernment of clarity from turbidity, while admitting that such present mirror-like awareness exists, and to claim that anything else apart from this mirror-like awareness is entirely the teaching of Māra—yet to remain fixedly attached to this present mirror-like awareness is likewise the teaching of Māra;
it is also called the teaching of the Natural Heretics (Svabhāva-vāda). To say that present mirror-like awareness is one's own Buddha is merely a matter of measurement and conceptual calculation.
Their speech is like the howling of a jackal; they still belong to the gate of sticky glue.

Fundamentally failing to recognize that self-knowing and self-awakening are one's own Buddha, they run outward in search of a Buddha elsewhere. They take the instructions of false spiritual friends regarding self-knowing and self-awakening as a mere medicine.
This treats the illness of seeking outwardly. Since one no longer seeks outwardly, once the illness has been cured, the medicine must be discarded.
If one clings to this self-knowing and self-awakening, it becomes the illness of *dhyāna*; such a person is a thoroughgoing *śrāvaka*. It is like water turning into ice:

though the ice is entirely water, it is difficult to hope for it to quench thirst. This is also called a "terminal illness" for which worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness; it has not been otherwise since beginningless time.
"Buddha. Do not interpret this as "Buddha. The Buddha is medicine for sentient beings; when there is no illness, one need not take medicine.
When both medicine and illness have been eliminated, it is like clear water. The Buddha is like licorice mixed with water, or like honey mixed with water; he is exceedingly sweet and delicious.
If it were merely like counting the ripples on clear water, then "not clinging" would not be incorrect; yet this "non-existence" is what is inherently present.
It is also said that this principle is what all people inherently possess. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas call one who points this out "the person who shows the pearl.

From the beginning, it has never been a thing. There is no need to know it or understand it; there is no need for "it being so" or "it not being so. Simply sever the dualistic extremes; sever existence.
Sentences are not sentences; they cut off the state of no-sentences and yet are not without sentences. Traces of either extreme do not appear; grasping at either extreme does not catch you.
Measurement and calculation cannot govern you. It is neither deficient nor complete; it is neither ordinary nor holy.
It is neither light nor darkness; it is not possessing knowledge, nor is it lacking knowledge; it is neither bondage nor liberation;

it is none of the various names and designations. Why is it not true speech? If one were to carve out space to produce the form of a Buddha, or if one were to say that space can be made blue, yellow, red, or white—this is like saying that dharmas do not exist.
There is a comparison. Because there is nothing with which it can be compared, the Dharma-body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical categories;

thus it is said that the holy body is nameless and ineffable. The gate of emptiness according to the reality of principle is difficult to approach, just as the *mahāśakunika* insect (the "great-end worm") can alight anywhere except upon a flame.
The minds of sentient beings are also like this: they can take objects of perception everywhere, yet they alone cannot [alight]...
To rely upon Prajñā while seeking a single point of knowledge or understanding from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is the demon of the spiritual friend, for it gives rise to verbal views.

If one makes the Four Great Vows, vowing that only after all sentient beings have been saved shall one first attain Buddhahood, this is the demon of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, for the vow is one of non-abandonment. If one observes the fasts and precepts...
Cultivating dhyāna and studying wisdom constitutes tainted roots of goodness (*sāsrava-kuśala-mūla*).

Even if one sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), manifests the attainment of perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*), and delivers beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, such that they all realize the fruit of a *pratyekabuddha*—this is a demonic root of goodness, for it gives rise to craving and attachment.

If, regarding all phenomena, one is entirely free from craving and defilement, such that the divine principle alone remains, and one abides in profound meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without further ascending, [that is true liberation].
This samādhi is a demonic state; because one has long indulged in it, when one reaches the supreme nirvāṇa—detachment and tranquility—it becomes a demonic activity.
If one does not depart from the various nets of Māra through wisdom, then even if one has mastered a hundred volumes of the Vedas, they are all merely dregs of hell.
There is no possibility of finding anything that resembles the Buddha. As for now, hearing this teaching, do not cling to any wholesome dharmas.
To seek dharmas such as existence and non-existence is to fall into emptiness. Not knowing how to abandon the root to pursue the branches is precisely what constitutes falling into emptiness.
To seek the Buddha, to seek bodhi, and to seek all dharmas of existence and non-existence is to abandon the root and pursue the branches. At present, coarse food merely sustains life;
it mends tattered clothes to ward off the cold, and when thirsty, one scoops up water to drink. Beyond these, everything else is merely a matter of existence.
Regarding the peerless Dharma, there is not even a hair’s breadth of conceptual attachment. Such a person gradually attains a portion of lightness and clarity.

A true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) neither clings to existence nor clings to non-existence, thereby liberating one from the ten phrases of demonic speech. (In the Master’s Recorded Sayings, it further states: "Right now, simply be free of these ten [phrases]:

a turbid mind, a greedy mind, a mind of desire, a defiled mind, a mind of anger, a clinging mind, a dwelling mind, a dependent mind, a grasping mind, and a yearning mind. Each of these single phrases contains three further phrases; if each and every one of them is penetrated beyond these three phrases, then all functions of illumination and application may be employed as they please, whether vertically or horizontally.)"

However, all movements, actions, speech, silence, weeping, and laughter are entirely the wisdom of the Buddha. I do not know whether these ten phrases of a turbid mind are themselves the ten phrases of Māra’s speech; one must certainly not depart from this meaning. When one speaks, it does not bind others;
in all one's discourse, one does not claim to be a teacher. One speaks like an echo in a valley;

though words fill the world, there is no fault in the mouth. Such a person is worthy of being relied upon. If one says, "I can speak and explain; I am the preceptor and you are the disciple," [then one is not so].

"Son, this is the same as the teachings of Mara. To pointlessly say, 'The Way exists where it is directly perceived,' or to pointlessly speak of whether one is a Buddha or not, or of Bodhi, Nirvana, and liberation, or to claim a single knowledge or understanding—seeing someone raise a hand or point a finger and saying, 'This is Chan, this is the Way'—such words bind people; they have no moment of stillness and are merely a burden."
This increases the monk's fetters. Even if one does not speak, there is still verbal transgression. It would be better to take the mind as one’s teacher rather than being taught by the mind.

Within the teachings of provisional meaning, there are those who are teachers of humans and devas, and there are those who are guides. Within the teachings of definitive meaning, one is not a teacher of humans and devas, nor is one taught by the Dharma;
one has not yet attained the profound mirror-like insight. For now, rely upon the teachings of definitive meaning, though traces of conceptualization still remain.
Father, if this were a teaching of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), it would only be fit to be spoken before worldly people who are deaf.

However, at present, simply not relying on or dwelling in any phenomena of existence or non-existence, nor dwelling in a state of non-reliance, and furthermore, not forming a conceptual understanding of such non-reliance—this is called a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). It is also said that the Buddha alone is the great spiritual friend. Why? Because...

There are no two [teachings]. All others are entirely called "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika) and are also called "the teachings of Māra. Now, this merely explains the phrase that shatters the two extremes:
regarding all phenomena of existence and non-existence, one should simply not be stained by greed or attachment, nor engage in matters of liberation and bondage.

There are no other distinct words or phrases used to instruct people. If one says there are separate words or phrases to instruct people, or that there is a separate dharma given to others, this is called being a non-Buddhist.

The Way is also called the teaching of Māra. One must recognize the language of definitive meaning (nītārtha) and the language of provisional meaning (neyārtha). One must recognize words of prohibition and words that do not prohibit.

One must recognize the language of saṃsāra. One must recognize the language of medicine and illness. One must recognize the language of metaphors for the inverse and the direct. One must recognize general and specific language.
To say that one attains Buddhahood through the practice of the Way implies cultivation and realization; it implies that the mind is the Buddha, and that this very mind is [Buddhahood].
"Buddha. This is spoken by the Buddha; it is a teaching of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*); it is non-restrictive speech; it is general speech; it is speech that combines and weighs;
it is speech concerning the margins of impure phenomena; it is analogical speech; it is dead speech; it is speech directed toward ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
It is taught by the Buddha that one does not attain Buddhahood through the practice of cultivation; there is neither cultivation nor realization, neither mind nor Buddha.

This is a teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), a prohibitive statement, a distinct statement, a statement of a hundred-stone load, a statement outside the teachings of the Three Vehicles, a statement of inverse analogy, a statement that demarcates the boundary of pure phenomena, a statement of arising, and a statement for those who have attained the stages and positions. From...

From the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, all the way to the tenth ground (*daśabhūmi*), whatever words or phrases exist are entirely categorized as the defilement of mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya-rajas*).
Whatever words or phrases exist are entirely subsumed under the side of afflictions (*kleśa-pakṣa*). Whatever words or phrases exist are entirely of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).

The teaching of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is upholding; the teaching of provisional meaning is transgression. On the ground of the Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*), there is neither upholding nor transgression—neither definitive nor provisional teachings.
All are prohibited. One discerns the ground from the sprouts; one discerns the clear from the turbid. It is simply the present mirror-like awareness (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
If one counts from the side of clarity, mirror-like awareness is not clarity; non-awareness is not clarity; even "clarity" itself is not it.
It is not impurity, nor is it non-impurity. It is not the holy, nor is it the non-holy. When seeing turbid water, one speaks of the water.
Regarding the affliction of turbidity: if water were clear, there would be nothing at all to say; to speak of it would only make that water turbid.

If there is a question asked of what does not exist, there is likewise a discourse spoken of what cannot be said. The Buddha does not preach the Dharma for the sake of being a Buddha; within the equal and true *dharmadhātu*, there is no Buddha who does not deliver sentient beings.
The Buddha does not abide in Buddhahood; this is called the true field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). One must distinguish between the host and the guest in speech; [this concerns] greedy defilement.
All phenomena of existence and non-existence are deluded by the objects of existence and non-existence; one's own mind is the Māra-king, and its illuminating function belongs to the subjects of Māra.
Simply by means of present discerning awareness, do not rely upon or dwell in any phenomena of existence or non-existence, whether worldly or supramundane.
Do not form conceptual understandings of reliance or non-reliance, nor rely upon or dwell in the absence of such understanding. Self-...

The mind is the Buddha; its illumination and function belong to the Bodhisattvas. Each and every thought (should be expanded) is the sovereign master; illumination and function belong to adventitious dust.
It is like describing water by means of waves: it illuminates the myriad phenomena without effort. If one can maintain tranquil illumination, there is no need for esoteric principles;

naturally, this will penetrate through past and present. As it is said: "The spirit has no function of illumination, yet its supreme function ever abides; it is able to serve as a guide in all places."

Master, the nature and consciousness of sentient beings have never before trodden the steps of the Buddha; it is a nature like sticky glue that has long adhered to all phenomena of existence and non-existence.
Consequently, they cannot suddenly ingest the medicine of the profound principle, nor can they suddenly believe when hearing words beyond the conventional.
For this reason, beneath the Bodhi tree, he remained silent in contemplation for forty-nine days, as his wisdom was obscured and difficult to penetrate.
To say that there is nothing by which the Buddha-nature of sentient beings can be illustrated is to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
to say that sentient beings have no Buddha-nature is likewise to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. To claim that there is a Buddha-nature is called the slander of attachment;

to claim that there is no Buddha-nature is called the slander of falsehood. As it is said: to assert that the Buddha-nature exists is the slander of exaggeration (*samāropa*), while to assert that the Buddha-nature does not exist is...
To say that the Buddha-nature neither exists nor does not exist is the slander of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
At first, one wishes not to speak [of it], for sentient beings would have no opportunity for liberation; yet at first, one wishes to speak of it.

Furthermore, sentient beings generate understandings based on words, whereby the benefit is slight while the loss is great; therefore, it is said: "I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana.

Looking back toward the past, one finds that all Buddhas of the past preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. What followed was merely the preaching through verses and the provisional establishment of names.
Originally, this was not the Buddha, yet it was pointed to as the Buddha; originally, this was not Bodhi, yet it was pointed to as...
He speaks of bodhi, nirvāṇa, liberation, and so forth; yet I know he cannot lift a load of a hundred piculs, so I give him a load of only one sheng or one he.
I know he finds it difficult to believe the teachings of definitive meaning (nītārtha), so I speak to him of the teachings of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
Thus, for the time being, wholesome dharmas may circulate, which is superior to unwholesome dharmas. When the limit of the good fruit is exhausted, the fruit of evil will arrive.
If one attains Buddhahood, then sentient beings arrive; if one attains nirvana, then birth-and-death arrives; if one attains illumination, then darkness arrives.
These are merely the overturning of the causes and effects of outflows (*āsrava*); there is nothing that does not reciprocate and respond.
If you wish to avoid witnessing such overturning events, simply sever the phrases of the two ends. Do not measure or calculate; do not let them concern you. Be neither Buddha nor sentient being.
Neither intimate nor distant; neither high nor low; neither level nor uneven; neither departing nor arriving. It is simply that one does not cling to words.
Like being on two sides of a canal, you cannot catch hold of it. It avoids the mutual comparison of suffering and pleasure; it avoids the reciprocal exchange of light and darkness.
True principle is neither real nor unreal; it is neither false nor non-false. It is not a thing that can be measured or numbered. To use an analogy:

Space cannot be cultivated or refined. If the mind forms even the slightest conceptual interpretation, it is immediately constrained by measurement and calculation, just as a divination omen is governed by metal, wood, water, fire, and earth.
It is also like sticky glue that adheres at five points; thus, the Demon King seizes one and carries them home at will.
Generally, all teachings consist of three interconnected phrases that are good in the beginning, middle, and end; the beginning is direct.
One must first teach them to give rise to a wholesome mind; having subsequently shattered that wholesome mind, only then can it be called "truly good.
A Bodhisattva is not a Bodhisattva, yet is named a Bodhisattva. Dharma is neither dharma nor non-dharma; it is entirely like this. If one were to speak of it as a single phrase alone:
This causes sentient beings to enter hell. If one speaks of these three phrases simultaneously, one enters hell oneself;
this does not concern the Master’s teaching. To realize that present awareness is one's own Buddha is the "goodness in the beginning.

Not remaining attached to this present awareness is the "goodness in the middle. Furthermore, not forming a conceptual understanding of non-attachment is the "goodness in the end. It is as explained previously.
Regarding the Buddha after the lamp: he is simply neither ordinary nor holy. Do not mistakenly say that the Buddha is neither ordinary nor holy.
The First Patriarch of this land said: "Being neither capable nor holy is the holiness of the Buddha. If one says the Buddha is holy, that too is incorrect.
From the nine grades of spirits, dragons, and animals, up to Śakra and Brahmā, all are able to undergo transformations; even the highest grade of spirits possess knowledge.
How could events spanning hundreds of kalpas across the past and present possibly be the Buddha?

For instance, when the body of an Asura King was exceedingly large—equaling twice the size of Mount Sumeru—and he realized his strength was insufficient during battle with Śakra, he led a host of a million troops into the hollow of a lotus fiber to hide.
His transformative powers and eloquence were not lacking; yet these are merely secular narratives and not the terminology of the Buddhist teachings. Section by section.
The laxity and the ascension and descent differ. That which is not yet awakened to or understood is called greed and anger;
once awakened, it is called the Buddha-wisdom. Therefore it is said: "It is not a different person from before; it is only that the sphere of one's practice has changed. Question:
"When cutting grass, felling trees, digging the earth, or tilling the soil, is there a karmic retribution? The Master said: "One cannot definitively say there is sin, nor can one..."
Regarding whether one has attained meditative concentration, it is said there is no offense; regarding whether there is an offense or no offense, the matter rests with the person concerned.

If one is defiled by craving for all phenomena—whether they exist or not—and possesses a mind of grasping and rejecting that fails to transcend the three propositions, this person is certainly said to have committed an offense.
If, however, one transcends beyond the three propositions, the mind is like space, yet one does not even form the thought of "space"; this person is certainly said to be without offense. Furthermore:

It is said: If one has committed a transgression and yet claims that the Way perceives no transgression, such a thing is impossible. If one has not committed a transgression and yet claims that the Way perceives a transgression, such a thing is also impossible.
According to the Vinaya, even in cases of fundamental delusion involving killing, or where one kills another through a chain of circumstances, the offense of killing is still not incurred;
how much more so for those who inherit the Chan lineage, whose minds are like empty space, wherein not a single thing is retained, nor is there any...
The characteristic of empty space: where would you place one's offenses? If there was an ancient [Buddha], there is also a present one;
if there was an ancient Buddha, there is also a present Buddha. If you attain it now, you will attain it until the very limits of the future. It is simply this single thought-moment.
This single thought-moment is not governed by any dharmas of existence or non-existence. From antiquity to the present, the Buddha has been nothing other than a human being.

Human beings are nothing other than Buddhas; they are also samādhi. One need not employ meditative concentration to enter concentration, nor employ dhyāna to contemplate dhyāna, nor employ the Buddha to seek the Buddha.
It is as the saying goes: "The Dharma does not seek the Dharma; the Dharma does not obtain the Dharma; the Dharma does not practice the Dharma; the Dharma does not see the Dharma.
One naturally attains the Dharma, yet there is no further attainment through that attainment. Therefore, a Bodhisattva should be thus.

This is right mindfulness regarding phenomena: utterly empty, it exists alone. Furthermore, there is no wisdom that knows this solitary existence; its nature is suchness (*tathatā*), not established by causes.

It is also called the "knot of essence" (*tattva-grantha*) and the "accumulation of essence" (*tattva-samudaya*). It is not known by wisdom, nor cognized by consciousness. It is beyond the reach of thought and deliberation;
it is a state of profound stillness where the essence is exhausted. All calculation and estimation have forever vanished, like the great currents of the ocean when the waves have subsided.
It does not arise again. It is also said to be like the waters of the great ocean when there is no wind and thus no rippling waves.
When one suddenly perceives these rippling waves, this is the coarse within the subtle. When the perception of perception vanishes, it returns to being the subtle within the subtle;

this is the realm of the Buddha. From this initial awareness, it is called the summit of samādhi, also called the King of Samādhis, and also called the wisdom of *jñeyāvaraṇa* (the obstruction to the knowable).
They give birth to all samādhis and confer the empowerment upon the crowns of all the Dharma-princes.

Within all forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, mental objects, and buddha-lands, they attain equal and perfect enlightenment. They penetrate both the internal and external without any obstruction whatsoever.
A single form is a single atom; a single Buddha is a single form; all Buddhas are all forms; all atoms are all Buddhas—all [are thus].
Form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are likewise thus.
Each one pervades all buddha-fields. This is the coarse within the subtle; it is a virtuous realm. It is that which is known, perceived, heard, and seen by all those who flow upward;
it is also that from which all those who flow upward are born and die. It transcends all existence and non-existence, and is what is taught by those who flow upward. It is also...
The upward-streaming nirvana is the unsurpassed path; it is the peerless mantra, the foremost teaching.

Among all teachings, it is the most profoundly deep, such that no one can reach its depths. It is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, like clear waves that can describe the functions of all waters—whether clear or turbid, deep or flowing, vast or great. Protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining...
"If you are able to do so, I shall at that time manifest for you a body of pure radiance. He further said: "Just as your own speech and so forth are such, mine are likewise so:
the sound of a single buddha-field, the fragrance of a single buddha-field, the taste of a single buddha-field, and the touch of a single buddha-field."
The affairs of a single Buddha-field are all like this. From here upward, reaching as far as the Lotus Treasury World, the dimensions in both length and breadth are entirely the same.
If one clings to the initial cognition as being the ultimate understanding, it is called the "summit-knot" (*mūrdha-grantha*) and is also called the "falling summit-knot.

This is the root of all worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). One naturally gives rise to views and knowledge, binding oneself without a rope; because of what is known, one is bound. There are two [types] in the world.
Fifteenth: Furthermore, there are all the gates of scattered afflictions that bind and attach others. This is first known;
when the two vehicles perceive this, it is called the *er-yen* (jñeya) consciousness, also termed "subtle affliction," which they then immediately sever. Once it has been severed, [they proceed].
It is called "the withdrawal of the spirit to dwell in the hollow cave"; it is also called "being intoxicated by the wine of samādhi," and "being bound by the fetters of Māra.

Sustained by the power of meditative concentration, one remains unaware as the world undergoes formation and destruction, nor does one perceive the outflows [of the afflictions] as they lead to other lands.
It is also called "the terrifying place of the deep pit of liberation. Bodhisattvas distance themselves from all such states in order to seek unsurpassed bodhi.

To aspire for nirvana in such a manner is still a perverse vow. Even when one's own five aggregates are being cut and mangled by others, to remain entirely free of afflictions and not give rise to even a single thought of "I" or "mine" regarding them—yet to rely on this state and maintain it without a single thought [of its impermanence], taking it to be the ultimate—is called the defilement of mental objects (*dharmaraja*).
Even those on the tenth stage cannot escape this; they flow into the river of birth and death, their minds sustained by the conceit of self (*asmimāna*).
Those whose consciousness pursues profit and fame claim, "I have attained all things without obstruction," yet this is merely self-deception.
The First Patriarch of this land said: "If the mind holds something as right, it must hold something as wrong. If you prize one thing, you will be deluded by that one thing.
To believe is to be deluded by belief; not to believe likewise constitutes slander. Do not prize anything, do not fail to prize anything; do not believe, do not disbelieve. Question:
"How is it that sentient beings lack Buddha-nature while insentient things possess it? The Master said: "From humans up to Buddhas is the attachment of sacred emotion;

from humans down to the hells is the attachment of ordinary emotion. If, at this very moment, one harbors a mind of stained attachment toward these two realms of the ordinary and the sacred, this is called 'sentient beings lacking Buddha-nature.
If, at this very moment, one [remains free of such attachment] toward the two realms of the ordinary and the sacred..."
Regarding objects and all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, there is absolutely no mind of grasping or rejecting, nor is there even a cognition or understanding of grasping or rejecting.
This is called "insentient things possessing Buddha-nature. It is simply because they lack emotional entanglement that they are called "insentient";

this is not the same as the insentience of wood, stone, empty space, yellow flowers, or green bamboo, which one might mistakenly take to possess Buddha-nature. If one were to say they do possess it, how could that be?
Therefore, one does not see in the sutras anyone who attains Buddhahood without having received a prediction (vyākaraṇa). It is simply like the present mirror-like awakening;

it is merely that it is not altered by sentient beings. It is like a verdant bamboo: there is nothing that does not respond to conditions, and there is nothing that does not know the proper time. It is like a yellow flower.
It is further said: "If one has ascended the Buddha’s steps, insentient things possess Buddha-nature; if one has not yet ascended the Buddha’s steps, sentient beings lack Buddha-nature.
This is the Small Vehicle perspective of Baizhang the Elder and the Younger; it must be that they had never seen Nanyang [Huiren].

When one has not yet awakened or attained understanding, it is called the "mother"; when one has awakened, it is called the "child. Yet, there is ultimately no such thing as awakening, understanding, knowing, or comprehending;
this is what is meant by "both mother and child having perished. All verbal teachings are merely for treating illness. Since illnesses differ, the medicines also differ.

Therefore, at times he speaks of the existence of a Buddha, and at times he speaks of the non-existence of a Buddha. These are truthful words used to treat illness; once the illness is cured, [the medicine is discarded].
If they are healed, each word is true speech. If the illness is not healed, each word is false speech;
thus, true speech becomes false speech because it gives rise to views. False speech is true speech because it cuts off the delusions of sentient beings.

Since the illness is false, it is treated solely by means of false medicinal antidotes. The ground of the sages is cultivated through the causes of the ordinary; the Buddha enters among sentient beings.

They are drawn by those of their own kind and guided by those who share their same channel. When the limbs and joints of hungry ghosts are ablaze with fire, he preaches the *Prajñāpāramitā* to them, causing them to resolve their minds [upon enlightenment].
If [the Bodhisattva] were exclusively situated in the stage of the noble ones (*āryabhūmi*), by what means could he reach that place and converse with them?
The Buddha enters among all classes of beings and acts as a boat or raft for sentient beings, undergoing suffering alongside them with boundless toil and exhaustion.
When the Buddha enters places of suffering, he likewise undergoes suffering together with sentient beings. Yet the Buddha alone possesses the freedom to come and go at will, unlike sentient beings.
The Buddha is not empty space; how could he not suffer when undergoing suffering? If one says he does not suffer, such a statement is contradictory and false. It is merely idle talk.
Do not speak erroneously of whether the Buddha’s supernatural powers (ṛddhi) are sovereign or not; you would simply bring shame upon yourself.

For now, I dare not say that the Buddha is conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), nor do I dare say that the Buddha is autonomous or non-autonomous, except when praising his medicinal prescriptions.
One does not wish to expose the ugliness of both ends. The Teaching says: "If a person establishes the Buddha’s Bodhi within the realm of 'existence' or 'is-ness,' that person incurs a great sin.
It also says: "It is as if one were speaking thus before a person who does not recognize the Buddha;
there would be no fault. Just as untainted cow's milk can cure tainted diseases, the cow does not dwell on high plateaus, nor..."
Dwelling in the low marshes—this cow’s milk is fit to be made into medicine. The high plateau is a metaphor for the Buddha; the low marshes are a metaphor for sentient beings. As it is said:
the Tathāgata’s true wisdom and *dharmakāya* are beyond all illness (*anupama-vyādhi*).

His eloquence is unimpeded, his ascent is sovereign, and he is neither born nor extinguished. This is called [the illumination of] birth, old age, sickness, and death, and their manifold pains and afflictions; this is darkness.
Having consumed a mushroom soup, he contracted dysentery and passed away; this was merely concealing his enlightened traces in darkness. Both light and darkness are sent away;
do not grasp, for there is nothing to grasp, nor even the absence of grasping. He is neither luminous nor dark. Born in the royal palace, he took Yaśodharā as his wife.
The realization of the Way through the eight phases is a conceptual construction of the śrāvakas and non-Buddhists; it is like saying that [the Buddha] does not have a body sustained by mixed food.
Cunda said, "I know that the Tathāgata will certainly not accept or eat [this meal]. First, one must possess both eyes to illuminate both ends of the matter.
Do not merely carry a single eye and walk toward only one side; otherwise, how could you ever reach the other? This is the merit.
The virtuous goddess followed by the woman of darkness—when a wise host refuses both, it is because the mind is now like empty space;
only then does learning begin to bear fruit. The High Ancestor of the Western Land said: "The Snow Mountains are a metaphor for Great Nirvana."
The First Patriarch of this land said: "Mind upon mind is like wood or stone. The Third Patriarch said: "Utterly forgetting all conditions. Caoqi said:
"Do not deliberate on good or evil at all. Our former teacher said: "Like a lost person who cannot distinguish directions. Master Zhao said:
"Closing off the intellect and blocking the ears, one awakens alone in the profound darkness. Mañjuśrī said: "Because the mind is identical to empty space, I pay homage to the Non-..."
Regarding the profound sūtras that one contemplates, if they have not been heard or upheld, then at this very moment, one merely perceives all phenomena as being either existent or non-existent;

one sees nothing and hears nothing, with the six sense-faculties blocked and sealed. If one can study and uphold the sūtras in such a manner, only then does one possess the capacity for true cultivation.
These words are harsh to the ear and bitter to the mouth, yet if one can act accordingly within them, then—up to this point.
In the second and third births, he is able to proceed to places where no Buddha resides and sit upon the Great Bodhimanda, manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment.

He transforms evil into good and good into evil; he causes the teachings of evil dharmas to instruct bodhisattvas of the ten stages, while causing the teachings of good dharmas to instruct those in the hells and the realm of hungry ghosts.
He is able to proceed toward the place of light to untie the bonds of light, and able to proceed toward the place of darkness to untie the bonds of darkness. (It is also said:)

From the Form Realm upward, giving is the disease and stinginess is the medicine. From the Form Realm downward, stinginess is the disease and giving is the medicine. It is further said: from humans up to the Buddha is gain; from humans down to hell is loss. The same applies to right and wrong. The Third Patriarch said: "Gain and loss, right and wrong—let them all go at once.
To pick up gold and turn it into earth, or to pick up earth and turn it into gold—one can accomplish these in a hundred ways, transforming and manipulating with complete freedom.
Even if there were someone outside worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges seeking salvation, the Bhagavān would immediately manifest his thirty-two marks.

He appears before that person, adopts their very voice, and preaches the Dharma for them, transforming them according to their individual capacities. He assumes diverse forms to respond to beings and manifests in all realms of existence.
To be free from "I" and "mine" still belongs to the realm of the other shore; it is but a minor application, yet it is also included within the great application of the Buddha’s gateway of activity.
His great body is hidden within formlessness, and his great voice is concealed within the soundless sound, as if—
Fire within wood; like the sound of a bell or a drum—when the conditions have not yet converged, one cannot speak of its existence or non-existence.

Rebirth in the heavens as a secondary reward is cast off like mucus or spittle. The Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices are like riding a corpse across to the other shore, or like escaping from a prison through a latrine hole.
When the Buddha manifests the thirty-two marks, they are called "filthy grease."

The *ābharaṇa* (robe) is free from the entanglements of goodness, free from the entanglements of evil, free from the entanglements of the Buddha, and free from the entanglements of sentient beings. Its measure and number are likewise so;
indeed, there are no entanglements of any measure or number whatsoever. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha is a person who has transcended entanglements and surpassed all measure.

His craving for knowledge and understanding of meanings and phrases is like a mother’s love for her child: she does nothing but give her son much ghee to eat, regardless of whether it is digested or not.

Know this: these words refer to the afflictions of receiving the honor and nobility of humans and devas across the ten stages; the afflictions of the meditative concentrations and meritorious bliss of the form and formless realms;

the afflictions of being unable to attain mastery over supernatural powers such as flying, ascending, concealing, and manifesting, or traveling everywhere to the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions to hear the Dharma;
and the afflictions of practicing the causes and conditions of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the study of emptiness and impartiality.

The afflictions of practicing the Middle Way; the afflictions of studying the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), the six supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);

the afflictions of cultivating the Mahāyāna mind and giving rise to the four great vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*); the afflictions of clear understanding from the first, second, third, and fourth stages (*bhūmi*);

the afflictions of various knowledges and views from the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth stages; and the Bodhisattvas of the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages who simultaneously illumine both [aspects].

The afflictions of the Truths, and even the afflictions of the millions of *asaṃkhyeya* practices leading up to the fruit of Buddhahood—these are merely the conceptual understanding of the meanings and phrases of desire.
One does not realize that these are, in fact, the afflictions of bondage; therefore it is said: "The river of views can sweep away even the fragrant elephant.
If one clings to the idea that one is inherently pure and inherently liberated, and considers oneself to be the Buddha, or the one who understands the path of Chan, this belongs to the self.

However, as for the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas): if they cling to the idea that [enlightenment] is attained through cultivation based on causes and conditions, they belong to the school of causal non-Buddhists.
To cling to existence belongs to the eternalist school; to cling to non-existence belongs to the nihilist school; to cling to both existence and non-existence belongs to the school of extreme views;
and to cling to neither existence nor non-existence belongs to the school of the view of emptiness. They are also called the deluded and ignorant.
"O outsider! Now, simply do not form views such as that of a Buddha or Nirvana;

Sa. Without cause, they form the perception of seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma; yet, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they are driven down to the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
This is not because they lack understanding, but specifically to serve as a model for all students, so that future learners do not form such perceptions or hearings.

The two Iron Ring Mountains represent being attached to all phenomena;

These are the severance of the three limits; these are the purification of the three karmas; these are the emptiness of the three wheels.

Sickness. It is that which manifests names and phrases. Furthermore, names and phrases do not themselves constitute names and phrases;

The Master said, "The very fact that you say it has no characteristic of movement is already movement. How could empty space ever say, 'I am without [movement]'?"
"The characteristic of movement—these are all your own emotional views. [The student] said, "Space has no characteristic of movement; yet that too is an emotional view.
The Master asked, "Earlier you asked what it was that he leaned upon. You already know the answer, so you should not say 'he leaned. Where would you intend to support him?"
[The student] asked: "If it cannot be that 'this very mind is Buddha,' then is it that 'this mind creates Buddha'? The Master said:

"'This very mind is Buddha' and 'this mind creates Buddha'—these are all conceptual constructs formed by the calculations of the deluded mind. Buddha is the person of wisdom; the mind is the master of accumulation."
Whenever one encounters an object, he immediately employs his wondrous function. Great Virtue, do not identify with the mind or identify with the Buddha;

even if you were to identify them, that would be what others call "ignorance regarding the knowable. Therefore, the Master of Jiangxi said: "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not an object.
This is merely to teach you, the people of later generations, how to practice. Students of the present day merely don these robes and stand by...
The student said, "I suspect such a trivial matter as this—can it really be resolved? You have said that it is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing;

The Master said, "You do not recognize that mind is Buddha, nor that wisdom is the Way. Since I have not attained even a trace of 'mind,' where else could it be?"

[The student] said, "Since it cannot be grasped as a whole, how does it differ from (or is it the same as) the great void? The Master said, "Since it is not a thing, with what could it be compared to the great void?
Furthermore, who would you have to distinguish it as being different or not different? [The student] said, "It cannot be that it is not this, not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing.
The Master said, "If you recognize this, you will still end up forming [a conceptualization of] mind and Buddha. [The student] said, "I beg the Master for instruction."
[The student] said, "I speak. The Master said, "I myself do not know. [The student] asked, "Why do you not know? The Master said, "How am I to tell you what to say?
[The student] said, "Does this not mean that you do not permit the student to understand the Way? The Master said, "What Way would you understand? And how would you go about understanding it?"
He said, "I do not know. The Master said, "Not knowing is actually good. If you take my word for it, you will be called a person of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Even if you were to see Maitreya appear in the world, he would still pluck the hair from your head. He asked, "How will this affect future generations?"
The Master said, "You should look for yourself; do not worry about those who come after you. [The monk] said, "Previously, you did not allow me to understand the Way.
Now, however, you say I should look for myself. I do not yet know how to do so. The Master said, "I grant that you have attained a dark realization and a subtle realization.
How do you understand it? [The monk] asked, "What is a subtle realization? The Master said, "Do you wish to imitate my words? Even if you were to speak like an old man..."
The monk said, "Venerable Sir, how is it? The Master replied, "If I had already understood it myself, there would have been no need for you to trouble the Abbot.
I beg your compassionate instruction. The Master said, "It is not right to point east and west to deceive people.

When you were being so complacent and easygoing, why did you not come to ask me back then? Now that you are clever and cunning, only then do you say, 'I do not understand. What is your purpose? "If you..."

The Master said, "What kind of talk is this, 'acknowledging' or 'not acknowledging'? [The monk] said, "When it comes to this point, I am even more at a loss.
The Master said, "If you do not understand, then I do not understand either. [The monk] said, "I am but a student, so I do not understand;

but the Master is a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), so you ought to understand. The Master said, "This fellow, when I tell you that I do not understand, who are you to discuss being a virtuous friend?"
Do not be clever or cunning. Look at the old masters of Jiangxi in their day.
There was a scholar who asked, "If water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-hu boat—how is this principle? The old master said, "Here there is neither water nor boat;
what do you mean by sinews and bones? Brothers, that scholar then simply desisted. Was this not effortless? Therefore:

[The student] said, "I have repeatedly sought the Way, yet the Buddha did not understand the Way. I shall cultivate it myself; what need is there to know [how]? The Master asked, "How do you cultivate it?
The Master said, "It cannot be conceived by thought or deliberation. To tell people: 'Cultivate in this way, practice in that way'—this is extremely difficult.
[The student] asked, "Do you permit a student to cultivate it? The Master said, "I, an old monk, cannot obstruct you. [The student] said, "As for me..."
"How should one practice? The Master said, "If you wish to practice, then practice; do not merely seek after others.

The student asked, "If one does not rely on the instructions of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), there is no way to attain realization. As the Master often says, one must understand before one can practice;
if one does not understand, one falls into the trap of cause and effect and lacks any autonomy. I wonder how one should practice so as to avoid falling [into such traps]."
[The monk] asked about cause and effect. The Master said, "There is no need for further deliberation.

As for cultivation, where would you not be able to go? [The monk] asked, "How can one go? The Master said, "You must not seek it by following after others. [The monk] said, "The Abbot has not yet spoken."
[The student] asked, "How should I, so-and-so, go about seeking it? The Master said, "Even if you were to speak of it, where could you find it?
Furthermore, from dawn until night, as you suddenly walk east or west, you do not even deliberate whether you can go or cannot go; others cannot possibly know what you are doing.
[The student] said, "When walking east or west, one does not think of anything at all—is that so? The Master said, "If it is like that..."
At that time, someone asked, "Who says this is right or wrong? He replied, "The Master always says, 'I do not go anywhere in any place;
no one can constrain me. This is called the Pervasive Samādhi and the Universal Manifestation of the Physical Body. Is this not the principle you refer to?"
The Master said, "If one speaks of cultivation, where does it not reach? I do not speak of being bound or unbound, nor do I speak of samādhi.
[The student] asked, "How is this different from attaining the Way of Bodhi through some dharma? The Master said, "I do not discuss difference or non-difference.
[The student] asked, "The cultivation you, Preceptor, describe is far removed from the Mahāyāna; I wonder how that can be so? The Master said, "I do not concern myself with its being different."
"It is not a matter of distinction, nor have you ever studied it. If we speak of studying the scriptures, there are already the masters of the sutras and śāstras;
their school is truly formidable. For now, it would be better for you to simply listen. The student asked, "Ultimately, how should a student understand this?
The Master said, "Regarding what you have asked, it fundamentally remains within the realm of causes and conditions. You simply cannot do anything about it, because of these conditions."
This is merely recognizing the affairs at the six gates. You should simply understand the Buddha’s side; then come and I will deliberate with you.
Brothers, do not pursue things in such a manner. Do not dwell upon it in this way. Do not rely on the words of the ancients, but practice the bodhisattva path.

He was the only person traveling alone. The Māra Pāpīyān led his retinue and constantly followed behind the Bodhisattva, seeking the place where his mental activities arose, intending to strike him down.
Thus he passed through immeasurable kalpas, yet could not find even a single moment’s deviation.
Just as he was about to take his leave with his retinue, after offering praise and making offerings, this was still within the stage of progressive cultivation.

As for those of middling or inferior capacity, they are at a loss; how much more so regarding the state where all effort is transcended? Take Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, for example—there is no further talk of them.
Brothers, how can you say that practice does not exist? A person who practices even for a single day is impossible to find. Nowadays, people merely follow others...
"Throughout my years, I have sought only the ultimate. Why do you merely dabble with your lips and tongue to produce intellectual interpretations?
[The student] said: "At such a time, there is no name for Buddha and no name for sentient beings. How could I possibly attempt to conceptualize it? The Master said:
"By saying 'there is no name for Buddha and no name for sentient beings,' you have already engaged in conceptualization. You are merely memorizing his words. [The student] said: "..."
"If it is thus, all matters belong to the time when a Buddha appears in the world; one cannot simply remain silent. The Master asked, "How would you speak?
He replied, "Even if one were to speak, words would still not reach it. The Master said, "If you say that words do not reach it, that itself is a reaching word."
"You are searching for things in vain like this. Who provides you with objects? [The student] said: "If there is no one who provides objects, then who is the person on 'that side'?
The Master said: "If you do not cite the scriptures, then from where can we discuss the Buddha? Since we do not discuss the Buddha, with whom could I, an old monk, discuss 'this side' or 'that side'?
[The student] said: "Although the fruit does not abide in the Way, the Way can serve as the cause. It is like...
"What? the Master said. "He was an ancient sage of the past. Now, one must not fail to observe the precepts. I am not he, and he is not me.
To act like Li-nu or Pai-gu is to walk the path with true ease; yet, if for even a single thought you differ from this, it is no longer so."
"It is difficult to practice. He asked, "In what way is it difficult to practice when there is even a single thought of difference?

The Master said, "The moment there is a single thought of difference, there are the two faculties of superior and inferior. This is not a matter of emotional views; you are merely following cause and effect. What further freedom do you have?
He asked, "I have often heard the Master say that the Reward Body and the Transformation Body are not the true Buddha, nor are they the preachers of the Dharma. I wonder about this—"

"How is it? the Master said. "Because it arises from conditions, it is not. [The monk] asked, "If both the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya* are not the true Buddha, is the *dharmakāya* the true Buddha?
The Master said, "That is already the *nirmāṇakāya*. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then even the *dharmakāya* is not the true Buddha.

The Master said, "Whether the *dharmakāya* is the true [Buddha] or not, this old monk has no tongue; I do not know how to speak of it. You may teach me how to speak, and then I shall be able to do so."
[The student] asked: "Apart from the three bodies, what dharma is the true Buddha? The Master said: "This fellow is quarreling with an old man of eighty or ninety;
I have already told you. What more do you ask about 'apart' or 'not apart'? You are like one trying to drive a wedge into empty space. [The student] said:
"I have humbly heard that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was spoken by the Dharma-body Buddha. How is this so? The Master said: "You just now said—"

"What kind of speech is this? The monk, who held the Way in high esteem (or perhaps asked), looked back at the Master and sighed, saying, "If it is the Dharma-body speaking, where would you listen for it?
The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Great difficulty, great difficulty! (*The Lamp of the Dharma* says at this point: "Go well, take care," and then stops;
however, the Master’s recorded sayings contain the following passage: "Look at Master Liang; he was a man from Shu who could expound upon the thirty-two [marks]."

While lecturing on this sutra and treatise at Jiangxi, he went to visit an elder monk at Kaiyuan Temple. The elder asked, "I have heard that you, Master, can explain and lecture upon the sutras—is this true?
The Master replied, "I dare not say so. The elder said, "With what do you lecture? The Master said, "I lecture with the mind (*citta*).

The elder said, "The *citta* is like a skilled performer, and the *manas* is like the conductor of the performance; how could you possibly explain and lecture [with such things]? The Master said, "Do not..."
Xuankong said, "It was indeed Xuankong who lectured. Xiu said, "But it was actually Xuankong who lectured. The Master [Zhang] shook his sleeves and departed. Xiu called out to the lecturer;
the lecturer turned his head. Xiu asked, "What is it? At that, the lecturer attained awakening. Brothers, look at how swift and sharp he was!
[The Master] said, "Ma. The monk said, "According to what the Master says, it is the Dharma-body preaching the Dharma.

The Master said, "If you understand it in this way, it is already the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya). The monk said, "Since it is the Response-body, does it not have one who preaches the Dharma? The Master said, "I do not know."
[The student] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Not understanding is actually good; it spares you the trouble of having to explain it away.
[The student] asked, "The scriptures say that where a Dharma-body Bodhisattva dwells, one sees the Dharma-body Buddha; at the stage of a Ground-rank Bodhisattva, one sees the Reward-body Buddha;
and those of the Two Vehicles see only the Transformation-body Buddha. Is this not the principle? The Master said, "My eyes have never looked at the scriptures, and furthermore—"
"One who has no ear-holes has never heard. You must see for yourself. If you maintain this mindfulness, then later on there will be nothing you can do about it.
It is like playing with a pearl while saying its light pervades everywhere; as long as the golden tray is present, you may have it.
But if the golden tray is suddenly snatched away, where do you play with the pearl? Where would you go to seek whether its light pervades or not? The student—
[The student] prostrated. The Master smiled and said, "Great difficulty, great difficulty! The ancients would have cursed you, calling you a hunter or a fisherman;
they would have called you a dung-carrier. Go now, take care! Addressing the assembly, he said: "Ultimate Truth is of one suchness; it functions secretly and operates subtly."
No one perceives it; it is called "non-outflowing wisdom" (anāsrava-jñāna), also termed "the non-outflowing inconceivable," and so forth.
It is the nature of emptiness and immovability, not the flow of birth and death. This Way is the Great Way, the unobstructed nirvana, wherein wondrous function is spontaneously complete.
Only then does one attain mastery over all spheres of practice; thus it is said that "among all spheres of practice, one acts without acting. Furthermore—
It is said that the Samādhi of Universal Pervasion universally manifests the form-body solely because no one knows its place of operation;

it leaves no trace, does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and the true principle is spontaneously realized while wondrous function is spontaneously sufficient. The Great Way is formless, and the true principle has no counterpart;
therefore, it does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and is devoid of coarse or subtle conceptualizations. As it is said: "Not hearing, yet hearing."
The Path of Great Nirvāṇa is not something that can be reached through hearing or not hearing. A monk asked, "The Great Way does not belong to seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing;
I wonder how one may realize it? The Master said, "One must realize that there is a silent resonance that naturally penetrates. This is also called the "enlightening cause" (*vidyā-hetu*).

It does not exist through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Seeing and knowing belong to conditions; they only arise in relation to objects. This spiritual and wondrous [nature] is inconceivable; it is not something that has a counterpart.
Therefore, it is said that its wondrous function is self-communicating and does not rely upon external things. Thus, it is called "penetration" (tong), not "reliance-based penetration" (yitong).
If one must depend on objects to first perceive it, then it is not the dharma of light or darkness. Therefore, it is said: "It is not the dharma of light or darkness."
Detached from existence and detached from non-existence, it penetrates the profound principles in secret; no one perceives or knows it.

This is also called "mysteriously uniting with true principle," which is not a matter of seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing. Therefore it is said: "With a stilled mind, one reaches the source; thus one is named the Tathāgata-Buddha.

Ultimately independent and autonomous, this is also called the "original fruit" (*mūla-phala*), which is not produced by a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*). Mañjuśrī said: "It arises solely from the cause of realization (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*)."
This is what is realized. It does not arise from causes of birth; from the very beginning, it has only taught people to realize the Way, with nothing else to seek.
If one attempts to construct a principle through deliberation, it all belongs to the realm of words and meanings—the doctrines of the Three Vehicles and Five Natures.
There is nothing that is not called "practice. If one possesses the necessary implements for every situation, one will attain success.
However, if one speaks of the Way, this is not it. To be consistently attached to them is to be constrained by them; this is also called "worldly wisdom.

The Teaching says that those scholars who are consistently attached to the Tripitaka act like hunters or fishermen; for the sake of profit and sustenance, they destroy the Mahayana. This is also called "greed."
This is the fulfillment of one's nature. Therefore it is said: "The Buddha did not realize the Way; I have cultivated practice myself. I possess my own wondrous function.
This is also called the "True Cause" (*zhengyin*). When one realizes that the six *pāramitās* are empty, then objects cannot confine me. This is why the Patriarch came from the West.
Fearing that you all might become deluded regarding the stages of cause and effect, I have come to transmit the Dharma to save those whose emotions are lost.
Once the nature of the flower has been suddenly awakened to, the nature is the seed-nature of the flower; it is also called the *bodhi*-flower. Thus, the Elder of Jiangxi said:
"It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. Although our predecessors spoke of "mind itself is Buddha," that was a statement made for a particular occasion.
The teaching that an empty fist or yellow leaves can stop a child's crying is something many people nowadays employ:

they call the mind "Buddha" and designate wisdom as the "Way," asserting that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all the Way. If one understands it in this way, how does it differ from the case of Yajñadatta, who lost his head and mistook a reflection for it?
Even if he were to recognize it, it would still not be his original head; therefore, the Great Being (Mañjuśrī) rebuked him.

Kātyāyana, to use a mind of arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of true reality is entirely a matter of emotional views. If one says that the mind is itself the Buddha, it would be like saying rabbits and horses have horns;
if one says the mind is not the Buddha, it would be like saying oxen and sheep have no horns. If your mind were the Buddha, [it would be so].
Furthermore, what use is it to deny the existence or non-existence of other forms? By what means is this the Way? For this reason, it is not permitted in the teachings.
It is better to take the mind as one's teacher than to let the mind be one's teacher. "The mind is like a stage actor; the consciousness (manas) is like the director.
Thus it is said that the Buddha possesses the Way. The mind does not depart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; all these belong to causes and conditions.
There is. All exist because they illuminate objects; they cannot be constantly illuminating. Therefore, neither mind nor intellect is the Way.
Furthermore, the Great Way is not a phenomenon of light or darkness. Although it appears as countless things, numbers cannot reach it, just as it was during the time of the empty kalpa.
There is no name for Buddha; there is no name for sentient beings. At such a time, this is precisely the Way. It is simply that no one awakens to it or perceives it;
it cannot be reckoned among things, and is thus called the Nameless Great Way. Yet even this already belongs to names and phrases.
Therefore, the True Principle is of one suchness and is beyond thought. As soon as there is thought, one is immediately constrained by the aggregates (skandhas), and the name "sentient being" arises.
There is a Buddha; since his appearance in the world, he has been called the "Man of Wisdom within the Three Realms. But what was he called before he appeared in the world? It is said:

"To have that which cannot be attained, and to give rise to great compassion amidst both being and non-being. When the Buddha appears in the world, he merely causes people to realize that the essence of the Way is neither ordinary nor sagely;
he calls this "returning to the source and reverting to the root" and "comprehending the Great Way through its essence. Now that [this day]...
Thus, one realizes the Way: that throughout immeasurable kalpas, the six destinies and four modes of birth have all involved coming and going;
these are merely temporary places of passage. The *Collection of the Original Practices of the Former Sages* states: "There is nowhere I have not traveled.

Although all sentient beings dwell in such places of passage, because they lack the cause of realization, they give rise to craving and desire; this is called being "entangled," whereby they fail to attain mastery.

For a moment at a crossroads, the clouds move and the moon travels; as the boat moves, the shore appears to shift. The deluded thoughts of sentient beings perceive that no thing remains stationary—how much more so when it comes to the capacity for principle to undergo transformation?
Now that you have realized this, you must proceed within [this inner realm], which is not the same as before.

This is because you take realization as the cause (*hetu*) in order to realize the fundamental fruit (*phala*). Thus, you realize that the aggregates (*skandha*) and realms (*dhātu*) are empty, and the six *pāramitās* are empty; therefore, you attain [liberation].

One would fail to abide as a Śrāvaka and would merely follow along with the passage of kalpas. Therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess the dual adornments of merit and wisdom as their cause of realization;
they realize that the essence of the six pāramitās is emptiness, and take this very realization as their enjoyment. For this reason, they do not harbor clinging knowledge.

One sees [the truth] and only then attains mastery. If there is knowing and seeing, one immediately belongs to the stages (bhūmi), and thus possesses a limited mental capacity (citta-mātra) that is partitioned by cause and effect;
such a person is called a "Buddha who repays causes and answers effects," and does not attain mastery. For this reason, the Great Sage rebukes them.

Because of internal and external views, the capacity of the mind is not exhausted, resulting in the two obstacles and two delusions; thus, the river of views can sweep away even the fragrant elephant.
Ultimate Truth has no form—how can it be known or seen? The Great Way has no form, for its principle transcends thought and deliberation.

Today, practicing the six *pāramitās*, one first exhausts the causes and realizes the fundamental fruit; thereby, one understands that these things are merely skillful means for provisional enjoyment.

Only then does one attain freedom; going and staying are sovereign and unobstructed. It is also called "the skillful means of diligent adornment," and it is also called "the subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body endowed with the thirty-two marks. This simply means not permitting the mind's measure to be partitioned.
If one lacks such a mind, then every place of practice—even a mere snap of the fingers or a joining of palms—is the direct cause. All myriad virtues are [thus perfected].
Being equally without end—(this character should likely be "作" [to act/manifest])—one first attains sovereignty. For this reason, celestial Māras and heterodox paths cannot find me;

it is called the "non-abiding mind" (amūla-citta), and is also termed "non-infiltrating wisdom" (an-āsṛti-jñāna). Its inconceivable, wondrous function is sovereign. Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are both the realms of the practitioner;
they all belong to the category of the "luminous phrase" (prakāśa-pada). If one realizes that the original source is not an ordinary thing, then...
Water cannot wash water. Why? Because from the very beginning there is no such thing. As the Sūtra says:
"In my royal treasury, there is truly no such sword. It also says: "The Goddess of Merit and the Woman of Darkness—a wise host accepts neither."
Therefore, the Way is neither light nor darkness; thus it is said that the ocean of nature is not the ocean of awakening.

When the ocean of awakening encounters conditions, it must confront objects, and therein its wondrous function operates, yet no one perceives or knows it. This is called the "extremely subtle dust-particle penetrating the golden water."
That which serves as the basis for a Bodhisattva is called the "receptacle of requisites. If water does not wash water, then its essence is neither light nor darkness;
it is also called "non-leaking wisdom" (*an-āsrava-jñāna*) and "unimpeded wisdom" (*an-āvaraṇa-jñāna*). If one is thus, one cannot be constrained by anything anywhere.
Yet now, you further seek to establish meanings and phrases, searching for victory and defeat, intellectual understanding, and verbal expressions, speaking of "sentient beings."
Even those who possess inferior existence, who seek the Buddha-bodhi as holy beings to save sentient beings, all belong to the realm of craving and are called "precept-breaking bhikṣus.
They are far removed from the Way. The Great Way is not ignorance; it has never been dark. It is not encompassed by the three realms, nor does it belong to the past, future, or present.
The Tathāgatagarbha is truly not concealed; when has the lion ever been in a cave? The five aggregates are fundamentally empty; when have they...
There is a locus. Furthermore, the Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it does not fall into any numerical categories. The Dharma is immovable and does not rely upon the six sense objects.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The Buddha-nature is permanent; the mind is impermanent. For this reason, wisdom is not the Way, and the mind is not the Buddha.
For now, do not call the mind "Buddha," and do not attempt to understand this thing through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. For the time being—this very thing!
Originally, there are no many names; wondrous function naturally penetrates, and numerical quantities cannot constrain it.
This is great liberation. Therefore it is said: "The human mind has no place of abiding; its tracks cannot be sought. Thus it is called non-leaking wisdom and inconceivable wisdom.
Observe how Cui, the Prefect of Chizhou, asked the Great Master Wuzu: "I have five hundred followers..."
"Why was it that only Master Neng alone received the robe as a token of transmission, while the others could not?
The Fifth Patriarch said, "Of the four hundred and ninety-nine people, all were proficient in the Buddha-dharma; only Master Neng was a person of transcendent capacity (some versions read:

'only Master Neng did not understand the Buddha-dharma'). For this reason, he transmitted the robe and the token. Cui said, "Thus I know that the Way is neither for the foolish nor the wise," and then he informed the Great Master.
"Everyone, you must all remember this. The Master said, "To 'remember' belongs to the sixth consciousness; it is unfit for those who are free from affairs—take care!
He further said, "For a moment, I have donned these soiled robes to explain this for the sake of others. It is not a thing of ordinary or sagehood.
From morning until evening, it never acts as a cause for others, nor has it ever acted as an effect for others. If it were to act as a cause for others, then..."
Lacking self-mastery, one is constrained by cause and effect and cannot attain freedom. When the Buddha had not yet appeared in the world, no one could comprehend this.

If we speak from the perspective of his appearance in the world, it is granted that there was a partial comprehension; however, this was merely a private realization of the profound principle, occurring spontaneously without a teacher. Fundamentally, there is nothing at all.

Their characteristics are of different natures. Therefore, if one were to depart from them, one would be identical to the Tathāgata. If both the *saṃbhoga*-buddha and the *nirmāṇa*-buddha were struck down together, where could they possibly remain?
This is not that I do not permit it; it is simply that even Maitreya acts as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
He vigorously practices the six *pāramitās*, and he can go anywhere at will. For what reason, then, do you not permit him? He has never been stuck in the state of an ordinary person.

Freedom. And how so? If you know it, you are immediately bound by the place of that knowing. If it were not thus, how could one not allow for it? That "other" has never undergone change or variation.

Therefore, the twelve divisions of the teachings definitively establish that it is not the self. The retributive and transformational bodies are not the true Buddha; do not mistake them for the Dharma-body. The fruits of retribution for both ordinary beings and sages are all mere shadows.
If you cling to them, they belong to the realm of impermanence and birth-and-death. Discussed in terms of the coarse and the subtle, not even a hair’s breadth is established.

When principle is exhausted and nature is fully realized, everything is entirely non-existent. It is like the time before the world was formed: vast, empty, and open, with no name for "Buddha" and no name for "sentient beings. This is the beginning.

There is a partial correspondence [to this]. One directly realizes that state over there, yet returns here to practice. Without realizing the stages of fruition of ordinary beings or sages, one speaks according to the fundamental nature:

It is like a withered tree; only when there is a slight degree of resonance does it begin to respond. It is further said:

"To simply realize that the nature [of mind] has remained unchanging throughout immeasurable kalpas is itself cultivation. To manifest wondrous function without dwelling [upon it] is the conduct of a Bodhisattva.

Obstructed, they wander through the hells as if in a transformed vision (*pariṇāma*; according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "transformed" should be read as "garden"). One cannot say that they lack functional efficacy.

For immeasurable kalpas, sentient beings have been deluded regarding their original nature and have failed to realize their own essence. Like clouds and dust momentarily obscuring [the sky], they become attached to various evil desires.

It is like the moon appearing to move when clouds race by, or the shore appearing to shift when a boat travels; for a brief moment on a forked path, they fail to attain mastery. Thus they plant [seeds of suffering].
They undergo various forms of suffering without being aware of it; yet even until this day, they have encountered their original nature, which is no different from today.

▲ Emperor Shunzong of the Tang dynasty asked Chan Master Ruman of Foguang Temple in Luoyang: "From where does the Buddha come? Where does he go when he passes away?

Since it is said that he dwells eternally in the world, where is the Buddha now? The Master replied: "The Buddha comes from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and goes toward the unconditioned when he passes away.
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is equal to empty space; it dwells eternally in the state of no-mind. When thought arises, it returns to non-existence."
Contemplate this: abiding, one returns to non-abiding; coming, one comes for the sake of sentient beings; going, one goes for the sake of sentient beings.
The ocean of pure True Suchness is profoundly still, its essence eternally abiding. The wise who contemplate well should no longer give rise to doubt or hesitation. The Emperor asked again:
"The Buddha was born in the royal palace and passed away beneath the twin śāla trees. He dwelt in the world for forty-nine years, yet he also said that there is no dharma to be taught. Mount...
The rivers and the great ocean, heaven and earth, as well as the sun and moon—all these, when their time comes, return to extinction.

Who could say they are not subject to arising and ceasing? Such are the doubts that remain. The wise distinguish them well. The Master replied: "The essence of the Buddha is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

it is through deluded sentiment that one falsely discriminates. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is equal to empty space; it has never undergone arising or ceasing. When conditions exist, a Buddha appears in the world; when conditions are absent, the Buddha [remains in quiescence]."
He entered nirvana, yet he transformed sentient beings everywhere, like the moon reflected in water—neither permanent nor annihilated, neither arising nor ceasing.
He had never arisen, nor had he ever ceased; clearly perceiving the state of no-mind, he naturally remained beyond verbal expression.
When the Emperor heard this, he was greatly delighted and came to hold the Chan school in even higher esteem.
