It is a classic example of the "seal of transmission" between master and disciple, wherein the ultimate truth is realized not through intellectual analysis, but through a direct, non-conceptual encounter. The dialogue between Lingmo and Shitou illustrates the "one word of accord" (*yiyun xiangqi*), a pivotal moment in the history of Zen where the lineage is passed from mind to mind. The subsequent exchange between Lingmo and his attendant regarding the "Buddha’s roar" further demonstrates the pedagogical skill of using paradox and the negation of conceptual categories to lead the student beyond dualistic thinking toward a state of non-dual realization. The final question—"Who hears it?"—points directly to the nature of self-awareness, which is the very ground of awakening. The attendant’s failure to respond underscores the fact that the Buddha’s roar cannot be grasped as an object of cognition; it is the very activity of consciousness itself, prior to the subject-object split. Thus, the story serves as a profound teaching on the nature of Zen enlightenment as a dynamic, living reality rather than a static state of being.

Those who attain it do not distinguish between the ordinary and the sage, nor between the foolish and the wise; yet for the most part, it remains a mere empty talk.

The Head held up a hoe. The Master took it and immediately made a gesture of weeding grass. The Head said, "You can only weed that;
you do not understand how to weed this. The Master had no reply.

The Master picked up the pure pitcher and poured it out before the spring. At that, the Spring ceased. Arriving at Mount Guishan, he entered the hall and hung his robes and bowl on the upper end of the platform.
Hearing that his senior brother had arrived, Guishan first assumed a dignified demeanor and came down from the hall to meet him.
"Look! When the Master saw him coming, he made a gesture of lying down. Baizhang then returned to his quarters. The Master departed.

Fayan Yi said, "Deng Yinfeng was truly strange, most strange; yet, in the end, he did not hit the mark.
He added, "At that time, the entire assembly emerged by mere coincidence. Cuiyan Zhi said, "These words contain a point of penetration;

As the government troops and the rebel forces were locked in combat, with victory and defeat yet undecided, the Master said, "I must go and resolve this calamity. He then cast his mendicant’s staff into the air and flew across it. The two [armies]...
The army officers and soldiers looked up in awe; the events corresponded exactly with his prior dream, and their hearts to fight immediately subsided.

Since the Master had manifested such spiritual wonders, he feared they might lead to the delusion of the masses, so he entered Mount Wutai. Before entering the Vajra Cave, as he was about to demonstrate his passing, he first asked the assembly:

"In various places, I have seen people depart from this life while sitting or lying down. Is there anyone who has passed away while standing? They replied, "There is. The Master said: [He then stood upright and passed away.]

"Is there anyone else who can stand on their head? [The assembly] replied, "We have never seen such a one. The Master then stood on his head and passed away; he remained perfectly upright, his robes hanging naturally over his body.

At that time, the assembly discussed carrying him to the cremation ground, but he remained motionless. Those from far and near gazed upon him, their expressions of wonder and admiration never ceasing.
The Master had a younger sister who was a nun; she was also present there at the time, and she patted him, saying reproachfully, "Elder brother, what..."
In the past, he did not follow the laws and precepts; now that he was dead, he continued to delude people. Thereupon, [the monk] pushed him with his hand, and he fell down with a crash.
He was subsequently cremated, and his relics were collected to build a stupa.
▲ Once, while Zen Master Wuliao of Guiyang was staying in a hermitage, a tiger chased a deer into the hut. The Master warded off the tiger with his staff, and the deer escaped.

▲ When Master Longshan of Tanzhou and his senior teacher, Master Mi, were traveling together with Dongshan, they saw vegetable leaves floating down a mountain stream.
Dongshan said, "There are no people in these deep mountains; why are there vegetable leaves flowing along? Is there perhaps a practitioner of the Way dwelling here? Thereupon, they...

While clearing away grass and traveling along a mountain stream for five or seven *li*, they suddenly saw the Master with an emaciated form and an extraordinary appearance. Setting down their luggage, they paid their respects.
The Master said, "There are no paths on this mountain; from where have you come, *ācārya*? Dōng replied, "Setting aside the matter of there being no path for a moment."
"From where did the Master enter? the Master replied, "I have not come from the wandering waters. Dong said, "How long has the Master resided on this mountain?
The Master replied, "Neither spring nor autumn has passed. Dong said, "Does the Master reside first, or does this mountain reside first?
The Master replied, "I do not know. Dong said, "Why do you not know? The Master replied, "I have not come from the realm of humans or devas."
Dongshan said, "What principle have you realized, Master, that you have come to dwell on this mountain? The Master replied, "I saw two clay oxen fighting and entering the sea;
until this very day, there has been no further news. Only then did Dongshan assume his full ceremonial demeanor and pay obeisance, asking:
"What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "Green mountains shroud white clouds. "What is the host within the guest?
The Master said, "Never leaving one's door for many years. "How far apart are guest and host? The Master said, "Waves upon the waters of the long river.
"When guest and host meet, what words are spoken? The Master said, "A clear breeze brushes the bright moon. Dongshan took his leave.
[The Master] withdrew. The Master then recited a verse, saying: "I have lived for long in a thatched hut of three bays; A single divine light shines upon ten thousand tranquil realms.
Do not bring是非 (right and wrong) to judge me; In this floating life, such artificial analysis is irrelevant. He spoke again: "A pond of lotus leaves provides countless garments;
A carpet of pine blossoms yields more than enough food. Yet, because the world has learned of my dwelling place, I must once more move my thatched hut."
He lived in deep seclusion within his dwelling. Because he burned down his hermitage, no one knew where he had gone; thus, people also called him Master Yinshan (Hidden Mountain).
Master Mengxi asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "I have come from Dingzhou. The Master said, "What extraordinary things have occurred in Dingzhou lately?
The monk said, "I have been staying at the guest quarters; I have heard only that salt is expensive and rice is cheap. It is truly miserable."
[The monk] spoke of "extraordinary matters. The Master said, "In my place, it is also just like this. I give monks coarse gruel and plain rice;
there are no extraordinary matters here. What are you looking for by coming here? The monk said, "I do not understand. I beg the Master’s compassion.
The Master said, "It is fortunate that you do not understand. If you did understand, I would concede half the principle to you. [The Head Seat]...
In the evening, the Master asked, "When you were just now examining the monk, why did you say, 'I concede half the point to you'?
The Master said, "I am grateful that you brought this up; otherwise, I would have forgotten it. The Head Seat said, "Please explain this for me, Master.
The Master said, "You have forgotten what came before and lost track of what followed; I too have lost track of what came after and forgotten what was before. Only then did the Head Seat depart.
The Master called him back and said, "You must not mention it. Lately, monks speak only of the high price of salt and the low price of rice, and they do not take the Buddha-Dharma as their concern.
To repeatedly bring this up would not be difficult for you to lose your very life."

He said, "I do not understand. The Master replied, "Clouds in the blue sky; water in the pitcher. Li bowed with joy and recited a verse:
"Refined is my physical form, like the shape of a crane; Beneath a thousand pine trees, two cases of scripture.
I have come to ask about the Way, with no other words— Clouds in the blue sky; water in the pitcher. Li asked again, "What are precept, concentration, and wisdom? The Master replied, "Poverty..."
"In this Way, there are no such worldly trappings. Li could not fathom the profound meaning.

The Master said, "If you, Prefect, wish to take responsibility for this matter, you must stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor. If you cannot relinquish the things of the inner chambers, it will immediately become a leakage."
Zhang Wujin’s verse says: Clouds in the blue sky, water in the jar; The eye follows the finger and falls into a deep pit.
The wildflowers cannot endure the bitterness of wind and frost; What need is there to speak of walking the bottom of the deep sea?

One night, as the Master was walking in meditation while ascending the mountain, the clouds suddenly parted and he beheld the moon. He let out a great roar, which echoed for about ninety li to the east of Linyang.
All the residents there claimed it came from their own neighbors. The next morning, they questioned one another in turn until they finally reached Yaoshan.
The disciples said, "Last night the Master let out a great roar on the mountain peak. Li wrote a poem for him, saying: "Having chosen this secluded dwelling, it suits my rustic sentiments;
Throughout the year, there is neither parting nor welcoming. Sometimes he ascends directly to the solitary peak, And under the moon, parts the clouds with a single roar.
He ascended the hall and said: "The Patriarchs taught nothing but protection. If greed or anger arise, you must guard against them most carefully."
Do not allow them to collide or strike one another. If you wish to know this, you must take up the withered wood and the stone;
truly, there are no branches or leaves to be found. Even so, you should examine it for yourself further; do not cut off speech.
I now speak these words for you to manifest that which is beyond speech; that other [reality] is fundamentally devoid of ears, eyes, and the like.
At that time, a monk asked, "What are the six realms of existence? The Master said, "Although this pivot of my essential teaching is within them, it has never been defiled.
The monk asked, "When one does not understand the afflictions within the body, what is the case? The Master said, "What characteristics do these afflictions have?
I simply want you to examine them for yourself. Furthermore, there is another type of person who merely memorizes [the teachings] on the back of a sheet of paper.
Language. It is mostly deluded by sutras and treatises. I have never looked at sutras, treatises, or commentaries.
You are simply lost in the confusion of phenomena and have strayed from your own home-ground, which is why you possess a mind of birth and death.

Before you have learned even a single word or phrase, a single sutra or treatise, you speak of what Bodhi and Nirvana are, and whether they are encompassed by the world or not. If you understand it in such a way, [you are mistaken].
This is precisely birth and death. If one were not bound by this continuity of gain and loss, there would be no birth and death.
You see how that Vinaya Master spoke of the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*—this is the very root of birth and death.

Nevertheless, though it is thus, even if one exhaustively searches for birth and death, they cannot be found; from the Buddhas above down to the ants below, all possess these long and short, good and bad [conditions].
The large and the small are not the same. If they do not come from without, where are there any idlers digging hells to wait for you?
If you wish to recognize the realm of hell-beings, it is those being boiled in cauldrons right now.

If you wish to recognize the realm of hungry ghosts, it is those who are currently full of falsehoods and lacking in substance, such that people do not believe them. If you wish to recognize the realm of animals, look at those who do not know [themselves] right now.

Those who do not distinguish between benevolence and righteousness, nor between kin and stranger, are they. Why must one wear fur and carry horns, or be slaughtered, dismembered, and hung upside down?

If you wish to recognize those of the human and celestial realms, it is those who, in their present purity and dignified deportment, hold the ritual pitcher and carry the alms bowl; they ensure liberation and will not follow along with the various destinies.
First, you must not discard this. This is not easily obtained. One must stand upon the peak of the highest mountain and walk upon the floor of the deepest sea;
practicing in such a place is no easy matter, and only then will there be a slight degree of resonance. Now that you have emerged into the world, [you must maintain it].
These are all people of many affairs; one cannot find a single person who is dull-witted and simple.

Do not merely take the words from the instructional manuals and consider them your own realization and knowledge. When you see someone who does not understand, do not give rise to contempt or disdain.
Such people are all icchantikas and non-Buddhists; this mind is simply not the mark. You must examine this thoroughly. Even to speak thus is still within the three realms.
This is a matter of the ultimate limit. Do not let it pass in vain beneath your patched robe. Reaching this point, it is even more subtle;

do not regard it as something trivial. You must know to hold it dear. On the sixth day of the eleventh month in the eighth year of Taixi, as he was about to pass away, he cried out, "The Dharma Hall is collapsing!
The Dharma Hall is collapsing! The assembly all took up pillars to prop it up. The Master raised his hand and said, "You do not understand me."
Yi then passed away. His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa at the eastern corner of the monastery.
Next is Chan Master Danxia Tianran of Dengzhou. He originally studied the Confucian classics.

While on his way to Chang’an to take the imperial examinations, he was staying overnight at an inn when he suddenly dreamed that white light filled the room. A diviner said, “This is an auspicious omen for the understanding of emptiness. Coincidentally, a Chan...
The official asked, "Where are you going, virtuous sir? He replied, "I am going to take the examination for office. The Chan master said, "How does taking office compare to selecting a Buddha?
He asked, "If one is to select a Buddha, where should one go? The Chan master said, "Nowadays, the Great Master Ma has appeared in Jiangxi;
that is the field for selecting Buddhas. You may go there. Thereupon, he went straight to Jiangxi. As soon as he saw the Patriarch, he uncovered his head with his hand.
Dazu looked at him for a long time and said, "Nanyue Shitou is your teacher. He immediately went to Shitou and presented his previous intention to him.
Shitou said, "Go and work in the fodder barn. The Master bowed in thanks and entered the quarters of the laborers (*xingzhe*), where he served as a cook in turn for three years.
One day, Shitou addressed the assembly, saying, "Tomorrow, clear away the weeds from the Buddha hall."

Mazu personally entered the hall to observe him and said, "My son is naturally so. The Master then descended from the ground and prostrated, saying, "I thank the Master for bestowing a Dharma-name.
Consequently, he was named Tianran ("Natural"). Mazu asked, "From where have you come? The Master replied, "Stonehead. Mazu said, "Stonehead..."

"The road is slippery. Will you trip and fall again? The Master said, "If I were to trip and fall, I would not have come here. He then took up his staff and traveled in all directions until he reached Huilin Temple.
It was a day of great cold, so he took a wooden Buddha and burned it for a fire to warm himself. The temple administrator rebuked him, saying:
"How could you burn my wooden Buddha? The Master struck the ashes with his staff and said, "I burned it to retrieve the *śarīra*.
The host replied, "A wooden Buddha—how could it have *śarīra*? The Master said, "If there are no *śarīra*, then take two more and burn them.
Thereafter, the host's eyebrows and beard fell out.
Baoning Yong said: "Setting aside for a moment the fact that the abbot’s eyebrows and beard fell out, tell me:
do Danxia’s eyebrows still remain? If you can see this, you will be a fellow student of the ancient Buddhas; if you cannot see it, you must strictly avoid denying cause and effect.
Zhenjing, ascending the hall, said: "Danxia burned the wooden Buddha; the abbot’s eyebrows and beard..."
It falls. [The Master] suddenly picks up his staff and says, "This is not a wooden Buddha. He then throws it down and says, "Who dares burn you?

"The various quarters of the school discuss this, saying that the temple master suddenly gave rise to doubt, which led to..."
This is a calamity. One does not realize that the temple administrator bought iron and obtained gold—a single instance of great wealth!

The monk asked, "Why did the temple administrator's eyebrows and beard fall off? Yunfeng said, "Seven openings, eight passages. The monk raised this question and asked Tianning.

he visited National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang.

The next day he went again to pay his respects. Upon seeing the National Teacher, he spread out his sitting mat. The National Teacher said, "No need, no need.
The Master stepped back, and the National Teacher said, "So it is, so it is. The Master then stepped forward again, and the National Teacher said, "Not so, not so.
The Master circumambulated the National Teacher once and departed. The National Teacher remarked, "The time since the Sage has passed; people are mostly indolent."
"Thirty years from now, it will be difficult to find this fellow," he said, as he went to visit Layman Pang.
Seeing the daughter Lingzhao washing vegetables, the Master asked, "Is the Layman here? The girl set down her vegetable basket and stood with her hands folded.
The Master asked again, "Is the Layman here? The girl picked up the basket and walked away. The Master then turned back. A short while later, the Layman returned.
The girl then recounted the previous conversation. The Master asked, "Is Danxia here? The girl replied, "He has gone. The Master said, "It is like smearing red earth on a cow's udder.
Lingzhao said, "Danxia discerns the field from its seedlings; Lingzhao recognizes the person through their words. Jiangshan Qin said, "Lay down the vegetables."
The basket arises right where it is; one picks up the vegetable basket, and it is extinguished wherever one goes. The layman said, "Red earth smeared on a cow's udder;
selling Yangzhou from inside one's own house. But tell me, what is it ultimately like? Everyone disperse, lest you increase the proliferation of idle talk.
On another day, he visited Layman Pang. Upon meeting at the gate, the Master asked, "Is the Layman at home?
The Layman replied, "When hungry, one does not choose one's food. The Master said, "Is Old Pang at home? The Layman replied, "Heaven! Heaven! and entered his house.
The Master said, "Heaven! Heaven! and returned. The Master asked Layman Pang, "What was it like when we met yesterday?"
[The Master] said, "It is like today. The layman said, "Bring forth yesterday’s matter according to the Dharma and make it into a 'Dharma-eye' (zongyan).
The Master said, "As for this Dharma-eye, can it contain Master Pang? The layman said, "I am within your eye. The Master said, "My eyes are narrow; where can you find a place to settle yourself?

The layman said, "How can these eyes be narrow? How can this body find a place to settle? The Master ceased speaking. The layman said: *Note: This dialogue occurs in the context of a Chan encounter between Mazu Daoyi and the layman Pang Yun. The term "zongyan" (宗眼) refers to the "eye of the school," the core insight or pivotal realization of the lineage.*
[The Master] further said, "Recite one phrase, and this dialogue will be complete. The Master also did not respond.
The gentleman said, "Among all these, no one can utter this one phrase. While the Master and Layman Pang were walking, they came upon a pool of water.
The Layman pointed at it with his finger and said, "Even so, you still cannot discern it. The Master said, "It is indeed impossible to discern. Thereupon, the Layman...
The Master scooped up water and splashed two handfuls upon the scholar. The Master said, "Not so, not so. The scholar said, "It must be so, it must be so.
The Master then scooped up water and splashed three handfuls upon the scholar. The Master said, "At this very moment, what can be done?"

The scholar said, "There are no external objects. The Master said, "Those who gain the advantage are few. The scholar asked, "Who is it that falls into disadvantage? The scholar came to visit the Master;
he stood before the Master for a short while and then departed. The Master did not look back. The scholar returned and sat down.
The Master, in turn, went before the scholar and stood there for a short while, then returned to his quarters. The scholar said, "You went out and I entered; has [the advantage] not yet been found?"
"There is a matter at hand. The Master said, "This old fellow goes in and out; when will he ever come to an end?
The Layman said, "There is not even a trace of compassion. The Master said, "He has led this fellow to such a state. The Layman said, "By what means did he lead him?"
The Master picked up the scholar’s head-wrap and said, "He looks exactly like a monk. The scholar took the head-wrap and placed it on the Master’s head, saying, "He looks exactly like a layman.
The Master responded with three "A-ho! sounds. The scholar said, "There is still a trace of something lingering."
The Master threw down his *fùtóu* (head-wrap) and said, "It looks just like a black silk cap (*wūshā jīn*). The scholar also responded three times.
The Master said, "How can you forget the breath of the past? The scholar snapped his fingers three times and said, "Moving heaven and shaking earth.
Because the Master was on his way to Mazu’s place, he encountered an old man with a young boy on the road. The Master asked, "Where do you live, sir?"
The old man said, "Above is heaven; below is earth. The Master said, "If suddenly heaven collapses and the earth opens up, what then?
The old man said, "Heaven! Heaven! The youth let out a single sigh. The Master said, "It is not without a father that a son is born.
Thereupon, the old man and the youth entered the mountains. [Later,] he asked a monk, "Where did you stay overnight? The monk replied, "At the foot of the mountain."
The guest stayed overnight. The Master asked, "Where did you eat? The monk replied, "I ate at the upper and lower [halls].
The Master said, "When someone gives food to you, does that person possess eyes or not? The monk was speechless.
Changqing asked Baofu, "When one gives food to another to eat, there is a share of gratitude; why then do you not possess eyes?
Baofu said, "Both the giver and the receiver are blind men. Changqing said, "If one brings forth the full extent of their spiritual capacity (*jī*), would they still be blind?
Baofu said, "Can you say that I am blind? Xuanguan examined this, saying, "Now tell me, was Changqing enlightened?"
This is Danxia’s intention. Was it that he was using his own family wealth? Tiantong Hua said:
"Since Danxia had already begun as a dragon but ended as a snake, Changqing and Baofu could only follow the error with the error.
Nevertheless, these two or three old masters do not know where this monk (the author of 'Lao') has fallen. Those who possess the eye for discerning the Dharma—please try to judge this!"
Xuedou Xian’s verse: "Exhausting one's capacity does not result in blindness; it is like pressing down a cow’s head as it grazes.

The various patriarchs—four times seven and two times three—bring forth precious vessels only to incur fault. The fault is deep, nowhere to be found; in heaven and on earth, all alike sink into the mud.
Fenyang Shanzhao, addressing the monks, said: "If you do not go up the mountain, how will you recognize Danxia?"
Baoning Yongdai, acting as the monk, said: "Today I have been exposed by the Master. He then ascended the hall and said:
"You entire family, you must carefully protect that single spiritual essence. It is not something you can create or describe through names;
what more need be said about 'realizing' it or 'not realizing' it? In the past, when I saw Shitou, he too taught only this: 'You must carefully protect...'"
Protect yourself from this matter; it is not something you can discuss. You and your entire family each have your own patch of ground—what more is there to doubt?
What "Zen" could possibly be something you understand? How could there be a Buddha to be attained?
The very word "Buddha" is never pleasing to hear. Look for yourself: skillful means, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity do not come from the outside.
Attained. Not clinging to the square inch of the heart-mind. Skillful means is Mañjuśrī; expedient means is Samantabhadra. What more do you intend to pursue?
There is no need for seeking through scriptures, lest you fall into emptiness. Nowadays, scholars are in a state of clamor and confusion, all of them "investigating Zen" and "inquiring about the Way.
Here in my place, there is no Way to cultivate and no Dharma to realize. Each sip of drink and each morsel of food—each is as it is.
It is your own portion; do not harbor doubts. Everywhere, there are those who are like this.
If you can recognize it, Śākyamuni is none other than an old ordinary person (the character for "old" should follow the *Chuandeng lu*). You must look into this for yourself;
do not let one blind man lead a crowd of blind men as you walk together into a pit of fire. Playing double-six in the dark at night—how can you hope to win? There is nothing to do; take care.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Changqing era, he told his disciples, "Prepare hot water for a bath; I wish to depart.
Thereupon, he donned his bamboo hat, took up his staff, and put on his sandals. He lowered one foot, which had not yet reached the ground, and passed away.
A monk from Jiangling came to visit Chan Master Dachu of Tanzhou. The Master asked, "When did you set out from Jiangling?
The monk held up his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). The Master said, "Thank you for coming from afar; you may go. The monk circumambulated the meditation seat once and departed.
The Master said, "If it were not so, how could one know the true nature of the eyes? The monk clapped his hands and said, "It would kill me!
I nearly made a false judgment regarding the various quarters [of the teaching]. The Master said, "You have truly grasped the principles of the Chan school."
The monk reported this to Danxia. Danxia said, "That may be acceptable according to the Dharma path of Dayuan, but it is not so here.
The monk asked, "I do not know how it is done here. Danxia said, "It is still three steps ahead of Dayuan.

The monk bowed, and Danxia said, "Many err in their judgments regarding the various quarters [of the Chan school]. Dongshan said, "If it were not for Danxia, it would be difficult to distinguish [the difference]."
Jade and Stone. Huanji said: "This monk has received the old master Dachu’s fist, yet he still returns with Danxia’s lethal hand.
Dongshan said, 'If it were not for Danxia, it would be difficult to distinguish jade from stone. Now, they have been distinguished. Is it jade? Is it stone?"

The Master said, "Please, Reverend, examine it setting aside raising the eyebrows and blinking the eyes.

"Master, what is the mind like? The Master said, "It is no different from the Abbot's. Mazu said, "That is none of your business.
The Master said, "Fundamentally there is nothing. Mazu said, "You, too, are nothing. The Master said, "Since there is nothing, that is the true thing. Mazu said, "The true thing cannot be grasped.
Your mind’s perception and measurement are such as this; you must guard and uphold it very carefully. Later, while presiding over the assembly, he ascended the hall and said: "Now, gentlemen..."
A student of the Way must recognize their own original mind. Only by pointing directly to the nature of that mind can one truly perceive the Way.

I see many of my contemporaries who take nothing more than a raised eyebrow, a blink of an eye, a single word, or a moment of silence as a seal of approval, regarding these as the essential core of the mind.
This is truly a failure to understand. I shall now clearly explain it for all of you; each of you must listen and receive it. Simply cast aside—
All deluded movements of thought and the objects perceived by the intellect are, in themselves, your true mind.

This mind has no contact whatsoever with external objects, nor even when one maintains a state of silent stillness; it is the mind that is the Buddha, requiring no cultivation or refinement. Why is this?

It responds to conditions and reflects accordingly, functioning with a clear, limpid spontaneity. Yet, when one investigates the locus of this functioning, it is utterly unfindable. To call this "wondrous function" is precisely it.
One’s original mind must be protected and sustained with great care; it must not be treated lightly. A monk asked, "When those within [the circle] meet one another, what is it like?
The Master said, "Already, they are no longer within. The monk asked, "What is it to be within? The Master said, "Do not act as if you were asking Māṇavaka (Han Wengong).
One day, Han Wengong visited the Master and asked, "How many years of age are you? The Master held up his rosary and said: [The number of beads].

"Do you understand? The official said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "One hundred and eight times, day and night. The official did not comprehend this and returned home. On the following day, he came again.
Upon reaching the gate, he saw the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) repeating the previous conversation and asked, "What was the meaning of that? The Head Seat clicked his teeth three times.

When he saw the Master repeat the previous question, the Master likewise clicked his teeth three times. The official said, "So it turns out that the Buddha-dharma has no... [The official remained speechless].
"Two kinds. The Master asked, "What is the principle behind this? The official said, "Just now, when I questioned the Head Seat, he answered in exactly the same way.
The Master then summoned the Head Seat and asked, "Was it you who answered in such a manner? The Head Seat replied, "Yes. The Master immediately struck him and expelled him from the monastery.
Fenyang Shanzhao’s verse says: "Understanding the deployment of the *jīfēng* (spiritual edge) is Master Dadian; Clearly knowing it is no small matter of karmic conditions.
The same clanging of teeth is viewed differently by the monastic community; Only after leaving the monastery did Lord Han find leisure."

One day, Duke Wen said to the Master, "My discipleship involves many affairs of state and military administration. I beg the Master for a single word regarding the essential points of the Buddha-dharma.
The Master remained silent for a long time. The Duke was at a loss. At that time, Sanping was serving as attendant;
he struck the meditation seat three times. The Master asked, "What is this? Sanping replied, "First move with concentration, then extract with wisdom. The Duke then said, "Master!"
The style of this lineage was lofty and austere. A disciple obtained an entry point through an attendant. A monk asked, "The waves of the sea of suffering are deep;
what shall serve as the boat or raft? The Master said, "Use wood as the boat and raft. The monk said, "If that is so, one will attain deliverance."

The Master said, "The blind remain blind as before; the mute remain mute as before. One day, while walking along the corridor with Yanghuozi, he encountered a monk who came forward to pay his respects.
The Master struck him across the mouth with the Yanghuozi and asked, "Do you understand?
The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Old wild fox Dadian has never let anyone down."
▲ Chan Master Kuang of Longbeard from Tanzhou went to Caoxi to pay homage at the Patriarch’s stupa. Upon his return, he visited Shitou.
Shitou asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Lingnan. Shitou said, "Has the single scroll of merit at the head of Dayu Ridge been completed yet?
The Master said, "It was completed long ago; it simply lacks the dot in the eye. Shitou said, "Do you wish for the dot to be applied? The Master—
[The Master] said, "Please do so. Daou then lowered his head and extended one foot. The Master prostrated himself. Daou asked, "What principle have you seen that you prostrate yourself?
The Master replied, "According to what I have seen, it is like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace."
Xuánjué challenged him, saying: "Tell me, when Long-beard answered, was he responding with eyes, or was he responding without eyes?
If he had eyes, why did you ask him to have his eyes opened? If he had no eyes, you also said that he had long since achieved it.
How do you resolve this? Fadeng spoke on his behalf, saying: "The Master may be said to have dimmed eyes."
As the Master was seeing to the monks' inquiries, he said, "Every step is a place for you to realize the truth; do you know this? The monk replied, "I do not know.
The Master said, "If you knew, what would I be able to do? The monk bowed, and the Master said, "I am not capable; you, however, are excellent.
When Layman Pang arrived, the Master ascended the seat and the assembly gathered. The Layman stepped forward and said, "Each..."
"Please examine yourself well. He then stood to the right of the meditation seat. At that time, a monk asked, "Without touching the master of the house, please let the Master answer my question.
The Master said, "Do you recognize Master Pang? The monk replied, "I do not. The layman then grabbed him and said, "What a pity!
What a pity! The monk was speechless. The layman then let him go. A short while later, the Master asked, "Did that monk just now receive a beating?"

"No," the scholar said. "I must wait until he is willing before I can obtain it. The Master said, "The layman sees only the sharpness of the chisel's tip, but does not see the squareness of the chisel's head.
The scholar said, "Such talk may be acceptable for me, but if outsiders were to hear it, it would surely not be good."
The Master said, "What is not good about it? The layman said, "Master, you see only that the tip of the awl is sharp;
you do not see that the point of the chisel is keen. A monk came for an audience. He circled the meditation seat once and stood there with a solemn air.

The Master said, "If this were the Dharma-seat of Shitou, not even a single drop would be required. The monk circled the meditation seat once again. The Master said, "But rather, it is just like this."
At that time, [the Master] did not readily acknowledge the monk’s place of origin. The monk then departed. The Master called out to him, but the monk paid no heed.

The Master said, "This fellow still lacks instruction. The monk turned back and asked, "Is there a person who does not receive it from another, who does not accept instruction, and who does not fall within the ranks?
Do you grant this? The Master said, "Meeting him, one does not meet him; meeting him, there must be something. The monk—

The Master then stepped back three paces. The monk, however, circled the meditation seat once. The monk said, "Not only is the eye of the school made clear, but the lineage of the teacher also has a firm basis.
The Master then struck him three blows. He asked another monk, "Where have you come from?
The monk replied, "From the Controlling Stone Hermitage on Mount Jiuhua. The Master asked, "Who is the abbot of that hermitage? The monk replied, "A venerable elder under Mazu. The Master said:
"What is his name? [The monk] said, "I do not know his dharma-name. The Master said, "He does not know it; you do not know it either.
[The monk] asked, "Where are the eyes of the Venerable Elder? The Master said, "If the Abbot himself had come in person, he would have had to receive a blow of the staff today as well.
[The monk] said, "Fortunately, we encountered the Master who let me off. The Master said, "A hundred years from now, even a monk like this will be hard to find."
Li Xingpo arrived. The Master asked, "Do you remember the events that took place when we were in Jangzhou? The nun said, "It would not be without the Master’s guidance that I would know.
The Master said, "There is much falsehood and little reality in what you say. The nun said, "What is there to hide?
The Master said, "I take pity on you as a woman and let you go with your staff. The nun said, "I certainly do not see any fault in the Venerable Elder. The Master said, "That is my own fault."
"In what place? The old woman said, "The Master has no fault; how could I possibly have a fault? The Master asked, "What is it like for one who has no fault?
The old woman then held up her fist and said, "In this way, everything becomes a perversion. The Master said, "Truly, there is nowhere to hide.
Seeing a monk, the Master seized him and said, "Lion cub! You belong to the species of jackals! The monk made a gesture with his hand as if brushing away his eyebrows.

The monk made a gesture of baring his teeth. The Master said, "Even so, you still lack the roar. The monk grabbed hold of the Master, who said, "You especially love to employ this single turn of phrase.
The Master gave him a slap. The monk clapped his hands three times. The Master said, "If you see that it accords with my style, would you be willing to act like this?
The monk replied, "In the end, it does not depend on anyone else. The Master made a gesture of twitching his eyebrows. The monk said, "You still lack the roar."
The Master said, "I suspect it does not depend on anyone else. A monk asked, "Without failing the sages of all past ages, what is the first phrase of the Long-Bearded One?
The Master said, "There is a mouth, but one cannot speak. The monk asked, "Why can the mouth not speak? The Master then offered this verse:
"The stone lion and the wooden girl— This first phrase is the pivot of all Buddhas. It cannot be spoken."
"How truly marvelous! This very point—do not harbor any doubt. After a long silence, he asked, "Which is it: the first phrase or the second? The monk replied, "Neither one nor two.
The Master said, "When you see the profit, you forget the awl; you still have much left to do. The monk bowed.

The Master picked up his tea bowl and said, "At this very moment, you do not fail the sages of antiquity. The monk said, "Directly pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood."

"Furthermore, how is it? The Master set down his tea bowl and returned to the abbot’s quarters. The monk followed him in. The Master raised one foot and said, "The great earth does not admit even a needle;
from where have you come? The monk replied, "Even Vimalakīrti himself would be unable to keep his mouth shut.
The Master said, "In this momentary encounter, we have met a fierce tiger again. The monk then made the sound of a tiger. The Master [struck him] with his staff.
The master held his staff in the manner of a leveled spear. The monk, however, seized it and said, "The great earth does not admit even a needle; from where could you have obtained this?
The master replied, "Not only would Vimalakīrti be silenced, but even Mañjuśrī would find his mouth sealed. The monk said, "A tiger struck by an arrow cannot be resisted.
The master gave him a slap and pushed him out of the abbot’s quarters.
▲ When Chan Master Huilang of Zhaoti Temple in Tanzhou first visited Mazu, Mazu asked him, "What do you seek by coming here?
He replied, "I seek the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Mazu said, "The Buddha has no knowledge or vision; knowledge and vision are merely demons. From where have you come?"
[The Master] said, "I have come from Mount Nanyue. The Patriarch said, "You have come from Mount Nanyue, yet you do not yet recognize the essential heart of Caoxi.
Return there at once; it is not appropriate for you to go elsewhere. The Master returned to Shitou and asked, "What is the Buddha? Shitou said, "You have no Buddha-nature.
The Master said, "What about all the wriggling, sentient beings? Shitou said, "Wriggling, sentient beings indeed possess Buddha-nature."
[Hui]xing asked, "Why does Huirang not have it? The Master said, "It is because you are unwilling to accept it. At these words, the Master entered into realization.
After he took up residence, whenever a student arrived, he would always say, "Go away! Go away! You have no Buddha-nature.
His manner of engaging students was roughly like this (at that time, he was called Dalarang).
▲ When Chan Master Zhenlang of Xingguo Temple in Changsha first visited Shitou, he asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
Shitou said, "Ask the pillar. Zhenlang said, "I do not understand. Shitou said, "I do not understand either.
The Master suddenly attained realization. Later, when he was residing there, a monk came to pay his respects. The Master called out, "Venerable One! The monk responded, "Yes? The Master said:
"You have come in vain. The monk asked, "Why did you not look at me, Master? The Master then rubbed his eyes and gazed at him; the monk was speechless (at that time he was called Xiaolang).
Zen Master Shilou of Fenzhou was asked by a monk: "I do not yet recognize my original nature; I beg the Master for a skillful means to point it out. The Master—
The monk said, "Shilou has no ears. The Master said, "I myself know that I am at fault. The monk asked, "Does the Old Monk also have faults?
The Master said, "My fault lies in the place where you are wrong. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
He then questioned another monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "From the land of Han. The Master asked, "Does the host of the land of Han respect the Buddha-dharma?"
Mao said, "Alas! Fortunately I have encountered you to ask this; had I been asked by someone else, disaster would have ensued. The Master said, "How so?
Mao replied, "Since I do not even see a person, what Buddha-dharma could there be to value? The Master said, "How many years since you received the precepts?
Mao replied, "Thirty years. The Master said, "If you truly do not see anyone, that is excellent," and he struck him.
▲ The Dharma Master Fotu of Famen Temple in Fengxiang Prefecture habitually held a single string of prayer beads.
He would recite three names: first, Śākyamuni; second, Yuanhe; and third, Fotu. As for all others, he would say, "What is this?
It is a wànduòqiū," and then pass over one bead, beginning again from the end. His conduct was extraordinary, and no one could fathom it.
▲ When Master Daotong Jì of Lǐzhōu was visited by Míhú leading a group of followers, as soon as they wished to meet him, the Master pulled his meditation seat around and sat facing the wall.
Míhú stood behind him for a short while, then returned to the guest quarters. The Master said:
This was indeed so. If he had not verified and refuted [the claim], later he would have been subjected to disparagement and exploitation. He ordered his attendant to request rice;
when the rice was brought, Mí (Miaoxin) instead dragged the meditation seat over and sat upon it. The Master then walked once around the meditation seat and returned to his quarters.
Mí then pulled the meditation seat down and led the assembly out to visit Layman Páng. The Layman said, "Do you remember when you were in your mother's womb?"
He spoke a single phrase and presented it to the Master, strictly instructing him not to analyze it through intellectual reasoning. The Master said, "This is still a matter of past lives.
The Layman said, "I told you from the start that you must not employ intellectual reasoning. The Master said, "How can one not fear such startling words?

The Layman said, "By your own understanding, Master, you may indeed be called 'startling. The Master said, "To not employ intellectual reasoning is itself to fall back into the trap of intellectualization."
The Master said, "It is not merely separated by one or two lifetimes. The Layman said, "A monk who eats his rice porridge may be scrutinized as he pleases.
The Layman snapped his fingers three times. One day, seeing Layman Pang approaching, the Master immediately shut the door and said, "Old man of many knowledges, do not let us meet.
The Layman said, "Sitting alone and speaking to oneself—whose fault is this? The Master then opened [the door].
The Master was just stepping out when the officer seized him, saying, "The Master knows much; I know much.

The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment this 'knowing much,' how much difference is there between closing a door and opening it, or rolling it up and spreading it out? The officer said, "Just this one question would kill me with its intensity.
The Master remained silent. The officer said, "Seeking cleverness and ending up clumsy. Question: How should one act throughout the twelve periods of the day?
The Master said, "Do you recognize the twelve hours? The monk asked, "What are the twelve hours? The Master said, "Zi, Chou, Yin, Mao.
The monk bowed. The Master presented this verse: Within the twelve hours, what thing is distinct? Zi, Chou, Yin, and Mao—I shall now explain them.
If you understand that all phenomena are but mind, they are empty; Then Śākyamuni and Maitreya will be resolved from this point on. 1.
One day, [Zhaozhou] asked Layman Pang: "This phrase has been rarely avoided by anyone throughout antiquity and the present.
Did you, Master Pang, manage to avoid it? Pang replied, "Yes. The Master repeated the previous question. The Layman said, "Where have you been coming from?
The Master said, "Not only now; even the ancients had this saying. The Layman performed a dance and went out. The Master remarked, "A mad old man!"
The "Wind-Crazed Old Man" (Fengdian Lao). When a scholar came to visit, he picked up a bamboo sieve and called out, "Master Datong!
Master Datong! The Master did not look back. The scholar said, "The school of Shitou has crumbled like ice melting away.
The Master replied, "If it were not for people like Master Pang, it would certainly be so. The scholar threw down the sieve and said, "I would rather have it be worth no more than a single cent."
[Mañjuśrī] held up a coin. The Master said, "Though the coin has no value, how can you dispute my debt?
Mañjuśrī performed a dance and withdrew. The Master then picked up a bamboo sieve and said, "Pang! Pang! Mañjuśrī said, "You want my sieve; I want your wooden ladle.
The Master performed a dance and withdrew. Mañjuśrī clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "Go back! Go back!"
The lineages of the Nanyue and Qingyuan schools were not yet settled regarding Dharma heirs.
[Next is] Zen Master Tianhuang Daowu of Jingzhou, a native of the Zhang family of Dongyang in Wuzhou. His physical presence was exceptionally distinguished.

He possessed innate wisdom from childhood. At the age of fourteen, he earnestly sought to leave the household life, but his parents would not permit it. He consequently reduced his intake of food and drink until they were compelled to grant him permission.

Upon entering the monastic order, he cultivated the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) with diligence; even during storms, rain, or the darkness of night, he sat in meditation amidst burial mounds, free from all fear.
He visited Guoyi of Mount Jing to receive the teachings of the mind, serving him assiduously for five years. He then visited Master Ma...
Zu repeated his previous interpretation and relied upon [Nanyue] for two summer retreats. Later, he visited Shitou and asked:
"Setting aside concentration and wisdom, by what Dharma do you instruct people? Shitou said: "In my place, there are no servants; what is there to set aside?
Zu asked: "How can one realize this? Shitou said: "Can you grasp empty space? Zu said: "If that is so, then from this day forward..."
He departed. The Head asked, "I do not know from where you have come—early or late? He replied, "Daowu is not a man from that side.
The Head said, "I already knew where you came from. He asked, "Why does the Master falsely accuse me? The Head said:
"You are present here now," [the Master] said. [The monk] replied, "Even though it is so, how ultimately can you show this to people of later generations?

The Master said, "Tell me, who is the person of later generations? At these words, the teacher attained sudden enlightenment, completely exhausting his former grasping for attainment that had arisen under the guidance of the two previous masters.
Miaoxi said, "Tell me, what exactly did he realize?

Later, while residing at Tiantong, he would sit and merely bow to all guests, regardless of their rank. When the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Lord Pei, who was the Governor of Jiangling, visited him...
He prostrated himself to inquire about the Dharma, but the Master received him without showing any special courtesy. Pěi Yù turned back toward [the monastery].

In the fourth month of the *dinghai* year of the Yuanhe era, the Master manifested illness and instructed his disciples to announce his passing in advance. When the full moon arrived, the great assembly came to inquire after his health; the Master suddenly called for the head cook.
As the cook approached, the Master said, "Do you understand? The cook replied, "I do not understand. The Master then picked up his pillow, tossed it to the ground, and [passed away].
Even after his passing into nirvana, he was sixty years of age and thirty-five years of *dharma*-age.
He succeeded Shitou and resided in the eastern part of the city. He had three disciples: Huizhen, Wenlai, and Youxian. The inscription for him was composed by Fu Zai, the Court Musician;
the records in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) are entirely consistent with Fu’s inscription, though they erroneously list Longtan as his master.
Dharma Heir:

Chan Master Daowu of the Heavenly King Temple, of the Cui clan of Zhugong, a descendant of Cui Ziyu of the Han dynasty. He left home at the age of fifteen and received full ordination at twenty-three.
At thirty, he visited Shitou; although he repeatedly received instructions from him, he did not attain realization. Subsequently, he visited Zhong.
The National Teacher (No. 34). Together with his attendant, Yingzhen, he traveled south to visit Mazu. Mazu said, "Recognize that your own mind is fundamentally Buddha;
it does not belong to gradual stages, nor does it depend on cultivation. Its essence is naturally suchness, and its myriad virtues are complete.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. Mazu instructed him, saying, "If you take up the position of abbot, do not leave your former location."

Having received the imperial decree, the Master returned to Jingmen. Not far from the city wall, he constructed a thatched hut. When a high-ranking military official came to visit him, the Master did not accord him special courtesy.

The official grew angry, seized the Master, and threw him into the river. Upon his return, he saw fires breaking out throughout the entire yamen, and heard the voice of the Heavenly King from the sky rebuking him in anger.
He immediately repented with grief and prostrated himself; the smoke and flames suddenly ceased, and everything returned to its original state.
As before, he went in person to the riverbank to welcome the Master. Seeing that the Master stood in the water without his robes being wet at all, he felt even greater reverence.
To the west of the prefecture, he built T’ien-wang Temple to provide for the Master. Longtan Xian asked, "How is it with the matter transmitted from the ancestors?
The Master said, "It is not that you cannot understand where you have come from. Longtan said, "This eye—how many..."
The man attained it fully. The Master said, "In shallow grass, even a reed grows tall. A monk asked, "What is the profound and subtle teaching?
The Master said, "Do not say that I understand the Buddha-dharma. The monk said, "But what of my lingering doubts? The Master said:
"Why do you not ask the old monk? [The monk] said, "I have already asked. The Master said, "Go! This is not where you shall dwell.
The Master often said, "How happy! How happy! Yet when his time of death approached, he cried out, "Suffering! Suffering! and further said, "King Yama has come to take me.
The temple administrator asked, "When the Imperial Commissioner threw the Master into the water at that time, did the spirit..."
"Form is immovable. How could it be like this now? The Master picked up his pillow and said, "Tell me, was it like this then, or is it like this now?

The head monk had no reply and subsequently passed away. This occurred on the thirteenth day of the tenth month of the *wuzi* year, the third year of the Yuanhe era (the *Linjian Lu* states the thirteenth year, *wuxu*;
however, the date corresponds to the third year, *wuzi*). He was eighty-two years old and had spent sixty-three summer retreats in meditation.
He succeeded Mazu and resided at Xicheng. He had one disciple, Longtan Chongxin. A stele was composed by Qiu Xuansu, the Regional Inspector of Jingnan.

Furthermore, there are the *Nanyue Stele* by the Tang literatus Gui Deng, the *Memorial on the Essential Teachings* by Pei Xiangguo (Guifeng Zongmi), and the *Epitaph for Mazu’s Stupa* by Quan Deyu; all of these identify Tianwang as the successor to Mazu.
Foguo Bai, Daguan Ying, Lü Xiaqing, and Zhang Wujin all composed works to refute the errors in the *Zhuan Deng Lu*.
Yet, because they were contemporaries—and shared other commonalities, such as having both visited Shitou and Mazu—they could not help but leave certain doubts unresolved.
Furthermore, when Yaoshan went to visit Shitou, Shitou remarked that his karmic connection should instead lie with Mazu.
Shanxuan attained great enlightenment under Mazu, yet he ultimately succeeded Touzi; both were descendants of Śākyamuni.
How can one distinguish between them?

▲ Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo in Hongzhou was a native of Min. He left home at the age of youth at Mount Huangbo in his own prefecture.
A protuberance on his forehead rose like a pearl; his speech was clear and resonant, and his disposition was serene and pure.

Later, while traveling to Tiantai, he encountered a monk who greeted him with laughter as if they were old acquaintances. Upon looking closely, [Xiyun saw that] the monk’s gaze pierced others. Thereupon, they traveled together.
It happened that the mountain stream was suddenly in flood. [Nanquan] cast aside his rain hat, set down his staff, and stopped.

The monk urged the Master to cross with him. The Master said, "If you wish to cross, brother, cross yourself. The monk immediately lifted his robes and stepped through the waves as if walking on level ground.
Looking back, he called out, "Come across! Come across! The Master said, "Tsk! You self-satisfied fellow! Had I known sooner, I would have cut off your shins. The monk sighed and said, "Truly..."
"You are a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma; I am not your equal. Having said this, he vanished. He went to the capital of Luoyang to beg for alms, chanting the sound of "filling the bowl.
An old woman appeared from between the thorn-bushes of her gate and said, "You are truly insatiable! The Master replied, "You have not yet given anything;
why do you reproach me for being insatiable? The woman laughed and closed her gate. The Master marveled at this, approached her, and spoke with her, after which she was greatly inspired.
The physician took his leave after a short while. The old woman told him, "You should go to Nanchang to see Master Ma.
Upon arriving in Nanchang, Master Ma had already passed away. He then went to Shimen to pay respects at the stupa.
At that time, Chan Master Baizhang was living as a hermit near the stupa, so he went to visit him. Baizhang asked, "Majestic and dignified, from where have you come? The Master replied, "Majestic."
Majestically he came from Lingnan. Zhaozhou said, "So majestic and so dignified—what business do you have here? The Master replied, "Being so majestic and so dignified, I have no other business.
He then prostrated himself and asked, "How do you point to the ancestral vehicle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
Zhaozhou remained silent for a long while. The Master said, "Do not let it be cut off for future generations. Zhaozhou said, "I thought you were someone."
The man then rose and entered the abbot’s quarters. The Master followed him in and said, “I have come specifically for this.
Baizhang said, “If that is so, you must not let me down hereafter. One day, Baizhang brought up the story of Mazu’s shout during his second visit;
the Master then attained realization (as seen in the chapter on Baizhang). One day, Baizhang asked the Master, “Where have you been? He replied, “I went to gather mushrooms at Mount Daxiong.”
When the mushrooms appeared, Baizhang asked, "Do you see the tiger? The Master then made the sound of a tiger. Baizhang took up his axe and made a gesture as if to strike;
the Master immediately struck Baizhang with a slap. Baizhang laughed heartily and departed. Later, he ascended the hall and said, "On the foot of Mount Daxiong there is a great tiger;
all of you must watch out for it. Today, the old fellow Baizhang has encountered it in person."
He encountered one mouthful.
In the *Biyanji* (Blue Cliff Record), it is recorded that after the Master had visited the Abbot but did not take his leave, the Abbot remarked later, "The Abbot [Dongshan] held him in deep esteem.
The next day, the Master took his leave of the Abbot. The Abbot asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am going to pay my respects to Master Ma. The Abbot said, "Master Ma..."
"The Master has already passed away. (Yuánwù said: "Tell me, when Huangbo asked that question, did he ask because he knew [the answer], or did he ask because he did not know?
The Master said, "I went specifically to pay my respects, but my karmic fortune was too shallow; I did not even get to see him once.
I do not know what words or phrases he had on his usual days. The Old Man recounted how [the Master] had been struck with a shout during his second visit three times.
The Master spoke in a dialect that was unintelligible to the Japanese. Upon hearing it, the Master involuntarily stuck out his tongue.

Baizhang asked, "In the future, will you not take up the lineage of Mazu? The Master replied, "Not so. Today, because I heard what you raised, I have been able to see Mazu’s great capacity and great function.
Yet, I do not yet know Mazu. If I were to succeed Mazu, my descendants would perish in the future. Baizhang said: [This is the end of the recorded exchange.]

It is said: "If one's insight is equal to that of the teacher, one possesses half the virtue of the teacher; only when one's insight surpasses that of the teacher is one fit to receive the transmission.
You possess a realization that far exceeds your teacher’s. (Yuanwu further said: "Tell me, when Huangbo asked this question, did he ask because he already knew, or did he ask because he did not know?
This case has already appeared in the chapter on Baizhang; it is recorded here again for further reference.
This is based on Yuanwu’s *niangu* (critical comments). As for the differences between the various versions of this case, there is no need to discuss them.

The *Tianbi Gong’an*, *Huiyuan*, *Sungu Tongyao*, and others all attribute it to Linji; this follows its inclusion within the Master’s chapter in the *Recorded Sayings of Ancient Worthies* and the *Línjiàn Lù*.
One day, while Zhaozhou was supervising the communal labor of clearing a field, he returned and asked the Master, "Master Yun, it must have been no easy task clearing this field.

The Master replied, "I simply performed my duties along with the assembly. Zhaozhou said, "You must have exerted yourself greatly. The Master replied, "How could I dare refuse such toil? Zhaozhou asked, "How much field did you clear?
The Master took his hoe and struck the ground three times. Zhaozhou then gave a shout, and the Master covered his ears and departed.
While the Master was at Nanquan attending to communal labor (*pǔqǐng*) and sorting vegetables, Nanquan asked, "Where are you going?
The Master replied, "I am going to sort vegetables. Nanquan asked, "With what do you sort them? The Master held up his knife. Nanquan said, "You only know how to act as a guest;
you do not know how to act as the host. The Master pointed with the knife three times. Nanquan said, "Everyone, let us go sort vegetables. One day, [the Master] carried his bowl toward Nanquan.
He took the seat of the senior monk. When Shishuang entered the hall and saw him, he asked, "Venerable sir, for how many years have you practiced the Way?
The Master replied, "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja. Shishuang said, "Even so, you are still the descendant of Old Master Wang. The Master then moved down to sit in the second seat.
Quanshu retired.
Guishan said, "He who deceives his enemy perishes. Yangshan said, "Not so; you must know that Huangbo possessed the mechanism for trapping tigers.
Guishan said, "The extent of your realization has grown this much. Xuedou said, "What a pity! Wang [the tiger].

"Master, one sees only the sharpness of the tip of the awl. Had I been Nanquan at that time, as soon as he said, 'Before King Wei-yin,' I would have immediately taken my seat in the second position, leaving Huangbo unable to rise for the rest of his life.
Even so, I must still save Nanquan. Miaoxi said, "Why wait for him to ask about the year?"
As he was performing his circumambulation, upon entering the hall and seeing him in the seat of honor, he took up his bowl and sat in the second seat.
Even had Huangbo possessed the "trap for tigers" device, where could he have applied it?
One day Nanquan said, "I, this old monk, have a 'Song of Herding an Ox. I ask you, Elder, to provide a response. The Master replied, "I already have a teacher of my own.

When the Master took his leave of Nanquan, Nanquan saw him off at the gate and held up the Master’s straw hat, saying, "Elder, your physical stature is of vast capacity, yet this hat is far too small.
The Master said, "Even so, the entire great trichiliocosm is contained within it."
Quán asked, "What about Master Wáng? The Master donned his bamboo hat and departed. While the Master was at Yángguān, he was performing prostrations in the hall.

At that time, Emperor Xuānzōng of the Táng dynasty was a novice monk (śrāmaṇera) and asked, "If one does not seek the Buddha, does not seek the Dharma, and does not seek the Saṅgha, Elder, what is it that you seek when you prostrate? The Master replied, "I do not seek the Buddha; I do not seek the Dharma."
He did not seek anything from the Sangha and constantly paid homage in this manner. Baizhang said, "What is the use of paying homage?
The Master then struck him with his palm. Baizhang said, "That was too coarse. The Master replied, "What place is this for speaking of coarse or fine? He then struck him again.
The Master had once dismissed his assembly while at Kaiyuan Temple in Hongzhou. One day, Prime Minister Pei Xiu entered the temple and was walking about.
Next, seeing a mural on the wall, he asked the temple master, "What is this painting? The master replied, "It is the true likeness of eminent monks.
The official said, "The true likenesses may be viewed, but where are the eminent monks? The master was at a loss for an answer. The official asked, "Is there any Zen practitioner here?
He replied, "Recently there was a monk who came to serve in the temple; he bears a certain resemblance to a Zen practitioner. The official then requested to meet him and said:

I recently had a question, but the various virtuous ones were reluctant to speak. I now request that the Master provide a single word in my stead. The Master said, "I pray the Excellency will pose the question.
The Excellency repeated his previous words. The Master called out in a clear voice, "Pei Xiu! The Excellency responded, "Yes? The Master asked, "Where are you?
At that moment, the Excellency understood the meaning, as if he had recovered a pearl from within his topknot. He invited the Master into his official residence and performed the rites of a disciple.
Chan Master Jìngshān Gǎo, when Administrative Commissioner Lǐ visited the mountain, took up this kōan and commented:
"Lord Péi followed error with error, completely shedding his sensory roots and dust. Huángbò bestowed compassion spontaneously, without expending any mental effort.
It is like the earth supporting a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering loftiness; it is like a stone containing jade, unaware that the jade is flawless."
Although this is so, Huangbo possesses only the "sword that kills" and lacks the "sword that gives life.
Today, if Grand Councilor Dazai were to ask Yunmen, "The true likeness may be beheld; where is the eminent monk?
Yunmen would likewise call out, "Grand Councilor! If the Grand Councilor responds, Yunmen would immediately say, "In the hall today..."
He offered special thanks for his support.
One day, Pei placed a statue of the Buddha before the Master and knelt, saying, "I request you, Master, to bestow a name upon it.
The Master called out, "Pei Xiu! The official responded, "Yes. The Master said, "I have finished bestowing the name upon you. The official prostrated himself. One day, Pei invited the Master.
Upon arriving at the prefecture, he presented a scroll of his own commentaries to the Master. The Master received it and placed it on his seat, not deigning to open or read it for some time.
Then he asked, "Do you understand? Pei replied, "I have not yet fathomed it. The Master said, "If you could understand it in this way, you would still be somewhat close;
but if it is expressed in paper and ink, how can there be my school? Pei then offered a poem in one chapter, beginning: "Since the Great Being..."
He transmitted the seal of the mind; with a round protuberance on his forehead and a body seven feet tall, he hung his staff for ten years while dwelling by the waters of Shu.

Today he crosses the banks of the Zhang River with his bowl floating. A thousand dragons and elephants follow his lofty steps; ten thousand miles away, fragrant flowers form a cause for supreme merit.
Those who wish to serve him as disciples do not know to whom he will entrust the Dharma. The Master showed no sign of joy.

Having received the Master’s instructions, Pei further studied the various aspects of the teachings in depth. He served his teacher with the etiquette due to a disciple, yet regarded Guifeng as a brother and friend.
He once personally transcribed five hundred fascicles of the Great Canon, and the writings he composed for the Fayuan (Garden of the Dharma) were held in high esteem by all quarters.
There were six newly arrived monks; five of them prostrated, while one among them lifted up his sitting mat and drew a circle in the air.
The Master said, "I have heard there is a very fierce hunting dog. The monk said, "It has come seeking the sound of the mountain goat."
The Master said, "The langur has no sound; come, seek it. [The student] said, "I have come seeking the langur’s tracks. The Master said, "The langur has no tracks; come, seek it.
[The student] said, "I have come seeking the langur’s footprints. The Master said, "The langur has no footprints; come, seek it.
[The student] said, "If that is so, then it is a dead langur. The Master then ceased speaking. The next day, he ascended the hall and said, "Yesterday you were seeking the langur..."
The monk Yang emerged. As he stepped out, the Master said, "Yesterday’s case was not yet resolved; I have retired for now. What do you say to this? The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "I thought you were a monk of true substance, but it turns out you are merely a scholar-monk.
He then struck him and drove him out. One day, the Master clenched his fist and said, "All the old monks in the world..."
"In this matter, if I let slip even a single thread of leniency, you will run wild in every direction; if I do not let it pass, it will not take more than a single squeeze.
A monk asked, "What is it like when you let slip a single thread of leniency? The Master said, "Running wild in every direction.

[The monk] asked, "What is it like when you do not let it pass and it does not take more than a single squeeze? The Master said, "Pǔ. The Master ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, the Master said:
The Master took up his staff and struck everyone at once, dispersing them. He then called out to the assembly; as the assembly turned their heads, the Master said, "The moon is like a drawn bow;
there is little rain and much wind. When asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? the Master struck him. One day, he ascended the hall for a discourse.
The great assembly gathered like clouds. The Master said, "What do you all seek? He drove them away with his staff, yet the assembly would not disperse.
The Master sat back down and said, "You all are nothing but fellows who eat dregs of wine.
To travel as pilgrims in such a manner brings you ridicule from others. You go wherever there are eight hundred or a thousand people; you cannot hope for anything else."
"How noisy! When I was traveling as a monk, if I encountered a man even beneath a blade of grass, I would strike him on the crown of his head with my staff.
If he were to feel the pain, I could have filled a cloth bag with rice and provided for him.
But if everyone were as easygoing as you are, how could there be such matters as these today? Since you all call yourselves..."
When traveling on foot, you must also apply some measure of spirit. Do you know that within the Great Tang there is no Chan master?
At that time, a monk asked, "The venerable elders of all quarters gather crowds to teach and transform; why do you say instead that there is no Chan master?

The Master said, "I do not say there is no Chan; it is simply that there is no master. (Later, Guishan asked Yangshan, "What do you say to this? Yangshan replied, "The king of geese chooses its milk; it has never been the kind of creature that confuses it with duckweed.")

Tianhuai said, "This is indeed difficult to discern. Wuzu Jie’s *Record of Monastic Sayings* says: "I thank the Master for explaining the principle so well. Chengtian Zong said: "Wuzu Jie’s eye illuminates the four quarters of the world; yet even he could not fully see Huangbo.

If one wishes to uphold the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, one must rely on a master of the Huangbo lineage. Shimen Cong said: "Huangbo’s instruction was truly extraordinary; however, as soon as he was pressed by Puna, he lost one of his eyes. Jingshan Daowu said: [The text continues: "Huangbo’s instruction was indeed marvelous... (Note: The provided text fragment ends with Jingshan’s name).

Now tell me: is this a sentence of *amṛta* (clarified butter), or is it a sentence of poison? Furthermore, there is a verse: "Only by putting on clothes upon one's body can one avoid the cold; Though food is spoken of at the mouth, one is never satiated. The 'Old Lady’s Zen' within the land of the Great Tang— Today, for your sake, I have annotated it to its end.

Fojian Qin’s Verse: "In the mountains of Huangbo he clearly revealed himself to the assembly; Within the land of the Great Tang he hid his form in the dark. A corner of his *kāṣāya* robe still drags upon the ground— Who among those in the monasteries has eyes to see? Fohui Quan’s Verse: "Without a teacher, he fills the land of the Great Tang;

Those who eat only dregs of wine cannot understand him. Passing idly through the bamboo temple, spring is already deep; Falling flowers scatter wildly, staining the color of the moss. Dharma Brother, do you not see that under Master Mazu...?
Of the eighty-four people who sat at the site of enlightenment, only two or three attained the True Dharma Eye of Master Ma;
Master Guizong of Mount Lu was one of them. Indeed, an ordained person must first know the matters transmitted from of old before they can truly succeed.
For instance, although Oxhead under the Fourth Patriarch spoke horizontally and vertically, he still did not yet know the pivotal bolt of the higher realm.
Only with such eyes can one distinguish between the factions of the heterodox and the orthodox. For the time being, you should attend to your own affairs;
you are unable to realize the truth, knowing only how to parrot words. You merely tuck them into your leather bag and go everywhere proclaiming, "I understand Chan.
But can this save you from birth and death? To treat the elder masters with such contempt is to invite five arrows into hell. As soon as I see you entering, I shall strike.
When you enter through the gate, you will recognize it immediately. Do you understand? You must exert yourself with urgency; do not treat this as a trivial matter.
If you spend your entire life merely wearing a single robe and eating what comes your way, those with clear eyes will laugh at you. In the end, you will be reckoned by mere commoners.
You should examine for yourself how far you have come: whose business is this? If you understand, then understand; if not—
The assembly dispersed immediately. [Baizhang] said to Gōngměi Páirén: "All Buddhas and all sentient beings are nothing other than this single mind;
there is no other dharma. This mind, from time immemorial, has never been born and has never ceased.
It is neither blue nor yellow; it is formless and signless. It does not belong to existence or non-existence; it is reckoned neither new nor old; it is neither long nor short."
It is great and not small; it transcends all limits, names, words, traces, and dualities. It is the very essence itself. To stir a thought is to deviate from it.
It is like empty space, without boundaries and impossible to measure. This one mind alone is the Buddha;
there is no difference whatsoever between the Buddha and sentient beings. It is only because sentient beings cling to appearances and seek outwardly that they fail to find it.
Through such revolving delusions, one causes the Buddha to seek the Buddha and the mind to grasp the mind; yet throughout kalpas and until the end of one's life, one will never attain it.

If one does not know how to let thoughts rest and forget deliberation, the Buddha will manifest before one’s very eyes. This very mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is none other than sentient beings.
When acting as sentient beings, this mind does not diminish; when acting as Buddhas, this mind does not increase.

Even the myriad practices of the six perfections and merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are inherently complete from the beginning, requiring no cultivation or addition. Encountering conditions, they are manifested;
when conditions cease, they are quiescent. If one does not resolutely believe that this is the Buddha, yet desires to practice by clinging to signs in order to seek merit—
All such applications are merely false conceptions; they run counter to the Way. This very mind is the Buddha—there is no other Buddha apart from it, nor is there any other mind.
This mind is luminous and pure like empty space, devoid of even a single trace of form or characteristic. To raise the mind or stir a thought...
This would immediately deviate from the essence of the Dharma and constitute attachment to signs (*nimitta*). Since beginningless time, there has been no Buddha who attached to signs;

he cultivated the six perfections and the myriad practices desiring to attain Buddhahood—this is merely the gradual path (*anupūrva-krama*). Since beginningless time, there has been no Buddha who followed a gradual path;
rather, it is simply the awakening to the One Mind, wherein not even the slightest dharma can be obtained. This is the true Buddha. The Buddha and sentient beings are in every way identical.
It is like empty space, which is neither mixed nor destroyed. It is like the great solar orb illuminating the four continents:
when the sun rises, its light pervades the world, yet empty space was never brightened; when the sun sets, darkness overspreads the world, yet empty space was never darkened.
The realms of light and darkness contend with one another, but the nature of empty space remains vast and unchanging.

The minds of the Buddhas and sentient beings are likewise thus. If one contemplates the Buddha as having the marks of pure radiance and liberation, and contemplates sentient beings as having the marks of defilement, turbidity, and the darkness of birth-and-death, one who forms such conceptions will not attain Bodhi even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, because of being attached to marks.
This single mind alone exists; there is not so much as a speck of dust’s worth of another dharma.
It can be attained: the mind itself is the Buddha. Nowadays, practitioners of the Way who do not awaken to the essence of this mind give rise to further thoughts upon that mind;
they seek the Buddha outwardly and practice by clinging to forms. All such things are evil dharmas and are not the path of Bodhi.
To make offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions is not as good as making offerings to a single mindless practitioner of the Way. Why? Because the "mindless" one is without [deluded] mind.
It is the mind of all things. The essence of suchness is, internally, like wood or stone—unmoving and unswaying; externally, like empty space—unobstructed and unimpeded.
It is without subject or object, without location or direction, without form or appearance, and without gain or loss.

Those who approach it dare not enter this Dharma, for they fear falling into emptiness where there is no place to rest. Thus, they look upon its precipice and retreat. Examples of this are found throughout the vast literature of inquiry.
[Those who] see [the truth] are as numerous as hairs; those who seek to know the view are like the hair, while those who awaken to the Way are like horns.

Mañjuśrī represents Principle (*li*), and Samantabhadra represents Practice (*xing*). Principle is the principle of true emptiness and non-obstruction; practice is the inexhaustible practice that is free from marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Avalokiteśvara represents Great Compassion, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta represents Great Wisdom. Vimalakīrti means "Pure Name. "Pure" refers to nature (*prakṛti*); "name" refers to...
This is their characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Since nature and characteristics are not different, he is named Vimalakīrti. That which is manifested by the great Bodhisattvas exists within every person;
