it is not separate from the one mind. To realize this is precisely it. Those who study the Way today do not seek realization within their own minds, but instead grasp at objects by clinging to appearances outside the mind;
they all turn their backs on the Way. As for the sands of the Ganges, the Buddha said they are sands. All...
When Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas pass over it on foot, the sand feels no joy; when cattle, sheep, insects, and ants tread upon it, the sand feels no anger;
toward precious jewels and fragrant scents, the sand feels no greed; toward excrement, urine, and foul odors, the sand feels no aversion.
This mind is the mind that is no-mind, free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Between sentient beings and all Buddhas, there is nothing further.

There is a distinction. Simply being able to be without-mind (*amanojñā*) is itself the ultimate. If a student of the Way does not directly become without-mind, even if they practice for kalpas upon kalpas, they will never accomplish the Way;
they will be fettered by the meritorious practices of the Three Vehicles and fail to attain liberation. Nevertheless, there are differences in the speed with which one realizes this mind:
there are those who attain the state of no-mind in a single thought-moment upon hearing the Dharma, while there are those who only reach it upon attaining the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding "attaining the mindless": once one attains the mindless state for a long or short duration and abides therein, there is nothing further to be cultivated or realized.
Truly there is nothing to be attained; it is real and not false. Attaining it in a single thought is exactly equal in its efficacy to attaining it through the ten stages (*bhūmi*);

there is no difference in depth or shallowness. It is merely that [those who follow gradual cultivation] have endured toil in vain over many kalpas. Whether creating evil or creating good, both are attachments to forms (*nimitta*).
To perform evil while attached to signs is to suffer in saṃsāra in vain; to perform good while attached to signs is to undergo toil and hardship in vain.

In neither case is it as good as immediately recognizing one’s own fundamental Dharma upon hearing these words. This Dharma is the mind; there is no dharma outside the mind. This mind is the Dharma; there is no mind outside the Dharma.
The mind is itself mindless, yet there is no "one who is mindless. If you attempt to make the mind mindless, the mind instead becomes something existent.
It is to be realized through silent resonance alone, transcending all conceptual thought. Therefore it is said: "The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.

This mind is the Buddha of primordial purity; every person possesses it. All sentient beings, down to the most minute insects, are of one essence with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, no different at all.
It is only because of deluded thoughts and discrimination that they create various karmas. Yet, within the fundamental Buddha, there is not a single thing [of this nature].
All phenomena are merely empty and pervasive, quiescent, luminous, wondrous, and peaceful. One awakens to and enters this deeply for oneself; it is right here and now.

It is perfectly complete and fully endowed, lacking nothing further. Even if one were to practice with diligence throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, traversing all the stages (*bhūmi*), when the moment of realization arrives, one realizes only that which was originally the Buddha. Nothing can be added above this. Yet, looking back...
The efforts exerted throughout kalpas are all but deluded acts within a dream. Thus the Tathāgata said: "In regard to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I have truly attained nothing.
Had I attained anything, Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed a prediction of my enlightenment upon me.
Question: "What is the Buddha? The Master said: "Your own mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the mind. Mind and Buddha are not different. This is what is meant by "immediate" (*jì*).

The mind is itself the Buddha. Apart from the mind, there is no other Buddha. [A questioner asks: "If one's own mind is the Buddha, then how did the Patriarch come from the West to transmit the Dharma?
The Master said: "The Patriarch came from the West solely to transmit the Buddha of the mind. He directly pointed out that the minds of you all are fundamentally the Buddha;
because mind after mind is not different, he was called the Patriarch. If you see this meaning directly, it is sudden [enlightenment]."
Transcending the three vehicles and all stages, one is fundamentally a Buddha, not something to be accomplished through cultivation. [The student] asks:

"If this is so, when the Buddhas of the ten directions appear in the world, what Dharma do they preach? The Master says: "The Buddhas of the ten directions appear in the world only to collectively preach the Dharma of the One Mind.
Therefore, the Buddhas secretly entrusted this essence of the Dharma of the One Mind to Mahākāśyapa. This essence of the Dharma of the One Mind is exhaustive.
Space pervades the Dharma-realm; this is what is called the Buddhas. As for the principle of the teachings, each phenomenon—how could you understand it through words and phrases?
Nor is it something seen within a single stimulus or a single object. This meaning can only be attained through silent resonance.
To attain it is to enter a single gate, which is called the Gate of the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta-dharmamukha). If you wish to realize it, simply know that there is no-mind.
Sudden awakening is simply awakening. If you apply your mind to study and grasp it, you will only move further away.

If there is no mind that discriminates between paths, and you are free from all grasping and rejecting, with a mind as still as wood or stone, only then do you have the capacity to learn the Way. [The student] asks: "Right now there are all sorts of deluded thoughts;
why do you say they do not exist? The Master says: "Delusion has no inherent substance; it is merely what arises from your own mind. If you..."
The conscious mind is the Buddha. The mind is fundamentally without delusion; why then do you give rise to a mind that further identifies with delusion?
If you do not produce thoughts or stir your mind, there will naturally be no delusion. Therefore it is said: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;

when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. [A questioner] asked: "Right now, at the very moment a delusive thought arises, where is the Buddha? The Master said: "You are aware of it right now."
When delusions arise, awakening is precisely the Buddha. If there were no deluded thoughts within, even the Buddha would not exist. Why is this so?

It is because when you give rise to the mind to form the view of being a Buddha, you then say there is a Buddha to be realized; when you form the view of being a sentient being, you then say there are sentient beings to be saved.
Every stirring of thought is entirely your own point of view. If all views are absent, then the Buddha exists.
"Where is he? As soon as Mañjuśrī gave rise to the view of a Buddha and the view of the Dharma, he was banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains.
[The Buddha] said: "At this very moment of awakening, where is the Buddha? The Master said: "From where does the question come? From where does awakening arise?
Speech and silence, movement and stillness—all sounds and forms—are entirely the work of the Buddha. Where would you seek the Buddha? You must not further place a head upon your head."
Head. Adding mouth upon mouth. Simply do not give rise to divergent views. Mountains are mountains; water is water; monks are monks; laypeople are laypeople.
The mountains, rivers, great earth, sun, moon, and stars—all are entirely nothing other than your own mind. The three thousandfold world-system is, in its entirety, your very self.
Where is there so much variety? Outside the mind there are no dharmas; before one’s eyes are the green mountains.
The world of empty space is brilliantly clear; there is not so much as a hair’s breadth that can serve as an object for your views and understandings.

Therefore, all sounds and forms are the Buddha’s eye of wisdom. Phenomena do not arise in isolation; they depend upon conditions to be born. Because it acts for the sake of sentient beings, it possesses manifold wisdom.
Throughout the day one speaks, yet what has ever been spoken? Throughout the day one hears, yet what has ever been heard? Thus, Śākyamuni’s four...
In the nineteenth year, Shou said, "I have never uttered a single word. He continued, "If it were so, where would Bodhi be? The Master said, "Bodhi has no such place.
Even a Buddha does not attain Bodhi, and sentient beings do not lose Bodhi. It cannot be attained by means of the body, nor can it be sought by means of the mind.
All sentient beings are themselves the manifestation of Bodhi. [The student] asked, "How is this so?"
He resolved to attain bodhicitta. The Master said, "Bodhi is unobtainable. You should now simply give rise to the mind that is without attainment.
To be certain that not a single dharma can be attained is itself bodhicitta. Bodhi has no place of abiding; therefore, there is no one who attains it."
Therefore it is said: "At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was not the slightest dharma that I could obtain; the Buddha then conferred upon me the prediction of enlightenment.
This clearly shows that all sentient beings are fundamentally *bodhi*; they should not seek to obtain *bodhi* anew.

When you now hear of the arousal of the *bodhicitta*, you imagine that by learning this one mind you will become a Buddha, intending only to act as a Buddha for yourself, regardless of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Even if one cultivates for kalpas, one will only obtain a reward-body Buddha or a transformation-body Buddha. What connection does this have with your original source, the true-nature Buddha?
Therefore it is said: "Seeking outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like you. It is also said: "This Dharma is equal, without high or low;
this is called Bodhi. This is precisely this original source, the pure mind, which is identical to that of sentient beings and all Buddhas in the world.
The realms, mountains, and rivers—whether with form or without form—pervade the worlds of the ten directions; all are equal, devoid of the marks of "self" and "other.

This fundamental source, the pure mind, is eternally self-perfect, luminous, and universally illuminating. Yet worldly people do not awaken to this; they merely identify the faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as the mind.
Being shrouded by these very faculties of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they fail to perceive the essence of their own brilliant clarity. Simply...
When the lower [levels of] mind are absent, the fundamental essence manifests of itself, like the great sun rising in the void, illuminating the ten directions without further obstruction.
Therefore, practitioners of the Way should not merely recognize seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, nor their activities and movements;

by emptying out seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, the path of the mind is cut off and there is no place for entry. One must instead recognize the original mind within the very state of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
However, the fundamental mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor is it separate from seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Simply do not give rise to views or interpretations based on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing; do not stir thoughts regarding seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing;

do not seek the mind apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing; and do not abandon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing to grasp at dharmas. It is neither identical with nor separate from them. Not...

Abiding without attachment, one is free and sovereign in all directions; there is nothing that is not a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). If you wish to know the essential secret, simply do not allow even a single thing to cling to the mind.
To say that the Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is "like empty space" is a metaphor for the identity of the *dharmakāya* and empty space:
empty space is the *dharmakāya*, and the *dharmakāya* is empty space. Ordinary people say that the *dharmakāya* pervades the locations of empty space, [but within] empty space...
The Dharma-body is all-encompassing. One does not realize that the Dharma-body is itself space, and space is itself the Dharma-body.
If one definitively asserts that there is space, then space is not the Dharma-body. If one definitively asserts that there is a Dharma-body, then the Dharma-body is not space.
Simply do not interpret it as space, for space is the Dharma-body; do not interpret it as the Dharma-body, for the Dharma-body is [space].
Space. Space and the Dharma-body have no different characteristics; Buddhas and sentient beings have no different characteristics;
birth-and-death and nirvana have no different characteristics; afflictions and bodhi have no different characteristics. To be free from all characteristics is itself the Buddha.
Ordinary people grasp at objects; practitioners of the Way grasp at the mind. When both mind and object are simultaneously extinguished, that is the true Dharma.

It is relatively easy to forget objects, but it is extremely difficult to forget the mind. People do not dare to forget the mind, fearing they will fall into emptiness where there is nothing to grasp or seek.
They do not realize that emptiness is fundamentally without emptiness—it is solely the one true Dharma-realm. Question: What is seeing one's nature? Answer: Nature is itself seeing.
Seeing is itself the nature; one cannot use the nature to further see the nature. Hearing is itself the nature; one cannot use the nature to further hear the nature.
It is only because you create the view of "nature" that you can speak of being able to hear or see the nature, whereby the duality of oneness and difference arises.
He clearly stated: "That which is already visible cannot be seen again. Why do you place a head upon your own head? He... [text fragment]... clearly stated.
Clarifying the Way is like scattered pearls upon a tray: the large are large and round, the small are small and round;
each is unaware of the others, and each does not obstruct the others. When they arise, they do not say, "I am arising"; when they perish, they do not say, "I am perishing.

Therefore, within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, there is nothing that does not accord with the timing [of reality]. Furthermore, sentient beings do not see the Buddha, and the Buddha does not see sentient beings. (The fourth [section]...)

The fruits do not see the four stages of approach; the four stages of approach do not see the four fruits. The three levels of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood do not see the two types of perfect and wondrous enlightenment;
the two types of perfect and wondrous enlightenment do not see the three levels of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood. Even so, water does not see fire, and fire does not see water;
earth does not see wind, and wind does not see earth. Sentient beings do not enter the dharma-realm, and the Buddha does not emerge from the dharma-realm.
Therefore, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no coming or going, and there is neither a seer nor that which is seen.

Since this is so, for what reason do you say, "I see" and "I hear," or claim that you attained awakening in the presence of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), or that the spiritual friend preached the Dharma to you?

Or that the Buddhas appeared in the world and preached the Dharma to sentient beings? Kātyāyana merely used a mind of arising and ceasing to transmit the Dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa); he was...
Vimalakīrti rebuked him, clearly stating: "All dharmas are fundamentally unbound; what need is there to liberate them? They are fundamentally unstained;
what need is there to purify them? Therefore it is said: 'The true mark is thus—how can it be spoken? You have now merely produced a mind of right and wrong and a mind of defilement and purity.
Having acquired a single bit of knowledge and understanding, you travel about the world, intending to [correct] others whenever you see them."
It must certainly be grasped. Who possesses the discernment to judge who is strong and who is weak? If it were as you suggest, heaven and earth would be as vastly different as they are;
what more could be said of "seeing one's nature"? Question: You have already stated that nature is seeing and seeing is nature.

Since nature itself is without obstruction and without limit, why is it that one does not see when an object intervenes? Furthermore, within empty space, one sees when close at hand, but not otherwise.
"How is it that one does not see when at a distance? The Master said, "This is you generating false and divergent views.
If you say that one does not see because of an intervening object, yet sees when there is no object, and thereby claim that the nature has obstructions, you are entirely out of touch with the truth.
The nature is neither seeing nor non-seeing; phenomena are likewise neither seeing nor non-seeing. For one who sees the nature, where is there that is not 'I'?"

This is the fundamental nature [of all things]. Therefore, the six realms and four modes of birth, as well as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, are all the essence of my own pure and luminous nature.
Hence it is said: "Upon seeing form, one sees the mind," for form and mind are not distinct.

It is only because one grasps at appearances and engages in seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing that one attempts to remove external objects in order to perceive [the mind]; such a person falls among those of the Two Vehicles and relies on supernatural powers for their vision.
[The opponent says: "It is understood. In empty space, one sees what is near but does not see what is far; this is categorized among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
[But you] clearly state that it is neither internal nor external, neither near nor far. As for 'that which is near yet cannot be seen,' this is the nature of all things.
If even what is near cannot be seen, what is the intent in further saying that what is far cannot be seen?"
Question: Does the Buddha exhaustively attain the end of ignorance? The Master said: Ignorance is precisely the place where all Buddhas attain the Way.
Therefore, dependent origination is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Every speck of dust and every color perceived immediately accords with the boundless principle of nature.
Raising the foot and setting it down does not depart from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The site of enlightenment is that which has nothing to be attained. I tell you:
precisely this non-attainment is what is called "sitting at the site of enlightenment. [The questioner] asks: "As for 'ignorance' (*avidyā*), is it light or is it darkness?
The Master says: "It is neither light nor darkness. Light and darkness are phenomena of alternation. Ignorance is simply not light; it is also not dark. It is simply..."
This is the fundamental illumination. It is neither bright nor dark; it is merely this single phrase that confuses the eyes of all people in the world.
Therefore it is said: "Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
That unimpeded wisdom (hui) transcends empty space; there is no place for you to engage in discourse. Śākyamuni’s measure is equal [to this].

Suddenly, a bodhisattva emerges from within a single pore of Samantabhadra and, with a single stride, traverses the entire trichiliocosm, yet does not leave that single pore. What capacity do you possess now to emulate him?
[The Master] said: "Since it cannot be learned, why is it said that 'the source of returning is non-dual, while expedient means are manifold'?"
[The questioner asked: "How is this so? The Master said: "'The source of returning has no duality' means that the true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature.
'There are many gates of expedient means' means that Śrāvakas perceive the arising of ignorance and perceive the cessation of ignorance;
Pratyekabuddhas perceive only the cessation of ignorance and do not perceive its arising, realizing quiescence in every thought-moment. As for the Buddhas, they perceive sentient beings..."

Throughout one's entire life one is born, yet there is no birth; throughout one's entire life one perishes, yet there is no perishing. This absence of birth and absence of perishing is the fruit of the Mahāyāna.
Thus it is said: "The fruit is full and Bodhi is perfect; the flower blooms and the world arises. Raising the foot is the Buddha; lowering the foot is the sentient being.
The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, are those for whom both principle and phenomena are complete; sentient beings are those for whom both birth-and-death and fulfillment are complete. One.
All things are complete and sufficient. Because they are sufficient, there is no seeking. You are now, in every thought-moment, studying the Buddha, yet you harbor resentment toward sentient beings.
If you resent and cling to sentient beings, this is to slander the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Therefore, since the Buddha appeared in the world, he held a refuse-basket to sweep away the filth of conceptual proliferation; he merely taught you to eliminate the mind of study from the past and to eliminate the mind of views.

When one attains exhaustion [of delusion], one does not fall into conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It is also said: "Carry out the dung. This is simply to teach you not to give rise to the mind.
If the mind does not arise, one naturally becomes a great sage. One must certainly not discriminate between Buddhas and sentient beings;
when there is no discrimination regarding anything at all, only then does one enter the gate of our Caoqi school. Therefore, the ancient sages of old have said: "I practice little..."
The Dharma-gate. Thus, non-action is my Dharma-gate; it is simply the gate of the single mind. When all people arrive here, none dare to enter.
It is not that there is nothing at all to be found, but rather that few attain it. Those who attain it are Buddhas. Be careful!
Now, those who study the Way must first eliminate all miscellaneous studies and external conditions. They must be resolute in their non-seeking. Resolute...
Without attachment, hearing the profound Dharma is like a clear breeze reaching the ear—passing by in an instant, never to be pursued again.
This is what is called deeply entering the Tathāgata-dhyāna and departing from the conceptualization of dhyāna. From the ancestral masters of old, only the One Mind has been transmitted.

There is no second Buddha; the mind itself is the Buddha. To transcend suddenly both the Equal and Sublime Awakenings, and to remain resolutely without flowing into a second thought—only then can one be said to have entered the gate of our school.
Regarding such a Dharma, you who are but ordinary people, when you arrive here, how do you intend to study it?
Therefore it is said: "The moment you conceive a thought, you are bound by the demon of conceptualization; yet it is not by non-conceptualization."
At that time, you will again be bound by the demon of conceptualizing thoughts (the character "demon" [魔] should be present here). This does not come from outside; it arises from your own mind.

Only for a Bodhisattva who lacks supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is its track impossible to find. If, at all times, your mind holds the view of permanence, you are a follower of the eternalist heretics (*śāśvatavāda*).
If you contemplate all phenomena as empty and yet form a view of emptiness, you are a follower of the nihilist heretics (*ucchedavāda*).
The Way. Thus, it is said that "the three realms are mind-only" and "all phenomena are consciousness-only. This is spoken for the sake of those with the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
If one speaks of the *dharmakāya* as the ultimate fruit, this is addressed to those of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood.
Therefore, the Buddha eliminates two types of ignorance: first, the subtle ignorance regarding the knowable; second, the extremely subtle ignorance regarding the knowable. Since the Buddha is thus...
That is so. Why then speak further of the two types of awakening—the ordinary and the wondrous? For this reason, all people desire only to move toward light and not toward darkness;
they seek only enlightenment and do not love afflictions or ignorance. Thus, they claim that the Buddha is awakening while sentient beings are delusion.
If one holds such a view, one will continue to transmigrate through the six realms for hundreds and thousands of kalpas, never finding cessation.

Why is this? Because it constitutes slandering the fundamental source-nature (*prakṛti*) of all Buddhas. Others have clearly told you that the Buddha is not enlightened and sentient beings are not ignorant;
for dharmas possess neither enlightenment nor ignorance. Thus, the Buddha is not superior, and sentient beings are not inferior.
Because the Dharma has neither strength nor weakness, even the Buddha is not wise and sentient beings are not foolish;

because the Dharma has neither folly nor wisdom. You stick out your head and claim to understand Chan; as soon as you open your mouth, the sickness breaks out. You do not speak of the root, but only of the branches; you do not speak of delusion, but only of awakening;
you do not speak of the essence, but only of its function. There is no place at all for your talk or argument. He [the Master] is entirely...
The Dharma is fundamentally non-existent, yet now it is not non-existent either. When conditions arise, there is nothing; when conditions cease, there is nothing that is not.

Fundamentally, it does not exist, because the fundamental is not fundamental. The mind is not mind, because the mind is not mind. Characteristics are not characteristics, because characteristics are not characteristics.
Therefore it is said: "There is no dharma, no fundamental mind; only then does one understand the mind and mental dharmas. The dharma is itself non-dharma; non-dharma..."
This is precisely the Dharma, because there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. These mind and mental factors suddenly and fleetingly give rise to a single thought;
one realizes it is like an illusion and like a transformation. Thus, one flows into the past Buddhas. Yet, the past Buddhas do not exist, and the future Buddhas are not non-existent.
Furthermore, they are not called "future Buddhas. The present moment does not abide from one instant to the next, so it is not called "present."

When the Buddha is present, and when the Buddha arises, one does not attempt to constrain him. Whether it be awakening or delusion, good or evil, one must never obstinately cling to them or attempt to sever them.
Just as when a single thought flickers up, it cannot be locked by a thousandfold bolt, nor can it be bound by ten-thousand-fathom ropes.
Since this is so, how could one possibly attempt to extinguish it or stop it? How could one even conceive of such a division?
I tell you clearly: you, O *ālaya-vijñāna*, how do you intend to sever it? It is like a mirage:
if you say it is near, it cannot be found even if you search throughout the ten directions; if you say it is far, when you look, it is right before your eyes.
When you try to pursue it, it moves further away; when you try to avoid it, it comes back to chase you. You cannot grasp it.
Yet, one cannot abandon it either. Since this is the case, we know that the nature of all dharmas is inherently so; thus, there is no need for sorrow or anxiety regarding others.
For instance, it is said that the preceding thought is ordinary and the succeeding thought is holy, like the turning over of a hand.
This is the ultimate of the teachings of the Three Vehicles. According to our Zen school, however, the preceding thought is not ordinary, nor is the succeeding thought...
Furthermore, it is not that the preceding thought is not the Buddha and the succeeding thought is not a sentient being;
therefore, all forms are the form of the Buddha, and all sounds are the sound of the Buddha. To bring forth a single principle, all principles are likewise so.
Seeing one phenomenon, one sees all phenomena; seeing one mind, one sees all minds; seeing one path, one sees all paths. One.
There is nowhere that is not the Way. When one perceives a single speck of dust, the mountains, rivers, and great earth throughout the ten directions are all likewise so.

When one perceives a single drop of water, one immediately perceives all the waters of nature throughout the ten directions. Furthermore, when one perceives all phenomena (*dharma*), one perceives the universal mind.
All phenomena are fundamentally empty, yet the mind is not non-existent. That which is not non-existent is wondrous existence; even this existence is not...
There is existence. Non-existence is itself existence; it is the wondrous existence of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Since this is so, the worlds of the ten directions do not transcend my single mind, and all lands of subtle dust do not transcend my single thought.
If this is the case, what can be said of "internal" and "external"? It is like the nature of honey being sweet: all honey is thus. One cannot say, "This honey is not sweet."
This is the ultimate suffering. Where could such a thing exist? Therefore it is said: "Space has no interior or exterior; such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Space has no middle; such is the nature of reality. Thus, sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, and Buddhas are themselves sentient beings."
Sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally of one and the same essence. Birth-and-death and nirvana, the conditioned and the unconditioned, are fundamentally of one and the same essence.

The mundane and the supramundane, even the six realms of existence and the four modes of birth, as well as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—whether possessing nature or lacking nature—are likewise of one and the same essence.
To say they are "the same" means that names and appearances are empty; existence is empty, and non-existence is also empty, throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The realms are originally one emptiness. Since this is so, where is there a Buddha who delivers sentient beings? Where are there sentient beings who receive the Buddha’s deliverance?
Why is this so? Because the nature of all phenomena is inherently thus. If one views it as spontaneous occurrence (*svabhāva*), [one falls into error].
You would immediately fall into the natural heretics. If you form the view of "no-self" and "no-what-belong-to-self," you will fall into the stages of the three worthies and ten sages.
How can you now, with a mere foot or an inch, attempt to measure the void?
He has clearly told you: "Dharma after dharma does not reach one another; for dharmas are inherently quiescent. They abide in their own place; they abide in their own place.
Truly so. Because the body is empty, it is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*); because the mind is empty, it is called the emptiness of nature (*prakṛtisūnyatā*);

because both body and mind are entirely empty, it is called the emptiness of the dharma-nature (*dharmatāsūnyatā*). Even the thousandfold divergent explanations do not depart from your own fundamental mind.

To speak now of bodhi, nirvāṇa, true thusness (*tathatā*), and buddha-nature as if they were distinct from the two vehicles and bodhisattvas is like pointing to leaves and calling them gold, or pointing to one's fist and calling it a clenched hand.
Regarding the teaching of the palm: when the hand is extended, the entire assembly—whether gods or humans—all see that within the palm there is not a single thing.
Therefore it is said: "Originally there was not one thing; where could there be dust?
Since there is originally no thing, the three periods of time are fundamentally non-existent. A student of the Way must enter directly with a single blade and see this very point.
This was only now attained. Therefore, the Great Master Dharmatrāta came from the Western Heaven to this land;

after passing through many kingdoms, he found only one person worthy of being a master, to whom he secretly transmitted the Mind-Seal. This seal stamps your original mind; by means of the mind, the Dharma is sealed.
Seal the mind with the Dharma. Since the mind is thus, the Dharma is also thus. It is identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Within the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, who is the person who receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), who is the person who attains Buddhahood, and who is the person who attains the Dharma?
He has clearly told you: Bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body, for the body is without marks; it cannot be attained by means of the mind.

Because the mind is without marks, it cannot be attained through its nature. Since this nature is precisely the original source-nature, the true and heavenly Buddha, one cannot attain a Buddha by means of a Buddha;
one cannot attain the markless by means of the markless; one cannot attain emptiness by means of emptiness;
one cannot attain the Way by means of the Way. Originally there is nothing to be attained; even non-attainment is unattainable.
It can be attained. Therefore it is said that not a single dharma can be attained; it is simply to lead you to realize your own original mind.
At the moment of realization, there is no mark of realization; there is neither realization nor non-realization, and even the mark itself cannot be apprehended.
Regarding such a dharma, those who attain it do so, yet the attainer does not consciously perceive it; those who do not attain it likewise do not consciously perceive it. Such is this dharma.
From the time of antiquity until now, how many have truly known this? That is why it is said: "How many people in the world have forgotten themselves?

If today, regarding a single mechanism, a single environment, a single scripture, a single teaching, a single era, a single moment, or a single name or character, you grasp them before the gates of your six sense-faculties, how are you any different from a wooden puppet on a mechanical device? Suddenly, if there were someone who came forth and did not—

Regarding those who form a conceptual understanding based on a single name or a single characteristic, I say that even if one were to search throughout the worlds of the ten directions, such a person could not be found, for there is no second person.
To succeed to the ancestral position is also called being of the Śākya clan;

because it is unmixed and purely singular, it is said that when the King attains Buddhahood, the princes shall likewise follow him into the homeless life. This meaning is extremely difficult to understand.
I only teach you not to seek. To seek is to lose it. It is like a foolish person who shouts once on a mountain;
the echo comes from the valley, and he immediately runs down the mountain to pursue it. When he finds it not, he shouts again, and the mountain peak echoes once more.

They likewise run up into the mountains to pursue it; thus for thousands of births and ten thousand kalpas, they remain merely people seeking sound and chasing echoes—vainly born and aimlessly dying men.
If you have no sound, then there is no echo. Nirvāṇa is without hearing, without knowing, and without sound.
To leave no trace and no sign—if one can attain such a state, one dwells somewhat in the same room as the Patriarchs. Entering the hall, he said:
"This very mind is Buddha. From the Buddhas above to the wriggling insects and sentient beings below, all possess Buddha-nature; they share the same essence of mind.
Therefore, when Bodhidharma came from the Western Heaven, he transmitted only the Dharma of the One Mind, pointing directly at all sentient beings."
One is originally a Buddha; there is no need for cultivation. Simply recognize your own mind and see your own original nature right now, and do not seek anything else.
How does one recognize one's own mind? That which is speaking these very words is precisely your mind.
If you do not speak and are not active, the substance of the mind is like empty space: it has no form or appearance, nor does it have any location.
It is not exclusively non-existent either; it exists, yet it cannot be seen. Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"The treasury of the true nature within the mind has neither head nor tail; responding to conditions to transform beings, it is expediently called 'wisdom.
When it does not respond to conditions, one cannot speak of its existence or non-existence; even when it is actively responding, it leaves no trace. Since you know this to be so:
Now, simply to dwell within non-existence is to tread the path of all Buddhas. As the Sūtra says: "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling on anything.
That all sentient beings revolve in birth and death is because their mental objects run about and their minds do not rest within the six realms, thereby causing them to undergo various sufferings.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The minds of those who are difficult to transform are like monkeys."
Therefore, by means of various methods, one restrains the mind and subsequently subdues it. Thus, when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. Hence, one knows that all dharmas are created by the mind.
Even humans, devas, hells, the six realms, and asuras—all are created by the mind. Now, simply practice non-mindfulness and bring [all activity] to an immediate rest.

Regarding all conditions: do not give rise to deluded thoughts or discriminations. There is no person and no self; there is no greed or hatred; there is no loathing or affection; there is no victory or defeat.
Simply eliminate these many kinds of deluded thoughts as they arise. By nature, one is originally pure; this is itself the practice of the Dharma of Bodhi and the Buddhas.
If you do not realize this meaning, then even if you study extensively and practice with diligent hardship, eating only wood, [it will be of no avail].
Those who wear grass garments yet do not recognize their own minds all engage in deviant practices; they become nothing but celestial demons, non-Buddhist heretics, or spirits of the water and land.
What benefit can there be in practicing in such a manner? Master Zhi said: "The fundamental substance is created by one's own mind; how can it be sought within words and letters?
Now, simply recognize your own mind and cease discursive thought and delusion; then worldly afflictions will naturally [subside]."
Śāriputra, Vimalakīrti said: "I have set out but a single bed and lie here ill; my mind does not stir.
Just as I now lie ill, with all objects of perception stilled and deluded thoughts extinguished—this is itself Bodhi.

If, however, your mind is now in turmoil and unsettled, then no matter how much you study to reach the stages of the Three Vehicles, the Four Fruits, or the Ten Bhūmis, you will ultimately remain among the ranks of ordinary beings and sages."
"Sit. All conditioned phenomena ultimately succumb to the power of impermanence; all have a limit to their duration. It is like an arrow shot into the air:

when its momentum is exhausted, it falls back down. To return thus to the cycle of birth and death—to practice in such a manner without understanding the Buddha’s intent—is to undergo hardship in vain.
Is this not a great error? Master Zhi said: "If one has not yet met a world-transcending enlightened teacher, it is a waste to take the medicine of the Great Dharma."
Now, at all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—simply practice being without-mind.
Be without discrimination, without dependence, and without attachment. Throughout the day, let things proceed spontaneously and freely, appearing like a simpleton.
Let the people of the world not recognize you; you need not even seek to be recognized by others. When the mind is unrecognized, it is like a dull stone, entirely devoid of [conceptualization].
Sewing up the cracks: when all dharmas pass through your mind without entering it, you remain solitary and unattached. Only when this occurs do you begin to have a slight degree of resonance.
To penetrate beyond the realms of the three worlds is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world. Not leaking mental characteristics is called untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
One does not create karma for humans or devas, nor does one create karma for the hells; no thoughts arise, and all conditions are exhausted.
Non-arising: this very body and mind is that of a free person. It is not that they do not arise at all;
rather, they arise according to one’s will. As the Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva has a mind-made body (manomayakāya). This is it.

If, however, you have not yet realized the state of no-mind and act while clinging to forms, all such actions belong to the realm of Māra. Even performing the Buddha-work of adorning the Pure Land constitutes karma. Thus it is said:
This is called a hindrance to Buddhahood. Because you are hindered by this, you are bound by cause and effect; you lack the freedom to go or stay as you wish.

Therefore, dharmas such as Bodhi are fundamentally not existent. What the Tathāgata has taught are all merely transformations of people, just like using yellow leaves as gold to temporarily stop a small child’s crying. In reality, there is no dharma named Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Now that...
If you understand this meaning, why exert yourself in vain? Simply follow conditions to exhaust old karma, and do not create new calamities.

When the mind is luminously clear, all former interpretations must be relinquished. As Vimalakīrti said, "Remove all that exists," and as the Lotus Sūtra says, "For twenty years he was constantly ordered to remove filth.
This refers solely to removing the place within the breast where one forms interpretations.
Furthermore, it is said that one must sweep away the dung of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Thus, the Tathāgatagarbha is inherently empty and quiescent, not retaining even a single dharma.

Therefore, a sutra states: "The lands of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty. If one claims that the Buddha-way is attained through cultivation and study, such a view has no connection whatsoever to the truth.
Or, if one treats the subject and object as distinct entities, raising an eyebrow or moving...
To meet with another and respond appropriately is called "attaining accord" (qihui); it is the realization and verification of the principles of Chan.
If one suddenly encounters someone who does not understand, one immediately says that they know nothing at all. If one manages to establish a logical argument against them, the mind becomes joyful;
if one is defeated by them and falls short, the mind immediately becomes despondent. To study Chan with such a state of mind—
What connection is there? Even if you manage to understand a little bit of principle, you have only attained a *caitta-dharma* (mental factor);
as for Chan and the Way, there is no connection at all. This is why Bodhidharma sat facing a wall, never allowing people to find a point of view;
thus it is said: "The cessation of contrivance is the Buddha-way; discrimination is the army of Māra. This nature is not lost even when you are deluded, nor is it gained when you are awakened.

It cannot be attained. The true nature of heaven is fundamentally without delusion or awakening. Throughout the entirety of the void-realm of the ten directions, it has always been the substance of my own one mind.
Even if you were to exert yourself in movement and activity, how could you ever depart from this void? This void is originally neither large nor small;
it is without outflows and without conditioned action; it is without delusion and without awakening. To see clearly, there is not a single thing to be found—neither person nor self.
The Buddha has severed even the slightest trace of conceptual measurement (*vikalpa*). He is without dependence and without attachment—a single stream of pure clarity.

This is the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena) of one's own nature; how could there be any room for deliberation? The true Buddha has no mouth and does not preach the Dharma;
the true listener has no ears—whom could he hear? Take care. It is also said: "If one simply lacks all mental activity, that is what is called untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*)."
In all your daily activities—walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—and in every word you speak, simply do not become attached to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Let every utterance and every blink of an eye be entirely identical to the untainted (*anāsrava*). As we move toward the future age of the Dharma’s decline, most who study the Way of Chan will be attached to all sounds and forms.
Why not let your mind be like my mind—identical to empty space, like a withered tree or a stone? Like...
Only when the cold ashes and dead fire have departed will there be a slight degree of correspondence.
If it is not thus, on another day you will be completely subjected to the interrogation of Old Man Yama. You need only distance yourself from all dharmas of existence and non-existence;

let the mind be like the sun-disk, ever present in the void, its radiance spontaneous, illuminating without the act of illuminating. This is no matter of reducing effort. When one reaches this state, there is no...
The place of resting is precisely the practice of the deeds of all Buddhas; it is to give rise to the mind by abiding nowhere.

This is your pure *dharmakāya*, named *anuttara-bodhi*. If you do not realize this meaning, then even if you acquire vast knowledge through study, practice with diligent hardship, and subsist on grass garments and wooden food, if you do not recognize your own mind, all such efforts are termed "false practices."
It is further said: "Now, at all times, you should simply practice non-mind. After a long time, you will surely attain it in reality.

Because your capacity is small, you cannot transcend [samsara] instantaneously; however, if you can persist for three, five, or ten years, you must find a point of entry, and then you will naturally come to understand.
Because there are greed, hatred, and delusion, one establishes the precepts, concentration, and wisdom; fundamentally, there is no affliction."
How could there be bodhi where there is affliction? Thus the Patriarch said: "The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to deliver all minds;
since I have no mind, what use have I for all dharmas? Above the fundamentally pure Buddha, one does not further attach to a single thing.
For example, although the void may be adorned with immeasurable precious jewels, it can never be made to abide [by them]. Buddha-nature is like the void;
although it may be adorned with immeasurable merit and wisdom, it can never be made to abide [by them]. It is only that one is deluded regarding one's original nature and thus fails to see it.
This is what is called the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground: all phenomena are established in dependence upon this mind. When encountering objects, they immediately...
If there is existence, it is because there is no object; if there is no object, then it is non-existent. One must not attempt to transform the pure nature into an objective conceptualization.

What are called concentration and wisdom are the vivid function of discernment—tranquil yet alert. To perceive, hear, sense, and know as being all conceptualizations upon an object is acceptable for the time being when speaking to those of middling or inferior faculties.
However, if one wishes to realize this through direct personal experience, none of these conceptual views should be maintained. Thus it is said.
The "transformed city" refers to the Two Vehicles, as well as the stages of the Ten Grounds, Equal Enlightenment, and Sublime Enlightenment;

these are all provisional teachings established for the purpose of guiding and attracting beings, and thus they are all considered transformed cities. As for the "Jewel Place," it is the jewel of the true mind, the Buddha-nature of one's own original self.

This jewel does not belong to the realm of emotional or intellectual measurement; it cannot be established through conceptual construction. Therein, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being, neither subject nor object. Where, then, could there be a city?
If one asks, "Since this is already a conjured city, where is the treasure place? the treasure place cannot be pointed out;
for if it were pointed out, it would have a specific location, and thus it would not be the true treasure place. Therefore, it is said to be "nearby" only, and its exact measure cannot be defined.
One must simply realize and accord with it through personal experience. As for the term *icchantika*, it refers to one who lacks faith. [This applies to] all those in the six realms of existence.
Sentient beings, even those of the Two Vehicles, who do not believe in the existence of the Buddha-fruit, are all called icchantikas who have severed their roots of goodness.

Bodhisattvas, however, deeply believe in the existence of the Buddha-dharma; seeing no distinction between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and perceiving that Buddhas and sentient beings share the same single *dharmatā*, they are called icchantikas of the roots of goodness.
Ordinary people are mostly obstructed by objects in their minds and by phenomena in their principles.

One constantly desires to escape from sensory objects (*viṣaya*) in order to settle the mind, and to conceal worldly affairs (*dharma*) in order to preserve principle (*li*). One does not realize that this is actually the mind obstructing the objects and principle obstructing the affairs.

Simply allow the mind to be empty and the objects will naturally become empty; simply allow principle to be quiescent and the affairs will naturally become quiescent. Do not apply the mind perversely.

Ordinary people for the most part are unwilling to empty their minds, fearing they will fall into nihilism (*śūnyatā*); they do not know that their own minds are fundamentally empty. This is the delusion of the foolish.
One eliminates phenomena, not the mind; the wise eliminate the mind, not phenomena. The Bodhisattva’s mind is like space:
all things are relinquished, and all merit performed is free from attachment. However, there are three grades of relinquishment:

relinquishing everything—outer objects, inner body, and the mind—just like space, without any grasping or attachment. Thereafter, one responds to things according to circumstances, wherein both subject and object [are non-existent].

To forget all of this is "Great Equanimity" (mahopekṣā). If one practices the Path and spreads virtue on one side, while simultaneously relinquishing them on the other with a mind free of expectation, this is "Middle Equanimity.
If one extensively cultivates various virtues with some expectation, yet upon hearing the Dharma and realizing emptiness, subsequently becomes unattached, this is "Small Equanimity.
Great Equanimity is like a torch held before one; there is no further confusion or awakening. Middle Equanimity is like...
A torch is held beside one; it is sometimes bright and sometimes dim. When one slightly relinquishes [the mind], it is like a torch behind one’s back: one does not see the pits and ditches.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva’s mind is like space, relinquishing everything. The past mind cannot be apprehended; this is the relinquishment of the past.
The present mind cannot be apprehended; this is the relinquishment of the present. The future mind cannot be apprehended; this is the relinquishment of the future.

This is what is meant by relinquishing all three periods of time. Since the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa, the mind has been transmitted from mind to mind through the Seal of the Mind (citta-mudrā).
Mind and mind are not different. If the seal is applied to emptiness, the seal does not produce a pattern; if the seal is applied to things, the seal does not produce a dharma.
Therefore, one uses mind to seal mind; mind and mind are not different. Since that which seals and that which is sealed are both difficult to harmonize, those who attain it are few.
Yet, mind is itself no-mind, and attainment is itself no-attainment. The Buddha has three bodies; the Dharma-body speaks of self-nature.
The Dharma of pervasive emptiness. The *saṃbhogakāya* teaches all pure dharmas; the *nirmāṇakāya* teaches the dharmas of the six perfections and myriad practices.

The *dharmakāya* teaching of the Dharma cannot be sought through speech, sound, form, or written characters. There is nothing taught and nothing realized; it is simply the self-nature of pervasive emptiness.
Therefore it is said: "There is no dharma that can be taught; this is called the teaching of the Dharma. The *saṃbhogakāya*...

The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) manifests whatever teachings are required according to the capacity of those who perceive it; it also adapts to circumstances and the faculties of beings in order to gather and transform them.
Since these are all not the true Dharma, it is said: "The *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma.
Question: "Originally there is not a single thing. Is 'no-thing' itself the truth? The Master said: "Even 'no' is not it. There is no place for 'bodhi' (awakening), nor is there any 'non-bodhi'."
Wu Zhihui asked: "Is not the empty space directly before one's eyes truly an object?
Is there not, then, a pointing to that object to reveal the mind? The Master said: "What kind of mind would you have me point out for you to see within an object?

Even if you were to see it, it would merely be the mind that reflects the object—just like a person using a mirror to look at their face. Though they may clearly see their own eyebrows and eyes, fundamentally..."
"It is merely a physical image; what concern is it of yours? The student said, "If it were not for this reflection, when would I ever see it?
The Master said, "If you involve yourself with causes and conditions, you will always have to rely on external things. When will there ever be an end to that? Have you not seen him say to you:
'When you let go of your hand, there is nothing for you; all your laborious talk of thousands of varieties is in vain'? The student said, "If he has realized it, then even the reflection—"
"Is it that there is no object? The Master said, "If there were no object, what further need would there be for illumination? Do not fall into the habit of talking in your sleep with your eyes open.
As soon as you form the view of being a Buddha, you are obstructed by the Buddha; as soon as you form the view of being a sentient being, you are obstructed by the sentient being.

Forming views of ordinary or holy, pure or defiled, and so forth—all become obstructions. Because they obstruct your mind, they collectively result in the cycle of birth and death. It was just like this.
It is like a monkey that lets go of one thing only to seize another, with no end in sight.

The Buddhas of the ten directions have, in reality, not attained even the slightest dharma which could be called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is simply the single mind, truly devoid of any differentiated characteristics and lacking even the slightest radiance.
Furthermore, there is neither victory nor defeat. Because there is no victory, there is no mark of a Buddha; because there is no defeat, there is no mark of a sentient being. [The interlocutor] asks:
"If the mind is already without marks, how can it be entirely devoid of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics used to transform and deliver sentient beings?
The Master says: "The thirty-two marks belong to the realm of 'marks. All marks whatsoever are empty and false. The eighty minor characteristics belong to..."
“Form. If one sees me by means of form, that person follows a perverted path and cannot see the Tathāgata.
Question: “Why did the Bodhisattva Anantagātra not see the crown-mark (uṣṇīṣa) of the Tathāgata? The Master said: “In reality, there is nothing to be seen. Why?
Because the Bodhisattva Anantagātra is himself the Tathāgata; he should not see him further. I am merely teaching you not to become a Buddha.”

One sees, yet does not fall into the side of the Buddha; one does not form the view of a sentient being, yet does not fall into the side of sentient beings. One does not form the view of existence, yet does not fall into the side of existence;

one does not form the view of non-existence, yet does not fall into the side of non-existence. One does not form the view of the ordinary person, yet does not fall into the side of the ordinary person;

one does not form the view of the sage, yet does not fall into the side of the sage. Merely to be free from all views is itself the boundless body (*anantakāya*). If there were any locus for views, [it would not be the boundless body].
They are called non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Non-Buddhists delight in various views, whereas the Bodhisattva remains unmoved by all views.
"Tathāgata" has the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. Therefore it is said: "Maitreya is also suchness; the multitude of sages and worthies is also suchness.
Suchness is non-arising; suchness is non-ceasing; suchness is without seeing; suchness is without hearing. The Tathāgata’s crown...
This is precisely perfect vision (*pariniṣpanna-darśana*), yet there is also no perfect vision; therefore, one does not fall into the extreme of perfection.

Thus, the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not fall into any numerical categories. For this reason, it is provisionally compared to empty space: it is as perfectly vast as the great void, neither deficient nor redundant, and is naturally free from affairs.

Do not forcibly discriminate external objects; once you engage in discrimination, it becomes consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore it is said: "Perfect realization is identical to the ocean of consciousness," flowing [onward].
Whirling like a tumbleweed, the practitioner of the Way should not doubt that the four great elements constitute the body; yet the four great elements are without self, and the self has no master.
Thus one knows that this body is without self and without master. The five aggregates constitute the mind; yet the five aggregates are without self and without master.
Thus one knows that this mind is without self and without master. It arises from the conjunction of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses.
Cessation is likewise so. Since the eighteen realms are empty, all things are empty; there is only the fundamental mind, vast and pure.

One who studies Prajñā does not perceive a single dharma that can be attained. They sever their intent toward the three vehicles, for there is only the one true reality, which cannot be realized or attained.
To claim, "I am able to realize it" or "I am able to attain it," is the mark of one with overweening pride (*adhimāna*). This is from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Those who brushed their robes and departed were all of this same class. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Regarding Bodhi, I have truly attained nothing; it is merely a matter of silent resonance.

When ordinary people are about to die, they should simply contemplate that the five aggregates are empty, the four elements are without self, and the true mind is not permanent—neither going nor coming.
At the time of birth, the nature does not come; at the time of death, the nature likewise does not go.

Depart! Abide in profound stillness and perfect quiescence; let mind and objects be as one. If you can simply do this, you will attain immediate and thorough realization right here and now, no longer bound by the three periods of time;
such a person is one who has transcended the world. You must not harbor even the slightest inclination or pursuit.
If you see auspicious signs, such as the Buddhas coming to welcome you or various manifestations appearing before you, do not have the mind to follow them away. If you see inauspicious signs...
Though various things manifest before one, there is no fear in the mind; simply by forgetting the mind and becoming one with the *dharmadhātu*, one attains mastery.
This is the essential point. It is simply to realize directly and suddenly that one’s own mind is fundamentally the Buddha:
there is not a single dharma to be attained, nor a single practice to be cultivated. This is the Unsurpassed Way. Question: The scriptures say, "To dissolve..."
"How could it be that after billions of kalpas of inverted thoughts, one does not pass through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* to attain the Dharma-body? The Master said:
"If one were to attain something through cultivation over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one would not attain it even in as many kalpas as there are sands in the Ganges.
If, however, one attains the Dharma-body within a single *kṣaṇa*, directly perceiving one's nature, this is still the ultimate discourse of the Three Vehicles' teachings."
Why is this? Because it views the Dharmakāya as something that can be attained. All such [teachings] are subsumed within the category of the provisional (neyārtha) teachings.

As for my Zen school, which has been transmitted from master to master since antiquity, we have never taught people to seek knowledge or seek understanding; we simply speak of "studying the Way" (*xué dào*).

This term "studying the Way" is already a phrase used for guidance and introduction. Yet, even the Way cannot be studied. If one harbors the intention of seeking through study and understanding, one instead creates...
One is deluded regarding the Way. The Way has no location; it is called the Mahāyāna mind. This mind is not within, nor without, nor in between; in reality, it has no location.
First, one must not form conceptual understandings or interpretations. It simply refers to the sphere of your current mental calculations.
If these mental calculations are exhausted, the mind has no location. This Way is celestial and natural; fundamentally, it has no name. Question: From the beginning until now, all [teachings] have...
[The student] said, "It is said that 'the mind itself is the Buddha. I do not yet understand which mind is the Buddha. The Master said, "How many minds do you have?
[The student] said, "Is it that the ordinary mind is the Buddha, or is it that the holy mind is the Buddha? The Master said, "Where do you have such things as an ordinary mind or a holy mind?
[The student] said, "In the teachings of the Three Vehicles, it is currently stated that there are ordinary and holy beings. Why does the Master say they do not exist? The Master said—
He said: "Within the Three Vehicles, I have clearly told you that the minds of ordinary beings and sages are illusory. Yet you do not understand this now;

instead, you cling to them as being existent and take the empty as real—is this not itself delusion? Because of delusion, the mind is confused. You need only eliminate ordinary sentiments and sagely states;
outside of the mind, there is no other Buddha. The Patriarch came from the West to point directly that the whole body of every person is [Buddha]."
"Buddha! You do not recognize this now; you cling to the ordinary and cling to the holy, racing outward and thus deluding your own mind. This is why I told you that the mind itself is Buddha.

If a single thought of emotion arises, one immediately falls into the various realms of existence. From time immemorial until this very day, there has been no difference, nor is there any separate dharma;
therefore, it is called the realization of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. He asked, "What is the meaning of 'immediately' (*ji*) as spoken by the Master?"
"What is the principle here? The Master said, "What principle are you looking for? As soon as there is a principle, the mind immediately becomes dualistic.

The student asked, "Your previous statement was that from time immemorial there has been no difference from today. How is this so? The Master said, "It is precisely because you are seeking it that you yourself create the distinction.
If you did not seek it, where would there be any difference? The student asked, "Since there is no difference, why bother to speak of it at all?"
The Master said: "If you do not recognize the ordinary and the sage, who is it that tells you 'it is'?
Whether it is 'it is' or 'it is not,' the mind is likewise not the mind. When both the center and the periphery are forgotten, where else would you seek to go?
Question: Delusion can obstruct the self-mind; I wonder, by what means may delusion now be dispelled? The Master said: "Arising of delusion and the dispelling of delusion—this too..."
"It is delusion. Delusion has no root; it exists only because of discrimination. You need only exhaust all attachments regarding both the ordinary and the sagely, and delusion will naturally vanish.
What more would you propose to do to dispel it? There must not be even a hair’s breadth of reliance or clinging.
This is called 'I shall surely attain Buddhahood even if I must give up both arms. Since there is no reliance or clinging, how can there be any transmission? The Master said:
"To transmit mind by means of mind. [The student] asked: "If it is the characteristics of the mind that are transmitted, why do you say that the mind itself is also non-existent?
The Master said: "To not grasp a single dharma is called 'transmitting the mind. If one realizes this mind, it is precisely no-mind and no-dharma. [The student] asked:

"If there is no mind and no dharma, how can it be called 'transmission'? The Master said: "When you heard it was called 'transmitting the mind,' you thought there was something to be obtained. Therefore—"

The Patriarch said: "When one recognizes the nature of mind, it may be called inconceivable. It is clearly understood as having nothing to be attained; when there is attainment, one does not speak of knowing.
If this matter were taught for you to understand, how could you possibly endure it? Question: "Does the Buddha deliver sentient beings? The Master said:
"In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers. Since even 'I' cannot be found, how can 'non-self' be found? Buddha."
Sentient beings and all things are ungraspable. [The questioner] asked: "If there are currently the thirty-two marks and the saving of sentient beings, how can you say they do not exist?
The Master said: "All that has form is entirely illusory. If one sees that all forms are no-form, then one sees the Tathāgata.
[The questioner] asked: "The Master is currently preaching the Dharma; how can you say there is neither Sangha nor Dharma? The Master said:
If you perceive any dharma that can be spoken of, you are seeking me through sound. If you perceive a self, that is a locus.
There is neither dharma nor non-dharma; dharma is itself the mind. Therefore, the Patriarch said: "When transmitting this dharma of mind..."
Among all phenomena, when have phenomena ever been real phenomena? When there is no phenomenon and no fundamental mind, one first understands that every mind is a phenomenon;

in reality, not a single phenomenon can be attained. This is called sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). As for the site of enlightenment, it is simply not giving rise to various views and awakening to the fact that phenomena are fundamentally empty.
This is called the "empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Originally there was not a single thing; where could there be any dust? If you grasp the meaning within this, you will roam freely.
[The student] asks: "What is being discussed in the *Yao*? How do the Buddhas practice great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings? The Master says:

"As for the Buddha’s compassion, it is called 'great compassion' because it is without conditions (*anālambana*). Regarding 'compassion' (*maitrī*), one does not perceive the existence of a Buddha to be attained."
The compassionate one does not perceive any sentient beings to be delivered. The Dharma they preach is without preaching and without demonstration;
those who hear the Dharma have neither hearing nor attainment. It is like a phantom person preaching the Dharma for phantom people. How can this Dharma be taken as the Way?
From the words of my spiritual friend, I have received, understood, and awakened to this compassion.
If you give rise to thoughts or stir your mind to learn his intellectual views, you will not awaken to your own mind; in the end, it will be of no benefit. Question:
What is it to transcend the three realms? The Master said: Do not deliberate upon good or evil; right where you are, you transcend the three realms. It is like this:
He has come into the world to destroy the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātu*). If there were no mind at all, the three realms would likewise not exist.
It is like a single mote of dust broken into one hundred parts: ninety-nine parts are non-existent and one part is existent; the Mahāyāna cannot then transcend them.
Only when all one hundred parts are non-existent can the Mahāyāna truly transcend them. The Patriarch directly pointed this out to all.

The fundamental mind and essential body of sentient beings are, from the very beginning, the Buddha. They are not produced through cultivation; they do not belong to gradual stages; they are neither light nor darkness.
Because they are not light, there is no ignorance (*avidyā*); because they are not darkness, there is no darkness. Therefore, there is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance.
Upon entering this gate of my school, you must pay close attention. To perceive it in this way is called [the True Dharma Eye].
The Dharma. Because one sees the Dharma, one is called a Buddha. When both the Buddha and the Dharma are absent, this is called the Sangha;

it is termed the "unconditioned Sangha" and is also known as the "Three Jewels in One Essence. Now, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek by clinging to the Buddha, does not seek by clinging to the Dharma, and does not seek by clinging to the assembly.
One should be without anything sought. Because there is no clinging to seeking the Buddha, there is no Buddha. Because there is no clinging to seeking the Dharma, there is no [Dharma].

Dharma. Because there is no grasping at the multitude of seekers, there is no Sangha. Question: What is the Way? How does one practice? The Master said: What is this "Way"? You wish to practice. Question:
How do the masters of various regions transmit the lineage, practicing Chan and studying the Way?
The Master said: These are words for guiding those of dull faculties; they should not be relied upon as ultimate. [The student] said: This is precisely what guides those of dull faculties.
[The student] spoke of people of superior capacity (*agradhika*). He did not yet understand how one would engage with such a person, nor what further teaching would be given.

The Master said: "If one is a person of superior capacity, where else would one go to seek it? Even one's own self cannot be found; how much less could there be any other dharma to be grasped by the mind? [The student] asked:
"Does the teaching not say, 'What is the nature of each and every dharma'? The Master replied: "If it were so, then there would be nothing at all to seek."
The Master said, "If it were so, it would save you mental effort. [The student] said, "If that were the case, it would be a total severance;
it cannot be non-existence. The Master said, "Who taught him to be non-existent? Who is he? You intend to seek him.
[The student] said, "Since you do not permit seeking, why do you again say, 'Do not sever him'? The Master said, "If you simply cease seeking, who then would teach [you otherwise]?"
“You have cut it off. You see the empty space before you; how do you cut it? He said, “Is this dharma obtainable, and is it therefore the same as empty space?

The Master said, “Empty space has never told you whether there is sameness or difference. I was merely speaking in that way for the moment, yet you immediately gave rise to a conceptual understanding here.
He said, “Does this mean one should not give rise to conceptual understanding regarding people? The Master said, “I...”

"It has never obstructed you. However, it must be understood that this belongs to the realm of emotion (*qing*). When emotion arises, wisdom is separated. [The Master] asked, "In this matter, do not give rise to emotion, is that so?
The Master said, "If you do not give rise to emotion, who would say 'it is'? [Someone] asked, "The Sixth Patriarch was unlearned in the scriptures;
how did he obtain the transmission of the robe and become the Patriarch? Yet, the Venerable Xiu was the head seat among five hundred monks and served as a teacher."
The Master had lectured on thirty-two sutras and treatises; why did he not transmit the robe?

The Master said, "Because they possess a mind—that is, they rely on conditioned dharmas—and take what they have cultivated and realized to be the ultimate truth. This is why the Fifth Patriarch transmitted it to the Sixth Patriarch.
At that time, the Sixth Patriarch merely attained a silent resonance, receiving the profound, secret intent of the Tathāgata; therefore, the Dharma was entrusted to him.

He said, "You have not yet seen the Way. 'The Dharma is originally without Dharma; where there is no Dharma, that too is Dharma. Now, at the moment of bestowing this non-Dharma, how has any dharma ever been a dharma?
If you understand this meaning, only then can you be called a child of the renunciant life, and only then will your practice be authentic.
If you do not believe this, why did the Venerable Ming run all the way to the summit of Mount Dayu to seek out the Sixth Patriarch? The Sixth Patriarch then asked him:"
"What do you seek in coming here? Do you seek robes, or do you seek the Dharma? The Venerable Ming replied, "I have not come for the sake of robes;
I have come only for the sake of the Dharma. The Sixth Patriarch said, "For a moment, collect your thoughts and do not deliberate upon anything good or evil. Ming then followed these instructions.
The Sixth Patriarch said, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—at this very moment—return to me, Venerable Ming."
"Before my parents were born, this face already came forth. Upon these words, he suddenly attained silent realization.

He then prostrated and said, "It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know for themselves. For thirty years, I have labored in vain within the assembly of the Fifth Patriarch.
Only today do I realize my former errors. The Sixth Patriarch said, "So it is. At that moment, one truly knows the Patriarch.
The Master came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha; it does not rely on words and phrases.
Have you not seen how Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Besides the transmission of the golden robe, what else did the World-Honored One transmit?
Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the bannerpole in front of the gate! This is precisely the hallmark of the Patriarchs.

The six perfections and the myriad practices—all these are merely gates of transformation for the purpose of engaging with sentient beings and delivering them; they are peripheral matters.

Even such states as Bodhi, True Suchness, the Ultimate Reality, Liberation, and the Dharma-body, extending all the way to the holy stages of the ten bhūmis and the four fruits, are entirely gates of deliverance;
they do not pertain to the Buddha-mind. The mind itself is the Buddha. Therefore, within all the various gates of the perfections, it is the Buddha-mind [that is fundamental].
First: If one is simply without a mind of birth-and-death, afflictions, and the like, then one does not employ dharmas such as bodhi.

Gone. The mind itself has ceased and is non-existent; how can it be further pursued? Question: How does one avoid falling into stages? The Master said:

Only when delusions have ceased can one be called a person of mastery. Furthermore, from moment to moment and thought to thought, do not perceive any signs;
do not recognize the three periods of past, present, and future. The past has no departure, the present has no abiding, and the future has no arrival.

when dispersed in various locations, each drop is perfectly round; yet when not dispersed, it remains but a single mass.
This one is all, and all is this one. The various forms and appearances are like houses: one leaves the house of a donkey and enters the house of a human.

When the teacher arrived at Yunju, Yunju said, "Old man, you are so advanced in years; why do you not seek a place to stay?"
The Master asked, "What is my dwelling place? Jiuyun said, "In front of the mountain there is the site of an old temple.

The Master said, "Where is my dwelling place? Zhunyu said, "Being so old and venerable, this is your dwelling place."
He did not know either. The Master said, "For thirty years I have been riding a horse, but today I have been knocked off by a donkey.

From past to present, there has been no decline; yet among the assembly, divergent interpretations abound and deliberations are manifold, burying the very essence of the school."

The essential point is this: there are erroneous judgments regarding names and phrases. Some say that every verdant bamboo shoot is *tathatā* (suchness), and every lush yellow flower is nothing other than *prajñā* (wisdom).
Others claim that mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees—every single thing—is the manifestation of the true mind;

why then should one focus solely on the cypress tree in front of the courtyard? Even a speck of dust, a hair, a tile, or a pebble is all part of the manifold layers of the single *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm).

It is inexhaustible; principle and phenomena are perfectly interfused. Some say that regarding the "cypress tree in the courtyard," one must directly realize it the very moment it is raised, seeing the whole body as the absolute truth. Zhaozhou speaks directly for others, speaking with utter sincerity: when hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps.

"The old monk is not within the realm of clarity. Do you still cherish and protect anything?

Question: "The Ultimate Way is without difficulty; it only dislikes discrimination. What is non-discrimination? The Master said:

The entire verse by Wuan says: "A single pulse penetrates directly through the gate; the traveler sighs in vain at the hardships of the road.
This is not for boasting of cleverness before others—it is the golden hammer that shatters ten thousand layers of barriers.
