A monk presented a portrait of the Master for inspection. The Master said, "Tell me, does it resemble me or not? If it resembles me, I shall beat you to death;
if it does not resemble me, I shall burn the portrait. The monk was speechless.
Xuánjué said, "Keep it as an offering.
The Master lifted up his bowl and said, "Thirty years from now, if you see this old monk, keep it as an offering;
if you do not see me, then smash it to pieces. Another monk said, "After thirty years, I dare say I shall see the Master. Thereupon, the Master smashed it.
The Master asked a monk, "Have you ever read the *Lotus Sūtra*? The monk replied, "I have.

The Master said, "'Wearing the patched robe in seclusion, falsely calling oneself an *āraṇyaka*, deceiving the people of the world'—how do you understand this? As the monk was about to prostrate himself, the Master said, "Did you come here wearing your patched robe?
The monk replied, "I came wearing it. The Master said, "Do not deceive me. The monk asked, "How can one avoid being deceived? The Master [remained silent].
He said: "Do not take my word for it.
Xuedou raised this case, saying: "Big as Zhaozhou may be, he is a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail. If you can discern this, you will see through Zhaozhou;
if you do not understand, each of you will simply wrap yourselves tightly in your patched robes—do not be deluded by Cui Feng.
"Good. Question:
Does a newborn infant possess the six consciousnesses? The Master said: "It is like hitting a ball on a steep current. The monk then asked Touzi:
"What is the meaning of 'hitting a ball on a steep current'? Touzi said: "Thought after thought, it never stops."
While Huineng was sweeping the ground, a monk asked, "The Master is a great *kalyāṇamitra*; why are you sweeping the ground? The Master said, "Dust comes from without.
The monk said, "Since this is a pure monastery (*ārāma*), why is there dust? The Master said, "There is not even a single speck.
A monk asked, "Do you receive those who come in such a manner? The Master said, "I do. The monk said, "What about those who do not come in such a manner? The Master said, "I do."

"Does the Master still receive [disciples]? He replied, "I do. The Master said, "Those who come in such a manner are received by the Master. But for those who do not come in such a manner, how would you receive them?
The Master said, "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak. My Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. There was a certain old woman.

A man was sent to offer money to request that the Tripitaka be recited. Once the Master had accepted the offering, he descended from his meditation seat, circumambulated it once, and said, "Tell the patron that the recitation of the Tripitaka is finished.
When the man returned and reported this to the patron, the patron said, "I have been requesting the recitation of the entire Tripitaka; why have you only recited half?"
Jingshan Daowu said: "Among the assembly, people deliberate, asking, 'What is that half-treasury?
Some say, 'Walk around once more. Some snap their fingers. Some cough once. Some give a shout. Some clap their hands.
Such understandings as these are simply a lack of shame. If it were that half-treasury, do not even mention Zhaozhou."
He circumambulated once more. Even if he were to circumambulate a hundred thousand million times, at the old woman’s station he would receive only half a *piṭaka*.
Even if he were to circumambulate Mount Sumeru a hundred thousand million times, at the old woman’s station he would likewise receive only half a *piṭaka*.
Even if all the old *śramaṇas* in the world were to circumambulate together in this manner a hundred thousand million times—
[One] circuit. Even if one were to take only the portion belonging to the old woman, it would amount to but half of the Tripiṭaka.

Suppose the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the universe—whether grasses or trees—were each to possess the mark of the broad and long tongue, and with different mouths yet one voice, were to recite [the Dharma] from this day until the end of the future;
even then, regarding the portion belonging to the old woman, it would still only amount to half of the Tripiṭaka. You all must...
"Do you recognize the old woman? After a long silence, he said: "The embroidered mandarin ducks are displayed for you to behold; the golden needle is not passed on to others. He asked:
"I have heard that you, Master, personally saw Nanquan—is this true? The Master replied: "In Zhenzhou, they grow large radishes."
Yuanwu Keqin said: "Some say, 'It has long been known throughout the world that Zhenzhou produces large radishes.
It has also long been known throughout the world that Zhaozhou visited Nanquan. Yet this monk asks again;
therefore it is said, 'Zhenzhou produces large radishes,' which is simply irrelevant. Master Cheng of Jiangxi judged this as a "dispersed saint. He said:
To ask about the east and answer about the west is called "not answering the question. It is not to enter his circle. If you understand it in such a way, how can you succeed?
Master Yuanlù said, "This is a peripheral remark; it is included among the Nine Bends (jiǔdài).
If you understand it in such a way, you have not even dreamed of it in your dreams. Furthermore, you bring disgrace upon Zhāozhōu."
The official asked, "When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the monastery master’s eyebrows and beard fall off?
The Master said, "In your honor’s residence, raw things are turned into cooked ones. Who is he? The official said, "My servant.
The Master said, "But he is indeed a skilled hand. Dai Fu Ma asked, "Does the Master still practice cultivation? The Master said, "If this old monk were to practice cultivation..."
"This is a calamity! Since you, Master, do not practice, whom will you teach to practice? The Master said, "Your Excellency is a person who practices.
He asked, "In what sense am I called one who practices? The Master said, "If you were not practicing, how could you have been thrust into the position of a human king?
You are being fed until you are raw and frozen, red and parched, with no end in sight to your release. "Your Excellency! [the Master continued.]
He shed tears and bowed in gratitude. He asked, "By what skillful means can one immediately hear that which has not yet been heard?

The Master said, "Set aside for a moment the question of 'not yet heard. What have you ever heard before? The monk asked, "Without departing from words and phrases, how can one attain solitary liberation?

"Go! The Master held up his whisk and said, "Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha, pass by quickly.

Plucking the willow blossoms, plucking the willow blossoms. Oṃ mānida li hūṃ phaṭ.

If the mind does not differ, then the myriad dharmas are as one. Since they are not obtained from without, why do you still cling to them so?
You are like a sheep, randomly picking up things and putting them into your mouth. When I heard Master Yaoshan say that when someone asks a question, simply tell them:

Son, do not let the sickness of the mind be the most difficult to cure. This nature existed long before the world did;
when the world perishes, this nature does not perish. From the moment you saw this old monk, you have never been anyone else;
you are simply this very host. Why seek this further outward? At this very moment, do not turn your head or change your brain. If you turn...
To change one’s head for one’s brain is to lose it immediately. A monk asked, “I have heard your teacher say that when the world is destroyed, this nature is not destroyed.
What is this nature? The Master said, “The four elements and the five aggregates. The monk said, “These are still subject to destruction. What is this nature?
The Master said, “The four elements and the five aggregates.”
Fayan said: "One is two; they are both ruined and unruined. How do you understand this? Try to judge it! Miaoxi said:
"The Great King in the military camp. Xuedou’s verse says: "The clay Buddha does not cross the water."

The Dharma. Even the True Dharma follows after the heterodox. In other places it is difficult to see but easy to recognize; here, with me, it is easy to see but difficult to recognize. It is also said:

"Who has committed the transgression? Later, he met the author of the *Zuochanzhu* (Seated Meditation Master), who said, "The old monk has not failed him.

He took leave of his preceptor. When his relatives heard that the master was returning, they all wished to come and meet him. The master heard of this and said, "The worldly dust of craving and attachment has no end;

He used to say: "If a seven-year-old child excels me, I immediately question him; if a hundred-year-old old man falls short of me, I immediately instruct him.
When he went to Zhaozhou’s Guanyin Hermitage, the Princes of Yan and Zhao arrived at the hermitage together to see the Master.
The Master sat upright and did not rise. The Prince of Yan asked, "Is the King of Men more venerable, or is the King of Dharma more venerable? The Master replied:
Whether among kings of men, he was the most honored among kings; whether among kings of the Dharma, he was the most honored among kings of the Dharma.

When both types of kings heard of him, they were delighted and submitted with reverence, providing offerings together. The Master’s ambition was to emulate the ancients; in maintaining the monastery, he lived through times of decay.

There were no upper or lower galleries in the Sangha hall, and as he prepared meals on the spot, a corner of his rope bed broke; he tied it up using a cord fastened to a piece of leftover firewood. This happened repeatedly.
Some wished for him to compose new works, but the Master did not permit it. He presided over the monastery for more than forty years without ever sending a single letter to a donor.
On the second day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Qianning era of the Tang dynasty, he passed away peacefully in the right-side reclining posture.
He lived to the age of one hundred and twenty and was posthumously titled Great Master Zhenji (True Limit).

The ten directions of the world are the eyes of the śramaṇa; the entirety of the ten directions of the world is the whole body of the śramaṇa.

The faculty of the eye returning to its source is named Mañjuśrī; the faculty of the ear returning to its source is named Avalokiteśvara;
the mind returning to its source is named Samantabhadra. Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s wisdom of wondrous discernment; Avalokiteśvara is the Buddha’s great compassion without conditions;
Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s wondrous practice of non-action. These three sages are the Buddha’s wondrous function; the Buddha is the true essence of these three sages. This is their function.
Thus, there are the provisional names of as many sands as there are in the Ganges; yet in essence, they are collectively named one Bhagavān.

While working in the garden with Master Shengguang, the Master suddenly pressed down on his hoe and looked back at Guang, saying, "The matter is not non-existent; however, as soon as one conceives a thought..."

A monk asked, "Since ancient times, have the sages of the past reached the true principle? The Master said, "They have. The monk asked, "How do they reach the true principle?
The Master said, "At that time, Huo Guang sold a counterfeit silver city to the Xiongnu; the contract document is still here."
"Who did this? The monks were silent. He addressed the assembly: "All dharmas are vast and open; what fetters them, what binds them?
You yourselves give rise to notions of difficulty and ease within them. The source of the mind is a single unity, extending throughout the ten directions.
Those of the highest capacity understand it naturally. Have you not heard Nanquan say: 'Such dull-wittedness is rare indeed in this world'? It is distinct and clear."
There is nothing that is not so. It is simply that you lack the resolve of a true man, which leads you to experience such exhaustion. Do you wish to understand this easily?

From antiquity to the present day, not a single ordinary person or sage has ever appeared before you, nor has there been a single word—whether good or evil—that has reached your portion. Why is this? Because goodness is formless.
In evil there is no characteristic of evil. Since the self (*ātman*) is already non-existent, what do you grasp as good or evil? What do you establish as ordinary or holy?
Do you believe this? Will you take responsibility for it? Where is there any place to evade it? It is just like trying to flee from one's shadow in broad daylight;
can you really escape it? If it is so now, it was so in the past; the present and the ancient are simultaneous. Do you [understand this]?
How can you fail to grasp this? The Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle; those who have realized it naturally spur one another toward progress.
Do not let trivial conditions obstruct the Great Matter. Have you not heard it said: "It is better to establish the Dharma for a lifetime than for anyone to forget their conditions all at once.
You who wish to understand Chan, each of you return to your robes and bowls and look within! [He] addressed the assembly: "Truly, how pitiable they are! How bitter!"
Facing death before others, what is there to be sought in these trifles of sound, form, lips, and tongue?
Let me ask you this: how do you go about seeking those two characters, "sound" and "form"? Do you understand? I say that sound and form are like bubbles;
is this for me to explain them away for you, or is it for me to seek out sound and form for you? Try to deliberate upon this; do not take it lightly. Zhi-gang, apply yourself with diligence.
If one understands the root source, it is ultimately nothing other than this. It is like a round mirror: when a man approaches, a man appears; when a woman approaches, a woman is revealed.

Even monks and laypeople, blue and yellow, mountains and rivers, and the myriad things—all according to their respective forms and characteristics—reflect within that single mirror, transmitting its radiance.
Yet this mirror does not possess many different natures; it simply has the capacity to reflect objects and make them manifest. O worthy one, have you yet recognized the mirror? If not...
The mirror of consciousness is entirely obstructed by men and women, blue and yellow, mountains and rivers, and the like, which block your radiance. Where is there any room for breath?
If the mirror of consciousness were removed, then even blue and yellow, men and women, the great earth, mountains and rivers, and all things with or without thought—[would all vanish].
Whether four-footed or many-footed, born from a womb, an egg, or moisture, or dwelling in heaven or hell—all find their respective measures and the duration of their kalpas within a single mirror.
Whether form or emptiness, all can be clearly understood therein; it is nothing other than this. Have you not heard the meaning of "all phenomena are like [a dream]"?
Time passes as swiftly as a flying arrow; do not let your days drift in vain. This Great Matter must certainly be resolved.
[The Master] understood and took it up. A monk asked, "What is the Great Perfect Mirror? The Master said, "No object whatsoever can adhere to it.
The monk pressed further, "Why can no object whatsoever adhere to it? The Master said, "You are yourself all objects. Can you, then, adhere to yourself?
O worthy one, you are fundamentally complete and inherently perfect; let there not be even a speck of dharma to obstruct you."

Only then will your eye-sight begin to be restored. If there is even a speck of dust that has not been exhausted, it will not be merely a single lifetime or half an eon that has cheated you of your skin-bag;
rather, within the dharmas of your life-force, faculties, and objects, you have created various monsters—mountain sprites and ghostly specters—who attach themselves to your practice.
To consider a little attainment as sufficient is to toy with a mere fragment of skin; such an attitude toward the Buddha-dharma is, in fact, a poison.
To deride the veneration of stupas and temples and to disparage those who uphold the sutras is like a worm within a lion’s body eating the very flesh of that lion.
O virtuous one, do you not see it? Within the vast emptiness before your eyes, is there even a single hair’s breadth lacking? If you can realize this within it—
A message: it is well to transcend the realms of both the ordinary and the holy, and to realize the wisdom of the mundane and the supramundane.
If one dharma is thus, so too are all dharmas. Do you, O virtuous ones, find joy in this? Addressing the assembly:

from the heavens and the human realm throughout the six paths of saṃsāra, down to the most minute insects and sentient beings, none have ever existed apart from this single portion of true suchness (*tathatā*).
There are some points here that seem contradictory. Do you still believe them? Can you truly accept them?

Generally speaking, when traveling as a pilgrim, one must possess the great root of faith and act as a true man before success can be achieved. Where else could one find such difficult-to-believe teachings?
Those ancients, upon hearing it said "this very mind is Buddha" or "this very mind is Dharma," immediately accepted it with conviction and lived in thatched huts wherever they were.
"In this stone chamber, we nurture the holy embryo, merely awaiting the maturation of the fruit of the Way. Why do you not now emulate them and practice?

You, O benevolent one, are most discerning; there is no admixture here at all. Cultivating one's livelihood and engaging in productive industry are not in contradiction with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
At the foot of Mount Zihu, there was a potter’s family who had no son. The husband and wife burned incense and offered prayers day and night. The Master [Huangbo]...
One day, after [the child] had passed away, [Dongshan] asked him, "What did you pray for? Tao told him the reason. The Master said, "You give me bamboo;
I shall give you a son. Tao then gave him bamboo. That evening, he experienced a miraculous dream and subsequently gave birth to a son.
Consequently, the people called the Master the Chan Master of Divine Power. During the Guangming era, he passed away peacefully without illness and was interred in a stupa at his home mountain.

▲ When Master Yunji Shizu of Zhongnan Mountain first visited Nanquan for an interview, he asked: "The *maṇi* jewel no one recognizes;

▲ At Xiaoyi Temple in Jizhou, Practitioner Ding was attending upon Chan Master Xingkong. The Master struck him with a staff and said, "I have blinded your original eyes.

"Setting aside for a moment following or not following, I ask the Master to point out east, west, south, and north. The Master then struck him.

"How do you act for the sake of sentient beings? Yun said, "I see only clouds rising over the azure peaks;

The Master gave a shout. Yun opened both hands. The Master said, "What limit is there to those who falsely accuse others? Yun covered his ears and departed. The Master said, "He is dead!"
This fellow was a man of his life’s calling.
When Chan Master Sanping Yizhong of Zhangzhou first visited Shigong, Shigong would constantly draw his bow and set his arrow to receive visitors.

"How about the 'arrow that brings people back to life'? Gong snapped his bowstring three times. The Master then prostrated himself.
Gong said, "For thirty years I have drawn my bow and set my arrow, yet I have only managed to shoot half a saint. He then broke his bow and arrow.
Later, he visited Dadian and recounted this story. Dadian said, "Since it is an arrow that brings people back to life, why did you identify it by the bowstring?"
The Master had no reply. Dadian said, "Thirty years from now, it will be difficult to find anyone capable of raising this story.
The Master asked Dadian, "Without pointing east or marking west, please give me a direct indication. Dadian said, "A stone man crouches at the mouth of the Yangtze River in Youzhou."
The Master said, "That was still like pointing east and drawing west. Huangbo said, "If one is a phoenix chick, one does not seek it elsewhere.
The Master bowed; Huangbo said, "Had you not possessed the latter phrase, the former talk would have been difficult to bring to completion."
▲ Master Benchong of Majiashan ascended the hall and said: "In these very activities and movements, do you accord with your original patriarch?

[The Master] went to give a discourse on tea. The Master said, "Do you even recognize your own mouth? He asked, "What is the mouth?

The monk prostrated. The Master said, "He often says that 'one nature is all natures'. Before the monk could speak further, the Master said, "You have brought shame upon the vision gained from your lifelong travels.

The Master said, "If I were to point it out to you, I would immediately lose the source. [The student] asked, "How is it so? The Master presented this verse:

"The mind is the substance of nature; nature is the function of the mind. Mind and nature are one and the same—who distinguishes them, who shares in them? To seek outside of delusion is to lose the source."
This alone is difficult to penetrate. From antiquity to the present, ordinary beings and sages alike are like illusions and dreams.
Fojian said: "Questions are not in vain; answers are not established for nothing. As soon as one follows the turn of words, ten thousand mountains confront one face-to-face."
Although there is both inclusion and exclusion within the subsequent verse, alas, it errs in its terminology. This old monk shall once again pass judgment upon it, and thus there is this verse:
"The mind is fundamentally not mind; nature is fundamentally not nature. When both mind and nature are extinguished, who is deficient and who is in excess?

To be decrepit and fundamentally empty is like applying moxibustion to seek out a disease. To delude oneself regarding the source by wandering outside of reality is to betray both the ordinary and the sage."
▲ Master Bensheng held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying: "If I hold it up, you immediately begin to construct intellectual interpretations regarding the time before it was held up.

Whenever he saw a monk, he would raise his staff and say, "All Buddhas of the three periods of time arise entirely from this. Few who confronted him attained a profound resonance with his meaning. Changsha heard of this.

The Master said, "The Way is like an outstretched hand; Buddha is like a clenched fist. Yangshan asked, "Ultimately, how is it?"
"This is indeed trustworthy and reliable. The Master struck the air three times with his hand and said, "There is no such thing; there is no such thing.

[The student] asked, "Is it still necessary to study the scriptures? The Master replied, "The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon are matters external to one's own nature.
If you set them up as an opposition, then mind and objects become two separate dharmas, and the subject and object function in tandem, giving rise to all manner of views and interpretations."
This is also merely wild wisdom; it is not yet sufficient to constitute the Way. If one does not set oneself in opposition to others, there is not even a single thing.
Therefore, the Patriarch said: "Originally there is not a single thing. Do you not see when an infant emerges from the womb?
Can one say at that time, "I understand the teachings," or "I do not understand the teachings"? At such a moment, one is unaware of whether there is the meaning of Buddha-nature or not.
When he grew up, he studied various forms of knowledge and understanding; upon emerging from his studies, he would say, "I am capable" and "I understand.
He did not realize that these were all merely adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*). Among the sixteen modes of conduct, the conduct of an infant is supreme.

The state of being "laughing and frolicking" serves as a metaphor for a practitioner of the Way who has abandoned the mind of conceptual discrimination and grasping or rejecting; therefore, the infant is praised as a fitting analogy.
Take it up. If one were to say that the infant is the Way, people today would misunderstand. One night, the Master was gazing at the moon with Yangshan.
Yangshan asked, "When this moon is crescent, where does the full phase go? When it is full, where does the crescent phase go?
The Master said, "When it is crescent, the full phase is hidden; when it is full, the crescent phase remains."
Yunyan said, "When it is pointed, the circular form is present; when it is circular, the pointed form is absent. Daowu said, "Even when it is pointed, it is not pointed;
even when it is circular, it is not circular."
▲ Chan Master Longtan Chongxin of Lizhou was a native of Zhugong. His family sold cakes. From his youth, the Master was exceptionally brilliant and extraordinary.

The Master lived in the lane adjacent to the temple and would regularly offer ten cakes each day to him. Whenever the Heavenly King (Wuheshang) finished eating, he would invariably leave some behind.
One of the cakes said, "I bestow this upon you so that it may provide shade for your descendants. One day, the Master thought to himself, "The cake was carried away by me;

why has it returned to gift itself to me? Is there some other profound meaning here? He went to him and questioned him. Huang replied, "This was brought by you; returning it to you—what fault is there in that?
Upon hearing this, the Master gained considerable insight into the profound principle and consequently entered the monastic life under him. Huang said:
"In the past, you honored merit and goodness; now you have faith in my words. You may be named Chongxin (Venerable Faith). Thereupon, he served diligently at the Master’s side.
One day, the Master asked him, "Since you arrived, I have not received instruction on the essential point of the mind.
Huang replied, "Since you arrived, I have never failed to point out the essential point of your mind. The Master said, "Where did you point it out? Huang replied, "When you brought me tea, I..."
"I will receive it for you. Come, bring the food; I shall accept it for you. When you perform the *vaṃdana* (bowing), I shall lower my head.
Where else would he not point out the essential heart-essence? The Master lowered his head for a long time. The Emperor said, "If you see, see directly;

if you deliberate, you are already mistaken. At these words, the Master attained immediate liberation. He asked again, "How does one maintain this? The Emperor said, "Roam freely according to your nature."
He lived freely according to conditions, simply exhausting the ordinary mind without any separate realization of a sage. Later, the Master went to Longtan in Liyang to reside there.

[The student] said, "I am fortunate to have met the Master. The Teacher said, "These are merely words that go beyond the ordinary.

The Fifth Generation after the Sixth Patriarch: The Venerable Elder Muzhou of Chen, whose name was Daoming. He was a descendant of the Chen clan of Jiangnan. At the time of his birth, a crimson light filled the room and auspicious clouds covered the sky;
these did not disperse for ten days. His eyes possessed the double pupils (*chongtong*), and his face displayed the seven stars. His physical features were [extraordinary].

He was extraordinary, standing out among men. Once, while visiting Kaiyuan Temple, he paid homage to the Buddha and saw a monk; as if returning to what was familiar, he spoke to his parents, expressing his wish to leave the household life.
His parents granted their permission, and he became a monk. Later, he maintained the precepts with rigorous discipline and mastered the Tripitaka.

Traveling to various regions, he attained the essential meaning under Huangbo. Monks from all quarters looked up to him with admiration, and all referred to him as a venerable elder. Afterwards, he resided at Kaiyuan.

"Why do you not come closer? At that moment, a monk stepped forward. The Master said, "The Rector is not here;
take him away yourself and give him twenty blows outside the main gate. The monk asked, "In what way have I erred? The Master replied, "To place shackles upon a collar.

He replied, "In what way am I speaking falsely? The Master said, "A novice does not belong here. When a person in purple robes and a Great Virtue arrives, they must pay their respects."
The Master held up his hat and its band, asking, "What is this called? [The monk] replied, "A 'Heaven-Pointing Hat' (*chao tian mao*).

[Mao] said, "It is a material phenomenon (*rūpadharma*). The Master said, "When you were granted the purple robe before the imperial curtain and lectured on the sutras in the presence of the Emperor, how could you have failed to observe the five precepts?

Jingshan Hongzhi said: "The Monk-Administrator and the novice have truly lectured on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, yet they simply do not know the origin of the sugar cake.

Although the old man of Muzhou was a spiritual teacher of a region, when it comes to 'the triple world is mind-only' and 'all phenomena are consciousness-only,' he ultimately could not comprehend it."
Question: "What is the true meaning of Caoxi? The Master said: "This old monk loves anger and does not love joy. Question: "Why is it so? The Master said:
"When meeting a swordsman on the road, one must present one's sword; if you are not a poet, do not offer your poem. The Master asked the Elder of Wuling:
"Once realized, even the tip of a hair swallows the vast ocean; only then does one know that the great earth is but a single atom."
"Dust. Elder, what do you say? He replied, "I ask who. The Master said, "I am asking you, Elder. He said, "Why do you not acknowledge my words?
The Master said, "If you do not acknowledge my words, I shall not acknowledge yours."
Xuedou took up the case and said, "Falling! Falling! He then added, "This old fellow with his entanglements deserves to have them cut through once and for all.
Taking up his staff, he asked, "Where has he gone?"
Question: "What is it like when a single phrase exhausts all expression? The Master said: "Your meaning has fallen. The student asked:
"Where, Master, is my meaning fallen? The Master said: "Thirty blows—whom would you have them eat? Question: "I am both a lecturer and a traveler, yet I do not understand the intent of the teaching.
What then? The Master said: "Truly, this is a sincere statement; you ought to repent. The student said: "I beg the Master for instruction."
The Master said, "If you had not asked, I, an old monk, would have kept my mouth shut and remained silent. Since you have asked, I cannot remain silent. The monk said, "Please speak, Master.
The Master said, "One's heart bears no grudge against others, and one's face shows no color of shame.
[The Master] asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk said, "I have arrived from over there. The Master said, "I am at fault. The monk said, "But the Master..."
[The monk] said, “I have attained it. The Master said, “You are carrying a yoke and confessing your crime!
He struck him across the back. Yunfeng Yuan said, “Why did Muzhou use such elaborate words? ‘Settle that matter!’—he struck him across the back.”
Question: "When one bows high to Śākyamuni but does not prostrate to Maitreya, what is it like? The Master said: "Yesterday someone asked this;
I chased him out. The questioner said: "Does the Master fear that I am not sincere? The Master said: "My staff is not here.
I will give you thirty blows with the handle of my broom for now. Question: "What is the phrase that is unobstructed wherever one encounters it? The Master said: "I do not..."
[The Master] spoke thus. [The monk] asked, "What do you say, Master? The Master said, "The arrow has already traveled a hundred thousand li beyond the Western Heavens;
it now awaits me within the Great Tang. There was a monk named Zongchan who came to visit and said, "I, Zongchan, inquire of the Master."
The Master said, "Stop. The monk stopped immediately. The Master scolded him, saying, "You do not even know your own name.
He added, "If there is a statement, there must be a judgment. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! The monk had no reply. A newly arrived traveler from another region came to pay his respects.
The Master rebuked him, saying, "Reverend, why have you stolen the monastery's fruit and eaten it? The monk replied, "I have only just arrived. Why does the Master say I have stolen fruit?"
The Master said, "The stolen goods are right here. He asked a monk, "How many new arrivals are there? The monk replied, "Five. The Master said, "Like a collapsing wall or melting ice.

The monk said, "The Master has never even asked such a question before. The Master said, "The thief uses the stolen goods as proof. He then asked a monk who lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

The man then took leave and returned to Mount Lu. He lived there for many years, eventually passing away. His remains were enshrined at the foot of the mountain. It is said that whenever the wind blows through the valley, the sound of a donkey braying can be heard. People call this the "Donkey Peak" (E-yu). This is why the verse says, "Three lifetimes of being a donkey—how can you ever escape? It is a matter of the principle of cause and effect. One must realize that the self-nature is originally pure and free from delusion; it is simply because one fails to recognize it that one wanders in birth and death. If one can suddenly awaken to the fact that the mind is originally Buddha, then one will naturally be liberated from the cycle of rebirth. This is what is meant by "the donkey is rare, but the rider is rarer still. If one can understand this, one will know that the original nature is inherently complete and lacks nothing. It is only due to the false thoughts of the deluded mind that one fails to perceive it. If one can cast aside all delusions and see into one's own nature, then one will attain liberation. This is the essential meaning of the teaching. One must strive to practice diligently and not allow oneself to fall back into the mire of worldly confusion. Only then can one truly transcend the realm of birth and death. This is the ultimate purpose of the Buddhadharma. May all practitioners take heed.

▲ Chan Master Zhixian of Xiangyan in Dengzhou was a native of Qingzhou. He traveled extensively to study under various masters.
During his time at Baizhang, he was naturally intelligent and quick-witted, yet he could not attain realization through Zen practice. Following Baizhang’s passing, he went to study under Guishan.

Guishan asked him, "I have heard that while you were with our late master Baizhang, when asked one thing you would answer with ten, and when asked ten things you would answer with a hundred. This is due to your cleverness."
"O you of keen faculties! You who understand through the intellect and perceive through consciousness—this is the very root of birth and death.

Returning to his quarters, he sought throughout all the texts he had studied over the years to find a single phrase with which to respond, but in the end, he could not find one. He sighed to himself and said, "A painted cake cannot satisfy hunger."
He repeatedly requested that Guishan explain it to him. Guishan said, "If I were to explain it to you, you would later curse me away. What I have spoken is my own;
it ultimately has nothing to do with you. The Master then took the texts he had studied throughout his life and burned them, saying, "In this life, I shall not study the Buddha-dharma.
I will simply be a long-walking monk who prepares gruel and rice, so as to avoid the burden of mental toil."
The Master then wept as he took his leave of Mount Mushi and traveled directly to Nanyang. There, beholding the traces left by National Teacher Huizhong, he settled down to stay.

He did not grasp at the branches. Suddenly, while he was beneath the tree, someone asked him, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

At that time, the Venerable Houtou Zhaoshang stepped forward from the assembly and said, "I do not ask about [the meaning] atop the tree; I ask about it before one has climbed the tree."

bring forth a question! Yuanwu Keqin said: "If you, as soon as you are born, [distinguish between] being on the tree and being under the tree, then you will be met with [this response]."

Sheng said, "The three holes of the round beads are known by everyone; please, Master, complete the previous statement. The Master struck him, and Sheng shook out his sleeves and departed.
The Master said, "Thirty years from now, you will go away beating your breast and weeping bitterly.
Later, when Shuzhu addressed the assembly, he said, "When I was at Dingshan thirty years ago, I was thoroughly deceived by him; it was no small matter."
Xuedou raised this case and said: "Dingshan’s application was indeed effective, yet how perilous it was!
Pishu knew it well enough, but he still lacked the eye for discerning the Dharma. Try to examine this and see."
The Master saw the Head Seat washing his robe and asked, "What are you doing? The Seat held up the robe to show him. The Master said, "What kind of robe is this that you are washing?
The Seat replied, "In Guanzhong, they use iron coins. The Master called for the Rector and said, "Move this man down from the seat and let him stay here."
▲ Master Mihu of Jingzhao Prefecture sent a monk to ask Yangshan, “In these times, is awakening still necessary?
Yangshan replied, “Awakening is not non-existent; however, it falls into the second rank. The Master deeply approved of this.
He then sent another monk to ask Dongshan, “What is that ultimate state? Dongshan said, “You must ask him yourself before you will know.”
The Master also approved of this.
Touzi Qing took up the Master’s question regarding Yangshan and said: "While it is acceptable for Yangshan to speak in such a manner, does he thereby escape falling into his own trap?
If he escapes it, there is yet another person who most decidedly does not approve. If he does not escape it..."
"Not so. This too falls into the second head. Although Mihu agrees with him, does he himself still have a way to emerge?
Everyone, try to examine this! If you can examine it through, both men will dissolve like ice melting away.
If you cannot examine it through, do not act rashly. He then recited a verse: "Borrowing from the peak of the emerald crags..."

He asked a person, "Pointing to the end of the mountain, you have not yet settled yourself. Although you may thus avoid the Chongyang commandment, how can this compare to the numinous sprout that does not violate the spring?
A monk asked, "Since ancient times, have the sages of the highest caliber attained the true principle or not? The Master said, "They have. [The monk] said, "As for that which is truly..."
"How do you understand the correct principle? The Master said, "At that time, when Huo Guang sold a counterfeit silver city to the Xiongnu, who was it that drafted the treaty?
[The student] said, "I have reached a point where I can only remain silent. The Master said, "This is like making someone stand as a guarantor on level ground."

Jingshan Daowu cited this case, saying: "As for the phrase 'Who wrote this contract?', if Jingshan had been that monk at the time, he would have uttered a turning word to stop this old fellow in his tracks.
But tell me, what word would he have uttered? After a long silence, he said: "If it were easy to obtain, one would simply regard it as something trivial."
When Master Yuankang went to visit Shilou, as soon as Shilou saw him, he drew up his legs and sat down.
The Master said, "How complete your majestic deportment is! Shilou asked, "What did you just see? The Master replied, "I have been pointlessly led astray by someone.
Shilou said, "It must be like this before it can be called true seeing. The Master said, "Alas! How many people have been deceived!"
"Come," said the Master. Baolou then rose from his seat. The Master said, "You have seen it, but you have not moved.
Baolou replied, "Even with all my strength, I cannot emerge from samādhi. The Master clapped his hands three times.
Later, a monk recounted this to Nanquan. Nanquan said, "No one in the world can judge the right or wrong of these two fellows.
If you could judge them, you would be a fellow student of theirs."
▲ While Wang Jingchu, the Attendant of Xiangzhou, was presiding over his duties, Master Mi arrived.
The official raised his brush to show him; Mi asked, "Can you also judge the void? The official threw down his brush and entered his residence, never coming out again. Master Mi became suspicious.
The following day, he sent Gushan, the Master of Offerings, to enter and probe his intentions; Mi also followed him there, hiding behind a screen.

While he was hiding in ambush to eavesdrop, the Master of Offerings sat down and immediately asked, "Yesterday, when Master Mi did not speak further after saying, 'I do not know what words there were,' why did you two no longer see each other?
The official said, "A lion bites a man; a Han-dog chases a clod of earth. Upon hearing these words, Master Mi suddenly realized his previous error.
He stepped out and laughed heartily, saying, "I understand! I understand! The official said, "If you understand, then..."
"It is not non-existent. Try to say something. Baizhang said, "Please, Attendant, demonstrate it. The Attendant then held up a single chopstick.
Baizhang said, "This wild fox spirit! The Attendant said, "This fellow has seen through it completely."
Daguai Zhe said, "Although Mishu was thus, he only managed to grasp a single fragment. Changshi said, "This fellow has seen through it;
he is much like one who strikes the watchtower while looking at the watchtower. Daguai said, "It is not so.
Although Changshi is but a layman, beneath his brush lies the power of life and death. Mishu is a virtuous teacher of a region, yet—"
One must not slip out of another’s grasp. At that moment, one should wait for the other to drop the brush and simply say, "I have always had my doubts about this fellow.
This is recorded in the *Recorded Sayings of Yuanwu*: When the Master first met Muzhou, one day Muzhou asked, "Why did you enter the hall so late today?
The Master replied, "I was watching the ball game. Muzhou said, "People hit the ball..."
The Duke was playing polo. The Master said, "Is it people who play polo? The Duke replied, "People get tired. The Master asked, "Does the horse get tired? The Duke replied, "It gets tired.
The Master asked, "Does the pillar get tired? The Duke was bewildered and had no answer. Upon returning to his private residence, he suddenly attained realization in the middle of the night.
The next day, he saw the Master and said, "I have understood the matter from yesterday. The Master [said], "... (The Master remained silent).
[The Master] asked, "Is the pillar exhausted? He replied, "It is exhausted. Thereupon, [Master] Zhou granted him approval. This is also seen in the *Sunggu lianzhu*.

“Where have you been? Zheng rose from his seat, leaned against the bed, and stood there. Gan said, “When you are at leisure, you speak of Chan like a cascading river;
why do you not say something? Zheng said, “What can be made of beating these two pieces of skin? Gan said, “And what can be made of not beating these two pieces of skin?

The Fifth Generation under the Sixth Patriarch.
Chan Master Linji Yixuan of Zhenzhou, a native of the Xing clan from Nanhua in Caizhou. From childhood, he bore the aspiration to transcend the mundane world.
His resolve was such that, upon shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he immediately aspired to the Chan school. Initially, while in Huangbo’s assembly, his practice was singularly pure.
At that time, Muzhou served as the First Seat (the head monk) and asked, "Senior Monk, how long have you been here?
The Master replied, "Three years. Muzhou asked, "Have you ever questioned the Master? The Master said, "I have never questioned him; I do not even know what to ask. Muzhou—
[The Master] said, "Why do you not ask the Abbot, 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? " The Master then went to ask him.
Before his voice had even ceased, Baizhang struck him. The Master came down [from the hall], and the Governor asked, "How did your inquiry go?
The Master said, "Before I had finished asking, the Abbot struck me; I do not understand. The Governor said, "Just go and ask again. The Master [went back].
[The Master] asked again. Baizhang struck him once more. Thus he asked three times and was struck three times.

The Master said to Prefect Zhou, "I have long benefited from your encouragement in inquiring about the Dharma, and I have repeatedly received the Master’s blows. I regret that due to my own karmic hindrances, I failed to grasp the profound meaning.
I shall now take my leave. Prefect Zhou said, "If you are going, you must first bid farewell to the Master before departing. The Master bowed and withdrew; Prefect Zhou went to the Master first.
At Huangbo’s place, it was said: "The monk who has come to inquire is indeed young in years, yet he is most extraordinary.
When he comes to take his leave, you should skillfully receive him; in the future, he will become a great tree that provides shade for all people under heaven.
The next day, the Master took his leave of Huangbo. Huangbo said, "There is no need for him to go elsewhere. Go directly to Daoyi at Tancheng in Gaoyang; he will surely [enlighten you]."

The Master said, "Three times I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I was struck.
I do not know whether I was at fault or not. Dayu said, "Huangbo’s heart is so earnest and compassionate for you."
"You have exhausted yourself to the point of collapse, yet you come here again to ask whether there is fault or no fault.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "So it was; Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not so very much. Yunyu grabbed him and said, "You bed-wetting little devil!
Just now you were asking about fault and no fault, and now you say Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is not so very much. What have you seen?"
"What is the principle here? Speak quickly, speak quickly! The Master struck Daoyu three times in the ribs.
Daoyu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo; it is none of my business. The Master took his leave of Daoyu and returned to Huangbo.
Upon seeing him, Huangbo asked, "This fellow comes and goes; when will he ever have an end? The Master replied, "It is only because your compassionate heart is so earnest. Then [Huangbo]—
Having finished his duties, he stood in attendance. Huangbo asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "Yesterday, I received the Master’s compassionate command to go visit Dayu.
Huangbo said, "What words did Dayu speak? The Master recounted the previous conversation. Huangbo said, "That old fellow Dayu is too talkative;
wait until he comes here and I will give him a thorough beating. The Master said, "Why say 'wait until he comes'? I would do it right now."
Baizhang struck him and followed it with a slap. Huangbo said, "This madman has come here to pull at a tiger's whiskers. The Master then shouted.
Huangbo called to his attendant, saying, "Escort this madman to the meditation hall."
Miaoshan raised this question to Yangshan: "At that time, did Linji obtain the power of Dayu or the power of Huangbo?
Yangshan replied, "He not only rode upon the tiger's head, but he also knew how to grasp the tiger's tail."
One day, while Huangbo was on a work assignment, the Master followed behind him. Huangbo looked back and saw that the Master was empty-handed, so he asked, "Where is the mattock?
The Master said, "Someone has taken it away. Huangbo said, "Come closer; let us deliberate on a matter together. The Master then drew near.
Huangbo held up the mattock and said, "This very thing—how can all the people in the world pick it up?"
He could not lift it up. The Master reached out his hand, seized it, and held it upright, saying, "Why is it now in my hands?
Huangbo said, "Today there is someone else who has been invited for communal labor," and he immediately returned to the temple. While the Master was hoeing the ground, he saw Huangbo approaching.
He stood with his hoe resting on the earth. Huangbo asked, "Is this fellow tired? The Master replied, "The hoe has not even been raised; what is there to be tired about?"
"Ma! Baizhang struck him. The Master caught the staff and gave it a shove, sending Baizhang falling over. Baizhang called out, "Venerable One! Help me up!
When the Venerable One helped him up, he said, "How can you tolerate this madman’s rudeness? As soon as Baizhang rose, he struck the Venerable One.
The Master was hoeing the ground and said, "In other places they burn the dead; here we bury them alive. One day, the Master...
While sitting in front of the Sangha hall, he saw Huangbo approaching and immediately closed his eyes. Huangbo then made a gesture of intimidation and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
The Master followed him to the quarters to pay his respects. The Head Seat was standing in attendance by Huangbo’s side.
Huangbo said, "Although this monk is a junior, he knows that there is such a matter. The Head Seat replied, "The old master’s heels..."

He did not acknowledge the ground [of the teaching], but instead cited a junior monk as evidence. Huangbo slapped him across the mouth himself. The Head Seat said, "If you had known, you would have understood.
While the Master was sleeping in the Sangha Hall, Huangbo entered the hall and saw him; he struck the head of the wooden board once with his staff.
The Master raised his head, saw it was Huangbo, and then went back to sleep. Huangbo struck the head of the board once again. Then...
He went up to the upper hall and saw the Head Seat meditating. He said, "The junior monks in the lower hall are meditating, yet you sit here;
why are you indulging in such deluded thoughts? The Seat replied, "What are you doing, you old fellow? Baizhang then struck the wooden board once more.
He then went out.
Guishan raised the matter and asked Yangshan, "As for Huangbo’s intention, what was it? Yangshan said, "Two colors, one match."
While the Master was planting pine trees, Huangbo said, "What is the purpose of planting so many pines in the deep mountains?
The Master replied, "First, to provide a scenic setting for the mountain gate; second, to serve as a landmark for future generations.
Having spoken, he struck the ground three times with his mattock. Huangbo said, "Even so, you have already received thirty blows from me. The Master struck the ground again.
Three times he let out a sigh, then one more sigh. Huangbo said, "Our school will flourish greatly in the world through you.
Later, Huangbo went into the kitchen and asked the head cook, "What are you doing? The cook replied, "I am sorting the rice for the monks' meal. Huangbo asked, "How much do they eat at one sitting?
The cook replied, "Two shi and five dou. Huangbo said, "Is that not too much? The cook replied, "I am still afraid it might be too little. Huangbo—[left the sentence unfinished].

He struck him. Holding up his head toward the Master, the Master said, "I shall examine this old fellow with you. As soon as Baizhang arrived and stood in attendance, the Master brought up the previous conversation.
The Master said, "The head cook does not understand. Please, Preceptor, provide a turn of phrase on his behalf.
Baizhang said, "Just bring it up. The Master said, "Are you being too much? Baizhang said, "Tomorrow he shall eat another meal. The Master said, "What are you talking about?"
"Come tomorrow. [Baizhang replied,] "I will eat right now. He then gave Baizhang a slap. Baizhang said, "This madman comes here again to pull at the tiger's whiskers.
The Master let out a shout and departed.
Guishan raised this question to Yangshan: "What was the intention behind these two venerable masters? Yangshan asked, "How about you, Master?
Guishan said, "Only by raising a son does one come to know a father’s compassion. Yangshan said, "Not so. Guishan asked, "And what about you, my son?
Yangshan said, "It is very much like inviting a thief to ruin one's house."
Mount Jing had a community of five hundred people, yet few came to seek instruction. Huangbo sent the Master to Mount Jing and said to him, "When you arrive there, what will you do?
The Master replied, "Once I have arrived there, I shall naturally have my own expedient means.

When the Master reached Mount Jing, he girded his waist and ascended the Dharma Hall to see the Abbot of Mount Jing. Just as the Abbot raised his head, the Master let out a shout. The Abbot was about to—
He opened his mouth. The Master shook his sleeves and departed. Shortly thereafter, a monk asked Jingshan, "What were the words and phrases of this monk just now?
[The monk] replied, "He gave the Master a shout. Jingshan said, "This monk comes from Huangbo’s assembly. Do you wish to know? Go ask him yourself.
Of Jingshan’s five hundred followers, more than half dispersed. The Master went up to Huangbo during the summer retreat.
At Poshan, the Master saw Pó reading a scripture. The Master said, "I took you for someone of substance; it turns out you are just an old monk who eats black beans.
After staying for several days, the Master took his leave. Pó said, "You arrived after the summer retreat has ended; why do you not stay for the rest of the summer?
The Master replied, "I came briefly to pay my respects to the Master. Pó then struck him and drove him away. The Master traveled some distance...
Li was suspicious of this matter and returned for the remainder of the summer. Later, he took his leave of Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "Where are you going?
The Master replied, "Not south of the Yellow River; I am going back north of it. Baizhang struck him. The Master grabbed him and gave him a slap.
Baizhang laughed heartily and called to his attendant, "Bring the meditation board and desk of our late master Baizhang here. The Master said, "Attendant, bring fire!"
Huangbo said, "Not so. You simply take it with you; hereafter, you shall cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven.

Longguang remained seated. The Master said, "A great *kalyāṇamitra*—do you have no skillful means? Longguang stared at him with wide eyes and said, "Ha! The Master pointed his finger and said:
"This old fellow has failed today. He went to Master Ping of Sanfeng.
Ping asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Huangbo. Ping asked, "What words or phrases did Huangbo have?
The Master said, "Last night, the Golden Ox met with calamity; even until now, no trace remains. Ping said, "The golden wind blows through the jade flute; who is this?"
Ping said, "I know your music. The Master said, "Directly penetrating ten thousand layers of barriers, not dwelling within the azure heavens.

Ping said, "This question of yours is far too lofty. The Master said, "A dragon gives birth to a golden phoenix; it breaks through the emerald lapis lazuli. Ping said, "Sit for a moment and drink some tea.
He asked again, "Where have you recently come from? The Master said, "Longguang. Ping said, "How has Longguang been of late? The Master—

The woman said, "It happens that Fenglin is not at home. The Master asked, "Where has he gone? The woman then walked away. The Master called out to her;
the woman turned her head back, and the Master simply continued on his way. (An alternative version reads: "The Master said, 'Who says he is not there?'")

The Master said: "They are like a mirror reflecting images, or like a bell sounding its note. Question: How does one enter this gate? The Master said: "If you wish to enter this gate, you must first pass through the barrier of the three worlds. If you can pass through it, then you may enter. Question: What is the barrier of the three worlds? The Master said: "The three worlds are within the mind; the mind is within the three worlds. If you can see the mind within the three worlds, then you will know that the three worlds are originally empty. If you can see the three worlds within the mind, then you will know that the mind is originally still. If you can see the mind and the three worlds as being simultaneously empty and still, then you have entered the gate. Question: What is the gate? The Master said: "It is the gate of the Great Way. Question: What is the Great Way? The Master said: "It is the way of no-way. Question: What is the way of no-way? The Master said: "It is the way that has never been walked. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the sound of an echo in a valley, or like the reflection of the moon in water. Question: How does one attain liberation? The Master said: "Liberation is attained when there is neither subject nor object. When the subject and object are both extinguished, then one attains liberation. Question: What is the meaning of this liberation? The Master said: "It is the liberation of the Great Void. Question: What is the Great Void? The Master said: "It is the void that is not void. Question: What is the void that is not void? The Master said: "It is the void that contains all things. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the sky covering the earth, or like the ocean containing the rivers. Question: How does one practice? The Master said: "Practice is the practice of non-practice. Question: What is the practice of non-practice? The Master said: "It is the practice that has never been practiced. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the light of the sun and moon, or like the fragrance of incense. Question: How does one realize the fruit? The Master said: "Realization is the realization of non-realization. Question: What is the realization of non-realization? The Master said: "It is the realization that has never been realized. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the blossoming of flowers in spring, or like the ripening of fruit in autumn. Question: How does one maintain the Dharma? The Master said: "Maintaining the Dharma is maintaining the Dharma of no-Dharma. Question: What is the Dharma of no-Dharma? The Master said: "It is the Dharma that has never been maintained. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the turning of the wheel of the Dharma, or like the transmission of the lamp of wisdom. Question: How does one protect the Sangha? The Master said: "Protecting the Sangha is protecting the Sangha of no-Sangha. Question: What is the Sangha of no-Sangha? The Master said: "It is the Sangha that has never been protected. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the harmony of the three jewels, or like the unity of the three bodies. Question: How does one serve the Buddha? The Master said: "Serving the Buddha is serving the Buddha of no-Buddha. Question: What is the Buddha of no-Buddha? The Master said: "It is the Buddha that has never been served. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the manifestation of the Buddha's body, or like the preaching of the Buddha's voice. Question: How does one benefit sentient beings? The Master said: "Benefiting sentient beings is benefiting sentient beings of no-sentient-beings. Question: What are sentient beings of no-sentient-beings? The Master said: "They are sentient beings who have realized that they are originally Buddhas. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the rain nourishing the crops, or like the wind moving the clouds. Question: How does one repay the kindness of the Triple Gem? The Master said: "Repaying the kindness of the Triple Gem is repaying the kindness of no-kindness. Question: What is the kindness of no-kindness? The Master said: "It is the kindness that has never been repaid. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the gratitude of a child for its parents, or like the devotion of a disciple for their teacher. Question: How does one uphold the precepts? The Master said: "Upholding the precepts is upholding the precepts of no-precepts. Question: What are the precepts of no-precepts? The Master said: "They are the precepts that have never been broken. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the purity of a clear mirror, or like the stillness of a calm lake. Question: How does one cultivate meditation? The Master said: "Cultivating meditation is cultivating meditation of no-meditation. Question: What is meditation of no-meditation? The Master said: "It is the meditation that has never been cultivated. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the clarity of the sky, or like the depth of the sea. Question: How does one study wisdom? The Master said: "Studying wisdom is studying wisdom of no-wisdom. Question: What is wisdom of no-wisdom? The Master said: "It is the wisdom that has never been studied. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the brilliance of the sun, or like the vastness of space. Question: How does one manifest the power of the Dharma? The Master said: "Manifesting the power of the Dharma is manifesting the power of no-power. Question: What is the power of no-power? The Master said: "It is the power that has never been manifested. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the majesty of a king, or like the strength of a lion. Question: How does one enter the realm of the Buddhas? The Master said: "Entering the realm of the Buddhas is entering the realm of no-realm. Question: What is the realm of no-realm? The Master said: "It is the realm that has never been entered. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the sovereignty of the Dharma-king, or like the freedom of the liberated sage. Question: How does one transcend the world? The Master said: "Transcending the world is transcending the world of no-world. Question: What is the world of no-world? The Master said: "It is the world that has never been transcended. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the transcendence of a lotus from the mud, or like the emergence of a phoenix from the egg. Question: How does one dwell in the ultimate truth? The Master said: "Dwelling in the ultimate truth is dwelling in the truth of no-truth. Question: What is the truth of no-truth? The Master said: "It is the truth that has never been dwelt in. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the stability of Mount Sumeru, or like the constancy of the flowing river. Question: How does one attain the state of non-arising? The Master said: "Attaining the state of non-arising is attaining the state of no-arising. Question: What is the state of no-arising? The Master said: "It is the state that has never arisen. Question: What is the meaning of these words? The Master said: "They are like the unborn nature of all phenomena, or like the unconditioned essence of the Dharma-body. Question: How does one realize the nature of emptiness? Yet guest and host are distinct and clear as a mirror; the Master merely points out the flower in one’s eye. Master Wujin said to me:
"Fenyang was the direct fifth-generation descendant of Linji. He is venerated by scholars throughout the world. Observe his handling of the essential framework..."

He merely discussed the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials. Now, as for his lineage of Dharma, [the character here should be deleted], they all claim that the words regarding the establishment of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials during this single period are of no benefit to the Way.

Rather, simply not giving rise to divergent views toward any phenomena, but remaining entirely ordinary—this is the meaning of the Patriarchs. Is this teaching correct or not? I said: "Layman, you have heard of it..."
"Having explained it thus, you have come to understand it clearly. How could you still doubt the guiding principles of Fenyang?

In the midst of the ocean of feverish affliction, it is the banner of the cool, tranquil, and quiescent Dharma. The raising of this banner is like a drum smeared with lethal poison:
when struck, all who hear it die; however, those who hear it from afar die later. Unless one meets an untimely death, even upon hearing it, one does not perish.
When Linji was still hale and hearty, Xinghua, Sansheng, Baoshou, and the Venerable Ding were present.

Among those who heard [the teachings] and died, there are still those who have awakened to their meaning even after more than a hundred years; these are precisely those who did not die an untimely death.

The "Middle Mystery" (Zhongxuan) is the essence of the Middle Mystery. this is truly lamentable. Xuefeng said: "The continuous flow of true permanence is the Dharma of Equality; it is simply that words are used to dispel [delusion]."
It is said that to use principle to dispel principle is called "being clear about what precedes but not what follows. This is merely the measure of partial realization of the Dharma-body;

To turn the pivot and shift the position, to exercise mastery over life and death, to grant or withhold as appropriate, to pass through birth and enter into death, to extensively benefit all beings, and to be utterly detached from the realms of form, desire, and attachment—this is the second phrase;

Cavernous Yang (Dongyang) pervades the entire realm of saṃsāra. Within this single true essence, the great function manifests before us; its responsive transformations are without fixed direction.

It is entirely functional and yet entirely non-functional; it is entirely arising and yet entirely non-arising. As a skillful means, it is called the "Gate of Compassionate Samādhi. This is the third phrase.
The ancients termed it the "Mystery within the Essence" (*tǐzhōng xuán*). Master Fushan Yuan also said: "It is the mystery within the intent, not [the mystery within] the meaning."
Regarding the meaning of "consciousness": the ancients were not worth mentioning, and Yuan was likewise deluded.
I cannot fail to clarify this. Wujin nodded in agreement. Jianfu Gu addressed the assembly, saying: "Sentient beings have wandered for a long time because they do not understand their own self.

When one studies the Buddha-dharma with a sentimental mind and seeks extensive knowledge and understanding, one is blown by the wind of that intellectual understanding into the sea of birth and death.

If this were true knowledge and understanding, then throughout all past lives, everyone would have studied it extensively, possessing great knowledge and insight, with eloquence surpassing others and a sharpness of wit so swift that their minds would never cease; yet such people remain no different from those who existed before the empty kalpa.
This corresponds [to past karma]. Because of this, one wanders through the evil realms for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, never again obtaining a human body.
Now, having emerged from birth and attained this human form, you remain beneath the *kāṣāya* robe; yet, as before, you extensively seek intellectual understanding and cannot still the mind.
Thus, you cannot avoid the cycle of the six destinies. Why not let the mind rest? Why not proceed in a state of being like one who is dazed or deluded?
He did not speak for five or seven years after departing. Thereafter, even the Buddha could do nothing for you. As the ancient masters said:
"Within a single phrase, the three mysteries must be fully present. Thus we know that this Dharma-gate of the three mysteries is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The Buddhas employ this Dharma-gate to deliver all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, causing them all to attain Buddhahood.

Investigation and Deliberation: Awakening to the Profundity within the Essence. As the ancient said, as Master Sengzhao remarked:

The Sixth Patriarch said: "You all, people of this world, your own minds are the Buddha; do not harbor further doubt. There is not a single dharma outside that can be established;
it is all your own mind. The mind gives rise to the myriad kinds of dharmas. He further said: "In..."
To manifest a jeweled-king land upon the tip of a single hair, and to turn the Great Dharma Wheel while seated within a minute speck of dust—such as this is right view.
To lack even a fraction of this is to fall into wrong view; there will then be superfluous dharmas, and one will fail to realize that all is but mind-only.
The monk asked again: "How are such words and phrases, as well as the timing and causal conditions, the 'Mystery within the Essence'? The Ancient said:

Such responses are what are called "conventional words" (he-tou-yu); they directly clarify the mystery within the essence, which is precisely like pouring foul water upon someone.

Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the mystery within the phrase (*jùzhōng xuán*). If one can clarify this, it is called "the path of penetration and transcendence," the pivotal mechanism of the higher realm, and also termed "one's own fundamental matter.

Zhongxuan said: In ancient times, it was said that when a bhikṣu asked the Buddha what Dharma he would preach today, the Buddha replied, "I will preach the Dharma of certainty.
He asked again, "What Dharma will you preach tomorrow? The Buddha replied, "The Dharma of uncertainty.
The monk asked, "Why is today certain and tomorrow uncertain? The Buddha said, "Today is certain; tomorrow is uncertain. A monk then asked Master Si, "How is this so?"
This is the great purport of the Buddha-dharma. He replied, "What is the price of rice in Luling?
Furthermore, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "I have heard that you, Master, personally met Nanquan; is this true? He replied, "In Zhenzhou they grow large radishes."

The answer is: "Three catties of hemp. If one awakens to and enters into a single phrase among such statements, all are comprehended as a whole.

Thus, within the essence, the profound mystery is realized, and views and understandings are simultaneously purified and exhausted. From this point onward, there is no longer any knowledge or vision of Buddha-dharma;

However, they merely attain a liberation through intellectual understanding and views, yet they still remain within birth and death and have not attained mastery.
Why is this? Because they have not yet awakened to the Way; thus, regarding all words and phrases concerning the realm of others, they call them "non-responsive talk."

In the present age, people take this as the ultimate standard, and it has spread widely throughout the world; thus, the ancestral style has been extinguished because of the persistence of words and phrases.
If one wishes not to involve oneself in words and phrases, one must clarify that which is the "mystery within mysteries.

A monk asked, "What kind of words, phrases, timing, or conditions constitute the mystery within mysteries? Gu said, "It is like when a non-Buddhist asked the Buddha: 'I do not ask about the word "existence," nor...'"

He asked a question without speaking. After the World-Honored One had remained silent for a long while, the outsider said, "The World-Honored One’s great kindness and great compassion have cleared away my clouds of delusion, enabling me to enter.

He replied, "I have no mental energy today; simply go ask Zhizang. The monk [went to ask him].

Only those who have attained awakening know this; if one looks back to the original school of the ancient patriarchs, it is not yet possible.
The monk asked, "The Three Mysteries must be perfectly complete all at once. If they are seen as not yet complete, what fault is there?

Each and every point must accord with the Three Vehicles. Within the responses, one must rely upon the proper timing, incorporate both principle and phenomena, and distinguish between guest and host;
only then can it be called "perfect. Otherwise, it is called "partial and withered. This person does so because they do not forget their knowledge and views.
The Eye of the Way is not yet clear; it is as if there were a speck of gold dust in the eye. You must further awaken to the mystery within the phrase before you may proceed.
If you merely awaken to the mystery within the phrase, you will indeed penetrate the Dharmakāya, yet you will instead become a slave to this very knowledge and vision.
In both cases, there is no actual realization. There remains attachment and aversion toward self and others, for they perceive objects as existing outside the mind;
thus, they have not yet clarified the "mystery within mystery. Many descendants of Yunmen and Linji are like this.

Any practitioner of the Way, even if they attain a certain kind of mysterious gate, must further clarify the "mystery within mystery" before they can avoid remaining stuck on the path of mere liberation.

Only then did he attain stability, his feet firmly planted upon the ground. The monk asked, "Since you say that one studies within the words and phrases, the blows and shouts of the Buddhas and patriarchs, why is it that some are entirely perfect while others are not? Take awakening as the standard. However, those who study are inferior and do not awaken to the Way; they merely acquire knowledge and views.

Such knowledge and views are the product of learning, not awakening. Therefore, they mistake words and phrases for the state of non-action, treating them as "pointing-out" words or "liberating" words.

To speak in terms of "seizing away," to speak in terms of "illuminating function," or to speak in terms of "simultaneity" and "non-simultaneity"—all these are the errors and delusions of false teachers, not the fault of sentient beings.
The original intent of the student is solely to awaken to the Way and see their nature;

however, because the teacher does not penetrate the Way, they merely use intellectual views to instruct them. Thus it is said: "My eyes were originally correct, but because of the teacher, they became distorted. (Seng)

[The questioner] said: "In the Master’s discourse on the Dharma-gate of the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan), since there are three names, there must also be three Dharma-gates, yet the phrasing for each is different.
How then can you say that within a single phrase, the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials (Sanyao) must be fully present? The Ancient [Master] said:
"The Dharma-realm of empty emptiness is fundamentally unconditioned (*asamskrta*). Yet, responding to conditions and manifesting itself, there is nothing it does not do. Therefore..."

The void of space and the world, the myriad phenomena in their array, the four seasons and the yin-yang, the cycles of stagnation and prosperity during the eight nodes, the flourishing and withering of plants and trees, the seven destinies of humans and devas, the sages, worthies, and all Buddhas, the five teachings and three vehicles, the scriptures of external paths, and all that is mundane and supramundane—all emerge from this.
Therefore, it is said: "There is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm; in the end, it returns to it."
Regarding this Dharma-realm, a sutra states: "All Buddhas and all the dharmas of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Buddhas emerge from this very sutra.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Within the tip of a single hair, one manifests jeweled royal lands."
Seated within a mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel. Vimalakīrti said: "Sometimes he acts as the sun or moon deities, or as Brahmā, the Lord of the World;
sometimes he becomes earth or water, and sometimes he becomes fire or wind. Master Li said:
"In the waters of wisdom within the ocean of the Dharma-realm, he manifests as fish and dragons; dwelling in the great mansion of Nirvāṇa, he appears as the Yin and Yang to transform beings."
Regarding "things," Zhenjue said: "The single moon universally appears in all waters; the moons in all waters are subsumed within the single moon.
The Third Patriarch said: "The one is all; all is the one. Therefore it is said that the myriad things are fundamentally non-existent;

they are established by grasping at the Real. The true nature is immeasurable, and its principle cannot be divided. Thus, one should know that the principle of the boundless Dharma-realm is the entire body [of reality].
It is omnipresent within every single dharma and every single atom. The *Avataṃsaka* states: "The nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) pervades all places—every sentient being and every land;
throughout the three periods of time, there is nothing left out, yet it has no form or characteristic that can be apprehended.
Upon reaching this state, every single dharma, every single atom, every color, and every sound is fully endowed with universal pervasion and mutual containment.
There are four meanings: the nature of reality is boundless, and phenomenal appearances are boundless. They interpenetrate yet do not mingle; they blend yet are not one.
How could one doubt that within a single word the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are not fully contained? The monk further asked:
"For what reason did the ancients insist that a single word must contain the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials? What was their intention? The Ancient replied:

all the words and teachings of the Patriarchs of the three periods of time originate from the "Mystery within the Words" (*chü-chung-hsüan*);

Great person, it is easy to understand. For instance, consider meeting the venerable elder Yunmen in person—he possessed a great reputation like Deshan Xuanmi, Dongshan Liangjie, Zhimen Guangzuo, and Baling Zhaode.

Yet, when it comes to the Three Essentials (san-yao), why do you alone fail to provide such a distinction? This is precisely the case.
He criticized those scholars who, mired in intellectual views, were unable to awaken to the Way.

The Middle [Way] does not possess the Three Mysteries and the Three Essentials. Now, when one expounds principles or narrates events, is this not a matter of intellectual views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*)?

Furthermore, since the scriptural vehicles already contain these meanings, why establish the School of the Patriarchs (*zongmen*) anew? Those of old, whose vital energy overwhelmed others, disparaged the scriptural vehicles as mere intellectual views;
yet when their own school failed to penetrate [the truth], they in turn cited intellectual views as proof. This is the first...
This is a mistake. What is meant by the fault of not recognizing the "live word" in Baolin’s three statements? It is said: Baolin truly grasped the essential meaning of Yunmen.
