If one asks about the school of Deva, he answers, "It is the non-Buddhists. If one asks about the "whiskered blade," he answers, "Sharp."
"Jian is. When asked about the similarities and differences between the ancestral teachings [of Chan] and the scriptural teachings, he replied, "They are not the same.
If one regards this as a dead word, one falls into the trap of verbal formulations. Now, observing the three words in his reply: if they are called "words," they lack logical consistency;

if they are called "not words," they all respond to the capacity of the interlocutor—they are living words. For the ancients to condemn them was an error. This is the second fault. What is meant by "dividing into two"?

You sow the seeds yourself; do you not realize the difficulty with which the Sages establish their teachings? It is said that the World-Honored One’s verse states: "The *ālayavijñāna* is subtle; its habitual tendencies are like a torrential stream.
Fearing that one might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it. Does this mean he spoke of the eighth consciousness as being real?
Then there would be the concern that one might be deluded regarding the absence of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Therefore, he spoke of it as being unreal.
Indeed, fearing that they might mistake delusion for annihilation, I have never openly expounded this; how difficult it is to establish such words!
To instruct Ānanda, I pointed toward the principle that delusion is itself truth, saying only: "There are two kinds of erroneous cultivation:
first, taking the攀緣心 (the攀缘心, the mind that clings to objects) as one's own nature; second, [taking] the consciousness-essence (識精), which is perfectly luminous and capable of giving rise to..."

Regarding those matters omitted by various commentators, they nevertheless did not wish to interrupt the flow of the text, fearing that it might give rise to two different interpretations regarding a single teaching;
thus, ancient masters established two distinct traditions of their own, which misled later students—this was the third failure.
The *Línjiàn Lù* states: "The Great Master Linji said: 'In general, when proclaiming the Dharma of our school, one must [do so] within a single phrase.'"
The Three Mysteries (san-xuan) are complete; within each mystery, the Three Essentials (san-yao) are complete. There are both mysteries and essentials.
Nowadays, most monks from various quarters render these words obscure and indistinct; only Chan Master Wude of Fenyang was able to masterfully penetrate their meaning.

He composed a verse to clarify them, saying: "The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; If you grasp the intent and forget the words, the Way is easy to approach. A single phrase clarifies—"
Illumination encompasses the myriad phenomena; on the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh. It is not only the Linji school that delights in discussing the Three Essentials;
the *Cantong qi* (Merging of Difference and Unity) composed by Shitou also fully possesses this principle.

I have once deeply contemplated it and found that it merely substitutes the terms "profound" (*xuan*) and "essential" (*yao*) with "illumination" (*ming*) and "darkness" (*an*). The text consists of only forty-odd lines, yet it expounds upon illumination and darkness.
[The Master] halved it. At the beginning of the chapter, he immediately inscribed: "The spiritual source is bright and pure; the branches and tributaries flow on in obscurity.

He further opened up and elucidated this by saying: "In obscurity, one must accord with the superior and middle [levels]; in clarity, one must distinguish between the clear and the turbid. When in obscurity, one must necessarily differentiate between superior and middle;
when in clarity, one must necessarily clarify the distinction between the pure and the turbid. This is the mystery within the essence. As for pointing this out...
To manifest the intent of this school, it is said: "The beginning and the end must both return to the source; the noble and the humble employ these words.

Thus, below, he extensively enumerates phrases concerning clarity and obscurity, which flow on and connect one after another without ceasing—this is the "Middle Mystery within the Ultimate" (*zhongxuan*).
When his discourse concludes, he further says: "I respectfully inform those who study the Mystery: do not let your time be spent in vain. O practitioners of the Way, day by day..."
To be able to employ [the Dharma] without missing the proper time or occasion is truly to repay the Buddha’s kindness; this is the "Mystery within the Center" (Zhongxuan).

When Zhaozhou was traveling and arrived at the monastery, he was washing his feet in the back shed when the Master asked him:
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou said, "I happen to be washing my feet. The Master stepped forward and made a gesture as if listening.
Zhaozhou said, "If you understand, then understand; why do you keep at this 'pecking'? The Master then returned to his quarters. Zhaozhou said: [The Master]... (implying he did not understand).
"Thirty years of wandering as a pilgrim—today I have mistakenly written annotations for others. The Master asked Xingshan, "What is the white ox on the open ground?
Xingshan said, "Hūṃ, hūṃ. The Master said, "Mute! Xingshan said, "What are you saying, Elder? The Master said, "This beast!
Magu asked, "Of the Great Compassionate One’s thousand hands and eyes, which one is the true eye? The Master grabbed him.
Zhuzhu said, "Regarding the Great Compassionate One with a thousand hands and eyes—what is the true eye? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
Gu pulled the master down from his meditation seat and sat back down himself. The master greeted him, saying, "How do you do? Gu hesitated, and the master immediately shouted.
He then pulled Gu down from the meditation seat again and sat back down. Gu then departed.
Tang further asked, "As for the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara, which one is the front?
The Master descended from his meditation seat, seized him, and said, "Where has the Twelve-Faced Avalokiteśvara gone? Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Tang turned around, intending to sit down.
The Master then struck him. Gu seized the staff, and they grappled with one another back to the abbot’s quarters.
The Master said, "I have not a single dharma to give to people; I merely treat illnesses and untie bonds.
It would be better for you to take my words from my mouth and then rest in non-action. He further said, "A single thought arises in dependence, yet it is unborn; thus one transcends."
Regarding the Provisional Studies of the Three Vehicles, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Those who study the Buddha-dharma today should first seek genuine insight.
If one attains genuine insight, one will be unstained by birth and death and possess freedom in going and staying; there is no need to seek anything further extraordinary."

"Excellence comes of its own accord, O follower of the Way! Just as the virtuous predecessors of old all possessed a path for transcending the ordinary, so too does this mountain monk point the way for others:
I simply want you not to be deluded by others. When you need to act, act; do not hesitate any further."
Why is it that students today do not attain it? The sickness lies in a lack of self-confidence.

If you cannot have sufficient confidence in yourself, you will immediately become frantic, pursuing every external circumstance until you are turned around by those myriad objects and lose your freedom.
If you can bring to rest this mind that incessantly runs after things, you will be no different from the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Do you wish to recognize this?

"Have you attained the patriarchs and Buddhas? "It is simply this person before you who listens to the Dharma. When the student does not believe this, they immediately run outward in search elsewhere.
Even if they were to find something, it would all be mere words, names, and forms; they would never attain the living meaning of the Patriarchs.

If one does not encounter this at such a time, for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one will wander through the three realms, driven away by the pursuit of likes and dislikes, ending up in the bellies of donkeys and oxen.
It arises within. O practitioner of the Way! According to my own perspective, it is no different from that of Śākyamuni.

In our daily manifold activities, what is lacking? The divine light of the six realms has never ceased for a moment. If you can see it thus, you will be a person of no concerns for the rest of your life.
Venerable Sir, there is no peace in the three realms; they are like a burning house. This is not a place for you to remain long.
While you remain here, the demon of impermanence kills in a single kṣaṇa, making no distinction between noble and base, old and young.
You must not be different from the ancestral Buddhas; simply do not seek outside. The light of your one thought-moment of pure mind is the Dharmakāya Buddha within your own house.
The light of your one thought-moment of non-discriminating mind is the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha within your own house. The light of your one thought-moment of non-deviation...
Apart from the light of the mind, this is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha within your own house. These three bodies are the very person listening to the Dharma right before you at this moment.
It is precisely because one does not run outward in pursuit that such efficacy exists. According to the masters of the sūtras and śāstras, however—
To take these three bodies as the ultimate limit is not how I, this mountain monk, see it. These three bodies are merely names and designations;
they are also the three bases. As the ancients said: "The body is established based on meaning, and the land is discussed according to its substance.
Thus, the Dharma-nature body and the Dharma-nature land are clearly known to be but shadows and light. Venerable sir, you should first recognize the person who plays with the shadows. This is all...

The source of the Buddha: every place is the dwelling where the stream of the Way returns. This physical body of yours, composed of the four great elements, does not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma.
Your spleen, stomach, liver, and gallbladder do not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma. Empty space does not understand how to preach or listen to the Dharma.
What, then, understands how to preach and listen to the Dharma? It is this very thing, vividly present before your eyes. This one—
This very form-segment is solitary luminosity. This is what is meant by "expounding the Dharma" and "listening to the Dharma.

If you can see it in this way, you will be no different from the Patriarchs and Buddhas. However, at all times, do not allow for even a moment’s interruption; it is present everywhere before your eyes.

It is only because feelings arise that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptualizations shift that the essence becomes distinct. For this reason, one transmigrates through the three realms and undergoes all manner of suffering. Regarding this, the Mountain Monk says:

There is no place of seeing that is not profoundly deep; there is nothing that is not liberated. O followers of the Way, the dharma of mind has no form, yet it penetrates throughout the ten directions.

When it is in the eyes, it is called seeing; when in the ears, it is called hearing; when in the nose, it smells fragrances; when in the mouth, it engages in discourse; when in the hands, it grasps and holds.
Running and rushing about on foot, it originally was one refined spirit, which divided into six harmonious combinations. Once the single mind is gone, there is liberation everywhere.

Where does the meaning lie in this talk of the mountain monk? It is simply because you practitioners cannot rest your minds of constant seeking and fall into the idle realms and conditions of the ancients.
You practitioners, take up the mountain monk’s view and cut off the realm of retribution.
The head of an emanation Buddha is like one whose mind has reached the fulfillment of the ten stages; the two types of awakening, Equal and Wondrous, are like men bearing shackles and chains;
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas are like filth in a latrine; and Bodhi and Nirvana are like stakes for tethering a donkey. Why is this so?
It is simply because the practitioners of the Way do not realize that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are empty; therefore, such obstacles arise.

If one were a true person of the Way, it would never be like this. One should merely be able to follow conditions to exhaust past karma, wearing clothes as they come by chance, walking when one wishes to walk, and sitting when one wishes to sit, without a single thought of aspiring for the fruit of Buddhahood. Why is this so? An ancient said:
He said: "If you wish to perform practice to seek the Buddha, know that the Buddha is the great omen of birth and death, O Great Virtue. Time is precious;

do not merely intend to dabble idly at home, practicing Zen and the Way, recognizing names and phrases, seeking Buddhas and Patriarchs, or seeking spiritual friends through mere intellectual speculation.
Do not err, O follower of the Way! You have but one father and mother; what more is there to seek?"
Look back at yourself. An ancient said, "Yajñadatta lost his head; when the seeking mind comes to rest, there is nothing more to do.
Venerable sir, you must simply remain ordinary; do not put on a pretense. There are some ignorant, shaven-headed soldiers who cannot distinguish between good and evil.
They immediately claim to see gods and ghosts, pointing east and drawing west, predicting fine weather or rain;
all such as these must eventually pay their debts before King Yama on the day they must swallow hot iron balls.

When the sons and daughters of good families are possessed by such wild fox spirits and demons, they immediately begin to act strangely and behave like blind, wretched creatures; the day will come when they must pay the price for their food.

O practitioners of the Way! You must earnestly seek the genuine insight that allows you to traverse the world with ease, so as to avoid being deluded in body and mind by these various spirits and demons.
Do not engage in further fabrication; simply remain in the ordinary state. As soon as you conceive a thought, you have already erred.
Furthermore, do not seek the Buddha; "Buddha" is merely a name and phrase. Do you recognize the one who is rushing about in pursuit? Three.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs of the ten directions throughout the ages appeared solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma;

the practitioners of the Way today likewise seek the Dharma solely for this purpose. Only upon attaining the Dharma is one finished; if it is not attained, one continues as before to transmigrate through the five paths.
What, then, is the Dharma? The Dharma is the mind-Dharma. This mind-Dharma is formless, yet it penetrates the ten directions and is manifest in use before one’s eyes; yet people do not believe it.
Consequently, they merely recognize names and phrases, seeking the underlying meaning within the words; this is worlds apart from the Buddha-dharma. O practitioners of the Way!
When I, this mountain monk, preach the Dharma, what Dharma do I preach? I preach the Dharma of the Mind-Ground.

This enables one to enter the pure and the defiled, the mundane and the sagely, the real and the conventional. Yet, fundamentally, it is not your own reality of the mundane, the conventional, the ordinary, or the sagely. It can [only]...

All things—whether ultimate or conventional, ordinary or sagely—are given names. Yet, O practitioners of the Way, among all these ultimate and conventional, ordinary and sagely things, not a single name can be established.
Grasp them and use them directly; do not attempt to establish names, for only then will you accord with the profound principle.
My teaching of the Dharma differs from that of everyone else in the world. Suppose Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were to appear before you, each manifesting their own body right here before your eyes.

He asked about the Dharma. As soon as he said, "I take my leave of the Master," [the Master] replied, "I have already understood it. "How is this so? "It is simply because my perspective is different.
Outwardly, I do not grasp at ordinary people or sages; inwardly, I do not dwell in the fundamental source. Having seen through the original Dharma, I no longer harbor doubts or errors.
He further said, "O practitioner of the Way, there is no place in the Buddha-dharma where one exerts effort; it is merely the ordinary state of non-action. Put on your robes and eat your food..."
"Eat your rice. Defecate and urinate. When weary, lie down. Fools laugh at me, but the wise understand. As the ancients said:
"To apply effort directed outward is entirely the way of a foolish and stubborn fellow. You should instead take charge wherever you are; in every place where you stand, there is the truth."

All objective conditions cannot be exchanged or altered. Even if one possesses habitual tendencies from the past or has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*), these shall all become the great ocean of liberation.
Yet, those who study Chan nowadays do not recognize the Dharma at all; they are like a goat that touches its nose and immediately puts whatever it encounters into its mouth.
They cannot distinguish between master and servant, nor differentiate between guest and host. Such as these allow their deviant minds to enter [the path].

One who merely follows the Way cannot be called a true renunciant; such a person is actually a true worldly householder. Now, one who has truly left the home-life must be able to discern the ordinary and the authentic view.
They must discern Buddha and Māra, discern the true and the false, and discern the mundane and the sage.
If one can discern in this manner, they are called a true renunciant. If one cannot distinguish between Māra and Buddha, they are precisely a renunciant in name only.
Entering a household is what is called being a sentient being who creates karma; such a person cannot yet be called a true renunciant.
Right now, there is the realization that Buddha and Mara are of one essence. A practitioner with clear eyes strikes both Mara and Buddha.
If you cherish the holy and loathe the ordinary, you will continue to sink and float within the sea of birth and death with no end in sight. At that time, a monk asked: "What is..."
"Buddha-demons," he said. "Please grant me instruction. [The Master] replied: "The place where your single thought of mind harbors doubt—that is the Buddha-demon.

If you can penetrate the fact that the myriad dharmas are unborn, and that the mind is like an illusion or a transformation, such that not a single speck of dust or a single dharma remains, and all places are pure, then there are no Buddha-demons.
'Buddhas' and 'sentient beings' are the two realms of defilement and purity. From the perspective of this mountain monk, there are neither Buddhas nor sentient beings."
Birth is neither ancient nor modern; when one attains it, one simply attains it, without being constrained by time or season. There is no cultivation or realization; there is neither gain nor loss.
At all times, there is no other dharma apart from this. Were there even a single dharma that transcended this, I would say it is like a dream or an illusion.
What I, this mountain monk, speak of is nothing other than the solitary, vivid clarity of the practitioner right now before their eyes as they listen to the Dharma.
Such a person is unimpeded everywhere, penetrating throughout the ten directions and attaining mastery over the three realms.
They enter all differentiated states without being turned back or diverted. In a single kṣaṇa, they penetrate the Dharma-realm; meeting a Buddha, they speak of the Buddha;
meeting a Patriarch, they speak of the Patriarch; meeting an Arhat, they speak of the Arhat; meeting a hungry ghost, they speak of the hungry ghost. Thus they travel and dwell in all places.
The earth. Teaching and transforming sentient beings, never for a single thought-moment has it been absent. Pure in every place, its light permeates the ten directions;
the myriad dharmas are of one suchness. O practitioner of the Way! You great man, today you finally know that there is fundamentally nothing to do.

It is only because you have not had sufficient faith that you pursue and seek from moment to moment, abandoning your head to search for your head, unable to rest of your own accord. Like a Bodhisattva of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching], you enter...

Manifesting the body within the Dharma-realm, one turns away from the mundane world toward the Pure Land, loathing the ordinary and rejoicing in the holy. For those of such a disposition, acceptance and rejection have not been forgotten;
the mind of defilement and purity still remains. This is not the case with the insight of the Chan school. It is simply the present moment, with no further temporal divisions.
Everything I, this mountain monk, say is merely a matter of medicine and illness treating one another for a time; there is no real dharma at all. If it is thus...
To see this is true renunciation. One may consume ten thousand taels of gold daily. O practitioners of the Way!

Do not, in your haste, have your faces branded by the seals of various teachers from all quarters who say, "I understand Chan; I understand the Way," with eloquence like a cascading river; these are all merely creating karma for hell.
If one is a truly authentic seeker of the Way, they do not perceive the faults of the world. You must urgently seek a true and authentic vision.
[The Master] said: "If you penetrate the true mind and awaken to the perfect clarity of its nature, only then will it be fully realized. Question: "What is the truly authentic insight?

I beg for further instruction. [The Master] said: "Simply enter everywhere—into the mundane and the sacred, into defilement and purity, into the lands of all Buddhas, into Maitreya’s tower, and into the world of Vairocana. It manifests in every place."

The earth undergoes formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. When a Buddha appears in the world, turns the Great Dharma Wheel, and enters *nirvāṇa* without remainder, one perceives no marks of coming or going.
Seeking his birth and death, they are utterly unfindable; he thus enters the realm of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmadhātu*).
He travels everywhere through lands and enters the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), seeing that all phenomena are entirely true and are all the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

(The *Yulu* states: "To see all dharmas as empty in their nature is to realize that none possess substantial reality. This is from the *Zhengfayan zang*. There is only the man of the Way who listens to the Dharma without dependence;
he is the mother of all Buddhas. Therefore, the Buddha is born from non-dependence. If one awakens to non-dependence, even Buddhahood is not attained.
To see it in this way is the true and correct understanding. Students do not comprehend this and cling to it as mere names and phrases, and thus they are caught by the ordinary and the holy.)

This is called "obstruction by names," which hinders the eye of the Path so that it cannot see clearly. Take, for instance, the twelve divisions of the teachings; they are all expressions intended to manifest the truth.
Yet students do not understand this, and instead give rise to interpretations based on the manifest words and phrases. These are all dependencies that fall within the realm of cause and effect;
one thus cannot escape the cycle of birth and death within the three realms. If you wish to attain freedom in going and staying within birth and death, [you must transcend these].

Right now, recognize the person who listens to the Dharma. Formless and signless, rootless and baseless, without a place of abiding, vividly alive—this is the very locus for the application of all manner of expedient means, yet it is simply without location (*yǔ-lù*; in the *Yù-lù*, the character "location" [所] is followed by the character "with" [以]).
The more you seek it, the further away it becomes; the more you pursue it, the more you miss it. It is called "the secret. O practitioners of the Way, do not mistake this for a dream or an illusion.
My son, in the midst of this brief interval between morning and evening, one returns to impermanence. What thing do you seek within this world as liberation?
Seek only enough food for a single meal to sustain yourself until the time passes; meanwhile, you must go in search of a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Do not follow after pleasures with complacency, leading to a life lived in vain and a death met by chance. Time is to be cherished; every thought-moment is impermanent.

On a gross level, one is oppressed by earth, water, fire, and wind; on a subtle level, one is oppressed by arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. Thus, one is beset by the four elements and the four marks of existence without end.
O followers of the Way, for now you must recognize the four kinds of signless realms, so as to avoid being tossed about and struck down by external conditions.
Question: What are the four kinds of signless objects? The Master said: "When a single thought of love arises in your mind, you are drowned by water.
When a single thought of anger arises, you are burned by fire. When a single thought of doubt arises, you are obstructed by earth. When a single thought of joy arises, you are blown away by wind.
If you can discern them in this way, you will not be turned by objects; rather, you will employ objects everywhere, surging eastward and drifting westward."
Sinking. The south surges up while the north sinks; the center surges up while the periphery sinks; the periphery surges up while the center sinks. Treading upon water as if it were earth;
treading upon earth as if it were water. Why is this so? It is because one has realized that the four great elements are like dreams and like illusions. O seeker of the Way:
you who are listening to the Dharma right now are not these four great elements, yet you are able to employ them. If you can see it in this way, then you may depart.

Abiding in freedom. From the perspective of this mountain monk, there is no dharma to be disparaged. If you loathe the ordinary and cherish the holy, you will be bound by the realms of the holy and the ordinary.
There are some students who seek the manifestation of Mañjuśrī on Mount Wutai; they have already gone astray.
Mount Wutai has no Mañjuśrī. Do you wish to recognize Mañjuśrī? It is simply that which functions before your eyes;
from beginning to end it is never different, and it is unimpeded in every place. This is the living Mañjuśrī: the light of non-differentiation within your single thought-moment.
Everywhere is universally good (Samantabhadra). If you can attain mastery with a single thought-moment, you will be liberated wherever you are;

this is the dharma of the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara. They manifest as both principal and attendant to one another: when they manifest, they manifest simultaneously; when they are hidden, they are hidden simultaneously. One is three, and three is one.

Only when you understand it in this way can you truly begin to contemplate the teachings. Now, regarding the Great Good Spiritual Friend (Mahākalyāṇamitra)... [beginning]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* or related Mahāyāna literature, specifically discussing the non-dual nature of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.)

Daring to slander the Buddha and the Patriarchs, you judge right and wrong by the standards of the world; you reject the teachings of the Tripiṭaka and insult the young novices, seeking out those who are either hostile or compliant.
Therefore, for twelve years, I have sought a single instance of karmic nature even as small as a mustard seed, yet I could find none.
If one were like this "Chan Master" who acts like a new bride, he would immediately be terrified and driven out of the monastery, rather than being given [instruction].
Having eaten his rice, he was uneasy and unhappy. Since ancient times, when senior predecessors have gone everywhere and people did not believe them, they were driven out;

it was only then that they came to know their own worth. If everyone everywhere were willing to accept you, what would you be worth? Therefore, when a lion roars once, the wild jackal’s head splits open.
You practitioners of the Way, all over the various regions you say there is a Way to cultivate and a Dharma to realize. But tell me first, what do you realize?
"What path does the Dharma cultivate? What is lacking in your current practice? Where do you seek repairs? Later generations of young monks will not understand;
they will immediately believe such wild fox spirits and demons who claim to tell the truth and bind others with their words, saying:
'Only when one's conduct accords with principle and one guards the three karmas can one attain Buddhahood. To speak in such a manner is like..."
A fine rain in spring. An ancient said: "When you meet a person who has attained the Way on the road, first do not speak of the Way. Therefore it is said:
"If a person attempts to cultivate the Way but the Way does not proceed, myriad perverse conditions will vie to arise. When the sword of wisdom is drawn forth, there is not a single thing."
The light has not yet manifested at the head, yet it is bright at the base. Therefore, the ancients said: "The ordinary mind is the Way.
O Great Virtue, what thing are you seeking? Right now, before your eyes, this person who hears the Dharma without dependence is vividly clear and never lacking.
If you wish to be no different from the Patriarchs and Buddhas, simply see in this way; do not allow yourself to be misled by doubt. You—
Mind and mind are not different; this is called the living patriarch. If the mind were different, then essence and form would be separate.

Because the mind is not different, essence and form are not separate. Question: "What is the state where mind and mind are not different? The Master said: "The moment you intend to ask, it has already become different.
Essence and form are each distinct. O practitioners of the Way, do not err! All phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, are devoid of self-nature."
Furthermore, there is no nature of arising; there is only the empty name, and even that name is empty.
You have mistakenly taken these idle names to be real—this is a great error. Even if they existed, they would all be objects of transformation based upon something.

There is a Bodhi based upon Nirvana, based upon liberation, based upon the three bodies, based upon object and wisdom, based upon bodhisattvas, and based upon Buddhas. You are currently within this realm of transformation based upon such things.
In the midst of the earth, what thing do you seek? Even the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are merely used-up paper for wiping away impurities.
The Buddha is an illusory transformation body; the Patriarch is but an old bhikṣu. Have you not yet been born of your mother?
If you seek the Buddha, you will be seized by the demon of the Buddha. If you seek the Patriarch, you will be bound by the demon of the Patriarch. If you have any seeking at all...
It is suffering. It is not as good as having nothing to do. There is a certain class of shaven-headed bhikṣus who say to those studying the Way:
"The Buddha is the ultimate; after practicing for three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, his fruition was fulfilled and he finally attained the Way.
O Dharma-stream, if you say the Buddha is the ultimate, for what reason did he lie on his side between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara eighty years later?
And he died. Where is the Buddha now? It is clear that his birth and death are no different from my own. You say that the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics constitute a Buddha;
then a Wheel-Turning Sage King should also be a Tathāgata. It is clear that these are but illusory transformations.

An ancient said: "The Tathāgata displays his physical form merely to accord with worldly sentiments; fearing that people might give rise to the view of annihilation, he provisionally establishes names for his stations.
The so-called thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics are but empty sounds. To have a body is not the essence of awakening; formlessness is the true form.
You say that the Buddha possesses the six supernatural powers, which are inconceivable, and that all the devas and immortals [are likewise so].
Asuras and powerful spirits also possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); should they not be considered Buddhas? Do not err, seeker of the Way! Consider this:
when the asuras fought with Śakra, Lord of Devas, and were defeated, they led their eighty-four thousand followers into the pores of a lotus fiber to hide.
Are these not sages? As for what this mountain monk has cited, these are all instances of karmic power and dependent power. Now, as for...

It is not so for the Buddha’s six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). When he enters the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), he is not deluded by form; when he enters the realm of sound (*śabdadhātu*), he is not deluded by sound;

when he enters the realm of fragrance (*gandhadhātu*), he is not deluded by fragrance; when he enters the realm of taste (*rasadhātu*), he is not deluded by taste; when he enters the realm of touch (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), he is not deluded by touch;
and when he enters the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), he is not deluded by phenomena. Thus, he penetrates all six—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena—and [remains unattached].

This is the mark of emptiness; it cannot be bound. This person who walks the path without reliance, though possessing the coarse substance of the five aggregates, is one who possesses spiritual powers that traverse the earth.
O followers of the Way, the true Buddha has no form, and the true Dharma has no marks. You merely fashion patterns and models upon these illusory transformations.
Even if you were to attain something through such means, it would all be nothing but wild fox spirits and demons; none of them are the true Buddha.

This is the view of the non-Buddhists. As for those who truly study the Way, they take nothing from the Buddhas, take nothing from the Bodhisattvas or Arhats, and take nothing from the excellence of the triple world;
they are utterly detached and independent, unrestrained by external things. Even if heaven and earth were overturned, they would not harbor a single doubt.

Should the Buddhas of the ten directions appear before them, they would not feel a single thought of joy; should the three miserable realms and the hells suddenly manifest, [they would remain unmoved].
I do not have a single thought of fear. Why is this so? I perceive that all Buddhas are of the nature of emptiness: they exist when transformed and do not exist when untransformed.
The triple world is but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Therefore, as for dreams, illusions, and empty flowers, why trouble oneself to grasp them?
Consider, O practitioners of the Way, those who are listening to the Dharma right now before you: they enter fire without being burned; they enter water without being drowned;
they enter the three miserable realms and the hells as if strolling through a garden; they enter the realms of hungry ghosts and animals without undergoing retribution.
Why is this so? Because there is no dharma to be disliked. If you cherish the holy and loathe the ordinary, you will sink and float within the sea of birth and death, mired in affliction.
It exists because of the mind; if there is no mind, what can afflictions constrain? Do not trouble yourself with conceptual discrimination or grasping at signs;

you will naturally attain the Way in an instant. If you intend to learn by following others through a weary and laborious process, you will ultimately remain within birth and death throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
It would be better to do nothing at all and sit cross-legged on the corner of a bed in the midst of the forest thickets.

O practitioners of the Way, if you wish to accord with the Dharma, simply do not give rise to doubt. When extended, it encompasses the entire dharma-realm; when withdrawn, not even a single hair’s breadth is established.
It is vividly and individually luminous, never lacking anything. The eyes do not see it; the ears do not hear it. What thing can you call it? An ancient said:
To say it is like a single thing is not the way. You should simply look for yourself; what more is there? Even speaking of it would be inexhaustible.
Each of you must exert yourselves. Take care, O seekers of the Way! This very function before your eyes is no different from that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If you do not believe this, you will seek it elsewhere; do not err. There is no dharma outside, nor can it be found within.

Rather than taking my words to heart, it would be better for you to cease your activities and be free from concerns. Do not continue what has already arisen; do not allow what has not yet arisen to arise.
This would surpass ten years of your traveling as a pilgrim. According to my own view, there is nothing like this.
There are many ways to put it, but it is simply this: wearing clothes and eating food as usual, passing the time without concern. When you encounter a Buddha, kill the Buddha;
when you encounter a Patriarch, kill the Patriarch; when you encounter an Arhat, kill the Arhat; when you encounter your parents, kill your parents;

when you encounter your kinsmen, kill your kinsmen. Only then do you attain liberation. Unrestrained by things, you penetrate through and attain sovereign freedom. If you can bring this single thought-moment to rest—
The place where you cannot allow a single thought-moment of your mind to rest is called the Tree of Ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance has no dwelling place;

ignorance has no beginning or end. If you cannot bring each successive thought to rest, you will ascend that Tree of Ignorance and enter the six realms and four modes of birth, donning fur and wearing horns. If you can bring it to rest, then it is [enlightenment].
The realm of the pure body: when you do not give rise to a single thought, you have ascended the Bodhi tree.

Regarding the supernormal powers and transformations within the three realms—emanating bodies through the power of the mind—there are a certain class of blind shavelings who, having finished their meals, sit in meditation and practice contemplation.
They grasp at thoughts and leaks, refusing to let them arise; they loathe clamor and seek stillness. This is the dharma of external paths. The Patriarch said:

If you dwell the mind to observe stillness, raise the mind to illuminate outwardly, gather the mind to clarify inwardly, or concentrate the mind to enter meditative absorption—such practices as these are all mere contrivances.
How can you, who are now listening to the Dharma in this manner, intend to cultivate it, realize it, or adorn it?
It is not something to be cultivated, nor is it something that can be adorned.
"Objects. If you were to instruct another on how to adorn them, all objects would indeed be adorned.
When I, this mountain monk, say that 'there is no dharma outside,' students do not understand and instead form a conceptual understanding directed inward.

They then lean against a wall and sit, pressing their tongues against the upper palate, remaining in a state of profound stillness and immobility, taking this to be the Buddha-dharma of the Patriarchal Gate. This is a great error. If you were to take it as such..."
It is the unmoving, pure realm that is the reality. You, however, identify ignorance as your master. As the ancients said:
"The profound pit of dark stillness is truly terrifying"—this refers precisely to this. If you were to identify the moving, then all grasses and trees would possess movement;
could they then be considered the Way? Therefore, that which moves is the element of wind; it is not [the Way].
That which moves is the earth element. Both movement and non-movement are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If you try to seize him where he moves, he stands where he does not move; if you try to seize him where he does not move, he stands where he moves.
It is like a fish submerged in a spring that leaps up by stirring the waves. Venerable Sir, movement and non-movement are these two kinds of objects. Return [to this].

This was the man who relied on nothing. Whether moving or unmoving, he remained ever-present. On the tenth day of the fourth month in the eighth year of the Yuanhe era (the Dinghai year), as he was about to manifest his passing, he spoke this verse of transmitting the Dharma:
"Following the current without ceasing—ask how it is so? True illumination is boundless—explain it to others as such.
Free from characteristics and free from names, no one can receive it; Once the 'blow-off-hair' sword has been used, it must be quickly polished. He then addressed the assembly once more.
[The Master] said: "After my extinction, you must not allow my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to be extinguished. Three sages came forward and said:
"How would we dare let the Master’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye be extinguished? The Master said: "In the future, if someone asks you about this, what will you say to him?"
The Master suddenly gave a shout. The Teacher said, "Who would have known that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be extinguished upon this blind donkey?
Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the northwest corner of the prefecture, and he was posthumously titled Huizhao.
Jiyin said, "One must urgently grind it. Chuanshi said, "One must simply vanish one's traces where there is a place to hide the body;
do not hide the body where there are no traces. Huanji said, "Jiyin only recognizes a vegetable knife;
he has not yet dreamed of the 'blowing-hair' sword."
The Record of Pointing at the Moon, Scroll Fourteen;
The Record of Pointing at the Moon, Scroll Fifteen:
The Fifth Generation after the Sixth Patriarch.
▲ Chan Master Qingzhu of Shishuang Mountain in Tanzhou was a native of the Chen family of Xingan in Luling. Initially, he studied the Vinaya, but suddenly abandoned it.
He traveled to Mt. Gui (Miaoshan) to serve as the rice steward. One day, while sifting rice, Miaoshan said, "Do not scatter the donor's rice.
The Master replied, "I shall not scatter it. Miaoshan picked up a single grain from the ground and said, "You say you will not scatter it?"
[He] scattered [the grain]. "What is this? The Master had no reply. Miu said again, "Do not underestimate this single grain;
hundreds of thousands of grains all arise from this one grain. The Master said, "Hundreds of thousands of grains arise from this one grain, but I wonder from where this one grain arises?
Miu laughed heartily and returned to his quarters. That evening, Miu ascended the hall.
He said, "There are insects in the rice for the great assembly; everyone, look well. Later, he went to visit Daowu.
The Master asked, "What is awakening that meets the eye? Daowu called out, "Attendant! The attendant responded, "Yes? Daowu said, "Fill the water pitcher.
After a long while, Daowu then asked the Master, "What was it you were just asking? As the Master was about to speak, Daowu simply rose and left. At this, the Master attained realization.
"I shall follow the ways of the world," he said, and spoke these words: "Within my mind there is a thing that has long been a source of affliction.
Who can remove it for me? The Master replied, "Both mind and thing are non-existent; to attempt to remove them only increases the affliction. He said, "Excellent! Excellent!
Thereafter, the Master withdrew from the world and mingled with the common folk at Táojiāfáng in Liúyáng, Chángshā. Wandering by day and dwelling by night, no one was able to [discern him].

Later, when a monk came from Dongshan, the Master asked him, "What words or phrases did your teacher use to instruct his disciples? The monk replied, "After the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said:
'At the beginning and end of autumn, brothers, whether you go east or west, you must head toward a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not a single blade of grass.
After a long silence, he asked: 'But as for that place ten thousand *li* away where there is not a single blade of grass—how does one go there?'"
The Master asked, "Has anyone offered a response? The monk replied, "No. The Master said, "Why did you not say, 'Stepping out the door is grass'?
The monk returned and related this to Dongshan. Dongshan remarked, "Liu Yang truly has an ancient Buddha!"
Miaoxi said, "Have you not heard it said: 'A single drop of lion’s milk scatters ten bushels of donkey’s milk'?
Dayang Yan said, "Even if one were to say directly now that they do not step outside the gate, the weeds would still be lush and overgrown.
Tell me, where should one go to practice? After a long silence, he said: 'Do not linger by the green herbs on the cold crag; sit upon the white snow.'"
Yunzong’s “not subtle” is not as good as Yuantong’s “well said. Now tell me, how would you express the single phrase beneath the heels of everyone here right now?
If you say, "Ten thousand miles, not a blade of grass," I grant that you have seen Dongshan.
If you say, "Stepping out the door is already grass," I grant that you have seen Shishuang. If you say, "Not stepping out the door is also..."
The grass stretches far and wide; I allow you to see Dayang. If you cannot say anything at all, I allow you to see Yansheng.
Why? Only a fine breeze comes upon the mat; no idle words fall into the human world.
The Master was in the abbot’s quarters. A monk asked from outside the window, "If you are only a few feet away, why can I not see your face?
The Master said, "It is nowhere hidden throughout the entire world. The monk reported this to Xuefeng, asking, "What is the meaning of 'nowhere hidden throughout the entire world'?
Xuefeng said, "Where is it that it is not Shishuang? When the Master heard this, he remarked, "What is this old fellow so obsessed with?"
Jiufeng heard this and said, "This old monk has committed a transgression.
Xuansha said, "The old fellow on the mountainhead has missed the mark. Dongshan Jia said, "He makes the local deity laugh to death.
Dongchan Qi said, "As for Xuefeng, did he understand Shishuang’s meaning, or did he not?"
[The Master] said: "If you understand, why did he say, 'Death is urgent'? If you do not understand, how would you explain it?
How could Xuefeng not have understood? Yet, while the Dharma itself is without difference, because their lineages of teachers differ, their interpretations vary."
He said, "The entire realm has never been hidden. One must have studied it before one can understand it; to speak recklessly is not permissible.
Huan Ji said, "This statement by Lord Qi takes illness as medicine. If the eyes flicker and move, one will enter hell like a shot arrow."

A monk asked, "Three thousand miles away, I have heard from afar that Shishuang has an 'unregarding' [attitude]. Is this so? The Master said, "Yes. The monk asked, "But when the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest, is this regarding or unregarding?
The Master said, "I say it does not startle the multitude. The monk asked, "Not startling the multitude means being in harmony with the myriad phenomena;

what then is 'unregarding'? The Master said, "The entire world has never been hidden. When the monk took his leave, the Master [said]: [Note: The final line "When the monk took his leave, the Master" indicates the transition to the next encounter, though the text provided ends abruptly.]
A monk asked, "If one goes by boat or goes by land? The Master said, "When you meet a boat, you go by boat; when you meet land, you go by land.
The Master added, "I say that halfway along the road it becomes somewhat difficult. The monk had no reply. Yun’gai asked, "I do not ask about the time when all ten thousand doors are closed.
But what is it like when all ten thousand doors are open? The Master said, "What of the matter within the hall? The monk said, "No one can receive him. The Master said, "Speak!"
"You have spoken quite thoroughly; yet you have only managed to express it eighty or ninety percent. The student asked, "I do not know for certain—how would you, Master, speak of it?
The Master replied, "No one recognizes him."
Miaoxi said: "A pair of iron hammers without holes; among them, one is the heaviest.
In the *Chuan Deng Lu*, regarding the Master Yu’s later words, it says: "Still, no one can receive him. Dongchan Qi asked:
"As for Shishuang’s intention, what was it? If you say they are the same, why did he previously not permit him? If you say..."
There is another principle at work here. Furthermore, he simply repeats it once more. But tell me, what was the intent of the ancient?
He asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "I am investigating the Way. The Master drew a line in front of him and said, "You came here with your feet pricked;
do you still investigate this? The monk said, "I cannot investigate it. The Master said, "Your monastic robe is like this..."
[Huizhao] said, "It is thick. Yet, for this very reason, one cannot examine this. The Master said, "Even though your cassock is thick, what can you do? You still cannot examine this.
[Huizhao] said, "In that case, even if the Seven Buddhas appeared in the world, they could not save you. The Master said, "What need is there to speak of the Seven Buddhas?
Even if a thousand Buddhas appeared in the world, they could not save you. [Huizhao] said, "You are far too dull-witted. The Master said, "How so?"
The monk said, "What about this? The Master said, "Go to the hall for meditation. The monk said, "Yes, yes. Prime Minister Pei arrived.

The Master picked up Pei’s ceremonial tablet (hù) and asked, "In the hands of the Son of Heaven it is called a jade scepter (guī); in the hands of an official it is called a tablet. Now, in my old monk’s hands, tell me, what do you call it?
Pei had no reply. The Master then left the tablet with him. Addressing the assembly, he said: "For those at the beginning of their practice..."
Before encountering the Great Matter, one must first recognize the head; then the tail will follow of its own accord. Shushan Ren came to attend him and asked, "What is the head?
The Master said, "You must simply know that it exists. He asked, "What is the tail? The Master said, "Exhausting the present moment. He asked, "What is it like when there is a head but no tail?
The Master said, "Even if you could spit out gold, what would you do with it? He asked, "What is it like when there is a tail..."
"How is it when there is no head? The Master said, "There is still something upon which he relies. [The monk] asked, "How is it when the head and tail perfectly correspond?
The Master said, "Even if he does not form such a conceptual understanding, I still do not grant him permission."
Later, a monk asked Jiufeng, "What is the head? Jiufeng said, "Opening one's eyes, one does not perceive the dawn. The monk asked, "What is the tail?
Jiufeng said, "Not sitting upon the ten-thousand-year throne. The monk asked, "What is it like when there is a head but no tail? Jiufeng said:
"In the end, it is not valued. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when there is a tail but no head? Feng said, "Though full, one has no strength.
[The monk] asked, "What is it like when the head and tail are perfectly matched? Feng said, "The descendants have gained strength; those within the room do not know."
The Master resided at Shishuang for twenty years. His disciples were many and mostly practiced *dhutāṅga* by sitting constantly without reclining, standing firm like stumps;

thus, the world called them the "Dried-Up Wood Assembly. When Emperor Xizong of the Tang heard of the Master’s reputation, he dispatched a special envoy to bestow upon him the purple robe, but the Master firmly declined and would not accept it.
On the day of Jihai, the second month of the fourth year of the Guangqi era (the Wushen year), he sat peacefully and passed away.
▲ Chan Master Jianyuan Zhongxing of Tanzhou served as an attendant to Daowu. Once, while passing tea to Daowu, Daowu held up the cup and asked, "Is this false, or is it correct?
The Master crossed his hands and stepped forward, gazing intently at Daowu. Daowu said, "If it were false, it would be entirely false;
if it were correct, it would be entirely correct. The Master replied, "I do not speak in such a manner. Daowu asked, "How then do you speak?"
When [Dongshan] was born, the Master took the cup from him, held it up, and asked, "Is this right or is this wrong? I replied, "You have not served me as my attendant in vain.
The Master then bowed. One day, while attending me as I went to a donor’s house for a funeral visit, the Master tapped the coffin and asked, "Is he alive or is he dead?
I said, "I will not say he is alive; I will not say he is dead. The Master asked, "Why do you not say?"
I said, "Not to speak, not to speak. When we had returned halfway, the Master said, "The Abbot must speak to me today;
if you do not speak, I shall strike the Abbot! I said, "Strike as you please, but as for speaking, I will not speak. The Master then struck me.
Upon returning to the monastery, I said, "You should leave this place; I fear that if the administrators find out, it will be inconvenient. Thereupon, the Master...
He took his leave and hid himself in a village temple. After three years had passed, he suddenly heard a youth reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra.

When it reached the passage, "To those who should be saved by the body of a bhikṣu, he immediately manifests in the body of a bhikṣu," he experienced a sudden and great awakening. He then burned incense and prostrated from afar, saying:
"I now know with certainty that the late master’s final words were never in vain. It was only because I lacked understanding that I previously harbored resentment toward him."
The Master said, "Since my late teacher has passed away, only Shishuang is the legitimate successor; he must provide proof for me. He then went to Shishuang.
Upon seeing him, Shishuang asked, "Where have you come from since leaving Daowu? The Master replied, "I have simply been staying at a village temple.

Shishuang asked, "Have you yet resolved the karmic connection regarding the previous occasion when you struck my late teacher? The Master rose and stepped forward, saying, "Please, Master, [let us discuss it]."
Shangdao asked for a turning word. Shishuang said, "I do not say it when one is alive; I do not say it when one is dead.
The Master then recounted the circumstances of his realization while at a village monastery and subsequently paid homage to Shishuang, where he prepared a vegetarian feast and offered repentance.
On another day, carrying a spade, he returned to Shishuang and walked back and forth from east to west and west to east across the Dharma Hall. Shishuang said, "Do..."
[Zhao] Mo asked, "I am seeking the sacred relics of the former master. Nanquan Shuang said, "The vast waves are immense and white billows overflow the heavens;
what 'sacred relics of the former master' are you seeking? Zhao Mo said, "This is precisely where one must exert effort. Nanquan Shuang said, "In this place, not even a needle can penetrate;
what effort could there be? Yuan Chi placed a spade upon his shoulder and departed.
Taoyuan Fu said: "The sacred remains of the former master still exist. Xuedou’s Verse: Rabbits and horses have horns;
oxen and sheep have none. Beyond a hair’s breadth, beyond a speck of dust— As vast as mountains, as lofty as peaks. The golden sacred remains still exist today.
White waves surge to the heavens; where can they be placed? Nowhere to be placed. A single sandal returned to the West—once lost. Yuánwù Qín said:
Some misunderstand this, saying, "It is not that 'not speaking' is the Way. They claim that "no phrase" is a "phrase," and that while rabbits and horses have no horns, they say they do;
while oxen and sheep have horns, they say they do not. This is simply a way to avoid being caught.
Sheshuo: "Little do you realize that the ancients, through a thousand transformations and ten thousand shifts, manifested such spiritual powers solely to shatter this ghost-cave of your cleverness.
If you can penetrate through it, there is no need for even a single word 'finished.
Rabbits and horses have horns; oxen and sheep have none. Beyond the slightest hair or speck of dust, they are like mountains and peaks. These four lines are like the *Mahāyāna*...
It is like a precious pearl; Xuedou has presented it to you in its entirety.
What follows is merely the formal conclusion based on the facts of the case.
One day, Master Bao’ai came to visit. The Master immediately rolled up the curtain and sat within the abbot’s quarters.

As soon as Bao’ai saw this, he lowered the curtain and returned to his guest seat. The Master ordered an attendant to deliver a message, saying, "It is no small matter for the Elder to have traveled so far;
you are still separated by the ford. Bao’ai seized the attendant and gave him a slap. The attendant said, "There was no need to strike me."
Jiā said, "The Abbot is here. Gài replied, "It is precisely because there is this old Abbot that I strike you.
When Jiā reported this back to the Master, the Master said, "You are still separated by a ford."
As Master Sengmi and Dongshan were walking along, they suddenly saw a white rabbit scurry past. The Master said, “How magnificent! Dongshan asked, “What do you mean?
The Master replied, “It is very much like a commoner being invested as a high minister. Dongshan said, “You are quite old yet you speak such words.
The Master asked, “And what about you? Dongshan replied, “A family of generations of official rank, now temporarily fallen into obscurity.”
While the Master was threading a needle, Dongshan asked, "What are you doing? The Master replied, "Threading a needle. Dongshan said, "As for the matter of threading a needle, how is it?
The Master said, "Every stitch is the same. Dongshan remarked, "Having traveled together for twenty years, have you been making such talk?
Is there really no such skill? The Master asked, "And what about you, Elder? Dongshan replied, "It is like the great earth."
Regarding the principle of the "ignition of fire," the Master asked: "There is nothing that the scope of one's wisdom and knowledge has not traversed.

At this point of direct cutting through, I beg for a word from the Master. Dongshan said, "How can you, Master, claim credit for your own realization? Because of this, the Master suddenly attained awakening; his subsequent utterances were no longer ordinary.
Later, while crossing a single-plank bridge with Dongshan, Dongshan crossed first and held up the bridge, saying, "Come across!"
"Come forward. The Master called out, "Jia Acharya. Dong then lowered the bridge planks.

[This concludes the entry for] Chan Master Shanhui of Jia Mountain in Lizhou, a native of the Liao family of Guangzhou. Having attained the Dharma from Chuanzhi, he lived in seclusion, hidden from the world;
students gathered around him like scales of fish. In the Gengyin year of the Xiantong era, he opened a teaching seat at Jia Mountain. When the Master was first there...
When Guishan was serving as the head cook, Guishan asked him, "What vegetables are you eating today? The Master replied, "Two years under the same spring.
Guishan said, "Attend well to your duties. The Master said, "The dragon dwells in the phoenix’s nest.

A monk asked, "Regarding the ancestral intent and the doctrinal intent established from of old, why does the Master say there is none? The Master replied, "Three years without eating a meal; before one's eyes, there is nothing."
The hungry man asked, "Since there is no such thing as a hungry person, why is it that I have not awakened? The Master said, "It is precisely because awakening has deluded you, O Kalyāṇamitra.
He then showed him this verse: "Clearly, there is no dharma of awakening; The dharma of awakening, instead, deludes people.
Stretch out your two legs and sleep; There is neither falsehood nor truth. A questioner asked, "When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what is it like? The Master said, "Directly..."

"One must brandish the sword. If one does not brandish the sword, the fisherman will nest in the trees. Later, a monk asked Shishuang, "What is it like when one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha?
Shishuang said, "He has no land; where would you meet him? The monk returned and related this to the Master (Xuedou).

After the Master finished his discourse in the hall, he said, "In the establishment of the gate, he is not as good as I am; yet in the profound discourse on entering into principle, he still compares favorably with Shishuang."
Shuang Baibu asked, "When the ancients spread their hair to cover the mud, what were they doing? The Master said, "The nine suns have been shot down, yet one obscuration still remains.
When that single arrow falls to the ground, the world will be plunged into darkness. There was a monk in the Master’s assembly.
He arrived at Shishuang. Upon entering the gate, he said, "I hope you are well? Shishuang replied, "Not necessary, O *śramaṇa*. The monk said, "If so, then take care.
He then went to Yantou and likewise said, "I hope you are well? Yantou let out two sighs. The monk said, "If so, then take care.
Just as he was turning to leave, Yantou said, "Though you are but a junior, you are indeed capable of maintaining your composure. The monk returned and related this to his teacher.
The Master ascended the hall the following day and called out, "Master, come forth—you who came yesterday from Shishuang Yantou.
He then recounted the previous dialogue exactly as it had occurred. When the monk had finished speaking, the Master said, "Does the assembly understand? If no one speaks, [I shall speak for you]."
"The old monk does not begrudge his two eyebrows; let me speak. He then said: "Although Shishuang possesses the sword that kills, he lacks the sword that gives life.
Yantou likewise possesses both the sword that kills and the sword that gives life. [He then] ascended the hall.
"I have lived on this mountain for twenty years, and I have never once raised a matter concerning the School of the Ancestors.
A monk asked, "I have heard it said that you, Master, have lived on this mountain for twenty years and have never raised a matter concerning the School of the Ancestors; is this true?

The Master replied, "It is true. The monk then overturned the meditation seat, and the Master ceased speaking. On the following day, he requested that everyone be assembled for communal labor and ordered a pit to be dug.
The attendant invited the monk from the day before and said, "For twenty years this old monk has spoken meaningless words.
Today I invite you, Venerable One, to beat this old monk to death and bury him in a pit. Please do so, please do so! If you do not beat this old monk to death," [he continued].

"The Elder would have beaten him to death himself; it was only by burying him in a pit that he could finally be rid of him. That monk returned to the hall, packed his belongings, and departed in secret.
Jiangshan Qin said, "When Jia Shan was turbid, both the head and the tail were turbid; when this monk was pure, he was pure from beginning to end.
Later people did not understand this and simply said, "This monk fled in secret for fear of being beaten to death. Little did they know that... [The text ends abruptly].
There is a needle within. This monk is indeed excellent; he simply lacks one turning word.

Had he waited for Jia Shan to say, "If you, Dharma-uncle, do not kill this old monk, then you shall kill yourself and bury me in a pit," he should have stepped forward and, with both hands, torn open [Jia Shan's] eyes, saying: "Cat!"
The Venerable Houtou came for an audience. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Hunan. The Master said, "Have you ever been to Shishuang?
He replied, "I had to pass through that main road; how could I not have reached it? The Master said, "I have heard there is a 'ball' koan at Shishuang—is this true?
He replied, "The Master must also watch closely before he can say so. The Master asked, "What is this 'ball'? He replied:
He could not leap out. The Master said, "What is this ball-stick? He replied, "It has no hands or feet. The Master said, "Go for now; I have not yet met you, Venerable One.
The next day, as he ascended the seat, the Master asked, "Was the one who arrived yesterday here yesterday? The monk bowed his head and responded, "Yes.
The Master said, "There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent is right before the eyes. It is not a dharma of the present moment, nor is it something heard by the ears."
As soon as his eyes reached [the Master], Xuansha said, "Though you ask today, it is nonetheless not so. Yunmen said, "Though the crescent moon is bright, it has no concern with heaven and earth.
Xuansha said, "Do not stir up a boiling cauldron," and he made a gesture as if to overturn the meditation seat. Yunmen said, "Wait, wait; proceed slowly."
The Head raised his fist and said, "Are you able to 'hit' this right before your eyes?
The Master said, "A true adept, a true adept. The Head then made a gesture as if to overturn the meditation seat. The Master said, "Everyone, look at this warrior!
As for the arrangement of the school's public display, I am not his equal; however, as for discourse that penetrates the ultimate principle—"
He is one rank above this mountain monk. The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "Apprehend the old monk at the tips of the hundred grasses;
recognize the Son of Heaven in the bustling marketplace.
Yunmen said: "A shrimp burrows through your nostrils; a venomous snake pierces you as your eyes. For now, let us turn toward these entanglements.
Lihuizhi said, "Miaoxi remarked: 'Jiashan blocked the birth and invited the arrow; Yunmen mistook the thief for his son.
Although this is so, those who recognize kindness are few, while those who betray it are many."
A monk asked, "What is the realm of Jia Shan? The Master said, "The ape carries its young back into the green peaks;
the bird picks up a flower before the azure cliffs.
Later, Fayan said, "For twenty years, I understood this only as a discourse on the realm. Fushan Yuan said: [The text ends here.]
Even if you do not take this as an object of conceptual understanding, you have still not reached it. Why? Because when the rhinoceros gazes at the moon, patterns form upon its horn;
when the elephant is startled by thunder, flowers enter its tusks.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The golden crow and the jade hare vie with one another for brilliance. When the sun is sat upon, the world falls into darkness.
The upper lip and the lower lip have never known each other. I tell you clearly: do not let your eyes look back at them. Why is this?"

The sun and moon are not sufficient to constitute illumination; heaven and earth are not sufficient to constitute greatness. One does not wield the axe in mid-air, nor does the master craftsman leave behind a trace.
Seeing one's nature leaves no room for Buddhas; awakening to the Way leaves no place for teachers. As the ordinary old monk says: "To see Gautama with one's own eyes is like looking at yellow leaves.
The entire Great Canon of teachings is this old monk’s sitting mat; the profound essence of the Patriarchs is the hammer that breaks [all attachments]."
Straw sandals: it is better to go barefoot than to wear these. Ascending the hall: Not knowing dawn; awakening does not depend on a teacher.

Leaping with its scales at the Dragon Gate, one does not fall into the hands of the fisherman. It is simply that the mind does not harbor private attachments and the tongue does not cling to the profound essence (*xuanzhi*).

This is precisely when one may be recognized as a true知音 (one who knows the sound). This is called the "congenital talk" (*jushenghua*). If you harbor doubt regarding the profound essence, you will only bring ruin upon yourself, O *deshi* (Venerable).
“Lí! A weary fish stops at a pond; a dull bird perches on a reed. The clouds and waters are not the *śrāmaṇera*; the *śrāmaṇera* is not the clouds and waters.
An old monk attains mastery over the clouds and waters—how about you, *śrāmaṇera*? He ascended the hall and said: “The enlightened does not go beyond the door;
the hollow does not nest in a tree. The eye does not look toward another’s position; the foot does not tread upon another’s position. The six gates are not...”

Concealed. No trace remains at the crossroads; the study does not halt at midday, and the intent does not establish itself in the profound. For a thousand kalpas, the eye does not borrow from the base of the tongue;
for ten thousand kalpas, the tongue does not look back upon the clarity within the eye. When the sublime faculty does not rely on the business of sharp edges, what matter is there here?
O *kalyāṇamitra*, let the thread on the tip of the pole be played with as you wish; do not disturb the clear waves, and your intent will naturally be extraordinary.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Since the time of the Patriarchs, people have misunderstood; this has been passed down to the present day such that the words and phrases of Buddhas and Patriarchs are taken as models for teachers.
If one acts in this way, one instead becomes a madman or a person devoid of wisdom. He merely points it out to you: 'The absence of dharmas is itself the Way.
The Way possesses not a single dharma. There is no Buddha to be realized, no Way to be attained, and no dharmas.'"
It can be taken up; there is no dharma to be abandoned. Therefore, the old monk says: "No dharma is present before one's eyes, yet the meaning lies right before one's eyes.
This is not a dharma of the present moment. If you seek to learn from the Buddhas and patriarchs, such a person has not yet attained the eye. Why?

Because all such things belong to that which is relied upon, and thus one does not attain autonomy. Originally, it is only because birth and death are vast and boundless that the nature of consciousness lacks any portion of freedom.
Seeking a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) across thousands and tens of thousands of miles requires one to possess the correct eye.

One must seek liberation from erroneous views and definitively investigate whether the birth and death before one’s eyes truly exist or truly do not exist. If there were anyone who could definitively attain this, I would grant you permission to emerge [from delusion].
Those of superior capacity clarify the Way upon hearing these words; those of middling or inferior capacity merely wander like waves. Why do you not turn toward it?

Within birth and death, you must certainly grasp [the truth]. Where else could you doubt the Buddha or the Patriarchs? A person of wisdom would laugh at you for attempting to substitute for your own birth and death.
If you do not understand, listen to another verse: "Toiling to uphold the dharma of birth and death, you seek only from the side of the Buddha."

The foregoing sets forth the correct principle; it is like extinguishing a fire to search for foam bubbles. On the seventh day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Zhonghe era, he summoned his attendants and said:
"I have discussed the Way with the assembly of monks for many years. Each of you should personally realize the profound purport of the Buddha-dharma."
"I shall now depart as this illusory body reaches its end. You must protect yourselves well, just as you did while I was alive.
Do not follow the common crowd in succumbing to grief. Having spoken these words, he suddenly passed away.
▲ Chan Master Datong of Mount Touzi in Shuzhou (who studied under Cuiwei; see the section on Cuiwei’s sayings). On another day, he asked:

Great Sameness dwells in quiescence—this is the proclamation of my Master’s school. Later, the Master resided at Tōji-in (Touzi Monastery), and was thus named Jikujū (Quiescent Abiding).

He says, "White. He waits again for black. Xuedou’s verse says:
"Having eyes within life is the same as being dead; why need one test a master regarding medicinal taboos?
Even the ancient Buddhas said they had never been there before; who knows who can scatter sand and mud? Jingshan Daowei’s verse says: "Grain."
The millet does not bloom with sunny splendor; instead, people compete to plant peach and plum trees in spring. This turns those who toil at the plow into half of the flower-sellers.
When Xuefeng arrived, the Master pointed to a stone slab in front of his hut and said to him, "All Buddhas of the three periods of time are contained within this.

The Master pointed at it with his staff. Xuefeng said, "Going east? Going west? The Master said, "You are a clumsy, lacquered bucket. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when one succeeds at a single blow?
The Master said, "Not a man of impulsive temperament. [The monk] asked, "What is it like when one does not rely on a single blow? The Master said, "Clumsy."
"Lacquered bucket. Feng asked, "Is there any ginseng here? The Master threw his mattock down in front of Feng.
Feng said, "In that case, I shall dig right here. The Master said, "A fastidious lacquered bucket.
When Feng took his leave, the Master saw him out the door, called out, "Dharma-candidate! Feng turned his head and responded, "Yes? The Master said, "Be well on your way."
Xuedou Xian, regarding the phrase "not a man of impetuous temperament," picked it up and said:

Monks, what kind of words should you have applied to Touzi? If you can speak them, then..."

He was by nature impetuous and throughout his life he brilliantly illuminated the Eye of the Patriarchs. If one were to be reckless or superficial, he would strike them once on the crown of the head—do not say he did not speak.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a newborn infant possess the six consciousnesses? Zhaozhou said, "Striking water on a steep current."
The "Ball" (Qiuzi). Later, a monk asked the Master, "What is the meaning of 'beating a ball on swift water'? The Master said, "Thought after thought, there is no lingering.
Xuedou Xian composed a verse on this: "The six consciousnesses are of no avail; I extend this one question. A master of the Way has already examined the source of this matter together with me."
In the vast expanse, a ball struck upon rushing waters; its falling place never stays—who can perceive it?
When a monk asked, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies? the Master descended from his meditation seat and stood there. Again the monk asked, "How far apart are the ordinary person and the sage?
The Master likewise descended from his meditation seat and stood there.
Xuedou Xian said: "Everyone knows this public case well enough. If it were presented in such a manner, all the monks under heaven would become nothing but members of a 'reciting-talk' society.
Does Xuedou have any point of excellence? Let me try to present it for the sake of the great assembly:
how far apart are the ordinary and the sage? Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood there. What is the 'Ten'?"
"Body Tamed. Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood there. Now tell me: is this the same as what was raised previously, or is it different?
If you say they are the same, I grant you, Elder, one eye. If you say there is something extraordinary and distinct, I likewise grant you, Elder, one eye.
Furthermore, let us open another path: how far apart are the ordinary and the sage?
"Please, Senior, give us a turning word. What is the 'Tamer of the Ten Bodies'? Please, Senior, answer with a turning word.
Not only will you have visited and seen Touzi, but you will also come to know the excellence of Xuedou.
