Question: "Are all sounds the voice of the Buddha? The Master said, "Yes. [The questioner] said, "Master, do not let the sound of a boiling pot scald your ears.
The Master then struck him. Question: "Are coarse words and subtle speech both returned to the primary principle (paramārtha)? The Master said, "Yes."
[The monk] said, "Is it permissible to call the Master a 'head donkey'?
The Master struck him. Miaoxi said, "Thief! Thief! He has been caught. He added, "Now tell me, which one is the real thief?
Which one is the straw thief? Xuedou’s Verse: Touzi, Touzi! His wheel of skillful means is unimpeded. To let go of one, he gains two. Together.
They are the same as this. How pitiable are those infinite people who play with the tide; in the end, they fall back into the tide and die.
Suddenly, they come alive: the hundred rivers flow backward in a tumultuous, surging rush.
Question: "Water is uniformly water; why is the sea salty while rivers are fresh? The Master said: "Stars in the sky, trees on the earth.
While the Master was in the capital attending a lay patron’s vegetarian feast, the patron brought a tray of grass. The Master clenched both hands and placed them upon his head.
The patron then proceeded to serve the meal. Later, a monk asked: "When you were in the capital attending that vegetarian feast, what was your intention?"
"What is the meaning? The Master said, "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. [The monk] asked, "Since you, Reverend, have resided on this mountain, what kind of realization (境界) have you attained?
The Master said, "A girl with twin-tails has white hair. During the Zhonghe era, bandits rose up in violence and the empire fell into chaos.
A madman wielding a blade questioned the Master, saying, "What are you doing staying here? The Master then spoke according to the occasion (隨宜).
The leader of the bandits heard this and prostrated himself in submission. He removed his own clothes to offer as alms and departed.

On the sixth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Qianhua era, he manifested a slight illness. When the assembly requested a physician, the Master said to them, "The movement of the four elements is a constant process of aggregation and dispersion;
you need not worry. I shall preserve myself. Having finished speaking, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away.
▲ When Chan Master Lingzun of Anle Monastery on Mount Qingping in Ezhou first visited Cuiwei, he asked:
"What is the true meaning of the coming from the West? Cuiwei said: "I will tell you when there is no one else here. After a long silence, the Master said:
"Nobody is here; I request the Master to speak. Weimi descended from his meditation seat and led the Master into the bamboo grove.
The Master spoke again, "Nobody is here; I request the Master to speak. Weimi pointed to the bamboo and said, "This stalk is so long; that stalk is so short.
Although the Master understood these subtle words, he had not yet penetrated their profound meaning. Later, when he went to reside at Dàtōng, he brought up this initial encounter.
Seeing the opportunity at Cuiwei, he said to the assembly: "The former master went into the mud and the water for my sake;
since then, I have failed to recognize what is good and what is evil. From that time on, the Master transformed and guided others. A monk asked: "What is the Great Vehicle?

He replied: "A well-rope. "What is the Small Vehicle? He replied: "A money-rope. "What is 'with outflows' (*sāsrava*)? He replied: "A strainer. "What is 'without outflows' (*anāsrava*)? He replied: "A ladle."
It is said: "A wooden ladle.
Fayan Wenyu said: "The Mahayana and Hinayana; the well-rope and the money-rope; the tainted and the untainted;
the bamboo sieve and the wooden ladle. Master Fachang Yu gave this instruction: "I want one who does not know Chan to act as abbot."
National Teacher Miaoxi said: "Tell me, is this a sentence of *amṛta* (clarified butter) or a sentence of poison?

Next is Chan Master Shandao Xuanjian of Dingshan in Dingzhou. He was the son of the Zhou family of Jianzhou. He entered the monastic life at the age of seven and received full ordination according to his years.

He studied the Vinaya-piṭaka with great diligence and thoroughly mastered the essential meanings of the various sūtras on the nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. He frequently lectured on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
At that time, Zhou Jin’gang was known as Chang. He would often say to his fellow students: “A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean suffers no loss;
a tiny speck is cast upon a blade’s edge, yet the sharpness of the blade remains unmoved. Whether one is a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), only I know this.

Later, hearing that the Zen seats in the South were flourishing, the Master felt a sense of unease and said: “For a renunciant, even after studying the majestic deportment of the Buddha for a thousand kalpas, ten thousand...”

"Even if one studies the subtle practices of the Buddha for kalpas, one cannot attain Buddhahood. A son of Māra from the south dares to speak of 'directly pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
I shall tear open his den and exterminate his kind, thereby repaying the Buddha’s grace.
He then took up the *Qinglong shuchao* (Blue Dragon Commentary) and departed from Shu. Upon reaching Liyang, he saw an old woman selling cakes by the roadside and stopped to buy some.
The Master was eating a cake as a snack when an old woman pointed to his shoulder-bag and asked, "What writing is this? The Master replied, "The *Commentary on the Blue Dragon* (*Qinglong shuchao*).
The woman asked, "Which sutra do you lecture upon? The Master replied, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The woman said, "I have a question; if you can answer it," [she continued].

He was offered some refreshments. When he replied that he had not received any, the other said, "In that case, please go elsewhere. [The Master] recalled the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which says:
"The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. He asked, "I wonder, Elder, which mind did you serve?
The other remained silent. Thereupon, he went to Longtan. Arriving at the Dharma Hall, he said, "I have long heard of Longtan; now that I have finally arrived..."
He came forward, but the pool was no longer there and the dragon had not appeared. Baizhang drew back his body and said, "You have personally arrived at the Dragon Pool.

The Master was speechless, and so he remained to dwell there. One night, while standing in attendance, the Pool said, "It is deep in the night; why do you not go out? The Master said, "I take my leave," and then departed.
He returned, saying, "It is dark outside. The Pool lit a paper candle and passed it to him. As the Master reached out to receive it, the Pool—
He blew it out again. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment and prostrated himself. Longtan asked, "What have you seen?
The Master replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the land.

On the following day, Longtan ascended the seat and said to the assembly, "Among you there is a man whose teeth are like a forest of sword-trees and whose mouth is like a basin of blood; with a single blow..."
"One cannot turn back once struck. At that time, he shall stand upon the summit of a solitary peak and establish my Way.
The Master then piled the commentaries and sub-commentaries before the Dharma Hall, raised a torch, and said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void;
to exhaust all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a vast abyss. He then burned them. Thereupon, he paid his respects and took his leave, arriving at Mí.
Shanshan led the Master up the winding path to the Dharma Hall. Passing from west to east, and from east to west, he asked, "Is there anything?
Is there anything? Shanshan sat there, completely ignoring him. The Master said, "Nothing, nothing. (Xuedou’s commentary: "He has been thoroughly exposed. He then departed.
Upon reaching the gate, he said, "Even so, one must not be careless. He then assumed his full ceremonial demeanor and re-entered to have an audience.
As soon as he stepped across the threshold, he held up his sitting mat and said, "Venerable Master. As Shanshan reached for his whisk, the Master gave a shout and swept his sleeves out of the hall.
(Xuedou added a comment: "He has been seen through. That evening, Guishan asked the head seat, "Was the newcomer here today?"
Zuo said, "At that time, he would have turned his back on the Dharma Hall and gone out wearing straw sandals.
Shanshan said, "This fellow will, in the future, pitch a grass hut atop a solitary peak and go about reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs."
Xuedou added a comment: "Adding frost to snow. He further offered this verse: "First, see through it; second, see through it.
Adding frost to snow, he nearly fell into peril. The Flying Cavalry General enters the barbarian court;
how many can emerge completely unscathed? Hurrying past, let nothing escape. Sitting amidst the weeds atop a solitary peak. Tsk! — Yuanwu Keqin.
Yunmen said, "Xuedou says he has been thoroughly scrutinized. Now tell me: was it Deshan who was scrutinized, or was it Guishan?
Miaoxi said, "When these two venerable seniors met in this manner, each lost one of their eyes."
Small Assembly. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Tonight I shall not answer questions. Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows of the staff.

The Master said, "Where are you from? He replied, "From Silla. The Master said, "Before you even stepped onto the ship's railing—" and gave another blow.
[He] gave him thirty blows.
Yuanming said, "The Great and Small Deshan [were like] a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail.

When the Great Garuda wishes to spread its sky-reaching wings, who takes note of the surging clouds across the six directions?
He further said, "If you understand this as two separate parts, there will be no connection at all. Then he acted like a dragon.
"Head and tail meet; yet one must reach the point where there is no further engagement. Since you do not understand it in this way, how can you ultimately grasp it?
Tell me, why did these two elders handle the matter in such a manner? Everyone, try to look at this with your own eyes. Xuedou Xian said:
"Although these two elders were skilled at cutting the long to patch the short and discarding the heavy for the light, they..."

"Even seeing the old fellow Deshan is not yet sufficient. Why? Because you do not realize that Deshan wielded the sovereign authority beyond the threshold and possessed a sword that—if one hesitates to strike when it must be struck—will invite chaos.

Many people, relying on intellectual understanding, say: "Wait for Deshan to ask, 'Where are you from? and then [the monk's response reveals his blindness]."
At that moment, he struck him across the face with his sitting mat, saying, "You fool! Had you acted like this, I would have let you go.
Now tell me, ultimately, where was this monk's point of blindness? The Master then struck him.
Xuangjue said, "In the monastic communities, this is called 'speech from below the diaphragm. Let us set that aside for a moment; as for what Deshan said, 'Those who come to ask questions—'"
"Thirty blows! What was his intention? Dagui Zhi said: "People all say that Deshan’s application of the teaching was excellent.
If you understand it in this way, have you ever even dreamed of it? Dagui says:
Deshan was so thoroughly shattered by this monk’s single push that he was like ice melting away. Nevertheless, today one must seek this [monk]."
Such a venerable elder is truly difficult to find.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "If you can speak it, thirty blows; if you cannot speak it, thirty blows.
When Linji heard of this, he said to Luopo: "Go and ask him why, if one can speak it, there are thirty blows. Wait for him to strike you."

Linji said, "I have always suspected this fellow. Nevertheless, do you recognize Deshan? As Puxiu hesitated, Linji struck him.
Once, while Linji was standing in attendance, the Master said, "I am weary. Linji asked, "Old man, why do you speak in your sleep?
The Master struck him. Linji overturned the meditation seat, whereupon the Master desisted.
Xuedou said: "These two practitioners possess the eye of simultaneous pecking and hatching; they have the function of simultaneous pecking and hatching.
Xuedou intends to snatch the deer from the mouth of a fierce tiger and divide the rabbit from the talons of a hungry hawk.
He dares to call Linji and Deshan both blind men. If there is anyone who can discern this, they may roam freely throughout the world. Miaoxi said:
Look at these two decisive men: when they happen to meet by chance on the road, it is natural that each has his own way of emerging.
Later, Chan Master Yunfeng Yue took up the case and said: "These two masters, one pressing and the other nudging, briefly reveal their style;
it is much like climbing a high mountain hand-in-hand. Even so, they cannot avoid being observed from the sidelines."
"The onlookers are ugly. But tell me, who is the bystander? After a long silence, he let out a shout.
According to what Miaoxi has observed, even Yunfeng could not avoid muddying the waters.
I would gladly grant both these old fellows a single indictment and bury them together in one pit. But tell me, where does the fault lie?
Longya asked, "When a student wields the sword of Moye and intends to take the Master's head, what then?
The Master extended his neck forward and said, "Eat! Longya said, "The head has fallen. The Master laughed loudly. Later, Longya went to Dongshan and recounted the previous conversation.
Dongshan asked, "What did Deshan say? Longya replied, "Deshan was speechless. Dongshan said, "Do not say he was speechless."

"Furthermore, take this head of Deshan’s that has fallen off and present it to me, the old monk, for inspection. At these words, Ya suddenly attained realization and prostrated himself in repentance and thanks.
A monk reported this to the Master (Linji), who said, "The old man Dongshan does not know good from bad. How long has it been since this fellow died?"
"What is the use of saving him? A monk came to visit; he stepped forward and assumed the stance of a wrestler.
The Master said, "Such rudeness deserves a blow from my hand. The monk brushed his sleeves and departed.
The Master said, "Even granting you this, you have only attained half. The monk turned around and let out a shout. The Master said, "I must strike you."

[The monk] first attained [realization]. He said, "There are people with clear eyes in all quarters. The Master said, "Naturally possessing eyes. The monk opened his eyes wide and said, "Cat! and then departed.
The Master said, "The Yellow River clears itself only once every three thousand years. The Master ordered his attendant to summon Yicun.
When Yicun came forward, the Master said, "I myself summoned Yicun; why have you come here? Yicun had no reply.
Xuefeng asked, "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of our school, does a student have any share in it? The Master struck him with a staff and said, "What are you saying?
Xuefeng replied, "I do not understand. The next day, he requested further instruction. The Master said, "In my school there are no words or phrases;
truly, there is not a single dharma to give to anyone. Because of this, Xuefeng attained realization.
When Yantou heard of this, he said, "The old man Deshan has a backbone as hard as iron; it cannot be bent.
Even so, within the gate of proclaiming the Teaching, he still falls short by a small measure.
Baofu asked Zhaoqing, "As for Yantou appearing in the world, what teaching did he have that surpassed Deshan's, such that you speak in this way?"
Qingyun said, "Do you not see Yantou say: 'It is like a person learning archery; only after a long time does one hit the mark'? Fokuang asked, "What is it like after hitting the mark?
Qingyun said, "Unfold your mat, Reverend; do you not recognize pain and itch? Fokuang said, "Today the Master has done more than just cite a story.
Qingyun said, "What kind of mental activity is yours, Reverend, in unfolding your mat? Mingzhao remarked, "How great [the Master's realization]!"
Zhaoqing: "To apply names and phrases is an error. A monk visited.
The Master asked the Rector, "How many new arrivals are there today? The Rector replied, "Eight people. The Master said, "Call them here;
I shall press them all down at once. Ascending the hall, he said: "When one has exhausted all knowledge, even the Buddhas of the three periods of time find their mouths hanging on the wall."
Above. There is still one person who laughs loudly, "Ha ha! If you recognize this person, your study of the Way is complete.
Alternatively, it may be considered a cryptic utterance of Deshan. Touzi Qian said: "Deshan is truly like having hidden away the moon over the heavens of Chu, yet leaving behind the stars of Han."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If you have no concerns within yourself, do not seek falsely. Even if you were to obtain something through false seeking, it would still not be attainment.
You need only be without concern in your mind and without a mind toward external affairs; then you will be spirit-like in your emptiness and wondrous in your voidness.

To speak of beginning or end regarding even a hair’s tip of this is entirely self-deception. Why? A single thought tied to even a hair’s breadth becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms."
When a fleeting emotion arises, one is bound in shackles for ten thousand kalpas. The names and titles of "saint" and "ordinary being" are all but empty sounds;
their extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not be burdened? And when you grow weary of them, they again become a great affliction.
"In the end, it is of no benefit. He addressed the assembly, saying: "Sons, from morning until evening, what business do you have?
Do not seek to flaunt your donkey lips and horse mouths by questioning that old fellow Deshan. I am not afraid of you at all. I wonder, sons, what doubts or suspicions do you have?
Lately, in this age of the Dharma’s decline, there are many demons and spirits roaming about the houses in great packs, saying:"
"I am a Chan master. I do not know how much of the Way of Chan you have learned; tell it to this old man.
You bald-headed slaves from all quarters, who teach you to practice for the sake of becoming Buddhas—how many Buddhas have you actually produced by running about to others' houses?
If there is nothing for you to learn, then why are you running about? If there is something to be learned, bring what you have learned here and present it."
Look at this old fellow! If even a single phrase does not accord with the truth, you must receive a severe beating before you will understand.

You have been bewitched by those old bald monks from all quarters, who claim, "I am a man of cultivation," and thus strike a hard pose and put on airs, appearing exactly like someone who has attained the Way.
Do not apply your mind in such a casual manner; otherwise, you will wander through the three realms for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes.
All these are states of having a mind. Why is this? When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise.

If you can achieve a single moment of non-arising, you will forever be liberated from birth and death, no longer bound by them. When you wish to walk, you walk; when you wish to sit, you sit. What else is there to do?
O worthy ones, I see that you all give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment wherever you go, yet you still seek it within the teachings of this old shaven-headed slave.

Downward! To study the Buddha-dharma and bear its burden, one should not spare even body or life. [Yet these people] have all had the eyes of their children nailed shut and severed the life-roots of their children;
they are just like two or three hundred harlots. They say, "I am the master who transforms others and establishes the Dharma-banner to open the eyes of future generations.
But can you save yourself? O virtuous ones, regarding such talk of practicing cultivation, have you not heard?
The Way. That old barbarian practiced for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; where is he now? After eighty years, he has died;
how is he any different from you? My children, do not be mad! I urge you: it would be better to rest, to go where there is no concern.
The moment you give rise to a single thought, you are already a member of Mara’s retinue—a layperson who has broken the precepts.
When you saw Deshan appear in the world, ten out of ten, five out of five, all intended to gather together to challenge him with difficult questions, hoping to leave him tongue-tied and speechless.
You are a mere puppet; why do you not come forth now? A needle kept inside a tattered sack—why do you not show your head? It is so!
A fine fellow. I wish to question you; be truthful and do not err. You, O worthy one, have been running about from house to house, saying, "I understand Chan, I understand the Way.
You pat your chest and rub your ribs, praising Yang and Zheng. But here, you must empty it all out before you can be at ease.
Simply ensure that externally you are not attached to sounds and forms, and internally you have no capacity for knowing or understanding; let your essence be free of both the ordinary and the sage.
What more is there to learn? Even if you were to master hundreds of thousands of subtle meanings, you would still be nothing but a "sore-eating ghost"—a mere malevolent spirit.
This void of mine: if you say it exists, it is not existent; if you say it does not exist, it is not non-existent.
To call it mundane, it is not mundane; to call it sacred, it is not sacred. It cannot be fixed in any place whatsoever. For you, it serves as the basis for the myriad dharmas.

Master: This old fellow dares not slander him. Thus, the Old Barbarian spat out much of the saliva of expedient means to tell you to go where there is no business and not to seek it outwardly. Yet you still refuse;
you wish to collect superior phrases and store them in your breast, using clever speech and your tongue to achieve your ends, wearing your coarse cloth skirt with pride.
People know me as a Chan master who seeks a place to show his face. If you hold such a view, I shall strike that ghost’s rump;
the day will come when you enter the Hell of the Plucked Tongue.

Everywhere you go, you seek people to say, "I am a guest from under the patriarchs," yet when questioned about the fundamental matter, your mouth becomes like a wooden stump. You then proceed to explain it to them.
"Bodhi, nirvana, suchness, and liberation—by extensively citing the teachings of the Tripitaka, you claim these are Chan and the Way;
this is merely deceiving the common folk. What connection does this have [to true realization]? You slander my ancestors. Old Hanshi’s own perspective was not like this."
Here there is no Buddha, nor is there any Dharma. Bodhidharma is but an old, scabby barbarian; the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages are dung-carriers;
the Two Awakenings of Equality and Subtlety are precept-breaking commoners; Bodhi and Nirvana are hitching posts for donkeys;

the Twelve Divisions of the Teaching are registers of ghosts and spirits, or paper for wiping pus from sores; and the Four Fruits, the Three Grades of Sages, the Initial Mind, and the Ten Stages—these are all [but such things].

Guarding ancient tombs—what ghosts! Even saving yourself is impossible. The Buddha is an old barbarian’s wooden bolt. (From "My Ancestors" down to this point is recorded in the *Huìyuán*). Yǎn of Yúnmén said:
"To praise the Buddhas and the Patriarchs, one must be an old man like Dēshān. O worthy ones, do not err. Your bodies are covered in sores; what business are you studying?
Having eaten your fill, you speak of True Suchness and Nirvāṇa. Is there still blood under your skin? One must be such a person.
Only a man of true capacity can attain this. Do not cherish the "sage," for "sage" is but an empty name.

Throughout the three realms and the ten directions of the world, if there were even a single speck of dust or a single dharma to be grasped, which you might then cling to, give rise to understanding for, and take as something to be preserved, valued, and cherished, you would fall entirely into the ranks of celestial Māras and externalists;
such is merely that which is acquired through study. It is also like a spirit or a wild fox that clings to grass and wood. All [such things are false].
"Disciples, in this place of mine, there is not a single dharma to provide you with an intellectual understanding.
I myself do not understand Zen; I am no enlightened teacher (kalyāṇamitra). I understand nothing at all.
I simply defecate and urinate, beg for food and clothing—what else is there? Old man Deshan advises you: it would be better to go back to your own proper nature immediately."

Rest! Do not act like madmen. Each person carries a corpse on their shoulders, wandering aimlessly everywhere, seeking to swallow the spittle from the mouths of old bald monks. They then claim, "I have entered the triple world;
I cultivate accumulated practices to nurture the holy embryo, vowing to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. When the old fellow Deshan sees such types as these, it is as if...
A poisoned arrow has entered my heart; flower-needles disorient my eyes. I have brought shame upon my ancestors and burdened my lineage.
You may scheme to represent me as a renunciant, but even the water offered by the donors of the ten directions cannot be consumed by one such as this. Do not even attempt to calculate it.
To dare to walk upon the land of another king’s realm, while your parents do not provide you with fine delicacies—is this not for no reason?
Do not misapply your mind; there will come a day when King Yama demands payment for your straw sandals.

He will pass a rope through your nostrils and tether you to a stake to repay your past debts. Do not say that this old man did not warn you. You all seem to have great merit, having encountered [this].
When Deshan appeared in the world, he untied your ropes for you, removed your headstall, and unloaded your pack, so that you might become a true person.
The three realms and six paths cannot confine you; there is no other method.
This is the brilliant, vast void—unobstructed and sovereign—not something you can adorn. From the Buddhas down to the Patriarchs, all [have realized this].
This Dharma is transmitted so that one may attain liberation. The entire Great Canon of teachings is merely intended to guide you people of the present day.

My sons, do not seek it elsewhere! Even when the little green-eyed barbarian monk Bodhidharma came here, he too was only teaching you to go about with no affairs, teaching you not to engage in contrived activity. Put on your clothes, eat your food, defecate, and urinate.
There is no longer any birth-and-death to fear, nor is there any nirvana to be attained, nor any bodhi to be realized;

you are simply an ordinary person with nothing to do. First of all, do not fold your hands and pose as a Chan master, seeking a way out by using clever words to bewitch the young, desiring to have others call you an "Elder. Within your own portion, there is not a single thing to be found.
Sheshuo: "People merely know that their consciousness is vast and expansive, yet day and night they ceaselessly fabricate strange phenomena.
They praise Yang and Zheng, claiming, 'I am a follower of Master Mazu of Jiangxi. Old Hans Deshan, moreover, was not even one of your kind;
I saw that Master Shitou did not recognize good from evil, which is why the old man reviled him. My sons, you simply must not become attached."
Regarding sounds, forms, names, phrases, meanings, and states; mechanical principles; good and evil, ordinary and sage;

grasping and rejecting, objective conditions; defilement and purity, light and darkness; existence and non-existence—when you can penetrate all these thoughts in this very way, only then are you a person of no affairs.
Even the Buddhas are not like you; even the Patriarchs are not like you. O worthy one, do not trample about; your footprints are already wide enough. Depart!
There is no path of dhyāna to be learned. If there were something to be learned and attained, that would be the view of the "two-headed, three-headed" heterodox practitioners (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, there are no supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) or transformations to be obtained. You claim that supernatural power is the mark of a sage;

yet the devas, nāgas, spirits, the five-fold transcendents, heterodox practitioners, and asuras also possess supernatural powers—would they, then, all be Buddhas? To dwell alone on a solitary peak—[one...]

He observes the fast of eating only eggs, sits upright without lying down, and performs prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day. He doubts the life and death of others, yet the Old Barbarian has said:

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the law of arising and ceasing. If you claim that one attains [realization] by entering meditative absorption, concentrating the spirit, and practicing quiet contemplation, then consider the Nirgranthas and other non-Buddhist teachers who also enter the great samādhi of eighty thousand kalpas—could they not be Buddhas? Clearly, this is heresy.

Seeing a spectral apparition, he said: "O Benevolent One, the Old Barbarian is not a sage. The Buddha is but the Old Barbarian’s wooden stake. I merely wish for you to discern what is good and what is evil;
do not cling to self and others, lest you be impaled by the stakes of the various sages, the stake of bodhi, or the stake of liberation. "Excellence! [he exclaimed].
"Names and words, and their subtle meanings, drown and bind you. Why is this? As long as a single moment of deluded mind is not exhausted, it is the continuity of birth and death.
O worthy one, time does not wait for man; do not let the days pass by in negligence. Time is precious.
This old man does not expect you, a mere rustic slave, to carry this burden. If you are willing, believe and accept it; if you are not willing, each person has [their own responsibility]."
"Take this bowl and carry it away. This old man does not seek anything from you. There are many old bald slaves in all directions who occupy a certain place, preaching Zen and speaking of the Way;
you must go quickly to learn from them and copy them. In this place of mine, I ultimately have not a single dharma to give to you people.
You gentlemen may ask and learn for the sake of intellectual understanding, but I, this old man, cannot do so."

They enter the Hell of the Uprooted Tongue. If there is even a single speck of dust or a single dharma shown to people and explained, saying that there is a Buddha, there is a Dharma, or that there is a Triple Realm from which one may escape—these are all merely wild fox spirits and enchantments. O virtuous ones, do you wish to recognize it?
It is simply empty space; not even a trace of dust can be found therein. It is pure in every place, its radiance penetrating through and through, manifest both inside and out.
Luminously transparent. Without affairs, without dependence, and without a place to rest—what matters could there be? From birth until death, this old man has been nothing but an old bhikṣu.
Though born within the triple world, he remains unstained by defilement. If you wish to attain liberation, where would you go?
Even if there were a place to go, it would still be a cage, giving Mara an opportunity to exploit you. O worthy one, do not employ your body and mind.
There is nothing to be attained. It simply requires that at all times you do not employ external sounds or forms;

rather, you should immediately cast off everything from where you have been practicing until now, suddenly shedding your fetters and forever leaving behind the entanglements of the hindrances. When not a single thought arises, the past and future limits are severed.
Without thinking or recollecting, there is not a single dharma that can meet the mind. How, O worthy one, do you intend to open your mouth?
Mouth. You have much knowledge and understanding; yet, have you ever recognized his face?
Even for those who have left the household life, including Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Ten Grounds whose minds are fully perfected, they cannot find his traces.

For this reason, the various devas rejoice, the earth spirits support his feet, the Buddhas of the ten directions offer praise, and the Demon King weeps. Why is this? Because this void is so vibrantly alive.
There is no root or stem; there is no place of abiding. If you reach this point, the moment your eyes flicker or move, you have missed the connection.
O worthy one, do not seek the Buddha; the Buddha is a great murderous thief who has deceived how many people, causing them to fall into the pit of the demon of lust!
Do not seek Mañjuśrī or Samantabhadra; they are but country slaves. How tragic! You are a dignified man of noble bearing, yet you consume their poison.

The medicine has taken effect. He pretends to have the face of a Chan master, seeing spirits and ghosts; later, he will go mad and run about to other houses, seeking a female diviner to cast a divination for him.
Then some ignorant, old, shaven-headed slave will immediately perform a divination for him and tell him:
"I shall teach you to worship the ghost-monks and ghost-buddhas of the Patriarchs, the ghosts of Bodhi and Nirvana. This is a little lewd woman; not understanding, he asks her.
"What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? This old bald slave then struck the meditation seat as a dramatic gesture, held up his whisk, and said:
"Fine weather, fine rain, fine lanterns. He artfully composed these words and forcibly created complications;
he spoke of mysterious paths and bird-tracks, and extended his hand. If one were to grasp such explanations, it would be like placing a precious vessel inside something impure. It is like...
To take human excrement and treat it as sandalwood incense—O worthy one, since you are a man of noble character and I am likewise so, with whom would you feel timid or weak?
All day long you go to the mouths of those old, shaven-headed slaves from all quarters to receive their spittle and phlegm, eating it without the slightest sense of shame or remorse.
Alas, alas! You have driven yourself mad; the law of cause and effect is perfectly clear. A water-buffalo pulling a plow and dragging a harrow is no different from you.
His eyes protrude; his strength fails him. A great club strikes your spine, yet you claim the Buddha’s food and clothing as proof that "I have practiced the Way.
If you do not comprehend the Great Principle, even if you were to pass through the Buddha's belly, you would still be nothing more than a functional arrowhead.
Having never encountered a true person, you mistake the flickering light at the gates of the six sense organs for enlightenment.
To speak of a "manifesto" (lùbù) from within the mouth is but a cryptic word and a wondrous phrase; its brilliance is sharp and new. Yet, alas, you yourself have no share in it.
O benevolent one, this is merely the spittle of others. Furthermore, there is another class who gather in groups of three or two to deliberate:
"Where is there no trouble? We shall pass through winter and summer; let us quickly discuss Chan and the Way. They think they possess understanding and realization.
"Virtuous One, you have formed such a view of the principles as a whole, seeking only what is convenient. How could there be such a principle? You shall enter hell one day;
do not say I did not tell you, my sons. Everywhere you go, you will not pick a single stalk of vegetable nor carry a single bundle of firewood.
When your merit is exhausted in a single morning, you will simply have to eat grass. You have consumed the offerings of the faithful in vain and falsely claimed the title of 'Participant' (Chan)."
"Disciple, you have further assumed the appearance of a Chan master, which is of no benefit to others.

As for your own state, throughout the twelve hours of the day, wherever you walk and act, your mind is constantly attached to external objects. When seeing people, you merely wish to be seductive and fickle;

you point east while speaking of the west, and though it is right before your eyes and on your lips, you truly do not see it. You only wish to use superficial words to test and gauge my understanding. I, this old man,"
What distinguishes you all? Gentlemen, do not seize upon a single moment of vision;

otherwise, you will hastily swallow his poisonous medicine like lustful women who observe neither fasts nor precepts—blind shavelings, monks as common as sheep, who overturn others and cast them into hell.
O worthy ones, do not casually look through the manuals, seeking phrases and meanings, or hunting for victory and defeat, passing them back and forth one to another.

[The Master] said: "When will you ever find rest? This old man’s exhortation is no evil thing; you must truly bring your own eyes with you to distinguish between the clear and the turbid, and to discern what is the Buddha’s word and what is the Mara’s word. Do not allow yourself to be deluded by others.

Therefore, all those superior names and phrases are merely the skillful means employed for a time by the Old Barbarian. You must truly find rest; do not rely on a single thing, lest you be led astray by him."

Constructing interpretations through language, discriminating between the near and the distant, being flighty, hollow, deceitful, and false, and recording the idle talk and long-winded speech of others—all these are merely *anumāna* (inference).
O Benevolent One, this old man only fears that you, my sons, will fall into pits and ditches, perform deeds of meager merit, lose your eloquence, and be content with a little.
Standing still in a quiet place, you are unwilling to advance, deluding yourselves amidst various objects and becoming distracted.
He runs after others, wandering through the myriad dharmas, because he does not believe that empty space is fundamentally without affairs and cannot be increased or diminished by others.
You all are like old crows whose bodies are in the void while their minds are on piles of dung, seeking only dead things to eat.
My sons, do not say that the old fellow Deshan has never entered the monasteries to deliberate; [he has]. (He raised his voice.)
He reviles them, showing no human feeling and fearing no karma, solely because his sons do not maintain their proper station but roam the four quarters,
frequenting the doors of others like female ghosts who carry messages from one to another, interpreting matters according to circumstances while never forgetting their own tracks and traces.
I myself have not yet established myself; I constantly carry a corpse upon my back, bound by shackles and chains for five hundred and one thousand li, until I arrive before Master Deshan.
I stand here with my eight limbs planted on the ground, as if I were in debt to you regarding the Way of Chan. Master, you must speak for me.
I shall demonstrate the total functioning of this old man to you. This great staff is armor to shield the rustic slave; he reviles the thief while his own face is pierced by arrows.

He does not recognize good from evil. When he comes before me, it is as if meeting a man from Lǐzhōu who serves a hearty meal of boiled fish and stew—this is merely to help you cast off your heavy burden, remove your shackles, and become a true person. Will you consent?
"Ma! If you are willing, then stay; if you are not willing, feel free to depart. Take care. Addressing the assembly: "When there are words, one mounts the tiger’s head and gathers its tail;
under the first phrase, the fundamental principle is clarified. When there are no words, the sharp edge of the pivot is laid bare, like a flash of lightning or a stroke of a whisk.
The Master was ill. A monk asked, "Is there anyone who does not fall ill? The Master said, "There is. The monk asked:
"What is it to be free from illness? The Master replied, "A-ye, a-ye. He further addressed the assembly, saying, "To feel for echoes in empty space is but to weary your mind and spirit.
When one awakens from a dream, one realizes it was not real; in the end, what event has actually occurred? Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away.
This was the third day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty.

The Fifth Generation under the Sixth Patriarch.
▲ Chan Master Liangjie Wuben of Mount Dongshan in Ruizhou was the son of the Yu family of Kuaiji. In his youth, he followed a teacher to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*.
When he reached the passage, "No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind," he suddenly touched his face with his hand and asked his teacher, "I possess eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth;
why does the sutra say they do not exist? His teacher was struck with amazement and marveled at him.

He said, "I am not your teacher," and immediately pointed him toward Mount Wuxie to pay respects to Chan Master Mo and receive the tonsure. At the age of twenty-one, he went to Mount Song to receive full ordination.
While traveling, his first stop was to visit Nanquan, where he happened upon a vegetarian feast being held on the anniversary of Mazu’s death.
Zhuanzi asked the assembly, "Tomorrow we shall prepare a meal for Mazu; I wonder whether Mazu will come or not. The assembly remained silent.
The Master (Xuefeng) stepped forward and said, "He will come when he has a companion. Zhuanzi remarked, "Though this youth is young, he is quite capable of being refined.
The Master replied, "Preceptor, do not suppress the noble to make it base. He then went to visit Miaoyan of Mount Huishan and asked, "I have recently heard of Nanyang..."
National Teacher Zhong had a dialogue concerning "insentient things preaching the Dharma" (*wúqíng shuōfǎ*) that I have not yet fully investigated.
Guishan asked, "Dharma brother, do you remember it? The Master replied, "I remember it. Guishan said, "Try reciting it once for me. The Master then recited it:
A monk asked, "What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas? The National Teacher said, "Walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles. The monk said, "Walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles..."
"Is this not insentient? The National Teacher replied, "It is. The monk asked, "Does it understand how to preach the Dharma? The National Teacher replied, "It preaches constantly;
it preaches with blazing intensity without interruption. The monk asked, "Why do I not hear it? The National Teacher replied, "It is you who do not hear it;
it cannot be said that it prevents others from hearing. The monk asked, "I wonder, what kind of person is able to hear it?"
The Master said, "All the sages have heard it. The monk asked, "Does the Master also hear it? The National Teacher said, "I do not hear it.

The monk said, "If the Master does not hear it, how do you know that insentient things can preach the Dharma? The National Teacher said, "It is precisely because I do not hear it that I am able to know."
"If I were to hear it, I would be equal to all the sages; you, however, would not hear me preaching the Dharma.
The monk said, "In that case, sentient beings have no share in it? The National Teacher said, "I preach for the sake of sentient beings; I do not preach for the sake of the sages."
The monk asked, "After sentient beings hear this, what then? The National Teacher said, "They are not sentient beings.

The monk asked, "On what scriptural authority is it based that insentient things preach the Dharma? The National Teacher said, "It is evident that words do not encompass the scriptures; this is not something spoken by gentlemen."
"Do you not see that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'The lands speak, sentient beings speak, and all things of the three periods of time speak'?
After the Master finished citing this, Muzhou said, 'I have it here as well, but it is simply rare to encounter the right person. The Master said, 'I do not yet understand.'"
The Master requested instruction. Guishan held up his whisk and asked, "Do you understand? The Master said, "I do not understand. He requested, "Please, Preceptor, explain it to me.
Guishan said, "The mouth born of one's parents shall never be used to speak for a son. The Master asked, "Are there others who, at the same time as you, aspire to the Way?
Guishan said, "From here, going to You County in Liling, there are interconnected stone chambers where Yungyan Daoyuan resides."

Baizhang said, "He once questioned me, saying, 'When a student wishes to follow a teacher, what should he do? I replied to him, 'You must completely cut off all leakage. Have you not seen how the ancients said that "heavenly flowers fell" and "stones nodded"? Even that did not concern one's own affairs; what else could it be but something trivial?
Now, you intend to take this finite body and mind and apply them toward the infinite—what possible connection can there be? It is like taking a square...
A wooden peg inserted into a round hole—how many contradictions and obscurities there are!
If this were not the case, even if you could speak with a profusion of flowers and brocade-like patterns, it would still be of no use; you would remain within the realm of consciousness and emotion.
All matters must be exhausted right here before one can be free from fault; only then can one attain liberation. If even a single hair’s breadth remains unexhausted, one will immediately be caught.
How much more so when worldly entanglements are even greater? To err by a hair’s breadth is to commit offenses as vast as mountains and peaks.
As the ancients said: "The place of learning is not mysterious; it is entirely a matter of common custom. If one cannot relinquish the things of the inner chambers, they all become leaks."
You must directly engage here in coming, going, and arriving; only by exhausting all affairs can you be free from fault.
It is like a person who has mastered every head and penetrated every object—such a one is merely called a "man of affairs," but is never called "noble.
Know that the path of the noble is distinct; it is the most profound and weighty in the world.
Precious things must not be brought before those who are honored and noble; one must know that this is inconceivable and should not be treated with mere superficial courtesy.
Thus the ancients said: "It is like two mirrors facing each other, their radiance reflecting one another's light, without any increase or decrease.
Is this not simply as it is? Yet even so, it is still called a matter of images and reflections. It is like the rising sun shining forth.
"In the world, clarity and brightness constitute one half. What is that other half called?
Nowadays, people do not recognize even the coarse and shallow matters at the gateway of light and shadow; they take these to be the affairs of the inner chamber—how could this possibly suffice?
He further said, "The matter of ascending to heaven must be cast away before the assembly; the matter of reaching completion must be set forth before the assembly."
He pushed it away. Throwing it to the ground, it made a sound like gold. "You must not turn your head back to look at it. What other use would there be for it?

Do you not see that when the Second Patriarch was then widely versed in poetry, books, and the Tripitaka of the holy teachings—seeing them as clearly as the palm of his hand—why did he still seek from Bodhidharma the settling of his mind?
From this, one should know that the matters within this gate are no ordinary affair. I...
Taste the words of Yunju; know the profound meaning of the noble and honorable. You must awaken to this yourself. Alas!
Those who governed the world by simply wearing their ceremonial robes were Yao and Shun. A monk asked Caoshan, "When a son returns to his father, why does the father not acknowledge him at all?
Caoshan said, "It is only natural that it should be so. The monk asked, "Wherein lies the affection between father and son? Caoshan said, "Only then..."
This established the bond between father and son. [A monk] asked, "What is the bond between father and son?
Shanshan said, "Even swords and axes cannot cleave it. Another monk asked, "What is the lion? Shanshan said, "No beasts can approach it.
[The monk] asked, "What is the lion’s cub? Shanshan said, "It is that which can devour its parents. [The monk] said, "If no beasts can approach it, why then..."
"Why was he instead swallowed by his son? Shanshan said, "Have you not heard it said: 'If the son lets out a roar, both grandfather and father are extinguished'?
He asked, "After they are extinguished, what then? Shanshan said, "The whole body returns to the father. He asked, "I wonder, at the moment the grandfather is extinguished—"
"Where has the father returned? Shanshan said, "The place of return is also exhausted. [The monk] asked, "Why did you previously say that his whole body returns to the father?
Shanshan said, "It is like a prince who can accomplish the affairs of an entire nation.
He added, "Dharma Teacher, you must not let this matter remain isolated or stagnant; you must surely scatter a few more blossoms upon the withered tree."—Touzi Ganwen.
Chan Master Touzi. A monk asked, "The father did not go there; why did the son go instead? Touzi said, "Is this not the business of another's house?
The monk asked, "Does the relationship between father and son still belong to effort? Touzi said, "It does not. The monk asked, "If it does not belong to effort, how is it so?
Touzi said, "Father and son each attain liberation for themselves. The monk asked, "Why is it thus? Touzi said: [The text ends here.]
"You have met me, Master Huayan Long. When you were young, you served Master Shimen Che. One day you asked Shimen:
'If one can simply find peace and ease wherever one is, one will naturally accord with the ancient tracks.
Although you had these words, when the mind of doubt has not yet ceased, what then? Shimen said: "Only by knowing that [the Way] exists can one find peace and ease wherever one is. It is like...
If a person lives in a prefecture or county and hears or sees thousands of wonders and hundreds of anomalies, they regard them all as ordinary matters;

unaware that such things exist, they remain at ease. It is like a person living in a village who, upon encountering even a slight display of sensory phenomena, becomes startled and spreads rumors of it being strange.
Master Dongshan once instructed the assembly, saying: "If you wish to know this matter, it is like a family raising three sons."
One is stationed in the prefecture, one in the village, and one in the county. One uses the money and goods of the household;
one uses the money and goods of outside places; and there is one who obtains neither the money and goods of the household nor those of outside places.
Now tell me: which one is appropriate for the prefecture, and which one is appropriate for the county?
One of them was staying in the village. A monk asked him, "Are these three not confused about the relative weight [of their offenses]?
Dōu replied, "Yes. The monk asked, "What is the point of origin for this person? Dōu said, "He knows that there is, yet he does not know that there is."
"This person is from where he originated," the monk asked. Dōng said, "I do not know for certain whether this person has departed from this day or not.
The monk said, "He has also departed from this very day. The monk said, "If that is so, then he belongs to 'merit' (*gong*). Dōng said, "Yes. The monk asked, "What kind of merit is it called?
Dōng said, "It is called the merit of having already accomplished the task. The monk asked, "Does this person still know that there is such a thing?"
The monk asked, "What about those within the prefecture? Dong said, "To know that there is [something] is to understand how to honor what is weighty.
The monk said, "If so, then those within the village have fully understood their transgression. Dong said, "Yes. The monk asked, "What is this person's point of transgression?
Dong said, "Not knowing that there is [something], yet calling oneself an 'ordinary person'—this is the person's point of transgression. Have you not seen the former master say: 'Now...'"?

At that time, those who study the Way must know there is a place for turning over [the body] before they can succeed. Long said, "The ancients knew this; were they then like people from a provincial town?
Or did they also have to reach it through 'receiving and honoring'? Dumen said, "Dongshan asked: 'How is it at the time of directing?
How is it at the time of receiving? How is it at the time of merit? And how is it at the time of shared merit?'"
"What is it like? [The Master said: "What is it like when you are working? A monk asked, "What is 'directing' (xiang)? [The Master said: "What is it like when you are eating?
[The monk asked,] "What is 'offering' (feng)? [The Master said: "What is it like when you are turning your back? [The monk asked,] "What is 'merit' (gong)? [The Master said:

"What is it like when you have set down your hoe? [The monk asked,] "What is 'merit shared with others' (gong-gong)? [The Master said: "It cannot be seen. [The monk asked,] "What is it like? [The Master said: "..."
"What is 'merit upon merit'? He replied, "Non-sharing. This is called the five stages of meritorious achievement (*guǒxūn wèiwèi*).
It is like a newborn dove whose downy feathers are most endearing; after a long time, it will naturally be able to fly high and soar far.
A monk asked Master Yúnjū Hóngjué, "What is that which the śramaṇa values most? Jué said, "The place where the mind-consciousness does not reach."

Hong Juefan said: "Regarding the fundamental tenets of the Dongshan school, there is a taboo against 'full completion' (shicheng) in speech; one does not wish to commit such an error, for to do so is called 'touching upon a taboo.

For instance, regarding the Five Ranks, it is said: 'If one can merely avoid touching upon the current taboos, that is already superior to the talent of those who had their tongues cut off in a previous dynasty.
Since Hongjue was a high disciple of Dongshan, the fact that his response was of such a nature—was this not [the case]?"
Is this not a matter of avoiding taboo? It is said that Dongpo was most skilled at employing analogies. He once remarked:
"By extrapolating from what I know to what I do not know, consider an infant: when first born, one guides them with speech; as they grow slightly older, one teaches them writing.
The mouth must reach the point of forgetting sound before it can speak; the hand must reach the point of forgetting the brush before it can write. This...
This is what I know. When the mouth cannot forget sound, then speech is difficult to coordinate with written composition;
when the hand cannot forget the brush, then calligraphy is difficult to master through carving and engraving.

Yet, when one reaches the ultimate state of mutual forgetting, then in describing the workings of the mind and responding to the myriad transformations of things, it happens suddenly and without self-awareness. Indeed, this is not a matter of avoiding taboo names.

"Revering the ten completions is the Dharma. Hongjue did not forget the Dharma; how could he otherwise have been able to recognize the fundamental principle? The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"All sages and worthies attain their distinctions through the Dharma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Hongjue applied this in his *Linjian Lu*, which further states:
"Now, all spoken teachings consist of three successive phrases, being good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end."
At the beginning, one must first teach them to give rise to a wholesome mind; in the middle, one shatters that wholesomeness; and only at the end can it be called "wholesome.
A Bodhisattva is not a Bodhisattva, yet he is named a Bodhisattva. Dharma is not Dharma, nor is it non-Dharma. It is entirely like this.
If one were to answer with just a single phrase, it would cause people to fall into hell; if one were to speak all three phrases at once, they would fall into hell of their own accord.

This does not involve the affairs of the teaching master. Thus, we know that the ancient great masters’ expounding of the Dharma was entirely based on the methods and regulations of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
those who do not understand take these words to be merely casual or arbitrary. This is the same intent as found in Asanga’s commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
When one with clear insight into the Way examines the fifteen characters of the title of Dongshan’s "Five Ranks" (*Wuwei*), [one perceives their profound significance].
Regarding the arrangement [of the verses]: the Elder Jiewu said, "From the center of the center, one goes to the biased; from the biased of the center, one arrives at the center;

from the combined, one reaches. Following the explanation of Jiyin, *Rendian yimou* (The Eye of the Human and Heavenly) changed "reaches in the combined" (*jianzhong dao*) to "arrives in the biased" (*pianzhong zhi*).
Huanjì said: "Many people point to the five ranks of Dongshan as 'ruler and subject.'"
Regarding the avoidance of speech that touches upon taboos and the value placed on the pivot of indirect expression (*huíhù*):

Linji’s use of the staff and the shout was intended to fully uphold the orthodox command and directly reveal the family style. Yet, one fails to realize that the use of the staff and the shout is itself the secret mandate of indirect expression and avoiding taboos;
and the avoidance of speech touching taboos and the value of indirect expression is precisely the wondrous function of the full upholding and direct pointing.

It is a matter of fortune. Furthermore, to not speak of "black" when it is black, but instead say "midnight charcoal," and not speak of "white" when it is white, but instead say "ancient mirror" or "old woman," is a form of evasive ambiguity that remains merely superficial.

Indeed, the existence or non-existence of all phenomena belongs entirely to conventional designations; they possess no ultimate reality. If one insists upon fixed names for them, it is entirely a false view. Therefore:

Dongshan uses black and white as a provisional means to demonstrate "reciprocal interplay" (*huixu*). He avoids direct confrontation and avoids total completion; these are dead words. Therefore it is said:
"Borrowing black to represent the provisional, he uses white to indicate the partial. The absolute does not abide in the absolute—midnight is empty and luminous.
The partial does not abide in the partial—daybreak is dark and obscured. This has been the way all sages and worthies have taught since antiquity; Dongshan specifically did this for [his disciples].

It is simply brought forth. How could there be any sage or worthy one in the world who, without employing indirect expression (*huixu*) or avoiding tabooed terms, would use ten instances of literal, "dead" language to instruct others?
Juefan says that where the mind-consciousness (*xinshi*) cannot reach is the tabooed term; yet he praises [the master] for forgetting dharma and consciousness to realize the essence of the school.
I fear that Hongjue would not have been willing to nod his head in agreement, for the mind-consciousness...
To say that "not reaching [the point]" constitutes a taboo violation would mean that Dongshan was not a Buddha.

Is it then the case that even "even if one were to bring it forth, there is nowhere to place words" is all a taboo violation? One cannot simply say that because Dongshan has passed away, there is no need to correct him.
As for the desire to simplify the "Middle of the Middle" into the "Extreme of the Extreme," I initially agreed with this view.
However, upon repeatedly examining the discourse on Dongshan’s Five Ranks, I realized it was not so. Why?

It is because "the ruler facing [the minister]" represents the "Extreme within the Center," while "the minister serving the ruler" represents the "Center within the Extreme. "Coming from the Center" refers to the Ruler...
This is the state. It is what Caoshan referred to as "originally having no things. When a student realizes this, it is their achievement; thus it is called "achievement" (*gong*).

It is like the contemplation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is the principle-dharma realm (*li-fajie*). Because the "correct" and the "partial" are both harmonized, it is called "shared achievement" (*gong-gong*).
This is like the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma*). "Merit upon merit" is like the non-obstruction between phenomenon and phenomenon.
Now, taking "shared merit" as the "partial-middle ultimate," those with non-reliant wisdom know this to be incorrect. Furthermore, ancient masters have said: "Phenomena do not exist independently.
To observe them in isolation is the realm of conceptual cognition (*jñāna*), not the realm of contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*). They further stated: "Form..."
In the "Middle" there is no "Emptiness. When both principle and phenomenon are utterly severed, then even "reaching the Middle" cannot be established; this is truly as Master Juefan said.
The Great Master’s expounding of the Dharma always adheres to the formal methods of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Miaoxi personally met various venerable ancestors of the Dongshan lineage and once received their secret transmissions within the meditation hall; when he cited the language of the Five Ranks, he likewise followed the "reaching the Middle."

This text has never been altered to be biased; it reaches the ultimate point. This, too, can serve as proof. Furthermore, regarding the matter of cutting out the tongue, Juefan cites He Ruo Bi while omitting Vasubandhu.

Since Vasubandhu slandered the Mahāyāna by practicing the Hīnayāna and intended to have his tongue cut off—an act that most directly touches upon a taboo—why did he set aside the close precedent to follow the distant one? Moreover, [he omits] "the Eye of Humanity and Heaven."
To assign the five princes to the five ranks and place the posthumously born (mashō) in the position of the legitimate heir is erroneous.

Furthermore, to equate the one born within the womb (naishō) with the one born by normal delivery (tanjō) is also incorrect. The one born by delivery is still subject to waiting [for succession], whereas the one born within the womb is capable of immediately inheriting the lineage.
Kakuhan has discussed this in great detail, as already recorded above; there is no need to elaborate further.
Furthermore, there are those who claim that the Dong lineage has fallen into excessive verbal explanation and is not as direct as Linji’s approach. This is also incorrect.
How do the guest and host differ from the ruler and subject? How do the four shouts differ from the five ranks? To be like blind men feeling an elephant is truly pitiable.

Tai said, "The fault lies within the midst of activity. The Master then called to his attendant and had him remove the fruit table.
Taisu Zhe said: "Do you all know where Dongshan has landed? If you do not, you will likely interpret this in terms of right and wrong, gain and loss.

even if all the people in the entire world were to come, they would not dare to look at it with a single glance."—Langye Jue.
Yun said, "If it were not for the old man Dongshan, how could he have discerned this? Nevertheless, even so, Dongshan still lacks one move.
Yungai Ben said, "Although Dongshan possesses the tongs and hammer for shattering empty space, he still lacks that one move."
Yet there were no needles or thread for mending. When he said that it was being put to use, he simply said, "Please, Head Seat, have some fruit.
If Head Seat Tai had been a true monk, he would have spat it out even after eating it.
Question: "If a snake swallows a shrimp, is it right to save it? Or is it right not to save it? The Master said: "If you save it, its two eyes will not see;
if you do not save it, its form and shadow will not be manifest."
Huanji said: "In the past, the Inspector of Hongzhou asked Mazu, 'Is it right to eat meat and drink wine, or is it not?
Mazu replied, 'To eat is the official’s emolument; to abstain is the official’s blessing.
When Zen Master Guoyi of Mount Jingshan was asked about two envoys staying at an inn where a post official had slaughtered a sheep for them, one of the envoys heard of this..."
One person saves; another does not save. Are their offenses and blessings different? Guo Yi said: "The one who saves possesses compassion;
the one who does not save possesses liberation. These three venerable elders—one was struck by thunder and swept away by lightning, yet he fell back into the leakage of views.

One person possesses the luster of pearls and the smoothness of jade, yet falls into the leakage of emotion. Another person is as lofty as a mountain and as deep as water, yet falls into the leakage of speech.
If one can discern each of these, one has eyes but is like one who is blind; if one cannot discern them, one has a mouth but is like one who is mute.
Furthermore, if anyone says that they have emerged identically from the mold without any discrepancy, beat your breast and weep aloud! You must!

"Having attained the Way, you have long since entered it. Feng said, "I have no mouth. The Master said, "Let us grant that you have no mouth;
now give me back my eyes. Feng was speechless. Once, while Xuefeng was carrying firewood, he dropped a bundle down in front of the Master.
The Master asked, "How much does it weigh? Feng said, "No one in the entire world can lift it up. The Master said, "How did it get here?"
At this point, Feng remained silent. [Xuefeng] asked: "When it is said, 'Diligently wipe away the dust at all times,' why is it that one does not obtain his robe and bowl?
I wonder, what kind of person is fit to receive them? The Master said: "One who does not enter the gate. [Xuefeng] asked: "As for one who does not enter the gate..."
“Will you get it back? The Master said, “Even so, I cannot help but give it back to him.
He added, “Even if one says directly, ‘Originally there is not a single thing,’ one still does not yet merit his robe and bowl.
Tell me, who merits them? You must provide a turning word here; tell me, what word can you offer? At that time, a monk offered nine [turning words].
Sixteen turns of speech were all rejected; only at the very last turn did he finally satisfy the Master’s mind.
The Master said, "Why did you not speak in this way earlier, Ācārya? Another monk had been listening secretly, yet he did not hear the final turn.

He subsequently requested instruction from that monk, but the monk refused to speak. Thus they followed one another for three years, and in the end, the monk would not provide the clue. One day, because...
The monk became ill. Another monk said, "I have requested you to repeat that previous story for three years, yet I have not received your compassion.
I shall not take it well; I will depart taking it poorly. He then took up a knife and said, "If you do not speak for me, I will kill you, Elder!
The monk was terrified and said, "Dharma-teacher, wait! I will speak for you. He then said, "Even if it were brought forth, there would be no place [for it to abide]."
The monk bowed in thanks.
Xuedou Xian said, "Since he did not accept it, his eyes must be open; had he accepted it, they would surely be blind.
Do you see the patriarch’s robe and bowl? If one enters the gate through this, then they are handed over with both hands—not only at Dayu Ridge."
"One at the head of the ridge cannot be lifted up. Even if all the people of the nation were to come, one would simply take it away slowly.
Tiantong picked this up and said: "Changlu is not like this; one must bring it forth. If you do not bring it forth, how can you know that it is not accepted?
One must not accept it. If you do not not-accept it, how can you avoid bringing it forth? That which is brought forth must necessarily be [so]."
"This eye does not grasp the bottom; truly it is blind. Do you understand? "It illuminates everything to the end while its essence has no dependence;
the entire body merges with the Great Way. Question: "Master, you usually teach students to practice the 'Bird Path. I do not yet know what the Bird Path is. The Master said: "Not..."
He met a man who asked, "How should one practice? The Master said, "You must simply proceed with no self-interest beneath your feet.
The man asked, "As for practicing the 'Bird Path' (vīthi), is that not the original face? The Master said, "Why, Venerable Sir, are you so inverted?
The man asked, "In what way am I inverted? The Master said, "If you were not inverted, why would you instead mistake the servant for the master?"
Lang asked, "What is one's original face? The Master said, "One does not travel the path of birds.
Later, Jia Shan asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Dongshan. Jia Shan asked, "What words or phrases did Dongshan use to instruct his disciples?
The monk said, "He usually teaches students to train in three paths. Jia Shan asked, "What are these three?"
Lu said, "The Dark Road, the Bird Path. He extended his hand. Shanshan asked, "Is there truly such a saying? Lu replied, "There truly is.
Shanshan said, "A guide for a thousand li; a draft for the recluse beneath the forest trees—how tragic!
Fushan Yuan said, "Were it not for the falling yellow leaves, how could one know that this is autumn?"
The Master asked a monk, "What is your name? The monk replied, "So-and-so. The Master said, "Who is the master of you, the venerable one?
The monk replied, "I am seeing him right now as I respond. The Master said, "Alas, alas! People of the present age for the most part are all like this;
they recognize only that which follows behind the donkey or the horse and take that to be themselves. This is precisely why the Buddha-dharma is sinking. This is 'the host within the guest.'"
[The Master] had not yet distinguished [the point]. How could one discern the "Lord among Lords"? The monk then asked, "What is the Lord among Lords?
The Master said, "You, *ācārya*, should say it yourself. The monk said, "If I were able to say it, I would merely be a 'lord among guests.
What then is the Lord among Lords? The Master said, "To speak thus is easy; to maintain continuity is very difficult. He then presented this verse: "Alas! To see..."
Nowadays, those who study the Way are in their thousands and tens of thousands, all recognizing the gateway. It is just like entering the capital to pay court to the Sovereign;
they reach the Tongguan Pass and immediately stop. There was a monk who was unwell and wished to see the Master. The Master went to him.
The monk said, "Master, why do you not save the sons and daughters of this household? The Master said, "Whose sons and daughters are you? The monk replied:
“Such-and-such a person is the son or daughter of a great icchantika family. The Master remained silent for a long time.
The monk asked, “What is it like when the four mountains press in from all sides? The Master said, “In my youth, I too passed beneath the eaves of people’s houses.
The monk asked, “Do you yield to them or not? The Master said, “I do not yield. The monk asked, “Where then would you have me go? The Master said, “To a field of parched grain stubble.”
He went inside. The monk let out a sigh and said, "Farewell," then sat down and passed away. The Master struck his head three times with his staff and said, "You only know how to go like that;
you do not know how to come back like this. One night during a formal assembly (*sengcan*), he did not light the lamps.
A monk came forward to ask a question, then withdrew. The Master ordered an attendant to light the lamp and then called for the monk who had just asked the question to come forward.
"Come forward. The monk stepped near. The Master said, "Bring me two or three ounces of flour and give it to this venerable elder.
The monk brushed his sleeves and withdrew. From that moment on, he attained realization. He subsequently gave up all his clothing and funds to provide a vegetarian feast for the community.
After three years, he took leave of the Master. The Master said, "Go well. At that time, Xuefeng was standing in attendance and asked, "As for this monk who has just departed, when will he return?"

[The monk] came back. The Master said, "He only knows how to go once; he does not understand how to come back. That monk returned to the hall and passed away while sitting beneath his robes and bowl.
