[Later,] the Master asked a monk, "Where have you come from? He replied, "I have come from traveling the mountains. The Master said, "Did you reach the summit? He replied, "I did. The Master said
"Is there anyone at the summit? He replied, "There is no one. The Master said, "If that is so, then you have not reached the summit.
He replied, "If I had not reached the summit, how would I know there is no one? The Master said, "Why do you not stay for a moment?
He replied, "I am not unwilling to stay, but someone in the Western Heaven does not approve. The Master said, "I have always suspected this fellow. A monk asked Zhuyou, "How is it?"
"This is the practice of a śramaṇa. Wuzu said, "Practice is not non-existent; however, if there is a realization [of it], one immediately deviates. Another monk brought this up to the Master.
The Master said, "Why did he not ask, 'I do not yet know what kind of practice this is'? The monk then presented these words to Wuzu. Wuzu said, "Buddha-practice! Buddha-practice!
The monk returned and reported this to the Master. The Master said, "Yizhou is still somewhat tolerable; New罗 (Xinluo) is the most painful."
The monk then asked, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa? The Master said, "The head is three feet long; the neck is two inches long.
The Master then ordered his attendant to take these words and ask them of the Venerable Sansheng Ruan. Sansheng pinched the attendant's hand once.
The attendant returned and reported this to the Master, who approved. While washing his bowl, he saw two crows fighting over a toad.
A monk asked, "For what reason does this reach such a state? The Master said, "Precisely because you, O *śrāmaṇera*, ask:
among the three bodies (*trikāya*), which body does not fall into the category of numbers? The Master added, "I have often applied myself most earnestly to this."
A monk asked Caoshan, “The former master said, ‘I have often been critical of this matter. What was his meaning?
Caoshan replied, “If you want your head, I will chop it off. He then asked Xuefeng, who struck him in the mouth with his staff and said, “I too have been to Dongshan.
Chengtian Zong said, “One phrase brings peace to the seas and rivers; one phrase brings wind [and rain].”
The high moon is cold. One turning phrase is like riding a thief’s horse to pursue a thief.
Suddenly, if a monk comes forth and says, "It is not so at all," one might grant him that he possesses a single eye.

[Zhaozhou] said with delight, "Such complications—have you even dreamed of the three old fellows? He added, "Why do you not apply a needle to the *gāohuáng* (the vital point between the heart and diaphragm)?"

The Master asked a monk, "What have you come to do? The monk replied, "I have come to serve my teacher with filial piety. The Master said, "In this world, what thing is most filial? The monk was unable to answer.
Cen Shangshu asked the Master, "Among the fifty-two stages of the Bodhisattvas, why is the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (Miaojue) not seen?
The Master said, "Shangshu, you see Wondrous Enlightenment directly before your eyes. A monk asked, "What is green?"
[The monk] asked, "What is the father of the mountain white clouds? The Master said, "That which is not dense and dark. [The monk] asked, "What is the child of the white clouds and green mountains?
The Master said, "That which cannot distinguish east from west. [The monk] asked, "What is the white cloud leaning all day long? The Master said, "It cannot be parted from.
[The monk] asked, "What is the green mountain that knows nothing at all? The Master said, "That which does not look back."
The Master and Yunju were crossing a stream. The Master asked, "How much water is there? Yunju replied, "It is not wet. The Master said, "A coarse fellow.
Yunju then asked, "How deep is the water? The Master replied, "It is not dry."
Wuzu Yan said: "When these two people speak in such a manner, is there still any distinction of superior or inferior?

Today, as I walk along and let my arm swing naturally, I shall explain it for all of you: 'The single phrase of crossing the water is not wet,' yet the pearl treasures in the storehouse are piled high;
'The single phrase of crossing the water is not dry,' yet with not even a single awl, how can one speak of poverty? This is the duality of dry and wet."
Neither path is traversed; let the green waters and blue mountains be as they are.
Entering the hall [the Master said]: "There is a person who, amidst a thousand or ten thousand people, does not turn his back on anyone and does not face anyone.
Tell me, what kind of countenance does this person possess? Yunju stepped forward and said, "I am going to attend the hall, Official. The official asked.
"Is there anyone practicing? The Master said, "Wait until you become a man, and then you shall practice.

He ascended the hall and said, "Is there anyone who does not repay the four debts of gratitude or the three realms of existence? The assembly remained silent. He spoke again, "If you do not realize this meaning, how can you transcend the afflictions of beginning and end?
You must ensure that mind after mind does not touch external objects, and step after step remains without a fixed location, maintaining this state constantly without interruption."
Only then can you attain resonance. You must simply exert yourself; do not let the days pass in idleness.
On one occasion the Master said, "If you realize the matter that lies beyond the Buddha, only then will you have some share in the discourse. A monk asked, "What is this discourse?
The Master said, "When you are discoursing, you, O *kalyāṇamitra*, do not hear it. The monk asked, "Does the Master hear it? The Master said, "When you are not discoursing, then you hear it."
A monk asked, "What is one who is above the Buddha? The Master said, "Not a Buddha.

Yunmen said, "It cannot be named; it cannot be described. That is why it is called 'not. Jingshan Daoyuan said, "The two venerable masters handled the matter of that which is above the Buddha in this way, but let us proceed slowly. Here, it is not so. For example:"
"What is this matter that lies above the Buddha? He seized his staff and struck him across the back, lest he remain hidden behind the root of "above the Buddha.

Because Cao Shan was about to take his leave, the Master then instructed him, saying: "While I was at the place of my late teacher Yunyan, I personally received the seal of the *Baoming Sanjing* (The Threefold Mirror of the Treasure)."
Obscure. The essential point of the matter is now exhausted; I entrust it to you now. The verse says: "Such a Dharma has been secretly transmitted by Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Now that you have obtained it, you should protect it well. Like snow in a silver bowl, or the bright moon hidden among the egrets—though the likenesses are not identical, one knows their place when they are mixed together.
The meaning does not reside in the words; the responsive opportunity also arrives. To move is to form a nest; to falter is to fall into a trap. Turn away!

It is neither contact nor non-contact; it is like a great mass of fire. It merely manifests as forms and patterns, yet these immediately belong to defilement. At midnight it is perfectly luminous, yet at dawn it does not remain revealed.
It serves as a model for all things, employing itself to uproot all suffering. Although it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not without expression.

It is like standing before a precious mirror, where form and reflection behold one another. You are not that [mirror], yet that [mirror] is precisely you. Like an infant of the world, [endowed with] the five...

The marks are fully complete. Neither going nor coming, neither arising nor abiding. Peaceful and harmonious. With phrases and without phrases, one ultimately does not obtain the thing, for the words have not yet been rectified.
The hexagram *Lí* (Fire) is doubled; the biased and the correct interact and turn back upon each other. Layered, they become three; when all transformations are exhausted, they form five.
It is like the taste of the *zhīní* herb; it is like a vajra. In the very center is the subtle embrace; striking and singing are both present.

The Way is universal, penetrating all paths; it accompanies one wherever one goes. To align with it is auspicious; it must not be violated or opposed. It is the wondrousness of true nature, belonging neither to delusion nor enlightenment.
Through the conditions of time and circumstance, it is silently yet clearly manifest. Subtly it enters the interstices of the infinitesimal; vast it transcends all spatial location.

A deviation as slight as a hair’s breadth fails to accord with the musical scales. Thus there are sudden and gradual approaches, established according to conditions, and these approaches are divided into their respective tenets.

This is precisely the compass and square; it is the ultimate goal of the fundamental principle (*zongtong*). It is the flow of true permanence, outwardly still yet inwardly wavering—like a tethered horse or a crouching rat.
The former sages took pity on this and established the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) for the sake of the Dharma. Following their delusions, they mistook black for white;

only when these inverted perceptions are extinguished will they sincerely admit their own error and seek to align with the ancient tracks. Please observe the ancients: when the Buddha-way was about to be perfected, he contemplated for ten *kalpas*.
A tree like a tiger’s maimed paw, like a horse’s white hind leg—these exist because of inferiority. A precious jade table and rare treasures exist because of their startling wonder.

A wildcat, a dog, a white ox—Houyi used his skill and strength to shoot a target at a hundred paces; yet when the arrowheads meet point-to-point, what has skill and strength to do with it? A wooden man sings, a stone woman dances;
this is not reached by consciousness or cognition, so how could it admit of thought or deliberation? Your servant respectfully...

A son who is compliant with his father is filial; one who is non-compliant is not filial. One who does not offer support is not an assistant. He acts secretly and employs himself in obscurity, appearing as if he were ignorant or dull-witted.
Yet, by being able to maintain continuity, he is called the Lord among Lords.

The *Zhizhengzhuan* (Biographies of Realization through Wisdom) was established by Chan Master Dongshan Wuben. Regarding the "Middle Way of Subtle Embrace" (*zhengzhong miaojie*) and the "Path of Penetrating the Source and Penetrating the Way" (*tongzong tongtu jiedai*), the *Zhuan* states:
Baizhang said, "To interpret the meaning based on the literal text is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three ages;

to depart from a single word of the sūtras is to be identical to the teachings of Māra. Therefore, regarding the fundamental principles outside the teachings (*jiaowai zongzhi*), whatever he revealed necessarily stated that one must rely upon the teachings.
If one speaks of "wondrous inclusion" (*miaoxie*), it is called "the central correctness. If one speaks of "inclusion of the path" (*xielü*), it is called "penetrating the source" (*tongzong*).

If one speaks of "inclusion and carrying" (*xiadai*), it is called "the thorough way" (*tongtu*). This is because they are fundamentally the same term, "inclusion and carrying," with the character "wondrous" added.

However, the expression "inclusion and carrying" must have a fundamental basis. As stated in the Mahāyāna definition of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): "That which is said to 'carry its own characteristic' (*daijixiang*) carries..."

Regarding the "concomitance with itself," there are two meanings for each. As for the term "concomitance" (*dai*), it has two senses: first, "carrying along" (*xiadai*), which means the cognizing mind directly carries the essence of the object while cognizing it;
second, "transformative concomitance" (*bian-dai*), which means the cognizing mind transforms and gives rise to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) while cognizing it.
When Caoshan saw Du Shun’s verse on the *dharmakāya*, he said: "My intention does not lie in such [a view]."
The Way is that which one creates for oneself, saying: "He is fundamentally not me; I am fundamentally not he.
Without me, he dies; without him, I remain. If he were like me, he would be a Buddha; if I were like him, I would be a donkey.
Not eating the stipend of the Empty King, why borrow a wild goose to transmit a letter? I speak this while lying across my body; look at the hair upon my back. Suddenly—
It is like singing a "White Snow" ballad; one might still fear it to be a "Ba" song. When I examine the words of Caoshan, they are all wondrously imbued with a profound grasp.

If the words were not so imbued, they would be like the mind that can take objects as its conditions, failing to grasp the essence of those objects. In that case, the object would have no self and the self would have no object;
the vital connection would be severed, and it would be nothing more than a conventional notion circulating in the world—not the true school’s principle. —Huanki (Phantom Guest)
It is said: In the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, when the cognizing mind directly grasps the essence of the object while perceiving it, this is "apparent with a real substrate" (*sādṛśyopādāna*).
When the cognizing mind arises as a transformed image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and perceives it, this is "with a real substrate but a solitary shadow" (*sasvabhāvapratibimba*).

Both of these belong to the realm of mental construction (*vikalpa*) and reside solely in the partial position of the "ministerial" stage. This [text] borrows from them to clarify the subtle grasping; it is the very path of our own school.
"Bian" (偏) means "partial," and "zheng" (正) means "correct. "Xie dai" (挾帶) means "to carry both together," which is "comprehensive. The Master further said:
"In the age of the Dharma’s decline, many people possess only dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*). If one wishes to verify what is true and what is false, there are three kinds of 'leakage' (*chōu*):
first is the leakage of views (*jian chōu*), where the faculty does not leave its station and falls into a sea of poison; second is the leakage of emotion (*qing chōu*)."

First is stagnation in orientation; the locus of vision becomes partial and withered. Second is stagnation in the turning away; the place of seeing is lopsided and parched. Third is leakage in speech;
one investigates the subtle but loses the fundamental source, the faculty is dim regarding beginning and end, and turbid wisdom revolves. You should understand these three types.
Juefan said: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "One should contemplate that the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are empty.
Subhūti, when a bodhisattva performs this contemplation, they do not allow the mind to become distracted. If the mind is not distracted, then one does not perceive dharmas.
If one does not perceive dharmas, then one does not realize [them]. It further states: "It is as if a garuḍa were soaring through the void."
Soaring with sovereign freedom, they do not fall for a long time. Although they sport within space, they do not rely upon it, nor are they obstructed by it.
In the past, Master Dongshan established the five ranks of partiality and correctness as a standard for the Great Dharma, and distinguished the monastics by means of the three types of leakage;
these were not arbitrary or contrived acts, but were all rooted in the Buddha.
This is the lingering intent [of the ancients]. Nowadays, when those in the monastic forests hear the term "leakage," they often snort with derision.
Even if Dongshan were to reappear, what could he possibly do?

Furthermore, regarding the three verses on the Essential Principles, the first, "The Hammering and Singing Proceed Together," states: "The golden needle and the double lock are both prepared; the paths harmonize."
The hidden is entirely pervasive; the precious seal is wondrous in the wind. Layer upon layer, the brocade seams open. The verse on the two golden locks and the mysterious path says:

In the midst of mutual clarity there is darkness; when effort is equalized, progress becomes difficult to perceive. When strength is exhausted, one forgets whether to advance or retreat; the golden lock is like a net stretched wide.

The third is "Not Falling into the Realm of the Ordinary or the Sage" (also titled "Neither Entering Principle nor Phenomena"). The verse says: Phenomena and principle are both not entered; Reflective illumination cuts off the subtle and profound.
Turning one's back on the wind, there is neither skill nor clumsiness; Like a flash of lightning or a spark, it is difficult to pursue.
Another verse says: The Way is without mind and accords with man; Man is without mind and accords with the Way. If you wish to know the meaning herein, One is old and one is not old.
Later, a monk asked Caoshan, "What is 'one who is old'? Caoshan said, "Not supporting. The monk asked, "What is 'one who is not old'?
Caoshan said, "A withered tree. The monk then related this to Xiaoyao Zhong, who said, "The three obediences and six duties."

The Master was unwell and sent a novice monk to deliver a message to Yunju. He instructed him, saying, "If he asks whether the Master is at ease, simply say, 'The path to Yunyan is about to be cut off. When you deliver these words, you must stand far away; I fear he might strike you. The novice took his instructions and went to deliver the message. Before he had even finished speaking, Yunju struck him with a staff. The Master said, "Bring him here. The novice returned and told the story. The Master said, "I have already struck him once for you. The novice replied, "He struck me first. The Master said, "He struck you because he recognized you as one of my own family. The novice said, "Even so, I am not spared from being struck. The Master said, "It is because you are my son that you are struck. The novice said, "Father and son both receive blows. In the third month of the Wuchen year of the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty, he manifested illness. The military governor of Min ordered a physician to attend him, but the Master said, "I am not ill," and ultimately refused the medicine.

He left behind a verse of farewell and entrusted the Dharma. On the second day of the fifth month, he went out to visit Lantian in the morning; returning in the evening, he bathed his body. At midnight, he entered parinirvāṇa.
He was eighty-seven years of age and fifty-nine years since his ordination.

Deshan gave the Master a bowl of water; the Master took it and drank it. Deshan asked, "Do you understand? The Master said, "I do not.
Deshan again gave the Master a bowl of water; the Master again took it and drank it. Deshan asked, "Do you understand? The Master said—
“No. Shanshan said, “Why do you not strip away that which you do not understand? The Master said, “I do not understand. Shanshan asked again, “What, then, would you strip away?
Shanshan said, “You are very much like an iron stake. After [the Master] had taken up residence there, Xuefeng visited him.
During their conversation over tea, Xuefeng asked, “Regarding the incident at Deshan when you were cutting wood—what was it about? The Master said, “At that time, my late teacher approved [of me].”
Wuzhuo said, "The Master left your teacher too early. At that moment, there happened to be a bowl of water before him. Wuzhuo said, "Bring me the water.
The Master then passed it to him; Wuzhuo took it and immediately poured it out.

The Sixth Generation under the Sixth Patriarch:
Chan Master Caoshan Benji of Fuzhou. He was the son of the Huang family of Putian, Quanzhou. In his youth, he studied Confucianism. At the age of...
19. At nineteen, he went to Ling-shi in Fuzhou to become a monk. At twenty-five, he received full ordination. He then visited Dongshan, who asked, "What is your name, *śrāmaṇera*?
The Master replied, "Benji (Fundamental Quiescence). Dongshan said, "Who is that? The Master replied, "He is not named Benji."

Shanshen esteemed him as a vessel of the Dharma. (This account is identical to the dialogue between Yunju and Dongshan; according to the *Sengbaozhuan*, the Master’s name was Danzhang, and this record follows that source. From this point on, he entered the Master’s room for formal training.
After lingering for several years, he took his leave. National Teacher Shan then secretly transmitted to him the essential tenets of the Dongshan school.

Shan asked again, "Where will you go? The Master replied, "I am going to the place where there is no change. Shan said, "In a place of no change, how can there be going? The Master said, "Even going does not involve change.
Thereupon, he traveled to Caoxi to pay homage at the ancestral pagoda; having returned from Luochuan, he settled there.
In Linchuan, there were beautiful mountains and waters, so he settled there permanently. Out of his aspiration for the Sixth Patriarch, he named the mountain Cao and addressed the assembly, saying:
"Ordinary sentiments and saintly views are like gold being melted away; on the mysterious path, one must practice mutual interpenetration.
Those who take up food for right livelihood must possess three kinds of 'falling' (degenerations): first, wearing fur and bearing horns; second, not severing sound and color."
Third, regarding "not receiving food": At that time, Choubunna asked, "What kind of fall is it to have hair on one's back and horns on one's head?

The Master said, "It is the fall of being of that same category. He asked, "What kind of fall is it to not cut off sound and form? The Master said, "It is the fall of following along. He asked, "What kind of fall is it to not receive food?
The Master said, "It is the fall of being noble and honorable. Then he said, "That which eats is precisely one's own fundamental portion."

Regarding phenomena (*dharma*), knowing they exist yet not grasping them is called "falling into the noble" (*ārya-patana*). Not clinging to the initial mind, yet knowing there is a self and the stages of sainthood, is called "falling into the category" (*nikāya-patana*).

If, at the moment the initial mind knows its own affairs and one turns the light back within, casting aside form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharmas*) to attain tranquility, then one achieves success.
Thereafter, one does not cling to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and so forth, following along with...
To divide it is to be obscured; to let it be as it is results in obstruction. Therefore, the six heterodox teachers were your teachers;
where those teachers fell, you likewise followed them into that fall. Only then may you take food—this "food" is precisely the food of right livelihood.
Furthermore, regarding the gates of the six sense faculties, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it is simply not being defiled by them that constitutes falling. Moreover—
This is the same as the previous case of leveling the ground; since even the fundamental matter itself is not grasped, how much less so other matters?

Whenever the Master speaks of "falling," he means that things are mixed together and cannot be categorized as distinct. Whenever he speaks of a "beginner," he means that those who have attained awakening are the same as those who have not yet awakened.

In the *Lamp Records* (Denglu), from "no ordinary sentiments or holy views" (*wúfánqíng shèngjiàn*) to "the third [case], not receiving food" (*zhì sān zhě bùshòushí*), there are forty-one characters.
In the *Forest Records* (Línjiānlù), from "no ordinary sentiments or holy views" to "mutual interplay" (*huíhù*), there are thirteen characters.

Furthermore, 'eating' refers to the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing that occur at the gates of the six faculties; it simply means not being defiled by them."

"Regarding 'falling into' (*wei-duo*): it is not the same as [the previous case]. This is Juéfàn’s (Juefan) interpretation of Caoshan’s words, whereas *Línjiān* (Línjiān) directly transmits Caoshan’s own words.

If one does not even grasp at one’s own fundamental task, how much less so for anything else? The words of the ancients were established with a sense of restraint. The *Zhizheng Chuan* states:
"The World-Honored One spoke of nine causes and nine conditions by which one dies before the completion of one's lifespan.
What are these nine? They are: eating without moderation; eating at an improper time; eating again before the previous meal has been digested; vomiting what has been produced [in the stomach];..."

One consumes it when it is digested and maintains this practice; one does not rely on medicine, nor does one know for oneself whether it causes harm or benefit, whether it is taken at the wrong time or in the wrong measure, or whether one engages in unchaste conduct—this is called "untimely death.

Observing from this perspective, I know that eating at the proper time prevents such a wrongful death; therefore, it is called "right livelihood through food. Huangbo said: "Those who have only just come forth these days..."

Practitioners of the Three Vehicles are all of this sort; they are all called those whose food is undigested. What is meant by "undigested food"? It refers to [mere] intellectual knowledge.
If not digested, they all become poisonous medicine; they are all categorized within the realm of arising and ceasing.
Since such things do not exist within True Suchness (tathatā), one knows from this that Caoshan valued the food of right livelihood and established the "three falls. Furthermore, he said:

[The Master] asked another monk, "What are you doing? The monk
“With whom as a companion on the Way can one immediately come to constantly hear what has not yet been heard? The Master said, “One who shares the same single blanket.
He asked, “This is still about the Master being able to hear it. What is it to ‘constantly hear what has not yet been heard’?

The Master said, “It is not the same as wood or stone. He asked, “Which comes first? Which comes after? The Master said, “Have you not heard it said that one constantly hears what has not yet been heard?”
Question: "When one ox drinks water and five horses do not neigh, what is it like? The Master said: "Caoshan understands how to guard his mouth.
When the Paper-Clothing Ascetic came to visit, the Master asked: "Are you not the Paper-Clothing Ascetic? The ascetic replied: "I dare not say so."
The Master asked, "What is the matter beneath the paper robe? The other replied, "Once the single fur cloak is hung upon the body, all phenomena are entirely as they are.
The Master asked, "What is the function beneath the paper robe? The other stepped forward, responded with an "Amen," and then stood there disrobing. The Master said:

"You only understand going in this way; why do you not understand coming in that way? The man suddenly opened his eyes and asked, "What is it like when the one true spirit does not rely on a womb? The Master said, "That is not yet subtle. The man asked, "What is the subtle?"
The Master said, "Not borrowed, not lent. Having said this, he respectfully took his leave and passed away. The Master presented a verse, saying:

"The nature of awakening is perfectly luminous, the formless body; Do not falsely cultivate intimacy or distance through intellectual views. When thought diverges, one is obscured from the profound essence; When the mind errs, it does not dwell as a neighbor to the Way.
Through emotional attachments, the myriad dharmas sink into the objective realm; With manifold discernment, one loses the original truth. Within such words..."
Quanhao understood it all. Being clearly free from affairs, he asked Elder Qiang, "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space;
responding to things by manifesting forms is like the moon in water. How do you explain this principle of 'responding'? He replied, "It is like a donkey looking down a well.
The Master said, "You have spoken quite a bit, but you have only captured eighty percent of it. He replied, "Master..."
Furthermore, how is it? The Master said, "Like looking at a donkey in a well. A monk cited the case where Yaoshan asked a monk, "How old are you?
The monk replied, "Seventy-two. Yaoshan said, "Is that seventy-two? The monk said, "Yes. Yaoshan then struck him. What is the meaning of this?
The Master said, "The first arrow might still be considered tolerable; the second arrow shoots deep into the person. [The monk] asked, "How can one avoid this staff?
The Master said, "Once the royal edict has been issued, the feudal lords yield the way. A monk asked Xiangyan, "What is the Way? Xiangyan said:
"A dragon’s roar from within a withered tree. A monk asked, "What is it like to be one who walks the Way? Yanyang replied, "Eyes within a skull.
The monk did not understand, so he went to Shishuang and asked, "What is it like to be a dragon’s roar from within a withered tree? Shishuang said, "It still carries a trace of joy."
[The monk] asked, "What are the eyes within the skull? Baoshou said, "They still carry consciousness.
[The monk] did not understand and asked the Master, "What is the dragon’s cry within the withered tree? The Master said, "The life-blood is unbroken.
[The monk] asked, "What are the eyes within the skull? The Master said, "They never dry up. [The monk] asked, "I wonder if there are any who can hear them? The Master said, "All have heard."
There was not a single person on earth who had not heard it. [A monk] asked, "I do not yet understand what verses are these regarding 'the dragon’s roar within the withered tree'?
The Master said, "If you do not know what verses they are, those who hear them will all perish. He then presented this verse: "The withered tree’s dragon-roar is the true seeing of the Way;
The skull, devoid of consciousness, has its eyes first opened. When joy and cognition are exhausted, the news is exhausted; How could the person themselves..."
Distinguishing the clarity within turbidity, Zhaojue Qin said:

"When mindfulness does not diverge and the mind does not err, one perfectly integrates the five stages of ruler and minister, leaps out of ignorance and the three poisons, and can then cause flowers to bloom upon withered wood and blow the pitch-pipe amidst cold crags. Behold him!
There were three veteran masters. One had penetrated the leakage of words; one had penetrated the leakage of sentiment; and one had penetrated the leakage of views.
If you can investigate and examine this well, you may walk alone upon the profound pivot. Do you understand thoroughly?
Do not linger by the cold crags while the strange grasses turn green; to sit amidst white clouds, the function is not yet subtle. —Jingshan Gao cites Yuanwu.
Having clarified the three types of linguistic penetration, he said: "Can you all discern them?
If you cannot discern them, I, Miaoxi, will not begrudge my eyebrows and shall explain them through for you. Xiangyan penetrated the leakage of words, yet he was bound to death by language.
Shishuang penetrated the leakage of emotion, yet he was driven to death by conceptual consciousness. Caoshan penetrated the leakage of views, yet he was..."
Seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing delude and kill; this has been clearly explained. Let those with eyes discern and grasp it. Jiyin said:
"When the consciousness of joy is exhausted, the news is exhausted. How can a person distinguish the clear within the turbid? This is what Daguan meant.
The biased and the orthodox interweave vertically and horizontally; one must keep far from the ten stages of perfection. One must penetrate the Dragon Gate; the Bird Path is unfit for travel.
The Stone Woman weaves amidst the frost; the Clay Ox plows within the fire. If one can escape both ends, a single branch of the ancient tree will flourish. This is it.
The Master read the Dharmakāya Verses composed by Du Shun and the Great Master (Fadashi), saying: "In my view, I do not wish to speak in such a manner.
His disciples requested that he compose another set himself. Having composed the verses, he also provided a commentary upon them.
The words run as follows: "He is fundamentally not me" (He is not I). "I am fundamentally not he" (I am not he). "If he lacks me, he dies" (I look up to you for life). "If I lack him, I... [die].
I am not him (yet he is not distinct from me). If I were like him, I would be a Buddha (but in truth, I am not a Buddha). If he were like me, he would be a donkey (neither position holds).
I do not eat the stipends of the Empty King; if I encounter imperial food, I must spit it out. Why rely on a wild goose to deliver a letter? (There is no correspondence.

I speak of singing with a horizontal body (and thus I sing); look at the hair on his back—it is not like yours. At first it seems like the "White Snow" aria (one might think it is White Snow), yet one still fears it may be something else.
A Bar Song (no commentary is transmitted for this line). A verse shown to students says: "Attaining realization through conditions, the response is swift;
Dissolving into the essence, the attainment of power is slow. That which flickers up has no original location; My Teacher spoke of it briefly as the inconceivable."
Jiyin said: "Observing it from this perspective, all the sages of the past have declared that when this single thought-moment arises, it is utterly ungraspable;
this is truly inconceivable. Since there is no distinct excellence apart from it, how could such realization not be swift?
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: 'By means of a small expedient, one swiftly achieves [enlightenment].'"
Bodhi asked, "If that is so, why do students not believe it? He replied, "Take Chan Master Shanhui of Zhulin, for example.
For the sake of Daowu, he went to see Chuanzi; upon hearing a single word, he attained realization.
After he had departed, he looked back, and Chuanzi said with a smile, 'This fellow suspects that I have something else. Thereupon, he capsized his boat. This was because he believed."
"The power is still slight; it is simply because one has not yet attained great penetration. Huanki said, "This is the hitching post for donkeys that has bound people for a thousand ages.
The Master composed a verse of four prohibitions, saying: "Do not travel the path of the mind; Do not don the garment of original nature.
What need is there to insist on 'just so'? Above all, avoid the time before birth. He addressed the assembly, saying: "In this lineage of the monastic robe, the principle must..."
This assembly (the character "assembly" likely should be placed above the character "must") must penetrate toward the ultimate reality; do not treat it as something trivial.
If you can clearly take this up and assume responsibility for it, you will turn all the sages behind yourself and only then attain true freedom.

If you cannot so turn them, then even if you have mastered the teachings to the full extent, you must still stand behind them with palms joined. How could you speak such grand words? If you cannot turn [them]...
When one attains mastery over oneself, then all coarse and heavy objects that arise will be brought under one's sovereign control.

Even if one falls prostrate in the mud, one still maintains this mastery. For instance, there was a monk who asked Yeshan, "Within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, is there also the meaning of the Patriarchs?
He replied, "There is. The monk asked, "If there is, why did Bodhidharma come again? He replied, "Precisely because there is."
The reason for coming here is surely not to act as a sovereign master and turn [the mind] back toward oneself?
As the sutra says: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.
What is called a *kalpa* (劫) refers to stagnation. To speak of "ten" is to mean completion; it is also said to mean the severing of leaks. It simply means that the ten paths have been cut off.
Not forgetting the great fruit, it is said that to remain fixated and attached is called "accepting things one after another.

Without distinguishing between noble and base, I have often observed those in the monastic communities who love to argue about this being one way or that being another; can they truly establish the matter?
Such talk is merely a path of discourse regarding future events. Have you not seen Nanquan say: "Even if you were ten times perfect, you would still fall short"?
"Master Wang’s 'Single Path'—this is indeed a most difficult matter. Upon reaching this point, one must be meticulous; only then can one attain clarity and mastery.
Whether in heaven, hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, or as an animal, it remains unchanged across all states of existence."
He is fundamentally the same person as before; it is simply that he does not travel the old path. If there is a mind of longing, one will again fall into attachment.
If one can break free, what is there to choose? An ancient worthy said: "I only fear you cannot enter the cycle of rebirth. What do you say to this?
It is simply that people nowadays speak of "purity" and love to talk about future matters; this illness is the most difficult to cure.

If it were merely coarse or heavy worldly affairs, they would be light; rather, the illness of "purity" is what is heavy. It is just like the "flavor of the Buddhas" and the "flavor of the Patriarchs."
All of these are merely attachments. My former teacher said: "To direct the mind toward it is to violate the precepts; to find flavor in it is to break the fast. But what do you call "flavor"?
It is nothing other than the flavor of the Buddhas and the flavor of the Patriarchs. As soon as there is a heart of longing, one has violated the precepts.
If one were to speak of breaking the fast or breaking the precepts as people do nowadays, then at the very moment of the three *karmavācanas*, they would already have been broken. If this is so—
Grossness, heaviness, and the afflictions of anger and ignorance are indeed difficult to sever, yet they are light.
If one is instead free from artifice, free from affairs, and pure, this is a state of heaviness beyond compare. The Patriarchs appeared in the world solely for this purpose; it was not for you alone.
At this time, do not act with indifference. It would be far better for a stray cat or a white ox to practice. This is not because they possess Chan or the Way;
rather, when will your various pursuits—seeking Buddhas and Ancestors, even up to Bodhi and Nirvana—ever come to rest and be accomplished?
All of these are but the mind of birth and death. Therefore, they are not as good as the stray cat or the white ox, who remain steadfastly ignorant.
They know nothing of the Buddhas or the Patriarchs, nor even of Bodhi and Nirvana, nor of the causes and effects of good and evil;
they simply eat grass when hungry and drink water when thirsty. If one can act in this manner, there is no need to worry about failing to achieve fulfillment.

Have you not heard it said: "When calculation fails, one knows that there is [a reality beyond it]"; thus, one is able to don fur and wear horns, pulling the plow and wielding the hoe. Having attained this opportunity—
It is appropriate. One has merely begun to compare them slightly; yet one does not see the worlds of Maitreya, Akṣobhya, and Sukhāvatī.
Such people are called "shameless and indolent Bodhisattvas" by those who have transcended the ordinary. This is also called the "death and rebirth of transformation.

Yet even this may still be considered a minor form of indolence. As for the fundamental matter itself, how should it be? You must be extremely careful and discerning before you can attain it. Every person...
There is a single seat-mat of ground. When a Buddha appears in the world, he cannot encroach upon it. If you practice with such an understanding, do not seek mere cleverness or sharp wit.
If you wish to know this matter: even if you were now to become a Buddha or a Patriarch, it is still just this.

Even if you were to fall into the three miserable realms, the hells, or the six paths of existence, it is still just this. Although it has no practical use, nevertheless, you cannot be separated from it.
It can be attained. One must first exercise mastery over it before it can be attained. If one exercises mastery, then it is immutable;
if one cannot exercise mastery, then it is subject to change. Have you not seen Yongjia say: "Vast and boundless, one invites calamity"? He was asked:
"What is meant by 'vast and boundless, one invites calamity'? He replied: "This very thing is it all. He was asked again.
[The student] asked, "How can one avoid it? [The Master] said, "If you know there is [a way], then you have attained it. Why would you need to avoid it?

Whether it be bodhi, nirvāṇa, afflictions, ignorance, and so forth—none of these require avoidance. Even down to the coarse and heavy matters of the mundane world, if you simply know they exist, you have attained them;
there is no need to avoid them. To avoid them is to undergo transformation and change. This applies even to becoming a Buddha or an Ancestor. Bodhi...
"Attaining nirvana—these calamities and misfortunes do not arise from minor causes. Why is this so? It is simply because of change.
If there were no change, one must attain freedom in every situation before it can be achieved. Zhong Wang of Nanping deeply revered the Master;
he sent envoys with formal invitations and instructions. The Master merely wrote a single verse on dwelling at Daming Mountain and entrusted it to the messengers.
Master Damei, having received the seal of mind from Daji, subsequently entered the old hermitage of Meizizhen in Siming.
There he bound up thatch to dwell in seclusion. During the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk under the jurisdiction of Yanguan who, while gathering walking staffs, [encountered him].
The monk became lost and arrived at the hermitage. He asked the Master, "How long have you been here? Baizhang said, "I have only seen the four mountains turn green and then yellow.
The monk asked again, "When one leaves the mountain path, where does one go? Baizhang said, "Go with the flow. Upon returning, the monk recounted this to Yanguan.
Yanguan said, "When I was in Jiangxi, I once met a monk; since then, I have not [seen him again]."
[The Master] knew of his whereabouts and wondered, "Could this be that monk? He then sent a messenger to summon him. Mei replied with a verse:
"An withered tree, broken and leaning against a cold forest, Has encountered spring many times, yet its heart remains unchanged. Even when woodsmen encounter it, they do not even glance at it;
How could a man of Ying hope to pursue it with such toil? A pond of lotus leaves provides countless garments, And the ground is covered with pine needles."
The flowers and food remained in abundance, yet he was soon discovered by the world; thus he moved his thatched hut deeper into the mountains.
The verse written by Master Ji for Nanping—“Withered wood is crushed” (*cuican kumu*)—is a single gāthā. The various机缘 (karmic conditions) concerning Plum are fully contained in the ninth fascicle.
This record, however, recounts the matter of Master Ji’s departure from Nanping and further describes the secluded elegance of Plum.
This is said to be the record of his "Fleeing in Fatigue. The subsequent verse is sometimes attributed to Master Yishan.
On a summer night in the year of Tianfu Xinyou (901 CE), the Master asked the administrator, "What date is it today? He replied, "The fifteenth day of the sixth month.
The Master said, "Throughout my life of traveling on pilgrimage, Caoshan always took exactly ninety days to constitute one summer retreat."
"I shall depart on my pilgrimage tomorrow at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.). When the time arrived, he sat in meditation with incense burning and passed away.
He had lived for sixty-two years and spent thirty-seven summer retreats in seated meditation. His disciples buried his entire body on the western slope of the mountain.
▲ Chan Master Daoying of Yunju in Hongzhou was a native of the Wang family in Yutian, Youzhou. He entered the monastic life at the age of seven at Yanshou Temple in Fanyang.
At twenty-five, he became a full monk (*bhikṣu*). His preceptor ordered him to study the *Śrāvaka* sections on the precepts (*piānjù*).
It was not to his liking, so he abandoned it to travel to various regions. Upon reaching Cuiwei, he went there to inquire about the Way.

At that time, a monk arrived from Yuzhang who highly praised the Dharma assembly at Dongshan. The Master then went to visit him. Dongshan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from Cuiwei.
Dongshan asked, "What words or phrases did Cuiwei use to instruct his disciples? The Master said, "Cuiwei makes offerings to the Arhats. I asked him:"
[Zhaozhou] was making offerings to an Arhat. [The Arhat] asked, "Will you return? Zhaozhou said, "What do you eat every day?
The mountain monk [Dongshan Liangjie] asked, "Is this really what you said? The Master said, "Yes. The mountain monk said, "It is not in vain that you have come to see a master.
The mountain monk asked, "What is your name? The Master said, "Daoying. The mountain monk said, "Speak further. The Master said, "Beyond this, it is no longer a name."
Daoying. Shanshan said, "Your words are exactly the same as those you spoke to Old Monk Daowu. The Master asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch?
Shanshan said, "When you, Dharma brother, have a thatched hut of your own in the future, if someone asks you, how will you respond?
The Master said, "Daoying would be at fault. Shanshan said to the Master, "I have heard that Dharma Master Sida was born in Japan."
"Does a country produce kings? The Master said, "If it were Si-da (Dafu), he would not even become a Buddha. Shan agreed with this. Shan asked the Master, "Where have you come from?
The Master said, "I have come treading over the mountains. Shan said, "Which mountain is fit for you to dwell upon? The Master said, "Which mountain is unfit for me to dwell upon?

Shan said, "In that case, the entire country has been occupied by you, O Acharya. The Master said: *Note: This dialogue is from the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps), featuring the encounter between Master Shishuang Qingzhu and his disciple Xuefeng Yicun.*
"Not so," said Shanshan. "If that is the case, then you have found a path of entry. The Master said, "There is no path.
Shanshan said, "If there is no path, how can you meet with this old monk? The Master said, "If there were a path, I would already be separated from the Master by a mountain.
Shanshan then said, "This son of mine will in the future be one whom thousands and tens of thousands cannot hold back. The Master then built a hermitage.
At Sanfeng, he did not attend the hall for ten days. Dayu asked, "Why have you not been coming to the meal recently?
The Master said, "Every day there is a celestial deity who brings me food. Dayu said, "I thought you were a man of substance;
it seems you still hold such a view. "Come back this evening," Dayu said. When the Master arrived in the evening, Dayu called out, "Attendant Ying! The Master responded. Dayu said:
"Do not think of good; do not think of evil. What is this? The Master returned to his hut and sat in silent meditation.
From that point on, the celestial being could no longer be found; after three days, he finally vanished. Guishan asked the Master, "What were you doing? The Master replied, "I was making soy sauce."
Mount [Shan] asked, "How much salt do you use? The Master said, "I add it as I go. Mount Shan asked, "What flavor does it have? The Master said, "It is attained.
Mount Shan asked, "When a great icchantika commits the five heinous crimes, where is their filial piety? The Master said, "Only then is filial piety perfected.

From that time on, Dongshan acknowledged him as the leader within the meditation hall. Later, when Official Liu Yu ended his rain-praying retreat and ascended the mountain to pay his respects, he questioned the Master.

[The Master] asked, "From where does the rain come? The Master replied, "It comes from the place where you, Official Duan, have asked. Official Duan then performed three prostrations and withdrew with joy.
After walking several paces, the Master called out, "Official Duan! The official turned his head back; the Master asked, "From where did your question come?
The official was speechless. He returned home and died three days later.
Dahui remarked, "Official Liu Yu ended up with nothing to say and returned home; three days later he died.
This was precisely because he had scratched at Hongjue’s itchy spot, yet he simply did not know the path for turning back. Had he been asked, 'From where have you come?
he should have simply performed the three prostrations as before and withdrawn with joy. This would have left Hongjue doubting for thirty years."
In the *Nian*, Dongping once asked an official, "What color is the wind? Xuedou then provided a verse on this: From where does the rain come? What color is the wind?
At the ten-thousand-fathom Dragon Gate, who has ever stayed overnight? Advancing and retreating together—who has suffered the mark upon the forehead?
What color is the wind? From where does the rain come? Without even a snap of the fingers, the tower [is revealed].
The gate opened; it was vast and imposing. The Master from the South had not yet returned.

The Master once ordered an attendant to deliver a pair of trousers to a practitioner who lived in a hermitage. The practitioner said, "I already have trousers provided by my mother," and ultimately refused to accept them.
The Master again ordered the attendant to ask him, "Before you were born of your mother, what did you wear? The practitioner— [remained silent].

He remained silent. Later, he passed away, leaving behind some *śarīra* relics. When these were brought to his teacher, the teacher said, "Even if one were to obtain eight bushels and four pecks of them, it would not be as good as having uttered a single turning word at that time.

While the Master was performing manual labor at Dongshan, he inadvertently killed a worm with his hoe. Dongshan asked, "What about this? The Master replied, "It does not die. Dongshan said, "The Second Patriarch went to Ye-du."

"Furthermore, how is it? The Master did not answer. Later, a monk asked, "Regarding the incident when you were at Dongshan where you killed earthworms by raking, was it not the case that you had no words [to explain]?
The Master said, "At that time there were words; it was simply that no one was there to witness them.
A monk asked, "From what do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise? The Master said, "They arise from deluded thoughts. The monk said, "And for me..."
The monk thought, "I can produce a bar of gold. Can I get it? The Master then stopped speaking. The monk did not accept this.
Yunmen said, "This is already a tangle; it cannot be settled. Had he waited until he said, 'I can produce a bar of gold. Can I get it?
I would have taken up my staff and struck him immediately."
A monk from Silla asked, "When Buddhatāpali met Mañjuśrī, why did he turn back? The Master said, "Precisely because he did not bring [Mañjuśrī] here, he turned back.

[Another] asked, "The scriptures say: 'If this person’s karmic offenses from previous lives should cause them to fall into the evil realms, by virtue of being treated with contempt by people in the present life, they will instead attain birth in heaven.
What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "As soon as there is movement, one falls."
The evil realms. When still, one is held in contempt by others. He said to the assembly: "What complicated matters are there in the Buddha-dharma?
Practice it and that is all. Simply know that the mind is the Buddha; do not worry that the Buddha cannot understand your speech.
If you wish to attain such a state, you must first become such a person. If you are already such a person, why worry? If you say that such a state is difficult, [then you have not yet attained it]."

Since ancient times, the virtuous ones of old have been pure and simple, acting in accordance with their true nature; fundamentally, they possessed no artifice. If someone were to ask them, "What is the Way?
they might sometimes answer, "Why are you making bricks, tiles, and wooden heads? This was because they originally possessed a solid foundation and real power at their very roots;
they were inconceivable people who could grasp soil and turn it into gold. If one lacks such a capacity, even if you can speak eloquently, it is of no avail.

It is like a cluster of flowers and a cluster of brocade; it is similar. To say directly that I emit light and shake the earth, and that there is nothing in the world superior to this, is to speak exhaustively of what would lead one to lose one's head.
Yet no one believes or accepts it. From the very beginning, it is simply because under one’s own feet there is a lack of power.
You all are like hunting dogs: you only seek out those who leave tracks. But when you encounter a wild goat hanging by its horns, it is not so.
However, no trace was to be seen, nor could his breath be discerned. A monk then asked, "What is it like when a wild goat hangs by its horns?
He replied, "Six times six is thirty-six. The monk asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. He said, "Have you not heard it said that there is no trace?"
The monk reported this to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "Your senior brother at Yunju is still there. The monk then asked, "What is it like when a wild goat hangs by its horns?
Zhaozhou said, "Nine times nine is eighty-one. The monk asked, "What is it like after hanging by the horns?
Zhaozhou said, "Nine times nine is eighty-one. The monk said, "How can it be so difficult to understand? Zhaozhou said, "What is there about it that is difficult to understand?"
He said, "I request that the Master provide me with instruction. Shouzhou said, "Silla, Silla. He then asked Changqing, "What is it like when a wild goat hangs from a tree branch?
Changqing said, "A fellow of the weeds. He asked, "And after he has hung there? Changqing said, "He is crying out in confusion."
[The monk] asked, "Ultimately, how is it? Qing said, "The matter of the donkey has not yet gone; the matter of the horse has arrived.
He asked again, "The World-Honored One has a secret word; Kāśyapa did not conceal it. What is the World-Honored One’s secret word?

The Master called the questioner by name and said, "Do you understand? [The monk] said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "If you do not understand, then the World-Honored One has a secret word."
If you understand this, Kāśyapa would not have concealed [the truth] and would instead have said: "When members of the Sangha speak or breathe forth words, there must be a source for them;
do not treat this with indifference. What kind of place is this? How could one accept it so easily? Whenever one asks about a matter, one must also recognize what is good and what is evil.
If one does not distinguish between the honorable and the lowly, nor knows what constitutes an offense, one will merely speak recklessly at random."

It is of no benefit. They travel together as a household, seeking out similar-sounding phrases wherever they go. Therefore, I have always told my brothers: "Do not take offense at our lack of similarity.
I fear that many of my fellow students will depart; first, do not bring them along. If you bring them, they will not be similar.
One must also look ahead in one's speech. An eighty-year-old man entering the examination hall is no small matter.

Childish play; this is no matter of mere complacency. If there is even a slight discrepancy in a single word, then it is as if one has traveled a thousand or ten thousand miles, making it difficult to bring oneself back under control.
This is because in the practice of the Way, people often take it lightly and fail to apply effort.

To strike the bone and break the marrow, there must be a profound reason. Words are like tongs and pliers, like hooks and chains; they must be made to flow in continuous succession before they can be effective. They are fully present in every single instance.
To clarify each and every thing—how could this not be the attainment of the wondrous matter? Those who study this one kind of path must investigate and exhaust its depths with great care;
they must be precise and exact, without the slightest deviation. When one reaches this point, what room is there for hesitation? What room is there for deliberation?
Those who move forward toward it must always maintain a sense of awe and keep their wings folded. This is so unless one is already one who knows.
A person naturally understands how to protect and cherish [their own conduct], never acting recklessly. Out of ten utterances, they cease nine times. Why is this so?
It is because they are constantly fearful that there may be no benefit. For one who has realized the essence, the mind is like a fan in midwinter; it is impossible for mold to grow upon their lips.
This is not a matter of forced effort; it occurs spontaneously and naturally. To attain such a state, one must be such a person.
Since you are such a person, you need not worry about such matters; yet such matters are difficult to encounter. It is also said:
"Even if you were to master the matters on the Buddha’s side, you would already be misapplying your mind.

Have you not seen that when the ancients spoke until the heavenly flowers fell and the stones nodded their heads, it still did not concern their own affairs? What else, then, is this trivial business?
Now, if you intend to employ this finite body and mind within the infinite, what connection can there possibly be? It would be as much a mismatch as trying to fit a square block into a round hole;
it is nothing but a clumsy, awkward affair. If there were no such thing, then even if you could speak with the profusion of clustered flowers and brocade, it would be of no use;
you would still remain within the realm of emotional consciousness. If you wish to deal with all matters, you must reach here.

Only when [the mind] is completely exhausted can one first attain freedom from transgression and truly emerge from the body. If there is even a hair’s breadth that has not been exhausted, one is immediately burdened by worldly dust;
how much more so if it is greater? To err by a hair’s breadth is to commit a transgression as vast as a mountain.
As the ancients said: "If the place of study is not profound, it is entirely mundane. Things of the inner chamber that one cannot let go of all constitute leakage. One must directly turn toward...
To grasp things here and take them away, to go and to come, and to exhaust all affairs—only then does one attain freedom from fault.
It is like a person who has mastered every head and penetrated every object; such a one is merely called a "man of affairs accomplished," but is never called "noble."
You should know that the single path of the Honored One is distinct; it is the most profound and most precious thing in the world.
One must not bring [ordinary things] toward the side of the Honored One; one must know this to be inconceivable and not treat it with mere superficial kindness. Therefore, the ancients said:
It is like two mirrors facing each other; their radiance reflects one another, shining forth without any increase or decrease.
Is this not the very same thing? Yet you still call it a matter of images and reflections. When the sun rises and its light illuminates the world, this clarity is one half;
what do you call that other half? People today have not yet recognized the gate and threshold of light and shadow.
To take such superficial matters and treat them as the innermost secrets of the house—how could that possibly suffice?
To know that the path of the Honored and Noble is distinct from these is to understand that the records of the lamp (the *Denglu*) contain nothing other than these various worldly sayings;
they merely state: "That which enters through the gate is not the treasure," and "Offered up, it does not become a dragon. These two lines alone are all there is.

It is further said: "Those who attain do not regard it as insignificant; those who are enlightened do not despise its application; those with true knowledge do not lament over it; and those who understand it feel no aversion toward it.
If one descends from heaven, one is immediately poor; if one wells up from the earth, one is immediately wealthy.
To emerge from within the gate is easy; to exit through the body is difficult. If one moves, one buries oneself ten feet deep; if one does not move, one is born right where one stands."
Miao. With a single word, he transcended all; he stood alone, preeminent among his contemporaries. His words need not be many; if they are many, they are useless.
A monk asked, "How is it that descending from heaven one is poor? He replied, "One does not prize what is obtained.

The monk asked again, "How is it that surging forth from the earth one is wealthy and noble? He replied, "Within nothingness, there may be something. He further said, "To realize that there is nothing at all is to attain it."
Having no designs, one speaks of nothing as being right; one's conduct has no dependence, and the mind has no place of attachment.

Only when these are exhausted does one attain faultlessness. Among the multitude, one is as if there were no multitude; though amidst no multitude, one is as if in the midst of a multitude. In the body, one is as if without a body;

dwelling in the world, one is as if without a world. Is this not freedom from affliction? One’s virtue transcends the myriad classes of beings, liberated from all fetters. [Thousands of people, ten thousands...]
People attain it; yet the Way should not be sought within oneself. If one attains it now, it is no different from when one first began. An ancient said:

"Having realized the matter of that side, you come back to carry out your affairs on this side. What kind of matter is there on that side? (The character "li" [李] should be read as "lü" [履], meaning "shoes," as below. What kind of matter is there on that side?
How, then, does one pack one's belongings here? Therefore it is said: "If you have something, do not bring it; if you have nothing, do not take it away.
To whom does that which is presently here belong? It is further said: "To embody this matter, you must be like a person who has just ceased breathing;
only then will you correspond with that person. If you can realize the intent of this person, only then will there be a slight [understanding]."
If one were permitted to speak of portions, there would be but a small portion of luggage. To be away for a brief moment is like being dead;
how much more so now, when one is away for years and months. If one were always present, why worry that household affairs would not be managed?
If you wish to know matters of the distant past, they reside only in the present. If you attain them in the present, you will attain them in the distant past as well.
It is like a person returning home from thousands of villages and ten thousand miles away: when they arrive, it is simply that; if it is so, then all is so; if it is not so, then all is not so.
Even if a blaze of light were to arise upon the crown of one’s head, it would still not be it. Yet it is capable of being all things, while all things are not it.
In practicing the Way, one spends the whole day coveting what is ahead and loses what is behind; if one looks at what is behind, one loses what is ahead.
It is like a person who does not move forward—what business could there be behind them?

A monk asked, "When someone enters wearing brocade and embroidery, why is it that after seeing the Master, they are left with not even an inch of thread upon them? The Master said, "It is as if one were walking through a palace of lapis lazuli."
Overthrow it! You must also shatter it to pieces! Then he said: "If there is even a hair’s breadth of something that has not been completely eliminated, one is immediately burdened by defilement;
how much more so if there is more? Have you not seen the common saying: 'The matter of ascending to heaven must be cast away before the assembly;
the matter of reaching perfection must be discarded before the assembly'? When it is thrown to the ground, it makes a sound like gold—there is no need to turn back and look at it. Himself...

What further use would there be for anything else? Did you not see that when the Second Patriarch was extensively learned in poetry and the classics, and possessed the Three Baskets of the Holy Teachings as clearly as if looking at the palm of his hand, why did he still seek from Bodhidharma the settling of his mind?
This shows that the matters within this gate are no ordinary affair. Therefore it is said: "The wise do not seek within words; one who has attained the person does not look for it in explanations."
It is not that he differs from ordinary people; he has simply ceased all worldly entanglements and is temporarily not on the road. There must be a reason for this:
it is not merely that he cannot find evil associates, but even good associates cannot be found. Where has he gone? He has gone through his entire being.

Return home; go to pay your respects. Only then can you escape the gates of the various realms of existence. You must leave the cage and free yourself from extraordinary dangers and hardships. It is further said:
"As if observing objects in the palm of one's hand—only when this is certain and certain may one act in accordance with conditions.
If it is so for one, it will be so for ten million. Yet among those ten million, there is not one or two; even one or two cannot be found."
I do not say that those who manifest the Way are not to be found; rather, such people are rare.

Those who manifest their own true nature are difficult to find, yet they are by no means non-existent—it is simply that they are exceptional. If you have not yet attained this state, do not force yourself to act as if you have.

To force yourself leads to affliction; affliction leads to falling away from the Way; falling away from the Way brings retribution upon oneself. Thus, one cannot see [the truth]. How can you speak such grand words?

Now that you have left the household life, you are like a prisoner released from jail. Be moderate in desire and content with little; do not covet worldly glory. Endure hunger and thirst, and set your will upon non-action (*wuwei*).
Having entered into the Buddha-dharma, even through ten births and nine deaths, do not abandon one another. Whether emerging from birth or entering into death, do not violate the Buddha-dharma.
Cut through nails and sever iron; do not betray the Tathāgata. There is no need for many matters; each of you should understand this for yourselves.
Take [the staff]. When there is business, approach; when there is no business, do not stand about.
To personally demonstrate the Buddha-dharma to the assembly—what more could be done than this? All is transmitted according to the Sangha Jewel.
The Master held the position of abbot for thirty years, and his Way spread throughout the world. His assembly reached fifteen hundred people.

Zhong Wang of Nanchang revered him as his teacher and vowed to take him as his teacher for all generations. In the autumn of the first year of the Tianfu era of the Tang dynasty, he manifested a slight illness.
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month, he preached his final instructions to the great assembly, recounting the intent behind the beginning and end of his appearance in the world.
The assembly was all moved with deep sorrow. On the third day of the first month of the following year, he asked his attendant, "What date is today?
The attendant replied, "The third. The Master said, "Thirty years from now, simply say, 'It is just this. Thereupon, he sat upright and passed away in peace.
▲ Chan Master Kuangren of Shushan in Fuzhou was a native of Xingan in Jizhou. He left home to become a monk under Chan Master Yuancheng of his own prefecture.
One day he informed his teacher that he intended to travel to the Eastern Capital to study the teachings. Before even a year had passed, he suddenly said:

"Seeking through written lines and counting characters—words are not as good as silence. Abandoning oneself to seek others—borrowed is not as good as the real. Thereupon, he went to visit Dongshan. It happened that...
Shan visited early in the morning. The Master went out to meet him and asked, "Regarding that which has not yet been spoken of, I beg the Master to grant me his instruction.
Shan said, "No one is willing to grant it. The Master asked, "Is it still possible to apply effort toward it? Shan said, "Can you apply effort toward it right now?

The Master said, "If effort cannot be applied, then there is no place for concealment. Later, on another day, when Shan ascended the hall, he said, "If you wish to know this matter, you must be like a withered tree."
The flowers bloomed; only then did they unite with others. The Master asked, "How is it when one does not deviate from the timing in any situation?
Shanshan said, "Reverend, this is a matter of meritorious achievement. Fortunately, there is the 'merit of non-merit. Why do you not ask about that?
The Master said, "Is the merit of non-merit not a person of that [other] side? Shanshan said, "Many people would laugh at you for asking such a question. The Master said:
"If it is so, then one has gone far away," [the Master] said. Mountan Yan said, "Far away is not 'far away'; it is not that it is not 'far away. The Master asked, "What is 'far away'?
Yanshan said, "One must not call him a person from 'over there. The Master asked, "What is 'not far away'? Yanshan said, "There is no place for discernment.
Yanshan then asked the Master, "In the empty kalpa, when there is no human dwelling, what kind of person is this?"
The Master said, "I do not know. Shanshan asked, "Does a person still possess an underlying meaning or intent?
The Master said, "Why does the Master not ask him? Shanshan said, "I am asking right now. The Master said, "What is that meaning? Shanshan did not answer.

When Dongshan passed away and his disciples had completed their funeral rites, the Master went to Daguang Moshan at Da Miao in Tanzhou. He arrived just as Moshan was addressing the assembly, saying, "A high-ranking traveler..."
"Scholar, you must simply sleep amidst sounds and forms; only by sitting and reclining amidst sounds and forms can you attain it.
The Master came out and asked, "What is the phrase that does not fall into sounds and forms? Yangshan held up his whisk. The Master said, "This is a phrase that falls into sounds and forms."
Miaoyan set down his whisk and returned to his quarters. The Master did not find this satisfactory and took his leave of Xiangyan.
Xiangyan said, “Why do you not stay for a while? The Master replied, “I have no affinity with you, Reverend. Xiangyan asked, “What is your reason? Try citing it for me.
The Master then recounted the previous dialogue. Xiangyan said, “I have a saying of my own. The Master asked, “What is it? Xiangyan said, “When words are uttered—”
"It is not sound; before the form, there is no object. The Master said, "It turns out there was someone here all along.

He then instructed Xiangyan, saying, "In the future, when you have a place to dwell, I shall come to see you," and then he departed. Later, Guishan asked Xiangyan, "Is that short monk who asked about the dialogue on sound and form still here?
Xiangyan replied, "He has already left. Guishan asked, "Did you mention him to him? Xiangyan replied, "I did."
"I have also encountered him before," [Yan] said. Guishan asked, "Try to recount it for me. Yan recounted the previous conversation.
Guishan asked, "What did he say? Yan replied, "He deeply approved of me. Guishan laughed and said, "I thought this short fellow had some merit;
it turns out he is merely at this level. If this man has a dwelling place in the future, there will be no firewood near his mountain."
He burned [the boat]. Being near water but having no water to drink, the Master heard that the Venerable Daomian of Daguang in Fuzhou was addressing the assembly, saying:

"The phrase with a word and the phrase without a word are like a vine leaning against a tree. The Master went specifically over the mountains to visit him. He encountered Daomian plastering a wall and asked immediately:

"I have heard the Master say, 'The phrase with a word and the phrase without a word are like a vine leaning against a tree. Is this so? Daomian said: "It is. The Master said: "Suppose one suddenly encounters..."
"The tree has fallen and the vines are withered; where do the words return? Baizhang set down his mud-plaster tray and laughed heartily, then returned to his quarters.
The Master said, "I have sold my cotton robe and traveled three thousand *li* specifically for this matter; why does the Master deceive me?
Baizhang called to his attendant, "Bring two hundred coins to give to this elder," and then instructed him, "Go..."
Later, there was the One-Eyed Dragon (Yunmen), whose point was made clear for his son. On the following day, when Guishan ascended the hall, the Master came forward and asked:
"The principle of the Dharma-body is a mystery beyond the profound; it does not fall within the realm of right and wrong. Yet this is still merely an affair on the level of the Dharma-body.
What is the matter that lies above the Dharma-body? Guishan raised his whisk. The Master said, "This is still merely an affair on the level of the Dharma-body."
Regarding this matter, Guishan asked, "What is the matter that lies beyond the Dharma-body? The Master snatched the whisk, folded it, and threw it to the ground, then returned to the assembly.
Guishan said, "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes, but difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk.

Later, hearing that Master Mingzhao Qian of Wuzhou had begun his ministry (Qian was blind in one eye), he went straight there to pay his respects. Mingzhao asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Min Province."
Yangqi Zhao came and asked, "Have you ever been to Dayang Baizhang? The Master replied, "I have. Zhao asked, "What words or phrases did he speak there? The Master recounted the previous conversation.
Zhao said, "Dayang can truly be called 'head straight and tail straight,' yet he simply did not meet a true connoisseur. The Master still did not understand.
Zhao asked again, "If suddenly the tree falls and the vines wither, where do the words return? Zhao said, "This would cause Dayang to laugh."

Zhuanshin attained great enlightenment upon hearing these words. He said, "It turns out that Huishan originally had a blade hidden within his smile. He then prostrated toward him from afar and repented his error.
Yangqi addressed the assembly, saying: "The phrase with meaning and the phrase without meaning are like a vine leaning against a tree. Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti let go their hands."
"Go back. Yangqi spoke thus; this too is merely looking at rusted iron. There is further speech;
do not misquote it. Miaoxi said: "The gentleman is moved by gain."
Zhao asked one day, "Tiger gives birth to seven cubs; which one has no tail? The Master said, "The seventh one has no tail.
When Xiangyan appeared in the world, the Master went to visit him, not failing on his previous appointment. As Xiangyan was ascending the hall, a monk asked:
"When one seeks not after the sages and does not value one's own spiritual nature, what then? Yanguan said, "When the myriad functions have ceased, even the thousand sages cannot be carried along.
As the Master was among the assembly, he made a sound of retching and said, "What kind of words are these?

Upon hearing this, Yanguan immediately descended from his seat and said, "Just now, when I spoke to that monk, there must have been something incorrect, which has caused my uncle to react in such a way. I do not know where the fault lies."
The Master said, "When the myriad functions have ceased, there is still something remaining; though not carried by the thousand sages, it is nonetheless obtained from others.
How can one be without fault? Yan said, "I beg the Master’s younger brother to speak. The Master said, "If I am to make you speak, you must first return the rites of teacher and disciple.
Yan then prostrated himself and repeated his previous question. The Master said, "Why do you not say: 'Acceptance and refusal cannot both be complete'?"
Yan said, "If you agree, what is it that you agree with? If you assent, to whom do you assent? The Master replied, "To agree is to agree with the thousand sages;
to assent is to assent to one's own numinous spirit. Yan said, "If my junior master speaks thus, I shall vomit [in despair] for thirty years to come."
After the Master took up residence there, he indeed suffered from vomiting. He recovered in the twenty-seventh year.

Thereafter, however, after every meal, the Master would pick at his own mouth and induce vomiting, saying, "Brother Xiangyan predicted that I would vomit while standing for thirty years; three years still remain.
Later, the Master asked Jingqing, "When one says 'yes' or 'no,' it cannot be total. How do you understand this? Jingqing said, "Total."
[The Master] said, "If you cannot agree, then how is it? Qing said, "Within this, there is no path of agreement.
The Master said, "Only then does it satisfy this sick monk's intention."

The Master arrived at Jia Shan. Jia Shan was presiding in the Dharma Hall when the Master asked, "I have heard your words, 'Before one's eyes there is no dharma, yet the meaning lies before one's eyes.
What, then, is the dharma that is not before one's eyes? Jia Shan said, "The night moon radiates its brilliance; the clear pool has no reflection.

The Master made a gesture as if to overturn the meditation seat. Jia Shan asked, "What about you, Layman (Dharmācārya)? The Master said, "'Before one's eyes there is no dharma'—it is utterly inconceivable."
He attained it. The Master said, "The great assembly, look at this one warrior! The Master went to visit Yantou. When Yantou saw him coming, he lowered his head and feigned sleep.
The Master stood before him; Yantou paid him no mind. The Master struck the meditation bench once. Yantou turned his head and asked, "What are you doing?
The Master replied, "Master, please stop dozing off. He then shook out his sleeves and departed. Yantou laughed heartily.

Laughing loudly, he said: "For thirty years I played with horse-riders; today I have been bucked by a donkey.
