On the following day, the Master again asked the monk, "The entire world of the ten directions is a single bright pearl.
How do you understand this? The monk replied, "The entire world of the ten directions is a single bright pearl. What need is there to understand it? The Master said:
"I know you are making your living inside a ghost cave. Because the Master was presiding over the funeral for Xuefeng’s passing, he gathered the assembly for tea on the third morning.
At the altar, the Master picked up a single cup and said, "I ask the assembly:
when our late master was alive, he would respond to whatever you said. Now, how will you respond? If you can say it, then our late master will have no [debt] toward you."
"Failed. If you say it cannot be attained, then the failure lies with the former masters. Is there anyone here who can say it? He asked this three times, but the assembly remained silent.
The Master then smashed the bowl and returned to his quarters. Later, he asked Zhongta, "How do you understand this?"
The Pagoda said, "What fault did my late teacher have? The Master then turned his back to the wall, and the Pagoda went out. The Master called to the Pagoda again; the Pagoda turned its head.
The Master asked, "How do you understand this? The Pagoda then turned its back to the wall, and the Master desisted. [He then] ascended the hall for discourse.
The assembly had gathered, so he took up his staff and drove them all away at once. He then turned back to the attendant and said, "Today I have reached a realization that is perilous;
I could enter hell as fast as a shooting arrow. The attendant replied, "I am glad to see the Master has returned to human form once more."
Cuiyan Zhi said: "Whether it be the Great or the Lesser Xuansha, before they have not reached the village, and after they have not yet arrived at the inn.
How can one speak of the path of transcendence? Daowu Zhen said: "Whether it be the Elder Zhi, the Great or the Lesser, he is merely one-sided and withered.
If it were Daowu, it would not be so: Xuansha and his attendant—each possesses a single eye."
The Master said: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a single plot of land whose boundaries on all four sides have been demarcated and sold to others;
only the central tree still remains the property of this old monk. The Master then uttered this statement:
The veteran masters of all quarters say: "To receive beings and benefit living things—how do you receive those three kinds of sick people?
For one suffering from blindness, you raise a mallet or brandish a whisk, yet they do not see. For one suffering from deafness, you speak words of samādhi, yet they do not hear.
For one suffering from muteness, you try to teach them to speak, yet they cannot speak. If you cannot receive them, there is no Buddha-dharma."
This was efficacious. At that time, a monk came forward and said, "Regarding the three types of sick people, do you permit this student to discuss them?
The Master said, "I do. "How would you discuss them? the monk asked. The monk then bowed respectfully and departed. The Master said, "Not so, not so.
Daowu Luohan said, "Guichen currently possesses eyes, ears, and a mouth; how will you receive him, Master? The Master said, "I am ashamed," and then returned to his quarters.
The Abbot said, "As for the three kinds of sick people, where are they right now?
Another monk said, "Not only do they deceive others, but they also deceive themselves. Fayan said, "When I saw Luohan raise this [question] at that time..."
The monk said, "I have understood the three types of sick people through this monk's words. Yunju Xi said, "As for this monk—does he understand or not?

If you say he understands, Xuansha also said it was not so. If you say he does not understand, why did Fayan say, 'I have understood the three types of sick people because of this monk's words'? The Elder came forward and said, "There is no need for this; come up here."
A Discussion. Everyone should know that there was a monk who requested instruction from Yunmen.
Yunmen said, "Prostrate yourself. When the monk rose from his prostration, Yunmen struck him with his staff.
The monk stepped back, and Yunmen asked, "Are you blind? He then called the monk forward; as the monk approached, Yunmen asked, "Are you deaf? Yunmen—
[The Master] asked, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not. The Gatekeeper said, "Are you not afflicted by muteness? At this, the monk had an awakening.
Yuanwu Keqin cited this case and then raised the following: When Wuzu Fayan was ascending the hall, he said, "One person understands but cannot speak;
another does not understand yet can speak. If these two people come to study with me, how will you distinguish between them?"
If you cannot discern these two, it is certain that you will not be able to untangle the entanglements and remove the bonds for others.
If you can discern them, the moment you enter the gate, I shall put on my straw sandals and run several rounds inside your belly.
He still does not realize it himself. "What bowl are you looking for? Get out! Do not mistake this for being blind, deaf, or mute.
Xuedou, citing this, then gave a shout, saying: "This blind, deaf, and mute fellow! If it were not for Yunmen..."
"An ass's year ago! Now there are some who, when you raise the mallet or hold up the whisk, they pay no mind;
when you tell them to come forward, they do not approach; when you ask, 'Do you understand? they do not respond. Can anyone anywhere deal with such people?"
If Xuedou could not deal with you—this pack of donkeys—what would you be good for?
With his staff, he drove them all away at once. Xuedou’s Verse: Blind, deaf, and mute; utterly beyond the reach of intellectual devices.
Above heaven and below heaven, there is only laughter and sorrow. Even Li Lou could not distinguish true colors; how could Shi Kuang recognize the dark strings? Who can compete?

It is like sitting alone beneath a vacant window; leaves fall and flowers bloom at their own appointed times. [The Master] asked again, "Do you understand, or not? It is an iron hammer with no hole. Miaoxi commented:

"Although this monk has attained realization, he has only realized Yunmen Chan. As for Xuansha Chan, he must buy new straw sandals before he can attain it. Miaoxi’s Verse on Xuansha: Sitting alone beneath the empty window, Leaves fall and flowers bloom in their own time. If you ask whether he understands, An iron hammer with no hole.
Though this monk has indeed awakened, He has only realized Yunmen Chan. Were it Xuansha Chan, He would need to buy straw sandals anew.
The words of the three kinds of sick people: through Yunmen’s “six non-inclusions,” do not wait for right and wrong to enter your ears;
those who knew you before will turn into enemies.
When the Master saw a deceased monk, he said to the assembly: "Before the face of a deceased monk is precisely awakening (bodhi) encountered at every turn;
it is the divine light from ten thousand miles, the mark behind the crown. Many students were bewildered by these words. At other times he said:
"All you venerable Chan practitioners, you have all come from traveling on pilgrimage, claiming that you practice Chan and study the Way for the sake of some extraordinary or sublime destination."
It should simply be like this. Ask here, ask there; if anyone can demonstrate it, I shall bear witness for you.
I recognize all that is right and wrong. Is there anyone? If not, know that you are merely chasing after profit.
Since you have come here, I now ask you: do you all have eyes? If you do, you ought to recognize it right now.
"You have attained it. Do you recognize it yet? If you do not recognize it, I shall call you one who is born blind and deaf.
Is that so? Are you willing to speak thus? O Zen masters, do not humiliate yourselves. This is your true reality; when has it ever been like this?
The Buddhas of the ten directions hold you upon their crowns, not daring to err by even a single fraction."
"Son, you simply say that this matter is something only I can know. Do you understand? Now, as for those who claim to be our successors, they all say, 'I inherit from Śākyamuni.
I say, 'Śākyamuni and I studied together. You tell me, with whom do you study? Do you understand? This is not at all easy.
To know it, one must have attained great enlightenment before one can understand; if one is limited by the boundaries of what one has realized, one will never be able to perceive it."
"Do you still recognize Great Enlightenment? It cannot be that which reflects before the skull;
it cannot be your speaking of emptiness, your speaking of non-existence, or your speaking of this side and that side. There are worldly dharmas, and there is one that is not a worldly dharma.
You sons of the Buddha, even empty space arises from delusive illusion. Now, if you are truly and greatly awakened—"
Go! Where is there any basis for such talk? When even the news of empty space does not exist, where is there any sequence of karma within the three realms?
That which arises through the conditions of father and mother, you have established as being prior or posterior. To say now that it does not exist is already a deceptive word;
how much more so to claim that it does exist? Do you understand? You have been traveling on pilgrimage for a long time, yet you, my son, claim to have attained awakening.
Matter. I now ask you: suppose there is a mountain peak or a sheer cliff, a place utterly remote from human habitation—does the Buddha-dharma exist there?
Can it be discerned? If it cannot be discerned, you have not yet arrived. I often say: "In the presence of a deceased monk..."
This is precisely awakening (bodhi) before one’s eyes. It is the divine light from ten thousand miles away, the mark upon the crown of the head.

If a person can perceive it, they will be able to emerge from the realm of the five aggregates and cast off the conceptual thoughts before their skull. (Tianyi Huai said: "Setting aside for a moment the face of the deceased monk, what exactly is that which is behind a living person?
It all comes down to nothing other than your own true human body; where else could there be another dharma capable of covering it?
"Do you know? Do you believe it? Can you take responsibility for it? You must exert yourselves with great effort! Ascending the hall, he said:
"The Way of the Buddha is vast and open; it has no fixed path. It is the gateless gate of liberation, the mindless mind of the Way-man.

It does not abide within the three periods of time, and thus it cannot be subject to rising or sinking. To establish it as something separate from reality is to deviate from the truth; it does not belong to the realm of conditioned creation. To move is to give rise to birth."

This is the root of death. To remain in stillness is to become intoxicated in the realm of dullness and torpor; to extinguish both movement and stillness is to fall into a state of voidness and oblivion;

to grasp both movement and stillness together is to possess a coarse and superficial buddha-nature. You must, therefore, face all sensory objects and conditions like a withered tree or cold ashes, yet when applied according to the occasion, you must not fail to act appropriately.
Like a mirror reflecting myriad forms without its radiance being disturbed, or a bird flying through the sky without being mixed with the void.

Form: thus, throughout the ten directions there are no reflected images; within the three realms, all traces of activity are severed. One does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going, nor does one dwell in the mind of the intermediate state.
There is no sound of a drum within a bell, and no sound of a bell within a drum; bell and drum do not intersect. In every phrase there is neither before nor after.
It is like a strong man extending his arm—relying on no external force—or a lion roaming about—never seeking a companion.
The Nine Heavens are utterly free of obscuration; where is there any need for penetration? This single segment of radiance has never been dimmed.

If you reach this state, the essence is tranquil and ever-vivid; within the blazing brilliance of the sun, there is no limit or boundary; in the space of perfect enlightenment, there is no movement or wavering.

Swallowing and illuminating heaven and earth, it shines forth in utter clarity. Now, as for the Buddha appearing in the world: fundamentally, there is no coming or going. Names and forms have no substance;

the Way is originally suchness (*tathatā*). Reality is naturally so by its own nature; it is not something to be attained through cultivation or realization. It simply requires that one remain empty and at ease, yet never obscure one's active functioning.
It does not involve itself in the mud of the mundane world. Within this, even a hair’s breadth cannot be fully described; to do so would be to become an attendant of the Māra-king.

The interval before and after a phrase is the difficult point for the student. Therefore, when a single phrase accords with the occasion, the eighty thousand gates are forever cut off from birth and death.

(The *Sengbao zhuan* reads: "When one phrase accords with the occasion, the paths of birth and death are cut off within the eighty thousand Dharma-gates. Even if you attain a state like the moon's reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night, it follows...
Striking it with no flaw; touching its waves without dispersing. This is still the business of the shore of birth and death.
Where the Path-walker dwells, it is like fire melting ice—it never returns to become ice again. Once an arrow has left the bowstring, it has no power to turn back.
Therefore, it refuses to dwell within the cage and turns its head when called. The ancient sages made no arrangements, and thus to this day there is nowhere [to find them].
If one arrives here, at every step one ascends the profound mystery; it belongs neither to the heterodox nor the orthodox. Consciousness cannot perceive it, and wisdom cannot know it.
To move is to lose the source; to awaken is to be deluded regarding the ultimate intent. Those of the Two Vehicles tremble with fear, and those of the Ten Stages are struck with terror.
The paths of speech are cut off, and the sphere of mental activity ceases. It is such that Śākyamuni closed his door in Magadha, and Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī.
False! Subhūti proclaimed non-explanation to manifest the Way; Śakra and Brahmā ceased listening as flowers rained down.

If it is thus manifested before one, what further matter is there to doubt? It has no place of abiding; it transcends past, present, and future; it cannot be delimited or constrained; it is beyond the path of thought and reason;
it is not produced by adornment; it is fundamentally true and pure. Whether in movement, speech, laughter, or silence, it is clearly manifest everywhere. There is nothing more.

Deficiency. People of the present age do not awaken to the principle within this; they recklessly involve themselves in worldly affairs and sensory dust, becoming stained and attached everywhere and bound at every turn.
Even if they should awaken, the realms of dust remain chaotic and names and forms prove unreal.

They then intend to settle the mind and withdraw their thoughts, subsuming phenomena into emptiness, closing their eyes and hiding their vision. As soon as a thought arises, they immediately attempt to shatter it, yet subtle conceptions persist.
To suppress [the mind] as soon as it arises—such a view is that of an externalist who has fallen into nihilism, a dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed.
Obscure and indistinct, devoid of awareness or cognition, they plug their ears to steal the very bell [they seek], merely deceiving themselves in vain.
If one were to clarify this point here, it would not be so. It is not a matter of hiding in a corner or lurking by the door; every phrase is manifest before us.

It cannot be deliberated upon and does not involve literary artifice. Fundamentally, it is severed from the realm of dust; fundamentally, it has no rank or position. For the sake of expediency, we provisionally name it "a child who has left the home."
Ultimately, there is no trace. Whether true thusness, ordinary beings, or sages; whether those in hell, humans, or devas—these are merely methods for treating a mad child.
Since even empty space undergoes no change, how could the Great Way have any rising or sinking? To awaken is to be free and unimpeded, never departing from the fundamental limit.
If you arrive here, there is no place for either ordinary beings or sages to stand. If you direct your intention toward the words, you will be drowned and destroyed by them.

If you rush outward in pursuit, you will fall into the realm of Māra. As for the state of Suchness (tathatā), there is nothing to be contrived; it is just like a furnace of flames that harbors not even a mosquito.
This principle is fundamentally level and plain—what need is there to scrape it away? Whether in motion or stillness, whether raising an eyebrow or not, [it is all this].
This is the path of true liberation. Do not forcefully employ mental deliberation, for such construction deviates from the truth.

If you reach this point, not even a hair’s breadth shall be accepted; to point toward it with the intellect is already an error. Even if a thousand sages were to appear here, they could not establish a single word.

Long may you stand in reverence. Again, he addressed the assembly: "The true essence of the ancient Buddhas constantly manifests in accordance with things. Its majestic application is manifest everywhere."

Radiance flows everywhere; appearing and disappearing with equanimity, it illuminates all heights and depths. Therefore, for the superior śramaṇa, the eye of the Way must first accord with the fundamental and clarify the mind;
only then does one reach the ultimate. The myriad phenomena of the universe share a single body and a common source;

they are vast and boundless—whence could there be any discussion of obstruction? Events from kalpas as numerous as motes of dust are all present before one's eyes. Yet ordinary people remain distanced by the passage of long years.

This leads to a departure from the constant nature [of reality]. With deluded minds, they identify with external objects, thereby turning their backs on the True Doctrine. Clinging to existence and stagnating in emptiness, they fail to encounter virtuous friends or fellow practitioners;
instead, they merely form their own private interpretations based on doubt and error. Even when they engage in discussion, it results entirely in mere intellectual conjecture.

When they eventually reach the ground where principles are investigated, they cannot distinguish between the correct and the false. This is especially true for those who, throughout their lives, have never even attempted to grasp the truth themselves. As for the former sages...
The ancient masters knew the proper time for themselves; they disciplined themselves and deferred merit. In mountain huts and rocky caves, an ancient master said:

"If the mind retains the measure of the holy, one still falls into the dust of dharmas; if what has already been seen is not yet forgotten, it still constitutes a leakage. One must not merely speak of observing fasts and maintaining precepts.

Sitting long without lying down, dwelling the mind in contemplation of emptiness, concentrating the spirit to enter meditative absorption—when you have done this, you shall depart. What connection does this have [to liberation]?

Even the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Western Heavens can enter the eight-thousand-aeon samādhi; they concentrate their spirits in profound stillness, close their eyes and hide their pupils, extinguish the body and annihilate consciousness.
Yet, once the aeons are complete, they cannot avoid the cycle of birth and death. This is because their eye of the Way is not clear, and the root of birth and death remains.
The source is not broken. Now, for one who has left the household life, it is not so; one must not be the same as other non-Buddhists.
You must be truly enlightened and penetrating, possessing great wisdom and vision, able to penetrate to the same depth as all Buddhas. In silent illumination, knowledge is forgotten;
in emptiness, the myriad phenomena are contained. Right now, where is there that is not you? Where is there that is not clear? Where is there that is not revealed?
Manifest! Why do you not understand it in this way? If you lack this ground, how can you deal with all manner of leaks during the course of time?
Everything will become empty and false. Which of these, then, is the place where you have gained strength throughout your life?

If you have not yet achieved realization as it truly is, you must urgently forget your meals and lose sleep during this critical moment, as if your head were on fire, as if you had lost your very life.
Settle your mind in stillness to save yourself; let go of idle attachments and bring the consciousness to rest, and only then will you have even a slight measure of intimacy with it.
If you do not act thus, then tomorrow or the day after, everything will be carried away by the workings of your discriminatory intellect; what freedom will you then have?
Now, you are actually no different from those insentient things that proclaim the Dharma with such clarity—earth, wood, stone, and rock all preach the Dharma. Is this not so?
It is eternally true, yet few are able to hear it. Only if one hears this teaching can there be any discussion.
But tell me: how does one discuss the Dharma spoken by the insentient? Try to say something; you must not simply say that there is no word and no speech.
He neither looked nor listened; he could not be spoken to, nor did he speak of his own accord when unasked. He praised the path he was practicing, yet he did not see Sudhana.
Having visited fifty-three spiritual friends, at the very end he saw Maitreya. In the mere twinkling of an eye, he snapped his fingers.
He attained entry into the gate. As soon as he had entered, the gate closed of its own accord.

Within the multi-storied pavilion (kūṭāgāra), he beheld hundreds of thousands of Buddhas relinquishing their bodies and receiving new ones throughout past lives, as well as the spheres of activity of the one hundred and twenty spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) he had visited;
these all appeared simultaneously within the pavilion to serve as witnesses for him. Sudhana’s doubts were instantly stilled. Generally speaking, this consists of three main sections.

Below, once this true revelation is fully established as a complete negation, it can then be deliberated upon. Thus, within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, one is identical to the pure lands of all Buddhas;
what more need one fear regarding birth and death? Furthermore, who among them knows that all dharmas are entirely devoid of substantial reality?
Even at the assembly on Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa heard it directly, yet it was like speaking of the moon. As an ancient worthy said:
Do not deliberate upon good or evil at all; it is like pointing at the moon with one's finger.

Even the stages of practice and liberation of the Three Vehicles, the holy virtues and fruits of a Bodhisattva’s nirvana, are all like flowers in the sky or the horns of a rabbit. As it is said: "Returning to observe the world..."
It is just like events in a dream; conditioned mental phenomena cannot be relied upon. As days and years pass, they yield no benefit at all.

This is simply because one has deviated from the Truth and abandoned the Source, yet still harbors aversion for mundane emotions and takes delight in the Holy Path. To form such views and cognitions is to remain within the limitations of others;
one casts off the five aggregates but does not leave them behind. It is not seen that "all conditioned formations are impermanent"—this is birth and death.
Dharma. You merely intend to move forward; how could you possibly understand it? Only when you have penetrated through to the core will you know it.
If you have not yet investigated it thoroughly, you should know that it is all mere empty talk—a teaching difficult for the world to believe. Only those with great capacity can clearly realize it.
If you penetrate it in this life, it will remain so for ten thousand kalpas. As the ancient masters said: "One must resolve it directly in this very life."
[The Master] withdrew. [He said: "Who could endure the remaining retribution through many kalpas? Be careful. Ascending the hall, he said: "I now ask you all: what matter can you take up and bear?
In what world do you establish your body and maintain your life? Can you discern this?

If you cannot discern it, it is just like pressing one's eyes until flowers appear; as soon as one perceives things in such a way, one is mistaken. Do you know? Right now, before your very eyes, it is manifest."

The existence of mountains, rivers, and the great earth; form, emptiness, light, and darkness; and all such various things—all are but the appearances of flowers seen by one suffering from a deluded eye-disease.
This is called inverted perception. Now, as for those who have left the household life, they recognize the mind and penetrate the source; therefore, they are called śramaṇas.
Since you have now shaved your hair and donned the robes, assuming the appearance of a śramaṇa, you possess the capacity to benefit both yourself and others. As it is said:
Now look at this ground, entirely black and vast, resembling ink. One cannot even save oneself; how then can one hope to benefit others?

O worthy ones, the matters of the Buddha-dharma involve great causes and conditions. Do not treat them with indifference or superficiality, nor gather together to engage in idle chatter and miscellaneous talk.
Time passes all too quickly; the light of life is difficult to obtain and is truly to be regretted. You who are great men—why do you not [strive for yourselves]?
Examine and reflect: look into what this matter is. As for the ancestral vehicle of the Buddhas from of old—it is the crown lineage of all Buddhas.
Since you are unable to take responsibility for it, I have therefore used skillful means to advise you: simply proceed through the gate of Kāśyapa and leap directly beyond.
This one gate transcends the cause and effect of ordinary beings and sages; it transcends the wondrously adorned world-ocean of Vairocana; it transcends that [other].
The skillful means of Śākyamuni have, from time immemorial, never taught that there is a single thing to be given to you as an object of visual perception.
Why do you not urgently investigate and grasp this for yourself? You must not say, "I shall wait for two or three lifetimes; after long accumulating pure karma, I will attain it.
O worthy one, what is the matter of the *zong* (the fundamental vehicle)? It cannot be obtained merely by applying effort and adorning yourself with practice.
"Go! You cannot go by means of the knowledge of others' minds or past lives. Do you understand? Consider this:

when Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he performed all these various displays and preached the twelve divisions of the teachings, like pouring water from one vessel into another, creating a grand spectacle of Buddhist ritual.
Yet, within this gate, not a single point can be used; not even a hair’s breadth of artifice can be employed. Do you know? It is just like..."
The matter of dreams is like talking in one's sleep; a śramaṇa should not emerge with his head out of it, for that would differ from the matter of a dream.

This is because he has recognized it. Do you understand? To recognize it is the great liberation, the person who has attained great penetration; therefore, he transcends both ordinary people and sages.
Born into freedom from death, detached from cause and effect, transcending Vairocana and surpassing Śākyamuni, you are not deceived by the causes and effects of ordinary beings or sages.
Nowhere can anyone recognize you; do you understand? Do not remain forever clinging to the net of love for birth and death.

Bound by the karma of good and evil, you are led away; you have no share of freedom. Even if you could refine your body and mind until they were as empty as space, even if you reached a state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness that does not waver, you would still not have escaped the *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness). The ancients called this "like a rushing torrent;
because the flow is so rapid, one is unaware of it and falsely deems it tranquil. To practice in such a manner is entirely to remain within the bounds of saṃsāra.
It cannot be so; one will continue to wander in saṃsāra as before. Therefore it is said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
This very fruit of the three vehicles is thus fearsome. If one lacks the eye of the Way, one will not reach the ultimate end.

How does this compare to the ordinary person of today on the broad earth, who, without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort, suddenly transcends all? Do you understand and save your mental energy? Would you still wish for such a thing?
I exhort you: I shall now stand here and wait for you to grasp it; I will not further instruct you to apply effort or refine your practice.
If you do not act this way now, when will you? Will you consent? Then he descended from his seat. Entering the hall, he said: "You people!"
It is like sitting in the middle of the great ocean, submerged up to one’s head, yet still stretching out one’s hand to ask others for water to drink.
A bodhisattva who studies Prajñāpāramitā must possess a great vessel and great wisdom before they can succeed. If one possesses such wisdom, [one may attain it].

Right now, one can break free and depart. However, if one’s faculties are dull, one must simply apply diligent effort and endure with steadfast will, forgetting fatigue day and night, losing sleep and neglecting food, as if mourning for a deceased parent.

If one proceeds with such urgency until the end of one's life, and furthermore receives the support and guidance of others, investigating the reality down to the very marrow of one's bones, it will not be difficult to grasp it. How much more so nowadays!
Who is a person capable of receiving and studying [the Dharma]? O virtuous one, do not merely memorize words and phrases as if you were reciting a *dhāraṇī*.
When you step forward with your mouth full of "dha-dha" and "ho-ho," and are caught and interrogated by others, you have no way out;
you then become angry and say, "The Master did not answer me. Learning in such a manner—how can it be called learning?
This is a great suffering. Do you understand? There is a certain class of monks who sit upon rope-seated platforms and claim to be "good knowledge-holders" (śāstrajña).
When questioned, they merely sway their bodies, move their hands, blink their eyes, stick out their tongues, and stare blankly.

Furthermore, there is another class who speak of "luminous clarity" and the "numinous spirit," claiming that the capacity for seeing and hearing resides in the "spiritual platform" of the cognitive faculty, acting as the sovereign within the field of the five aggregates (skandha). To act in such a manner is to practice goodness in vain.
Knowledge deceives people greatly. Do you understand? I shall now question you:
if you take this "bright and alert" state to be your true self, why does it fail to be bright and alert when you are dozing off?
If it is not your true self during sleep, why is there a time of brightness? Do you understand yet? This is called "mistaking a thief for one's own son."
This is the root of birth and death; it is the arising of deluded thought. Do you wish to know the source of this root? I shall tell you:

that which is "brightly manifest and spiritually aware" exists only because of the dharmas of the external objects—forms, sounds, fragrances, and so forth—and through them, discrimination arises. One then says, "This is the brightly manifest and spiritually aware.
If those external objects did not exist, this "brightly manifest and spiritually aware" of yours would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.
O Benevolent One, where does true reality reside? If you now wish to attain mastery over the field of the five aggregates, you need only recognize your own secret vajra-body.
An ancient sage said to you: "Perfectly complete and all-pervasive, it extends throughout the entire realm of dust.
I shall now explain this briefly for you; the wise can understand through analogy. Do you still see the south?

In Jambudvīpa, all the activities and undertakings performed by people of the world—those various mental states and actions for maintaining the body and sustaining life—none of them are established without relying upon the light of the sun.
Yet, does the substance of the sun itself possess such manifold mental activities? Does it have any pervasive movement at all?
If you wish to recognize the adamantine essence (*vajra-svabhāva*), you must likewise view it in this way. It is simply this.
Now, the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the lands of the ten directions; form and emptiness, light and darkness;

as well as your own body and mind—all these are entirely manifested through the pervasive and perfected majestic radiance [of your original nature]. Indeed, they are nothing other than the successive manifestations of the karma created by all classes of beings, including devas and humans.
The retribution of birth and existence—whether sentient or insentient—is none that does not rely upon your majestic radiance.
Even the Buddhas’ attainment of the Way and their fruits, their reception of beings and benefitting of life, are all entirely dependent upon your majestic radiance.

As for this adamantine essence, do ordinary people and Buddhas exist within it? Does your mental activity exist within it? One cannot say they do not; yet one must not simply proceed as if they were present. Know this.
"Ma! Since you possess such extraordinary and marvelous capacity to manifest yourself in the presence of the light, why do you not clarify and grasp the cause?
Why, instead, do you follow others to make your living within the ghost-realm of the five-aggregate field of the body? You are simply deceiving yourself right now."
Suddenly, the demon of impermanence arrives; the eyes roll wildly, and one clings to the view of a self and the view of a life.
At such a time, it is extremely difficult to bear. It is like the great suffering of a living turtle shedding its shell. O worthy ones, do not harbor a drowsy understanding.
And so you depart. You have not yet been able to cover even a hair’s breadth [of the truth].
Do you realize this? There is no peace within the three realms; it is like a burning house. Furthermore, you are not one who has attained true peace and happiness;
you merely form large crowds and interfere in the affairs of others, flying here and there like wild deer in the fields, seeking only food and clothing. If you act in such a way, how can you...?
You walk the path of another king—do you understand? Kings and ministers do not detain you; your parents have released you to leave the home life;
donors from the ten directions provide you with food and clothing; and the local spirits and dragons protect you.
Yet, you must possess a sense of shame and know how to repay their kindness; do not fail these people. On this long bench, line up and sit down to consume [your meals].
"You are about to depart. You say it will be peaceful and happy, but that is not yet so. All this has been sustained by you through the nourishment of gruel and rice;

now you will change until you resemble a rotting winter melon, and then you will be buried in the earth. Your karmic consciousness will be vast and茫然 (vastly bewildered), with no foundation to rely upon.
Why, O śramaṇa, have you come to such a state? As for all those wriggling creatures upon the great earth, I call them the kalpa of hell."

Abide! If you do not understand this now, tomorrow or the day after, you will enter the wombs of donkeys and horses, pulling plows and dragging harrows, bitting iron and bearing saddles, being pounded by pestles and ground in mills, and being burned and boiled in water and fire. It will be extremely difficult for you to endure;
you must be truly fearful. This is your own doing—do you know? If you were to understand it right now, throughout eternal kalpas, you would never have [experienced such suffering].
"I have this news to tell you. If you do not understand this, the causes and conditions of these afflictions and evil karma will not cease for one or two kalpas;
they will last as long as your own adamantine life-span. Do you know? A questioner asked: "As for the ultimate vehicle (zongcheng) hereafter, how should one discuss its principles?
The Master said: "Few people listen. The questioner said: "I beg the Master to speak directly. The Master said: "It is like being deaf."

"Ma! Furthermore, he said: 'O Benevolent One, now that we have no other recourse, I must suppress such majestic radiance and urge you with bitter words through hundreds of thousands of skillful means, whether in this way or that. Yet, all that we have shared as friends has resulted in nothing but inverted views.
This throat, lips, and mouth of mine have achieved nothing but the karma of a wild fox spirit to deceive you. I replied: "I, too—"
Do you understand? As for whether there is fault or no fault, only I know it myself; how could you possibly comprehend it?
If such a person were to appear, they would willingly submit to censure. Truly, being a master is no easy task; one must be a true *kalyāṇamitra* to truly understand this.
Even though I am now providing such expedient means to assist you, you still cannot grasp it. Is this not so?
In the midst [of this], he purely raises up the essential vehicle (zongsheng). Where will you place it? Do you understand? Forty-nine years were but expedient means.
As for the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were a million followers, yet only Kāśyapa alone heard it directly;
the rest did not hear it at all. Tell me, what is that matter which Kāśyapa heard directly? You must not say it was like...
Coming, there is no speaking; speaking is non-speaking. Kāśyapa heard what cannot be heard, and thus he attained that which must be departed from.
This cannot be the fruit of your cultivated causes, nor the fundamental matter of the adornment of merit and wisdom—do you understand?

For instance, when it is said, "I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, which I entrust to Mahākāśyapa," my words are like speaking of the moon. When Caoxi held up his whisk, was it not likewise like pointing at the moon? Therefore...
The Way is a matter within the Patriarchal Vehicle (Zongcheng) inside the Great Tang. I have never seen a single person raise it up and proclaim it.

Even if someone were to do so, all people throughout the great earth would lose their lives; it would be like an unperforated iron mallet, causing everyone at once to lose their edge and be rendered tongue-tied.
You people are fortunate to have encountered me; disregarding my own life, I shall share with you this inverted knowledge and vision.
"Follow your own wild mind; only then will there be a place for you to pose a question. If I did not allow you to know and hear me in this way, where would you find me?
Do you understand? It is a great difficulty; exert yourself! Take care. He ascended the hall and said:
"The sun-wheel in the vast void is what establishes all people. The vast void is present right now—how do you all perceive it? It fills the eyes."
Looking, one does not see; listening with ears full, one does not hear. If you cannot discern these two points, you are but a dozing fellow.

If you can penetrate them thoroughly, you will sit upon all ordinary beings and sages, and sit upon the three realms. Your dream-like body and mind will be such that there is not a single thing even as large as the point of a needle to serve as a condition or a counterpart.
Even if all the Buddhas were to appear and manifest infinite supernatural powers and transformations, [it would remain so].
Throughout all these myriad nets of teachings, not even a single hair’s breadth has been applied; they merely assist the gate of sincere faith for beginners.
Do you understand? The waterbirds and forest trees can indeed grasp the essential principles most precisely; it is simply that few people listen.
This is not a matter of external affairs. To be a celestial demon or a non-Buddhist is to betray kindness and violate righteousness;

for humans and devas within the six realms of existence to act thus is to deceive themselves and succumb to madness (it should be "deception"). If the śramaṇas of today do not realize this matter, they instead become men who merely dally with shadows, floating and sinking within the sea of birth and death—when will they ever find rest?
Fortunately, you yourselves possess such a vast and magnificent tradition, yet you are unable to carry it forward.
"Furthermore, you must act as the sovereign within the field of the five aggregates. Do you still see it in your dreams?
Such vast territories—who could possibly be their sovereign? The great earth cannot support them, and empty space cannot contain them; how can this be considered a small matter?"
If you wish to attain thorough penetration, right here and now, you must become clearly enlightened. I do not instruct you to grasp even a single dharma as small as a speck of dust;
I do not instruct you to discard even a single dharma as slight as a hair. Do you understand? It is further said:
If you truly accept this for yourself, then regardless of whether you are a beginner or have entered the monastic community, it can be said that you have long been together with all people.

[He] steps forward. He is no less than the Buddhas of the past; he is like the waters of the great ocean, which all fish and dragons, from their first birth until old age, equally inhale, swallow, and enjoy.
Therefore it is said: "One who has first resolved for enlightenment stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the ancient Buddhas.
It is also said: "Your faculties have all become perverted; the ancients used the medicine of infinite wondrous efficacy to heal them."
This is the therapeutic antidote. Even reaching the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), one has not yet attained true awakening; thus, one knows that the Great Matter is no small thing.
When the ancients contemplated it, they were as if mourning the death of their parents; today, you brothers treat it as if it were trivial. Where else is there someone who can resolve this for you?
It is a pity that your time is being wasted in vain. Why not investigate it for yourself in secret and examine it with meticulous care? Until—
There is no place of attachment; naturally cease all conditions and depart. It is further said:

When these people see dangerous and evil things, or see tigers, knives, swords, and various such matters threatening their bodies and lives, they give rise to boundless fear and terror. What is this like?
It is just like a painter in this world who paints a depiction of the hells, fashioning tigers, knives, and swords;
having finished it, he looks at it intently and yet becomes terrified by it himself. You people here are exactly the same.
All these various things you perceive as existing are produced by your own illusions; you become terrified by them yourselves, and it is not someone else who is doing this to you.
It is past. Do you now wish to awaken from this illusory delusion? Simply recognize your own adamantine eye.
If you recognize it, I have never taught that there is even a speck of dust that can be manifested. Where else could there be tigers, wolves, knives, or swords to intimidate and frighten you?
Even up to Śākyamuni, such artful maneuvers cannot find a place to show their heads. Regarding this—
As I have told you: the Eye of the Śramaṇa grasps the world firmly; it encompasses heaven and earth, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of leakage.
Where else could there be a single thing for you to perceive or know? Do you understand? Why do you not urgently investigate this?

The Master [said]: "The Great Dharma is swift and difficult to raise; those of superior capacity are rarely encountered. Students rely on words to produce understanding, and follow their illumination while losing the source. Thereupon, he showed [the following]:
The Three Phrases of the Essential Principle state: The first phrase is to simply take responsibility for oneself. It is already fully perfected;
throughout the ten directions of the world, there is nothing else. It is none other than you yourself. Who else could see? Who else could hear?

All that exists is the activity of your own mind-king, which is entirely the unshakable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). It lacks only your own taking responsibility for it. This is called "opening the gate of skillful means" to enable [understanding].
You believe there is a portion of true permanence that flows on, extending through past and present, such that there has never been anything that is not it, nor anything that is not non-it.
However, this statement merely establishes the Dharma of equality. Why is this? It is simply using words to dispel words and using principles to pursue principles;

it is merely the ordinary nature and characteristics used to engage with things and benefit sentient beings. Furthermore, regarding the fundamental tenet, this still only clarifies what has come before.
After failing to understand this, they label it "one-flavor equanimity" or "plain reality. This is merely the measure of partial realization of the *dharmakāya*;

there are no words that transcend the ordinary, and one dies beneath the words, lacking any freedom. If one knows the measure that transcends the ordinary, one will not be driven by the demons of the mind.
Once [this truth] enters one's hands, it is immediately transformed into a state of natural ease; speech penetrates the Great Way and does not fall into the trap of complacent indifference.

This is what is called the first sentence of the fundamental tenet. The second sentence involves turning the cause toward the fruit; it does not cling to the principle of ordinary, uniform suchness (*tathatā*).
It is expediently termed "shifting positions to meet the occasion," wherein life and death are exercised with mastery, and bestowing or withholding is applied according to suitability.

Entering birth and entering death, one extensively benefits all beings. Completely transcending the realm of form, desire, attachment, and views, this expedient means is called the Buddha-nature that suddenly leaps beyond the three realms.
This is termed the simultaneous clarification of two principles and the concurrent illumination of two meanings;
it is unmoved by the two extremes, and its wondrous function manifests before one. This is called the governing tenet of the second phrase. As for the third phrase, know...

There is the fundamental nature and characteristic of great wisdom, which penetrates excessive views; it is clear in the yin and deep within the yang, vast and encompassing the realms of the sands of Ganges.

This single true essence manifests great function, responding and transforming without fixed direction. It is entirely functional and yet entirely non-functional; entirely arising and yet entirely non-arising.
These skillful means are called the Gate of Compassionate Samādhi; this is what is termed the third phrase of the governing principle.
Huanji said: "Sha [Wenying] claims that Kāśyapa heard it directly from the Buddha himself, yet he speaks of it as if discussing the moon while presenting it with such dogmatic certainty.
By means of these three statements, he has come to vie with the ancient Abbot of the Pagoda. Is this truly so? How could it be so?
Master Hong was fond of the curious and boasted of his erudition; it is not necessarily all true—there are many instances of this kind."
The Master had a verse that said: "The divine light ten thousand miles away is the mark behind the crown; when it sinks beneath the crown, where can one look?
The task is done and the intention has ceased; this trace of arrival pervades every place. The wise person, upon encountering it, seizes it at once;
do not wait until in an instant you lose your head. He also said: "Xuan Sha’s path of travel is unique; people of the present day must know it well. The three months of winter..."
The yang energy was at its peak. It was the time when frost fell in the sixth month. There are words that have nothing to do with the tongue; there are wordless phrases that are most essential.

If you understand my final phrase, few in this world will know it. On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty (the Wuchen year), he manifested illness and passed away.
The Master’s physical stature was short and small, yet his spirit was overflowing. Those who listened beneath his Dharma seat...
[He] lived to the age of seventy-four and sat in meditation for forty-four summer retreats.
Chan Master Hui-ling of Changqing in Fuzhou first visited Lingyun and asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

Lingyun replied, "The donkey’s business is not yet over, and the horse’s business has already arrived. The Master did not attain realization. He then visited Xuefeng and brought up the previous conversation.
Feng said, "Are you not a native of Suzhou? The Master replied, "How could I not know that I am a native of Suzhou?
When Xuansha saw this being raised, he said, "I fear his karmic conditions do not lie with the Abbot; let him come down here. I shall speak to him.
The Master went to Xuansha’s place and recounted the previous conversation. Xuansha said, "You are the Way-farer Ling."
"How is it that you do not understand? The Master asked. "I do not know the meaning behind Lingyun speaking thus; what is his intention?
The monk said, "It is simply that the Way of Ling is not to be sought externally. The Master asked, "How about you, Master? You speak of my name in this way; I cannot fail to recognize it.
I beg you, Master, to explain the principle. The monk said, "You are a man from the Two Zhe regions; I am..."
[A monk] from Fuzhou asked, "How is it that you do not understand? The Master said, "I truly do not understand. [The monk] begged the Master to explain it for him.
The Master said, "Have I not already explained it to you? The monk said, "I have come here specifically to beg the Master to explain it for me."
"Do not deceive me like this. The Monk said, "Do you hear the sound of the drum? The Master said, "I cannot fail to recognize the sound of the drum.
The Monk said, "If you hear the sound of the drum, it is only you. The Master said, "I do not understand. The Monk said, "Go eat your congee first, then come back.
After the Master had finished eating his congee, he went up [to the hall] and said, "I beg the Venerable One to explain it to me. The Monk said, "No."
[The Master] said, "I have finished eating my congee. The Teacher [Xuefeng] said, "I beg the Venerable One to explain this clearly;
do not deceive me. I shall take my leave and return home. Xuefeng asked, "When you came here, by which path did you come? The Teacher replied, "By the path from Dayu.
Xuefeng said, "When you go back, you will also go by the path from Dayu. How can you say that I am deceiving you? Thus he went back and forth with Xuefeng in this manner.
Fengxue Sha sat for twenty years, wearing out seven meditation cushions, yet he did not understand this matter. One day, as he rolled up the curtain, he suddenly attained great enlightenment.
He then composed a verse, which said: "How very strange! How very strange! Rolling up the curtain, one sees the whole world.
If someone asks me what my school is, I pick up my whisk and strike them right on the mouth. Fengxue said to Sha: "This fellow..."
"Thoroughly remove it. Sha said, "Not yet. This is merely a composition of the conscious mind; you must further examine it before it is acceptable.
In the evening, when the assembly of monks came up to pay their respects, Feng said to the Master, "Tou-tou Bei has not yet consented to you.
If you truly possess correct awakening, bring it forth for the assembly. The Master then offered this verse: "Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. Only man..."
Only when one is self-accepting does one become intimate [with the truth]. Formerly, I mistakenly sought it along the road; today, upon looking, it is ice within fire.
Feng then looked at Sha and said, "It must not be further composed by the conscious intellect.

The Master asked Feng, "The single path transmitted by all the sages of antiquity—please, Master, grant us an instruction. After a long silence, Feng remained still. The Master performed a prostration and withdrew. Feng then smiled.

The Master entered the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects. Xuefeng asked, "What is this? The Master replied, "Today the weather is fine; it is good for drying the wheat. From that time on, in responding to questions, he never failed to accord with the profound principle (*xuanzhi*). When Baofu was about to depart and return to Xuefeng, he said to the Master, "If the Abbot of the Mountain asks you about my news, how will you respond? "There is a little," [Fromzhan] said. "Tell me, what is this Way? The Master said, "To whom should I entrust it?
[Fromzhan] said, "Although Congzhan has these words, there is likely no such thing. The Master said, "If that were so, then your future path would depend entirely upon you, O Dharma brother.
The Master and Baofu were touring the mountains. Baofu asked, "An ancient said, 'At the summit of Mount Miaofeng. Is it not just this?"
[The monk] said, "Even so, there is none. The Master said, "It is indeed so, but it is a great pity.
A monk asked Gushan, "As for Changqing speaking thus, what was his intention?
Gushan said, "If Master Sun had not spoken these words, one might say that skulls would cover the wilds."
The Master was at West Hall. He asked the Senior Monk Xian, "There is Elephant Bone Mountain here; have you ever been there? Xian replied, "I have not.
The Master said, "Why have you not been there? Xian said, "Because I have my own fundamental matter to attend to.
The Master asked, "What is this fundamental matter of yours, Senior Monk? Xian then lifted up a corner of his patched robe. The Master said, "Is it merely this?"
“This one. Do not add anything more. He asked, “What did the Elder see? The Master said, “How can you have a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail?
He questioned a monk, “Where have you come from? The monk replied, “From Gushan. The Master said, “Gushan has a phrase that does not cross the stone gate.
If someone asks about it, what will you say? The monk replied, “Last night I stayed at Baoci. The Master struck him across the back.
"I strike you! Furthermore, how is it? The monk said, "If you, Master, were to administer this blow, you would not have received the offerings of devas and humans in vain.
The Master said, "How many times should I let you off? A monk asked, "How can one attain freedom from doubt and delusion?
The Master then extended both hands. The monk did not offer further words. The Master said, "Ask me again and I will tell you. When the monk asked again, the Master bared his shoulder.
[The Master] sat down. The monk prostrated. The Master asked, "How do you understand this? The monk replied, "Today the wind has risen.
The Master said, "To speak thus is the understanding of one who is not yet settled. Within the past and present, what essential point do you have that can equal Changqing?
If you can bring it forth, I will allow you to be the host of this discourse. The monk merely stood there. The Master then asked, "Who are you?"
"Where is that person? [The monk] said, "A person from the north. The Master said, "Three thousand li to the south or north—why do you study false speech?
The monk had no reply. Xuefeng asked, "I saw when Guishan questioned Yangshan about where all the sages of the past have gone.
Yangshan said, 'Some are in the heavens; some are among humans. What do you say is Yangshan’s meaning?"
Sheng asked, "Master, if one were to ask about the place where the sages appear and disappear, would it be improper to speak in this way? Feng said, "You are entirely unwilling to accept [the truth].
He continued, "Suppose someone were to ask you, how would you answer? The Master said, "Simply say, 'Wrong. Feng said, "In that case, it is you who are not wrong.

The Master said, "How is that any different from being wrong? [Later,] he ascended the hall and said: "If you encounter a fellow traveler on the Way, you pass each other with shoulders touching; thus, in a single lifetime..."
The period of study is concluded. Entering the hall: "When everything has been thoroughly cleaned and tidied away, you step forward and ask me for the self.
I strike you once across the back. If that one blow reaches you, you will surely feel shame; if that one blow does not reach you, where then do you understand it? Entering the hall:
"If everyone were like this today, the Old Barbarian (Bodhidharma) would have cause for hope. *Baoshou* (Precious Seal).
Fú said, "If it were all like today, the Old Barbarian would be utterly hopeless.
Xuánjué said, "To speak in such a way—is this the language of meeting, or is it not the language of meeting?"
▲ When Chan Master Congzhan of Baofu Monastery in Zhangzhou was fifteen years old, he paid his respects to Xuefeng as his preceptor.
He traveled through the regions of Wu and Chu, and later returned to serve him. One day, Xuefeng suddenly called out to him, "Do you understand?

As the Master was about to step forward, Xuefeng struck him with his staff. At that moment, the Master realized his place of return. He frequently consulted Changqing regarding the skillful means of the ancients and the present.

▲ Chan Master Youzhang of Ruilong Monastery in Hangzhou was the nephew of the Tang Prime Minister Xiahou Zhi.

At the age of seven, while visiting Huizhao Temple, he suddenly requested to leave the household life. Xiahou would not permit it, so the Master immediately ceased eating and drinking. Since he could not be dissuaded, [Xiahou finally consented].
He granted his request. Later, when Yinxin was at Baishui, he traveled to Jiangling.
There, Master Tengteng said to him, "Go to Tiantai and settle where you find tranquility; stay wherever you encounter peace.

Furthermore, he met Master Hanzhan, who said to him, "Forty years from now, there will be a Bodhisattva beneath Mount Jinzhou who shall rule over the region south of the Yangtze. At that time, my Way..."

How flourishing! When the Master entered the imperial palace, he resided at Fudang Monastery in Jing’an County. In the third year of the Tiānyòu era, Qián Shangfù (the Senior Uncle) respectfully invited the Master to his capital, where he greatly honored and exalted the White Dharma (*śukladharma*).
His records of being "boisterous and simple" perfectly accorded with the following discourse from the High Seat:
"In recent years, this old monk has traveled throughout the regions beyond the Yangtze River, including Lingnan, Jing, and Hu; wherever there were assemblies of realized teachers..."
There is no one among those who have come to consult me in the forest who does not seek this for the sake of today’s gathering with you all—each desiring to know the destination.
Yet, throughout all quarters, there is never a divergent teaching; it simply instructs each person to bring their frantic mind to rest and cease seeking from others.

One merely accords with circumstances while abiding in reality, yet there is no reality to be accorded with. One utilizes things according to the occasion, yet there is no occasion that can be utilized.
Even if one were to show compassion through bitter words, one could not call day night; even with further skillful means, one could never point east and call it west.
Should one be able to do so, it would simply be a supernatural feat or a magical trick, and would have nothing to do with me. If it is merely a matter of repeating words...
This is the way of such people. Failing to reflect upon themselves and recognize their error, they simply wish to pluck flowers from the sky and grasp the moon from the waves.
Will they ever succeed in applying their mental power? You should now each withdraw and contemplate this for yourselves.

If you suddenly come to accept it, only then will you know that the old man of Rui Long, having no other choice, went to great lengths to lead you back. Do you accept it now? The second year of Tiancheng, Dinghai (1027), the fourth month.
Month [X]. The Master entered the residence of the Shangfu (Grandfather) to take his leave, entrusting him with the protection of the Dharma.
He passed away at the appointed time. Chan Master Baozi Zangyu was asked by a monk: "When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when thought changes, the essence becomes distinct.
But what is it like when emotion has not yet arisen? The Master said: "Obstructed. The monk asked: "When emotion has not yet arisen, what is it that is obstructed? The Master said: "This."
This young man had not yet met his destined teacher.
▲ Chan Master Wenyuan of Guangfeng Monastery on Yunmen Mountain in Shaoyou was a native of Jiaxing. His secular surname was Zhang.
In his youth, he relied upon Vinaya Master Zhicheng at Kongwang Temple to leave the household life. Possessing a keen nature and innate wisdom, his eloquence was as if bestowed by heaven.
Upon reaching maturity, he shaved his head and received full ordination at the altar in Pilin. He attended Master Cheng for several years, thoroughly investigating the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Because he had not yet clarified his own fundamental matter, he went to visit Muzhou. As soon as Muzhou saw him arrive, he closed the door; the Master then knocked on it. Muzhou said:
"Who is it? The Master replied, "It is I. The Governor asked, "What are you doing? The Master said, "My own matter is not yet clear; I beg the Master for instruction.
The Governor opened the door, looked at him once, and then closed it. The Master continued to knock on the door like this for three consecutive days. On the third day, [the Governor finally spoke].
The Governor opened the gate. The Master then pushed his way inside. The Governor immediately seized him, saying, "Speak! Speak!
As the Master hesitated, the Governor shoved him out, shouting, "A carriage wheel from the time of Qin! He then slammed the door, injuring the Master's foot.
From this, the Master attained awakening. The Governor pointed him toward Xuefeng. When the Master arrived at Xuefeng’s manor, he saw a monk and asked, "Elder, are you going up the mountain today?"
"Go there," he said. The monk replied, "Yes. The Master said, "Deliver this kōan to the Abbot, but you must not say it was the words of another.

The monk replied, "I understand. The Master said, "When you reach the mountain monastery, as soon as the assembly has gathered for the Abbot’s formal lecture, go out, clasp your hands behind your back, and stand upon the ground, saying: 'Old man, why do you not remove that iron cangue from around your neck?'"
"Take it off. The monk followed his teacher’s instruction exactly. Seeing the monk speak in this manner, Xuefeng descended from his seat, seized him by the chest, and said, "Speak quickly!
Speak quickly! The monk had no reply. Xuefeng pushed him away and said, "That was not your words.
The monk said, "It was my words. Xuefeng said, "Attendant, bring the rope and staff! The monk said, "It was not my words; it was..."
A senior monk from Zhongshang in Zhejiang was at Zhuangshang; he sent someone to tell [Xuefeng] that I had come to speak with him.

Xuefeng said, "The assembly has gone to Zhuangshang to welcome five hundred virtuous teachers. The next day, the Master went up to Xuefeng. As soon as Xuefeng saw him, he asked, "For what reason have you reached such a state?
The Master then lowered his head. From that point on, they were in accord. They refined their understanding together for many years in secret.
He was granted the seal of the lineage.
The *Yuanwu Biyánjí* states: "The Master inherited the intent of Muzhou and went to see Xuefeng.
Upon his arrival, he immediately stepped forward from the assembly and asked, 'What is the Buddha? Xuefeng said, 'Do not speak in your sleep. The Master then bowed. He resided there for three years."
One day, Xuefeng asked, "What is your realization? The Master replied, "My realization does not differ by so much as a single hair from that of all the sages of the past.
(From the *Sengbao zhuan*: He went to visit Xuefeng. At that time, Xuefeng was sitting atop a stack of timber preaching the Dharma to the assembly.
The Master stepped forward and looked at him intently, saying, "A three-hundred-jin iron yoke upon your neck!")
"Why do you not take it off? Feng said, "Why have you come to such a state? The Master wiped his eyes with his hand and walked away. Feng was struck by this in his heart.
The next day, he ascended the seat and said, "There is a turtle-nosed snake on South Mountain; everyone, look carefully as you pass in and out.
The Master then tossed his staff out [of the hall], and Feng was again seized with alarm and trepidation. From that time on, those of his caliber changed their perspective.
The three records contain accounts of the Master’s time at Xuefeng; their differences are as follows. Consequently, I have recorded them together here for reference.
While the Master was at Xuefeng, a monk asked Xuefeng: “What is it that, when one’s eyes meet the Way, one does not understand it? When one sets foot upon it, how can one know the path?”
Fengyun said, "The blue sky! The blue sky! The monk did not understand, so he asked the Master, "What is the meaning of 'the blue sky'?
The Master said, "Three catties of hemp; one bolt of cloth. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "I further offer you three feet of bamboo.

When Fengyun heard this, he was delighted and said, "I have long harbored doubts about this cloth-clad monk. After the Master left the mountain ridges, he traveled everywhere to visit various teachers. This was during the time when the Master was on pilgrimage.

He encountered a presiding master who was serving as abbot at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. At the time of the midday meal, Xuefeng held up his alms bowl and asked him, "If you can speak of this, I will give you my bowl.
The master replied, "This is merely the business of an emanation Buddha. Xuefeng said, "As a presiding master, you have not even attained the status of a slave.
The master said, "I do not understand. Xuefeng said, "Ask me, and I will tell you. Only then did the master prostrate himself.

He prostrated. Feng then stepped on him and knocked him down. [The Master] said, "I attained it seven years ago, and only then did I see it. The Teacher said, "It is you who attained it seven years ago, and only then did you see it.
He replied, "Yes. The Teacher said, "Wait another seven years before you truly attain it. The Teacher was at the assembly of Master Yun in Zhejiang.
One day, while drinking tea, [Zhaozhou] raised the case of Master Yunmen’s *chuyu* (pith instruction), which said: "Seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing are the Dharma;
yet the Dharma is apart from seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. What is it? A monk standing nearby said, "It is certainly seeing.

[Zhaozhou] replied, "Now, all that is seen, heard, perceived, and known before one's eyes is the Dharma, and yet the Dharma itself cannot be apprehended. The Master clapped his hands once, whereupon Master Yunmen raised his head.
The Master said, "There is still one move missing. Yun said, "When I arrived here, I did not understand. The Master went to Dongyan. Dongyan asked, "What have you come to do?
The Master said, "I have come to draw near. Dongyan said, "Why are you wandering about so recklessly? The Master said, [I am here].
[The Master] was temporarily away. Yank said, "If you recognize your error, you will attain it. The Master asked, "Why are you running about so wildly? He went to Shushan Ren.
Ren asked, "Bring me a single phrase from the place where you have gained strength. The Master said, "Please ask in a loud voice. Shushan then asked in a loud voice.
The Master laughed and said, "Are you eating porridge today? Shushan said, "I am eating porridge. The Master said, "You are shouting wildly."
Mo arrived at Wo-long and asked, "One who has realized their own nature—do they still perceive a self? Long replied, "If one does not perceive a self, only then has one realized the self.
He asked again, "That which is learned upon the long rows of meditation beds—what rank of capacity is that? Long replied:
"This is the second capacity. [Wumen] asked, "What is the first capacity? Long said, "Tight leather sandals.
Miaoxi said, "Riding the thief’s horse to pursue the thief’s band; borrowing the old woman’s shawl to bow for New Year’s greetings."
Upon arriving at Guizong, a monk asked, "The great assembly has gathered like clouds; what should they discuss? Guizong said, "In twos and threes.
The monk said, "I do not understand. Guizong said, "In threes and twos. The Master then asked the monk, "What was the essential meaning of Guizong's words?
The monk said, "He came entirely in this manner. The Master said, "Have you ever been to Longya in Tanzhou? He replied, "I have been there."
The Master said, "A fellow who is searching for wild roots has arrived at Tiantong. Tiantong asked, "Have you reached a definitive conclusion? The Master replied, "What do you mean, Preceptor?
Tiantong said, "If you do not understand, you are wrapped up right before your eyes. The Master said, "If one understands, one is wrapped up right before one's eyes.

He then went to Ehu, where he heard the Abbot ascend the hall and say, "Do not speak only of those who have not yet attained realization; even those who have long been immersed in it are still floating and pressing against the surface."
