If you do not see it, do not speak recklessly. [The Head Seat] asked: "As for saying 'floating and pressing,' what does that mean? The Master said: "A cangue upon the head and shackles upon the feet."
[The monk] said, "If that is so, then there is no Buddha-dharma. The Master said, "This is the realm of great beings such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
When the Master arrived in Jiangzhou, the Minister Chen invited him for a meal. As soon as he saw [the Master], he asked: "I do not ask about the Confucian classics;
I have my own preceptors for the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings. What is the matter of a patch-robed monk’s traveling on pilgrimage?"
The Master said, "How many people have you questioned about this? Fushan replied, "I am questioning you, the Venerable One, right now. The Master said, "Set that aside for a moment;
what is the meaning of the Teachings? Fushan replied, "Yellow scrolls and red axes. The Master said, "This is merely words and letters; what is the meaning of the Teachings?
Fushan replied, "The mouth wishes to speak, yet words fail it; the mind wishes to contemplate, yet thoughts falter."

[Shushan] forgot [the answer]. The Master said, "When the mouth wishes to speak, the words fail; this is because it is opposed to having speech. When the mind wishes to contemplate, thoughts are forgotten;
this is because it is opposed to deluded thinking. What is the meaning of the teaching? Shushan was speechless.
The Master said, "I have heard you, Minister, recite the *Lotus Sūtra*; is that so? Shushan replied, "It is. The Master said, "The sūtra says: 'All livelihoods and productive enterprises are all..."
The true mark does not contradict [the conventional]. Now tell me: how many people have fallen from their positions in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception?
The Minister was speechless. The Master said, "Minister, do not be so hasty. You have cast aside the Three Sutras and Five Treatises to enter the monastic groves specifically."
Even after ten or twenty years, it would still be beyond remedy. When the Śāstrin (Shangshu) again managed to encounter him, he prostrated and said, "I, this person, am guilty of transgressions.
Later, he arrived at Lingshu. This was a dark sign of his destiny to receive the prediction of Zhisheng as the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*).
Initially, while Zhisheng was at Lingshu, for twenty years he did not appoint a head seat, constantly saying, "My head seat has already been born; my head seat..."
He was a cowherd. My head seat (śrāmaṇera) had traveled on pilgrimage and attained enlightenment. One day, he ordered the assembly to strike the bell; the head seat was waiting outside the main gate.
As the assembly went out to welcome him, the Master arrived. Baoshu said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time. He immediately invited the Master to serve as the head seat.
Shortly thereafter, the regional lord Liu intended to raise an army and personally entered the monastery to ask Baoshu to decide upon its merits and faults. Baoshu had already known this beforehand.
He sat peacefully and passed away. The ruler asked an administrator, "When did the Master fall ill? He replied, "He was never ill.

Just now he sealed a letter and instructed me to present it to Your Majesty. The ruler opened the letter and found a note that read: "The Eye and Lamp of Humanity and Heaven, the Senior Seat in the Hall.
The ruler realized the Master’s intent and immediately ceased hostilities, inviting the Master to succeed him in propagating the Dharma. Not long after...
After several moves, he arrived at Yunmen Guangtai Temple. A monk asked Master Shengfa, "It is said that 'striking the void produces sound, yet striking wood produces no sound.
What does this mean? The Master struck the air with his staff and said, "A-ya! A-ya! He then struck the head of a wooden board and asked, "Does it make a sound?
The monk replied, "It makes a sound. The Master said, "This worldly fellow! He struck the board again and asked, "What do you call this?"

[The Master] made a "ma" sound. Because his feet were lame, he always carried a staff while walking. Seeing that the assembly was about to go on a communal work assignment (*fangqing*), he raised his staff and said:
"Look, look! The people of Uttarakuru see how difficult it is for you to carry firewood;
they come to wrestle with you in the middle courtyard as an offering to you, and further recite the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for you, saying: 'The wisdom of all-knowledge is pure and non-dual.'"
There is no duality; there is no distinction and no interruption. A great multitude surrounds him, remaining for a long time without dispersing.
He then says: "You people have come here for no reason. What are you looking for? This old monk does nothing but eat his meals and defecate. What else could he possibly do?
You all travel to various quarters to practice Zen and inquire about the Way. Let me ask you: what have you attained from those travels?"
"What is the matter? Try to bring it up. Thereupon, having no choice, he himself recited the verse of Sanping:
"This very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing. He looked back at the monk and said, "What do you call 'seeing and hearing'?
He spoke again: "There is no further sound or form to present to you. He said to the monk, "What sounds or forms are there in the head? He spoke again: "If one understands within this..."
“Completely nothing,” he said. To the monk, he asked, “What matter is there? He added, “As for essence and function, what does it matter whether they are divided or not?
Then he said, “Speech is essence; essence is speech. Raising his staff, he said, “The staff is essence; the lantern is function. Is this divided or undivided?
Have you not seen it said: ‘The wisdom of all wisdoms is pure’? Upon hearing the striking of the meal drum, he said, “The sound of the drum!”
[He] bit through his seven-strip robe, then pointed to a monk and said, "Bring the cat here. After a long while, he asked, "Tell me, why was the drum placed there?
No one in the assembly could answer. He then said, "It was placed there because of its hide.
I usually say that all sounds are the Buddha’s voice and all forms are the Buddha’s form; the entire earth is this Dharma-body. You have been in vain..."
The Buddha-dharma’s knowledge and vision is like this: when you see a staff, simply call it a staff; when you see a house, simply call it a house.
In the *Transmission of the Lamp*, it is said that when a master ascended the hall and heard the sound of a bell, he remarked:

"The world is so vast; why does the sound of the bell strip away one's seven-strip robe? Jingshan Hongzhi Gao composed a verse on this: "The sound of the bell strips away the *uttarāsaṅga*; The azure sky is the very robe."
The Hu-er boy by the eye had no choice; with a single arrow, both eagles fell from his hand. What he picked up was originally just a gander among the trees.
Upon entering the Sangha hall, the monks rose in competition to welcome him. The Master stood and said, "Shitou spoke of 'mutuality' and 'non-mutuality.
A monk then asked, "What is non-mutuality? The Master pointed his finger and said, "This is the sounding board."
[The Master] said, "The head. He asked again, "What is mutual interpenetration? [The Master] said, "What do you call this board-head?
He questioned a newly arrived monk: "You have traveled on foot through all quarters, saying, 'I know there is. Bring me the three thousandfold world system here!"
[The Master] placed it upon his eyelashes. The monk said, "Yes. The Master said, "Why has Qiantang left the capital three thousand li away?
The monk said, "How could that concern him? The Master said, "You hollow-cheating fellow! He asked the Head Seat, "Are the great earth and the heavens the same as yourself, or are they different?
[The Head Seat] said, "The same. The Master said, "Then all living beings—moths, silkworms, and ants—are [the same as you]."
[The monk] said, "The same is the distinct. The Master said, "Why do you meet me with weapons? [The monk] asked, "An ancient said, 'There is a matter of the ultimate limit.
What is this matter of the ultimate limit? The Master said, "What can you do? It is in my hands!
[The monk] pressed further, saying, "I am asking about the matter of the ultimate limit. The Master then struck him with his staff and said, "Hūṃ! Hūṃ! This is precisely when one must break through!"
The Master requested further instruction, saying, "One such as this merely knows how to cause disorder everywhere. Come closer; I ask you:

when you are usually on the long benches discussing 'upward' and 'downward,' or 'surpassing the Buddhas and transcending the patriarchs,' do you say that an ox has the principle of surpassing the Buddhas and transcending the patriarchs? The monk replied, "Someone asked about that just now."
The Master said, "This is something learned on a long-bench (monastic dormitory). Do not say 'it exists' when it does not exist, nor say 'it does not exist' when it does.
A monk asked, "If it exists, why would one further wear fur and carry horns? The Master said, "I know you are merely a person who parrots words.
He added, "Come, come! Let me ask you again: all of you carry your staffs slung across your shoulders and say, 'I am...'"

"Regarding the case of being imprisoned for failing to pay taxes: Miaoxi said, 'This old fellow is truly intolerable; he has usurped a surname, occupies government land, and moreover refuses to pay the grain tax.'"
The Master said: "I will not question you regarding the period before the fifteenth day; but after the fifteenth day, bring me a single phrase.

Xuedou’s Verse: Take away one; pick up seven. Above, below, and in the four directions, there is no equal. Walking slowly, he tramples the sound of flowing water;
looking out freely, he traces the tracks of flying birds. The grass is lush; the mist is dense. Wildflowers grow in profusion by the crags.
A snap of the fingers brings sorrow to the Śūnyatā-deva. Do not move it! To move it is thirty blows.
[The Master] strikes with his staff. He says, "An ancient Buddha intersects with a pillar—what stage of spiritual capacity is this? A monk asks, "What is the meaning of this?

The Master says, "A single length of rope, bought for thirty cash. He then provides a substitute for the previous statement, saying, "Clouds rise on the southern mountain; the northern mountain descends."
It rained. The monk asked again, "How about thirty cash for a single silk sash? The Master said, "I’ll give it to you. Xuedou’s verse says:
Clouds on the South Mountain, rain on the North Mountain; The four sevens and two threes meet face-to-face. In the kingdom of Silla, he once ascended the hall;
In the kingdom of Great Tang, the drum has not yet been struck. Suffering within joy, joy within suffering—who says?
Gold was to him like dung and soil.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month of the first year of the Qiandao era, the Master went to the capital at the summons of the Lord of Guang, where he was lodged and provided with offerings.
On the *jiazi* day of the ninth month, he returned to the mountain and said to the assembly: "I have been away from the mountain for sixty-seven days; let us now inquire [of the time]."
“What about your activities during the sixty-seven days? The assembly was unable to respond. The Master said, “Why do you not say:

‘The Master eats much noodles in the capital’? A monk came to pay his respects; the Master then picked up his *kāṣāya* and said, “If you can say something [about this],” [he would grant you the robe].
"It has fallen inside the fold of my *kaṣāya* sleeve. If you cannot speak, you shall remain sitting in a ghost cave.
[The Master asked,] "How about this? He spoke on his behalf, saying, "I have no strength."
Miaoxi said, "In the Western Heaven, they cut off heads and sever arms; here, I take it upon myself to go out.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "An ancient worthy said: 'Medicine and illness treat one another. The entire earth is medicine; which of these is your own self?"
He then said, "When meeting the lowly, one is immediately noble. The monk asked, "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master clapped his hands once, held up his staff, and said, "Take this staff!
The monk took it and snapped it into two pieces. The Master said, "Even if you were as capable as this, you still deserve thirty blows of the staff."
Xuedou’s verse: "The entire earth is medicine; which of these is your own self? "The entire earth is medicine;
how could past and present be so mistaken? Shutting the door, one does not build a carriage; the open road is naturally vast and empty. Mistake, mistake!
Even the nostrils that reach toward heaven have been pierced through."

Ascending the hall, when the assembly had gathered, the Master pointed with his staff at those before him and said: "The great earth, heaven and earth, and all the buddhas as numerous as motes of dust—all are contained within this very space.
Who can dispute over the Buddha-dharma or seek victory and defeat? Is there anyone here who can offer a word of admonition?

When no one could offer an admonition, he said, "Wait, let this old man admonish you for you. A monk stepped forward and said, "We request the Master to admonish us. The Master replied, "This wild fox spirit!"

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The eyelashes span across the ten directions; the eyebrows soar upward through heaven and earth and penetrate downward into the Yellow Springs and Mount Sumeru, blocking your throats.
Is there anyone who understands this? If there is someone who understands, I shall drag Zhanpo over and wrestle for the forehead with Xinluo!"
Miaoxi said: "This is a great divine mantra; this is a great illuminating mantra; this is the unsurpassed mantra; this is the mantra of the peerless.
It can eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false. Do you people wish to recognize Yunmen? Have you not heard it said:
"The three stages must all be urged by everyone together"?

"A single arrowhead pierces the three barriers" (*Zhizheng chuan*).
The Yunmen school has three phrases: "The cover and lid within the heavens," "The eye and the scale," and "Not involving worldly conditions.

"Your Honor, pass through here. The Master said, "If that is so, then you have not fallen into false conceptualization. The Master said, "Give me back the pivot of the discourse!

Section: Addressing the Assembly. During the day, people come and go; during the day, they are distinguished from one another.

Suppose, suddenly in the middle of the night, someone were told to fetch an object. Before it has even reached its destination, how would you fetch it? [The Master] spoke on their behalf: "How many people have you deceived? Addressing the Assembly:

For those who are deluded about themselves, every path they encounter is obstructed. For those who have awakened to their original nature, why do they still have the perception of the four great elements? [The Master] spoke on their behalf: "..."
"Yizhou produces *fuzi* (aconite); Jianzhou produces ginger. [The Master] addresses the assembly:

"When the ancestral masters of the past and the Buddhas of the three periods of time preached the Dharma, why did the mountains, rivers, great earth, grasses, and trees not depart? He provides the answer on their behalf:

"A newly arrived monk performs his duties. [The Master] addresses the assembly: "Since you know where they come from, tell me: in which kalpa were there no ancestral masters? He provides the answer on their behalf: "I, this person, am now..."
[The monk] said, "It does not hit the mark.
Jingshan Hongdao said, "Yunmen was also like a thief whose heart is filled with trepidation. Jingshan is not so;
since he knows where it comes from, tell me, in which kalpa has there been no patriarchs? It is not that he intends to 'strike the grass,' but rather he wishes to startle [the listener]."

[The Master] held up a snake and addressed the assembly: "Spreading a net that covers the heavens to strike dragons; spreading a silk net to catch shrimp and clams. Tell me, where do the snails and oysters fall?
[He] provided the answer on their behalf: "One with eyes. [He] addressed the assembly: "Folding in half and splitting into three—the needle-case and the nostrils are right here."
"Where? Bring them out one by one for me to see. [The student] replied, "Superior, middling, and inferior.
Miaoxi said, "Leaning against the gate and peering through the window, you play with your own spirit."
Addressing the assembly: The staff has transformed into a dragon and swallowed up heaven and earth. From where do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come? Addressing the assembly:

Within the lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma (*ekayāna*). Tell me, is one’s own self within the Single Vehicle Dharma, or outside the Single Vehicle Dharma? [The Master] speaks on their behalf: "Enter."
Miaoxi said, "In vain, a scene of sorrow.
He addressed the assembly, saying, "Do you wish to recognize the Patriarch? Pointing with his staff, he said, 'The Patriarch is leaping about right above your heads!'"
Do you wish to recognize the eyes of the Patriarch? They are beneath your feet. He further said: "This is the food and drink used for sacrifices to ghosts and spirits;
yet, even so, the ghosts and spirits are never satiated."
Miaoxi said, "Have you not heard it said that one retains delusions to moisten rebirth? At that moment, a monk standing nearby coughed once.
Miaoxi said, "When an old fellow speaks thus, what fault is there? As the monk hesitated, Miaoxi struck him.
The assembly raised the case of Guankui’s ascent to the hall: "The ten directions have no walls; the four sides have no gates. Pure and naked, bright and clear—there is nothing to grasp.
The Master said, "To raise [the case] is easy; to come forth from it is very difficult. [Guankui] asked, "Does the Abbot not approve of you speaking in this way?
The Master said, "Did you just raise it in that manner? [Guankui] said, "Yes. The Master said, "You donkey!"
One year, [Nanquan] dreamed of Guankui, who said, "My words remain. Nanquan said, "I ask you:
where there are no walls on the ten directions and no gates on the four sides, tell me, what matter are Mahābrahmā and Śakra discussing?"
[The monk] said, "How could this interfere with other matters? The Master shouted, "A fellow who eats his rice by following the crowd!
The Master said, "In the past, the old masters all spoke 'talk that descends into the weeds' for the sake of compassion; one must recognize a person according to their words.

If it were 'talk that emerges from the weeds,' there would be nothing of the sort. If it were such [as you suggest], there would be talk of a 'heavy understanding. Have you not seen the Monk Yangshan?"
He asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Mount Lu. Yangshan asked, "Have you ever visited the Five Elders Peak? He said, "No.
Yangshan remarked, "Dharma brother, you have not truly traveled the mountains; this was merely a conversation spoken out of compassion for you."
Taisu Xiu said: "People nowadays all say that out of compassion there is talk of 'descending into the weeds.
They only know how to grasp at the moon, yet they fail to realize the depth of the water. Had Yunmen been careful with his words at that time, I wonder how later generations would have discussed it?
Yet the water-jelly has no eyes; to seek food, it must rely on the shrimp. —Xuedou.
Verse: Leaving the weeds, entering the weeds—who can seek them out? Layer upon layer of white clouds; the red sun shines bright. Looking left, there is no flaw;
looking right, one is already old. Do you not see? Hanshan’s son set out too early. Having been gone for ten years without returning, he has forgotten the path by which he came.
The Master said, "I do not dare hope that you will have waves against the current; yet even the intent to go with the current is difficult to find.
He then related how when Liang-sui first visited Magu, as soon as Magu saw him coming, he went off to weed the fields.

When Liang-sui arrived at the place where Magu was weeding, Magu paid him no attention at all and returned directly to his quarters, closing the door behind him. Liang-sui went to knock on the door for three consecutive days.
On the third day, as soon as he knocked at the gate, Gu asked, "Who is it? He replied, "Preceptor, do not deceive Liangsui.
Had I not come to pay my respects to you, Preceptor, I would have been led astray by the sutras and treatises for the rest of my life. The Master said, "There was already a wave against the current;
now that you have entered, this is the meaning of going with the current. This is also called the 'moment of releasing both. He then gave him instruction.
"Assembly, do not say that I am merely deceiving you today. Forced as I am, I must create a scene of disorder before you all.
Should a person of clear eyes see this, it will become a source of ridicule; now there is no avoiding it. Let me ask you all:
from the very beginning, what matter has ever been lacking? To tell you that 'there is nothing' is already [too much]."
This is to let it sink into oblivion. Nevertheless, one must reach this very state before it can be attained.
Do not ask haphazardly just to satisfy a quick tongue; your own mind will remain dark and murky. Great matters lie ahead for tomorrow and the days to come.

If your faculties and thoughts are slow and hesitant, for the time being, look toward the gateways of transformation and edification established by the ancients; look east and west and see what kind of principle this is.
Do you wish to understand? It is all because of yourself. Since immeasurable kalpas past, your delusive thoughts have been thick and heavy;
as soon as you hear someone speak, you immediately give rise to doubt, questioning the Buddha, questioning the Dharma, and questioning the ancients.
From above looking down, one seeks understanding; yet as one turns toward it, one sinks further into entanglement.
The moment you direct the mind toward it, you have already missed the mark—how much more so when there are words and phrases? Is it perhaps that not directing the mind is the way?
Do not misunderstand this! What else is there? Take care. Furthermore, he said: "In Jiangxi they speak of ruler and subject, father and son; in Hunan they say it is not so. As for me here—"
At that moment, it was not like this. After a long silence, he said, "Do you still see the wall? He spoke again: "From the beginning until now, what kind of matter has this been?
Now, being constrained and having no other choice, I shall speak to you all: throughout the entire earth, what object exists that could serve as a condition or an opponent for you?
If there were even so much as the point of a needle to act as a separation or an obstruction for you, [it would not be so]."
"Pick it up and bring it here for me. What do you call 'Buddha'? What do you call 'Patriarch'?
What do you call the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars? What do you take to be the four elements and the five aggregates?
When I speak thus, people call it the talk of an old woman from a village of three households. Should one suddenly encounter a genuine traveler of the path who hears this—
"What do you say? [The Master] grabbed his feet and dragged him down the steps. "What offense is there? Even so, on what principle do you act in this way?
Do not speak recklessly here just to satisfy your own tongue; one must be a true man before such a thing is possible.
If you were suddenly to find me at the heels of this old fellow, you would have nowhere to go and your legs would be broken. What then?"
This is a transgression. It is exactly so. Is there anyone here now who can ask a question regarding the discourse of the *zongmen*?
Wait until this old man has finished giving one turn of the answer. Eastward or westward! He also said: "Bring the entire universe at once and place it upon the lashes of your eyes.
When you people hear such words, I do not dare hope that you will come forward impulsively and seize the old monk.
He gave her a slap and said, "Wait; look carefully and slowly. Is it there? Is it not? What kind of principle is this?
Even if you were to understand it here, should you encounter a true monk, I would break your legs with a blow of my staff. He also said:
The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the canon—whether explained horizontally or vertically—have been expounded by the old masters of the world in every possible way.
Now, bring me the principle you have expounded even as much as the point of a needle, and let us see it. To speak in such a manner is already like trying to revive a dead horse with medicine.
Nevertheless, how many are there who have actually reached this realm? I do not dare hope that you can find it within your words.
An echo. Within every phrase, the blade is concealed; a single blink of an eye reveals a thousand differences. When the wind is calm and the waves are still, it is said again:
"My affairs have left me no choice, so I speak to you all: 'Right here there is nothing'—this already constitutes a mutual obscuration.

Yet you wish to step forward further, seeking understanding by chasing words and following phrases, creating a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, and setting up broad arrays of difficult questions. This is merely to exhaust yourself.
To gain a single instance of verbal fluency is to move further and further away from the Way; when will there ever be a time of rest?

If this matter were contained within words, then how could the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings not possess words? For what reason, then, is there said to be a "separate transmission outside the teachings"?
If it were obtained through scholarly understanding or intellectual ingenuity, then consider the holy ones of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*): their preaching of the Dharma is like clouds and rain.
It rains. Yet he was still rebuked for seeing the nature [of reality] as if through a fine gauze screen.

By this it is known that all those with a mind are worlds apart from the heavens and earth. Nevertheless, if one is a person who has attained the bottom, how could the fire of the Way ever burn their mouth?

How then should one proceed? Zhaozhou said, "If you claim to have reached the ultimate bottom, can that mind of discursive knowledge still fathom it?
From this, the Master gained entry through faith. Later, he resided at Tiantai for over thirty years without descending from the mountain, where he extensively mastered the Three [Teachings].
In his studies, his conduct was solitary and steadfast. Beyond his practice of meditative stillness, he constantly perused the *Nāga-kośa* (the Buddhist canon).

He was held in high esteem by those both far and near, who commonly referred to him as "Dajing Shouzuo" (Great Stillness Senior Monk). Once, someone asked him: "Disciple, whenever I sit in meditation at night, my thoughts fly about in confusion.

I do not yet understand the method for subduing them; I pray that you will grant me instruction. The Master said: "If, while sitting peacefully at night, your thoughts fly about in confusion, then..."
Take this scattering mind and investigate the place where it scatters. When you investigate and find no such place, then where does the thought of scattering exist?
Turn back and investigate the investigating mind itself; then where is the mind that performs the investigation? Furthermore, the wisdom that can illuminate is fundamentally empty.
The objects of perception are likewise quiescent. That which is quiescent yet not-quiescent is because there is no person who can bring about quiescence.
That which illuminates yet does not illuminate is because there is no object to be illuminated. When both object and wisdom are quiescent, the mind and its deliberations are at peace.

One does not seek out branches externally, nor does one dwell in meditative concentration internally. Both paths are extinguished, and the single nature is serene. This is the essential method for returning to the source.
Regarding the Way: the Master, having observed the meaning of "illusion" within the teachings, composed a verse and asked the assembly of students:
"If all dharmas are like illusory existences, then committing various transgressions and evils should entail no fault. Why, then, do the karmic actions one performs not fail to be forgotten?"
Relying upon the Buddha’s compassion, he arose to provide guidance and inspiration. At that time, the Elder Xiaojing replied: "A phantom person raises a phantom wheel of protection;

phantom karma can summon what is to be treated as a phantom. Failing to understand that phantoms give rise to various phantom sufferings, one realizes through awakening that both are like phantoms and are unconditioned.
Both of these two Elders passed away at their original mountain.
▲ Chan Master Daokuang of Zhaoqing Temple in Quanzhou served as the head of the kitchen staff under Changqing.
He frequently engaged in conversation with the assembly of monks. One day, Changqing saw him and said, "What is all this fussing about in your mouth every day?
The Master replied, "If one does not work for a day, one does not eat for a day. Changqing said, "In that case, you are sharpening your bow and notching your arrows."
The Master said, "I am waiting specifically for Weichi to come. Baizhang Qing said, "What happens after Weichi has arrived?
The Master said, "I will cause his sinews and bones to cover the ground and his eyes to bulge out. Qing then went out.

Later, while they were working together carrying mud, the Master stopped mid-path with his staff and asked a monk, "Are you carrying mud up the cave or down the cave? The monk said, "Up the cave. The Master struck him once.

He then asked Mingzhao, who dropped his mud-laden pole, stood with palms joined, and said, “Please, Master, examine me. Thereupon, the Master ceased.
Jingshan Daokai said: "Although Zhaoqing had indeed set his mind at rest, how could Mingzhao possibly have been satisfied?

▲ One day, Layman Wang Yanbin, the Grand Tutor, entered the Buddha Hall at Zhaoqing. Pointing to an alms bowl, he asked the hall master, "What kind of bowl is this?

"Do not let the old monk down.

To respond to the capacity of beings yet lack skillful means—how pitiable is this one-eyed dragon! Never before have you displayed your fangs and claws;
now that the fangs and claws are revealed amidst clouds and thunder, how many times has the wave gone against the current?
▲ Master Xingchou Gushan said to his disciples: "Though I am no longer here, I have never ceased to act for the sake of you, my brothers.

If you fully comprehend how to repay your debt of gratitude (ōnhon) while constantly acting for others, I grant that you have transcended conceptual understanding and intellectual knowledge within the field of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).

If you cannot yet fully comprehend this, you must still wait until you repay your debt of gratitude by opening your two flaps of skin [to speak] before you can truly be said to be acting for others. Thus he preserved [the lineage].
You have not yet emerged from the conceptual thoughts of intellectual understanding; for this reason, the ancients called it "the livelihood of ghosts" or being "a guest beneath the frog’s robe.
If you wish to achieve swift resonance, you must right now, standing as you are, verify and recognize it directly.
"What fault is there? It is not so. Your faculties and thoughts are hesitant; therefore, investigate further through both day and night.
Suddenly, one day you may perceive it. Do not be satisfied with a mere glimpse.

You must continue to probe and exhaustively investigate, even into brothels and wine shops—whether things are defiled or pure, good or bad—using what you have seen as your guide until you have reached the end."

This is the realm. Entering it is like entering the Vinaya. If one were to see even a single dharma as small as a hair’s breadth, and thus fail to see this very matter, I would call that the obscuration of ignorance.
One must simply not see any dharma as a separate entity; only then can one attain perfect completeness.
Upon reaching this point, one can further turn and cast [the mind] with freedom, opening and closing at will, leaving no seams or traces—like water.
Entering water is like fire entering fire, wind entering wind, or space entering space.
If one can act in this manner, they can directly draw a single sword and sever the web of doubt for all people under heaven, such that the "one" is not treated as something resembling a duality.
Therefore, the ancients said: "When great functions flourish, every movement is entirely true. If there were a person who reached such a state, who [could stop them]?
How could I dare to step forward and speak of right or wrong? Why? Because this person is a man who transcends all limits and measurements, having penetrated beyond cause and effect;
nowhere can he be bound or constrained. Brothers, if you can be like this, then it will suffice.
If you have not yet attained this, you must simply act with integrity (this character should be "zhai" [to give] rather than "yu" [with]). Do not speak or breathe recklessly;
do not cause yourself to sink and fall. Do not let immeasurable kalpas pass until such a time arrives. Then one speaks of repaying kindness, but it is not said here.

The Commandant said, "How did you manage to get here? The Master said, "I specifically thank the Grand Commandant for understanding my words.

"Come," [the Master] said. "And how is it? Long said, "Life and nature are difficult to preserve. The Master said, "In that case, you have been swallowed by him.

▲ Yiyuan Kaiming Chan Master of Wujishan in Quzhou was the son of the Xu family of Wuxing. He was born in the third year of the Qianfu era of the Tang dynasty.
On the night of his birth, a wondrous fragrance filled the room and a crimson light shone as brightly as day. During the Guangqi era, he accompanied his father while he was stationed in Xian’an.

His father attempted to force him to marry, but the Master did not consent; he subsequently traveled to various regions and attained spiritual resonance with Jingqing, after which he returned to visit his parents.

The parents then established a separate residence south of the city wall to fulfill the Master’s aspiration. Beside the residence was the temple of Minister Chen, where there was a statue of Chan Master Lin.

When the Master went to pay his respects, he lost sight of where the Master had gone. Later, when the Prefect performed a sacrifice beneath the shrine, he saw the Master in meditative absorption (dhyāna) amidst a thicket of bamboo behind the temple;
ants were gnawing at his robes, and withered leaves reached his thighs. Some have said: [this was a manifestation of his spiritual power].
This was Xuefeng Yicun, the son of the military commander Xu Zhenjiang. From this samādhi, he would suddenly emerge and suddenly enter.
Chan Master Nü of Zihu did not yet know the depth of the Master’s realization and asked, "The state of concentration you dwell in is merely that of the Lesser Vehicle.
At that time, the Master was just drinking tea; he held up his tea bag and said, "Is this great or small? Nü was struck with awe. He subsequently went to visit Tangshan in Kuochang.
Chan Master Deyan asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "My surname is Xu. De said, "Who permitted you [to become a monk]? He replied, "There is no distinction.
De silently recognized his potential and subsequently ordained him. Once, he ordered him to gather peaches, but the disciple did not return for ten days.

De went to search for him and found the master leaning against a rock while picking peaches, absorbed in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). De snapped his fingers to rouse him and lead him out. During the Kaiyun era, he traveled to Jianglang Rock.
Beholding a stone niche, he said to his disciple Huixing, "I shall enter meditative absorption within this; you must wedge the door shut with stones and not harbor thoughts of me.
Huixing followed these instructions. The following year, Huixing felt that his master had passed away; he opened the niche to look upon the Master.
His white hair fell over his shoulders, and his chest was still warm. He slowly rose from his meditation of his own accord, appearing completely unchanged in countenance.

He returned once more to Wugu. At that time, Minister Shen Gong was stationed in Xin’an; he commanded the monk Shou Rong, a scholar of the Abhidharma, to interrogate Master Fu regarding the signs of his meditative absorption.
The Master did not engage him in debate. Shou Rong held a slight contempt for him, yet the people of Xin’an vied with one another to paint portraits of the Master and revere them.

In every instance, they obtained śarīra relics. Consequently, [Wang] Rong felt ashamed and submitted; he paid homage to the image and apologized for his transgressions, and likewise obtained śarīra relics.

He sighed, saying, "From this day forward, I shall not dare to fathom the sequence [of the Dharma] through my profound understanding. When King Qian Zhongyi was moved by the Master’s appearance in a dream, he dispatched an envoy to bring a painted image.

Just as it happened, the King suffered from an eye ailment; upon unfolding the image and performing prostrations, it appeared exactly as seen in the dream, and śarīra relics fell like rain, [healing his eyes].

He recovered his health suddenly and completely; consequently, he was granted the honorary title "Kaimei" (Illuminator). When Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty heard of the Master’s power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he offered him special honors and invited him to court.

The Master did not go; however, the Emperor specifically had a palanquin brought to fetch him. They conferred in the private chamber, and Taizong deeply accorded with his views. Shortly thereafter, the Master requested to return home.

In the first year of the Chunhua era, he manifested parinirvāṇa. His age was one hundred and fifteen; his dharma-age was fifty-seven. Upon cremation, a white light illuminated the heavens, and relics of five colors were produced.
In the third year of the Zhenghe era of Emperor Huizong, a large tree by the roadside in Jiazhou was broken by the wind.

Inside it was a monk in meditative concentration, his hair and beard covering his body and his fingernails encircling him. Upon this being reported to the throne, the Emperor ordered that he be carried on a palanquin to the capital.
The Tripitaka Master Dharani from the Western Heaven was commanded to rouse him from his samādhi with a golden *kaṅkha*. He then asked, "In what era’s monastic community do you belong?
He replied, "I am Huichi, the younger brother of Dharma Master Huiyuan of Donglin. While traveling to Mount Emei, I entered samādhi beneath this tree. Is Dharma Master Huiyuan still well?
The Tripitaka Master said, "Dharma Master Huiyuan was a man of the Jin dynasty; he passed away seven hundred years ago."
After several years, Sengchi finally entered a state of stillness. Daozang asked, "Since you have arrived here, Master, where do you wish to go?
Sengchi replied, "To Chenliu County. He then re-entered meditative absorption. The Emperor composed three verses and ordered that an image of him be painted and distributed. The verses read:
"A venerable ancient sage for seven hundred years— Who can know the news from within his samādhi? How could he compare to one who returns to the West with a single shoe? He was born... [text ends]
What need is there to laboriously carve wood for a hide? To hide a mountain in a marsh is also to hide one's own person. In this world, there is no path of concealment to which one can cling.
Send word to Zhuang Zhou: cease your deliberations; it is not within the tree that one who bears the burden of seeking resides. A sentient body is not insentient;
each and every person possesses this very body within the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If you understand that Bodhi fundamentally has no tree, you need not—
With great effort, I inquire of Lu Neng.

[Zhao] Jian. At this, the Master [Baizhang] had a profound, mystical resonance with the profound essence of the teaching. When holding up or waving the whisk, he said: "This is the inexhaustible resource of Caoxi; people of the time call it 'the emergence of horns. I, the mountain monk..."

"Next year, on the second day of the second month, I shall part from you and temporarily depart. My ashes shall be scattered across the four forests, so as not to occupy the land of the donors.
On the twenty-eighth day of the first month of the following year, the local people vied with one another to enter the mountains to pay their respects; yet the Master was still in good health.
The inquiries were conducted as usual. On the first day of the second month, the prefectural official led the various officials to the mountain to pay their respects.
They stayed through the night. On the second day, after the midday meal, the Master ascended the hall to take his leave of the assembly.

At that time, Elder Yuanying came forward and asked: "The clouds grieve and the mists darken; the great assembly is choked with sobs. Before we part, please grant us one word. The Master extended one leg. Yuanying said, "Dharma..."
"The mirror does not face this land; where else, then, does the precious moon shine? The Master said, "It is not within your realm.

Ying said, "If that is so, then as bubbles arise and bubbles perish, they originally return to the water; the coming and going of the Master is its original constancy. The Master made a sighing sound.
After exchanging further words with several monks, he returned to his quarters. At the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.), he asked the assembly, "The World-Honored One..."
"When will the time of my parinirvāṇa be? He replied, "At the hour of the rat on the fifteenth day of the second month.
The Master said, "Before the hour of the rat today," and then he sat peacefully and passed away. He had lived in the world for seventy-eight years and spent sixty summer retreats in meditation.
▲ Chan Master Baofu Qinghuo went to visit Shuilong. Long asked him, “Master Huo, which venerable elder have you visited? Have you attained enlightenment yet?
He replied, “I once visited Dazhang and gained a point of conviction. Thereupon, Long ascended the hall, gathered the assembly, and called out, “Master Huo, come forward!
Burn incense before the assembly and speak of your realization; I, the old monk, shall [grant you the seal].”
"You are my witness. The Master stepped out from the assembly and held up the incense, saying, "The incense has already been offered.

As for awakening—whether one awakens or not. Long was greatly pleased and granted him permission. As the Master was about to pass away, he left behind this verse: "Let the people of the world cease to say the road is difficult;
The bird-path and the sheep’s gut are but a few inches apart. Take care, O Nüxi! To you, the waters by the riverbank, I return to the vast sea; I return to the mountains."
He immediately went to Zhu’an on Mount Guihu. After a short while, he said to his disciples, "After my passing, you shall offer my remains to the insects and ants;
do not erect a tomb or stupa. Having spoken these words, he secretly entered the mountains at the head of the lake, sat upon a flat rock, and passed away peacefully and solemnly.

The disciples searched everywhere until they were able to receive his final instructions. An extension of seven days was granted, yet in the end, not even a single insect or ant had caused any damage.

You rush outward in pursuit; that is why you have come here. Even if it were Śākyamuni Buddha himself, I would give him thirty blows of my staff.

To study the Way, one must possess the eye for studying the Way; to realize the ground, one must attain the phrase of realizing the ground.

one falsely conditions upon external objects and discriminates among reflected phenomena. Sometimes the meaning reaches the mind, but the phrase does not reach it.

It is like blind men feeling an elephant; each speaks of a different aspect. Sometimes both meaning and phrasing reach their full expression, shattering the realm of empty space and illuminating the ten directions with light.
At other times, neither meaning nor phrasing reaches its mark; the sightless man runs hither and thither, suddenly unaware as he falls into a deep pit.

The monk said, "I was sitting in the back storage area. The Master said, "To whom did you address your statement? The monk said, "To my master."
The Master brought up a story. He asked, "What is the surname of the host? The monk said, "He has no surname. The Master asked, "What is his given name?
The monk said, "He has no given name. The Master said, "In that case, you do not recognize the host. The monk then gave a shout. The Master did not respond.
Huanji said, "Shimen did not answer; was he accepting him or rejecting him?
A monk asked, "If one can turn things over, they are the same as the Tathāgata. I wonder, how does one turn over the three gates and the Buddha hall?

The Master said, "I will tell you, but will you believe me? The monk replied, "The Master speaks the truth; how could I dare not believe? The Master said: [Note: The text provided ends with the Master's response to the monk's affirmation of his words.]
This lacquer bucket. [A monk] asked: "When the ancients sought fire, what was their underlying meaning? The Master said: "Let it go out. [The monk] asked:
"What is it like after it has gone out? The Master said: "The first and third days of the month. Because he was constructing the Qīngliáng River embankment, a monk asked:

"If one were suddenly to encounter a flood that reaches the heavens, would you still be able to dam it? The Master said: "Above it supports heaven; below it supports earth. [The monk] asked: "As for the kalpa-ending fire..."
"If it is already completely transparent, what then? The Master said, "Transversely emerging, vertically vanishing.

In the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings), it is recorded that the Master asked the steward: "The Qingliang Dam was built by you; when a flood suddenly comes surging toward the heavens, can the dam still hold?
The steward replied, "It is right there inside. The Master asked, "With whom does it keep company? The steward was speechless. The Master then invited him [to stay].
The Master answered on his behalf, saying, "It has already passed through Silla. Later, the monk asked again, "If a monk suddenly encounters a great flood, what then? and so forth;
this was the same as the previous case.
The monk asked, "When not a single thread is left hanging, and the net of Dharma is boundless, why is there still delusion and enlightenment? The Master said, "Two buckets."
One Shoulder Load. A monk asked, "If a fire breaks out in one place, you may go ahead and try to extinguish it. But what if fires break out simultaneously from all eight directions?
The Master said, "Quick! The monk asked, "Is there still a way to escape? The Master said, "If you seek an escape, you will be burned to death. The monk bowed.
The Master said: "Even if you do not seek to escape, it will still burn you to death. Ascending the hall, he said: "A white cat with fierce claws and talons;
raised in the hall, no insects pass by. This is clearly the method for securing one's position atop a tree; one must strictly avoid leaving words open to outsiders.
What is the phrase for 'leaving words open to outsiders'? Do not misquote me! Ascending the hall, [he spoke on] the fifteenth day.
Before the fifteenth day, all Buddhas are born; after the fifteenth day, all Buddhas pass into extinction. Before the fifteenth day, all Buddhas are born;
you must not leave my presence. If you leave my presence, I have a hook with which I shall catch you.
"After the fifteenth day, when all Buddhas have passed into extinction, you shall not remain here with me. If you remain here, I have a awl to prick you! Now tell me:
on the very fifteenth day itself, is it the hook that is used, or is it the awl? Thereupon he spoke a verse: "On the very fifteenth day, The hook and the awl are both stilled at once.
If you further intend to ask 'How?', [He pricks him with the awl.]** *(Note: The final line of the verse is traditionally accompanied by the Master striking the student with the awl.)*
When the sun rises again, the Master was staying at Shimen. The Prefect, acting on personal animosity, flogged and humiliated him.
Upon his return to the assembly, the monks greeted him from the left side of the road. The Head Seat stepped forward to pay his respects and said, "The Prefect has wronged you;
he has so grievously insulted the Master. The Master pointed to the ground and said, "A heap of bones rises from level earth. As he spoke, a mound surged up following his finger.
The local governor heard of this and sent men to scrape it away, but it surged back up as before. Later, the governor’s entire family died in Xiangzhou.
Furthermore, a monk asked, "Is there still Buddha-dharma in the deep mountains and rocky cliffs? The Master said, "There is.
The monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs? The Master said, "A strange stone shaped like a tiger; fire burns it."
"The pine trees have the bearing of dragons. Master Wujin (Wu-jin Ju-shi) cherished these words; yet, the *Shimen Lu* alone does not record these two matters.
Both were personally recounted by Miaoxi (Miao-xi) to Master Wujin (as the saying regarding "deep mountains and steep cliffs" is now included in the *Huiyuan*).
▲ When Chan Master Yuanlian of Guanghui Monastery in Ruzhou first relied upon Zen Master Zhenjue of Zhaoqing, he was occupied daily with the tasks of cooking and tending the fires.
On one occasion, while he was reciting a sutra, Zhenjue saw him and asked, "What sutra are you reciting?
He replied, "The Vimalakīrti Sūtra. Zhenjue said, "The sutra is here; where is Vimalakīrti? The Master was at a loss and had no answer.
He paid his respects and wept, saying, "A man of great character, having been questioned by another, has no words to offer—how can he not feel ashamed?
Thereupon, he visited venerable masters in Min, traveling to more than fifty of them, yet none could accord with his realization. He then proceeded to Shoushan in Henan.
Shoushan asked, "Where have you recently departed from? The Master replied, "Hanshang. Shoushan held up his fist and said, "In Hanshang, is there still..."
“Is there such a thing? The Master said, “What kind of bowl is this that makes a sound? Shanshan said, “Blind! The Master said, “Exactly so,” gave a single rap, and then departed.
On another day, he asked again, “When a student has personally reached the Treasure Mountain but returns empty-handed, what then?
Shanshan said, “A torch before every door. At that moment, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, “I, this humble one, did not... [The text here is incomplete].
"Even the tongues of the old monks throughout the world would doubt this," said [Zhaozhou]. Xuefeng asked, "How is it that you understand?
Speak to me and let me see. The Master replied, "It is simply the water-garnet sand on the ground. Xuefeng said, "You have understood. The Master then bowed.
Miaoxi said: "Tell me, do you think that Master Nian would have approved of Guanghui?
If you say he approved, why did he not give him a blow? If you say he did not approve, why did he not give him a blow?
If anyone can provide an answer to this, Miaoxi will give them a blow."
Minister Yang Yi asked, "There is no Maitreya in heaven; there is no Maitreya on earth. In what place, then, does he reside? The Master said, "Beating bricks and striking tiles.
Xu Langzhong, while serving as the Commissioner of the Grain Transport for Western Sichuan, went to visit the Master.
He happened to meet him before the Buddha statue. Xu said, "Should I bow first to the Buddha, or should I bow first to the Elder? The Master said, "A shrimp swallows a whale."
Xǔ said, "If that is so, then you will not bow at all. The Master said, "Director Xu, you have fallen into a trap of words.
Xǔ said, "Elder Xu possesses the one eye. The Master then brushed him away with his sleeve. Xǔ said, "Today I see through you," and he prostrated himself.
The Master saw the *Zhimen Gāngzōng Gē* (Song of the Essential Principles of Zhimen), which says: "The wasp does not cling to its old nest; the fierce general..."
He would rather die at home. [Jiufeng] said, "Brother Zu, why exhaust yourself with so much effort?
When I usually speak of Chan, it is like a fan in one's hand: when raised, there is wind; when not raised, there is not even a single breath of air.
Since you call yourself a master of our school, yet you give people the actual dharma—take a torch and look closely! To open your mouth in such a manner is truly shameless."
[The Master] said, "Too little. Yantou said, "If one were to give the true Dharma to others, even the earth could not contain it.

Do you understand? You must investigate this thoroughly; do not just stare at one another. What are you doing here? Addressing the assembly, he said: "The Buddha-Dharma is fundamentally without affairs.
All the sages of the past were merely fabricating wonders, artificially creating complications, degrading the noble to the base, and burying their descendants. Furthermore..."
Yunmen, Zhaozhou, Deshan, and Linji—though they died, they were not yet truly awake; for a lifetime, they suffered indignity. Here with this old monk, it is not so:
even if Śākyamuni Buddha himself were to appear, I would exile him to another world, forcing him to leave no trace behind.
Why do I act thus? To spare my descendants the worry of losing their own selves. When the old monk speaks in this way, you all—
"How do you all understand this? If you can understand it right here, will you not feel a sense of joy and liberation?
I shall teach you how to cast off your coarse woolen robes and become a truly free and easy monk. But if you still do not understand, there will be new branches next year;
the wind of vexation will continue to blow without ceasing. A monk entered the room to seek instruction and said, "Just now, Master..."
[The Master] said, "This very speech is Śākyamuni coming forth; he too shall be banished to another world.

Before [the monk] had finished his remark, the Master said, "If you understand it in such a way, you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow. The monk asked, "I do not yet know how one should understand it.
The Master struck him. As the monk hesitated, the Master said, "Do you understand? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Today this mountain monk does not avoid—"

I have investigated this from all quarters and exposed it for you. To take this profound resolve and offer it to the lands of the dust motes—this is precisely what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
When Miaoxi finished speaking, he exclaimed, "A fine person is unwilling to act; one must insist on lying in excrement!"

In the third year of the Jingyou era, the year being Bingzi, on the twenty-sixth day of the first month, he displayed four circular diagrams (*maṇḍala*), each inscribed with the characters for tiger, dog, rat, and ox, and hung them at the entrance of his quarters. He subsequently passed away on the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month.
During the Jingde era, this master was held in the highest esteem by eminent scholars and officials, and furthermore, he enjoyed great renown.
Longevity. To know in advance when one’s retribution has ended is the hallmark of a true master.
At Tietie Foyuan, Chan Master Zhisong had a fellow practitioner arrive. Upon seeing him, the Master asked, "Do you still remember our acquaintance?
As the head of the visiting group hesitated, the second monk struck the head with a *zuoju* (a formal sitting mat) and said, "Why do you not respond quickly?"
To the Abbot, the Master said: "One arrow, two targets.
At Renwang Monastery, Chan Master Chu Ping asked Shoushan, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Shoushan gave a shout. The Master bowed; Shoushan raised his staff. The Master said, "Old Abbot, you have no world! Shoushan threw down his staff.
Zhàng said, "A person with clear eyes is difficult to deceive. The Master said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated.
When Chan Master Hanzhi Menhuǐ was serving tea to the monk-envoy from Beita, the Master rose, bowed, and said, "Envoy, please take a seat closer to me.
The envoy said, "How would one dare to nest upon the head of a hawk? The Master said, "If you hold it up respectfully, it will not be intimidating."
Long struck his sitting mat once. After the tea was finished, he rose and said, "Just now, I have inadvertently offended the Master.
The Master said, "Du the Chan Guest from Jiangnan—what second bowl do you seek?"
▲ Prime Minister Wang Sui, a lay practitioner, visited Shoushan and attained the meaning beyond words. From then on, he practiced deeply and clearly realized the Great Dharma.
At the time of his death, he wrote this verse: The lamp in the painted hall has already been extinguished; Toward whom do I point my fingers to speak? Coming and going are fundamentally ordinary;
The spring breeze sweeps away the lingering snow.
▲ Chan Master Yuantong Yuande of Luzhou lived incognito at Shanglan Temple in Nanchang.

When Song Qiqiu arrived, the assembly of monks hurried forward to welcome him, but the Master continued reading his sutras as if nothing were amiss. Qiqiu asked, "What sutra are you reading? The Master held up the sutra to show him.
Qiu found him extraordinary, and he subsequently became renowned. Later, the ruler invited him to Jinling. Afterwards, he resided at Yuantong Monastery on Mount Lu.
When Cao Han crossed the river and entered the temple, the meditators fled in terror, but the Master sat in meditation as usual.
When Cao Han arrived and the Master did not rise, Cao Han said angrily, "Have you not heard of the General who kills without blinking? The Master stared at him intently and said, "How do you know?"
"Is there a master who does not fear birth and death? Han was thereby startled and sighed with increased admiration.

Han asked, "Why did the Chan practitioners disperse? The Master said, "They gathered when the drum was struck. Han sent a subordinate officer to strike it, but no one arrived. Han asked, "Why did they not come?
The Master said, "It was because you had a murderous intent; that is why they did not come. Thereupon, he rose and struck it himself, and the Chan practitioners then assembled.

Han bowed and inquired after the strategy for securing victory. The Master said, "This is not something known by those who practice Chan. Whenever the Master presided over various monasteries, he was indifferent to matters of coming and going;
he would simply sit in silent repose, yet his disciples naturally established their own rules of conduct.

Throughout his life, he wore a single-layered robe and skirt, fastening the folds together with a cord. At night, he would extend the skirt to serve as a blanket. In the second year of the Taiping Xingguo era...
On the seventh day of the tenth month of that year, he ascended the hall and said, "Today is the day I shall sever all worldly ties.
He left behind his patched robe and the wooden sandals he wore, instructing his disciples to pile up green stones to form a stupa for him.

He said, "In the future, if this stupa turns red in color, it shall be my return. Thereupon, he passed away in a state of profound stillness. He had lived for eighty years and spent sixty-three summer retreats in meditation.
Huan Ji said: "Master De’s preaching of the Dharma is like clouds and rain; yet people of the world do not hear it because they have ears that listen [only to the mundane].
As for those who are deaf, even now they continue to hear the unceasing sound of his thunder."
▲ At Mount Dayang in Yingzhou, Chan Master Jingxuan became a fully ordained monk at the age of nineteen.

He studied the definitive meaning of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), and none could equal him in his lecture halls. Soon thereafter, he abandoned them to travel as a wandering mendicant.

Upon first arriving at Liangshan, he asked, "What is the formless site of enlightenment? Liangshan pointed to Guanyin and said, "This was painted by the scholar Wu. As the Master was about to offer a reply, Liangshan—
Ji Su asked, "Which of these has form, and which is formless? The Master then attained realization and prostrated himself.
Ji Shan said, "Why do you not utter a single phrase? The Master replied, "I would not decline to speak one, but I fear it would merely fill out paper and ink."

Shanxiao said, "These words shall be inscribed upon a stele. The Master offered this verse: "In my former days as a novice, I studied the Way in delusion; I sought out knowledge across ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains.
Though I tried to discern the ancient from the present, I could never truly comprehend it; To speak directly of 'no-mind' only served to increase my doubt.
Now, having been pointed out by you, Master, like the mirror of the Qin dynasty, I see clearly the time before my parents were even born. Now that I have awakened, what [more remains]?"
Attained. At night, he released a black chicken that flew off with the snow. Master Shan said, "This can revive the school of Dongshan. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:

"All you practitioners of Zen, you must clearly understand the phrase of ordinary non-arising, the phrase of wondrous mystery and lack of partiality, and the phrase of essential clarity and inexhaustibility."
The first phrase penetrates the single path; the second phrase lacks guest and host; the third phrase carries both together.
To speak the first phrase is for the lion to stretch; to speak the second phrase is for the lion to turn back and look;
to speak the third phrase is for the lion to crouch upon the ground. In letting go, it pervades the ten directions; in seizing, it cuts off everything at once. At this very moment—act!
"How can you communicate this message? If you cannot communicate this message, I shall offer it to King Chu tomorrow.
[The student] asked, "What is the phrase of ordinary non-arising? The Master said, "White clouds cover the green mountains; the peaks of the green mountains are not revealed.
[The student] asked, "What is the phrase of wondrous mystery and impartiality? The Master said, "In the jeweled palace, there is no one who does not stand in attendance."
"If you do not plant the *wutong* tree, the phoenix will not come. [The student] asked, "What is the phrase that embodies infinite clarity?
The Master said, "When the hand points to space, heaven and earth revolve; the stone horse turns back from its path and emerges from the gauze cage. [The student] asked, "What is the lion’s yawn?"
The Master said, "In the end, there is no intention to look back; how could one willingly fall into the ordinary? [The monk] asked, "What is 'the lion’s backward leap'?
The Master said, "Moving about and returning, all is returned to the Father; though great functions arise in abundance, the essence remains without deficiency.

[The monk] asked, "What is 'the lion crouching on the ground'? The Master said, "Utterly transcending the mechanism of coming and going; throughout past and present, there is no change or variation. A monk asked, "Regarding the deceased..."
When the monk passed away, [a questioner] asked, "Where has he gone? The Master said, "When did the deceased monk pass away? [The questioner] said, "But what can we do about seeing him off?
The Master said, "A strand of silk thread upon the flames of a red furnace; amidst the heavy clouds, it does not nod its head.

The Master’s spiritual presence was extraordinary and magnificent. From his childhood, he ate only once a day. While residing at Dayang, he never stepped beyond the boundary of his quarters, nor did he turn over on his side.
He did not attend the formal assembly for fifty years. On the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Tiānshèng era, he took leave of the assembly.
Three days later, he sent a verse to Minister Wáng Shù; its gist was: "I am eighty-five years old; having cultivated the causes, I have reached this point.
If you ask where I shall return, my *uṣṇīṣa* will finally be impossible to behold. He set down his brush and passed away. When the Master first entered the assembly,
There were two disciples, Cheng and Piu, who were renowned as extraordinary and outstanding; both passed away before their master.

When [Zhaozhou] reached the age of eighty, he lamented that there was no one to succeed him in the Dongshan (Dongzong) lineage. He then entrusted his topknot image and a verse to Fushan Yuan, instructing him to seek out a vessel of the Dharma.
Fushan found Touzi Qing and charged him with continuing the Dongshan lineage; the details of this account are found in the chapter on Fushan.
▲ Chan Master Chongxian of Xuedou in Mingzhou was the son of the Li family of Suining Prefecture. He left the household life under the venerable Renxian of Puan Monastery.
After receiving full ordination, he took up the sutras at the lecture hall, investigating principles and exhausting the profound mysteries.

His interrogations were as swift as galloping horses, and his eloquence and discernment were unrivaled. He first visited Zhimen, where he immediately posed this question: "If one does not give rise to a single thought, how can there be [existence]?"
Guo-men summoned the Master to come forward. As soon as the Master drew near, Guo-men struck him across the mouth with his whisk.
The Master prepared to open his mouth, and Guo-men struck him again. At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. He remained for five years, mastering the Way in its entirety.

Thereafter, he traveled widely to visit Chan Master Dongshan Cong. Whenever a new arrival came to inquire after him, Dongshan would immediately ask: "What is the meaning of the water buffalo of Mount Gui?"
"How is it? Most who answered him failed to accord with the Master's intent. When the Master arrived, he asked as before. The Master said, "This is merely a signpost for later generations.
As the Master was about to speak, the Master struck once with his sitting cloth and then departed. The Master said, "Come here first, Upāsaka!"
The Master said: "Before entering the hall. When the Master arrived at Dàlóng as the guest prefect (*zhikè*), one day [the abbot] asked him: "Those who speak and those who remain silent are not it;
that which is neither speech nor silence is even more so. To say 'all together' is entirely not it. Cast this aside, and the Great Function manifests before you."
The people of the time knew that he existed, yet they did not know how the Great Dragon was. The Dragon asked, "Do you have such a view and understanding?
The Master said, "This old fellow has crumbled like a collapsing wall and melted away like ice. The Dragon said, "I grant you thirty blows! The Master bowed and returned to the assembly.
The Dragon then called out, "The monk who just now asked the question, come here! The Master stepped forward. The Dragon asked, "For what reason did the old monk [crumble] like a collapsing wall?"
The ice was melted away. The Master said, "You have seen only your own failures. Long made a face and said, "How unbearable! How unbearable! The Master then withdrew.
Later, he recounted this to National Teacher Ya of Nanyue. Ya said, "Great Dragon, why do you not give him his proper fodder?
The Master replied, "The Master must still travel on foot. He then asked Lohan Lin, "Regarding 'the Dharma is thus' or 'not thus,' how would you point it out?"
Nanlin said, "It is simply because it is so by the nature of things. The Master said, "The assembly, take note of my koan," and with a sweep of his robe, he returned to the assembly.
Later, while descending from the hall, Nanlin had an attendant invite the Master to the abbot’s quarters and asked him, "Elder, why did you not agree with me just now?
The Master replied, "The Abbot is the contemporary patriarch; how would I dare not agree? Nanlin said, "You..."
He abruptly shook out his robes and returned to the assembly. The Master asked, "Do you permit me to speak the Way? Lin said, "Go ahead and speak.
The Master gave a single rap and went down. He then went to study under Dayu Zhi, with whom he traveled for the longest period, alongside Yunfeng Yue.
Later, when he appeared in the world, he burned incense at the North Pagoda (namely, at the temple of Zhimen), who was his Dharma heir.
A senior disciple named Dayulong asked, "Why do you not burn incense for your former master? The Master replied, "In the past, a monk asked my former master, 'What is the firm and solid Dharmakāya?
My former master said, 'Mountain flowers bloom like brocade; mountain stream water is as deep blue as indigo. I have now composed a verse on this karmic connection, thereby repaying his kindness."
Yunfeng Yue knew that the Master would not succeed to Zhi, so he went specifically to test him. One day, while walking through the mountains with him, Yue suddenly said:
"Entering a field of weeds, one does not pick; one simply plucks whatever grass comes to hand. What is ever absent from what meets the eye? Why do you not speak when the moment arrives?
The Master picked up a stalk of grain and showed it to him. Yue did not approve, saying, "Even in a dream, I have never seen such a thing. The Master—

[The Master] said: "You are unwilling to rest right where you are. A monk asked: "Having left the ancestral seat of Cui Feng, you have now arrived at the Dharma center of Xuedou. I wonder, are these one or two? The Master said:
"If a horse lacks the power to travel a thousand li, it is in vain to pursue its wind-like gallop. The monk said: "In that case, when the clouds disperse, every house has the moon.
The Master said: "A fellow who has the head of a dragon but the tail of a snake. Six newly arrived monks came to pay their respects. As they approached, [the Master] immediately—
The Master questioned the head monk: "One who serves as a high-ranking general must have seven things at his side.
When two blades clash, what do you do? The monk said, "I have long heard that Cuiyan possesses this one move. The Master said, "I let that one move pass; now return me the price for my straw sandals!
The monk then gave a shout. The Master struck him with his staff. The monk seized the staff and struck the Master once. The Master said, "Not yet."
Upon arriving at Cuifeng, [the Master] said, "I give you twenty blows! The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Stand to one side for now;
ask the second. The monk was utterly bewildered. The Master said, "Receive this verdict as it stands.
After they had finished drinking tea, the Master seized the head monk and asked, "Regarding the previous case, it is thus here; how would you present it in the hall? The monk...

The monk remained silent. The Master struck him with his sitting mat and pushed him out. The Master asked a newly arrived monk, "Where are you from? The monk lifted up his sitting mat. The Master said, "A shrimp cannot leap out of its basket. The monk said, "I can leap! The Master struck him. The monk said, "I can leap even further! The Master struck him again. The monk then ran away. The Master called him back, and the monk prostrated himself, saying, "I have offended you, Reverend. The Master said: "No offense at all. The monk then departed. The Master said to the assembly, "This fellow has a bit of spirit; he is not one who will submit easily. He then struck him once more. The monk turned around and said, "What was that for? The Master said, "To see if you were truly a man. The monk said, "If you had struck me earlier, I would have hit you right back. The Master laughed and said, "You are indeed a man. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "Do you understand this exchange? If you do, you may go forth and act as my successor; if you do not, you must continue to practice diligently. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am leaving now. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the Way. The monk bowed and departed. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a true man of the Way. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not lose your integrity. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great capacity. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not abandon your resolve. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great strength. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget your original vow. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great wisdom. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the Buddha's teaching. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great compassion. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the Dharma. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great skill. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the Sangha. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great virtue. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the precepts. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great discipline. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the meditation hall. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great stability. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the dining hall. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great mindfulness. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the bathhouse. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great purity. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the latrine. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great humility. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the mountain gate. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great resolve. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the temple grounds. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great integrity. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the path. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great insight. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the truth. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great realization. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the mind. The monk bowed and left. The Master said to the assembly, "He is a man of great awakening. He then struck him once more. The monk said, "I am going. The Master said, "Go, but do not forget the self.
