However, because my late teacher left behind an unfinished case, I have come forth to settle it with him. At that time, a monk asked, "What is this unfinished case of the late teacher?
The Master struck him and said, "If the grandfather does not settle it, the trouble will fall upon the grandson."
Sun asked, "Where does the fault lie? The Master said, "The fault lies with me; the calamity reaches you.

When the Prince of Jiangnan was still the Duke of Zheng, he received the mind-to-mind transmission from the chamber of Fayan. Upon hearing this question, the Prince said, "What unresolved case did my late teacher have?
The Master replied, "I am currently analyzing it for him."
Cuiyan Zhi said: "Exerting one's utmost effort for the sake of the assembly brings disaster from within one's own gate. Tiantong Jue said:
"If this monk were a true man, he would have come forth and overturned the meditation seat.

Not only would he have found his own way out, but he would also have spared his descendants from the lingering calamities of his ancestors' unfinished business. Yuanguan Ju said: "I, this mountain monk, am humble."
My intention is fundamentally like this. My coming forth today is solely for the sake of the founding patriarchs;
there is a ready-made public case (gong'an) that I shall proclaim before the assembly. Let those who do not spare their own lives come forward and test it!
If there is no one, I shall have no choice but to pick it up and play with it myself. (He lets out a shout and strikes the meditation seat with his whisk.)

[The Master] took his seat. ▲ Chan Master Qingsong of Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou went to study under Fayan. Fayan pointed to the rain and said to the Master, "Every drop falls into the eyes of the Senior Monk.
At first, the Master did not understand the meaning. Later, while reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he was moved to realization and received [the Dharma] from Fayan.
Seal of Approval. He ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas of the ten directions are always before you; do you see them?
If you say you see them, do you see them with your mind or with your eyes? Therefore it is said: 'All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished.
If one can understand in this way, the Buddhas are constantly manifest before one. Furthermore, he said: 'When seeing form, one sees the mind. Now, what do you call that?"

Consider this: the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the myriad phenomena in their array; and the appearances of blue, yellow, red, white, male, female, and so forth—are these the mind or not the mind?
If they are the mind, why do they instead become material objects? If they are not the mind, yet it is said that "upon seeing form, one sees the mind.
Do you understand? It is simply because of delusion regarding this that one falls into inversion, resulting in all manner of differences.
Within that which is devoid of identity or difference, one forcibly creates identity and difference. Yet, if you can now directly accept it as it is, your original mind will suddenly open up;
it is luminously clear, with not a single thing to be seen or heard. If you seek liberation apart from the mind, the ancients called this "searching for the source in the waves";
such a person will find it extremely difficult to achieve awakening.
▲ Chan Master Daoheng of Baizhang in Hongzhou went to study under Fayan. He requested instruction on the story of the outsider asking the Buddha whether he would speak of existence or non-existence.
Before he had finished his explanation, Fayan said, “Stop, stop! Do you intend to understand this by looking for the World-Honored One’s long silence?
From this, the Master attained awakening. Ascending the hall, [Fayan] said: "In truth, there is nothing to do. Each of you..."
Each one is a Buddha. What further doubt could there be? Having reached this point, an ancient said: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action.
This is the field for selecting Buddhas; with an empty mind, they return as the valedictorians. But what is meant by an "empty mind"?
It is not merely closing one's eyes and sitting in cold stillness that constitutes an empty mind; that is precisely the conceptualization and interpretation of the conscious intellect. Above...
Do you wish to understand the emptiness of the mind through the sitting? Simply recognize your own mind, and you will see that the mind is empty.
Therefore it is said: "The past has already passed; do not calculate the future. Sit upright and without concern; who has ever called out to you?
Even if someone were to call out to you, Master, would you respond or not? If you respond, who is it that calls out to you? If you do not...
He responds to others, yet he is not afflicted by deafness. The essence of the three periods of time is empty; furthermore, he is no mere block of wood. Thus the ancients said:
"When the mind is empty, one can see the Dharma King. Do you see the Dharma King? It is simply this old, sick monk.
Furthermore, do not say that his self-substitution was good. Take care! Ascending the hall, as soon as the assembly had gathered, he said: "Go drink tea. Or...

When the assembly gathered, he would say, "Be careful" (*zhēnzhòng*). At other times when the assembly gathered, he would simply say, "Rest. Later, there was a verse that said: "Bai Zhang has three secret phrases:
'Drink tea,' 'Be careful,' and 'Rest. If you can directly take them up in this very moment, I dare guarantee that you have not yet reached the ultimate."
Jianfu Gu raised this saying to show the assembly, saying: "Great assembly, as for Master Heng’s composition of this verse—tell me, what was his realization?
Do you know where he gained or lost? If you wish to understand, look at him during the three occasions he ascended the hall:
he was like a good person. But later, when he composed this verse, it was as if a blemish had appeared on his face."
These two lines of characters were carved [upon the stone]. If one is a person of thorough understanding and a man of realization, they will know immediately upon their being raised.
For those of later learning and beginners, it is difficult to discern and distinguish them. I, this old monk, shall provide you with a commentary from the beginning:

"Baizhang has three secrets; the thief’s own body is already exposed. "Drink tea; take care; rest"—the stolen goods are brought forth. To directly accept [this] right now—dare I guarantee that you have not yet?

Chè: This is very much like passing judgment while still clutching the stolen goods. Nevertheless, you worthy ones must possess the eye that discerns phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-cakṣus*) before you can provide authentic testimony.
If you cannot distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, you may be said to be "bluntly grasping at Buddha-nature.
You must further consult the wise and virtuous; otherwise, it is a pity to live and die in vain.
▲ Chan Master Daoyan Yongming went to visit Fayan. Fayan asked, "Aside from your formal inquiries for instruction, what sutra are you studying?
The Master replied, "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Fayan asked, "Under which category do the six aspects—totality, particularity, sameness, difference, formation, and disintegration—fall?
The Master replied, "The text is found within the 'Ten Stages' chapter (*Daśabhūmika*). According to its principle, all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds..."
"Does emptiness also possess the six characteristics? Master [Zhaozhou] had no reply. Yan said, "Ask me. The Master then asked, "Does emptiness also possess the six characteristics?
Yan said, "Emptiness. Thereupon, the Master attained awakening; he leaped for joy and prostrated in thanks. Yan asked, "How do you understand this?
The Master replied, "Emptiness. Yan approved. Later, on another occasion, because of the four... [text fragment].
The multitude of men and women entered the monastery. A monk asked, "In the Vinaya it is said that if one hears the sound of hairpins and bracelets through a wall, it is called breaking the precepts.
Seeing gold and silver intermingled, or crowds of people dressed in vermilion and purple, is this breaking the precepts or not? The Master said:
"What an excellent point of entry! Yan said. "In the future, you shall have five hundred disciples who will be held in high esteem by kings and lords.
Later, while at an ancient temple in Quzhou, he was reading the Tripitaka. Once, during a period of seated meditation, he saw Mañjuśrī manifest his form;
unable to contain himself, he rose and prostrated. Subsequently, when he went to Hangzhou to pay homage at the Aśoka Stūpa, he knelt and placed it upon his head, weeping tears.
A rain of śarīras fell. The Master asked the monk in charge of the stupa, "If people have not seen them with their own eyes, can it truly be said that they exist?
The monk replied, "According to the records, they are hidden within the inner corner and appear from afar like a suspended bell.

The Master’s doubts were not yet resolved, so he prostrated himself in earnest worship without ceasing for a moment. Suddenly, he saw the śarīras outside the suspended bell, crawling and wriggling as they moved.

The Master was filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy. Furthermore, Dashi Guangwen, acting as a patron (*dānapati*), invited him to his mountain retreat to perform the thirty-seven-day Samantabhadra Repentance.

Suddenly, he saw the elephant of Samantabhadra beneath the pavilion at the triple gate of the temple; the elephant’s trunk was extended straight, resting upon the place where the repentance was being performed.
On the eighteenth day of the ninth month of the second year of Jianlong (the *Xinyou* year), he manifested his passing into *nirvāṇa*. He entered...
At the edge of the coffin, a white light radiated forth during the day, seen by the entire assembly. During the cremation, the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting.
There was a butcher who, reflecting on his own evil karma, bared his chest and approached the pyre to beg for some; in an instant, he obtained seven grains.
▲ One day, a newly arrived monk came to visit Chan Master Huiming of Bao'en Temple in Hangzhou. The Master asked, "Where have you recently departed from?
The monk replied, "The capital city. The Master said, "Venerable sir, now that you have left the capital city to come to this mountain, the capital city is bereft of you."
"Regarding this 'surplus' of the Elder: if there is a surplus, then phenomena exist outside the mind; if there is a deficiency, then the mental phenomena are incomplete.
If you can explain the principle, you may stay; if you do not understand, you must leave. The monk had no reply.
Miaoxi spoke on his behalf, saying, "The Master cannot deceive me, nor can I deceive the Master.
He added, "Is there anyone present who can now utter a phrase that deceives one another?
If you can, I shall grant that you have leaped through the diamond ring and swallowed the thorny jujube."
The Master asked the senior monk Pengyan, "Among all the sages of the past and the virtuous predecessors, was there anyone who did not attain awakening?
Yan replied, "How could any of the sages or virtuous predecessors fail to have attained awakening?

The Master said, "When one person awakens and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions completely vanishes. Yet today Mount Tiantai stands towering and prominent; how can it vanish?"
He departed. Yan had no reply. Master Ziyuan, the Elder, asked, "What is the samādhi of the present moment?
The Master said, "Do you hear it? Ziyuan said, "I am not suffering from deafness. The Master said, "Indeed, you are suffering from deafness."
When Imperial Envoy Liao entered Yunju Qingxi Chan Master’s quarters, he saw the portrait of Fayan and asked, "What kind of fruit is this before the portrait?
The Master replied, "It is artificial fruit. Liao said, "Since it is artificial fruit, why is it being used to make offerings to the portrait?
The Master said, "I simply want you, Imperial Envoy, to recognize what is artificial."
▲ Zen Master Zhiiyi of Luohan Temple in Zhangzhou asked a monk, "Where have you been this summer?
The monk replied, "I was with Upāsaka Wuyan. The Master said, "Did you ever inquire after him? The monk said, "I did inquire after him.
The Master said, "How could one inquire after Wuyan? The monk said, "If one were Wuyan, where would there not be inquiry?"
The Master shouted, “It is just like asking an old brother! The Master was eating *bingdan* (steamed cakes) with the Elder Yandu.
Yandu said, “A hundred kinds, a thousand varieties—their substance is not two. The Master asked, “What is this non-dual substance? Yandu picked up a *bingdan*.
The Master said, “You are merely clinging to the hundred kinds and thousand varieties. Yandu said, “That too is just the Master’s own point of view. The Master said, “Indeed.”
"You are also like the style of hair-combing of Old Man Luo Yong. When the Master was about to pass away, he said to the assembly:
"Tonight my four elements are not in harmony. Clouds rise and birds fly; the wind moves and dust stirs. Amidst this vast expanse, is there anyone who can bring it under control?
If one can bring it under control, we shall never recognize each other for eternal kalpas. If one cannot bring it under control, I shall be seen by you at all times. Having spoken, he passed away.
He passed away in silence.

▲ Chan Master Wensui of Baoci in Jinling once studied the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* and composed a word-by-word commentary with topical divisions for it, claiming that his work deeply accorded with the intent of the scripture.
He went to visit Fayan, who said, "Does the *Śūraṃgama* not contain the principle of the 'eight returns'?"
The Master said, "Yes. Yan asked, "To what does clarity return? The Master said, "Clarity returns to the sun. Yan asked, "To what does the sun return? The Master was at a loss.
Yan then commanded him to burn the notes he had written. Only then did the Master follow Yan’s request for instruction.
▲ Zen Master Xuanze of Jinling Baoyuan Temple asked Qingfeng, “What is the student’s own self?
Feng replied, “The child of fire (Bingding) comes seeking fire. Later, he visited Fayan. Fayan asked, “Where have you come from?
The Master said, “From Qingfeng. Fayan asked, “What words did Qingfeng say? The Master recounted the previous dialogue. Fayan said, “How would you act in this situation, Senior Monk?”
[The monk] went to see the Master. The Master said, "Bing and Ding belong to fire; yet you seek fire further—this is like seeking oneself by means of oneself.
The monk said, "If one understands it in this way, how can it be right? The Master said, "I am simply like this. I do not know how you, Reverend, understand it."
Fayan said, "Ask me, and I will tell you. The Master asked, "What is the student's own self? Fayan said, "The child Bingding comes seeking fire.
At these words, the Master attained sudden enlightenment. On the day he opened the hall for his formal inauguration, Prince Li and Fayan were both present in the assembly.
A monk asked, "When the dragon roars, mist rises; when the tiger howls, the wind arises. I know this is what has come forth—"
"Regarding the matter of the limits of the world: why did you not understand when it came to this? The Master said, "Understand it well.
The monk raised his head to look at the Master, then looked at Fayan, and withdrew into the assembly. At that moment, Fayan and King Li both turned pale with alarm.

Fayan returned to his quarters and ordered an attendant to summon the monk who had been questioning him. Fayan said, "The question you asked just now—" [He was about to grant him the seal of certification.]
"You possess eyes. Before this assembly of humans and devas, why do you not bow? You have merely covered your eyes with your sitting mat.
Three days later, that monk spat out light and passed away.
▲ Chan Master Guizong Cezhen was originally named Huichao. He visited Fayan and asked, "I, Huichao, inquire of the Master:
what is the Buddha? Fayan replied, "You are Huichao. From this, the Master attained awakening.

Yuanwu Keqin said: "Among those who deliberate on this in various quarters, many offer intellectual interpretations, saying that Hui-chao was himself the Buddha, which is why Fayan answered as he did.
Some say it is very much like riding a cow while searching for a cow; others say..."
The very place where you ask is it; what connection could there be? If you understand it in such a way, not only do you fail yourself, but you also deeply wrong the ancients.
Xuedou’s verse says: "The spring breeze cannot stir the riverside lands; the partridge cries out amidst the deep flowers.
When the three-tiered waves rise high, the fish transforms into a dragon; yet the foolish man still scoops water from the night pond."
Yuanwu said: "In Jiangxi and Jiangnan, many people offer two kinds of interpretations for the verse: 'The spring breeze of the River Kingdom cannot stir it.
This refers to Hui-chao; this news is such that even the spring breeze of the River Kingdom cannot stir it.
'The partridge cries amidst the deep flowers'—this refers to the vast clamor of the various quarters' deliberations, which is like the cry of a partridge."

"Crying within deep flowers—what connection is there? You do not realize that these two lines from Xuedou are actually just one line, intended to be seamless and without flaw. He clearly says to you: 'His words are correct; his speech is correct.
It covers heaven and earth. When someone asked, 'What is the Buddha? Baizhang said, 'You are Huichao. — Xuedou.
The Way: The spring breeze of the River State cannot rouse it; the partridge cries amidst the deep flowers. If you can realize it here, you may stride alone through the crimson heavens;
this is far more than merely a fish transforming into a dragon when the waves are high. If you treat it as an emotional interpretation, [you have missed it].
This is like a fool still bailing out water from a pond at night. In the past, the venerable Master Duan also had a verse that said:
"With three large copper coins, I bought a sesame cake; having eaten it into my belly, I no longer hear of hunger."
This verse is excellent; however, it is not as well-phrased as Xuedou’s wording.
Later, after taking up residence [at a monastery], he ascended the hall and said: "Venerable elders, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing can only occur once.

As for 'having understood,' is that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, or is it not seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing? Do you wish to understand? I shall explain it thoroughly for you, venerable elders."
It is so. You must wait until you attain awakening before you may understand it. I have stood here for a long time; take care of yourself.
▲ Chan Master Shaoxian of Tong’an was soliciting tiles from Mount Yungai to build a hall.

Someone asked, "Since this is already Mount Yungai (Cloud-Covered), why do you need to solicit tiles? The monk had no reply. The Master spoke on his behalf, saying: "The tiles have met their destined person."
▲ Chan Master Guanyin Congxian ascended the hall. When the assembly had gathered, he sat in silence for a long while and then said:
"Mañjuśrī deeply praised the layman. I wonder, did the layman receive this praise or not? If he received it, where is the layman?
If he did not receive it, Mañjuśrī could not have spoken in vain. How do you all understand this? (Taiping Xingguo Era)
In the ninth month of the eighth year, he said to the Donor, Assistant Director Yuan: "I, this old monk, shall return to my hometown in two or three days.
Yuan said, "The Master is advanced in years; why do you still long for your hometown? The Master replied, "I am returning home to find some good salt to eat."
Yuan could not fathom his words. The following day, the Master sat upright and passed away without illness.
At Xingshan Monastery in Luojing, Zen Master Qilun had reached the end of his life while serving as a court official under Li Jixun. A monk asked him:
"This Dharma abides in its fixed position; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. I do not know, Master Li Gong, where you have gone?
The Master said, "I was just about to be asked by you. [The monk] said, "If that is so, then my question was in vain. The Master said, "You are remarkably sharp-witted."
▲ When the Zen Master Jinchan of Guxian was attending Dharma Eye (Hōgen), Dharma Eye asked him: "A monk once said, 'Since leaving this place, where have you been coming from?
He replied, 'I have come from entering the mountain ranges. Dharma Eye said, 'Not easy. The monk said, 'I have traveled across all those mountains and waters in vain.
Dharma Eye said, 'Even those many mountains and waters are not bad. At these words, the monk was speechless. The Master [Jinchan] commented on this:

The eleventh generation descendant of the Sixth Patriarch:
Chan Master Chiming (Cibian) Shichuang of Tanzhou, surnamed Li, was born into the Qingxiang clan of Quanzhou. In his youth, he was a scholar.
At the age of twenty-two, he received the full precepts at Yijing Monastery on Mount Xiang, south of the city. His mother was a woman of great virtue.
He traveled abroad to wander through various regions. The Master had joined eyebrows and elegant eyes; he was tall and robust, yet he did not conform to conventional standards.

Wherever he went, he was rebuked by senior elders as being too young for the monastic community (*saṃgha*). The Master laughed with a rugged, defiant air and said, "When dragons and elephants trample, they do not heed the footprints of the small."
This was not something an ass could endure. He once carried a chest of antiquities on a bamboo staff slung over his shoulder as he traveled between Xiangyang and Mian.

While staying at Shouzhi Valley Spring, he joined forces with others to enter Luoyang. Hearing that Chan Master Fenyang Zhao’s reputation for the Way was preeminent in the world, he resolved to personally rely upon him.
At that time, the imperial court was in the midst of a campaign against Hedong, and heavy troops were stationed throughout Luzhou and Zhezhou.

Many urged him not to go, but the Master paid them no heed. He crossed the great river and ascended Mount Taihang. Changing his clothes to resemble those of a servant, he concealed his identity among the ranks of fire-drill soldiers.
Sleeping in the open and lodging in the grass, he reached Longchuan and eventually approached Fenyang. Master Zhao admired his vigor;

however, after two years had passed, he still did not permit him to enter the inner chamber. The Master went to visit Zhao, who, sensing his resolve, would surely revile and scold the attendants to test him.

He disparaged all other quarters, and whatever he taught consisted entirely of worldly and vulgar matters. One night, he complained, saying, "I have been at this Dharma assembly for two summers now, yet I have received no instruction.
My thoughts have only increased in worldly toil; time has slipped away in an instant, and since my own fundamental task remains unclarified, I have lost the benefit of leaving the household life.
Before he had finished speaking, Master Zhao gazed at him intently and scolded him, saying, "How can such a person know [the Way]?"
Shi [the attendant] dared to trade insults with me. I became angry and raised my staff to drive him away. As the Master prepared to intervene and rescue him, Emperor Zhao covered his mouth.

The Master attained great enlightenment and said, "Now I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary circumstances. He served him for seven years before taking his leave to visit Chan Master Tangming Song.
Song said to the Master, "The Palace Secretary Yang Dainian possesses high insight; his entry into the Way is steady and substantial."
"You must not fail to see me. The Master then went to see Dainian. Dainian asked, "We do not recognize each other face-to-face, yet from a thousand li away our ways are the same.
The Master said, "I have recently received an invitation from the Mountain Gate. Dainian said, "You are truly full of empty talk.
The Master said, "I left Tangming last month. Dainian said, "Just now I regretted asking you. The Master said, "An adept. Dainian then gave a shout. The Master said:
"Exactly so," said Nianfu. The Master drew a line with his hand. Nianfu stuck out his tongue and said, "Truly a dragon and an elephant.
The Master asked, "What do you mean by that? Nianfu called for the guest master to bring tea, saying, "It turns out he is one of our own household. The Master remarked, "Indeed."
"It is not enough. After the tea was finished, he asked again, "What is the one phrase for the sake of others? The Master said, "Thoroughly.
Zhang Nian said, "If that is so, then it is like a bride in a long skirt dragging through the mud. The Master said, "Who could equal you, Inner Secretary?
Zhang Nian said, "A true master, a true master! The Master said, "I grant you twenty blows. Zhang Nian patted his knee and said, "What is this place?"
"Where is it? The Master clapped his hands and said, "I cannot let this pass. Yuanan laughed loudly.
He asked again, "Do you remember the circumstances of Tangming’s enlightenment at that time? The Master said, "Tangming asked Shoushan, 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Shoushan replied, 'On the banks of King Chu’s city, the Ru River flows eastward. Yuanan said, "It is just these words."
"What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A lantern hanging over the water. Yan said, "If that is so, then I have failed the ancients.
The Master said, "If you, Inner Secretary, have doubts, seek another teacher. Yan said, "A three-legged toad leaps up into the sky.
The Master said, "Leap as you please. Yan then laughed heartily. He was lodged in the refectory, where he questioned Zhizheng day and night regarding the Dharma. Because of this—

Upon hearing of his past deeds and former conduct, he regretted that he had seen him so late. While in the imperial court, he said to the Prince Consort (Fu-ma Du-wei) Li Gong Zunxu, "Recently I encountered a man of the Way who is truly a lion of the West River.
Li replied, "I am constrained by official protocol and cannot go to pay my respects; what can be done? Yuan An remained silent.
Upon returning, he told the Master, "Lord Li is one among those who follow the Buddha-dharma; he has heard of your reputation for the Way from afar."

He arrived with a sincere desire to see [the Master]. However, because the regulations did not permit him to accompany his attendants into the presence of the Master, he went to pay his respects to Master Li at dawn.
Upon reading the visitor’s card, Master Li sent a young attendant to inquire: "If you can speak the Way, you shall be granted an audience with the Abbot."
The Master said, "Today you have come specifically to visit me. He then instructed his attendant boy, saying, "Carve white characters upon the stele;
plant green pines along the path. The Master said, "Were it not for this festival day, such an occasion would surely be difficult to encounter on other days.
The boy stepped forward again and said, "The Commandant says: 'If that is so, then I shall go to meet the Venerable. The Master said, "From head to foot. Thereupon, the official...
[The Master] came out. Once [the official] was seated, he asked, "I have heard that there is a golden-haired lion in the West River.
Is this true? The Master said, "Where did you get such news? The official then gave a shout. The Master said, "A jackal howling. The official shouted again. The Master said, "Exactly so."
The Duke laughed heartily. The Master took his leave. The Duke asked, "What is the one phrase for you, Venerable, as you depart?

The Master said, "Take good care of yourself. The Duke said, "How is this any different from other places? The Master said, "And what about you, Excellency? The Duke said, "I shall give you twenty blows!
The Master said, "Solely for the sake of its wide circulation. The Duke shouted again. The Master said, "Blind! The Duke said, "Go well," and the Master departed.
“Very well, very well,” he replied. From then on, he came and went between the gates of Yang and Li, taking the Dharma as his friend.
After a long time, he took leave to return to Hedong. Nan’an asked, “Do you have a single phrase to entrust to Tang Ming? The Master said, “The bright moon shines upon the traveler at night.
Nan’an said, “That does not quite fit. The Master said, “It may still be bearable at the deepest of night; after midday, it brings even more sorrow to people. Nan’an—
Yuan’an said, “The Vajra statue before Kaibao Temple has recently sweated; why is that? The Master said, “I know.

Because his mother was old, he returned to Jūn Prefecture and relied upon Chan Master Dòngshān Cóng. Cóng ordered him to lead the assembly. Previously, Fényáng had said to the Master:
"I have traveled everywhere to study the descendants of Yúnmén, yet I have harbored a regret that I have not yet seen Cóng. Therefore...
The Master relied upon him for three years and then went to visit Chan Master Yin of Shending. Shending was a senior disciple of Shougang;

his reputation was preeminent at the time, and among the monks, none could rival his extraordinary brilliance. He had resided on the mountain for thirty years, and his disciples’ spirit overwhelmed those of all other quarters.
The Master did not cut his hair and wore tattered clothes; speaking with a Chu accent, he announced himself as a dharma-nephew to gain entry.
The entire assembly burst into laughter. Foding sent a youth to ask, "Venerable sir, whose successor are you?

The Master looked up at the roof and said, "I saw Fenyang in person. Foding then stepped out with his staff; looking back, he saw the Master standing tall and majestic, and asked, "Is there a 'Lion of the West River' in Fenzhou?
The Master pointed behind him and shouted, "The roof is collapsing! The youth fled backward, and Foding turned to look after him.
He appeared alert and vigorous. The Master sat upon the ground, slipped off one shoe, and showed it to him. Old Ding forgot his question and lost sight of where the Master was.
The Master slowly rose, adjusted his robes, and as he walked away, spoke: "To see the person is not as good as hearing of their reputation.
He then departed. Ding sent someone to pursue him, but could not catch him. Sighing, he said, "Is there such a son in Fenzhou? He then went to Daoyi at Dayu.
While at the Master’s quarters, Dongzhishi sat for a moment; he opened his box, took out some incense, and prepared to burn it. The Master asked, "How do you burn it?
Zhishi then placed the incense into the incense burner and lit it. The Master pointed at him and said, "What a clumsy fellow! You go about doing things this way again.

A monk asked, "When seeking stillness amidst the clamor, how should one proceed? The Master replied, "Sleeping with your head on a hemp sack. A monk asked, "When the fires from the four mountains come surging forth..."
"What? the Master asked. [The monk] said, "Things arise following people. [The Master] asked, "When traveling on foot and not meeting anyone, what then?
The Master said, "A fishing line twisting in the water. [The Master] asked, "You polish a three-foot sword to go and transform those who are unjust;
what is your intention? The Master said, "Go well. The monk said, "Understood. The Master said, "Look! The monk clapped his hands once and returned to the assembly. The Master said, "Finished."
A monk asked, "What is it like when there is reason but it cannot be expressed? The Master said, "Suffering. The monk said, "In that case, my tongue is pressed against the upper palate.
The Master let out a single sigh. The monk said, "I thought the beard was red. The Master said, "Have you ever even dreamed of Xinghua’s heels?
Another monk asked, "Where have you recently come from? The monk replied, "Clouds pass over a thousand mountains, all green. The Master said, "You are in a hurry."
"What is it? he asked. The monk said, "The cry of wild geese passing over the water is mournful. The Master then shouted; the monk also shouted.

The Master then struck him; the monk also struck him. The Master said, "Look at this blind fellow! By right, I should drive you out through the three gates. But considering that you are a newcomer, sit and drink tea.
The Master then asked Chief Seat Xianying, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "Jinluan. The Master said, "Last summer..."
"Where were you last year? He replied, "At Jinnian. "Where were you the summer before last? He replied, "At Jinnian.

"I shall have the attendant from the storehouse brought here to examine you. For now, have a bowl of tea prepared to moisten your mouth. [This was said by] Yong the Head Seat.
Master [Yunmen] went with Yong to Fenyang. Yong never exhausted its subtlety; though he followed the Master for twenty years, he never attained liberation.
One night, as they sat around a brazier deep into the night, the Master struck the charcoal with a fire-tongs and called out, "Yong, Head Seat!

"I see it in a dream. Now tell me: what excellence does the Zen of the Patriarchs possess? If you seek the principle within words, you will mislead future generations.
Even if you were to take it up under the blow of the staff, you would still be failing the former sages. The myriad dharmas are fundamentally at rest; it is only people who create their own clamor.
Therefore, when this mountain monk dwells at Fuyan, he sees only the realm of Fuyan.
Rising late and sleeping early, sometimes clouds arise from the azure peaks, and sometimes the moon sets behind the cold pond. The kalavinka birds fly and sing before the Prajna Terrace;
the fragrance of the śāla flowers wafts beside Mount Zhurong. Grasping my lean staff, I sit upon the flat stone with the monks of the Five Lakes, from time to time—
Speaking of the profound mystery, with head covered in ash and face smeared with dust, he dwells at Xinghua, seeing only the house style of Xinghua.

Welcoming and seeing off guests, the gate connects to the city; carriages and horses crowd together. Fishermen’s songs resound through the Xiang River, and monkeys cry on Mount Lu; the sounds of strings, flutes, and folk songs enter the ears at every moment.
Furthermore, he daily discusses Chan and the Way with eminent men from the four seas, forgetting the passage of years and months. Now tell me: [what is this?]

In the year Wuyin of the Baoyuan era, the Imperial Guard Commandant Li sent an envoy to invite the Master, saying, "Among the Dharma friends within the realm, there are only you and Yang Daian. Daian has abandoned me."
However, I have been feeling quite frail and aged in recent years. I have endured death just to see you once more. You then sent a letter to the Military Governor of Tan to earnestly invite him.
The Master was moved by compassion and, accompanied by his attendant, traveled eastward by boat. On the boat, he composed a verse, saying: "The long river flows on without end;
when shall we reach the Imperial Capital? Now that we have caught a favorable breeze, there is no need to ply the oars. Upon arriving at...
In the capital, he met with Master Li. Within a month, Master Li indeed passed away. At the moment of his death, he drew a circle and offered a verse to the Master:
"The world has no support; mountains and rivers present no obstruction. The great ocean contains a mote of dust; Mount Sumeru holds a mustard seed."
[The Master] picked up his head-wrap (*fuhou*) and untied his waist-belt. [The Layman] said, "If you seek birth and death, ask the leather bag.

The Master asked, "What is the original Buddha-nature? The Layman replied, "Today is as hot as yesterday. As soon as these words were spoken, the Master asked him, "What is the single phrase for the moment of departure?
The Master said, "Originally there is no obstruction; wherever one goes, it is square or round as appropriate. The Layman said, "In the evening..."
He arrived feeling extremely exhausted and no longer responded to conversation. The Master said, "Where there is no Buddha, manifest as a Buddha. Thereupon, the official passed away peacefully.
Emperor Renzong, who took great interest in the school of emptiness, heard of Mr. Li’s transformation and his dialogue with the Master; he marveled at it for a long time.
The Master wept bitterly and bid farewell at the burial mound. By imperial decree, he was granted an official boat to return south, and on the way—
He said to his attendant, "I have suddenly contracted a wind-paralysis; look, my mouth and lips are already slanted. The attendant stamped his foot on the ground and cried, "What shall we do?
Throughout your life you reviled the Buddhas and cursed the Patriarchs, yet now this has come to pass! The Master said, "Have no worry."
"I shall correct this for you. With his hand, he adjusted [the master's position] back to its former state and said, "From now on, I will no longer neglect you.
Subsequently, in the first year of the Mingnian era, on the fifth day of the first month, he bathed, took leave of the assembly, sat in the lotus posture, and passed away.
He had lived fifty-four years and spent thirty-two summer retreats in the monasteries. The son of Lord Li inscribed this account of his conduct upon his memorial stele.

Xinghua. He concealed his entire body at Shishuang. When the Master was first with Fenyang, Fenyang one day, on the pretext of dreaming of his deceased parents, ordered the storehouse to prepare wine and meat for an offering.
Once the offering was completed, he gathered the assembly of monks and commanded them to eat it.
No one would listen. Yang continued to eat and drink as before. The assembly said, "A monk who consumes wine and meat is not fit to be a teacher.
They all dispersed, leaving only Yang, Da-yu, and six or seven others remaining.

On the following day, Yang ascended the hall and said, "All these idle spirits and wild ghosts have been sent off with nothing more than a single platter of wine and meat. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "In this assembly there are no..."
"Branches and leaves; there is only the ultimate reality.
[The Master] descended from his seat. Master Xing of Xianxian was stern, cold, austere, and plain; the monastics feared him.
Fushan Yuan and Tiantai Hui went to attend upon him during a time of bitter cold and snow. Xing scolded and drove them away, even splashing them with water. As for others...
The monks were all incensed and departed; only Huairang remained, sitting calmly with his robes soaked by the water. Xingsheng said, "If you do not leave, I shall beat you.
Huairang replied, "The two of us have come from thousands of miles away specifically to attend upon the Master.

How could we leave because of a single ladle of water? Even if you were to beat me to death, I would not go. Xingsheng then ordered him to be enrolled as a resident monk and subsequently entrusted him with the succession.

Huiyuan served as the *dianzuo* (steward). As the community suffered from hardship and austerity, Huiyuan secretly took some oil and flour while on an official inspection tour to prepare a five-flavor congee for the monks.

When the official returned and learned of this, he calculated the value of the items and imposed a fine. After Huiyuan had assessed his robes and bowl to repay the debt, the official beat him and drove him out.
Consequently, Huiyuan took up residence in a corridor room. When the official went out and saw him there, he again demanded rent money. Huiyuan held out his alms bowl...
The Mayor exchanged his money for it and returned it to him without any sign of difficulty. Upon reflection, [the Master] said, "Yuan truly has the intention to practice Chan.
He then summoned him back.
At the Chuzhou Langya Mountain Chan Master Huijue Guangzhao’s hall, a monk came forward and drew a circle.
"Perfect Circle. The Master picked up his staff. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him and said, "Speak!
The monk said, "I will not speak. The Master asked, "Why will you not speak? The monk replied, "The Buddhas of the three periods do not go beyond this.

Incident: The mountain had long been without water, and the community suffered greatly from this hardship. Suddenly, a spring emerged from among the mountain rocks; its water was sweet, cool, and pure.

The Prefect, Lord He, subsequently named it "The Spring of Reappearance. On the fourth day of the fifth month in the sixth year of the Yuanfeng era, after bathing and ascending the hall to bid farewell to the assembly, he wrote this verse:
"Two places where I have served as abbot, yet nothing has assisted the Way. Be careful, all of you!"
The man did not need to search further; he dropped his brush and passed away.
▲ Zen Master Qingpou of Xingyang in Yingzhou was serving as a garden head under Dayang. While he was planting melons, Dayang asked:
"When will the melons ripen? The Master said, "They have already ripened and rotted away. [The monk] said, "Pick out the sweet ones and bring them here.
The Master said, "Who would eat them? [The monk] said, "Those who do not enter the garden. The Master said, "I wonder who it is that does not enter the garden."
"Will you eat it too? The monk asked, "Do you recognize him? The Master said, "Although I do not recognize him, I cannot help but give it to him.
Yang smiled and departed. A monk asked, "When Sāgara emerges from the sea, heaven and earth tremble; when meeting face-to-face, what is the matter?
The Master said, "The Golden-Winged Bird King presides over the universe; who among them is one who has emerged? [The monk] said, "If one suddenly encounters..."
"When he emerges, what then? The Master said, "It is like a hawk seizing a pigeon. If you do not believe me, you shall know it as true only when it is verified before your own skull.
[The monk] said, "If that is so, I shall fold my hands at my chest and retreat three paces.
The Master said, "You turtle beneath Mount Sumeru; do not wait until you suffer another defeat and turn back."
Huanji said: "Master Pofu did not recognize the thief and further handed over the Great Axe to him; this is truly pitiable and painful. While lying ill, Dayang asked:

If there were no bubbles and illusions, there would be no way to accomplish the Great Matter. If you wish to accomplish the Great Matter, recognize these bubbles and illusions. How so? The Master [replied].
Yang said, "That is still a matter of 'this side. What about a matter of 'that side'? The Master replied, "The crimson sun shines across the earth;
no flowers grow at the bottom of the sea. Yang laughed and said, "Are you so very alert? The Master gave a shout and said, "I thought you had forgotten!

▲ When Chan Master Xianru of Mount Luofu first arrived at Dayang, Dayang asked, "Where are you from?

He replied, "I do not know how to soar through the air. Yangshan said, "How then did you get here? He replied, "At every step I am not lost to the directions; throughout my entire being there is no place of distinction."

▲ Chan Master Tianyi Yihuai of Yuezhou had been a fisherman by profession since his youth. His mother dreamed that a star fell upon her house, after which she became pregnant.
When the boy was young, he would sit at the stern of the boat and release every fish he caught; though his father scolded and whipped him for this, he paid it no mind.

Huairang said, "I too am without measure; you too are without measure. What about you? The teacher was speechless. Huairang struck him and said, "You are full of empty talk!"

Zhaozhou subsequently served as the water-carrier. While drawing water, his carrying pole suddenly broke, and he attained enlightenment. He composed a verse of realization: "One, two, three."
Four, five, six, seven. Standing alone on a ten-thousand-fathom peak, he snatches the bright pearl from the jaws of the black dragon. With a single word, he exposes Vimalakīrti’s flaws.
Juewen struck the desk and praised him as excellent. Addressing the assembly, [the Master] said: An ancient said, "A single void atop the mountain of the five aggregates;

This is the place where the living emerge from the road of the dead.
If you can examine it with clarity, cast off the cap of dripping fat and strip away the foul-smelling cloth tunic.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "A wild goose flies across the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water. The goose has no intention of leaving a trace; the water has no mind to retain the shadow.

Let it go, and there are a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses; bring it back, and there is a solemnity and a profound earnestness. When used..."

When the banana tree hears thunder, it blossoms; when the sunflower faces the sun, it turns. You worthy ones, when the banana tree hears thunder and blossoms, does it have ears?

The Master said, "The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, explained this in detail at the assembly of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra to distinguish it for Ānanda.
Yet you still do not believe; you take that which investigates, pursues, and seeks after as the mind. [Ānanda] encountered the Buddha...

This is a rebuke. That which investigates, pursues, and tracks is consciousness (*vijñāna*). If one follows the characteristics of dharmas with consciousness, then affliction is called consciousness and not mind (*citta*).
"Intention" (*manas*) means recollection; it is the recollective thought that arises toward past objects, and it is entirely a deluded consciousness.

The mind is not involved in affairs. The mind is neither existent nor non-existent; it is unstained by existence or non-existence. The mind is neither defiled nor pure; it is not sullied by defilement or purity.

Even states such as delusion and enlightenment, or ordinary person and sage, and activities such as walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, are all merely false consciousness—they are not the mind.
The mind is fundamentally unarisen and, even now, does not cease. If one knows that one’s own mind is thus, one knows that it is likewise for all Buddhas. Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:

"The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), for it is free from falsehood. Since the Master [Bodhidharma] transmitted the teachings of the various periods of the Buddha's life to this land, we have not seen their complete collection;
furthermore, the three schools of Tiantai, Xianshou, and Ci'en—representing the natures-and-phenomena (xìngxiàng) traditions—are mutually contradictory.

He then constructed a multi-storied pavilion to host eminent monks who were masters of the three schools of thought. As they engaged in mutual debate, he reached a critical point where their views conflicted;
there, he resolved the matter by means of the essential tenets of the Mind School (*cittamātra*).

Consequently, he compiled sixty sections of profound and secret scriptures, along with three hundred works from the sages and worthies of India and this land, to support the doctrines of the three schools. These were arranged into one hundred fascicles and titled the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Source).

Recorded. Scholars throughout the world transmit and recite it. A monk asked: "Regarding the Mirror of the Source as expounded by the Master, you establish the principle of the Single Mind alone, which is able to encompass immeasurable Dharma-gates. Does this mind contain all phenomena, or does it give rise to all phenomena?
If it gives rise to them, does it arise from itself, arise from another, arise from both together, or arise without a cause?"
The answer is: This mind does not arise from anything, nor is it horizontal; it is neither other nor self. How is this known? If one says it contains all phenomena, that is horizontal.
If one says it gives rise to all phenomena, that is arising from [a cause]. If one says it arises of itself, then how could the mind further give rise to a mind?
If one says it arises from another, then it cannot be self-existent; how much less can there be an "other"? If one says...
If they arise together, then since neither self nor other exists, with what could there be "togetherness"?
If you say they arise without a cause, one should consider that even when a cause is present, arising is not permitted; how much less so when there is no cause? The monk said:

"If it is truly not produced by any of the four natures, then why did the World-Honored One say that the mind-faculty gives rise to mental consciousness, and that the mind is like a worldly painter who leaves nothing undone?"
"It is created from the mind. If this is so, is it not then self-arising? Furthermore, it is said that the mind does not arise in isolation;

it necessarily arises by depending on conditions. When there are conditions, volition arises; when there are no conditions, volition does not arise. Is this not then other-arising? Moreover, it is said:
"The six types of contact, as causes and conditions, give rise to the six types of sensation, whereby all phenomena are acquired. If this is so, is it not then co-arising? Furthermore, it is said:
The twelve links of dependent origination are not created by Buddhas, devas, humans, or asuras; their nature is simply so. One might then ask:

"Does this not mean they arise without a cause? The Master smiled and said: "The Buddhas respond to conditions according to their differences, bending down to accord with the capacities of all beings.

To generate goodness and destroy evil, they lead them into the primary truth (paramārtha-satya). These are the skillful words of the four kinds of *siddhānta*, like using an empty fist [to teach a child]."
"I am merely showing it to a small child; how could there be any real dharma? The monk asked, "In that case, are all dharmas the mind?
He replied, "If they were, then duality would be established. The monk said, "If this is truly so, then is nothing established at all, and is everything 'neither'?
He replied, "To say 'neither' also establishes duality. Have you not heard what the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: 'The true Mañjuśrī is without being Mañjuśrī. If he were to exist...'"
"Is this so? It is indeed two Mañjuśrīs. Yet today, it is not that I am without Mañjuśrī; within this, there truly are no such dual characteristics of 'is' and 'is not.

" The monk asked, "Since there are no dual characteristics, would it be acceptable for the principle to be one? He replied, "Since 'is' and 'is not' already deviate from the Great Principle, 'one' and 'two' likewise turn their backs on the Perfect Teaching.
The monk asked, "How should one apply the mind in order to accord with this principle? He replied, "When both object and wisdom are forgotten."

"How do you explain the 'seal' (mudrā)? The monk said, "In this way, speech and thought are severed; the paths of mind and intellect are cut off. [The Master] said, "This too is but forced speech, turning according to another's intent.
Though one wishes to hide one's form, one has not yet forgotten the traces. The monk asked, "How can one attain the state where both form and traces are forgotten?
[The Master] said, "Fundamentally, there are no traces. How can one speak of forgetting them? The monk said, "I understand now. It is essential..."
It is like a person drinking cold water—their coolness or warmth is known by themselves. You must await the moment of great awakening; then you will spiritually and brilliantly realize it, saying:
"Within this gate of mine, there is neither the principle of delusion nor awakening, nor clarity nor lack of clarity. Letting go completely, as for you, there is not a single thing."
To speak in a thousand ways through mere toil and hardship—this matter cannot be shouldered by anyone who is not of superior capacity or great vessel.
An ancient worthy said: "Throughout the entire world of the ten directions, one cannot find a single person to serve as a companion.

He further said: "There is only this one person who inherits the ancestral seat; there is ultimately no second person. If you have not yet reached this in person, it is in vain that you exhaust your spirit and thoughts. Borrowing...
It is said: "The profound within the profound; the wondrous within the wondrous. These are merely words from among the gates of skillful means intended to assist others in entering [the Way].

When one looks back at them during the time of direct realization within one's own domain, they are all seen as the teachings of Māra—vain and floating minds with many clever views that cannot bring about the fulfillment of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). They are merely the traces of forms and words, arising when literary patterns manifest.
"All of these are attachments to the gates of expedient means; they are delusions regarding the true path. One must let go of oneself from the top of a hundred-foot pole before one can succeed.
A monk said, "I pray you, grant me your final word. He replied, "A conjured person asks a phantom man; an echo answers the sound of a spring.
If you wish to realize my fundamental teaching, it is like a clay ox walking upon the water. Furthermore, he once said to his disciples: "Now, as for..."
The true lineage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is precisely True Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). As soon as one has a place of faith, one is capable of benefiting others.
If we discuss the gate of cultivation and realization, all quarters say that one's merit has not yet equaled that of the various sages;

yet, according to what is permitted within the teachings, even a bodhisattva at the initial stage can know it by analogy, and it is also permitted to reach an understanding through the provisional teachings. First, one enters through faith based on hearing and intellectual understanding; subsequently, with...
In non-thought, there is accord with reality. If one enters the gate of faith, one immediately ascends to the rank of the Patriarch.

Now, taking present-worldly matters as an illustration: among all worlds, there are three ways of knowing—first, through inference; second, through direct perception; and third, through knowledge derived from teaching.
Regarding the first, knowledge through inference: for instance, this present body of outflows experiences dreams every night. What is seen within those dreams is good...
In the face of evil objects, sorrow and joy appear vividly; yet upon awakening, one sleeps peacefully upon the bed—how could these have ever been real?
They are all merely the products of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within a dream. By this analogy, one may know that the affairs of the waking state are all as unreal as those in a dream.
Indeed, the objects of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—are fundamentally the eighth *ālayavijñāna*.

The objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is transformed solely by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). If it is an object of the present, it is the discrimination of the manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

if it is an object of the past or future, it is the conceptualization of the solitary, distracted mental consciousness. Although the objects of dreaming and waking differ, both do not transcend the mental consciousness;
thus, the principle of "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*) is clearly illustrated by this analogy. This is the second point, known through direct experience.

This means that it is clear regarding the object itself and does not depend on establishing a comparison. For instance, when one presently perceives objects such as blue or white, the objects are fundamentally empty of self-nature;
they do not say, "I am blue" or "I am white. All of these are portions of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) together with the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Conceptual discrimination [arises] as to whether something is blue or white; it is through the mind that it is distinguished as "form," and through speech that it is designated as "blue.

All of these are mental verbalizations, falsely established by oneself. Because the six sense objects are insentient, their substance does not establish itself, nor do their names call themselves forth.
Just as it is with a single form, so it is with all phenomena: they all lack intrinsic nature and are entirely mental verbalizations. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are fundamentally...
The world is tranquil, yet people themselves are noisy. Therefore, when the mind arises with intention, the myriad objects all exist; when the mind arises as empty, the myriad objects are all empty.
Thus, emptiness is not empty of itself—it is empty because of the mind. Existence is not existent of itself—it is existent because of the mind.
Since it is neither empty nor existent, there is only consciousness and only mind. If the mind were absent, where would the myriad dharmas find their resting place?
Furthermore, objects of the past have never truly existed; yet, as soon as they are recollected, they suddenly manifest before one. If such thoughts do not arise, the objects do not appear either.
This is something all sentient beings can know through their daily experience, requiring no effort to achieve and needing no cultivation to attain.
Anyone with a mind can verify this for themselves. Thus, the former masters said: "It is like a great root..."

A person who knows that there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) constantly contemplates their own mental verbalization as the object. At the time of this initial contemplation, although they have not yet attained the state of a sage (*ārya*), by partially understanding mental verbalization, they are a bodhisattva.
Regarding the third [category], those who know through the teachings: the *Mahāyāna-sūtra* states, "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only.
This is the fundamental principle manifested, the primary meaning of the definitive teaching. — Master [Hui-chung] (Note: The term "師" at the end indicates the closing signature of the commentary.)
Riding upon the power of his great vows, he served as a patron of the Dharma for China. During fifteen years at Yongming, he ordained one thousand five hundred disciples;
when he entered Mount Tiantai to administer the full precepts, approximately ten thousand people participated. He constantly conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the seven assemblies of followers.

By night he offered food to spirits and ghosts; by dawn he released various living creatures; six times a day he scattered flowers; and throughout the day and night he practiced and maintained his discipline.
For one hundred and eight days, he remained without ceasing through both cold and heat. His reputation spread to foreign lands;

thirty-six monks from Goryeo crossed the sea to inquire about the Way and received the Master’s seal of transmission. The King of that country sent a letter expressing the etiquette due to a gate-disciple.

On the twelfth month of the eighth year of Kaibō, he manifested illness. At the hour of the dragon on the twenty-sixth day, he burned incense and addressed the assembly, then sat in the full lotus posture.
Thus he transformed others. He lived through seventy-two years of the world and sat in meditation for forty-two summers. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Daci Mountain. Hong Juefan said:

"When I first read the *Xingxinglu* (Record of Self-Practice), which records his deeds day by day—one hundred and eight items—I calculated that his physical appearance must have been withered, emaciated, and frail.
Yet when I saw his portrait, he appeared majestic and robust; how virtuous he was!"

In the *Yinji*, it is recorded that Cai Shi used his official salary to release living beings. When he was sentenced to death by beheading, he expressed joy at the moment of execution, saying, "I have saved tens of thousands of lives and am now dying;
what regret could there be in death? The authorities heard this and were struck by its strangeness, so they released him. He subsequently became a monk.
This must have been an account of his practice of releasing life while serving as a local commander; however, neither the *Zhuan* nor the *Denglu* mention his execution.
[The author] says: It is not yet clear upon what basis that book relies.
▲ Chán Master Zhìfēng of Huáyán Monastery on Wǔyún Mountain in Hángzhōu produced foul-smelling blood when he was born; his skin and body were fragrant and pure.
After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he frequently dreamed of ascending Mount Sumeru and beholding three Buddhas seated in a row: first Śākyamuni, then [Maitreya].
They all prostrated at his feet, yet they did not recognize the third honored one, merely gazing upward at him.
Śākyamuni Buddha said to them, "This is the Lion-Moon Buddha (Siṃhacandra), who will serve as Maitreya’s teacher. Only then did they prostrate.

Later, upon reading the Tripitaka, it was found to correspond exactly with the dream. Furthermore, after receiving the Dharma from the National Teacher (Guoshi), one day he entered the Samantabhadra Hall for a banquet.
As he sat, a divine being suddenly appeared and knelt before him. The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a deity who protects the precepts.
The Master said, "I have long-standing karmic transgressions that I have not yet extinguished; are you aware of them? He replied, "What sins does the Master have?
There is but one minor oversight. The Master asked, "What is it? He replied, "Whenever you rinse your bowl, the water is also the property of the donor. Yet, every time the Master pours it out..."
"To discard it would be improper. Having finished speaking, he vanished. From then on, the Master drank all the water used for washing his alms bowl until it was gone.
After doing so for a long time, he consequently developed a spleen ailment, which only recovered after ten years.

Whenever one discards food, drink, saliva, spittle, excrement, urine, or the like, one should snap the fingers and silently recite the mantra, casting them away with a mind of giving. (From the *Denglu*).
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "All you senior monks, you all abandon one spiritual friend to seek another, and everyone claims this follows the model of Sudhana’s southern journey.

But let me ask you, seniors: when Sudhana took his leave of Mañjuśrī and set out for Mount Wonderful Peak to visit the Bhikṣu Meghashvara, why was it that upon arriving at that location, he instead met Meghashvara on a different peak? What is the underlying intent of the teaching here?"
The intent of the Patriarchs is a single expedient means; ultimately, there is no separate principle. If they can clearly realize that, then this [my teaching] will also be manifest.
All you venerable elders gathered here before me now: is this meeting or not meeting? Is this place the Wondrous Peak or a different peak?
If you can depart from here with such understanding, you may be said not to have failed me, and you will always see De-yun.
"O Bhikṣu, have you never for a single moment forsaken [this practice]? Can you still maintain your faith?

In the fourth year of the Kaibao era, the general Ling Chao established a monastery at Wuyun Mountain and invited the Master to reside there. Every time the Master went out with a large fan to beg for money, he would purchase meat to feed the tigers.
The tigers would always come to meet him and carry him back to the mountain on their backs. In the second year of the Yongxi era, he passed away and was interred in a stupa at the monastery.
▲ Chan Master Ba’en Yong’an of Hangzhou passed away in the seventh year of the Kaibao era. As he was bidding farewell to the assembly, a monk asked:
"In the past, the Tathāgata’s True Dharma Eye was personally transmitted to Kāśyapa; I wonder, what is the profound style of our Master?"
"How shall one realize this after a hundred years? The Master said, "Where have you seen Kāśyapa come from?
[The monk] said, "If that is so, then I shall accept it with faith and practice accordingly, never forgetting this principle. The Master said, "The Buddha-Dharma is not a matter of such a principle.
Having spoken, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away. Upon cremation, his tongue remained unburnt, soft and supple like a red lotus flower. It was enshrined.
At the Samantabhadra Bodhimanda, [he met] Chan Master Yu’an of Shangfang at Ruizhu Monastery in Wenzhou. The Master served under Tiantai and studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Upon reaching the passage: "When knowledge and vision establish further knowledge, this is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and vision are without seeing, this is nirvāṇa," the Master then...
He read it by breaking the phrasing, saying: "When knowledge and views are established, that very knowledge is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and views are absent, this is itself nirvana.
Upon hearing this, someone remarked to the Master, "You have broken the phrasing! The Master replied, "This is the point where I attained awakening."

Unchanging throughout his entire life, he was then known as An Lengyan (An of Lengyan). In the spring of the first year of the Zhidao era, as he was about to pass into nirvana, his dharma heir Yunren stood in attendance.
The Master spoke a verse to him, saying: "It is not a matter brought from the mountain peaks; How could it have been transmitted from Mount Kukkutapāda?
Since antiquity, all sages and worthies have been thus; It is not I alone who fashion it for you today. [He then] entrusted [the teaching to him].
Having given these instructions, he bathed his body, changed his robes, and sat peacefully. He ordered the coffin to be carried to the chamber; after a long while, he entered it himself.
After three days, the disciples opened the coffin and beheld the Master lying in the auspicious posture on his right side. The fourfold assembly was overcome with grief and lamentation.
The Master then rose again, ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, and rebuked them with these admonitions: "Whoever opens my coffin again in the future shall not be my true disciple."
Having finished speaking, he entered the coffin once more and passed away.
Huanki remarked, "Master An not only read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* with broken phrasing; even his passing was broken-phrased.
Zen Master Benxian of Ruiluo Temple in Wenzhou went to study under Tiantai. Guided by the dialogue concerning the wind and the banner, he attained awakening.

Later, he resided at Rui鹿 (Mount Rui). His feet never trod upon city walls or market towns, and his hands never handled wealth or silk. He did not provide bedding or furnishings, nor did he wear garments of silk or cocoons.
He observed the midday fast from dawn until dusk, remaining in meditative seclusion throughout the day; from evening until morning, he instructed and exhorted his disciples.

For more than thirty years, his resolve became ever more steadfast. Addressing the assembly, he said: "When I first beheld Tiantai, I attained realization immediately upon hearing his words. Yet, within those thousand days..."

Amidst the four modes of deportment, it was as if an object were obstructing his chest, like dwelling with an enemy. One day, he suddenly attained a sharp realization, as if washing one's face and touching one's own nostrils.
He composed three verses, saying: "It is not the wind or the banner that moves; it is your own mind that moves.
This has been transmitted from of old down to the present day. Henceforth, those who wander like water and clouds who wish to understand: The Patriarch was truly a fine connoisseur."
It is also said: "If you see form and thereby see the mind, when someone comes and questions you, you will find it difficult to answer.

If you seek out principles and speak in many ways, you will have betrayed the three matters of your lifelong practice as a monk. It is also said: "Throughout vast kalpas, it has always been thus. Thus, it is the same as heaven and the same as earth.
Being the same as earth and the same as heaven, what form could it take? What form could it take? There is nothing that is not it."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra proclaims that 'the Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm. Is this truly so?

Now, if the Buddha-body has already filled the Dharma-realm, then in the realms of the Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, humans, devas, asuras, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, and animals, there would be nowhere left to stand. To argue in such a manner is utterly preposterous."

It is commonly said that all phenomena arise as mere manifestations of the mind. Now tell me: are the six objects currently perceived by the five (or rather, six) sense faculties the same as you, or are they separate from you?
If they are the same, why do they not form a single mass? If they are separate, how can it be said that there is only this one mind?
You must apply yourself with great intensity; the Buddha-dharma is no ordinary matter. *Shang* (Part One).
[The Master] ascended the hall and said: "Do you all see the bamboo grove hermitage, the mountains, the waters, the monastery buildings, and the assembly of people?

If you say you see them, then the mind has external dharmas. If you say you do not see them, how can you deny that the bamboo grove hermitage, the mountains, the waters, the monastery buildings, and the assembly of people are vividly present right here?
Do you understand such an instruction? [The Master] ascended the hall and said: "In the teachings of Tiantai..."
It is said that there are three gates: the gate of Mañjuśrī, the gate of Avalokiteśvara, and the gate of Samantabhadra.
Regarding these, the gate of Mañjuśrī is all forms; the gate of Avalokiteśvara is all sounds; and the gate of Samantabhadra is arriving without moving a step.
My way, however, holds that the gate of Mañjuśrī is not all forms; the gate of Avalokiteśvara is not all sounds; and as for the gate of Samantabhadra—what is it?
Do not say that you have set aside the discourse of the Tiantai teachings. For now, I shall retire. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:

"In general, regarding the study of the Way, it is not necessarily the case that studying 'questions' constitutes the study of the Way; it is not necessarily the case that studying 'selections' constitutes the study of the Way; it is not necessarily the case that studying 'substitutes' constitutes the study of the Way;

it is not necessarily the case that studying 'alternatives' constitutes the study of the Way; it is not necessarily the case that studying the 'picking apart' of the sūtras and śāstras constitutes the study of the Way."
To study by means of extraordinary words is not necessarily true study. To grasp at and break down the extraordinary words of the Patriarchs is not necessarily true study.

If you engage in such study, even if you attain mastery in all seven ways and eight directions, if you still lack a point of realization within the Buddha-dharma, you are called a person of "dry wisdom.
Have you not heard the ancient masters say: "Cleverness cannot withstand birth and death"? Dry...
How could wisdom ever escape the wheel of suffering? If you people would study, you must study with true sincerity;

you must investigate while walking, investigate while standing, investigate while sitting, investigate while sleeping, investigate while speaking, and investigate while remaining silent. At all times, during every task you perform, you must investigate.
Incorporate this into all activities. Having already engaged in inquiry during such times as these, tell me:
whom do you inquire about? What words do you inquire about? At this point, you must personally arrive at a state of clarity;
if it is not so, you are called a person of mere haste, and there will be no realization of the ultimate principle. Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an instance: A monk asked Chang [Chanshi]:
"Sha. When Nanquan passed away, where did he go? Sha said, "He became a donkey for the eastern neighbor and a horse for the western neighbor.
The monk said, "I do not understand. Sha said, "If you want to ride him, ride; if you want to dismount, dismount.
The Master said, "If it were a person seeking to transcend the three realms and practice cultivation who heard these words, they would undoubtedly be filled with doubt and alarm."
"Da! Where has Nanquan gone after his passing? "One person said: 'He became a donkey at the eastern house and a horse at the western house. Another understood it by saying:
'A thousand transformations and ten thousand changes do not go beyond the eternal and true. Yet another understood it by saying:
'One must understand how he acts among different species before one can truly grasp these words. Still another understood it by saying: 'The eastern house is Nanquan; the western house is Nanquan.'"
Some understand it by saying, "The young master of the eastern house; the young master of the western house.
Some understand it by saying, "What is the eastern house? What is the western house? Others understand it by braying like a donkey and neighing like a horse.
Some understood it by saying: "What do you call the donkey of the eastern house? What do you call the horse of the western house? Some understood it by saying:
"Since you asked about passing away, the answer lies in the question itself. Some understood it by saying: "He has gone to where the pillar stands exposed."
Some have offered this interpretation: "The one from the eastern house becomes a donkey; the one from the western house becomes a horse. In what way does this diminish Nanquan?

Such interpretations by various schools all find a place of peace within the Buddha-dharma. But when Nanquan passed away, where did he go? [The text says: "The one from the eastern house becomes a donkey;
the one from the western house becomes a horse. Students do not understand this; they simply mount when they wish to mount and dismount when they wish to dismount. This—
This matter does not require many principles to understand. If you see the nature of the Dharma-realm, there is nothing more to do.
Take care. [Ascending the hall: "All of you, when you sleep soundly at night, you are unaware of anything.
Since you are unaware of anything, let me ask you: at that time, did you possess your original nature, or did you not? If you say that at that time..."
There is an original nature. Furthermore, one does not realize that all things are no different from death.

If you say that at that time there was no original nature, yet when sleep suddenly ends and one awakens, one perceives as before; do you understand? One does not realize that all things are no different from death.
He suddenly awoke from sleep and perceived everything as it was before. At such times as these, what is this? If you do not understand, each of you must investigate it for yourselves.
Do not stand idly by when there is nothing to do. In the second month of the first year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, he said to his senior disciple, Ruzhou:
"You may construct a stone niche. On the full moon of the eighth month of autumn, I shall pass away. Ruzhou received the command and completed the work immediately.
When the time arrived, scholars and commoners from near and far rushed to pay their respects and gaze upon him. On that day, he received visitors as usual.
At noon, he sat in the abbot’s quarters, his hands forming the *ratnamudrā* (jewel seal), and asked Dayzhou, "The ancients said: 'Riding on the tiger's head, one strikes the tiger's tail.
As for the matter of the center, what is it? Dayzhou replied, "It is also just like Dayzhou. The Master said, "You ask me. Dayzhou then asked, "Riding on the tiger..."
"Striking the tiger at its head or its tail—what about the matter of the center, Master? The Master replied, "I too cannot bring it forth.
Having said this, he suddenly opened one eye, looked with a faint gaze, and passed away.
Hong Juefan said: "I have always marveled that while the former sages were in their daily lives, their wit and eloquence were inviolable;
yet on their final days, they all withdrew their radiance and extinguished their spirit. Dongshan said, 'My reputation for idleness has already faded.
Linji said, 'Who would have known that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would perish at the hands of this blind donkey? Now Xian also says, 'I too am playing.'"
"Not coming forth. Alas, is there not a profound essential here?
Zen Master Yuanqi of Yandang in Wenzhou was asked by a monk: "The night moon spreads its light; why is there no reflection in the azure pool?
The Master said: "An adept playing with reflections. The monk walked from east to west and stood there. The Master said: "Not only..."
Playing with shadows, and moreover, fearing one’s own head.
▲ Once, while Master Hongshou of Xingjiao Monastery in Hangzhou was working together with National Teacher Huizhong, he attained realization upon hearing a piece of firewood fall.

He composed a verse, saying: "Flung down, it is not another thing; Laid crosswise or lengthwise, it is no mere dust. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth— The entire body of the Dharma King is revealed.
After he had settled there, Wang Gong Sui, the Minister of the Household, once passed by the Master. The Master sat naturally, wrapped in his coarse woolen robe and basking in the sun.
Wang bowed down, and the Master pushed aside his rush mat so that they could sit together on the ground. They conversed with laughter all day long before Wang departed. The gatekeeper... [text ends]

Shan was a preeminent disciple of Ciming; the Master prided himself on having personally seen Ciming and believed that no one in the world could equal him.
