One day, while walking together in the mountains, as their discussion became sharp and incisive, Fashan picked up a piece of tile and placed it upon a flat rock, saying, "If you can utter a turning word regarding this, I will grant that you have personally seen Ciming.

The Master looked left and right, intending to respond; Fashan rebuked him, saying, "To hesitate in thought and let the mechanism of the mind cease—your intellectual consciousness has not yet penetrated through."
"How could I have dreamed of such a thing? The Master was filled with shame and trepidation; he immediately returned to Shishuang.

When Ciming saw him coming, he rebuked him, saying, "A true itinerant monk must know the proper timing. What urgent business is it that you have come here so early, before the summer retreat has ended?
The Master wept and said, "Brother Shan harbors a poisonous heart that ultimately obstructs people; therefore, I have come to see the Master. Ciming suddenly asked, "What is the Buddha?"
Dafangyi said, "Cloudless sky arises above the ridge; the moon exists within the heart of the waves.
Ming opened his eyes wide and shouted, "Your head is white and your teeth are gone, yet you still hold such a view! How will you ever escape birth and death?
Dafangyi was struck with awe and begged for instruction. Ming said, "Ask me. Dafangyi repeated the previous words and questioned him. Ming roared with a shout, "Cloudless!"
"A moon rises upon the ridge; it falls into the heart of the waves. Upon these words, the Master attained great enlightenment.

Later, because the Head Seat was unwell, the Master sent an attendant to inquire after him. In the evening, the Head Seat came in person to offer his thanks. The Master said, "The Dharma-body is unwell."
The Master’s physical body was unwell. Zuo came to inquire after him. The Master said, “Washing a clod of earth in the mud.
Zuo said, “The Master always employs this device. The Master said, “Last night, why did the crown of Śakra, Lord of Devas, fall to the ground?
Zuo had no reply. The Master said, “Clouds rise on the southern mountain; rain falls on the northern mountain,” and then he shouted him out. This was because of the Master.
Huang Guobo asked Elder Baizhang Hua, "Since you are Baizhang, why are you so short and small? Hua replied, "Today is a fine, clear day.
Huang did not grasp the meaning and requested the Master to provide an alternative response. The Master said, "Just ask it again. Huang asked once more.
The Master said, "Walking hand-in-hand along the southern side of Mount Sumeru. Huang stood there reflecting for a moment, then asked, "What is the essential meaning of this?"
"What? the Master asked. Huang said, "A mosquito on an iron ox. Huang then paused in thought and said, "I do not understand.
I beg the Master to explain this for me. The Master said, "Leave your wife and children behind and come;
I will explain it for you. Huang said, "As for the Master himself, can you still travel? The Master said, "At Shanglan Temple, I see off guests a hundred thousand times a day."

The Master said to National Teacher Nan: "In the future, when I am a master of the soup-and-rice (a monastery) at the crossroads, if there is a monk coming from Huangbo, I shall certainly examine him.
National Teacher Nan said, "Why wait for another day? I will act as a monk from Huangbo; you may test me now.
The Master then asked, "Where have you recently come from? He replied, "Huangbo. The Master said, "I have heard it said that at Huangbo..."
"The head is old, yet the heels do not touch the ground. "Is that so? [The Master] asked. The monk said, "From where did you receive this news, Senior?
The Master replied, "Someone has transmitted it to me. Nan-chuan laughed and said, "In fact, it is your own heels that do not touch the ground.
The Master also laughed heartily and departed. Hao-wen asked a monk, "When Lu-tsu saw monks coming to visit him for instruction, why did he simply face the wall?"

He departed. As no one had yet grasped his essential point, he himself composed a verse, saying: "Severing the ten thousand mountains at once, I urge people to eliminate the difficulty of right and wrong.
Recently there has been no news from Chiyang; Indeed, in those days, I did not witness it with my own eyes.

When the Master was about to enter extinction, he manifested illness that was exceedingly severe. He spread straw mats upon the ground and rolled back and forth without ceasing for a moment. Zhe attended him.

The man shed tears and said, "Throughout my life I have reviled the Buddhas and scolded the patriarchs; why do you now act in such a manner? The Master gazed at him intently and rebuked him, saying, "Do you also hold such views?
He then rose and sat in the full lotus position. Calling to his attendant, he had incense burned; as the smoke arose, he passed into nirvana.
▲ Chan Master Zanyuan of Mount Jiang in Jinling was a distant descendant of the Great Being (Mahāsattva). He entered the monastic life at the age of three and became a full monk (*bhikṣu*) at seven.
At fifteen, he began his travels to seek teachers and visited Ciming. Upon seeing him, Ciming said, "Go, go; attend to the stable. The Master then brayed like a donkey.
Ciming remarked, "Truly a vessel of the Dharma," and appointed him as his attendant. There, he assisted with pounding grain and splitting firewood, blending seamlessly into the daily toil.
[He remained there for] ten years. After Ming passed away, he was buried at Shishuang. The Master cultivated [the land] for eight years before departing.
He served Chan Master Xian of Jiangshan as an elder brother. After Xian passed away, the Master succeeded him on the seat. Lord Wang Jinggong associated with the Master like brothers;

he questioned the Master about the intent of the Patriarchs, but the Master did not answer. The Lord pressed him further, and the Master said: "Your Excellency has three obstacles to your *prajñā*. You have come close..."
"The substance of the Way is one. Over successive lifetimes, it may reach a state of pure maturity. The official said, "I wish to hear the explanation of this.
The Master replied, "Your Excellency’s vital energy (*qi*) is robust and great, yet your worldly affinities (*saṃsāra*) are deep.

Possessing such robust and great energy while encountering such deep worldly affinities, you will inevitably take upon yourself the heavy burden of the world and harbor the ambition for universal governance. Since whether you are employed or set aside cannot be determined, your mind has not yet attained tranquility."
With a mind that has not yet attained equanimity, how can one who harbors the ambition to govern the world ever achieve the state where "a single thought encompasses ten thousand years"?
Furthermore, you are prone to anger, yet your studies still cling to mere principles; in the Way, this constitutes the folly of intellectual knowledge. This is the third point.

To regard fame and profit as if shedding one's hair, and to find sweetness in simple austerity like a *dhūta* ascetic—this is what approaches the Way. For now, you should cause the teachings of the Vehicle to flourish.

"It is well. The Duke bowed twice and accepted the instruction. When the Duke’s prestige shook the world, there was no month that passed without news of him. Yet the Master never once opened the letters to look at them.
When the Duke resigned from his government post and his boat arrived at Shitou, he had already entered the monastery by the second watch.

The Master came out to meet him, gave a single bow, and withdrew. The Duke sat with his attendants gathered around him, and guests filled the hall. Looking about, the Duke asked where the Master was. His attendants...
The man replied, "He has been sleeping for a long time. The Duke had built a hut at Dinglin and would frequently travel among the mountains;

whenever he felt a sense of agitation, he would go to the Master and sit facing him in silence until day’s end before departing. The Duke’s younger brother, Pingfu, was by nature bold and unrestrained, yet upon seeing the Master, he was struck with awe and showed him great respect.
He asked about the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, but the Master did not answer. Pingfu pressed him insistently to explain it.
The Master said: "Buddhas and patriarchs are no different from ordinary people. That which makes them different is their ability to guard their own thoughts.
A tree atop a high peak must have a root; its root lies in the tiniest sprout. Water that floods the heavens must have a source; its source lies in a mere trickle.
To stir a thought without cause within the pure and tranquil mind is perilous and precarious—worse even than a tree atop a high peak. It surges forth with vast power."

"It is rampant, exceeding even the floods that reached the heavens; how could it be moved? The Buddhas and Patriarchs transmitted the Dharma to one another, invariably exhorting them with earnestness:
'Guard and uphold it well for yourself. Pingfu asked, 'Does the Buddha-dharma end here? The Master replied, 'The most beautiful is not ornate; the most profound words are not prolix.
Now, ornamentation and prolixity are far removed from the Way, yet the vulgar world employs them. This was like the Duke of Shen’s discourse on governance."
Regarding the laws of the world, it is said that those who govern do not rely on many words, but rather on how they practice them; how much more so, then, for the supramundane Dharma?

Whenever a guest arrived, regardless of their rank, he would exchange no words beyond the customary greetings of "Are you well? or "How are you? He would then close his eyes as if entering meditative absorption.

Once, while he was serving food to the monks, word suddenly came that the kitchen and storehouse were on fire, and the flames had already reached the Chaoyin Hall. The assembly scrambled in panic, spitting out their food.

The Master ate and drank as usual; when he had finished his meal, he asked nothing. On another occasion, while he was outside the city walls, a madman entered the monastery, killed a monk with his own hands, and then committed suicide.
Their corpses lay side by side. Those nearby ran to report this, and armed guards crowded the road. When the Master returned and passed the place where the corpses were, he did not look at them.
He ascended the meditation hall and sat upright; his attendants stood to one side, hoping the Master would issue some instructions.

The Master closed his eyes as he did on ordinary days; [the monk] was ultimately unable to request instruction and departed. The Master upheld the essential points of the school; his pedagogical thrust was swift and sharp.
A monk asked, "What is the meaning of Luzu’s wall-gazing? The Master replied, "The affairs of the abbot are many. [Another] asked:
"What is a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)? The Master said, "A butcher slaughtering oxen and skinning sheep. [The questioner] asked, "Why is it so?
The Master said, "Karma lies within. In the first year of the Yuanyou era, he suddenly said, "I wish to return to Eastern Wu. He hurriedly prepared his departure and soon passed away.
A monk asked Zen Master Daoning Daoquan of Hongzhou, "What is the white ox on the open ground?

The Master placed a pair of fire tongs across the brazier and said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "The head is not lacking, and the tail is not superfluous.
When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the temple steward’s eyebrows and beard fall off? The Master said, "Thieves do not strike those who are already empty-handed."
**The Poor Child’s House** At Tong’an. Seeing a monk pass away, a monk asked, “Since it is Tong’an, why does the sick monk pass away?

The Master said, “Giving alms is not as good as paying back one’s debts. A monk asked, “Dīpaṃkara possessed right view; why did he pick up the flower and then smile? The Master said, “He could no longer restrain his impatience.

A monk asked, “For what reason do the Chan practitioners of the world come forth? The Master said, [“To seek the Way. (Note: The original text ends here with "出," which typically implies "to come forth" or "to emerge.")
"This is not permitted. The Master said, "It is often like this. A monk asked, "The scriptures say that one first realizes that sentient beings are originally Buddhas.
Why, then, are there afflictions and bodhi? The Master said, "Licorice is sweet; yellow bitter gourd is bitter.
[The monk] said, "In that case, they become two things. The Master said, "You understand this quite well. [The monk] asked, "Since it is already..."
“The single true Dharma-realm—why does it have a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions? The Master said, “The roots are deep and the leaves are lush.
[The student] asked, “I wonder, can one ever transcend this? The Master said, “Seeking cleverness and ending up with clumsiness.”
▲ Chan Master Wuzhen of Daowu in Tanzhou addressed the assembly. He cited Dongshan, who said: "On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice;
before the steps of the Buddha Hall, dog excrement falls from the sky. On the tip of the banner pole, a *zhuizi* is being fried;
three monkeys toss coins at night. The Old Monk says it is not so: "A three-faced *lilu* cat treads upon the moon; a pair of white oxen hold [the world] in their hands."
Holding smoke, wearing a crown, a green rabbit stands in the courtyard cypress; a shell-shedding turtle flies up into the heavens.
This old monk’s entanglements have been completely seen through by all of you. The old man Dongshan is truly extraordinary.
Even so, he could only manage three or four steps; he did not even pass the "seven-jump person-jump. Tell me, where does the crux lie?

"Where? Today this old monk, without sparing a single hair on his eyebrows, bestows everything at once. After a long silence, he said: "Excessive caution diminishes one's virtue; silence truly possesses merit. Let the vast ocean change as it may, I shall never speak for you.

[The Master] asked: "What is the meaning? The Master replied: "What place is there? Today this old monk, without sparing a single hair on his eyebrows, bestows everything at once. After a long silence, he said: "Excessive caution diminishes one's virtue; silence truly possesses merit. Let the vast ocean change as it may, I shall never speak for you. [The Master] asked:
"What is constant illumination? He replied, "A Mount Sumeru atop the point of a needle. "What is tranquil illumination? He replied, "The waters of the ocean within one's eyebrows.
"What is primordial illumination? He replied, "Leaping and bounding within one's straw sandals. The questioner withdrew.

The Master said, "Constant illumination, tranquil illumination, and primordial illumination—beneath one's straw sandals, there is constant leaping and bounding. Furthermore, understand this: a Mount Sumeru atop the point of a needle."
The water within his eyebrows was always vast and shimmering. He asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From the Sangha Hall.

The Master asked, "What did the Holy Monk say? The monk stepped forward and said, "I do not presume to inquire further. The Master said, "If you become a donkey for the eastern neighbor, you will become a horse for the western neighbor.
The monk asked, "Where does the fault lie? The Master replied, "Ten thousand li away in Yuzhou. Ascending the hall, he broke the scales and weights. With what [will you measure]?
The weight has been fixed. Set aside the bowl, the spoon, and the chopsticks; with what will you eat?
It would be better to go into a village of three households and cast the divining stalks east and west. If you suddenly hit upon it, you will strip away your nostrils.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Last night the thunder shook the earth; this morning the drizzling rain falls. The parched are moistened, and the myriad things sprout forth. But tell me, what of Jiazhou?"
"How long are the Great Image’s whiskers and beard? Is there anyone who can say?
If you can say it, the Iron Ox of Shanyu is the Bodhisattva Sadāparibhūta. If you cannot say it, Earth-Dweller (Tusu) will pull out your nostrils!
The Master asked a monk, "The beginning was not reached; the end was excessive. As the monk prepared to lift his sitting cloth, the Master pointed and said, "Depart!"
[The Master] set aside his sitting mat. "How would you say it? The monk asked, "From where did the Master obtain this news? The Master struck him.

As the monk prepared to pick up his sitting mat, the Master struck him again, saying, "Blind fellow! The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him once more, saying: *Note: This dialogue is from the *Wumenguan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 19, featuring Master Wuzu Fayan.*
"Sit down and drink some tea. The monk sat down. The Master asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Shishuang. The Master said, "It is no wonder that the master is bedridden with illness.
The head of the monastery asked, "How has your health been lately, Preceptor? The Master replied, "The one who prepares the gruel and rice has lost his strength.
After a long silence, he asked, "Do you understand? The head replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A mouse carries a pestle on its tail."
Several monks arrived for the first time to pay their respects. The Master said, "Are you all monks from Zhejiang?

They replied, "We are monkeys warming themselves by the fire. The Master said, "Why are you jumping about? The monks said, "Today we have had the honor of meeting the Master. The Master said, "I humbly wish you continued prosperity."

The monks remained silent. The Master then struck them. While the Master was in Ciming’s assembly, one day he carried a basket of snails around the monastery, saying, "I am selling snails," and commanded the assembly to offer words of response; none were in accord with the truth.
An elderly monk, seeing him from behind the curtain, looked at the Master with his eyes and then threw himself down and lay there. The Master set down the basket and walked away.

▲ Chan Master Chaoxin of Dinghui Temple in Suzhou asked a monk, "Regarding National Teacher Huizhong’s statement that 'insentient things preach the Dharma,' how do the venerable masters of the South deliberate upon this?
The monk said, "Everywhere it is said that the six sense organs function interchangeably. The Master said, "The scriptures state that there are no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
With what, then, would they function interchangeably? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him across the back with his staff.
Strike. ▲ Zen Master Fang of Jiangshan in Yuezhou was asked by a monk, "What is the Immovable Honored One? The Master said, "Wearing only his cotton robe, he passes through the marketplace.
The monk said, "I do not yet understand. The Master said, "Riding a donkey, he tramples the waves of Lake Dongting. The monk said—
"Passing through the third-level waves, listen exclusively to a single clap of thunder. The Master said, "Stretching out one's hand, one cannot even see one's own palm.

[The student] asked, "Does this allow a student to advance further? The Master said, "Treading upon the ground, one addresses the void. [The student] said, "Beneath the Gate of Thunder, a cloth drum finds it difficult to sound.
The Master said, "Upon an eight-petaled flower ball, there is no need to embroider a red banner. [The student] said, "Thirty years hence, this..."
The story was widely circulated. The Master then struck him.
While he was composing two cases, he added another case below them:
Question: "A rushing torrent crossing a blade; a swift flame passing through the wind. I wonder, does the school of Mount Jiang permit such borrowings?"

[The monk] said, "No. The Master said, "The sky is cold and the days are short; the nights grow even longer. [The monk] said, "A brocade curtain embroidered with mandarin ducks is difficult for travelers to see.
The Master said, "From within the skull, the vital breath surges toward heaven. The monk called out, "Preceptor! The Master said, "The head of a rooster and the tail of a phoenix."
[The Master] said, "People everywhere are washing in the mud. Jiangshan brought it forth and painted it. The Master said, "Jiangshan is acting as a guest today;
I hope you, O Ācārya, will transmit this well. Even so, I shall not let you off. Thereupon, he struck the meditation seat once.
▲ Chan Master Tan of Xingjiao Monastery in Xuanzhou was a silversmith. While sharpening and polishing vessels, he attained awakening and immediately left the household life.
He went to study under Langye, whose teachings and words he suddenly realized. Later, he relied upon Tianyi, who appointed him as the abbot of Xingjiao.
There, the attendant from Xuedou, Shengzong, came forward and asked: "Before the Buddhas appeared in the world, everyone’s nostrils reached the heavens. After they appeared in the world..."
"Why have you been so silent? The Master said, "Before Jizu Peak, the wind is still.
Zong said, "Not yet; speak further. The Master said, "Great snow fills Chang'an. Zong said, "Who understands this meaning? It makes me think of Nanquan.
He then brushed his sleeves and returned to the assembly, refusing to prostrate himself. The Master said, "Xinxiang’s teaching has lost ground today," and he departed.
The Abbot sent someone to invite Zong to come. The Master said, "Just now, you gave a wrong response to a single phrase before this assembly of devas and humans;
why did you not prostrate yourself to cover it over? Zong said, "A great man has gold beneath his knees; how could he be willing to prostrate himself before an eyeless old monk?
The Master said, "I have another phrase for you. Zong then proceeded to explain his previous words until the point where they reached the character "wei" (末).
At the place where the path was being repaired, the Master said, "I have thirty blows of the staff which I entrust to you to strike Xuedou. Zongli bowed.
▲ Chan Master Kequan of Guizong in Jiangzhou was a native of Hanzhou. He studied under Langye and attained sudden enlightenment through a single phrase. Later, he resided at Guizong.
At that time, Guo Gongfu, who served as the Magistrate of Nanchang, was on very close terms with him, yet [he] was [subjected to] the jurisdiction of the Prefectural Governor.

Jùn sent a letter to Gōngfǔ, saying: "My karmic ties in this world still extend for six years. However, as the local governor is pressing me so hard, I must cast off my remaining breaths and take rebirth into your family.
I pray you do not obstruct me. When Gōngfǔ read the letter, he was both surprised and delighted, and he nodded his agreement.
In the middle of the night, his wife saw the Master enter her bedchamber in a dream; she cried out in alarm, "This is not where the Monk comes from!"
Gongfu shook him and questioned him about this; he told him of his dream. Gongfu laughed and took out a book to show him; indeed, she was pregnant. When the child was born, they named him Xuānlǎo.
By the end of his first year, his memory and questioning were as they had been before. At three years of age, Băizūn Duān passed by Gongfu's residence and saw him for the first time.
[Zhaozhou] immediately said, "My nephew has come. Yun said, "How many years have passed since you parted from the Master? Xuan counted back on his fingers and said, "Four years.
Yun asked, "Where did you part? He replied, "At Bailian Village. Yun asked, "What is your proof? He said, "Father and Mother; tomorrow they will invite the Master for a meal.
Suddenly, the sound of a cart being pushed was heard. Yun asked, "What is that outside the gate?"
"What sound? Yun made a gesture with his hand as if pushing a cart. Yun asked, "What about after it has passed? He replied, "Two ruts on level ground.
Indeed, after six circumambulations, he passed away without illness.
▲The Lecturer Zixuan of Changshui in Xiuzhou was a native of Jiaxing in the commandery. From the time he shaved his head, he recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* without ceasing.
Following Master Hongmin, as he reached the passage on the "two aspects of movement and stillness being clearly non-arising," he attained a profound realization.

He said to Dao Min: "Even 'beating the void' or 'striking wood' still falls within the realm of the trap and the snare; even 'raising one's eyes' or 'lifting one's eyebrows' has already become a matter of deliberation.
Only by departing from these two paths can one accord with this principle. Dao Min patted him in confirmation. However, wishing to explore the source of Chan, he knew not where to turn.
Hearing that the Way of Langye was esteemed in his time, he immediately went to his seat. Just as the master was ascending the hall, he stepped forward and asked: "Purity and stillness—"
"Fundamentally thus. How is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Langya Pengleng replied, "Pure and fundamentally thus.
How is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? The Master attained realization and bowed in gratitude, saying, "I wish to serve you with the water vessel and towel.

Langya said to him, "The tradition of your school has not flourished for a long time. You should rouse your resolve to support it and repay the Buddha's kindness; do not treat it as something different."

Zong served as his intermediary. Accordingly, he performed two prostrations to decline the invitation. Later, while residing at Changshui, he received daily instructions from [his master] and addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Way is not attained through words or symbols; Chan is not known through conjecture or deliberation. To realize the meaning and penetrate the essence, there has never been any other method.
For this reason, both schools looked up to him. He once composed commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and other scriptures, which became widely circulated throughout the world.
▲ Chan Master Wenyue of Yunfeng on Mount Nanyue was the son of the Xu family of Nanchang. He was short and small in stature, yet possessed a refined and elegant beauty.

At the age of nineteen, he took up his staff and traveled extensively throughout the Jianghuai region. He would often sit silently beneath the meditation platform, recollecting the words of venerable elders.
He pondered this, saying: "I have heard that Linji stayed at Huangbo for three years, yet Huangbo did not recognize his potential.

The Venerable Master Chen instructed him to inquire about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma; though he asked three times, he was beaten each time, and I have never heard of Huangbo ever patiently instructing him.
It was only upon reaching Dayu that he attained enlightenment and became the founder of the Jiangxi school. The instruction given to me by this venerable elder cannot have been in vain."

"What I wish to hear is different," [the Master] said. He then went to see Dayu (Daoyou). Just as he arrived, Dayu was ascending the seat and said, "Everyone has gathered here to eat some vegetable soup.
If you call it 'a ladle of vegetable soup,' you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow. He then descended from the seat. The Master was greatly startled. That night, he went to the abbot’s quarters.
Dayu asked, "What do you seek by coming here? He replied, "I seek the Dharma of the mind. Dayu said, "The Wheel of Dharma has not yet..."
[The Master] turned [the bowl]. "The Wheel of Food turns first; only later is one born with physical strength and vigor. Why do you not go out to beg for food for the sake of the assembly?
I am occupied with enduring hunger; how have I the leisure to explain Zen to you? The Master did not dare disobey. Not long after, Yuyuan moved to Cuoyan.

Once the Master had completed his formal resignation from Yuyuan, he again went to Cuoyan to request instruction. Cuoyan said, "Do you not think that when you first settled here, the walls of your house were still thin?"

During a period of snow and frost, it was appropriate to beg for charcoal on behalf of the assembly. The Master also accepted this command. When the task was completed, he proceeded to build his own quarters.
Yunyan said, "The Buddha-dharma does not fear being ruined. [The abbot] added, "The Hall Office is short-staffed; I now trouble you with this duty. The Master accepted it without joy.

The Master harbored a lingering resentment toward Master Yan, which did not leave his mind. While he was sitting on the rear platform, the hoops of a wooden bucket suddenly came apart and it fell from the rack.
At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and clearly perceived the full scope of Yan’s teaching methods. He hurriedly put on his *kāṣāya* robe and went up to the dormitory hall.

Yan met him with a smile and said, "Venerable Vinaya Master, rejoice! Your great matter is now completed. The Master bowed twice without uttering a single word and departed. He served under Yan for eight years.
Later, he appeared at Cuiyan. At that time, the head seat led the assembly out to welcome him and asked, "I do not ask about the lineage of Deshan;
what is the great function of Linji? The Master said, "Where have you come from? As the head seat hesitated, the Master struck him.
As the head seat was about to respond, the Master shouted, "Lead the assembly back! The entire assembly was awed and submitted. A monk asked, "The peak mountain..."
"Are there still Buddhadharmas on these precipitous cliffs? The Master said, "There are. [The monk] asked, "What are the Buddhadharmas of the mountain peaks and precipitous cliffs?
The Master said, "A monkey climbing up a tree in reverse."
Miaoxi said, "If a person believes, accepts, and practices this, the task of their lifelong study will be completed.
Once, when [a monk] entered the room, he raised the case of a monk asking Zhaozhou, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? The Master then gave a shout.
The monk was left bewildered. The Master then asked, "What did Zhaozhou say? As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him over the mouth with his whisk.
A monk asked, "The Buddha did not convert his own country; why does the Master return to his hometown to preside over a monastery? The Master said, "I let this one point pass.
The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him. Ascending the hall, he said: "When one has not yet realized that objects are but mind, all manner of conceptual discriminations arise.
Once one realizes that objects are but mind, such discrimination no longer arises. Knowing that all phenomena are but mind, one immediately abandons the external."
"Dust-like appearances. All you virtuous practitioners of dhyāna: consider the great earth, mountains, and rivers; light and darkness, form and emptiness—all phenomena manifest before you.
How can you speak of the principle of 'letting go'? If you understand this clearly, you are still only halfway there;

you must know that above this there is yet another aperture. He then descended from his seat. At the conclusion of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall. A monk asked: "In the West, they used a wax man..."
[The Master asked: "What is the proof? [The monk replied: "Venerable Sir, what is the proof here? The Master said: "An iron ball. [The monk] said:
"There would be no place for me to apply effort. The Master said: "You are merely a follower of words. Ascending the hall, he said: "Cease right now, and cease at once.
If you seek a time of completion, there is no time of completion. If you attempt to understand this matter through words or speculate upon it with the faculty of thought..."
Heaven and earth are vastly different. A true man of great capacity—even if he were to cut through both halves with a single stroke—would still not be in accord.

How much less so when, called away by others, he is smeared with the superficialities of the abbot’s quarters, pointing and lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Treatise of Zhaolun*, discussing sense bases and objects, form and dharmas, the upward and downward paths, existence and non-existence, gain and loss?
At some future time, he will not find his proper place when death comes. Furthermore, in recent times, there is yet another kind of person...

This patriarch has spent twenty or thirty years racing for fame and reputation, doing nothing but instructing others. He merely tells them not to fall into his words and phrases, which he calls "penetrating sound and form.

Passing down from one to another in this manner, they have thereby confused and harmed the religious teachings and deluded later generations. How bitter, how bitter!
In my royal treasury, there is no such sword. If you all continue to practice wandering as you do now, you are merely those who wait by the stump beneath the forest of pure breezes.

The cool hares gradually move away as the spring grass turns green. [He] descended from his seat. On the eighth day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Jiayou era, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly and spoke this verse:

"The Lion of Duan is too lazy; Before he dies, his teeth have already rotted away. At the two times of the day, he accompanies the assembly to the hall; He is always on time for the rice gruel and the meal."
"It is not settled. It would be better to die now; to sleep forever and have no concern for any worldly affairs. First, one need not attend to officials;

[The official] said, "If you have an illness, you shall be exempt from punishment according to the law. The Master replied, "I am fully aware of your kind intention, and thus I did not dare speak falsely;

in truth, I have no illness. He accepted his punishment with equanimity and was sent into internal exile (bianguan) to Zizhou. Those who followed him increased even more. The following winter, by imperial decree, he was released to live at ease.
He built a hermitage on Fuyong Lake and addressed the assembly, saying in brief: "Now, those who leave the household life do so out of weariness with the mundane world..."
Exert yourself to seek liberation from birth and death. Rest the mind and cease discursive thoughts; sever all攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to external conditions).
When encountering sounds or forms, be like flowers growing upon a stone; when seeing profit or fame, be like grit in the eye.

Since beginningless time, you have surely experienced these things many times before—why must you now cling to them with such bitter persistence? If you do not stop now, when will you ever stop? Be able to exhaust [this cycle] this very day.
At that time, what further matter could there be? If one attains a state where the mind is free from affairs, even Buddhas and Patriarchs are but enemies;
all worldly matters naturally become indifferent, and only then does one correspond with that "other side.

Have you not seen how Yinyang refused to see anyone until his death, how Zhaozhou refused to speak of it until his death, how Biandan gathered acorns and chestnuts for food, and how Damei [did likewise]?
Lotus leaves served as clothing. Daozhe of Zhiji wore only paper; Sengxuan Taishangzuo wore only plain cloth.
Shishuang established the "Hall of the Withered Tree" and sat and slept with his disciples solely to cause them to die their own minds.
Touzi had people prepare rice to cook and eat together, desiring that they might realize the matter for themselves. Indeed, the various sages of antiquity have provided such precedents.
"If there were no superior quality, how could one accept it with such ease? O worthy ones, if you investigate this thoroughly, you will certainly not fail others;
if you are unwilling to take responsibility for it, I fear you will find it difficult in the future. He further said:
"Today, as I speak of our lineage to you all, I am already not acting with propriety; how could I go on to ascend the hall, enter the room, and strike the gavel?"
Brandishing the whisk, knitting his brows, and glaring with wide eyes; striking east and shouting west, he was like one suffering a fit of epilepsy.

He did not see that when Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing the wall for nine years at Mount Shaoshi, and that the Second Patriarch went so far as to stand in the snow and cut off his own arm—truly, one could say they endured every hardship.
Yet, Bodhidharma never uttered a single word, and the Second Patriarch never asked a single question.
[The Master] said: "Can one call Bodhidharma 'not acting for others'? Can one call the Second Patriarch 'not seeking a teacher'? He then composed five verses to describe the style of his school.
The first says: "The wondrous song does not depend on the tongue. The verse states: "In every land, in every atom, and in every place he speaks;
where there is no Chan to study, Sudhana studies. Even Śāriputra understands the news; the rain of flowers falls upon the cliff."
The first bird did not carry it away. The second [case] is: "A dead snake suddenly emerges from the grass. The verse says: "Scorched by the sun and blown by the wind, buried within the grass;
Stirred by its poisonous breath, it becomes perverse once more. If one were to pry open its dead mouth in the dark, Chang'an would remain as before, with no people coming or going.
The third is the "Recitation on the Needle and the Dry Bone. The verse says: "To live again from within death is extraordinary; He uses it secretly..."
Each household has its own head. At midnight, the skull chants a single song: "The red flames of the ice-river are yet cool and refreshing.

Fourth is "The Iron Saw and the Three Platforms. The verse says: "It is not a melody of *gong* or *shang*; who can harmonize with it in a single performance? Where can Boya lay his hands? This song has been long since ancient times.
Fifth is "The Uninterrupted Continuity of Past and Present. The verse says: "In the One Dharma, there are originally no ten thousand."

The Dharma is empty; within it, how could there be any realization of perfect penetration? It was thought that the news from Shaolin had been cut off, yet the peach blossoms still smile at the spring breeze.
On the fourteenth day of the fifth month in the eighth year of the Zhenghe era, he requested a brush and wrote this verse:
"I am seventy-six years old; my worldly ties are now exhausted. In life I do not crave heaven, and in death I do not fear hell. Letting go..."
Transversely situated beyond the three realms, he moves freely and spontaneously; what constraints could bind him? After some time, he passed away.
Chan Master Ba’en of Da Hong Mountain in Suizhou was surnamed Liu and hailed from Liyang in Wei. His ancestors were all eminent scholars.

Before reaching the age of twenty, the Master presented a plan for statecraft and was ranked among the highest in the imperial examinations. Later, weary of the mundane world, he petitioned the court to request permission to retire his official cap and girdle.
Fengwei became a monk. The Emperor granted his request, whereupon he devoted himself to the Way of the Patriarchs. Upon reaching Touzi, he realized the essence of the mind before long.

Touzi said, "You are one who has returned; you should protect and uphold it yourself. He was on friendly terms with Zhang Wujin, who once sent a letter inquiring about the essential tenets of the Three Teachings, stating:
"In the third fascicle of the *Qingliang Shu*, it says that the heterodox views of the Western Regions do not go beyond..."

There are four views. The Confucian and Daoist traditions of this region likewise do not transcend these four views. For instance, when Zhuangzi and Laozi reckon "spontaneity" (*ziran*) as the cause capable of producing the myriad things, this is a false cause.
The *I Ching* states that the Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*) gives rise to the two polarities; taking the Supreme Ultimate as the cause is likewise a false cause.
If one claims that "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way" and that it can produce the myriad things, this too is a false cause.

If one reckons that "One" is empty and non-existent, then it would be without cause. Now, I suspect that the "spontaneity" (*ziran*) of Laozi is not the same as the "spontaneity" of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Heavens.
Why do I say this? Laozi said: "Always be without desire to contemplate its subtlety; always have desire to contemplate its boundaries.
When there is no desire, there is constancy; when there are boundaries, one has already entered his Way. This is what is called...

How could there be any talk of "false causes"? The *I Ching* says: "The alternation of one Yin and one Yang is called the Way (*dharma*); the unfathomability of Yin and Yang is called the Spiritual (*shen*).
That which is spiritual describes the wondrous operation of all things; it is quiescent and unmoving, yet when stimulated, it penetrates and brings about the affairs of the world.
Now, you would instead destroy the Way of the transformation of Yin and Yang, labeling it a false cause, and cast aside that which is unfathomable.

"O Divine One, how could there be anything to say? I hope you will provide instructions after reading this paper, so that I may sever the net of doubt. The Master replied: "The schools of the non-Buddhist outsiders in the Western Regions are manifold;
yet, when their essential convergence is examined, they do not go beyond the four views of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence.

These are the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of both existence and non-existence, and the view of neither existence nor non-existence. This is because [they] do not take the one mind as..."

If one speaks of "the Way," then the Way is not possessed by me; therefore, it is called an "external way. If one does not see that all phenomena are themselves the mind, then phenomena will vary according to one's views;

therefore, this is called "false view. For example, if one says they "exist," then with existence comes non-existence. If one says they "do not exist," then with non-existence comes the absence of existence.

When there is both existence and non-existence, views of existence arise in competition; when there is neither existence nor non-existence, views of non-existence then arise. If one says they both exist and do not exist...
The view of neither existence nor non-existence is likewise so. Indeed, if one cannot free oneself from various views, there is no means to clarify one's own mind;

and if there is no means to clarify one's own mind, one cannot know the Right Path. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Regarding the teachings expressed through words and phrases, those of small intelligence falsely discriminate.
Unable to comprehend their own minds, how can they know the Right Path? It further says: "There is..."
To "see" is itself a defilement; this is not yet true seeing. Only by remaining far removed from all views does one thus see the Buddha.

Judging by this, the paths of the heterodox and the orthodox differ precisely because their realizations regarding "seeing" are distinct. Thus, Liang-qiing [Zongmi] noted that while the systems of Zhuangzi and Laozi reckon that the Dao and the Natural Law (*dharmatā*) can give rise to the myriad things, the *Yījīng* states that the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*) gives rise to the two polarities (*liáng yí*), namely the alternating Yin and Yang.

Yang is called the Way (*dharma*). To take the spontaneous Great Ultimate (*tài jí*) as its cause, and to claim that the alternation of one Yin and one Yang constitutes the Way capable of generating the myriad things, is to posit a false cause.
To reckon the One as non-being (*śūnyatā*) is to posit no cause at all. Let us attempt to discuss this: Now, the three realms are but mind;
the myriad conditions are of a single principle. Because the mind arises, phenomena arise; because the mind ceases, phenomena cease. Extending this reasoning broadly...
It encompasses all phenomena yet is not existence; it unifies and synthesizes them, reaching the ultimate state of quiescent extinction yet is not non-existence.
It is neither non-existence nor not non-existence; it is neither existence nor not existence. Once these four attachments have vanished, the hundred negations are thereby dispelled.
Then, natural causality becomes mere sophistry, and both emptiness and reality are equally provisional names. As for what is said:
The Great Ultimate (Tàijí) and Yin and Yang can give birth to the myriad things; their constant non-existence and constant existence constitute the gateway to all wonders.

That Yin and Yang are unfathomable is what is called the boundless spirit. Although the sages established teachings and provided various means for enlightenment, since these differ from the single mind, how could they not be the four views?
How is this made clear? It is because emptiness and non-being constitute the Way (Dào), and the Way is thus non-being. If...
It is spontaneous. Whether it be the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) or the alternation of Yin and Yang as the Way (Dào), the Way is "existence.

That it is eternally non-existent and eternally existent means it is both existence and non-existence. That Yin and Yang are unfathomable means it is neither existence nor non-existence. Some former scholars have said:
That which wondrously transforms all things is called the "Spirit" (shen); thus it is not a thing. To treat every single thing as a [separate] thing is likewise non-existence.
Therefore, the great masters of India all regarded the existence of dharmas external to the mind as heterodox, while taking the principle that "all phenomena are but mind" as the orthodox teaching.
This is because when the mind is taken as the fundamental principle, all views naturally vanish; though their words may differ, they are not sufficient to be considered [contradictory].

They are different. If one holds that there are phenomena external to the mind, then various views will compete to arise; though their words may occasionally coincide, this does not suffice to constitute true agreement.
Nevertheless, the sages of Confucianism and Daoism certainly were not unaware of this truth, yet they maintained it without discussing it.
This was because they did not immediately and explicitly point to the single mind as the source of all phenomena; even if they spoke of it, they did so without further elaboration. For example:
The non-Buddhist practitioners of the western heavens are all great *upāya* bodhisattvas manifesting through transformation.

They display various activities that give rise to diverse views and exhaustively elaborate on heterodox paths, precisely in order to demonstrate that the Buddha-dharma is the true path. This is why it constitutes the Way of the Sage.
Both the exoteric and esoteric teachings are the fundamental principles; they cannot be known through mere intellectual speculation. Thus, an ancient said:

"In the past, before the True Doctrine had arrived, Confucius merely took it as a point of mental focus. Now that we know where the ultimate principle resides, we ought not to continue clinging to provisional teachings.

However, to know that a teaching is provisional does not necessarily mean one truly understands the provisional; only by knowing that the provisional is itself the real does one truly understand the provisional.
This is also the fundamental intent behind the establishment of teachings and the composition of words by the Duke of Zhou, Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi;
it is the beginning and the end of the great causal conditions of a single matter. Thus, the three teachings share one mind, following the same path though by different tracks.
Ultimately, the source of the Way is fundamentally beyond words and speech. Were it not for the Great Being Vimalakīrti, who could have understood this meaning?
▲ Zen Master Yuanzhao Zongben of Huirin Temple in Tokyo was the son of Guan Shi of Wuxi. He visited Tiantai (Tianyi).

[The Master] attained the patience of the realization of the arising of dharmas (*utpatti-dharma-kṣānti*). He did not yet know what dharma was being taught.

Tianqin said, "I am teaching this very dharma. [The Master asked,] "What is this dharma? After a long time, the Master attained enlightenment and slept peacefully; his snoring was so loud that those who heard it were weary of it.

Regarding his name as a student: the Master asked, "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action (*wuwei*). Since it is called 'non-action,' how does one study? Li had no reply.
Emperor Shenzong held the Master in the highest esteem and once summoned him for an audience; the Master remained composed and at ease.

this is what truly constitutes being a companion. Those who heard this were moved without exception. He emerged into the world at Rui Guang Monastery. On the day he ascended the Dharma hall, he gathered the assembly and struck [the gavel].

A drum began to roll upon the ground, spinning and vibrating with a thunderous sound. The assembly was startled and retreated. A monk stepped forward and said, "This is an auspicious omen that the Dharma-thunder of this Master shall shake the earth.
As soon as he finished speaking, the monk vanished from sight. From then on, the Dharma assemblies flourished daily, and the congregation constantly numbered five hundred.
While he resided at Jingci Temple, there was a woman of the Zhang family whose daughter had died; her mother dreamed that the daughter appeared to her because of the retribution for her offenses.
She became a snake. Upon awakening, she was found beneath her coffin; [the Master] took her to his teacher, who preached the Dharma for her and ordered her to be returned to her original place.
Suddenly, a black cicada flew over the coffin and the snake died. The mother made a vow, saying, "If she is truly my daughter, let her enter my cage.
She indeed entered. The Master again preached the Dharma for her. That night, he dreamed that the woman said to him, "Fortunately, we have both been liberated from our two-fold retribution."
On the *jiazi* day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Yuánfú era, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bathed and lay down.
His disciples gathered around him and entreated him, saying, "The Master’s Way pervades the world; today you must not fail to leave behind a verse.

We pray that you will exert yourself to rise and sit upright. The Master gazed at them intently and said, "Fools! Even in my ordinary days I am too lazy to compose verses; why should I do so now on purpose?"
"What is this? [the master asked]. "Usually, when I wish to lie down, I lie down; I cannot sit up specifically for you today. He then took up his brush and wrote in large characters:
"My final affairs are entrusted to Shou-rong. He threw down his brush and lay down feigning sleep. When they shook him, he was already gone. The Master lived in seclusion at Lingyan in Su.
His disciples subsequently enshrined his entire body in a stupa there.
