Though it is said that the rivers and mountains of the southeast are distant, My eyes face the numinous light and the wondrous sound. Wang Xianmu first met [him] at the beginning of the Han dynasty.

He ascended the seat and, looking about him with his eyes, realized his original mind. I have heard it said of Aśvaghoṣa that when the Tathāgata was in the world, the physical forms and minds of sentient beings were particularly sublime;
thus, when he uttered a single perfect sound, all understood according to their own kind.

Now, more than two thousand years have passed since the era of the Buddha, yet he has been able to cause kings, dukes, and nobles to awaken upon hearing his reputation and to perceive the truth upon beholding his countenance.
As for the realization [of this], the power of his great vows and true compassion is such that he is truly without shame in fulfilling his duty to perpetuate the lineage.
He was Chan Master Fashou of Fayun Temple in Dongjing, the son of the Xin family of Qinzhou. His mother dreamed of an old monk seeking lodging;
upon waking, she became pregnant. Previously, there had been an old monk at Maiji Mountain who, together with the Venerable Lu of Yingqian Temple...
Shan once wished to travel abroad from Lu. When he was about to depart, he said to Ru, "In the future, you should seek me out before Zhupu Slope and below Tiechang Ridge.
Later, when Ru heard of this place, a child was born there. He went to visit him, and the child smiled at him.
At the age of three, the boy wished to return with Ru; he subsequently adopted Ru’s surname. At nineteen, he sat for the scriptural examinations and attained full ordination.

He was fully equipped with the study of the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and had profoundly mastered their subtle meanings; yet, he harbored considerable doubts regarding the Chan school.

Upon reaching Huguo Monastery in Suizhou, he read the stele inscription for Chan Master Jingguo, which recorded: "A monk asked Baoci, 'What is Buddha-nature? Baoci replied, 'Who does not possess it?'"

He asked again about the "pure fruit. Daokao replied, "Who possesses it? The monk was thereby enlightened. The Master laughed heartily and said, "How could the Buddha-nature dare to have existence or non-existence?

Moreover, you say you were enlightened because of this [fruit]. The monk felt his spirit pierced by indignation. Hearing that Dharma Master Huai’s dharma assembly was flourishing, he went directly to pay his respects.
Huai looked stern and sat with a grave air; tears fell from the monk's eyes, soaking his robes. At first, the Master found him easy to deal with.
Huishou wiped away his tears and asked, "What sutra does the Master lecture on? The Master replied, "The Avataṃsaka. He asked, "What is the central tenet of the Avataṃsaka?
The Master replied, "The Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is its tenet. He asked, "What is the central tenet of the Dharma-realm? The Master replied, "The mind is its tenet."
He asked, "What is the fundamental principle of the mind? The Master had no reply. Huai said, "A difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth.

You must examine this for yourself; there will surely be an awakening. Later, when the Master heard a monk cite Baizhang’s inquiry to Baoci—asking, "How is it before any emotion has arisen?"—Baoci replied, "Separated.
At that moment, the Master suddenly attained great enlightenment. He resided at Changlu in Zhenzhou, where his assembly numbered over a thousand, including Quan.
When Elder Jiao ascended the seat, the assembly looked at him with smiles, and no one came forward to ask a question.
Master [Wuzu] stepped forward, bowed, and hurriedly asked, "What is the self of Fa-xiu? Jiao smiled and said, "Fa-xiu has an iron face; does he not know his own self? The Master replied:
Those in authority are deluded. The Elder Fú of Chánglú was universally admired for his resolve to uphold the Dharma;

however, his insight into the Way was not clear, as he frequently used the offerings he received to load onto boats and transport them upriver to provide meals for monks. When the Master heard of this, he went to verify whether it was true or false.
Upon arriving, he happened to see Fú ascending the hall and saying: "Entering a desolate field, one does not pick; one may kill with reckless abandon, acting according to the hand."

"Even picking up a blade of grass is still slightly better. He then descended from his seat. The Master was greatly astonished and said, "If this is how one speaks of Chan, who would say they do not understand?
This is what is called 'arising and ceasing' in other quarters. He then went personally to the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects and related the preceding events in detail.
Fengfu again requested further instruction on the words of his teaching. Fengfu proceeded to explain the meaning according to the literal text.

The Master said, "If it were like this, people everywhere would not idly say that you do not understand Chan. Fengfu did not accept this. The Master said, "Please strike the bell to assemble the assembly.
There is the Venerable Fashou here; he will settle this with the Abbot. Fengfu then withdrew. Li Bashi was skilled at painting horses. The Master—

He rebuked him, saying, "You are a scholar-official renowned for your painting skills; moreover, you paint horses hoping others will praise your mastery. That your skill has entered so deeply as to penetrate into the belly of a horse is itself enough to cause alarm.
Thereupon, Li Bashi (Li Gonglin) ceased his brushwork. The Master (Fozhao) urged him to paint an image of Avalokiteśvara to atone for his transgression. Huang鲁直 (Huang Tingjian).
Lu Zhi composed flowery and erotic verses, which the Master also censured and rebuked. Lu Zhi laughed and said, "Will you then place me in the belly of a horse?

The Master replied, "Because you use flowery language to stir up the lustful hearts of people throughout the world, it will not merely be the belly of a horse; you shall surely be reborn in the Avīci Hell.
Huang was struck with awe and repented, subsequently applying himself with vigor to seek the Way. On the eighth month of the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, he passed away.
As he was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, he called for his attendant, changed his robes, and sat upright. He spoke this verse: "When coming, there was nothing; when going, it is empty.
The affairs of south, north, east, and west are all the same. Abiding in the six sense bases provides no benefit.

After the Master had remained silent for a long while, the Chief Administrator Huìdāng stepped forward and said, "Why does the Master not speak the final word? The Master replied, "Take care, take care. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
[He] passed away.
▲ Chan Master Fajian of Yanyen was also a successor of Tianyi. Upon arriving at Ruyi Monastery on Mount Huang, he saw dilapidated houses and broken walls that could not shield against wind and rain.
Fajian sought to reside there; after ten years, a great mansion had been miraculously completed. Then—

He departed and traveled down the Yangtze and Han rivers, crossed the two provinces of Zhejiang, ascended Mount Tiantai, and traveled upstream along the Huai and Wen rivers. Wherever he went, he engaged with sentient beings to benefit them;
he never failed in his speech, nor did he ever fail in his treatment of people. In his later years, he resided at Yanyen Temple in Wuning.

His dwelling consisted of only a few wooden pillars for a thatched roof, and his broken bed lacked a mattress. The Master was exceptionally content with these conditions. The District Magistrate, seeking to rectify the local elite, planned to renovate the temple entirely.

The Master smiled and said, "The Dharma of the donor is fundamentally for the purpose of saving others. To force someone to practice now when they have not yet awakened their resolve is called 'merely performing labor';
it is not called 'Buddhist activity. After ten years of his residence, the monastic community was established, and monks arrived there as if returning home."

The Master and Master Xiu were brothers by affinity; they were well-suited to one another. The monastery where Xiu resided was more magnificent than any in the world, and his preaching of the Dharma was like clouds and rain.
His majestic radiance was such that he could be considered a brother to [the Master], joining wings to soar through the heavens.
Xiu sent a letter inviting the Master, but upon reading it, the Master merely smiled. When a monk asked him the reason for this, the Master smiled and said: "I..."
At first, seeing that Xiu possessed a brilliant spirit, I thought he was someone with whom one could converse; yet now, after this, I know his folly.
A foolish person is precisely one with whom it is impossible to speak. The questioner stared at him for a long time and asked, "Why is that? The Master replied, "It is the law of a bhikṣu."

"One should travel the four directions with a single bowl. Since Xiu was unable to do so, he instead erected a large building at a major crossroads and begged for food from the public to support several hundred idle men. Is this not folly? The Master often said to people:

"All matters follow conditions; this is the Dharma of peace and happiness. In the seventh month of the Jiazi year of the Yuanfeng era, he commanded his disciples to retrieve the administrative documents from the abbot’s quarters and burn them in a fire.
He entrusted the affairs of the monastery to a monk. On the day of Xinwei in the eighth month, he passed away.
▲ The layman Yang Jie of the Ministry of Rites, courtesy name Cigong and style name Wuweizhe, traveled extensively to study under various renowned masters. In his later years, he followed Tianyi.
Tianyi frequently cited the kōan dialogues of the elder Pang, instructing him to investigate and penetrate them to a profound depth. Later, he served as a sacrificial official at Mount Tai.
One day, at the first crowing of the cock, he beheld the sun rising like a platter and suddenly attained great enlightenment. He then took his leave of the elder Pang with this verse:
"When a man grows old, he must marry; when a woman grows old, she must wed. What leisure do I have to further discuss talk of non-arising? He then wrote a letter and sent his robe.
Yi Chen-shan met Chan Master Huifeng Kai. The official asked, "How many years has it been since we parted?
Kai replied, "Seven years. The official asked, "Have you been studying the Way? Have you been practicing Zen? Kai replied, "I do not play these drums and pipes.

The official said, "In that case, you have merely wandered through mountains and waters, accomplishing nothing at all. Kai replied, "It has not been long since we parted, yet you are already so skilled in disparaging others."
Jian laughed heartily. The Master had a verse for departing this world, which said: "Nothing to be attached to, nothing to be abandoned.
Within the vast void, 'zhi-hu-ye-zhe' (the particles of Chinese grammar). Taking what is mistaken as correct, I go to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss."
▲ Chan Master Fajian of Mount Jiang in Jinling was later summoned by imperial decree to reside at Zhikai Chan Temple in the Great State Preceptor’s Monastery.
He asked the assembly, "I am departing for Zhikai and leaving Mount Jiang; which course of action is correct? The assembly remained silent and had no response.

The Master took up his brush and wrote this verse: "Not Buddha, not mind—vain is the deliberation; Obtaining the skin or the marrow—idle is the discussion. At the moment of departure, treasure [this]."
He held his fellow practitioners of Chan in high esteem. Outside his gate, a thousand mountains were bathed in the setting sun. Having finished writing this, he sat upright and passed away.

▲ During the early Xuande era of the Xuanhe period, Emperor Huizong issued an edict throughout the empire requiring all monks and nuns to become *de-shi* (virtuous scholars). Master Daming Mei Fa Ying of Mingzhou [was among those affected].
The Master composed a commentary on the *Laozi* with a free hand and presented it for inspection; the Emperor praised it as excellent.

Others considered this flattery, but the following autumn, when an imperial decree was issued to reinstate the monastic community of monks and nuns throughout the realm, the Master alone remained steadfast in his resolve not to change.

At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, he rose at dawn wearing a birch-bark cap, a crane-feather cloak, holding an ivory tablet, and wearing vermilion shoes. He ordered the drum to be beaten to assemble the congregation and ascended the seat. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The orchid is fragrant..."

Chrysanthemums in spring valleys, chrysanthemums by autumn fences—each thing has its own time for flourishing and withering. Formerly, monks and nuns were abolished so that the Way could be exclusively served;
later, when the Way was leveled and flattery prevailed, monks and nuns were restored. But tell me, how were the forms and appearances of these monks and nuns restored?

Taking up his crown, he showed it to the assembly and said: "My head has always been as round as the moon; though I wear this cap upon my hair, I do not become an immortal. Today I cast it down, and there is nothing more."
He blocked the way, emitting divine light that illuminated the azure sky. He cast it to the ground, changed into monastic robes, and holding up a crane-feather cloak (*he-chang*), he said:
"In days of yore, the Tathāgata traded for a leather garment; for many years I have felt ashamed to wear this crane-feather cloak. Return to me the robe of a manly Tamer of Men;
you should know that this object is not suitable. Having said this, he threw it down. Then, raising his official tablet (*xiang-jian*), he said: "I do so because I find the meditation board too..."
Without cause. Who would have thought he would be deceived by that elephant tablet? Why, today, has he suddenly let it go? An old immortal official retired from office throughout the heavens.
He casts it down. Taking up his vermilion shoes, he says: "Dharmatrāta took one pair back with him; from then on, his descendants walked barefoot.
Borrowing his vermilion shoes to replace the hempen sandals—do not say that the times are difficult and hinder one's hands. To transform into a Peng bird..."

"Meeting [him] is not like meeting the Kun-bird. To paint a tiger and fail to complete it so that it instead resembles a dog—throw it away! He threw down his staff, held it crosswise, and said, "Today this staff has transformed into a dragon;
it shall split apart the myriad layers of Mount Hua. Then, leaning the staff upon his shoulder, he said, "Be careful, O Buddha-mind, true and holy sovereign!
May you well employ the virtue of Yao to revitalize our lineage. He cast down the staff, closed his eyes, and passed away.
▲ The Senior Monk Faming of Kaiyuan Temple in Xingzhou attained the Dharma and returned to his hometown, where he lived in a state of carefree detachment.
He was fond of wine and gambling; when drunk, he would sing several stanzas of Li Yu’s lyrics. People called him the "Drunk Monk.

One day, he said to the assembly of monks, "I shall depart tomorrow morning. Do not go elsewhere. The assembly laughed at him in secret. At dawn the following day, he adjusted his robes and went forth.
Sitting in his seat, he called out loudly, "I am departing! Listen to one verse from me! When the assembly heard this, they rushed to look at him.

The Master then said, "Throughout my life, I have stumbled and tumbled within intoxication; yet even within intoxication, there was discernment. Tonight, when the wine has sobered, where will the willows be?
The morning breeze and the waning moon. Having finished speaking, he became silent. When they shook him, he had already passed away.
▲ The Magistrate Liu Jingchen, whose courtesy name was Xingchao, initially had no faith in the Buddha-dharma.
He encountered Chan Master Donglin Zong, Wu Dizhi, and consequently became intoxicated with the Way of the Patriarchs. Subsequently, he visited Hui-lin Chong.
When a monk asked Xuedou, "What is the original source of all Buddhas? Xuedou replied, "The cold colors of a thousand peaks. Upon hearing these words, [Liu] attained realization.

After more than a year, he served in the administration of Luocheng. He went to visit Guishan Lingyou at Mount Shao; as he was about to leave his post and take his leave of Lingyou, Lingyou said, "With such dedication as you apply yourself, why worry that you will not attain awakening?
Hereafter, should there arise extraordinary states or immeasurable joy, you must quickly collect [your mind].
If you can collect it, you will become a vessel for the Dharma; if you cannot collect it, you may lose your sanity. Not long after, he visited again.
Zhikai asked about the causes and conditions [of his awakening]. Haikong said, "An ancient said, 'The ordinary mind is the Way.
Throughout your twelve periods of the day, you emit light and shake the earth, yet you do not realize it yourself. You seek outwardly, becoming increasingly estranged and distant.
Your doubts grew ever deeper until one night, when you entered the room. Haikong then cited the story of Venerable Prajñātāra responding to King Gopāla regarding the seeing of nature."
The Master asked a question of the Duke, but the Duke was unable to respond. His doubt was profound. Upon returning home, he went to bed; at the fifth watch, he awoke.

While reflecting on the matter, he beheld various extraordinary signs: his inner and outer being became transparently clear, his six sense faculties trembled, and heaven and earth seemed to revolve, like the moon appearing when the clouds part.
Overjoyed beyond measure, he recalled the instructions of Mount Shao and restrained himself. When dawn broke, he hurried to Zhihai.
He informed [Baizhang] of what he had attained, and Baizhang took this as evidence. He then said, "Furthermore, you must be able to put it into practice before you have truly mastered it.

The Master asked, "Do you not require actual cultivation? Baizhang replied in a stern voice, "What kind of matter is this? How can you speak of 'cultivation'? The Master then attained deep realization.
He then composed the "Essay on Clarifying the Way and Admonishing the Confucians" to warn the world, saying:
"Clarifying the Way lies in seeing one's nature. That which I have realized is nothing other than seeing one's nature. As Mencius said:
"The mouth’s desire for flavors, the eyes’ desire for colors, the ears’ desire for sounds, the nose’s desire for odors, and the four limbs’ desire for ease and comfort—these are the nature. Yangzi...
It is said: "Seeing, hearing, speaking, appearance, and thinking are what the nature possesses. One who perceives this can clearly understand the Way.
You should know that the Way is not far from man; man’s relation to the Way is like that of fish to water—they have never for a moment been separated from it.
It is only because they delude themselves and pursue external objects that they follow the Way all their lives without realizing it. The Buddha is called the Great Awakened One; the Confucian...
It is called "prior awakening. This simply means to awaken to this. An ancient person once said: "Throughout past and present, nothing has ever fallen away;
it is clearly right before one's eyes. He also said: "The Great Way is merely right before one's eyes, yet for all its importance, it is difficult to perceive within that very presence.
Furthermore, he said: "Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; morning after morning, one rises together with him."
Rising and sitting, he is always present; speaking and remaining silent, he dwells together with you. If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is simply this voice.
This Buddha’s speech is the most intimate path: when standing, one sees him as if before one’s eyes;
when in a carriage, one sees him leaning upon the crossbar. Looking for him, he seems to be in front; suddenly, he is behind. Seek him to the left.
The above is where one encounters the source. This is the most proximate expression of the Way by the Confucian scholars.
Alas, this Way can only be transmitted through the mind; it does not rely on written words. Thus, when the World-Honored One held up a flower, the wondrous mind was transmitted to Kāśyapa.

When Bodhidharma faced the wall, the essential tenet was entrusted to Huike (Shenguang). Once the six petals had unfolded, the thousand flowers vied in their splendor, branching into schools and establishing lineages.

Schools. Each has its own tradition; thus, some blink their eyes or raise their eyebrows, clench their fists or point their fingers; some strike with staffs or shout, brandish fly-whisks or tap gongs;
some hold tridents or draw bows, roll balls or dance with ceremonial tablets; some drag stones or carry earth, beat drums or blow hair-whisks;
some remain silent or speak a single word, sigh once or smile once—even down to all manner of such expedient means, these are all [the direct transmission].

It is for all people; yet because it is so intimate, many are at a loss as to how to approach it. Those who catch even a fleeting glimpse of it find nothing separating them from it by so much as a hair’s breadth.

Should they hesitate or linger, however, they are separated by ten thousand miles. Those who wish to clarify the Way should not neglect this. Transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, it continues unbroken to this day.
This truly accords with what our Confucian tradition calls "being stirred to indignation without yet expressing it," and "opening the way without opposition."
Thus it is. My own attainment truly lies within this gate. Reflecting upon our own Confucian tradition, we find that this Way has existed there from the beginning.

How excellent were the words of Confucius: "He silently apprehends them and embodies them; he unifies them with a single thread. Therefore, the Way exists in the mere glance of the eye, and its meaning is conveyed by pointing at one's palm.
All such instances accord with the wondrous purport of the Chan school and capture the true pivot beyond formal teaching. However...
The Way of Confucius was transmitted to Zisi, and Zisi transmitted it to Mencius. After Mencius passed away, the transmission was lost;
what has been handed down to the world is merely the written word. Therefore, my study must seek self-realization before it may cease.
Fortunately, one night I attained enlightenment, such that everything seen by my eyes and heard by my ears [was transformed].
Whatever the mind conceives, whatever the mouth speaks, and whatever the hands and feet move—there is nothing that is not wondrous.

Having attained this for a long time, one sees it increasingly manifest before oneself; yet whenever one attempts to impart it to others, they are unable to receive it, and only then does one realize its wondrousness.
Thus, the Way indeed cannot be transmitted through written words. Alas! This Way is transmitted when there is the person [to receive it]; if there is no such person...
Such people have long since vanished. Now that I have encountered one, who else might resemble him?

Whether such a person will exist until the end of my life or not remains unknown. Therefore, I have composed this record, eulogy, song, and discourse to disseminate his story, and have further written this chapter to instruct my disciples.

Huanji said: "If the Signatory could not have a sudden flash of insight amidst the cold colors of the thousand peaks, he would instead bring upon himself the misfortune of joining the ranks of the tailless monkeys, wandering through the cycle of rebirth—how tragic!"
▲ Chan Master Weizheng of Jingtu Monastery in Hangzhou maintained a most rigorous discipline. Vice Minister Jiang Tang was a friend of the Master outside the monastic walls.
One day, Jiang said to the Master, "I have guests gathering tomorrow; I hope you will come to sprinkle them with the nectar of your teaching. The Master gave his word.
The next day, Jiang sent a messenger to invite him, but the Master handed him a verse, saying: "Yesterday..."
I once set a date for today; as I stepped out the door leaning on my staff, I reflected further: "As a monk, it is fitting that I dwell among the crags and valleys.
To be present at a banquet for a state official would be most inappropriate. In the end, he did not go. Someone asked him, "The Master is renowned as a Chan master, yet you do not speak of Chan.
Why is this? The Master replied, "Day and night, the myriad phenomena expound it for me. Language has its limits, but—"
This Dharma is inexhaustible; it is what is called the inexhaustible treasury of creation. Because the Master constantly rode a yellow calf, he was popularly called "Zheng the Yellow Ox.
(Record of Pointing at the Moon, Volume 25)
*The Record of Pointing at the Moon*, Scroll Twenty-Six.
The Thirteenth Generation under the Sixth Patriarch.
Chan Master Huanglong Zuxin Huitang Baojue of Longxing Prefecture was a student in his youth who enjoyed a reputation for excellence.
At the age of nineteen, he became blind. His parents permitted him to leave the household life, whereupon his sight was restored. He studied under Yunfeng Yue for three years;
finding him difficult to deal with due to his stubbornness, the Master informed Yue that he intended to depart. Yue said, "You must go and rely upon Master Huangbo Nan.

Upon arriving at Huangbo, the Master did not achieve great enlightenment for four years. He then took his leave again and went back to Yunfeng, only to find that Yue had passed away. He then settled there.
Shishuang was reading the *Transmission of the Lamp* when he came upon the passage where a monk asked, "What is the bamboo grove of great merit?
Fufu replied, "One stalk, two stalks leaning. The monk said, "I do not understand. Fufu said, "Three stalks, four stalks bent.

At this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment and thoroughly perceived the workings of the two masters. He returned directly to Huangbo; as soon as he unfurled his sitting cloth, Nanquan said, "You have already entered my [Dharma gate]."

[The room] was closed. The Master leaped for joy and said, "The Great Matter has always been like this. Why did the Abbot teach people to 'examine the phrase' and search for it with every possible means?
Nan-pu said, "If I had not caused you to investigate in this manner until you reached a state where the mind has no application," [the matter would not have been realized].
"To see for oneself and to affirm for oneself—that is precisely where I have buried you.
The *Sengbao zhuan* states: "The Master moved with ease and swam through the crowd, remaining submerged among them. From time to time he went to resolve his doubts regarding Yunmen’s sayings.
Nanquan Gong said: 'Once you know it is such a matter, simply let it be. Why do you expend so much effort?'"
The Master said, "It is not so. As long as there is even the slightest doubt remaining, one has not yet reached the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa).

How then could one move with such freedom—'seven strides and eight gallops,' turning heaven and earth? He then visited Cuiyan Zhen, who marveled greatly at him. He stayed in his service for three years, after which Zhen passed away.
He returned to Huangbo, where Master Nan appointed him to share the teaching seat. When Master Nan moved to Huanglong, the Master [followed].
He again visited Master Yue of Letan. Yue had entered the profound through the sutras and śāstras; when he heard of [Huangbo’s] reputation, he sometimes laughed at the Master.

But the Master did not cease his journey, saying: "Is this not like descending from a lofty tree to enter a secluded valley? The Master replied: "He uses the attainment of one who has something to attain to guard what precedes and block what follows;
I use the learning of one beyond study to serve as the central point for the hundred rivers."

The Master was standing with Xia Yigong engaged in conversation when they reached the *Zhao lun* passage concerning how "the myriad things are taken as one's own self" and how "sentient and insentient beings share a single essence.
At that moment, a dog was lying beneath the incense table. The Master struck the dog with his ruler and then struck the incense table, saying:
"The dog has sentience and departs; the incense table lacks sentience and remains still. How can sentience and insentience be one?"
He attained the realization of oneness. Duke Li was unable to respond. The Master said, "As soon as one engages in discursive thought, it becomes a superfluous dharma.
How could one have ever realized that all phenomena are oneself? He once discussed the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* with a monk, saying:

"When thirty-two thousand lion thrones made of precious jewels entered the small room of Vaiśālī, why did they not encounter any obstruction? It was because this was the supernatural power manifested by Vimalakīrti."
Is this to distinguish it from other provisional methods? Indeed, because this Dharma is difficult to believe, these auspicious signs are manifested.
Only those who are able to believe will finally know that what has existed from the beginning is inherently present. Why, then, must one be made to believe immediately? It is said:

if there is no entry through faith, the small will necessarily obstruct the great. Nevertheless, since faith already exists, from where does the Dharma arise? Furthermore, he spoke a verse: The Pavilion.
The moment one gathers the mind before the gate, the door opens without even a snap of the fingers. Since Sudhana departed, there has been no news;

yet outside the gate, spring arrives and the grass grows green of its own accord. The layman Wu Dunfu claimed to have encountered many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and that his own mind-ground was bright and pure.
While casually reading the biography of Deng Yinpeng, he saw that after the master passed away while standing upside down, his robes remained aligned with his body.
It fell off. He suddenly wondered about it, saying, "That transformation was extraordinary and thus unfathomable; why then did the robe also conform to it? He asked the Master about this.
The Master said, "Now your robe is hanging down to the ground; do you still wonder about that? He replied, "I have no further doubts."

The Master smiled and said, "Since you have no doubt about this, then that [other case] was merely a transformation in reverse; the robe also conformed to the body—what cause for doubt could there be?
At these words, Dunfu attained liberation.

In the *Luohu Yayu*, it is recorded that when Peng Qizi, the Governor of Jiujiang, questioned Wu Difu regarding the discernment of this matter, he asked: "When a person approaches the end of their life, is there a final instruction? The Master replied: "There is. Peng asked:
"I wish to hear its explanation. The Master said: "Wait until I am dead, and then I shall explain. Peng rose with increased reverence and said: [The Master then spoke].
"This matter must wait for the Abbot before it can be settled. The Master went to see Chan Master Yu of Fachang. Yu asked, "I have heard that the Abbot has constructed a thatched hall;
is the work already finished? The Master replied, "It is finished. Yu asked, "How many workers were employed? The Master said, "Only a few hundred workers were used.
Yu said indignantly, "A truly fine thatched hall! The Master clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "But first, we must have the whole world [to fill it]."
The Master ascended the hall and said: "If one only clarifies one's own self but does not awaken to what is before one's eyes, this person has eyes but no feet.
If one awakens to what is before one's eyes but does not clarify one's own self, this person has feet but no eyes. Judging by these two types of people..."
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, there is always something harbored within the breast. Since this thing is in the breast, the signs of unease are constantly before one’s eyes.
Once they are before one’s eyes, every movement becomes an obstruction. How can one attain peace and stability? Did not the Patriarch say:
"To grasp it is to lose the proper measure; one will surely enter a deviant path. To let it go naturally, its essence has neither departure nor abiding"?
Huanji said, "What a fine red-tailed carp! A pity it was drowned in a jar of minced vegetables.
On the day Master Nan passed away, the teacher composed a verse, saying: "The time of the ancients' departure is today; Today, as before, they do not come.
Since they do not come now, nor did they go then, White clouds and flowing waters wander in vain. Who?
The scale and the ruler are said to be level; yet within the straight, there is still the curved. Who says that the principles of things are uniform? Planting hemp, one still obtains millet.
Piteous are those people who rush about under heaven; six times six is originally thirty-six.

Hong Juefan said: "The 'poor son' in the Lotus Sutra fell to the ground as soon as he was pursued; when Constantly-Not-Light (Sadāparibhūta) spoke directly to him, he was immediately beaten and reviled.
These two cases are instances of not knowing that within the direct there is the indirect—like planting hemp and harvesting millet."
In his room, the Master constantly raised his fist and asked the monks, "To call it a 'fist' is to encounter resistance;
not to call it a 'fist' is to turn one's back. What would you call it?"
The *Luohu Yayu* states: When the Layman Wujin met Chan Master Doushuai Yue, he attained a realization of the truth.
He then inquired of Yue about the "house style" (*jiafeng*) of Huitang and wished to go there to visit him. Yue said, "This old man is nothing more than a single fist.
Thereupon, [Wujin] secretly sent a letter to Huitang, saying: "The Layman Wujin possesses worldly wisdom and eloquence; he is no match for you, sir."
When the Master delivered his teaching with a single blow of his fist, how could Dao’an have known there was a matter beyond the gates of the School?
Not long after, Wujin traveled to Huanglong and visited Huītáng at Xiyuan. First, he secretly inscribed a verse upon the wall of the hermitage, which read:
"Amidst a mass of chaotic clouds, several peaks rise high; The man of transcendent learning flees here to hide. Alas, the worldly..."

The official learned of his dwelling place. His vanguard gave a shout that scattered the monkeys and apes. He then slowly inquired about the affairs of the Chan school (Zongmen), and [the Master] indeed showed him the "fist" koan.
Wujin silently calculated that it did not exceed what Yue had anticipated; thus, he changed his mind. Thereupon, he composed a verse, saying:
"I have long looked toward the dragon within the Yellow Dragon Mountains; Upon arriving, I see only an old man tending the mountain. One must know that..."
Beyond the point where the fists touch, there is another "single point of the numinous oxhorn" that penetrates all.

When Linyuan was serving as attendant, he sought the theme for Huichang’s portrait, saying: "Three questions were posed to strike back; the profound mechanism transcended the Vulture Peak. A single punch was shown."
"Exposed in his naked body upon the Dragon Peak, he was wealthy and noble when heard of, yet poor when seen.
In his old age, he sings aloud as he returns home in joy; let people call him the 'Mountain-Dwelling Old Man. When Huang Tai-shi Lu-zhi heard this, he laughed and said:
"What Wujin says is like a single point of the mystical rhinoceros horn that penetrates all. This coarse fellow is merely providing ear-holes for empty space."—Lingyuan.
He composed a verse to clear up the matter, stating that this was a case of writing a single character without including the strokes. Alas!

To say that Wujin (Wuzhun Shifan) lacked insight into the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen) is to be called one who possesses the "eye" [of discernment]. Yet, based on the words of others, he misjudged the Master at Heitang;

where, then, was his power of critical appraisal? Although Yue (Foyan Qingyuan) had gained the favor of Wujin and emerged from his gate, he was narrow-minded and envious, causing trouble for the monastic community (Conglin).
This is merely a matter of words. Huànqì said, "Regarding Dōushuì’s description of this old man as 'nothing more than a single fist,' one can say he has wondrously captured his very marrow.
His letter to Huìtáng was a sincere revelation of his heart. Wújìn referred to Huìtáng as "The Old Mountain Dweller," a title of honor surpassing even the ten epithets of a Buddha.
Língyuán composed a verse for him, which was like rowing a boat downstream; Lǔzhí [likewise]...
[The Master] laughed. Because the wind fanned the fire, Zhongwen said such things; even if Doushuai Wujin were to laugh until his nostrils split, how could he ever make Huidang nod in agreement?

Now, with both feet brushing the void, I shall surely become a donkey if not a cow.

He struck a circle with his torch and said, "I shall settle this grievance right here," and he threw the torch, which ignited upon contact. He enshrined the remains in a stupa to the east of the Pujue Stupa.
A Letter to Senior Secretary Han Zonggu on Cultivating the Residual Habits (*vāsanā*) after Awakening, based on the *Guifeng Zhang*.
Yun’ang Zhenjing Chanshi, also known as Baofeng Kewen of Longxing Prefecture, was the son of the Zheng family of Xiafu. He spent the summer retreat at Daming Mountain (Daming Shanzhu).
There he heard the following dialogue cited: A monk asked Yunmen, "Is it true that the Buddha-dharma is like the moon reflected in water? Yunmen replied, "Clear."
There was no way for his doubt to penetrate. The Master then attained understanding. He went to see Huanglong, but it did not accord with him.
He remarked, "I have a fine point; this old fellow does not recognize me. He then went to Xiangcheng to see Master Shun.

Shun asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Huanglong. Shun asked, "What sayings or phrases has Huanglong had recently? The Master said, "Recently, at Huanglong, the Prefecture..."
The Prefecture commissioned the Elder of Huangbo. When the Dragon (the Master) uttered his words, he said: "Reciting hymns on the bell tower; planting vegetables beneath the bedframe.

as for the Buddha-dharma, he has not even dreamed of it yet. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and finally understood Huanglong’s point of application.
When Chusheng was first lecturing at a monastic assembly, he happened to strike the window lattice with his fan, causing it to make a sound. Suddenly, he recalled a passage from the teachings:

"If drums were struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they would be heard in all ten places at once. Because of this, he attained great enlightenment. He informed his original lecturer, who instructed him to go seek out a teacher.

After Qie delivered this statement, he remarked that his teacher had been a novice when he first studied the sūtras and śāstras, yet he had eclipsed the lecture halls of the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang.

While traveling along the Longmen Gorge, he saw a clay statue of a bhikṣu in the corridors of a temple; with its eyes closed as if in meditative absorption, it caused him to suddenly feel a sense of self-disillusionment.

The Master said, "In that case, I, your student, have attained mastery. Huanglong asked, "What about the shoes on your feet?"
He replied, "I obtained it for seven hundred and fifty wen at Mount Lu. Long said, "When did you ever attain mastery?
The Master pointed to his sandals and said, "When have they not been free? Long marveled at this.

One day Long said, "Just now I ordered an attendant to roll up the curtain and asked him, 'What is it like when the curtain is rolled up? He replied, 'It illuminates all under heaven. When I asked him to let the curtain down..."
"How is it at such a time? He replied, "Water cannot flow through. "How is it when one neither rolls up nor lets go?
The attendant was speechless. "What do you say to this? The Master said, "The Abbot must first escort the attendant to the Nirvana Hall before he can succeed.
Long said, "A man from Guansi truly has no head. He then looked toward a monk standing nearby. The Master pointed at him and said, "Even this monk has not yet dreamed of it."
The Dragon laughed heartily.

When the Master first traveled abroad, he was traveling together with two other monks. Upon arriving at Guyin, they met Xue Daitou, who asked, "When three people travel together, there must be one person of wisdom.
What is this 'one person of wisdom'? The two monks were speechless. The Master stepped forward and stood upon his shoulder.
At the sound of his voice, [the Master] let out a shout. Xue raised his fist and assumed a wrestling stance. The Master said, "There is no need for further examination.
Xue dragged his staff and chased him out. Xue then went to see Chan Master Cizhao of Shimen.

When the Master was residing at Dongshan, a monk asked: "The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states that the afflictions of the ground of ignorance are themselves the immovable wisdom of all Buddhas, which all sentient beings inherently possess.

It is only because the essence of this wisdom has no nature and no basis that it cannot realize itself; it realizes itself only by encountering conditions. Now, what are these afflictions of the ground of ignorance?"

"This immediately becomes the Immovable Wisdom (Acalajñāna) of all Buddhas. Its principle is profoundly deep and extremely difficult to comprehend. The Master said, "This is most clear and can be understood.
At that time, a young boy was sweeping the ground; the Master called to him, and as the boy turned his head, the Master pointed at him and said, "That is not the Immovable Wisdom.
He then asked, "What is Buddha-nature? The boy looked left and right, appeared bewildered, and departed.
The Master said: "This is not the affliction of the dwelling-place (bhūmi). If one can realize this, one becomes a Buddha right now. He asked a lecturer:

"When the calamity of fire arises, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all consumed by the flames. Is the world and empty space also destroyed? The lecturer replied: "The scriptures contain explicit teachings on this;
how could there be any reason for it not to be so? The Master said: "Where would you place all these ashes and embers?"
"Where? the lecturer asked. With a dry-mouthed smile, he replied, "I do not know. The Master also smiled and said, "What you have lectured upon is merely the words on paper.
While residing at Guizong, it was just as he was escorting the remains of Master Fayan for cremation. At that time, the rain had recently cleared, and the ground was slippery.
Suddenly, he slipped and fell. The assembly scrambled to support him and help him up. The Master held up a torch and said, "Fayan!"
The cremation. Guizong suffered a fall; he presented this to the assembly, having nothing further to say. Liu Yiweng once studied under Foyin and was quite conceited.
One day, upon seeing the Master, he asked, "For how many years has the Elder been performing plays?
The Master replied, "I am waiting specifically for the actors to arrive. [Liu] said, "I will not enter this community. The Master said, "But what can you do? You are here right now."
In this hall, Liu Ni was acting as the attendant. The Master clapped his hands and said, "Frog Zen; you can only leap once.
Later, while sitting together, Liu pointed to the Master’s robe and asked, "What do you call this? The Master replied, "Zen robes. Liu asked, "What is Zen?"
The Master then shook his sleeves and said, "I cannot shake them off. Liu was speechless. The Master gave him a blow and said, "Your skill is such as this;
how dare you examine an old monk? Langzhong Qian Yi visited the Master. After they had conversed for a long time, Qian went to the latrine.
The Master ordered an attendant to lead him out from the west side. Qian suddenly asked, "Since it is the 'east office' (latrine), why go toward the west?"
"Go," the Master said. "How many people go eastward seeking [the truth]? (Later, Dahui commented on this, saying: "Aha! This was Zhaozhou asking Touzi about 'not being permitted to travel at night;

one must arrive by dawn. Yet even these words are not as good as this one. When the Master went to visit Qian, a mastiff escaped out. The Master avoided it, and Qian said jokingly, "A Chan practitioner who instructs dragons and tigers—do you now fear a dog?
The Master replied instantly, "It is easy to subdue a tiger hiding in a rocky cave; it is difficult to tame a dog that guards its master."
When he arrived at Zhai Long, Qian praised him. Later, when the various monks from Nankang gathered together, Fo Yin arrived last.
The Master asked, "Why have you come so late from Yunju? He replied, "Because I was wearing straw sandals and passed through the belly of Guizong;

that is why I am late. The Master said, "In that case, you have been swallowed by Guizong. He replied, "But how can one not spit it out? The Master said, "If you cannot spit it out, then defecate it."
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "Sengcan the Venerable said: 'If you wish to seek the Buddha-way with the mind, ask empty space;
only then will you emerge from the dust. Now that you are seeking the Buddha-way, what does empty space say to you?
At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master laughed loudly.
The monk asked, "What is there to laugh at? The Master said, "I am laughing at you for generating interpretations based on words. The monk said, "I merely happened to lose the point.
The Master shouted, "Do not prostrate! The monk then returned to the assembly. The Master laughed again and said, "Generating interpretations based on words. A monk asked:
"One person wishes to leave Chang'an; another person wishes to enter Chang'an. I do not know which one comes first.
The Master said, "How many people have been puzzled by this? [The student] said, "Night travel is forbidden. The Master said, "A mosquito piercing an iron ox.
[The student] said, "An old ape cries in the ancient trees atop the mountain; new geese descend upon the level sands at the river crossing. The Master said, "The people of Chang'an..."
[The Master] entered [the room]. "How do you practice? The monk replied, "In spring, Mount Hua is green.
The Master said, "Although this monk is young, he is one with whom it is worth discussing. A monk asked, "Master Yunmen wished to strike down Śākyamuni Buddha with a single blow;
you, Reverend, now wish to bury Yunmen within a heap of refuse. I wonder, Reverend, will there still be any transgression for you?"
The student said, "I allow you to examine it; is there anything [to be found]? The Master said, "Do not be hasty.

The student said, "The Master sits and cuts off Mount Lu; why do you not recognize this statement of mine? The Master said, "Thirty blows! The student said, "Guan. The Master said, "Dian. The student said, "Zha.
The Master said, "I spare you because you act as a street-walker (mendicant). In the Master’s room, he asked a monk, "Is it finished yet? The monk said—
“I have not yet understood,” [the monk] said. The Master asked, “Have you finished eating your porridge? The monk replied, “I have. The Master said, “Then why do you say you have not yet understood?
He asked again, “What is that sound outside the door? The monk replied, “The sound of rain. The Master said, “Then why do you say you have not yet understood?
He asked again, “What is right before you? The monk replied, “A screen. The Master said, “Then why do you say you have not yet understood? He asked again, “Do you understand? The monk replied—
"No," he replied. "Listen to this verse: 'Accomplishing all matters according to conditions, what is lacking in daily life? Everything is simply ordinary; naturally, there is no inversion.
King Shu asked, "In all other sutras, the time and place are invariably indicated at the beginning. Why is it that the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* alone does not do so?
The Master said, "What is expounded here is the foremost vehicle, directly pointing to the daily activities of sentient beings as they manifest."

[The Master] said: "It belongs neither to the present nor to the past; it is simply that this old monk and you, Excellency, now together enter the Great Radiant Treasury (Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha) and sport in samādhi, acting as host and guest to one another.
This has nothing to do with time or place. He asked again: "The Sūtra says, 'All sentient beings have realized perfect enlightenment' (*sarvasattvāḥ pariniṣpanna-bodhim adhigatāḥ*).
Yet Guifeng [Zongmi] takes 'realized' (*zhèng*) to mean 'endowed with' (*jù*), claiming it is a scribal error in the translation. How is this? The Master said: "Perfect enlightenment..."
If [your] argument can be revised, then the *Vimalakīrti* may also be revised. Does the *Vimalakīrti* not say:

"One does not realize enlightenment by extinguishing sensation"? Now, to realize enlightenment without extinguishing the aggregate of sensation is identical in meaning to the realization of universal awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Thus, Guifeng’s statement is incorrect. (Signed: Shu.
The King was greatly delighted, praising him for many days. He addressed the assembly: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are of one body with me.
Feet-head and feet-tail, horizontal and vertical, in every direction. When fire breaks out on the continent of Uttarakuru, it burns the eyebrows of Śakra;
the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea cannot endure the pain and lets loose a thunderbolt that overturns the mountain torrents."
The mountain peaks topple; dark clouds fill the vast sky. At the crossroads, Old Zhao, the "Liao" surname man, starts awake from his drunken stupor, claps his hands, and laughs heartily, saying:
"In the city of Yunchang, there have been few thieves lately. He then picks up his staff and says: "Thieves! Thieves! He ascends the hall.
His trousers have no crotch; his pants have no opening. On his head are three or five pecks of green ash. This is Old Zhaozhou.
"You are young and fond of showing off. Thus it is said: 'In the state of Qing, men of talent are esteemed; in a wealthy household, children are arrogant.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The World-Honored One’s samādhi was unknown to Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa’s samādhi was unknown to Ānanda. For what reason was this so?"

I know. It is simply that there is a profound difference. When the three virtues and six flavors are offered to the Buddha and the Sangha, they are universally provided as offerings to all beings of the Dharma-realm, including humans and devas.
Yet the assembly, including the head seat, remains unaware of this samādhi. Why are they unaware? Because they do not recognize one another face-to-face.
Opening the ticket, unfolding the bowl, picking up the spoon, setting down the chopsticks—the assembly’s samādhi is such that each is unaware of the others.
Why are they unaware? Again, he picks up his staff and holds it crosswise, saying: "I observe the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus.
He strikes the ground with the staff and descends from the seat. Entering the hall, he cites an ancient: "Like a pearl on a platter, it turns of itself without being nudged. Only...
It is like the great assembly opening their bags and spreading out their bowls, picking up spoons and grasping chopsticks;
in all activities performed at any time, why would one need another person to push them before they turn? This extends even to Yunmen’s "moldy cake," Zhaozhou’s "cypress tree," and Deshan’s "staff."
Linji’s shout—what need was there for anyone else to push him over before he turned? It is simply that you people have not awakened and have instead misunderstood.
Furthermore, what does this have to do with Hu-bing, the cypress tree, the staff, or the shout? Have you not seen the Great Master Huineng say:
"If in a single thought you know your own error, your own numinous light will constantly manifest"? [Addressing the assembly: The Buddha-dharma...

These two words are truly difficult for anyone to master. There are those who do not trust in their own Buddha-work, relying instead on a mere semblance of the ancients' influence, upon a semblance of prajñā, upon the realms of what is known, and upon dharma-gates of fixed characteristics.

As soon as they move, they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust, becoming stuck and unable to escape. Or, when students come, it is like using a seal to stamp clay; they pass it down to one another through such imprinting and transmission.
It is only that you have mistaken yourself, and thereby you have also misled others. Under the gate of Dongshan, there is no Buddha-dharma to give to people;
there is only a single sword. To every person who comes, he cuts them off one by one, so that their life-force does not remain and both seeing and hearing are extinguished.
He then meets them before their parents were yet born. Seeing them about to approach, he immediately cuts them off. Thus it is.
Thus, even though a sharp sword may be keen, it does not slay one who is innocent. Is there anyone here who is innocent? Even so, they shall receive thirty blows of the staff.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In the lineage of Dongshan, sometimes we mix mud and water; sometimes we stand like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.
You people of all quarters, if you intend to see Dongshan in the place where he mixes mud and water, Dongshan will not [be found] there."
While you are mixing mud and water, you intend to see Dongshan at the place where "a thousand fathoms stand like a wall.
Yet Dongshan is not to be found at the place where a thousand fathoms stand like a wall. While you are intending to see Dongshan everywhere, Dongshan is not to be found anywhere.
Even if you intend not to see Dongshan, the nose-rope is still in Dongshan’s hand. You intend to fall into a deep sleep.
He also gave a sudden tug on the nose-rope; one could see his eyes flicker, yet he did not recognize him.
It does not matter that you do not recognize Dongshan; it is enough simply to recognize your own self. Addressing the assembly: At the ancient cave of Xinfeng, ten thousand peaks compete to converge;

at the true source of awakening, a thousand forests vie to cluster. This is a preeminent site throughout past and present, where the Buddha-work has flourished for a long time. Therefore, in the past...
Once Master Riwu Ben proclaimed, saying: "There is only the Buddha-bodhi; this is the true place of reliance. He then gave a shout and said:
"If you still go on acting like this, you are stuck right here! O Zen practitioners, as for what the Master said:
If you act in this way, you will immediately be there. But tell me, what is the meaning? Do you know where it lands?
There are many in the monastic communities who discuss this. Some say: "Hearing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma is like giving birth to an enemy;
how much more so to have a place to rely upon? For this reason, they were scrutinized by Master Wuben. Others say: "Wuben simply wants people to cease."
Settle it. Some say that Wuben saw only the sharpness of the chisel’s tip, but did not see the squareness of the chisel’s handle.
To match things in such a way—how could you have even dreamed of those ancients? Since it is not like this, then how is it?
All you Zen practitioners, this great matter must be investigated with meticulous care; one must not be coarse-minded. When practicing Chan, investigate it thoroughly to the very bottom.

Within the Gate of the Patriarchs, there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions; the paths of concealment and manifestation diverge. Only those of great wisdom can clearly perceive them;
from this point downward, their limits cannot be fathomed. Nowadays, most people merely embrace a child who does not cry or strike a perfectly clean ball;

they cast out a boat with its mooring ropes still attached or wash themselves while clinging to a bridge pillar. Both parties are men of stature—who among them lacks their own share? If you can see through this clearly, [you will understand].
He drives away the oxen of the plowman and snatches the food from the mouths of the hungry; yet he enters fire unburned and enters water unsunken. Ascending the hall, [the Master said:
"In the past, there were five hundred arhats who, using their six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), sought to subdue a venomous dragon but could not succeed at all.
Suddenly, a venerable elder arrived from another region. The assembly said to him, 'We have exhausted our spiritual powers, yet we cannot subdue it.'"

"The Venerable One might be able to subdue it. The Venerable One then snapped his fingers once, and the dragon immediately submitted. "O practitioners of dhyāna, based on this, is there a distinction of superiority or inferiority, or not?

If one says there is none, then five hundred people exerted their full supernatural powers and all said they could not do it, yet this Venerable One merely snapped his fingers once and the venomous dragon was subdued.
Since there is indeed a distinction of superiority and inferiority, how can [one say there is no difference]?"

If you have attained clarity regarding this, you become a man of the Way who transcends the ordinary; whether moving or still, coming or going, the five eyes cannot behold you, and the ten powers cannot know you.
You are worthy of receiving offerings from devas and humans, consuming ten thousand taels of gold daily.

If you have not yet attained clarity regarding this, the mountain gate is holding a vegetarian feast today to make offerings to the Arhats; for now, follow the crowd and open your bedding on the long communal beds.
He displayed his alms bowl and descended from the seat.
Huanji said, "If one were to understand this through the parable of Xiangwang obtaining the dark pearl, one would immediately be devoured by a venomous dragon.
He then gave a small informal sermon to the assembly, saying, "Is there anyone else who wishes to ask a question? After a long silence, he said, "I almost let it pass," and then gave a shout.

Again, he raised his whisk and said, "Ya-ya! Throughout the entire world of the ten directions—whether ordinary or holy, monastic or lay, grass or wood—all turn beneath this whisk to become Buddhas and Patriarchs. Without before or after, they are liberated all at once.
Is there anyone who is not liberated? If there were, their life would hang by a thread. Then, clapping his hands, he said, "Know gratitude!"
Such people are few. Regarding this matter, one discusses reality, not illusion. One must investigate with genuine investigation; one must awaken with genuine awakening.
If there is even the slightest bit left unexhausted, one falls entirely into the realm of Māra. Have you not seen the ancient saying: "On level ground there are countless dead;
to pass through the thornbush forest is to be a true adept"? Nowadays, most people merely attain a state where body and mind are stilled.
Extinction. The past and future limits are severed; a single thought-moment passes as ten thousand years. Cease! Rest! It is like an incense burner in an ancient temple—cold and still.

To take this as the ultimate is not yet to know that one is instead obstructed by this sublime state, such that right knowledge and vision cannot manifest, and spiritual powers and radiance cannot be revealed. Or...
There are those who cling to the notion that the ordinary mind is the Way, regarding this as the ultimate principle.

To them, heaven is heaven, earth is earth, mountains are mountains, waters are waters, monastics are monastics, and laypeople are laypeople; the "great month" has thirty days and the "small month" has twenty-nine.
Such people merely cling to grass and lean upon wood, remaining unaware and unconscious, led straight into delusion. Suddenly, when questioned, [they are at a loss].
"You ask, 'How is my hand like the Buddha's hand? and I say, 'It is the Master's hand. You ask, 'How is my foot like a donkey's foot?
and I say, 'It is the Master's foot. Everyone has a place of birth-connection (*jōen*); what is the place of your own birth-connection, Venerable?
You say, 'I am a person of such-and-such a province. What kind of talk is that? Do not misunderstand. In all matters of action and conduct, one must..."
One must simply follow one's ordinary path. Believing it to be secure and certain, one proceeds with the conviction that this is the right way.
Not daring to move even a single step elsewhere for fear of falling into a pit or a ditch, one is like a person born blind traveling for a long time.
With a single staff, not an inch can be abandoned; one grasps it tightly and relies upon it to go forward, depending on it at every step. Day after day...
If the eye of the Way opens wide, you will suddenly realize your former errors. Cast aside the staff, let go with both hands, and the ten directions will be vast and empty.
Moving freely in all eight directions, east, west, south, and north, there is nothing that cannot be; how could you continue to rely solely on the gates of others or follow in their footsteps?
What joy is there in that for yourself? Ultimately, how is it so? Have you not seen Yunmen Daoyuan?
The Way of the Teacher. Yet today, most of the elder monks throughout the world rely on inherited lineages and intellectual learning;

they produce nothing but verbose complications, stamped from printing blocks and cast from molds. If one were to understand clearly for oneself, why not deal with everything as it arises in the moment?
Furthermore, we do not see that the Great Master Linji said, "What I have here is the living meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West," and then...
It is used as soon as it arrives; wherever one stands, everything is true. He does not say, "How was it in the past? How is it now? Nor does he say, "This word is acceptable;
that word is not. "Where is the false? Where is the real? Try to bring forth even a hair’s breadth of a truly real principle for me to see.
This is simply because the person's own eyes are not open; they have no place of their own vision and have been proceeding in this way all along.
Receiving echoes and grasping at shadows, they observe hundreds of taboos, entangling and binding themselves.
Even if one were to speak in such a manner and suddenly perceive things with clear and unimpeded insight, it would still be like staring wide-eyed from within a coffin.
Now, is there anyone who possesses the wisdom of no-teacher and spontaneous wisdom—one who does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? Such a resplendent man of great character—*chi chi*.

"Chattering away! A thousand transformations, ten thousand shifts. Is there anyone who can do so? After a long silence, he said: "If there is none, then watch this old monk ride the mountain behind the altar and leap into all of your eyes."
[The Master] turns his back. Seven ups and eight downs; he has gone off to revile the Buddha and scold the Patriarchs.
He lets out a shout and descends from the seat. *Zongmen Wuku* says: After Chan Master Zhaojue moved from Letan to Huxi, he accepted the invitation of Wang Zichen, the Guanchen.

Following the opening of the hall, all neglected matters were restored. When he ascended the hall for a *xiaocan* (small session of private instruction), there was no [fixed schedule for] entering the room.

The Master said, "This is because [Zhēnjìng] took ordinary, mundane affairs as his illumination and realization, establishing neither cognitive views nor intellectual understanding as the Way.
Furthermore, he did not seek wondrous awakening, yet he took the virtues of all Buddhas and Patriarchs—Deshan, Linji, Cao..."

The Dharma-gate of True and Sudden Enlightenment for Perceiving One's Nature, established by Yunmen, takes as its core principle the teaching from the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* that the mountains, rivers, and great earth are all objects manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind; this is considered the ultimate, transcendent discourse.

This is also a form of establishment [of false views]. To claim that the ancients’ discourse on the profound and their explanations of the wondrous constitute Chan is to misrepresent the former sages and blind the descendants who follow.
Those who have no sinews in their eyes and no blood under their skin follow such precedents in their inverted ways, remaining complacent and unaware—truly pitiable.
