Only then can one truly attain it. Thus, the staff of Deshan and the shout of Linji both lead to the thorough realization of non-arising; they penetrate to the very top and the very bottom, reaching a state of harmonious mastery.
Only when the Great Function manifests before one can one appear and disappear at will. This is intended for those who wish to take up the entire burden with their whole being.
Retreat and guard the great realm of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. Yantou said, "A person who has attained it merely guards a state of leisurely ease;
throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, being without desire and without dependence, they naturally transcend all samādhis. Deshan also said:
You need only ensure that there is no concern within the mind; when there is no concern within the mind, it is empty yet spiritual, still yet illuminating.
If one speaks of beginning and end even to the extent of a hair-tip, it is entirely self-deception. Since this has already been clarified, you must put it into practice.

Simply take a step back; the further you retreat, the clearer it becomes. The more you fail to understand, the more power there is. As soon as a divergent thought arises, or as soon as a deliberate intention is conceived—
Immediately, one must fiercely sever [the continuity of thought] so that it does not persist; then wisdom will shine through with penetrating clarity. With every step, one treads upon solid ground.
How could there be any high or low, hatred or love, opposition or compliance, or any discrimination made therein? The habitual tendencies of ignorance arise and vanish in an instant;
over a long period, they will naturally lack the power to disturb the person. That the ancients used the metaphor of "herding an ox" was indeed true.

What is called "longevity" refers merely to people. To be direct and concise, the most essential point is first to eliminate the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), thereby making one empty, still, tranquil, and harmonious.
Let things proceed spontaneously and freely; as they proceed spontaneously and freely, there is no grasping or rejecting regarding any phenomena (*dharma*).

In every sense-faculty and every object-field, one becomes suddenly liberated in accordance with the moment. Abiding in solitary operation and solitary illumination, the essence of illumination stands alone, such that self and others are one.

It is like this: directly beneath, there is nothing that can be established through illumination. It is like cutting a single strand of silk; with one cut, everything is severed, and one spontaneously understands how to make a living.

Even the view of Buddha and the view of dharmas are not permitted to arise; then the defilements and karmic consciousness will naturally melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress. Furthermore, it is said:
whenever you encounter conditions or meet objects, do not fail to take them up and carry them along—how could it stop at this alone?
This life is all there is. Even if one were to reach the furthest reaches of the future and realize immeasurable holy bodies, these would still not be the place of ultimate rest.
One must simply retreat with single-minded devotion; do not set limits for yourself. To Counselor Han, he said:

"The ancients said, 'To speak ten feet is not as good as to practice one foot. This is because the power of concentration and wisdom turns back karmic conditions; it is precisely for the sake of awakening."

One must be alert, courageous, and resolute; this shall be enjoyed for thousands and hundreds of lifetimes. As for the various kōans of past masters, there is no need to understand them all exhaustively.
If you achieve clarity in one instance, then every instance will be like that. How could its myriad transformations ever alter or change its inherent power and function?
Addressing Old Man Fang Qing, he said: "The breast is empty and vast, not retaining even a hair’s breadth [of conceptualization]."
The hair [of the head] is suddenly void and凝 (stilled); words and thoughts are cut off. One directly accords with the original source, merging into boundlessness.
Only when one spontaneously attains the wondrous wisdom that is inherently present yet non-attainable can one be called "faith reached" and "vision penetrated.
Yet, if there still remains even a trace of subject and object, one falls into the dust of conditions; then, in the end, one has not yet attained it.
Corresponding to the instruction for nuns on the cultivation of the Way: One directly reveals that from the very beginning, the wondrously perfect true mind has been inherently complete.
When encountering objects or conditions, one knows immediately where one’s attachments lie; yet, by merely clinging to this state, one becomes afflicted and unable to emerge from it.
Consequently, one creates a habitual trap, establishing illumination and function upon sensory stimuli and objective circumstances, shouting "Hah! and clapping hands, glaring with eyes wide open.

Eyebrows! This is a case of making a special effort. If you further encounter a master of true substance, he will strip away all such intellectual understanding for you, so that you may directly realize the original state of non-action, non-affair, and no-mind.

Only then will you recognize shame and know when to rest, remaining perpetually in profound stillness; even the Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot find the place where such a one gives rise to a thought, let alone anyone else.
One’s vision may be equal to that of the Buddha, yet there still remains the obstruction of the Buddha-ground.

Although the Great Master, in his dealings with people, did not establish fixed nests or leave behind manifest traces, after a long time his disciples have come to falsely recognize these as such; this too is a nest.

This is because they take what is nestless to be a nest, and what is without manifest traces to be manifest traces. You must reach them so that [these attachments] are exhausted; do not let them sit by the stump waiting for a hare.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of anything to be done. Already, affairs have arisen; ultimately, even Buddhahood is not established—what then can be called a sentient being?
Even Bodhi is not established—what then can be called affliction? Transcending freely and eternally liberated, one receives blessings in accordance with the moment.
If you wish to attain intimacy, first do not seek it. To seek and obtain it is already to fall into intellectual understanding; desist!

When you rest until the state where not a single thought arises, this is precisely "penetrating through" (tòtuō). You do not fall into the dust of sensory emotions, nor do you dwell in conceptual thoughts;

you are suddenly and utterly transcendent. Thus, there is nowhere in the entire world that you are not hidden from; every object and every situation becomes a complete manifestation of great function.
Each and every thing flows forth from the very breast of your own self. As the ancients said, this is called "operating one's own family wealth. Once attained, it is attained forever.
How could there ever be an end to such enjoyment? It is like a great dead man whose breath has already ceased;

having reached the ground of one's own fundamental nature, there is great rest and great repose. Mouth, nose, eyes, and ears have no mutual cognition, and hands, feet, neck, and back do not reach one another.
Thereafter, facing cold ashes and extinguished fires, there is clarity in every aspect; amidst withered waters and rotten stumps, every thing is thus illuminated.
To the attendant Shixin, I say: When not a hundred things occupy the mind, one is perfectly interfused without boundaries, and the entire being is empty and still.
Whatever one does is never subject to doubt; this is called the manifestation of one's original nature. Yet, as soon as even a hair’s breadth of thought arises—
Regarding the view of the head: if you wish to act as a sovereign, you will immediately fall into the realms of the aggregates (*skandhas*).

You will be ensnared by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, by gain and loss, and by right and wrong. Half-drunk and half-awake, you will be unable to settle yourself. To speak according to reality:
it is simply that amidst the clamor and bustle, you are able to maintain control and conduct yourself as if there were not a single thing. Penetrating to the very top and bottom, directly beneath—
Perfectly accomplished, it is utterly devoid of form or appearance; yet it does not abandon effort nor obstruct action.

Whether speaking or remaining silent, whether arising or falling, it is ultimately no other than oneself. Should one perceive even the slightest obstruction, it is entirely a product of deluded thought.

One must simply allow it to be free and unimpeded—like the vast empty sky, like a bright mirror set upon its stand, like the brilliant sun shining in the heavens. Whether moving or still, whether departing or...
Come! It is not obtained from without. Let the teachings be free and at ease; do not be bound by the Dharma, nor seek liberation through the Dharma.
From beginning to end, bring everything into a single whole. Where could there be worldly dharmas apart from the Buddha-dharma?

Where could there be Buddha-dharmas apart from worldly dharmas? Therefore, the Patriarchs point directly to the human mind. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* values the person who is detached [from conceptualization].
The signs are as follows: for example, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, without relying on the power of another, one should thus examine this essential point.
It is well to practice long-term self-retreat and physical investigation so that there may arise a place of true realization and authentic awakening;
this is itself to be constantly and universally attending upon immeasurable and boundless great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). [This was] shown to Layman Liang. Simply let the mind be mindful.

Serene and still. It is precisely in the midst of confusion and turmoil that one should apply effort. When applying this effort, it must penetrate to the very top and bottom without the slightest omission;
it is fully manifested as it is, arising from nowhere else but itself. Only this single great function turns with effortless spontaneity.
What need is there to speak further of worldly truth or Buddha-dharma? They are held equally and identically. As days pass and years deepen, [this realization becomes ever more firm].
Naturally, beneath his heels, it is solid and certain; he is simply a fine elder who has directly realized and certified the truth, like water entering water.
[This was] shown to Imperial Censor Jiang. Whenever I receive scholars and officials, they often say that worldly affairs entangle them so much that they have no leisure to attend to this matter;
they wait until they have somewhat cleared away these distractions before they intend to apply their minds to investigate it. Although these are sincere words, [they are nonetheless a delusion].
They take only worldly toil as their business, bobbing up and sinking down until they are thoroughly matured in a state of worn-out dregs;
they simply call this "mundane affairs. They further wait until they have cast off these worldly conditions before they can enter the Way.

How could that which is called "walking all day long yet never walking, using all day long yet never using" be something other than mundane toil? Is there some separate, great cause apart from such toil?
Is it not so? Little do you realize that upon this great mass of jewels, the light of great jewels is radiated, illuminating heaven and earth.

Yet, failing to reflect and take responsibility for this yourself, you go further to seek it elsewhere, only increasing your toil; how could this be the ultimate essential? If one possesses the great capacity, [it is otherwise].
There is no need to look at the words and phrases of the ancients or their recorded sayings (gong’an). Simply, from the time you rise in the morning, maintain a state of stillness and quiet the mind.
Whenever you are called upon to perform any action, as you perform each and every one, further raise your awareness and examine it closely:
from where does it arise? What kind of thing is this that can produce so much? Once you have penetrated through this amidst the conditions of the mundane world, all things will be resolved.
There are no conditions that are not already thus; what need is there to reject or select?
This very state can transcend all schools and categories, transforming the burning house of the triple world into a pure, unconditioned, and cool Great Place of Practice.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "When a son of the Buddha dwells in this stage, it is the enjoyment of the Buddha; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, he is always therein."

Among these, this one matter—even if the Buddhas of the three periods of time were to appear in the world and guide beings through immeasurable wisdom, insight, and skillful means—would still be limited.
Even if the patriarchs of successive generations and the old masters of the world were to provide hundreds or thousands of questions and answers to uphold it, they too would be limited.
It is better to investigate it beneath one’s own feet. Regarding Wei-yin...
Prior to the King’s arrival, even beyond the kalpa of emptiness, one must have the spirit of a great man to enjoy the treasures of one's own house wherever they may be.
Only then does one possess such strategic resolve; neither relying on the words or instructions of others, nor succumbing to their deception.
From morning until night, with the inhalation not dwelling within the realms of the aggregates and the exhalation not engaging with the myriad conditions—this is the ultimate.
This is the essential point. It is simply because each person has personally turned their back on this matter.
At the gates of the six sense organs, they recognize light and recognize shadows, yet they find no joy; instead, they say, "What can be done? I have doubts.
But tell me, from where do these doubts arise? You also ask why you cannot speak it. It is precisely this very inability to speak it.
What is it? It is because you are unable to turn the light back upon yourself to directly take charge. The Patriarch said:
"Within your own portion, there is such numinous light and such sovereignty. Yet all sentient beings wander through the dust of emotions and cannot attain liberation.
Even if one were to provide various demonstrations regarding this great matter of cause and condition, they would still be [merely] according to their capacity.
The objective realm falls within the dust of the emotions. Do you understand? It is simply that when not a single thought arises, one will have a slight degree of resonance with the truth.
This is the small assembly instruction for the conclusion of the retreat. The Master said: "Gathering the cause to bring forth the fruit; being cautious at the end to protect the beginning.

At this moment, a single segment of causal conditions is fully perfected. The nesting place of the sages and the root-stump of birth and death are shattered by a single blow and severed by a single stroke. If...

This is a work that encompasses all directions; those who have reached the realization of the ultimate return can look upon it and understand its intent. But for those of later generations and beginners, how are they to find their footing?

Consider this: before the distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas was made, prior to the empty kalpa, and on the other side of King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara—was there still the establishment of retreats and the breaking of retreats?
Nevertheless, even if a thousand sages were to appear here, they would have to stare with open eyes and mouths agape.
Setting aside for a moment that realm, consider this very moment: where lamps and candles cast their light upon one another, and men sit or stand in solemn stillness;

where the high is heaven and the thick is earth; where mountains are mountains and waters are waters; where existence is existence and non-existence is non-existence; where long is long and short is short.
At this very moment, are you the same as or different from the time before King Ābhāsvara, beyond the kalpa of emptiness?
If you can be bold and clear within this state, there is no dharma before your eyes and no mind within your breast; looking upward, you do not see the various sages.
Below, one does not see ordinary beings; externally, one does not see any objective realms; internally, one does not see the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind.

Thus, one is able to penetrate and unify with all things. What need is there to speak of establishing or dissolving the retreat? With a single blow of the hammer, the nests of sages and worthies are shattered;
with a single stroke of the sword, the roots of birth and death are severed. Even if Linji, Deshan, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra were to appear—

Even those who are immeasurable and boundless, possessing great liberation and immense majestic power, as numerous as the sands of countless rivers—coming in vast waves—they cannot be extinguished by a single pinch.
But upon what do they rely? "Had he not shot the stone tiger at Lan-tien, he would have nearly killed General Li.
[The Master] addressed the assembly: "Heavenly beings and hell-dwellers, grasses, weeds, humans, and animals—the six classes and four modes of birth."

Whether minute or vast, near or far, there is nothing that is not true. However, because you have not yet penetrated to the very root and foundation, your ordinary thoughts and mental stirrings constantly revolve within the stream of defiled karma and consciousness.
You have never turned the light back to reflect upon yourself; therefore, you suffer in vain through the cycle of birth and death and fail to attain true enjoyment.
Addressing the assembly: At this very moment, it is like letting go of one's hand over a precipice—casting off the body and surrendering one’s life.

Cast aside seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Cast aside bodhi, nirvana, suchness, and liberation. Whether pure or defiled, cast them all away at once, so that the teaching becomes utterly naked and pristine.
Then, spontaneously, upon hearing it once, one will awaken to a thousand things. From this point on, take full responsibility for it directly;
then, turning back to examine the workings of the Buddhas and patriarchs, you will find they are no different from your own self. This is...

Entering the midst of a bustling marketplace, where the four classes of people throng in great numbers, engaging in commerce and trade until the wind whistles and the birds chirp, one perceives that all these are no different from oneself.
Only then does the Buddha become one with sentient beings; afflictions become one with bodhi;
mind becomes one with objects; light becomes one with darkness; right becomes one with wrong—and so on, even unto the thousandfold differences.

Ten thousand distinctions are all one; only then can one churn the long river into butter and curd, transform the great earth into gold, and make it all into a single expanse, yet even "one" does not stand.

Only then will walking be walking, sitting be sitting, putting on clothes be putting on clothes, and eating food be eating food—like a bright mirror set upon its stand: when a Hu comes, a Hu appears; when a Han comes, a Han appears.
Hanxian: "From the very beginning, he makes no calculations, yet manifests perfection wherever he is. He shows himself as a turtle on the courtyard floor;
many see those who are clever, talented, and quick-witted, but their roots are floating and their footing shallow.

They immediately recognize shifts and transformations within words, and taking this to be unsurpassed in the world, they consequently increase the thorns of views, flaunting their abilities and their understanding, and boasting of the sharpness and fluency of their speech, thinking—"
The Buddha-dharma is simply like this. Yet, when it comes to the conditions of sensory realms, one fails to penetrate and transcend them;
because of this, one falters and retreats, which is truly lamentable. Therefore, the ancients truly underwent every kind of demonic temptation and hardship.
Even when their bodies were cut into seven pieces, they did not stir a single thought; their resolve was as firm as iron and stone until they finally transcended birth and death.

It is entirely effortless. Is this not the transcendence of a great man? To Shilong Zhizang: Since the time of the Patriarchs, there has been a commitment solely to the direct transmission and pointing out;
there was no fondness for "carrying water and dragging mud," nor for issuing proclamations or establishing nests to obstruct people.
Indeed, throughout the more than three hundred assemblies of Śākyamuni, he established teachings according to the capacities of his audience and set forth models for the world.
Duan Zhouche said: "Therefore, the final direct and concise approach connects with those of the highest capacity.

Although from the twenty-eighth generation after Kāśyapa, there was little showing of mechanical devices and much manifesting of principles, at the moment of transmission, there was none who did not receive face-to-face guidance—like overturning a banner pole, like casting a needle into a bowl of water, like displaying the mark of the circular halo, or like holding a red banner and grasping the light."
Jian said: "It is like an iron stake. Regarding the verse for transmitting the Dharma: "Dharma broke the five schools; he established a doctrine with the non-Buddhists; the world was at peace;
'I turn over your heaven, you dog'—all these were divine maneuvers of swift agility, beyond the reach of conjecture or deliberation.
It is further said: "The late Master Wuzu was throughout his life solitary and austere, rarely granting approval to anyone; he remained dryly and starkly so."
Standing like a sheer cliff, he relies solely on this one point. He often said of himself: "It is like leaning against Mount Sumeru;
how could I fall into empty gestures or use slick-headed tricks to deceive people? Taking a flavorless iron sorrel-paste ball, he thrusts it right at the student's head, forcing them to chew upon it.
He must wait until the student’s "bottom of the bucket" falls away and they lose all such evil knowledge and views from their breast.
Without being entangled by even a single thread, and having penetrated [the truth] until it is utterly pure, one may then begin the process of forging.
Only then can one withstand blows and kicks; subsequently, one is shown the Vajra King’s Precious Sword.

Having tested whether they are truly capable of practicing and bearing this burden, such that everything is purified until not a single thing remains—where mountains are truly mountains and waters are truly waters—one must further turn toward that other side, where even the net of the thousand sages cannot detain them.

In this state, one accords with the transmission of the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye from one's ancestors; yet, when it comes to its practical application for the sake of sentient beings, one must still drive the plowman’s ox and snatch the food from the hungry man.
When one attains verification through the ten stages of perfection without any leakage, one is truly a practitioner of the Way of this ancestral house.
In the kingdom of Magadha, [Bodhidharma] personally enacted this command; at Shaolin, facing the wall, he fully upheld the orthodox lineage.

Yet, people of the time have fallen into error and confusion, and thus they value remaining silent, believing that there are no seams or gaps and nothing to be grasped—a state of "standing like a wall ten thousand fathoms high.
They fail to realize that this is merely their own fundamental matter; instead, they indulge their intellectual consciousness and calculations, taking this to be a "high view.
This is a great illness. The matter of the ancestral tradition has never been like this. Yantou said: "It is just a tiny bit revealed right before one's eyes. As it is said: "Like..."
The spark from striking flint, the flash of lightning—if you cannot grasp this, do not harbor doubts; this is the place where those of the highest path tread.
Unless one knows that there is something beyond, no one can know it. Zhaozhou’s “Go drink tea,” and Bimoyan holding up his staff.

Xuefeng’s rolling the ball, Heshan’s beating the drum, Juzhi’s single finger, Guizong’s dragging the stone, Xuansha’s “not yet thorough,” Deshan’s staff, and Linji’s shout—all these are ways of penetrating to the very top and bottom, directly cutting through the tangles of entanglement.

These great capacities and great functions differ in a thousand ways and ten thousand variations, yet they all converge in a single source. They can be used to untie the stickiness and remove the bonds for others; yet if one follows [them]...
To provide an explanation: one must immediately grant the fodder of the fundamental portion.

Just as seven *shu* of donkey’s milk will all be dispersed by the addition of a single drop of lion’s milk, if you wish for the transmission to be maintained at your feet in an unbroken and enduring succession, you must not yield to human sentiment and must not allow it to be treated lightly;
only then is it authentic. The final phrase is where one finally reaches the secure barrier. How true!
These words—transcending birth and death and upholding the true command—are entirely this very moment.
Only those who step upon the pivotal bolt at the summit will fully comprehend them. To Li Jiazhong: if you can nurture the fundamental root from within, [you will realize it].
From the point where the Buddhas and Patriarchs directly point it out, one immediately strips off the greasy patchwork robe until one is bare and naked.
One accepts this directly; it does not come from without, nor does it emerge from within. At that very moment, there is vast openness, and one clearly realizes this nature.
What more need be said of the minds of humans and Buddhas? It is like placing a single drop of snow upon a red-hot furnace—how could it remain?
In other realms, there are likewise as many *trāyastriṃśa* heavens. For this reason, this school does not establish written words or phrases;

it is granted only to those of the most superior faculties. Like a whirling wind, a swift thunderclap, a flash of lightning, or a shooting star, they realize the truth in its entirety, severing the root of birth and death, shattering the shell of ignorance, and becoming free of doubt.
They attain immediate and sudden enlightenment, which continues to unfold throughout the twenty-four hours of the day.
All matters and conditions are entirely perfected as supreme, wondrous wisdom. Why, then, rely on loathing clamor to seek stillness, or abandoning that to grasp this?

One is true, and all are true; one is fully realized, and all are fully realized. Addressing the assembly: If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of time and season.
When the time and season arrive, its principle will manifest of itself. If the time and season have not yet arrived, the ground of principle remains [unmanifest].
Before dawn, one’s karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, with no fundamental basis upon which to rely. I venture to ask you, sirs: what season is it right now? Is it the hour of dusk?
Is it the hour of the *xiaocan* (informal discourse)? Is it the hour when one sits or stands with solemn dignity?
Is it the hour of speaking of Chan or speaking of the Way? Is it the hour when the myriad phenomena intermingle?
Do you understand the timing? Is it not the case that the state of mind and the environment are one and the same at this very moment?
If you are so muddled and vague, then I am glad there is no connection between us. Tonight, all of you gentlemen are gathered here for a brief while;
the mountain monk will not begrudge his own eyebrows as he gives a definitive critique of this particular season. It is just like you all sitting here listening to the mountain monk’s drum.
Two pieces of skin are used as a means for the passage of time; this falls squarely within the realm of ordinary sentiment.

You must know that this mountain monk has never uttered a single word, and you have never heard a single phrase. Each of you and this mountain monk possesses a great matter that transcends past and present and is utterly beyond conceptual knowledge and views.
It is pure, naked, and starkly clear; each is unaware of the other, and each is not [to be grasped by] the other.

Arriving, they penetrate sound and form, transcending Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you can take a step back and turn toward yourself, shedding emotional dust and conceptual thoughts, discarding memory and discrimination, and casting off verbal expressions, hearing, seeing, sensing, and knowing, as well as right and wrong, gain and loss—you will suddenly, in this very moment, have a flash of realization.
You will then share the same knowledge and vision, the same speech, and the same actions as the Buddhas of antiquity.

This single essence and characteristic is not only identical to that of all the sages; it is also identical to the ancestral masters of successive generations and the elder monks throughout the world.
Extending downward to the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence—including the vinegar-fly and the midge—there is nothing that is not identical.

It is not deluded by external objects, nor is it disturbed by intellectual understanding. It does not fear birth and death, nor does it crave nirvana. It is expansive and ordinary, conforming to the times.
Spontaneous and effortless—whether in motion or stillness, in action or conduct, everything is nothing other than liberation.

One can transform all objective realms and master all speech. This is not only the case for ordinary people; even among the ancients, there was none who did not enter the Way through this very moment.
Have you not seen how Zhaozhou first studied under Nanquan and awakened to the fact that the ordinary mind is the Way? Later...
When someone came to ask about the meaning of the "coming from the West," Zhaozhou would immediately respond, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
This extended even to his saying, "In Zhenzhou, they grow large radishes," and "In Qingzhou, I made a hempen shirt that weighed seven catties. It was not only Zhaozhou;

Deshan attained this opportune moment when he would strike a person as soon as they entered the gate, and Linji attained this opportune moment when he would shout as soon as they entered the gate. Muzhou...

When the State Governor attained this opportune moment, he immediately said, "I grant you thirty blows for this ready-made public case. This opportune moment was realized upon the single finger of Guizong; it was seen at the place where Niaoke blew on a tuft of cloth. To speak of the essential point: [The text continues with the following: "Even if you were to attain the Way in a single phrase, you would still not avoid the thirty blows. Even if you were to attain the Way in a hundred thousand phrases, you would still not avoid the thirty blows. Why? Because the Way is not in the words. If you seek the Way in the words, you will surely fall into the pit of views. If you do not seek the Way in the words, you will surely fall into the pit of silence. Therefore, the ancients said: 'If you meet a person who knows, do not speak with them; if you meet a person who does not know, do not speak with them either. If you meet a person who knows, speaking with them is like adding frost to snow. If you meet a person who does not know, speaking with them is like pouring water into a deep abyss. Thus, the Way is not in the words. If you wish to see the Way, you must first see the person. If you wish to see the person, you must first see the mind. If you wish to see the mind, you must first see the nature. If you wish to see the nature, you must first see the source. If you can see the source, you will naturally see the nature. If you can see the nature, you will naturally see the mind. If you can see the mind, you will naturally see the person. If you can see the person, you will naturally see the Way. If you can see the Way, you will naturally see the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha, you will naturally see the patriarchs. If you can see the patriarchs, you will naturally see the ancestors. If you can see the ancestors, you will naturally see the Buddhas of the three periods. If you can see the Buddhas of the three periods, you will naturally see all sentient beings. If you can see all sentient beings, you will naturally see yourself. If you can see yourself, you will naturally see the entire world. If you can see the entire world, you will naturally see the Dharma-realm. If you can see the Dharma-realm, you will naturally see the Great Matter. If you can see the Great Matter, you will naturally see the Great Function. If you can see the Great Function, you will naturally see the Great Liberation. If you can see the Great Liberation, you will naturally see the Great Nirvana. If you can see the Great Nirvana, you will naturally see the Great Awakening. If you can see the Great Awakening, you will naturally see the Great Enlightenment. If you can see the Great Enlightenment, you will naturally see the Great Perfection. If you can see the Great Perfection, you will naturally see the Great Sameness. If you can see the Great Sameness, you will naturally see the Great Non-duality. If you can see the Great Non-duality, you will naturally see the Great Oneness. If you can see the Great Oneness, you will naturally see the Great Emptiness. If you can see the Great Emptiness, you will naturally see the Great Stillness. If you can see the Great Stillness, you will naturally see the Great Tranquility. If you can see the Great Tranquility, you will naturally see the Great Peace. If you can see the Great Peace, you will naturally see the Great Bliss. If you can see the Great Bliss, you will naturally see the Great Joy. If you can see the Great Joy, you will naturally see the Great Freedom. If you can see the Great Freedom, you will naturally see the Great Sovereignty. If you can see the Great Sovereignty, you will naturally see the Great Authority. If you can see the Great Authority, you will naturally see the Great Power. If you can see the Great Power, you will naturally see the Great Virtue. If you can see the Great Virtue, you will naturally see the Great Merit. If you can see the Great Merit, you will naturally see the Great Benefit. ▲ Chan Master Jicheng of Jingyin in Dongjing, together with Fazu of Yuanwu, Cishou, and ten great Dharma masters—totaling one thousand monks of both the Chan and Lecture schools—attended a vegetarian feast at the residence of Grand Marshal Chen Liangbi. At that time, Emperor Huizong went there in private to observe.

Among them was one who was an adept of the *Avataṃsaka*, a "tiger among scholars" in the Xianshou school. Addressing the assembly, he asked: "Our Buddha established his teachings ranging from the Small Vehicle up to the Perfect and Sudden.
Only after sweeping away both emptiness and existence to realize the true and eternal, and subsequently being adorned with the myriad virtues, can one be called a Buddha.
I have often heard that in the Chan school, a single shout can transform an ordinary person into a sage. How does this compare with the various sutras?"
The treatise appears to contain contradictions. Now, if a single shout can enter the five teachings of our school, it is considered a correct teaching;

if it cannot so enter, it is considered a false teaching. The various Chan masters looked toward their teacher, who said: "What the Dharma Master has asked is not sufficient for the response of the three great Chan masters.
The Junior Elder of Jingyin may be able to leave the Dharma Master without further doubt. The teacher—
"Summon Shan. Shan responded, "Yes. The Master said: "What the Dharma Master calls the 'Teachings of the Lesser Vehicle of the Dull-Witted' refers to the meaning of existence.
The 'Initial Teachings of the Mahayana' refer to the meaning of emptiness. The 'Ultimate Teachings of the Mahayana' refer to the meaning of neither existence nor emptiness.
The 'Sudden Teachings of the Mahayana' refer to the meaning of being both existent and empty simultaneously. As for the 'Perfect Teachings of the One Vehicle,' they refer to—"
It is the principle that what does not exist exists, and what is not empty is empty.

For instance, my single shout is not only able to penetrate the five teachings, but can also penetrate all fields of craftsmanship, arts, and the hundred schools of thought. The Master then let out a thunderous shout.
The Master asked Shan, "Did you hear it? Shan replied, "I heard it. The Master said, "Since you heard that this one shout was 'existence,' you can enter the Hinayana teaching.
A moment later, he asked Shan again, "Did you hear it? Shan replied, "I did not hear it.

The Master said, "Since you did not hear that the previous shout was 'non-existence,' you can enter the Initial Teaching. He then turned to Shan and said, "When I first gave that one shout, you said..."
"There is. When the sound of the shout has subsided, you again say, "There is not. To say there is not implies that it was originally real; to say there is implies that it is now unreal.
Neither being nor non-being allows one to enter the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao). At the moment I utter a single shout, "being" is not being, for it exists because of non-being.
At the moment there is no shout, "non-being" is not non-being, for it exists because of being. This is precisely being.
It is simply non-existent. One who can enter the Sudden Teaching must know that this single shout of mine does not function as a single shout;

it transcends both existence and non-existence, and both intellectual understanding and emotional attachment are forgotten. When the Way is present, not even a speck of dust can be established; when the Way is absent, it pervades the void horizontally and vertically.
This very single shout enters into hundreds of thousands of millions of shouts, and those hundreds of thousands of millions of shouts enter into this single shout.

Suddenly emerging before the trigger-mechanism, where even a crow’s flight cannot pass. He remained for seven days, his complexion as [vivid as before].
[The Master] Sheng.
▲ Chan Master Anmin of Huazang in Jiankang Prefecture initially gained renown for lecturing on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

He went to visit Yuanwu, who recounted to him the karmic occasion of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant. Zhaozhou commented: "It is like a person writing characters in the dark; the characters..."

Although he had not yet attained realization, his literary brilliance was already manifest. Where was it that this brilliance was manifest? The Master harbored doubts in his mind and went to seek instruction from Master Wuxue.
Wuxue asked, "What sutra do you lecture on, Preceptor? The Master replied, "The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Wuxue said, "In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are 'the seven locations where the mind is sought' and 'the eight returns that distinguish seeing. Ultimately, where does the mind reside? The Master offered many explanations of his understanding, but Wuxue—
In all cases, he was unwilling to accept it. The Master requested further instruction. Baizhang Wuzhu told him to compose a verse on the theme "The Pattern is Already Manifest.

By chance, a monk requested instruction on the *Ten Mysterious Gates of Discourse*. When [the monk] raised the question, "What is the appearance of the Mind-Seal? Wuzhu said in a stern voice, "The pattern is already manifest.
Upon hearing this, the Master attained realization and subsequently sought formal certification. Wuzhu then applied his authentic tongs and hammer to him, and the Master—
[Zhaozhou] was at a loss for words. One day he said to Baizhang Huaiwu, "Master, stop citing these stories; let me speak on them instead. Huaiwu consented.
Zhaozhou said, "When you habitually brandish the mallet or raise the whisk, is that not what is taught in the sutras: 'All phenomena in all worlds'?"
"All these are the wondrous, luminous true mind of bodhi. Wuzhuo laughed and said, "So you have been making your living right here all along?
The Master replied, "When I let out a shout or strike the meditation seat, is that not 'turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature,' whereby that nature achieves the unsurpassed Way?
Wuzhuo said, "Have you not seen it stated in the sutras that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks? The Master [nodded].

Upon hearing these words, he was suddenly relieved (according to the Luohu edition: "he was struck with awe and had no words to respond"). Having awakened, he left Sichuan and resided at Jia Shan, where the Master attended him. During a night assembly, the Master said:
Wu asked a monk who had questioned Yantou, "How is it when the ancient sail has not yet been hoisted? Yantou replied, "The donkey in the back garden is eating grass.
The Master did not understand and sought a definitive resolution. Wu said, "Ask me. The Master repeated the previous dialogue, and Wu said, "The cypress tree in the courtyard.
At that moment, the Master attained complete clarity and said to Wu, "As the ancients said, 'It is like a single drop falling into a vast abyss. It was indeed extraordinary.
Not knowing that the great ocean had been cast into a single drop, Wuguang laughed and said, "What can be done with this fellow?
Not long after, he was ordered to share the seat [with the Master]. Later, he went to visit Foguan. Foguan asked, "Foguo has a phrase that he never casually spoke to others;
has he ever spoken it to you? The Master replied, "Shut that dog's mouth! Foguan shouted, "That is not the principle! The Master—
[Zhaozhou] said, "No one has snatched away your bag of tea and salt; why do you cry out? Yanjian said, "If Foguo had not spoken for you, I would have spoken for you.
The Master said, "When you have doubts, O Monk, leave the monastery and go elsewhere to study. Yanjian laughed loudly.

▲ Chan Master Daoyuan of Zhaojue in Chengdu went to visit Daobei Dao. While contemplating the words, "Vast emptiness—no sage," he suddenly burst into laughter and said, "Bodhidharma has been here all along.
Daobei praised him. He subsequently went to study under Fojian and Foyan, both of whom recognized his potential.
Next, he visited Yuanwu at Jingshan; however, Yuanwu did not approve of him. When Yuanwu moved to Yunmen...
He lived there and followed the Master. Although he had attained a degree of faith and entry, he remained suspicious because he felt that something obstructing his chest had not yet been removed.

Once, when Yuanwu asked the assembly of disciples, "When birth and death arrive, what will you do? a monk replied, "The incense altar laughs at the Abbot. Yuanwu then asked the Master, "What about you?
The Master said, "The grass bandit has been utterly defeated. Yuanwu said, "If someone were to ask you this, how would you respond?"
As the Master was about to answer, Huineng (Wu) spoke with overbearing arrogance, saying, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. At that moment, the Master attained complete realization.

Huineng struck him with his fist, and the Master clapped his hands and laughed loudly. Huineng asked, "What did you see that you act like this? The Master replied, "I have not yet repaid the blow of your poisonous fist."
He did not forget [his realization] even through the kalpa of death; his awakening returned him to the clarity of enlightenment (*zhāojué*).
He was appointed as the head of the assembly. When Chan Master Fóxìng Fǎtài of Dàméi in Tánzhōu resided at Jiāngshān under Yuǎnwù, the Master served as the *zuòyuán* (head of the assembly).
There was a monk named Zhòng'ān who came to visit Yuǎnwù and questioned the Master; he subsequently received the essential instruction. When the Master later resided at Dèishān...
He sent An to Mount Jiangshan to deliver a letter of succession to Wuzhuo. At that time, Wuzhuo was sitting in his study. An approached him, holding the letter.
Wuzhuo said, "You have traveled a thousand miles to reach me; you have not disgraced our ancestral tradition. The public case is already established—how do you communicate it?
An replied, "Presented face-to-face, there is no further evasion. Wuzhuo said, "This is from Deshan; which one is yours?"
Xuansha sent the letter. Baizhang An said, "How could there be a second person? Wuzhuo Wu said, "What about the one behind you? An then passed the letter to him.
Wuzhuo said, "A master Chan guest; Tianran is still here. An said, "I entrust it to Jiangshan," and then he sent a formal letter to the Head Seat and the assembly.
In front of the Sangha Hall, the Head Seat asked, "Xuansha’s blank paper—where does this come from?"
Anan held up the letter and said, "Do you see it? The Head Seat reached out his hand to receive it. Anan took it back and said, "I have long kept this essential point hidden;

I did not strive to speak of it hastily. Today I present it to you; I hope you will deign to examine it. The Head Seat then gave a shout. Anan said, "A masterful Head Seat! The Head Seat shouted again. Anan struck him with the letter.
As the Head Seat hesitated, Anan said, "You do not yet understand three, eight, or nine. The Head Seat was left speechless. Anan said, "Not understanding three, eight, or nine—" and he departed.
He ceased his inner brooding. Then, striking the book once, he said, "Receive it! Wuzu and Foyan stood in the Dharma Hall, watching for his move.
Wuzu said in a stern voice, "I am going to kill my Head Seat! Foyan said, "It is like two official horses trampling one another; what evidence is there?
An said, "What need is there to speak of 'official horses trampling'? This is precisely the treading of dragons and elephants."
Wu said, "Bring him here, bring him here. An returned to the Dharma Hall. Wu said, "I am the head seat among my five hundred followers;
why did you strike him? An replied, "The Master should receive a beating as well.
Wu looked at Fuyan, who stuck out his tongue. Fuyan said, "Not yet. He then turned to An and asked, "Suppose one were empty-handed, holding a hoe—"
An: "A buffalo walks; a person passes over a bridge. The bridge flows, but the water does not flow. Wuzhuo asked, "How do you understand this?
An bowed low and said, "All that I have offered is the truth. Wuzhuo laughed and said, "So, you are truly one of our own family.
He then went to the place of Master Wuzu Fayan. Wuzu asked, "What is it that is spoken of in the scriptures? An said, "The patterns are already manifest."
Zizhao said, "Ultimately, what are you saying? An said, "Brandishing the precious sword in broad daylight. Zizhao said, "Come closer; here one does not recognize even a single character.
An said, "Do not feign defeat. Zizhao looked at his attendant and said, "Which monastery's monk is this?"
Dongshan said, "How many people have been caught in doubt? Guishan’s attendant replied, "He has previously served under the Master.

Dongshan said, "I am surprised he is so slippery-headed. The attendant then said, "He was once treated with neglect by the Master. Dongshan then took the letter and held it over the incense burner while reciting:
*Namo Samantabhadra-nāma*. Dongshan stepped forward and merely snapped his fingers. Dongshan [repeated this] a second time.

He arrived at Mount Jiangshan to spend the summer retreat. Baizhang Weixian invited him to share his seat and receive guests. In the autumn, when An took his leave to return home, Weixian asked, "What do you require?
An replied, "For short songs, I need ten or more feet; for long verses, only three or two words suffice. Weixian praised him with a verse.
Later, An appeared in the world at Lingyan in Dingzhou.
If the source is not deep, the stream will not be long. Master An received the Dharma from Foxing; as his special envoy, he was highly esteemed within the monastic communities.
From this, one can know the reach of Foxing’s influence. Alas! Why were the forests so lush in the past, while today they are so desolate?
▲ Zen Master Yuanjue of Mount Xiang’er in Meizhou was originally named Yuánjué. When the Prefectural Governor filled out the official registration form, he mistakenly wrote "Yuán.

Since the Master’s clan name was indeed Yuán, the governor jokingly said to him, "Is it permissible to have a name consisting of only one character? The Master replied, "One character is already too many."
Shou regarded this as extraordinary. He traveled extensively throughout various regions. Later, he relied upon Fóxìng to recount his insights. Fóxìng said, "You are far too distant.

Every time Fóxìng cited the four characters of the *Lotus Sūtra*—"opening, showing, awakening, and entering"—he would command him to provide a response, saying, "Only when I nod my head vertically will it be correct.
Once, due to a lapse in his duties, he was dismissed from office. During the period of his prohibition, having no one to rely on, he stayed in the home of a layman. One day...
While reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* daily, he reached the passage, "Furthermore, one does not even know what the house is or what the fire is," whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment.
Upon completing his retreat and returning home for a visit, Xingjian nodded in approval. At that time, Yuanwu was at Yunju; the Master went there to communicate his realization.
Wuha said, "This is originally a pure place. Why are you defecating here? At these words, the Master’s doubts were instantly resolved.

▲ Chan Master Zhongren of Zhongtianzhu in Lin’an Prefecture investigated the sutras and treatises to their depths, yet he had not yet attained realization in the Gate of the Patriarchs (the Chan school).

Yuánwù resided at Tiānníng Monastery. At dawn, the Master went to visit him. Yuánwù was just then conducting a *rùshì* (entering the room) session for the assembly. Upon seeing him, the Master felt deep reverence and submission; he stepped forward with vigor.
Yuánwù said, "To interpret the meaning based on the scriptures is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three ages;

to deviate from a single word of the scriptures is to speak like a demon. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! As the Master was about to respond, Yuánwù struck him across the mouth with his staff, causing him to lose a tooth. Thereupon, the Master attained great enlightenment.
▲ Chan Master Huayan Zu’jue of Zhongyan in Meizhou was intelligent from childhood; he could recite anything after seeing it once.
He authored a book to refute Buddhism, whereupon a terrifying vision suddenly appeared before him. Repenting his transgression, he left the household life and relied upon Chan Master Huimù Neng.

Not long after, an abscess broke out on his knee, which no physician could cure for five years. Consequently, he completed his *Huayan Helun* (Comprehensive Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), and that night he experienced a miraculous dream. At dawn—
He immediately cast aside his staff and began to walk. One day, while reciting the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs," he came to the passage:

"The Buddha-body has no birth, yet it can manifest birth; the nature of phenomena is like empty space, and all Buddhas abide therein. Without abiding and without departing, the Buddha is seen everywhere.
He then attained realization of the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka*. He once lectured at the Qianbu Hall, where his discourse was grand and expansive, and the assembly...
Everyone sighed in admiration. Just then, Chan Master Jing of Nantang arrived and said to him, "I observe that your lecturing and exposition are peerless in the southwest;
it is only a pity that you have not yet transcended the marks of words and letters. If you were to seek the Way beyond the mundane world, you would be the Zhi Jin-gang of today."
The Master joyfully concluded his lectures and traveled south. He relied upon Yuanwu at Zhongfu Mountain. One day, he entered the inner quarters for instruction. Yuanwu cited Deshan’s saying:
"When there are words, one treads on the tiger’s head and gathers up its tail; beneath the first phrase, the fundamental principle is clarified.

When there are no words, the sharp point of the faculty is exposed, like a flash of lightning. "How do you understand this? Yuanwu asked. The Master was unable to respond. He then devoted himself to intensive practice day and night.
Jiū attained sudden enlightenment. He presented a verse to express his realization, saying: "My home is atop a solitary peak; for many years the door has been half-shut.

I lament that my own body is already old; I have entrusted my livelihood to my children and grandchildren. When Wù saw it, he gave his approval. The following day, Jiū entered the inner quarters. Wù asked:
"Regarding yesterday’s *gong'an*, what do you say? As the Master was about to respond, Wuzhuo gave a shout and said, "The Buddha-dharma is not a matter of such logic.

The Master remained for another five years, becoming even more bewildered and distressed. Later, while at Mount Lu, he read Chan Master Fushan Yuan’s *Treatise on Eliminating Attachments*, which states:
"If one says that awakening involves partiality toward the near and the distant, how could there be a stinking tree growing within a sandalwood grove?"
The grass was suddenly cleared away, and he attained sudden enlightenment. He composed a verse and sent it to Wuzhuo, saying: "Stepping out the door, I return as before to the weeds;
the heavenly net is vast and wide, impossible to escape. Who would believe that karmic conditions leave no place of refuge? Returning home, I need not fear loud voices.
Wuzhuo was greatly pleased and held it up for the assembly, saying, "Jue has attained thorough penetration of Huayan."

▲ When the Emperor issued a decree requiring monks to become "virtuous scholars" (de-shi), Chan Master Tanyuan of Mingyin in Pingjiang Prefecture entered Tou-tuo Rock, subsisting on pine nuts to preserve his life.
Later, he relied upon Yuanwu. One day, when Yuanwu raised a drumstick to strike the drum, Tanyuan suddenly attained enlightenment regarding the Great Dharma.

Thereafter, whenever anyone questioned him about the Dharma, he would invariably respond, "Do not concern yourself with it. Consequently, people also referred to him as the Elder "Don't-bother-with-it" (Mo-li-hui).
▲ When the Head Seat Daozu of the Zhaojue Monastery in Chengdu first met Yuanwu, he attained enlightenment under the teaching "the mind is itself Buddha.

After some time, Yuanwu ordered him to share the seat [of the abbot]. One day, while conducting a private interview with the assembly, the Master suddenly asked, "When birth and death arrive, how can one avoid them?
The monk had no reply. The Master threw down his whisk and passed away peacefully. The assembly...
Everyone stared in astonishment. When Huineng heard of his arrival, he summoned him, saying, "Head Seat Zu. The Master opened his eyes and looked at him.
Huineng said, "Rouse your spirit and pass through the barrier. The Master nodded his head and immediately passed away.
▲ Xu Fu, styled Shichuan, served as a Grand Secretary. Whenever he accompanied his father, the Dragon-Tu Official, to visit Fachang and Lingyuan, they would engage in discourse all day long;

yet when the official heard of these matters, he regarded them with disdain. However, upon the passing of Fachang—which occurred amidst mere smiles and conversation—the official marveled at this and began to believe deeply.

Later, while observing the mourning period for his father, he felt that there was no way to repay his boundless debt of gratitude, and thus requested Lingyuan to return to the home to perform the ancestral rites.
When Yuan ascended the seat and finished the exchange of questions and answers, he said: "O virtuous ones, it is as if Longtu has read ten thousand scrolls of books;
like water being passed from one vessel to another, not a single drop is lost. But tell me, where does he usually keep them?
Now, after the consciousness is cast off, where will this person who possessed those ten thousand scrolls of books go to put them? Upon hearing this, Gong [was enlightened].
Feeling a sense of liberation and attainment, he then said, "I have no regrets. Yuan descended from his seat and asked, "Scholar, what did you just see that you speak thus?
The official replied, "If there were anything seen, I would be failing the Master."
Yuan said, "If that is so, then I am not as good as this old monk. Gong asked, "What kind of mental state does the Master have? Yuan laughed heartily.

At the beginning of the Jingkang era, while serving as a Ministerial Official (Wailang), he joined with several fellow officials of like mind to hang his alms bowl in Zemo Hall at Tianning Temple, where he applied himself diligently to the study of Yuanwu.
Yuanwu also rejoiced in his transcendent insight. One day, he went to [Yuanwu’s] quarters...
Ji-liao pointed to Wu’s crown and said, "This old fellow has not yet even planted his heels on the ground. Wu looked at him and said, "How could a turtle ever escape from inside a jar?
Ji-liao said, "I am glad that this old fellow has now planted his heels on the ground. Wu said, "..."
"Do not slander others; it is best to leave. The Master retired.
Later, Zhao Lingjin, the Prince of Jun, visited Yuanwu at Mount Oufu. The Master joyfully accepted him as his disciple to be forged in the furnace of his teaching.

However, Yuanwu did not grant him any concessions. Zhao pressed his request insistently, to which Yuanwu replied: "If you wish for this matter to reach its true resonance, you must simply undergo a death once."

He finally attained realization. The Master [Wuzu] intuitively understood this and once recorded it in a brief account, which states in part: "My family was poor and suffered robbery; who knew that everything had been stripped away?
The empty room was uninhabited; how many times did bandits come and strike it? Upon awakening, I saw that he had entrusted me with this matter, ordering me to provide protection.

In the winter of the Gengshen year of the Shaoxing era, the Master went to visit Dahui. When Dahui heard of this, he ordered the drum to be beaten to summon him into his quarters. The Master joyfully approached, carrying incense in his sleeve.
Huì said, "Regarding the story of Zhaozhou washing the alms bowl, how do you understand it, Layman? The Master said, "What bowl are you looking for? He then brushed his sleeves and went out.
Huì rose, grabbed him by the collar, and said, "The ancients attained enlightenment right here; why do you not attain it?
As the Master was about to reply, Huì struck him and said, "What bowl are you looking for? The Master said, "Only then did I return this old fellow."
Yes. One day, while returning from court, Layman Puxian Li Miyuan, a subordinate minister, was crossing the Tianjin Bridge when his horse leaped.
Suddenly he attained realization, and sweat poured from his entire body. He went straight to Tianting Monastery; just as he arrived, Yuanwu came out of the gate and saw him from afar.
He then called out, "Householder, you may rejoice; your great matter is now concluded. The official said in a stern voice, "Monk, why are your eyes clouded?
Huineng then gave a shout. The official also shouted. Thus, their exchange was swift and sharp; whenever he engaged in dialogue with Huineng, he never yielded on the spot.
When he was later transferred to the Ministry of Personnel, still in the prime of his life, he suddenly requested a clerical stipend and retired to Lianjiang in Min, where he built a hermitage.
He enjoyed himself. One day, manifesting a slight illness, he requested hot water to bathe. Upon finishing his bath, he sat cross-legged and composed a verse, saying:
"Needless to speak of the herdsman and the protector from of old; today they are clearly revealed. The void crushes down Mount Sumeru—what need is there to speak of the path beyond?
Having cast aside his brush, he passed away.
▲ Fan County Lady of Chengdu had lived as a widow for many years; she usually sat but never lay down.

Hearing that Yuanwu was residing at Zhaojue Temple, she went there to pay her respects and requested instruction on the causes and conditions for entering the Way. Yuanwu instructed her to contemplate:
"It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not a thing—what is this? For a long time, she found no realization. Fan wept and said to Yuanwu: "What expedient means does the Master have?"
[The Master] then provided a skillful means for him to understand easily. Wuzhuo said, "There is indeed a skillful means. He then had [Wuzhuo] simply look into what this thing is.
Later, he attained realization and said, "So it was so near all along!"
"The Arsenal of the Zen School: What expedient means does Master Zhi have that might allow me to understand it easily? Wuzhuo replied, "There is an expedient means:
it is not mind, not Buddha, and not a thing. At these words, Fan attained awakening and said, "I see now how near it has always been!"
▲ Chan Master Wenshu Xindao of Changde Prefecture studied the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) school and considered his understanding to be ultimate.

A fellow resident challenged him, saying: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Yet, before our eyes, the ten thousand phenomena are distinct and vivid; where, then, is 'mind' and 'consciousness'?"

The Master was at a loss. He then traveled extensively to seek instruction from various teachers. Upon arriving at Taiping, he heard that during the night session, Foguan had raised the koan of Zhaozhou’s “Cypress Tree” and cited Jue Tiezui’s remark:
“The former master did not say such words; do not slander the former master. This caused him to experience great doubt.
After having been alert and attentive for a long time, one night he suddenly attained enlightenment. He immediately went to the master’s quarters intending to recount what he had realized.
Upon seeing him arrive, Master Jian closed the door. The Master said, "Preceptor, do not deceive me. Jian said, "The ten directions have no walls; why do you not enter through the door?
The Master punched a hole in the window paper. Jian immediately opened the door, grabbed him, and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master—
Holding a mirror with both hands to his head, he made a spitting sound with his mouth and departed. He then presented this verse: "Zhaozhou has a story about the cypress tree;
Zen practitioners have passed it down throughout the world. Most merely pluck the leaves and seek the branches, Unable to understand directly at the source.
Master Jue says there are no such words— This is truly reviling one’s face with foul speech. If a Zen practitioner possesses..."
"An eye that penetrates all directions. One should take pleasure in discerning the true from the false within this.
Jia-Deep (Jian-shen) approved of this. ▲ Chan Master Longya Zhicai of Tanzhou received the Dharma from Fo-jian. Later, he visited Huanglong Sishi.
Sishi asked him, "If you understand the first phrase, you understand the final phrase; if you understand the final phrase, you understand the first phrase."
The first phrase: set aside for a moment the beginning and the end. Regarding Baizhang’s “Wild Fox” story—how do you understand it?
The Master said, "Entering the door, I already knew the understanding he had brought; why trouble myself to raise it again, trampling the mud beneath my feet?
Xinfeng said, "The new elder has died at the hands of the Senior Monk. The Master said, "Though the words differ, the ultimate principle is without discrepancy. Xinfeng...
[The monk] asked, "What is this matter that is without differentiation? The Master said, "If you do not strike the horn of Huanglong, how can you know the pearl beneath his chin?
[The monk] immediately struck him. Ascending the hall, he cited the small *sōsan* (informal sermon) of Sīxin, which said:

"If one discusses this matter, it is like a family with three sons. The first son is intelligent and wise; he filially supports his parents, receives guests who come and go, and manages the household."
The second son was fierce, stubborn, and cunning; he was greedy and lustful, addicted to wine, and would lie sprawled across the streets and alleys, ruining the family estate.
The third son was blind, deaf, and mute; unable to distinguish between beans and wheat, he was incapable of anything but eating his meals.
Among these three, Huanglong intended to select one for use. There were still forty days remaining; within death there is life, and within life there is death.
"Death. Among deaths, there is constant death; among lives, there is constant life. Use these four lines to test the monks of the world.
The Master said, "What do you call 'four lines'? What are the surnames and names of these three men?
If you can recognize them, you shall walk hand-in-hand with Huanglong, without the slightest interval between us. If this is not yet so, I cannot help but offer flowers upon borrowed water."

It is so. The three persons share a single body; their function is non-function. The four lines share a single sound; they are both empty and not empty. If you wish to recognize the three persons and the four lines:

when the golden crow first rises, it is a mass of red. When the Master first resided at Yuelu, on the day he opened the hall for the assembly, a monk asked: [The rest of the text follows as provided in the source.]
"Deishan’s staff and Linji’s shout—today I request that you, Master, pick them up for us. The Master said, "Suru suru.
[The monk] asked, "In 'suru suru,' is there still the meaning of the West? The Master said, "Suru suru. Because of this, the monastic community called him "Talent-Suru.
He resided at Longya and later moved to Yunkyai, governing the assembly with austerity; the monks revered him.
Wei. On the full moon of the eighth month in the year Wumao (1138) of the Xiangshu era, he suddenly gathered the assembly to entrust them with the affairs of the monastery. He then wrote this verse:
"On the day of the Mid-Autumn Festival in the year Wumao, my life as a renunciant and my duties as abbot are finished.

As I depart, even my own self does not exist; what empty space could there be to seek? His final instructions were as usual. On the twenty-third day, he again gathered the assembly and asked: "Nirvana and birth..."

"Death is entirely empty flowers. Both 'Buddha' and 'sentient beings' are merely figurative designations. How would you all handle this? When the assembly offered their responses, none were in accord.
The Master shouted, "Suffering! Suffering! Then he said, "White clouds surge from the earth; the bright moon hangs in the sky.
Having finished speaking, he passed away with a broad smile.
▲ Chan Master Shouxun of Heshan in Anjishou visited Fojian. He joined the assembly in seeking instruction, yet for a long time he made no progress.
He then wrapped his shroud and declared, "If I do not attain thorough penetration in this life, I vow never to unroll it.
Thereupon, he sat by day and stood by night as if mourning the loss of a parent. After more than seven weeks, Fojian suddenly ascended the hall and said: "The myriad phenomena and..."
The myriad phenomena are all sealed by a single Dharma. Upon hearing this, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
He went to see Huikuan, who said, "What a pity—a bright pearl has been picked up by this madman.

He then interrogated him, saying, "Lingyun said, 'Since the moment I first saw the peach blossoms, until now I have had no more doubts. What is it that he does not doubt? The Master replied, "Do not—"
Daolinyun said, "I have no doubt. Even now, though I search for a place of doubt, it is utterly unattainable. Yuanjian said, "Xuansha said, 'It is truly correct, most truly correct;
yet I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate. Where, then, was his lack of penetration?
The Master said, "I deeply understand how the Master’s compassionate heart is so earnest. Yuanjian approved. As the Master rose from his prostrations, he presented a verse, saying: "Day after day..."
Gazing at the sky, he did not raise his head; only when the peach blossoms were in full bloom did he lift his eyes.
Even if you possess a net that covers the heavens, once you have penetrated this secure barrier, you may simply rest. Jieyi instructed him to protect and uphold [the Dharma].

That evening, he spoke to the assembly in a stern voice, saying, "This time, Seat-Holder Xun shall sleep soundly. When Yuanwu heard of this, he suspected it was not yet so and said, "I must investigate him."
It was only after some time that he finally attained realization. He then sent someone to summon him, and they went together to wander the mountains. By chance, they arrived at a mountain pond;
Wuzhuo pushed the Master into the water and immediately asked, "What was it like before Niutou saw the Fourth Patriarch? The Master replied, "The pool is deep, and the fish gather there."
Wu asked, "What is it like after seeing? The Master said, "A tall tree invites the wind. Wu asked, "What is it like when one has seen and when one has not yet seen?

Yuanfan patted the official on the back and said, "How wonderful! Thereupon, the official attained realization. In the Ding-si year of the Shaoxing era, he was appointed as a Censor-in-Chief.

"Totu de-bde. Sūḥ sīri svāhā. Regarding the Seal of Wisdom, he spoke in verse, blending the Sanskrit and the Chinese (Tang) languages into a single whole:
"Alas, you worldly man! To attain this samādhi! Later, while serving as the Governor of Qiong Prefecture, he remained serene and withdrawn in his duties without weariness.

He passed away. Although he manifested the appearance of a high-ranking official, his reputation as a venerable elder was renowned throughout the four seas.
In the autumn of the twenty-third year, he requested retirement. He informed his relatives and acquaintances in advance, setting the thirtieth day of the tenth month as the time for his passing.

On that day, he had a high seat prepared in the rear hall and received guests as usual. Between the hours of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. and the Snake (9–11 a.m.), he descended the steps, faced the imperial palace, and performed a solemn prostration. He then requested—

Master Gui’s eyes turned red, and he eventually passed away. Because many of the Tripitaka collections at famous monasteries had been destroyed during the Jianyan era and thereafter, the Master commissioned the printing of one hundred twenty-eight sets.

▲ Chan Master Shitou Zihui of Diaoyutai in Taizhou was a stone mason by birth. Having received the *Lotus Sūtra* through oral instruction from others, he was able to recite it.

He entered the service of Dawsui, where he performed the duties of sweeping and sprinkling water. When ordered to quarry stones from the cliff, he did not let go of his hammer and chisel, yet he never ceased reciting the sūtra.
Seeing this, Dawsui said to him: "Today there is the clatter of stones; tomorrow there will be the clatter of stones. This is birth and death."

Having arrived, how shall we settle this? The Master (Zhaozhou) therefore performed a ritual of respect and requested the ultimate Dharma. Zhaozhou immediately ordered him to cease his recitation of the sutras and instead contemplate the karmic encounter regarding Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman.
The Master kept this thought in mind at every moment. After some time, while he was chipping away at a stone that was somewhat hard, he struck it with all his might.
Suddenly, seeing a flash of fire, he attained sudden and thorough realization. He ran to the abbot’s quarters, prostrated himself, and presented his understanding.
The verse says: Having exhausted all effort, there is not a single trace left. The sparks of fire scatter, yet they were originally right here.
[Zhaozhou] said with a smile, "You have attained thorough penetration. He then offered this verse on Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman: "The three armies do not move, yet the banners flash."
"The old wife is precisely the foot of the Māra-demon. Zhaozhou’s handleless iron broom sweeps away the dust and smoke until all is empty and desolate.
Following this, he was granted monastic robes; he was popularly known as "Huishi" (Stone-Returning).
▲ Chan Master Shiyuan of Liangshan in Changde Prefecture ascended the hall. He cited the story of Yangqi’s three-legged donkey and addressed the assembly, saying:
"To stir up boiling water, nothing is better than extinguishing the fire; to block a flowing stream, nothing is better than cutting off the source.
This is the clear mirror of the sages and the orthodox discourse of the Buddha-dharma; it lies precisely herein. This—
Regarding causes and conditions: nowadays in the monastic communities, there are many who proclaim the teachings and not a few who engage in deliberation.
Some simply say that the masters have no fixed principles; whatever is asked, they answer off the cuff. This may seem plausible, but it is merely a semblance.
This is still not it. If you proceed in this manner, you will merely understand it as a dry state of non-action; you will fail to see Yangqi’s point of application.
Furthermore, how will you deal with the myriad distinctions and various gateways of the Patriarchs?

There are also those who understand it solely from the perspective of the Buddha, which has no connection to one's own self. An ancient said: "Whenever there are words or phrases, each and every one must..."
"Resolve it back into oneself. But how so? Furthermore, there is another type who always understands it only as "oneself," discarding the ancient masters' point of application.
They know only to clarify the matter of one's own self, yet they do not know how to deal with the ancients' skillful means (*upāya*).
Being unable to dispose of them, they are like someone trying to bathe while clutching a bridge pillar; they simply cannot let go. This—
This, too, is a sickness. Furthermore, there are those who instead seek understanding at some distance from the feet [of the teaching]. This ailment is the most difficult to cure.
For this reason, his words possess a subtle artistry that is difficult for students to grasp; as soon as they attempt to apply their minds, they have already missed the mark.
Former masters called this the "Fayan Qiyuan School. One must be a member of his own household to reach such a field.
Only when one’s ground is fit for transmission may it be passed on; otherwise, one is said to "die guarding the path of goodness.

even among those in the monasteries of the world today who have emerged to serve as teachers, there are few who truly comprehend it.
If you wish to understand this, you must look lightly beyond the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvarakalpa, prior to the empty kalpa. Seize it and act;

press down and turn. Then, taking a single step before the ten-thousand-fathom peak, you can encompass past and present and cut off the tongues of all people under heaven. Is there anyone now who is like this? If there is, come forth!

▲The Minister Mo Jiang, whose courtesy name was Shangshu Zhaoxu, while serving in Western Shu, visited Nantang to inquire about the essentials for resolving his doubts.
Nantang instructed him to maintain mindfulness toward the "good place. At that moment, as he happened to enter the latrine and smelled a foul odor, he suddenly covered his nose with his hand;

the blue-eyed barbarian monk smiles and nods his head. (Nantang was the honorary title of Daisui.)
▲ Layman Wang Xiao, whose courtesy name was Guanfù, resided at Zhaojue Temple. One day, upon hearing the sound of the board signaling the end of meditation, he attained a realization.

▲ Chan Master Daochuan of Wuweijun and Yezhu was the son of the Di family of Kunshan.

Initially serving as a bowman for the county, he heard that the Senior Seat (Shouzuo) Qian of Dongzhai was expounding the Dharma for both monastics and laypeople, so he went to follow him. He practiced seated meditation without weariness.

One day, having failed in his duties, he was subjected to flogging; it was beneath the blows of the staff that he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He then resigned from his service and relied upon Qian, who [subsequently] changed his name for him.
He was named Daochuan (River of the Way). The Master said, "Formerly you were called Disan; now your name is Daochuan. 'Chuan' is simply 'san.
