The Master was the son of the Xi family of Xuancheng. His mother dreamed of a monk with a dark-complexioned face and a prominent nose, escorted by divine beings, who entered her bedchamber and asked where he resided;
she replied, "To the north of the mountain. Upon waking, she became pregnant.

On the tenth day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Yuanyou era of Emperor Zhezong (the Jisi year), at the hour of Si, the Master was born. A white light permeated the room, and the entire district spoke of it.

He was different from others. At the age of sixteen he left home [the *Denglu* records this as twelve, which is incorrect; this follows his chronological biography], and at seventeen he shaved his head.

He immediately took delight in the affairs of the Chan school and read extensively through the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of various masters. He especially favored the teachings of Yunmen and Muzhou, yet he once harbored doubts regarding the five houses of the Chan lineage.
Originally, he was merely a single Dharma. Where could there have been so many lineages? By nature, he was brilliant, elegant, and unconstrained;

at nineteen, he began his travels. He first arrived at the Beidu Hermitage in Taiping. The hermitage master received him with great reverence, saying, "Last night I dreamed that the temple deity informed me that Master Yunfeng Yue was coming;
he commanded me to wait for him with solemnity. It was because of this that the elder Beidu [received him].
He showed his delight to the Master, who read through it once and mastered it by heart. People consequently said that he was the reincarnation of Yunfeng.
Having visited Chan Master Mingji Cheng of Xuanzhou, he requested instruction on Xuedou’s *Niangu* (Verses on Ancient Cases) and *Songgu* (Eulogies on Ancient Cases).

Without offering a single word, Cheng directed him to see for himself and speak for himself; the Master immediately penetrated the subtle meaning. Cheng sighed and said, "Gao must be a person of another rebirth. He passed away.
At Dayang in Yingzhou, he met the senior seat holder Yuan, Master Weishan Daoqian, and Senior Seat Holder Jian.

The Master served under these three masters for a very long time and fully mastered the essential tenets of the Caodong school. He observed that whenever they transmitted the Dharma, they invariably applied incense to their arms to signify that the transmission was not made in vain, reciting:
"The Chan school possesses a lineage of transmission; how could it be a teaching where Buddhas and patriarchs merely realize and awaken for themselves?"

He discarded them (as Fangfu Wen Poshuo said: "There is indeed a gate of awakening, but it is simply not right to bring in all these 'household affairs'—such as the five ranks of mutual interplay between the biased and the correct, or the five princes—and pass them on.

The Master asked, "Which one are you? Guang replied, "Today I have caught this old thief. The Master deeply approved of him. Later, the attendant Jinli had long served the Master, silently investigating the story of the bamboo stick, yet he made no progress.

One day, after the private interview was concluded, he requested instruction. The Master said, "You are a man from Fuzhou. Let me give you a metaphor: it is like taking a fine-grade lychee, peeling off the skin and shell, and placing it in your mouth; the only thing you cannot do is swallow it. Jinli could not help but let out a laugh.

The Master said, "If the Abbot swallows it, it will be a disaster. Later, the Master asked again, "As for the lychees swallowed the other day, it was simply that you did not know their flavor. Baizhang Li said, "If one were to know the flavor, it would become even more of a disaster. The Master approved of this.
As soon as he saw a monk enter, he said, "That is not it; go out! The monk immediately left. The Master said, "A man of immeasurable capacity has been turned around by the flow of words.
Then another monk entered, and the Master likewise said, "That is not it; go out! But this monk instead stepped forward.
The Master said, "I have already told you it is not so. What more do you seek by coming forward? He then struck him out.
Another monk entered and said, "Just now, those two monks did not understand the Master's meaning. The Master lowered his head and let out a single sigh; the monk was left at a loss.
The Master struck him and said, "In fact, it is you who understand my meaning. As soon as the next monk entered, the Master said, "You do not understand;
get out! The monk immediately left. A third monk then entered, and the Master likewise said, "You do not understand; get out! The monk also left.
Yet another monk entered, and the Master said, "Of the two monks who just came in, one understands how to gather in [the teaching], while the other does not."
"Let go! [The Master] said. "One person lets go but does not know how to gather it back up. Can you still discern this? A monk said, "I accept this as my own record.
The Master said, "After you have accepted it, what further good news is there? The monk clapped his hands once and departed. The Master said, "In thirty years, he will realize it.
[Later,] a monk asked, "When one encounters a man who has attained the Way on the road, one does not respond with speech or silence. At such a time—"
"How is it? The monk said "Zhenzhong" (Take care) and departed. The Master laughed loudly. Next, another monk came. The Master said, "Just now I asked that monk:
'When a person who has attained the Way meets you on the road, how do you respond—not with speech, nor with silence?
He said 'Zhenzhong' and departed. Do you say he understood or not? The monk was about to bow in greeting when the Master struck him out. [The Master] asked a monk: "No..."
"Who is it that takes all dharmas as its companion? He replied, "A faceless man. The Master said, "Just now there was a monk who spoke like that;
I have already beaten him out. The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him. [The Master] questioned a monk:
Regarding the story of Xiangyan climbing the tree: "How do you understand it? [Xiangyan] said, "Singing the *zhègū* [partridge] song in the spring breeze.
The Master said, "The Venerable Houtou said, 'I do not ask about his being on the tree; bring me a phrase before he has climbed the tree. How would you respond to that?
[Xiangyan] said, "I have already spoken to the Master just now. The Master said, "Singing the *zhègū* song in the spring breeze."

[The monk] spoke of what was on the tree; [the Master] spoke of what was under the tree. The monk prepared to respond, and the Master struck him. A monk asked, "I have been practicing Chan but have not attained it.
Where does my illness lie? The Master said, "The illness lies right here. The monk asked, "Why then am I unable to attain it?"
The Master said, "You are a fellow who wets his bed while awake! I am going to beat you off! He asked a monk, "What was the meaning of the National Teacher’s three calls to his attendant?
The monk replied, "When the fish swim, the water becomes turbid. The Master said, "Do not let the pot boil over! The monk was speechless, so the Master struck him.
He then asked another monk, "Master Mazu said, 'Since the time of chaos, for thirty years I have never lacked salt and sauce. What does this mean?"
"What is it? [the monk] asked. "It is according to one's household, whether abundant or frugal," he said. The Master said, "What a fine 'according to one's household, whether abundant or frugal'!

It is simply that you do not understand. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him. A monk requested instruction on the story of Jia Shan’s realm. Before the monk had finished speaking, the Master gave a shout.
The monk was at a loss. The Master asked, "What were you asking? As the monk prepared to speak, the Master struck him repeatedly and shouted him out. [Another] asked:
The monk said, "The Way does not require cultivation; one simply must not defile it. The Master asked, "What is this Way that is undefiled?
The monk replied, "I do not dare say. The Master asked, "Why do you not dare say? The monk said, "For fear of defiling it. The Master called out in a loud voice:
The practitioner brought a dustpan and broom. The monk was at a loss. The Master struck him out and asked, "The wisdom of all-knowledge is pure;
it is non-dual, without division, without distinction, and without interruption. How do you understand this? The monk replied, "The wisdom of all-knowledge is pure;
it is non-dual, without division, without distinction, and without interruption. I simply understand it in this way."
The Master said, "Bring me the cat. The monk was speechless. The Master then shouted and drove him out.
He asked another monk, "Do you remember the *huatou*? The monk replied, "I do not remember it. The Master said, "What business is it of yours to come here? He struck him.
He then asked a monk, "The Fifth Patriarch said that Zhaozhou’s 'the dog has no Buddha-nature' is ten thousand times superior to [the case of] the cat. As he spoke, [he struck him].
"What? he asked. [The monk] replied, "The wind blows and the grass bends. The Master said, "You must not speak recklessly. How do you understand this? The monk was speechless.
The Master said, "A mere follower of empty words," and struck him out. As soon as the Master saw a monk enter, he said, "Śākyamuni Buddha has arrived!
The monk stepped forward; the Master said, "Not so," and struck him. Then another monk entered, and the Master likewise—
[The Master] said, "Śākyamuni Buddha has arrived! The monk greeted him face-to-face and then departed. The Master said, "That was quite like a real one.
As soon as the monk entered, the Master said, "All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, beasts, donkeys, and horses;
the cypress tree in the courtyard, three pounds of flax, a dried piece of dung—what a shameless thief you are! [The monk] said, "I have long known that the Master possesses..."
"This is the essential point. The Master said, "I have already needlessly entered the weeds; you do not even know the stench of my excrement.
The monk brushed out his sleeves and left. The Master said, "Alas, how bitter! Buddha! He then asked an attendant, "How many people have entered the room?
How many have been able to express it, and how many have not? The attendant replied, "I simply watch."
The Master suddenly extended his hand and said, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand? The attendant replied, "The weather is cold;
please, Master, let us roll up your sleeves. He then departed. The Master followed him, striking him with a bamboo staff, and said, "Tell me, was that a reward for you or a punishment?
A monk requested instruction, saying, "I do not know where I shall go when I die. The Master said, "Tell me, right now, what is this?"
"Is he alive? Is he dead? The monk said, "Alive, I will not say; dead, I will not say. The Master said, "You have acted as a servant to Jianyuan.
The monk hesitated, and the Master struck him out. Another monk came forward, and the Master said, "That monk just now suffered a defeat;
do you know it? The monk said, "I know. The Master likewise struck him out. He asked another monk, "Yantou..."
As soon as he stepped across the gate of Deshan, he asked, "Is this ordinary or is it holy? Deshan gave a shout; Yantou bowed. What was his intention?
[The monk] said, "What a fine message! The Master said, "Where is the 'fine' part? The monk then shouted. The Master said:
"With that shout of yours, there was no master present. [The Master] went out and asked a monk, "It cannot be like this;
it cannot be not like this; it cannot be both like this and not like this. How about then? The monk said, "It can be all of these. The Master said:
He cast aside the sweet peach tree and climbed the mountain to pluck sour pears. He asked a monk, "Tell me, does Chan receive the teachings?
The monk replied, "A single iron bar stretching ten thousand miles. The Master said, "But what can you do? There is Maitreya within Guanyin Temple.
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him out. He asked another monk, "What is your name? The monk replied, "Faru. The Master said, "The Buddha Hall..."
"Is it so, Your Honor? [The monk] replied, "It is so. The Master said, "I have been seen through by you, old monk. As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him.
Later, while visiting with Elder Niaolong during a conversation regarding Feng Jichuan, the Master said: "In the past, there was an official who asked the Great Sage of Sizhou, 'What is your surname?
The Sage replied, 'My surname is He. The official asked, 'In which country do you reside? The Sage replied, 'I reside in the country of He. What is the meaning of this?"
The Dragon said, "The Great Sage was originally not surnamed He, nor was he a native of the land of He. Feng laughed and said, "The Great Sage definitely was surnamed He and lived in the land of He.
This exchange continued back and forth several times, until he finally sent a letter to the Master requesting that he resolve this public case.
The Master said, "There are sixty blows; I shall give thirty blows to the Great Sage for being improper in saying his surname was He."
"Thirty blows for Jichuan! It was improper for him to ask, 'What is the surname of the Great Sage?
If he were the Elder Wolong, I would have told him to take it upon himself and leave. One day, they went together to Ming'an. Seeing a skull painted on the wall, Jichuan offered this verse:
"The corpse is here; where is the person now? Only then do we know that the single spirit does not dwell within the skin-bag. The Master did not [approve].
[The Master] agreed. He composed a verse himself, saying: "This very physical form is that person; a single spiritual soul within a skin-bag;
the skin-bag is the single spiritual soul. When Zhang Zishao arrived, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "When Dadian drove away the Head Seat for the sake of Han Wen Gong, what was his intention?
The Master said, "A catfish climbing a bamboo pole—traveling a thousand li in a single day. The monk further asked, "I, your student, have not yet..."
[The student] said, "I understand. I beg the Master’s compassion. The Master said, "There is still a second ladle of foul water remaining.
[The student] asked, "As for the Head Seat, who also knocked his teeth three times—where does the fault lie? The Master said, "The fault lies in the knocking of the teeth. [The student] asked, "..."
"Do not slander the Head Seat. The Master said, "What principle have you seen that leads you to speak thus?
He replied, "Who knows the distant mist and waves? There is surely another way of thinking. The Master said, "Do not slander Jingshan.
He replied, "Suppose the Minister asks the Master today how old he is; how would you respond? The Master said, "Point toward..."
The monk said, "He was one hundred and twelve years old. The Master continued, "Can you call this slandering Jingshan? The monk replied, "And you, Master, are slandering the Minister as well.
A monk asked, "An ancient said, 'It is like a man climbing a tree, holding a branch in his mouth, with neither hand grasping a branch nor foot treading upon the trunk.
I wonder, does such a person still have the capacity to answer a question? The Master said, "The answer has already been given."
Jin said, "The student asks about the story of the tree; why did the Master answer while sitting under the tree?
The Master said, "It was precisely because you were asking from beneath the tree. Jin said, "Can you deceive the eyes of the assembly? The Master said, "Truly, one cannot deceive them.
Jin said, "As for when the tree had not yet grown and no news had yet moved—where could Xiangyan have obtained it?"
This phrase has come forth. The Master said, "It comes from within your own lacquer bucket.

The student asked, "As for what the Master said—that to call it a 'bamboo stick' is to encounter resistance (chu), and not to call it a 'bamboo stick' is to turn one's back (bei)—is there still a way to benefit others in this?"
The Master said, “No. The student asked, “If that is so, then it becomes a mere empty fabrication. The Master said, “An empty fabrication. He then continued:
“It is like a man climbing a tree, holding a branch in his mouth, with neither hand grasping a branch nor foot treading upon the trunk.

If someone beneath the tree asks about the meaning of the Westward Journey, to answer him would mean losing one’s life; not to answer would mean violating the questioner’s inquiry. At that moment, Xiangyan just—
When he spoke thus, there was one who could not agree with him from the sidelines; he was called Upādhyāya Houtou.

Stepping forward from the assembly, he said, "I do not ask about that which is upon the tree; bring me a phrase for that which is beneath the tree. The Master said, "Dangerous! Xiangyan laughed heartily.
The Master said, "Dangerous! These two dangers at Jingshan—one danger is like the sky covering all and the earth supporting all;
another danger is such that there is no way to reach it. Is there anyone who can discern which is which?

If you can discern them, not only will you have personally seen Xiangyan, but you will also leave Head Monk Houtou with nowhere to establish his body or maintain his life. If you cannot, then Jingshan..."
I shall present a koan to provide a commentary for all of you: if you call it a bamboo stick, you contradict it;
if you do not call it a bamboo stick, you turn your back on it.

Regarding the essential method for responding [to this question], the Buddha said: "If there is one who wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, they should purify their mind so that it is like empty space.

Remaining far removed from discursive thoughts and all forms of grasping, they shall cause the mind to encounter no obstacles wherever it turns. The realm of the Buddha is not an external realm characterized by signs."
The Buddha is the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). If one desires to know this realm, it is not attained through elaborate cultivation or realization;
rather, one must purify the sense-faculties (*indriya*) from the defilements of adventitious afflictions (*āgantukakleśa*) that have persisted since beginningless time.

Like the vast expanse of space, one should remain far removed from all grasping within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and from false, unreal conceptualizations (*vikalpa*). It is also like...
"Empty space is that toward which this effortless, wondrous mind is directed; naturally, it will be without obstruction. (Shown to Li Xianchen). It further says: "An ancient worthy said:
'In seeking an ox, one must follow its tracks; in studying the Way, one prizes the absence of mind. When the tracks are found, the ox returns; when there is no mind, the Way is easy to seek.
What is called 'no-mind' does not mean being as insentient and dull as earth, wood, tiles, or stones."
To know means that when encountering objects and conditions, the mind remains steadfast and unmoving; it does not grasp at or cling to any phenomena.
It is utterly vast in all places, unobstructed and unhindered, untainted by anything, yet it does not dwell even in a state of non-taint.
One contemplates the body and the mind as being like a dream or an illusion, yet one does not dwell even in the realm of dreams, illusions, or emptiness. To reach such a state is what is meant.
Only then can it be called true non-mind; this is not merely the "non-mind" spoken of with the lips.

If one has not attained true non-mind and relies solely on what is said, how does this differ from the heterodox meditation of silent illumination? Simply attain the root, and do not worry about the branches.
Emptying this mind is the root; once the root is attained, then all manner of speech and all manner of wisdom will emerge daily.

To respond to things and follow conditions—whether in the seven perversions and eight inversions, or in joy or anger, liking or disliking, compliance or resistance—all these are merely secondary (the "branches").
If one can maintain self-awareness within the state of following conditions, then there will be neither deficiency nor excess. (Shown to Huang Boceng.
Having studied this Way, whenever you encounter objects or respond to conditions throughout the twelve periods of the day, you must not allow evil thoughts to continue in succession.
Or, if you fail to maintain mindfulness and a single evil thought arises, you must immediately sharpen your focus and pull your head back around.
If you simply follow after it continuously without interruption, not only will it obstruct the Way, but you shall also be called a person lacking wisdom.
Long ago, Guishan asked Lan’an, "In the twelve periods of the day, what should you devote yourself to? An replied, "Tending the ox. Guishan said:
"How do you herd it? An said, "Once it has entered the grass, I pull it back by the nose. Shanshan said, "You truly herd the ox.
A student of the Way who restrains evil thoughts should be like Lan’an in herding the ox; then, in time, they will naturally become proficient.
(Shown to Li Xianchen). He also said: "Do not grasp another’s bow; do not ride another’s horse. Of others...
One does not know what matters will arise. Although this is a common saying, it can also serve as a provision for entering the Way. One must constantly examine oneself from dawn until dusk;

if one perceives that there is even a slight tendency toward partiality or deficiency regarding matters that greatly benefit others or oneself, one must immediately take warning and must not be negligent.
It is further said: Formerly, Master Daolin dwelt atop the long pines of Mount Qinwang.
The people of the time called him Master Niaoke (Nest-in-a-Tree). When Minister Bai Juyi was stationed in Qiantang, he went specifically into the mountains to visit him.
He asked, "The place where the Chan Master sits is very precarious. The Master replied, "I, an old monk, have nothing precarious. You, Minister, are far more precarious.
The Minister said, "My position governs the rivers and mountains; what precariousness could there be? The Master said, "Fuel and fire [are in constant conflict]..."
"Interacting, the nature of consciousness does not remain still—is this not perilous? He asked again, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good. [The monk] said, "Even a three-year-old child knows how to say that. The Master said:
"A three-year-old child may be able to speak of it, but an eighty-year-old man cannot practice it. Bai then paid his respects and departed.
Now, wishing to save effort and mind, do not concern yourself with whether the three-year-old child can or cannot speak of it, nor whether the eighty-year-old man can or cannot practice it.
Simply take this saying as sufficient: "Commit no evil. Whether you believe it or not, that is the end of it.
This is also correct. Please reflect upon this. It is further said: "The people of the world manifest ignorance while feigning goodness.
Although their goodness may not yet be perfected, how could it not surpass those who lack integrity and shame, and who rely on the pretext of goodness to commit evil?

In the teachings, this is called 'the ground of practice being untrue, resulting in a circuitous fruition. If one can instead maintain a straightforward mind and straightforward conduct, one may directly attain unsurpassed Bodhi."
This is the deed of a true great man. The events of kalpas as numerous as dust motes exist only in the present moment.

If you realize this now, the events of kalpas as numerous as dust motes will instantly dissolve and vanish like ice. If you do not realize it now, even after passing through further kalpas, it remains exactly thus.
Such a Dharma has been eternally constant since antiquity; it has never shifted or changed by so much as a single hair’s breadth.
It is further said: "The worldly affairs of defilement are like a chain of linked rings, continuing without interruption. One should seek opportunities to reduce them as soon as they arise;

for since time immemorial, one has become habituated to them through practice. If one does not strive to contend with them, then over the passage of years and months, one will sink deeper into them without realizing it.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month [the day of death], one will suddenly find oneself at a loss for what to do. If you wish to achieve this, [you must act now].
If one wishes to be free from confusion at the time of death, one must not be confused while currently engaged in one's activities.
It is impossible to be free from confusion at the time of death while being confused in one's present conduct. Furthermore, it is said:
There is a certain kind of person who, in the morning, studies the sutras, recites the Buddha’s name, and performs repentance; yet in the evening, they indulge in verbal karma by reviling others.
On the following day, they perform prostrations and repentance as before, continuing this as their daily practice throughout the year. This is the height of folly.
They fail to realize that the Sanskrit term *kṣamā* (懺摩) means "repenting of one's transgressions," which refers to severing the continuity of such mental states. One—
To sever [the defilements] so they never recur, and through a single confession to ensure they are never committed again—this is the intent of our Buddha’s repentance.

Students of the Way must not fail to understand this. Furthermore, it is said: "A student of the Way, throughout the twelve periods of the day, must always maintain a state of tranquility and non-entanglement within the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
One must also practice seated meditation to prevent the mind from becoming heedless, keeping the body steady and unmoving for a long duration."
Through long-term cultivation and mastery, the body and mind naturally become tranquil and steady, and one possesses a portion of inclination toward the Way.
It is only the deluded perceptions of distracted sentient beings that [mistake] this for the perfection of tranquility (*śamatha-pāramitā*).

If one clings to the state of stillness as being the ultimate, then one is held captive by the heterodox meditation of "silent illumination" (*mozhao*). The Sanskrit term *prajñā* is translated here as "wisdom. There has never been anything more luminous than this.
Prajñā. Those who harbor greed, hatred, and delusion have not yet realized clear prajñā;
those who harm sentient beings with such poison act in direct opposition to prajñā—how can they be said to possess wisdom?
(Shown to Chen Cizhong) When the matter of birth and death is held in mind, the mental faculty is already rectified. Once the mental faculty is rectified, one responds to conditions in daily life.

At that time, do not exert effort to forcefully dispel [distractions]. Since there is no need for forceful expulsion, there will be no error or deviation. When there is no error or deviation, right mindfulness becomes uniquely liberated.

When right mindfulness is uniquely liberated, the principle follows the transformations of phenomena. When the principle follows the transformations of phenomena, phenomena attain integration with the principle.
When phenomena attain integration with the principle, effort is saved. The very moment one perceives this saving of effort, it means one has attained the study of this Way.
This is the place of power. Where one gains power, one saves infinite effort; where one saves effort, one gains infinite power.
(Shown to Ra Myeong-bil) This matter can only be shouldered by those who are clever and sharp-witted. Yet, if they are clever and sharp-witted, they lack the capacity to shoulder it.
For although the entry point is easy for the clever and sharp-witted, it is difficult for them to maintain it; this is because their depth of entry is not very profound.

It is because their power is weak. Those who are clever, intelligent, and sharp-witted, upon merely hearing a good spiritual friend speak of the matters within this [Dharma], immediately have their eyes dart about;
they have already used their mind, intellect, and consciousness to grasp and understand it. Such people create obstacles for themselves and will never have a time of awakening throughout kalpas.
While calamities caused by external ghosts can still be remedied, this is a haunting caused by one's own family spirits.
It cannot be averted by propitiatory rites. Yongjia said: "The depletion of the Dharma-treasure and the destruction of merit—none of these arise except from this mind, intellect, and consciousness.
This is what is meant. (Shown to Li Xianchen) The hindrances to the Way posed by the mind, intellect, and consciousness are more perilous than venomous snakes or fierce tigers.
Why is this? Even venomous snakes and fierce tigers can still be avoided; yet the wise person of keen intelligence takes the mind, intellect, and consciousness as their dwelling place.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they have never for a single moment failed to interact with them.
As days pass and months deepen, without knowing or realizing it, they become fused into a single mass—not by any deliberate effort to become one, but because of this.

Since time immemorial, one has practiced until this single path has become thoroughly familiar. Although one may suddenly recognize it for what it is and wish to distance oneself from it, such separation is impossible.
Therefore it is said: "A venomous snake or a fierce tiger can still be avoided, but the mind, intellect, and consciousness—truly, there is no place for you to avoid them.
(Shown to Luo Mengbi) Most scholar-officials seek the state of non-attainment with a mind that still harbors the desire for attainment.
Attaining the Dharma. What is meant by "having a mind that attains"? It refers to those who employ cleverness and sharp intelligence to deliberate and calculate.

What is meant by the "Dharma of non-attainment"? It refers to where deliberation does not operate and calculation does not reach; it is where cleverness and sharp intelligence find no place to settle.
One does not see the Elder Śākyamuni at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, where Śāriputra earnestly made his three requests.

One must reach the point where there is no opening for a word to be uttered; only then can one, with all one’s strength, attain this Dharma which cannot be understood through thought or discrimination.
This is the ultimate realization of Śākyamuni Buddha, the prototype of his opening of the gate of expedient means and his revealing of the true aspect.
In the past, the Zen Master Xuefeng Zhenjue, out of the urgency of this matter, [did so] three times.
He went to Touzi and visited Dongshan nine times, but their karmic conditions did not harmonize.

Later, hearing that Deshan Zhou, the "Vajra Master," was teaching, he went to his quarters. One day he asked Deshan, "Regarding the ancestral style of our school, by what dharma do you instruct people?
Deshan replied, "In my school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma shown to people. He later asked again regarding the ancestral school...
Regarding the matters within the Vehicle: does a student still have a share in them? Deshan held up his staff and struck him, saying, "Say something!
It was beneath that blow that Xuefeng finally shattered his lacquer bucket.
Viewed from this perspective, even a modicum of cleverness, sharp wit, calculation, or deliberation is of no use whatsoever in this gate. As an ancient worthy said: Prajñā...
It is like a great mass of fire; if one approaches it, it will scorch one's face. As soon as one deliberates or reflects, one falls into the realm of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Yongjia said: "The depletion of the Dharma-treasure and the destruction of merit—none of these fail to arise from this mind-consciousness.

Thus we know that the mind, intellect, and consciousness do not merely obstruct the Path, but also cause people to fall into the seven inversions and eight perversions, committing all manner of unwholesome deeds. Since there is a finality [to this], [one must be vigilant].

This mind of the Way must possess a resolute will; until one reaches the state of great rest, great repose, and great liberation, one must vow not to retreat or fall away for the remainder of this life.
There is not much more to the Buddha-dharma, yet it is difficult to encounter over the long term.
The affairs of worldly toil and defilement are like a chain of hooks, continuing without interruption. Those whose resolve is inferior often find themselves willing to submit to them.
One becomes a companion to it; unaware and unknowing, one is dragged away by it.
Only if a person has cultivated the power of past vows will they be willing to step back and reflect. Yongjia also said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature."
The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. The Dharma-body is realized as being without a single thing; it is the original nature, the self-existent, true Buddha.
If you contemplate in this manner, suddenly, at the point where thought cannot reach, you will see the Dharma-body that is devoid of even a single thing.
This is precisely the place where the person transcends birth and death. As for the "Dharma of non-attainment" mentioned previously, it cannot—
To seek with a mind that grasps at attainment—this is precisely the point. For a lifetime, scholars and officials have made their living within the realm of calculation and deliberation;
as soon as they hear a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) speak the Dharma of non-attainment, doubt arises in their hearts and they fear falling into emptiness.
Whenever Miaoxi sees someone speaking in this way, he immediately asks: "It is precisely because of this fear of falling into..."
"Emptiness" means returning to emptiness and non-existence. There are ten items comprising five pairs; they cannot be fully analyzed or categorized.

Generally, people take conceptualization and calculation as their habitual dwelling place. When they suddenly hear talk that cannot be grasped through thought or calculation, they become utterly bewildered and find no way to grasp it.
What they fail to realize is that this very state of having no way to grasp it is precisely where one rests.
This was the time when his life and spirit were at their peak. He established a bond with a fellow seeker; they met at Yimen during the Jingkang era.
At that time, he was in the full vigor of his prime, and he already knew there was this great matter of karmic destiny (not recorded in the narrative).

However, because he had extensively mastered a multitude of books and delved too deeply into the Nine Classics and Seventeen Histories, his intelligence was excessive and his intellectual pathways were overly complex.
Your power of concentration is too slight; you are dragged away by the circumstances of daily life as they arise.
Therefore, beneath your heels, you cannot achieve that sudden "crack" of realization or that decisive "snap" of severance.

If, from time to time, right mindfulness remains present and your fear of birth and death does not waver, then as days and months gradually pass, that which is raw will naturally become matured, and that which is matured will naturally become manifest. Furthermore, who is it?
This is the realm of the matured: it is that which is clever, sharp, and characterized by deliberation and calculation. What, then, is the realm of the raw?

It is bodhi, nirvāṇa, true thusness, and buddha-nature—beyond thought and discrimination, unreachable through weighing, measuring, or conjecture, and where you have no room for mental contrivance or arrangement.
Suddenly, when the time arrives, it may manifest through the circumstances of the ancients entering the Way.

Whether while reading the scriptures, or during daily activities in response to circumstances—whether good or bad, whether the body and mind are distracted, or when adverse or favorable conditions appear before one, or even when the consciousness of body, mind, and intellect momentarily attains stillness—one may suddenly trip over the pivot and overturn it;
this is no small matter. (Shown to Xu Dunli) A scholar who has extensively read many books does so fundamentally...

Rather than benefiting one's own consciousness, one instead memorizes the words of the ancients, storing them within one's breast to serve as resources for worldly affairs or as handles for conversation.
Little do they realize that this is contrary to the intent of the sages' teachings—what is called "counting another's treasures all day long while having not even half a coin of one's own.
The same applies to reading and studying the Buddhist teachings: one must see the moon and forget the finger; one must not rely on the words themselves.
This gives rise to understanding. An ancient worthy said: "The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to deliver all minds. I have no mind; what use have I for all dharmas?
If those with resolve who read books and study the teachings can act in this way, they will embody the intent of the Sage to some small degree.
(Shown to Li Xianchen) He further said: "Lately, in the monastic communities, [people] take the marvelous words and subtle..."
Regarding the exchange of questions and answers, they serve as causes and conditions for making distinctions and are used to entice those who study superficially;

these people fail to grasp the fundamental reality. When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they do so only fearing that others will not understand. Even when there are teachings involving concealment, they employ incidental analogies and parables merely to enable sentient beings to awaken and enter [the truth].
For example, when a monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha? Mazu replied, "This very mind is the Buddha. At this—
Regarding this realization, what further distinctions are there? Not realizing it here is precisely the very mind that is Buddha;

this is the causal condition for the distinction. For those who practice Chan, when examining the scriptures and the circumstances of the ancient masters’ entry into the Way, they should simply leave the mind empty.
They must not seek the profound or the marvelous, nor seek realization and entry within sounds, names, phrases, or meanings. If such a mind arises, [it is an obstacle].
This immediately obstructs one's own correct knowledge and vision, such that for kalpas on end there will be no point of entry. Panshan said: "It is like throwing a sword into the air;
do not debate whether it reaches its mark or not—it must not be treated with negligence. Vimalakīrti said: "The Dharma transcends the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
If you wish to penetrate this Dharma, you must first clear away the gates of the six sense organs so that not even the slightest transgression remains."
Suffering. What is meant by "calamity and suffering"? It is being driven about by forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, and mental objects, and being unable to distance oneself from them.
This refers to those who seek knowledge and views, searching for intellectual understanding within the scriptural teachings and the words of the ancient masters.

If one can, within the scriptural teachings and the causes and conditions for entering the Way described by the ancient masters, not give rise to a second thought, but directly realize the place of return, then—
Within one’s own realm or another’s realm, there is nothing that is not as one desires; there is no lack of mastery. When Deshan saw a monk enter the gate, he would strike him with his staff;
when Linji saw a monk enter the gate, he would shout at him. The venerable masters of all quarters call this "seizing [the student] by the face" and "directly handing it over.
Miaoxi calls this "the first-rate kind of dragging through mud and water. Even if one were to proceed toward a single...

Under a single blow of the staff or a single shout, one should be able to take it all upon oneself; yet such a person is already no true hero. They have already been doused over the head with a ladleful of foul water.
How much more so when, under a single blow of the staff or a single shout, they seek something extraordinary or search for a subtle understanding—this is the mark of one who lacks spirit.
Furthermore, regarding those who lack spirit (as shown to Deng Zili): Formerly, Marshal Li Wenhe went to study under [the Master].
Chan Master Cizhao Cong of Shimen realized the essential tenets of Linji. He had a verse that said:
"To study the Way, one must be an iron man; Upon touching the heart-mind, judgment is immediate. Directly seize supreme Bodhi; Pay no heed to any right or wrong."

"Exquisite indeed are these words! They may serve as seeds of illumination and as an aid for triggering the awakening. (Shown to Li Xianchen) It further states: "The Buddha is the medicine for sentient beings.
When the sickness of sentient beings is eliminated, the medicine is likewise of no further use.

Yet, if the sickness has departed while the medicine remains, one enters the realm of the Buddha but cannot enter the realm of Māra; this [remaining] sickness is equal to the sickness of sentient beings that has not yet been eliminated."
When the illness is cured, the medicine is discarded; when both Buddha and Mara are swept away, one begins to have a slight degree of resonance with this great matter of causal conditions.
The Buddha is one who has finished his business within the realm of sentient beings; sentient beings are those who have not finished their business within the realm of the Buddha.
If you wish to attain such oneness, simply let both Buddha and sentient beings be cast down at once; then there will be neither "finished" nor "unfinished."

An ancient worthy said: "If you merely understand that phenomena are non-phenomena, and you can see forms and hear sounds without being deaf (as shown by Nian Miaozheng), this person knows the principle that worldly conditioned things are empty, false, and unreal.
However, when encountering circumstances and conditions, if they suddenly collide before you and you do not follow them away, you will certainly have your nostrils pierced by them."
It is because, since time without beginning, that which has been familiarized has become too familiar, while that which is raw remains too raw.
Although one may momentarily recognize this and break through it, in the end, the power of the Way cannot overcome the power of karma. Now, what is the power of karma? It is the familiarized.
What is the power of the Way? It is the raw. However, the power of the Way and the power of karma originally have no fixed measure; one need only observe their manifestation in daily life.
It is simply a matter of being deluded or undeluded. If one is deluded regarding the power of the Way, then one is overcome by the power of karma.
When the power of karma prevails, every touch and movement becomes an obstruction. When every touch and movement becomes an obstruction, one becomes stained and attached everywhere.

When one is stained and attached everywhere, one takes suffering to be happiness. Therefore, the Elder Śākyamuni said to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra: "You take the characteristics of form and emptiness to oppose one another."
They contend for possession of the Tathāgatagarbha, yet the Tathāgatagarbha conforms to form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

Therefore, within it, the wind moves and the void is still; the sun is bright and the clouds are dark. Sentient beings are deluded and distressed, turning their backs on enlightenment and uniting with the dust of the senses;
thus they give rise to worldly appearances through the toil of defilement. This is what is meant by being obscured by the power of karma while the power of the Way is defeated. Śākyamuni—
The Old Master further said: "I unite my wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor born—with the Tathāgata-garbha;
yet the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it, the one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes the one."
The small manifests the large; the large manifests the small. Without moving from the site of enlightenment, one pervades the realms of the ten directions.
One’s body contains the infinite space of the ten directions; upon a single hair-tip, one manifests jeweled king-lands, and while sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
To say that this is the locus of actualization where the power of the Way overcomes the power of karma is not so; for both [powers] ultimately revert to being illusory.

If one abandons the power of karma while clinging to the power of the Way, I say that such a person does not understand the Buddhas’ skillful means of preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate. Why? Because the Elder Śākyamuni said: "If one grasps at the marks of dharmas..."

This is to become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. If one grasps at the mark of non-dharmas, one likewise becomes attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas. This refers to what was previously stated:
that the power of the Path and the power of karma have no fixed measure. If there is a man of wisdom who takes the power of the Path as his weapon to eliminate [afflictions].
The power of karma. Once the power of karma is eliminated, even the Way is illusory. Therefore it is said: "It is merely by means of provisional names that sentient beings are guided.
When one has not yet realized the breakthrough, there are thousands of difficulties and ten thousand hardships; once the breakthrough is realized, what difficulty or ease can there be?

Master Pang said: "Ordinary people are narrow in their resolve and capacity; they falsely claim there are difficulties and ease. To be free from marks is like space; it fully accords with the wisdom of all Buddhas.

The characteristics of the precepts are also like space, yet deluded people create for themselves the act of 'maintaining' them. They refuse to pull out the root of their sickness, merely playing with flower branches.
Do you wish to know the root of this sickness? It is nothing other than this very attachment to what is difficult and what is easy."

Those who give rise to false notions of acceptance and rejection fail to uproot this fundamental ailment; they will continue to drift and sink within the sea of birth and death, truly having no time of emergence.
Long ago, when the scholar Zhang Zhuo was pointed toward the source of his illness by a venerable master, he immediately understood and said:

To sever afflictions is to increase one's illness further; to strive toward True Suchness (Tathatā) is likewise a deviation. To follow worldly conditions according to their measure is to be without obstruction;
Nirvana and birth-and-death are equal to flowers in the sky. One must attain directness, harboring no doubt regarding the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and no doubt regarding birth-and-death.
Simply always allow your mind to remain vast and open. When circumstances arise, deal with them as they come, like still water or a clear mirror.
When good or evil, beauty or ugliness arrive, there is not even a hair’s breadth to escape. Know for certain that this state of no-mind is naturally inconceivable.
(To Lü Shunyuan) If you wish to recognize the Dharma, it is true suchness, the Buddha-nature, and bodhi.
To realize nirvana is this. Do you recognize the illness? It is deluded thought, inversion, greed, anger, and false views.
Nevertheless, apart from deluded thought and inversion, there is no true suchness or Buddha-nature; apart from greed, anger, and false views, there is no bodhi or nirvana.
Tell me, are they separate, or are they not separate? If they are separate, one remains while the other departs, and the illness becomes even deeper.
If one does not distinguish them, this is precisely the coarse and superficial Buddha-nature and the clumsy True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Ultimately, how can one explain the principle of "removing the disease but not removing the dharma"? There are some people who, hearing such talk, immediately say:

"The dharma is itself the disease; the disease is itself the dharma. They claim that as long as there is verbal expression, there is no real meaning. To follow True Suchness in this way is, in fact, a deluded inversion.
If you think that greed, anger, and false views are all the Dharma, then, following such delusions, true thusness, Buddha-nature, bodhi, and nirvana are all illnesses.
With such a view, do not say, "I wear the patched robe"; even as a servant to a master of the seat, you have not yet attained it.
Why? You must know that there are countless dead people on level ground; indeed, pass through them.
One who can deal with the forest of thorns is a skilled hand. As the ancients said:
"Even if there were a dharma that surpassed nirvāṇa, I would say it is likewise like a dream or an illusion.

If one can, within this dream-like illusion, realize it as it truly is, understand it as it truly is, cultivate it as it truly is, and practice it as it truly is—using the dharma of suchness to tame oneself—one gives rise to the Great [Vehicle].
With a compassionate mind, they employ various skillful means and are further able to subdue all sentient beings; yet, regarding these sentient beings,
they do not form the notion of "subduing" or "not subduing," nor do they form inverted notions,
nor notions of greed, anger, or false views, nor notions of true suchness, Buddha-nature, bodhi, or nirvana, nor notions of a disease to be removed or a dharma to be removed.
Do not harbor thoughts of preserving one part or discarding another, nor of division. Since such thoughts do not exist, there is the single path of pure, equal liberation.

(Wei Gong requests the ascent of the seat. Since it is said to be empty and illusory, then at the time of its creation it is illusory; at the time of its reception it is illusory; at the time of cognition it is illusory;
and at the time of delusion and inversion it is illusory. This is true for the past, the present, and the future alike.
This is an illusion. To know today that it is not real is to use illusory medicine to treat an illusory illness. When the illness is cured, the medicine is discarded;
according to this principle, one remains simply the person of former times. If there were a separate person or a separate dharma, that would be the view of a demon or a heterodox teacher.

(Answer to Zeng Tianyou) It is further said: "If even in the time it takes Maitreya to snap his fingers, Sudhana was able to suddenly forget all the samādhis realized by his various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), how much more so the habitual tendencies of beginningless, false, and evil karma?
If one were to take the sins previously committed as real, then all present and current phenomena would likewise be substantially existent—even one's official rank and wealth."

I hope that all your cherished attachments are entirely real; that you can distinguish between what is for future use and what is appropriate for the present conditions, such that you are not robbed by external objects;
that when looking at documents piled upon your desk, you are able to set them aside; that when encountering worldly things, you are able to turn away from them;
that when dwelling in a place of stillness, you do not harbor discursive thoughts; and that in investigating this very matter, you have no distracting notions. Thus, Huang—
The Master Laozi said: "The mind does not falsely grasp at past phenomena, nor does it covet or cling to future events;
it dwells nowhere in the present. One thoroughly understands that the three periods of time are entirely empty and quiescent.
As for past events, whether they were good or evil, there is no need to deliberate upon them; deliberation obstructs the Way. As for future events, there is no need to calculate them; calculation..."
It is chaotic. Whether present circumstances before you are favorable or adverse, there is no need to fixate on them;
for if you fixate, they will disturb the mind. Simply respond to everything as it arises according to conditions, and naturally this principle will be realized.
Adverse circumstances are easy to overcome; favorable circumstances are difficult to overcome. That which opposes my will requires only a single [thought].
The character for "patience" (ren) requires constant vigilance; in a moment, it passes away. When circumstances flow naturally, there is truly no place for you to evade them.
It is like a magnet and iron meeting: they join together in one place without either being aware of it. If even insentient objects behave thus, how much more so for sentient beings!
How much more so for those whose active ignorance remains entirely within, making their living there;
in such a state, if they lack wisdom, they remain unaware and unknowing, being led into the net by others, only to seek an exit from within it.
Is this not indeed difficult? Thus the former sages said: "To enter the world such that nothing remains outside of the supramundane—this is precisely this principle.
Recently, there has been a class of practitioners who have lost the skillful means;
they often mistake active ignorance for entering the world, and then forcibly arrange mundane dharmas as being the supramundane state where nothing remains.
How tragic this matter is! Unless one has made a vow from former lives, one will immediately recognize this [delusion] as broken, maintain mastery, and not be led astray by others.
Thus, Vimalakīrti said: "The Buddha speaks of abandoning lust, anger, and delusion as liberation for those with overweening pride;
for those without overweening pride, the Buddha says that the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is itself liberation. If...
To avoid this error, within the midst of adverse and favorable conditions, one must be without the marks of arising or ceasing;
only then can one truly leave behind the name of "one who has attained superior pride. Only in this way can one be said to have entered the world, and is called a man of real power.
All that has been explained above is what I, Miaoxi, have personally experienced throughout my life; even now, I practice in exactly this manner. May it be so.

Your Excellency, taking advantage of your physical vigor and strength, has likewise entered this samādhi. (To Vice-Director Da Lou: Having read your letter in detail, I now know that among the four modes of deportment, there is no interval of interruption;
you are not deprived by worldly busyness. Amidst the turbulent current, you frequently exercise intense self-reflection and never fall into negligence.
Your resolve for the Way becomes ever firmer as time passes, which deeply satisfies my humble mind. However, in this world...
The afflictions of worldly toil are like a blazing fire; when will they ever end? While in the midst of this clamor, you must not forget the matters of the bamboo chair and rush mat.
Having long applied your mind to states of stillness and victory, these are precisely what you require for use amidst the bustle.
If you gain no strength within the clamor, it is as if you have never practiced your cultivation in stillness. This is because your prior conditions have been muddled by distractions.
Now, as I lament receiving this retribution, I alone dare not obey your command. If one stirs such a thought, it obstructs the Way. An ancient worthy said:
"If you recognize your nature while following the current, there is neither joy nor sorrow. Vimalakīrti said: "For example, lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land;
they grow in low, damp, and muddy soil. The Old Barbarian [the Buddha] said: "True Suchness does not abide."

The intrinsic nature accomplishes all phenomena in accordance with conditions. As it is further said: "Responding to stimuli in accordance with conditions, there is nowhere it does not pervade, yet it constantly dwells upon this seat of Bodhi.
How could this be a deception of people? If one were to consider stillness as right and bustle as wrong, [one would be mistaken].
This means that one seeks the true mark by destroying worldly marks; one seeks quiescence by departing from arising and ceasing.

When you prefer stillness and loathe clamor, this is precisely the time to exert effort. Suddenly, amidst the clamor, you will overturn the news of stillness. This power is worth ten million billion times more than sitting upon a bamboo chair or a rush cushion.
(Answer to Zeng Tianyou) Having just attained tranquility of body and mind, you must— (Note: The final sentence is left incomplete as the source text ends abruptly.)
Exert yourself! Do not seek refuge in a place of quietude; the teachings call this the "frightful deep pit of liberation.
You must learn to turn like a rolling wheel, like a gourd upon the water—free and easy, unrestrained, entering the pure or the defiled without obstruction or sinking.
Only then will you have even a slight measure of intimacy within the gate of the patch-robed monks.
"If you merely manage to hold a child so that it does not cry, what use is there in that? (He showed the emptiness of wisdom. Linji said:
"If you can bring to rest the mind that incessantly pursues [objects], you will be no different from Śākyamuni Buddha himself. This is not a deception of people;
for even a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage, because the mind seeking Buddha-wisdom is not yet fulfilled, is called 'affliction. It is simply that there is no place for you to settle."

This is the arrangement. It is impossible to anticipate even a single point outside of it. Several years ago, there was a lay practitioner named Xu who recognized the gateway and the household register.
He sent a letter presenting his understanding, saying: "In daily life, everything is empty and vast; there is not a single thing with which to form a correspondence.
Only then does one know that the three realms and the myriad dharmas are fundamentally non-existent. It is truly peaceful, blissful, and refreshing."
He lived with a mind that could let go. He expressed this through a verse, saying: "Do not cling to places of purity; purity will bring one exhaustion.
Do not cling to places of pleasure; pleasure will drive one to madness. Like water that conforms to its vessel, it follows whatever shape—square or round, short or long."
Letting go or not letting go—consider this further with great care. Within the three realms and the myriad dharmas, where else could they possibly have their home?
If you simply remain thus, this matter will become greatly distorted. To inform you, Layman Xu: your own kinsmen are bringing about calamity.
Open wide the eye of the thousand sages; there is no need for frequent prayers and exorcisms (to Shi Yan Ziqing).

For a student of the Way, it is easy to empty the environment in daily life, but difficult to empty the mind. If the environment is empty but the mind is not, the mind will be overcome by the environment.
Simply empty the mind and the environment will naturally become empty. If the mind is already empty, yet you further give rise to a second thought, desiring to empty the environment, then this is...
If this mind has not yet attained emptiness, it will again be seized by external objects; as long as this affliction is not eliminated, there is no way to escape from birth and death.
As the elder Pang Gong presented this verse to Mazu: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action.
This is the field for selecting the Buddha; with an empty mind, one returns having passed the imperial examination. Once this mind is empty, what further thing exists outside of the mind?

And yet, can it be empty? Reflect on this (shown to Huang Boceng). When the mind does not run outward in pursuit, is free from false conceptualization, and does not rely upon various sensory objects, then this very house of fire and the toil of worldly afflictions are themselves the place of liberation and transcendence from the three realms. Why is this?
Does the Buddha not say: "To be without reliance and without dwelling amidst all objects, to be without discrimination, and to clearly perceive the Dharma-realm as vast and great"?
Establishing [the stages], they realize that all worlds and all phenomena are equal and non-dual.
Therefore, by the power of the wisdom of their own practice, Bodhisattvas on the Far-Going Ground (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi) transcend all followers of the two vehicles.

Although they have attained the treasury of the Buddha’s realm, they manifest as dwelling within the realm of Māra; although they have transcended the path of Māra, they manifest the practice of Māra’s arts; although they manifest as being the same [as others]...
They practice the ways of non-Buddhists yet do not abandon the Buddha-dharma; though they manifest compliance with all worldly conventions, they constantly practice all supramundane dharmas.
This is the true skillful means within the dust and toil of the burning house. For those who study Prajñā—
If one abandons these skillful means and instead conforms to worldly afflictions, one will certainly be seized and held by Māra.

Furthermore, within such conforming circumstances, they perversely propound their own logic, claiming that afflictions are themselves bodhi, and ignorance is itself great wisdom; thus, step by step, they walk upon existence.
They speak only of emptiness with their mouths, yet do not reproach themselves for being dragged along by the power of karma;

furthermore, they teach others to repudiate cause and effect, saying that drinking alcohol and eating meat are not separate from bodhi, and committing theft and engaging in sexual misconduct do not hinder prajñā. Such people as these—

Malevolent demons and poisons have entered their hearts and viscera, yet they remain entirely unaware of it. To seek to escape the toil of worldly existence under such conditions is like pouring oil onto a fire to extinguish it—how lamentable!

(This demonstrates True Suchness. Furthermore, it is said: Only after one has attained thorough penetration can one say that afflictions are identical to Bodhi and ignorance is identical to Great Wisdom.
Within the originally vast, quiescent, and wondrous mind, there is pure, perfect, and luminous clarity.
It is utterly vast and empty, without a single thing that can act as an obstruction, like the great void of space. Even the word "Buddha" is an external object;
how much more so could there be the dust and toil of afflictions to serve as its counterpart?
This matter is like the clear blue sky and the bright sun—resplendent, pure, unchanging, and unmoving; it neither decreases nor increases, being present in the daily activities of every person.
It responds to conditions; it is luminous in every head and manifest in every object. One cannot grasp it, yet it ever remains when let go.
Vast and unimpeded, it is clearly empty and void. Like a gourd upon the water, it cannot be pulled or entangled.
Since antiquity, those who possess the Way have used it to emerge from and submerge within the sea of birth and death with complete freedom.
The essence and its enjoyment are complete, lacking nothing and leaving nothing behind. One does not perceive any state of birth-and-death or worldly affliction (*saṃsāra-kleśa*).
It is like splitting sandalwood: every fragment is [the whole]. What could one use to constitute birth-and-death and worldly affliction? From where would birth-and-death and worldly affliction arise?
When the cause is gathered and the fruit is realized, where then would they be placed? Since there is no place for them to abide, then even the Buddha is an illusion.
Dharmas are like illusions. The twenty-five states of existence within the three realms, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements—all are utterly empty and vast.
When one reaches this state, even the single word "Buddha" has no place to abide.
If even the word "Buddha" finds no place to rest, where then could true suchness, Buddha-nature, bodhi, or nirvana exist? Thus, Master Fu said: "I fear..."
In human life, one cuts through views; for the time being, one establishes provisional names. Those who study the Way must understand that they cannot proceed in a single direction.
Regarding the causes and conditions for the ancients entering the Way: they sought the profound, they sought the subtle, they sought the extraordinary, and they sought intellectual understanding.

Yet they were unable to see the moon and forget the finger, failing to cut everything through with a single stroke. As Yongjia said: "From an empty fist, one gives rise to real understanding. This is the root.

Within the phenomena of the objective world, one falsely fabricates and clings to monstrosities; amidst the five aggregates, twelve bases, eighteen elements, and the afflictions of the twenty-five realms of existence, one delusively imprisons oneself through attachment. The Tathāgata calls such a person "one who is to be pitied. As the Master Yantou said:
"If you simply have no desires and no dependencies, you are yourself the Benevolent One (Śākyamuni). In the end, there is only this one parent."
This lump of flesh that was born, when not even a single breath arrives, immediately falls under the jurisdiction of another. Aside from this lump of flesh, what else is there?
What can you take as something extraordinary, mysterious, or sublime? What can you take as bodhi, nirvana, true suchness, or buddha-nature?

There are two matters that must be kept close to the tip of the nose: first, where one dwells; and second, not knowing where one will go after death.
Amidst tea and rice, in stillness and in bustle, one must be diligent in every thought-moment, as if constantly owing a debt of a million strings of cash with no way to repay it.
The chest and heart are oppressed with distress; there is no way to evade it. One cannot seek life, yet one cannot seek death.
At such a time, the paths of good and evil are both about to be severed. When you realize this moment, it is precisely when you must apply yourself with effort.
Right here, examine the *huatou* (critical phrase). A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No."
When looking, do not use measurement; do not use commentary; do not seek to understand through intellectual analysis;
do not take responsibility at the point where words are uttered; do not construct logic at the point where [the mind] is raised; and do not fall into the state of empty stillness.
Do not attempt to awaken through equanimity of mind; do not seek to comprehend by relying on the words of the masters;
do not fall into the trap of "non-affairs. Rather, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, constantly maintain mindfulness at all times: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature, or not?"
There is nothing. When you have become thoroughly familiar with this "calling forth" (tisi), it transcends verbal deliberation and mental reflection;

within the square inch of your mind, there is a state of being unsettled, like biting a raw iron peg—when there is no flavor at all, do not by any means let your resolve falter. When you reach such a moment, it is indeed a favorable sign.
Have you not seen the ancient master say: "The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to deliver all minds; I have not one..."
Exert yourself with all your heart. Of what use are all the dharmas? It is not only thus under the gate of the Patriarchs;
the entire Great Canon of teachings spoken by the Buddha is entirely this same principle. Yet sentient beings have heavy obstructions from evil karma;

as soon as they get out of bed each day, their consciousness becomes distracted and scattered, calculating fame and profit, carrying around the burden of self and others, and falling into deluded thoughts and inversions from dawn until dusk.
Like links of a chain or rings of a hook, they continue in succession without interruption, and one never grows weary of them.
Suddenly, a single thought arises, and one directs the mind toward this very gate to contemplate it, immediately seeking to understand the workings of the mind, intellect, and consciousness.

Yet, as nothing can be arranged or settled, affliction arises; one wishes to stop at once, yet there is no end to the reasons for which people speak in such a manner—those who do so are beyond counting. Śun...

The original companions of the Way, however, were not like this. Having realized that all manner of things within the realm of deficiency are empty and illusory, they focused their minds with single-minded intent upon investigating the matter beneath their own heels: from where does birth come, and to where does death go?
Since they knew neither the place of origin nor the destination, there remained now a vivid, solitary clarity that distinguished right from wrong for others.
Whether it be good or ugly, there must be a determination as to whether it exists or not, whether it is real or illusory.
One must simply wait until it is like a person drinking water who knows for themselves its coldness or warmth, rather than receiving instructions from the mouths of others.

Suddenly, with a single burst of realization, one arrives at the ultimate state of peace, great rest, and great cessation; only then does one truly accept it oneself. Bring this scroll here to seek [instruction].
Instruction: Grasp the brush and let it fly at random; thus, a single tangle of complications is formed. Now, things do not arise in isolation; their arising must have a cause.
If you persist in interpreting this as a mere tangle of complications, how can you ever succeed? Have you not seen that in the past, Master Zihu said:
"The Patriarch’s coming from the West was simply this: winter cold and summer heat, night dark and day bright."
It is simply because you disciples have no intention, yet create intentions; you cause trouble where there is no trouble;
you forcibly construct "inner" and "outer" where there is neither inner nor outer; and you frivolously speak of "east" and "west" where there is neither east nor west.
For this reason, your *śamatha* cannot be clear, and thus your faculties and objects cannot be mastered with freedom. Judging by this, Shun-yuan never came to Miaoxi to seek Dharma words. Miaoxi...

Xiyuan has never written a single character. Whether it be winter’s cold or summer’s heat, the darkness of night or the brightness of day, from within, without, and in between, or east, west, south, and north—it has never been altered, increased, or decreased by even a hair’s breadth. Why is this?
In my school there are no words or phrases, nor is there a single dharma given to others. Since not a single dharma is given to others, that which you are writing right now is precisely this.
What is it? That which is called "cold in winter and hot in summer, both inside and out" — what is that?
That which has never shifted by so much as a single hair’s breadth in the east, west, south, or north — what is that? *Tut!* Even "existence" cannot be found.
Non-existence cannot be apprehended. Winter’s cold and summer’s heat cannot be apprehended. The internal, the external, and the intermediate cannot be apprehended.
One who speaks thus cannot be apprehended; one who receives such speech cannot be apprehended.
Not even a single hair’s breadth can be apprehended. Neither the primordial source nor the wondrous joy can be apprehended. It is ungraspable.
Attainment is also unattainable. Within this unattainability, one simply attains it. When Shunyuan reached this point, how should he have practiced?
This very "how should he practice? has no place for attachment. Only then does one not even accept these words.
Since these words are not accepted, Miaoxi has nothing to say, and Shunyuan has nothing to hear. This state of having nothing to say is—
The true teaching is this: that which is without hearing is true hearing. Thus, Wondrous Joy (*Abhirati*) is identical to Shun-yuan; Shun-yuan is identical to Wondrous Joy.
Wondrous Joy and Shun-yuan are non-dual and cannot be divided; they are without distinction and without interruption.
When the Great Statue of Jiazhou eats yellow gall (*hanyanglian*), the Iron Ox of Shanfu has his mouth full of bitterness. Is it bitter or not? Look clearly: there is nothing to be found.
Look! Alas! That mind which, when alive, does not know its place of origin and, when dead, does not know its destination, has not yet perished.
This is precisely the state where birth and death intersect. Simply, at this very point of intersection, observe the pivot of the koan.
A monk asked Master Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou said, "No. Simply take up this doubt: that while alive, one does not know where one comes from...
When the mind that does not know where it goes at death is shifted onto the "Wordless," then the entangled mind will no longer function.
Once the entangled mind ceases to function, the mind that doubts whether one comes from birth or goes toward death will be severed.
Simply hang over the precipice at the point where [the doubt] is about to cease but has not yet ceased. When the time and conditions arrive, suddenly—*pèn!*—with a single blow, it is finished.

If you can sacrifice your life, only then will you be willing to take the initiative yourself.

at that moment, you will finally believe that stillness is precisely the time of bustle, and bustle is precisely the time of stillness, and speech is precisely silence.
The time of silence is itself the time of speech. One need not rely on questioning others, nor will one naturally fall prey to the heterodox talk and confused doctrines of false teachers.

When performing any action, what form or segment does it possess? Once the task is accomplished, it follows the movements of my own mind.
There is nothing that does not encompass, and there is not the slightest excess. At this very moment, by whose power of grace do you receive it?

It is like a person drinking water: they know its coldness or warmth themselves; it cannot be described to others, nor can it be presented to others. As the former masters said: "If one speaks of realization, it cannot be shown to others;
