Regarding the point of awakening: only those who have already realized it, attained it, believed it, and awakened to it can silently accord with one another.
Those who have not yet realized, attained, believed, or awakened to it do not only lack faith themselves; they also do not believe that others possess such a realm of experience.
Elder Layman, your natural disposition is close to the Way. It is evident that whatever you do is free from attachment; it would be even easier for you to [understand] otherwise.
If one compares this to others, nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine out of ten thousand parts have already been saved; it requires only one final exhalation to complete the task.

When scholar-officials study the Way, they often fail to engage with it substantively. Aside from mere verbal discussion and mental deliberation, they are left utterly bewildered, with no place to set their hands or feet.
Do not doubt that this very state of being at a loss for what to do is precisely where the excellence lies.
In this state, one merely desires in the mind to grasp it through deliberation and wishes in speech to explain it with clarity; yet one does not realize that this is precisely where one has erred.
The Buddha said: "The Tathāgata uses all manner of metaphors to explain various matters, but there is no metaphor capable of explaining this Dharma.
Why? Because the pathways of mind and intellect are severed; it is inconceivable. Thus, one should know by faith that it transcends the realm of deliberation.
It will certainly obstruct the path to enlightenment. If one attains the severance of the past and future limits, the pathways of mind and intellect will naturally cease.
Once the pathways of mind and intellect have ceased, whatever various matters are spoken of are all this very Dharma.
When this Dharma is clarified, that very place of clarity is itself the inconceivable realm of great liberation. This realm itself is likewise inconceivable. Realm.
Since it is inconceivable, all metaphors are also inconceivable; various phenomena are also inconceivable.
Even this very inconceivability is itself inconceivable. This statement, too, has no place of attachment.

Even this state of non-attachment is inconceivable. Thus, through successive inquiry into phenomena, dharmas, analogies, and realms, it is like a ring without beginning or end; having neither point of origin nor point of exhaustion, all are inconceivable dharmas.
Therefore it is said: "The Bodhisattva dwells in the inconceivable, yet within it he engages in contemplation."
It is inexhaustible. Entering this inconceivable state, both thought and non-thought are utterly quiescent;
yet one must not abide in that state of quiescence. If one were to abide in the state of quiescence, one would be governed by the measure of the *dharmadhātu*.

In the teachings, this is called the affliction of the *dharmārambaṇa* (dharma-dust). One must extinguish the measure of the *dharmadhātu*, so that all manner of supreme qualities manifest simultaneously.

Only when [all conceptualization] has been utterly exhausted can one truly behold such things as "the cypress tree in the courtyard," "three pounds of hemp," "a dried piece of excrement," "the dog has no Buddha-nature," "swallowing the waters of the West River in a single gulp," or "the East Mountain walks upon the water.

If one suddenly penetrates through a single phrase, only then is it called the "Infinite Dedication of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-apramāṇa-pariṇāmanā*). One sees it as it truly is; one sees it as it really is.
Acting thus and employing things as they truly are, one is able to manifest jewel-king lands upon a single hair-tip and turn the great wheel of Dharma within a speck of dust.
One accomplishes all manner of dharmas and destroys all manner of dharmas;

everything is governed by me, just as a strong man extends his arm without relying on external force, or as a lion roams about without seeking a companion. Such are the various supreme and wondrous realms.
When the realms manifest before one, the mind is not startled or amazed. When various conditions of evil karma manifest before one, the mind feels no fear or dread.
Amidst the four modes of daily conduct, one follows circumstances with relaxed ease, wandering freely and spontaneously.
Only when one reaches this state can it be said that there is neither heaven nor hell. Yongjia said: "There is neither person nor Buddha. Great.
The thousand sands of worlds are like bubbles in the ocean; all sages and worthies are like lightning flashes.
If this old man had not reached this state, how could he have spoken such words? Many have misunderstood these words; if one has not thoroughly penetrated the root source, [one will surely err].
Unable to refrain from forming interpretations based on the literal words, one then asserts that "all things are non-existent," thereby negating cause and effect.
One treats all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas and Patriarchs as mere falsehoods, claiming they are intended only to delude and mislead people.

If this malady is not eliminated, one will wander aimlessly and recklessly, inviting calamity and disaster. The Buddha said: "The empty, false, and floating mind gives rise to many clever views. If not...

If you cling to existence, you cling to non-existence; if you do not cling to these two, you will instead engage in conceptual calculations and speculative deliberations between existence and non-existence.
Even if you recognize this sickness, you will certainly remain stuck in a deluded inversion regarding that which is neither existent nor non-existent.

Therefore, the ancient sages spoke with bitter urgency and earnestness, instructing one to leave behind the four propositions and cut off the hundred negations, striking a single blow to resolve everything into two parts, so that no further thoughts or reflections arise.

First: "Seated, one cuts off the summit of the thousand sages. As for the "four propositions," they are: existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, and both existence and non-existence.
If one can penetrate these four propositions, then when seeing it said that all phenomena truly exist, I will likewise accord with them and speak of existence;
yet, I shall not be obstructed by this "true existence. When seeing it said that all phenomena...
If they say that things truly do not exist, I also accord with them and tell them they do not exist; yet this is not a mere worldly emptiness or voidness.
If they see and say that all phenomena both exist and do not exist, I also accord with them and tell them they both exist and do not exist;
yet this is not frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). If they see and say that all phenomena neither exist nor do not exist, I also accord with them and tell them so.
"Neither existent nor non-existent; furthermore, they are not contradictory. As Vimalakīrti said:
"The six heterodox teachers fell into error, and you have likewise followed them into that same fall. (This was in response to Zhang Yangshu. Zhaozhou said:
"Every day, except for the two meals of porridge and rice, this old monk has no other occasion for the distracted use of mind. Now tell me, where has this old fellow gone wrong?"

If you can recognize his true face here, only then may it be said that walking is Chan and sitting is Chan, and that whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, the essence remains at peace.
If you have not yet reached this state, you must constantly take a step back and look beneath your own feet.
Investigate thoroughly and minutely: "I am one who can know the likes and dislikes, the strengths and weaknesses of others; whether they are ordinary or sage-like, existent or non-existent.
Pushing the investigation further and further until you reach a point where there is nothing left to investigate—like a rat entering a cow's horn.
Suddenly the stolen heart is severed; this is precisely where you, the person, set down your four-cornered feet and sit securely at home (shown to Xiong Shuya).
I have learned with deep sorrow that your fifth son has passed away due to illness. The affection between father and son endures through a thousand births and a hundred kalpas.
The flow of affection and attachment—imagine yourself in such a state. (There must be some corruption or omission here. It is impossible [for such things to exist].

Within the world of the five turbidities, all things are various illusions; not a single one is real. I entreat you: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, constantly maintain this contemplation.
Then, as days pass and months deepen, it will gradually be worn away. However, when you are truly in a state of affliction, examine it minutely and interrogate it thoroughly from its source.
From where does it arise? If you exhaustively investigate the place of its arising and find nothing, then from where does this underlying affliction of the present moment come?
At the very moment of affliction, is it existent or non-existent? Is it empty or substantial? Investigate and investigate until the mind has nowhere to go.
If you wish to reflect, simply reflect; if you wish to weep, simply weep. Weep and weep until you have no more tears; reflect and reflect until you have no more thoughts.
Go! When you have shaken off and exhausted the many habitual tendencies of affection and attachment within the *ālayavijñāna*, it will naturally be like ice returning to water;
thus you shall return to that original state which is without affliction, without deliberation, and without sorrow or joy.
One enters the mundane and the supramundane without remainder. Mundane phenomena are the Buddha-dharma; the Buddha-dharma is mundane phenomena.

The nature between father and son is one and the same. If a son were to die and the father felt no affliction and had no thoughts of him, or if a father were to die and the son felt no affliction and had no thoughts of him—would that still be possible? If one forcibly suppresses such feelings when weeping...
Furthermore, one does not dare to weep; when contemplating, one also does not dare to contemplate.

This is specifically an attempt to oppose the Way of Heaven and extinguish the nature of Heaven, like raising a sound to stop an echo or pouring oil to extinguish a fire. When in the midst of affliction (*kleśa*), it is entirely nothing other than an external matter;
one must simply not form thoughts of it being something external. Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; it is the illusory, empty body."
This is the Dharma-body. It is true speech, real speech; it is not deceptive and not false speech. Once you have seen it thus, neither deliberation nor affliction can be found.
One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation; any other contemplation is not so.
This is called "erroneous contemplation. Since the erroneous and the correct have not yet been distinguished, one must apply diligent effort.

This is the definitive meaning of Wondrous Joy (*Abhirati*). Do not speak of this before those who lack wisdom. (Response to Wang Yanzhang) The daily activities and manifestations of sentient beings are ignorance (*avidyā*).

When they follow along with ignorance, they give rise to joy; when they oppose ignorance, they give rise to affliction (*kleśa*). Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not like this; they borrow ignorance in order to...
To perform the work of a Buddha. Sentient beings take ignorance as their dwelling place;
to oppose them is to destroy their dwelling, whereas to comply with them is to guide them according to their attachments. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"The host of afflictions is the seed of the Tathāgata. As Yongjia says: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body. Thus...
This principle was also [taught] to Zhang Taifu Yizhi: "Examine thoroughly beneath your own heels:
from where does this person who attains wealth and honor come? Where will this person currently enjoying wealth and honor go in the future?

Time is not some other thing; simply look at this very point: the head-word (*huatou*). When a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha?
Yunmen replied, "A dried piece of dung. Just bring up this story; when all your clever stratagems are suddenly exhausted, you will awaken.

You must by all means avoid seeking out texts for citations or engaging in reckless speculation and commentary. Even if you were able to provide a clear explanation through such commentaries, [it would be of no avail].
To have such a lapse is entirely the livelihood of ghosts. If the doubt has not been resolved, life and death will intermingle.
If the doubt is resolved, then the mind of birth and death is severed. When the mind of birth and death is severed, the vision of Buddha and the vision of dharmas perish.

If even the vision of Buddha and the vision of dharmas have perished, how much less would one give rise again to the views of sentient beings and afflictions? Simply take that which is bewildered and distressed...

Shift the mind onto the dry dung pellet and strike it once, holding fast. Then, the mind that fears birth and death, the mind that is bewildered and distressed, the mind that calculates and discriminates, and the mind that seeks cleverness will naturally cease to function. When you realize they no longer function, do not fear falling into emptiness.
Suddenly, at the very point where you have struck and held fast, all news and signs vanish; there is a sense of incomparable joy and liberation for the rest of one’s life.
Once the flow of news has been cut off, the views of a Buddha, the views of dharmas, and the views of sentient beings will arise;

yet, through conceptualization and discrimination, one may employ cleverness to expound upon principles, all of which will not hinder one another. In the four modes of conduct during daily life, simply remain constantly relaxed and open.
Whether in a quiet place or a noisy one, constantly use the "dry dung picket" to rouse yourself. As days pass and months come, the water buffalo will naturally become proficient.
First, you must not give rise to further doubts elsewhere; once the doubt regarding the dry dung picket is shattered, the doubts as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will all be shattered at once.
(Answer to Lü Longli; shown to Ceng Tianyou: Do not merely focus on the words and phrases of the ancients as if stacking a pagoda.)

This is like a child’s play: one layer finished, another begins; it is a waste of effort with no end in sight. Simply maintain the mind in one place, and there is nowhere it will not reach the bottom. When the time and conditions arrive, you will naturally strike it and bump into it, and suddenly, with a great startle, you will realize it.

Is there still a fault in not giving rise to a single thought? He said: "Mount Sumeru. When nothing at all can be brought forth, what then? "Let it go. If you cannot resolve your doubt here, simply investigate right here;

there is no need to create further complications for yourself. In response to Lü Juren, he said: "A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but a single doubt. If the doubt is broken upon the *huatou*, then a thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are broken all at once. If the *huatou* is not broken, then for the time being, deal directly with it."

To abandon the "head-word" (hua-tou) and instead give rise to doubt regarding texts, give rise to doubt regarding the scriptures and teachings, give rise to doubt regarding the public cases (gong-an) of the ancients, or give rise to doubt amidst the mundane toil of daily life—all these are the retinue of demons and spirits.
Once you have established this mind, first of all, do not be hasty; for haste leads to delay. Nor must you be lax, for laxity leads to indolence.
It is like the method of tuning a lute: the tension and looseness must hit the middle way before a melody can be formed.
Simply, in the midst of daily activities and in response to circumstances, observe from time to time that which is capable of discerning right from wrong and straight from crooked for others.
By whose power of grace do you receive this? Ultimately, from where does it flow forth? Search and examine it again and again;
the path by which you have always been born will become familiar. Once that place of birth is familiar, then that familiar place will, in turn, give rise to birth. What is that familiar place?

It is the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the twenty-five states of existence. It is ignorance, karmic consciousness, and volition.
The mind-consciousness that calculates and discriminates flashes and flickers day and night, like a wild horse that never pauses for rest.
This very chain causes people to wander through birth and death and leads them to commit unwholesome deeds.
Once this chain arises, however, Bodhi, Nirvana, True Suchness, and Buddha-nature will manifest before one. At the moment they manifest, it is likewise...
Since there is no measure of direct manifestation, the ancient masters realized it through their own realization and explained it thus: "When responding to the eye, it is like the thousand suns;
the myriad phenomena cannot escape their shadows and forms. When responding to the ear, it is like a deep valley; great and small sounds are never lacking.
Such matters do not require seeking from others nor borrowing the power of others; they spontaneously manifest and respond within the conditions of the environment.
"Vivacious and lively! You have not yet attained such a state. For now, take that mind which contemplates the worldly dust and toil, and turn it toward the place where contemplation cannot reach.
Try to contemplate there (referring to the practice of contemplating the 'wordless' *hua-tou*, etc.). [This was said in response to Rong Maoshu.

Since you already know that this great matter of causal connection is definitely not obtained from another person, you should then immediately and completely relinquish external objects, at all times..."
Push and investigate beneath your own heels. Pushing and investigating again and again, you will find no "pushing mind" within, nor any "object pushed" without.
It is pure and naked, bare and clear, with nothing to grasp. Like a gourd floating on water, it cannot be moved by anyone;
it is eternally vast and open, such that one cannot constrain or entangle it.

It is attained. As soon as it is struck, it moves; as soon as it is touched, it turns. Thus sovereign, thus suddenly liberated, thus numinous and holy—it does not share the same path as the thousand sages, nor does it borrow from the patch-robed monks. It can directly issue commands to the Buddhas and Patriarchs, such that the Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot command it.
When a person recognizes this kind of matter, they should immediately exert their full brilliance and focus toward the hundred [doubts].

Take another step beyond the tip of the measuring pole. If one can take this step, then one is no different from the youth Sudhana, who took a single step within a pore of Samantabhadra’s body and traversed worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Walking in this manner until the end of all future kalpas, one would still be unable to know even a single pore.
The sequential order of the oceans of lands, the treasury of the oceans of lands, the distinctions within the oceans of lands, the universal entry into the oceans of lands,
the formation of the oceans of lands, the destruction of the oceans of lands, and the adornments of the oceans of lands—

all such boundless realms as these are not attained through outwardly directed thought or deliberate effort in cultivation and realization. They are simply the Way that has been fundamentally complete beneath one’s own feet.

This is indeed the principle. I have not seen Master Deshan say: "If you simply remain non-active toward the mind and mindless toward phenomena, then you will be empty yet spiritual, void yet wondrous.
If there is even a hair’s breadth of talk regarding the beginning or end of this, it is all self-deception."
Why is this? A single thought tied to the slightest degree becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting emotion arises and one is shackled for ten thousand kalpas.
Holy names and mundane titles are all but empty sounds; extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not be burdened?
When you grow weary of them, they again become a great affliction. To speak thus is like striking the head of a stone man with a staff—*baò!* (a sound of sudden realization).

To speak plainly of the actual reality: what was said previously—that internally one does not perceive a mind capable of inference, and externally one does not perceive an object to be inferred—is precisely this principle.
This principle is more readily perceived when looking at it through concrete phenomena.
If you turn toward the mental faculty to engage in deliberation and calculation, you will become increasingly remote and distant from the truth.
This is why, at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, Śākyamuni Buddha could only save an eight-year-old girl;
at the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, he could only save a young boy; and at the assembly of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, he could only save a butcher. Observe these three individuals.
As for the manner of attaining Buddhahood, how has one ever sought realization from without? Despite all the diligent cultivation and study, the Buddha said only this:
"I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. He spoke only of providing such a guarantee;
he certainly did not say there is a dharma to be transmitted that causes you to run abroad in search of it before you can become a Buddha. Fortunately, there is...

Given such a fundamental nature, why do you not believe it? If you can, at this very moment, believe with direct penetration—neither seeking outwardly nor grasping for realization within the mind—then throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, you will be liberated wherever you are. Why is this?
Since you no longer seek outwardly, the inner mind is tranquil; since you no longer grasp for realization within the mind, external objects...
Tranquil and secluded. Thus the Patriarch said: "Circumstances and conditions have neither good nor evil; good and evil arise from the mind.
If the mind does not insist on naming them, from where would deluded sentiments arise? Since deluded sentiments do not arise, the true mind is free to know all-pervasively.

One should understand that the internal mind and external objects are but a single matter; one must by all means avoid viewing them as two separate things. Recall how Miaoyan asked Yangshan: "Miao..."

Regarding the "wondrously pure and luminous mind," Yangshan asked, "Can it be called a 'phenomenon'? Guishan replied, "Just so, just so.
(The Master Shizhong’s detailed account of this event is not recorded here. He was subsequently given the title "Layman Wujing" (Wondrously Pure). The Master Shizhong exhorted him:
"Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, even in moments of haste or distress, you must never forget the meaning of the wondrously pure and luminous mind. When deluded thoughts arise..."
You must exert effort to cast it aside. Simply take up the monk’s question: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? and Zhaozhou’s reply: "No.
As you take this up again and again, even the one who takes up this saying will not be seen to exist.

Then, even this very awareness that does not see anything existing will not be seen to exist. After that, these words will have no point of reception; suddenly, within this state of having nothing to receive—
The place of reception: when one does not consciously perceive the loss of voice during a great laugh that lasts for a single circuit, this is precisely the place of returning home to sit securely.

(Shown to Zhao Shichong) Yantou said: "If you wish to propagate the Great Teaching at a later time, it must flow forth from your own breast one by one, covering heaven and earth; only then is it the deed of a true man. Yantou’s words were not [mere rhetoric].
This alone clarifies the spiritual capacity of Xuefeng and may serve as a model for ten thousand generations of those who study this Way.
What is called "flowing forth from the breast" is one's own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) since beginningless time; it is inherently complete from the start.
As soon as a second thought arises, one falls into conceptual inference (*anumāna*). Conceptual inference is a dharma obtained through the adornments of external objects.

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the matter of that which existed before one's parents were born, beyond the realm of King Wei-yin. That which is attained through direct perception possesses coarse power;
that which is attained through inference (*anumāna*) possesses weak power. One with coarse power can enter the realm of the Buddha and can also enter the realm of Māra.
One with weak power may succeed in entering the realm of the Buddha, but will often retreat from the realm of Māra.
They are beyond counting. This matter does not depend on being clever or sharp-witted, nor does it depend on having dull faculties or shallow understanding.

To speak according to reality, it is simply taken as the standard mark by a single spray of water hitting the ground. As soon as one receives this news, whatever words or phrases there may be do not stand apart from the truth;
wherever they are established, that very place is the truth itself. This is what is meant by "flowing forth from the breast. It is because...

To cover heaven and encompass earth is simply this; it is not a matter of composing words to seek something extraordinary that others cannot express, nor is it a matter of a "brocade heart and embroidered mouth" with clever and novel phrasing, which one then claims flows from the depths of one's own breast (addressed to Zeng Shuchi).
If you wish to study this Way, you must investigate it beneath your own feet. As soon as you involve yourself in even a hair’s breadth of intellectual views, you have already missed the mark.

The news from beneath the heels has been communicated; once this news from beneath the heels is thoroughly understood, all manner of knowledge and views are nothing other than matters beneath the heels.
Thus the Patriarch said: "When speaking of knowledge and views, knowledge and views are themselves the mind; when the mind is present, it is knowledge and views; knowledge and views are right now.
If one does not stray from this present moment for even a single thought, one is directed toward that which lies beneath the heels.
Suddenly cast away all knowledge and views, and you will walk hand-in-hand with the Patriarch.

Since you have not yet reached this state, take care not to fall into error regarding knowledge and views (as indicated by the sequence of characters). To study worldly dharmas, one relies entirely upon verbal discussion and mental deliberation;

to study world-transcending dharmas, the use of verbal discussion and mental deliberation keeps one far removed from the truth. Did the Buddha not say: "This Dharma is not within the sphere of thought or deliberation"?

This is something that can only be understood by those who are distinct [from the ordinary]. Yongjia said: "The depletion of the Dharma-treasure and the destruction of merit—none of these fail to arise from this mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Indeed, the mind, intellect, and consciousness are the den of deliberation and discrimination.

If you truly wish to shoulder this great matter of karmic conditions, I urge you to exert your utmost vigor and take this very thing as your vanguard when advancing and your rearguard when retreating.
The root of the demon of birth and death is severed with a single stroke; this is precisely the moment of emerging.

It is only at such a time that one can truly employ the mouth to discuss it or the mind to contemplate it. Why is this? Once the eighth consciousness is eliminated, the demon of birth and death has no place to dwell.
When the demon of birth and death has no place to dwell, that which was used for calculation and discrimination is entirely transformed.
If there is no wisdom more subtle than this, not even by a hair’s breadth, that can act as an obstruction for me—this is why it is said:
"Observing the sequence of phenomena, one discriminates with wisdom; having definitively determined right from wrong, one does not violate the Seal of the Dharma.
Upon reaching this stage, whatever cleverness one employs and whatever principles one expounds are all the realm of great quiescence, great ultimate realization, and great liberation. Furthermore...
It is not some other thing. Thus Panshan said: "The whole mind is Buddha; the whole Buddha is the person. This is it.
Until you have attained such [realization], you must, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, never allow the mind, intellect, or consciousness to gain the upper hand.

After a long time of pure cultivation, you will naturally reach a state where there is no need to exert effort to dispel [delusions]. (Shown to Xie Kuoran) Ordinary calculating and arranging is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Sentimentality—that which flows and migrates through birth and death—is also the functioning of consciousness; that which is fearful and terrified is also the functioning of consciousness.
Yet those who study the Way today do not recognize this as a sickness; they merely bob up and down within it.
As the scriptures say, "They follow consciousness rather than wisdom," and for this reason, they obscure the radiance of their original ground and their fundamental nature.

Face and eyes. If at some moment you can let go completely, without a single thought of calculation or deliberation, and suddenly stumble and step upon your own nostrils, then this very consciousness and emotion is itself the wondrous wisdom of true emptiness; there is no other wisdom to be attained.
If there were something else to be attained or something else to be realized, then it would not be so. It is like a person who, when lost, calls the east "west."
When one acts toward the west, upon reaching the moment of awakening, that very west becomes the east; there is no separate east at all.
This wondrous wisdom of true emptiness shares its lifespan with the great void of space. Within this very great void, is there even a single thing that can obstruct it?
Although it does not receive even a single object as an obstruction, it does not hinder various objects from coming and going within space.
This wondrous wisdom of true emptiness is likewise: the defilements of birth-and-death, of ordinary beings and sages, cannot stain it by so much as a single speck.

Although they cannot stain it, it does not obstruct the coming and going of birth-and-death, ordinary beings, and sages therein. (Answer to Zeng Tianyou) The fire of the mind blazes fiercely, shimmering without ceasing.
Greed, anger, and delusion follow one another like a chain of linked hooks, continuing without interruption.
If one lacks a fierce and resolute will, as the days and months pass by, one will unwittingly be seized and held by the demon of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*).

If, however, one can for a single moment realize that conditioned arising is non-arising, one need not depart from greed, anger, and delusion; by employing the seal of the Demon King in reverse, one drives away all demonic hordes.
To act as a protector of the Dharma is not a matter of forced effort; it is simply because the nature of the Dharma is thus (as shown by Xie Kuoran).
Zen is not found in places of stillness, nor in places of clamor, nor in the realm of conceptualization and discrimination, nor in the sphere of daily activities responding to conditions.
Nevertheless, one must by no means abandon places of stillness, places of clamor, the sphere of daily activities responding to conditions, or the faculty of thought.
[The Master] consulted the *Fenbie chu* (Discriminating Places). Suddenly his eyes opened: "All these are matters within one's own house" (he showed this to Vice Minister Nie).
If you do not lose clarity amidst the conditions encountered in daily life, then as the days and months gradually pass, it will naturally coalesce into a single whole.
Where are these places of encountering conditions? They are when you are joyful, when you are angry, when you are adjudicating public affairs, and when you are exchanging greetings with guests.
When gathering with wife and children, when contemplating good and evil, and when encountering circumstances and conditions—these are all moments of a sudden, single burst.
(Shown to Xiong Shuya) Remember this principle ten thousand times over: it is simply because it is too near.
It does not go beyond the range of one’s own eyes; where the eyes open, it pierces immediately, and where the eyes close, nothing is lacking.
When the mouth is open, it is spoken; when the mouth is closed, it is likewise spontaneously manifest.
If you intend to give rise to a thought or stir a mind to take charge of it, you have already missed it by eighty thousand miles (in response to Liu Yanchong).
Regarding the saying "The dog has no Buddha-nature," it is like a man hunting a thief who already knows the thief’s lair but has not yet caught him. Please act quickly.
Marvelous! There must not be even the slightest interruption. At all times—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; when reading books and history;
when practicing benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and sincerity; when serving elders; when instructing students;
or when eating porridge or rice—one must grapple with it. Suddenly, the sack is dropped. What more need be said? (Shown to Wang Shengxi)
An ancient worthy said: "If you simply prepare a heart of resolve, you will certainly not be deceived. I only fear that you yourself lack sufficient faith;
thus, amidst the conditions of daily life, you may be carried away by external circumstances and fail to practice the *kung-fu* with single-mindedness, resulting in interruptions.
When there are such interruptions, the mind cannot help but be restless and disturbed. Yet, in the very moment of this restlessness and disturbance, it is precisely a state of excellence."
Regarding the timing: the Buddha said, "At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; yet do not suppress or extinguish those deluded minds.
Abide within the realm of deluded perceptions without applying analytical knowledge; and within this lack of analytical knowledge, do not discriminate what is real.
This is precisely that principle. This principle cannot be explained to others; it can only be known the moment it is raised by one who has attained realization through direct experience.

[The Master] points to the place where [the letter] fell (indicating Xie Kuoran). He instructs: Since receiving my previous letter, whenever you encounter situations amidst the bustle that cannot be avoided, you have constantly conducted self-inspection;
yet, you have not yet applied the actual work of cultivation. This very state of being unable to avoid it is itself the work.
If you were to apply further effort to this inspection, you would instead distance yourself from it even further.
In the past, the Elder Huayan of the Wei Prefecture said: "The Buddha-dharma is present in the midst of daily activities—in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining;
in drinking tea and eating meals; in speaking and conversing; and in all that one does. Even when raising the mind or stirring a thought, it is not [the Buddha-dharma] itself.
It is precisely at this point where there is no place to hide or evade that you must most strictly avoid stirring the mind or giving rise to thoughts of inspection."—The Patriarch.
The Master said: "When discrimination does not arise, the void clarity illuminates itself. Furthermore, Layman Pang said: "In daily activities there is no distinction;
it is only I who am naturally in harmony. At every turn there is neither grasping nor rejecting; in every place there is no discord. Who assigns the titles 'red' and 'purple'?"
"Even on a mountain peak, not a speck of dust remains. Spiritual powers and wondrous functions consist simply in carrying water and hauling firewood. Furthermore, the former sage said:
"Whatever is conceptually discriminated or calculated by the mind—all that which is the manifestation of one's own mind—is entirely like a dream.

Take this to heart! When you cannot avoid [the present moment], do not further attempt to deliberate with the mind. When there is no deliberation, everything is spontaneously perfected; nor is there any need for principle."
It has nothing to do with being sharp or dull; it is entirely unrelated to matters of sharpness or dullness, nor does it concern matters of stillness or distraction.
Precisely when one can no longer avoid it, suddenly the sack is dropped, and one cannot help but clap one's hands and laugh aloud.
Remember this, remember this! If even a hair’s breadth of effort were used to seek realization in this matter, then—
It is like a person grasping at and rubbing empty space with their hands; it only serves to increase one's own exhaustion (shown to Chen Jiren).
As long as emotional consciousness has not been shattered, the fire of the mind will flicker incessantly. At such a time, simply maintain the "head-word" (*huatou*) of your doubt.
For instance, when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does even a dog have Buddha-nature? Zhaozhou replied, "No. Just keep this up.
Tear it up and lift it up! It is not from the left; it is not from the right. Furthermore, you must not attempt to awaken through the ordinary mind.
You must not take responsibility at the very moment the phrase is raised. You must not grasp it as something mysterious or sublime.

You must not deliberate upon it in terms of existence or non-existence. You must not speculate by conceptualizing it as the "non-existence of true non-existence. You must not sit idly in [this state].
There is nothing within the inner armor. Furthermore, one must not seek realization in the place where the spark from striking flint meets the flash of lightning;
one must simply reach the state where there is no mind to employ. When the mind has nowhere to rest, do not fear falling into emptiness—this very point is the excellent state.
Suddenly, like a rat entering a cow’s horn, one will see the ultimate resolution. This matter is neither difficult nor easy; it can only be realized by those who have planted the seeds in past lives.

Having attained the depth of the *prajñā* and *sarvajñatā*, and having served true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) throughout beginningless and vast kalpas, one has cultivated and acquired right knowledge and right view.
Within the subtle consciousness (*liṅ-vijñāna*), as one encounters circumstances and conditions, this manifests in the sphere of active conduct (*samudācāra*).
"Striking it, bumping into it—just as if one were in the midst of a crowd of ten thousand people and recognized one's own parents.
At such a time, there is no need to ask others; the mind that seeks will naturally cease its wandering.
Yunmen said, "It is not that it exists when spoken and does not exist when unspoken. It is not that it exists when deliberated upon and does not exist when not deliberated upon."
When measured by time, it simply does not exist. Furthermore, he himself raised the question: "Tell me, when there is no deliberation, what is this?

Fearing that people might not understand, he further said: "What else could it be? (Answering Zhang Anguo). Generally speaking, those who have more than enough experience in the world have long been stuck in the midst of worldly toil;
suddenly, having received instructions from someone, they apply themselves to practice in a state of stillness and silence.
Now, when one suddenly attains a state of mind free from concerns, one may mistakenly take this to be ultimate peace and happiness.
Little do they realize that this is like pressing down grass with a stone; although for a time all signs of activity seem to cease, how can the roots remain?

How, then, could there ever be a time of realizing the profound stillness of *nirvāṇa*? To bring true, authentic stillness before oneself, one must, amidst the blazing process of arising and ceasing, [penetrate its nature].

Suddenly leaping forth, without moving so much as a hair’s breadth, one stirs the long river into butter and curd, and transforms the great earth into gold. Seizing and relinquishing at will, killing and giving life with total freedom—there is nothing that cannot be accomplished for the benefit of self and others. (Shown by Fu Jishen) Formerly, Venerable Yan-yang asked Zhaozhou: "When not a single thing can be brought forth, what then? Zhaozhou said: [The dog has no Buddha-nature. Fu Jishen added: "If you can understand this, you will see that even if you were to take up the entire universe and cast it into the furnace, it would not be too much; even if you were to fill the void with all manner of things, it would not be excessive. This is why it is said: 'A single word, like a thunderbolt, strikes the heart; a single phrase, like a sharp sword, severs the root. It is not that there is nothing to bring forth, but that there is nothing to be grasped. If you can let go of everything, then even if you were to bring forth the ten directions, they would be nothing more than a single blade of grass. He then recited a verse: "The Great Way is originally vast and open; How could there be anything to bring forth? If you try to grasp it, you lose it entirely; If you do not grasp it, you possess it all. The ancient sages have already passed away; The current generation is lost in confusion. If you wish to know the true source, Do not seek it outside of yourself. He then said: "If you can understand this, you will see that the Buddhas and patriarchs have never been separate from you. If you cannot understand this, you will wander through birth and death for aeons. Therefore, I say: 'If you can leap out suddenly, without moving a single hair, you can stir the long river into butter and curd, transform the great earth into gold, and exercise mastery over seizing and relinquishing, killing and giving life. For the benefit of self and others, there is nothing that cannot be done. He then showed the verse by Fu Jishen.
