[Zhaozhou] said, "Put it down. Yan Yang asked, "Since you have not brought a single thing here, what is there to put down?
Zhaozhou said, "If you cannot put it down, carry it away. At these words, Yan Yang attained great enlightenment.
Furthermore, a monk asked an ancient worthy, "When a student is unable to cope with things, what then? The ancient worthy said, "I, the old monk, am also unable to cope. The monk said—
"Because the student is still on the stage of training, how can he be dealt with? But the Abbot is a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra);
why can he, too, not be dealt with? An ancient worthy said, "If I could deal with him, I would simply take away this 'inability to deal with him' from you.
At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. The point at which these two monks were enlightened is precisely the point where Lord Lou was deluded.
The point where Lord Lou harbored doubt is precisely the point where the two monks asked their questions. "Dharmas arise from discrimination; they likewise perish through discrimination.

To extinguish all dharmas of discrimination—this dharma is without arising or ceasing. (Answer to Lord Lou) A Letter on Dreaming and Awakening Sent to Xiang Bogong (See in the chapter on Master Longqing Xian).
Instruction: The thirtieth day of the twelfth month has already arrived; one must attend to daily practice.
One should observe in this manner; then the worldly mind of affliction will naturally dissolve away.
Once the mind of affliction has dissolved, tomorrow will again be as it was before: "In early spring, it is still cold. As the ancient masters said:
"If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season. This very season is precisely when the Yellow-Faced Old Man appeared in the world.

The time of attaining Buddhahood—sitting upon the Vajra Seat, subduing the armies of Māra, turning the Wheel of Dharma, delivering sentient beings, and entering Nirvāṇa—is no different and no distinct from the time of realizing emptiness, namely the "thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month.
Upon reaching this point, one should simply observe in this manner. To observe in this way is called right observation; to observe otherwise is called wrong.
Contemplation: while the false and the true are not yet distinguished, one cannot avoid being subject to the shifting changes of time.
If you wish to be free from the influence of time, simply let go all at once. Let it go until there is nothing left to let go; even this saying must not be grasped.
As before, you are simply the Layman Who Understands Emptiness (Jie Kong Jushi), and no other. (Answer to Liu Jigao) Master Zhangjing said: "The ultimate principle is beyond words."

It is said: People of the time do not understand this; they strenuously practice other matters, taking them to be spiritual power, yet they do not know that one's own nature is fundamentally not an object of the sensory realms.
This is a subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation. All its discerning awareness is unstained and unimpeded; such radiance has never ceased or been abandoned.
From past kalpas until now, it remains steadfastly without change, just as the solar disc appears the same whether viewed from afar or nearby.
Illumination, though it reaches all forms, does not unite with anything. This spiritual torch and wondrous clarity do not require refinement;

yet, because one fails to realize this, one grasps at objective phenomena. This is merely like pressing the eyes and falsely perceiving flowers in the sky—exhausting oneself in vain and needlessly passing through kalpas.
If you can turn the light back upon yourself, there is no second person; in every movement and action, the true nature (dharmatā) remains unimpaired. Left.
As for what you have just said regarding your own dull faculties, try this: reflect back and look within. Can that which knows itself to be dull actually be dull?
If you do not turn the light back upon yourself to reflect, but merely cling to your dull faculties, your afflictions will only increase.
This is to pile further delusion upon delusion, like adding more empty flowers to an existing cluster of empty flowers. Simply listen: can that which knows its own faculty to be dull truly be dull?
It is certainly not dull. Although one must not cling to this dullness, one must likewise not discard this dullness while practicing.
Taking up or discarding, being sharp or dull—this depends on the person, not the mind. This mind is of one essence with the Buddhas of the three periods of time and is non-dual.
If there were duality, then the Dharma would not be equal. To receive the teaching and transmit the mind are both empty.
Delusion! To seek the truth by searching for reality only leads to further divergence. One need only know the mind of oneness without duality;

it is certainly not found within the realm of sharp or dull faculties, nor between acceptance and rejection. Then, one shall see the moon and let go of the finger, cutting through everything with a single stroke.
If you remain hesitant, calculating before and after, this is merely producing a false understanding based on an empty fist held up as a finger. This is the root [of delusion].
Within the phenomena of the objective realm, one falsely fabricates the strange and bizarre; within the aggregates and elements, one delusively imprisons oneself, with no end in sight.
(In response to Chen Jiren) I have humbly received your news that you have closed your doors and ceased socializing, setting aside all worldly affairs.

Morning and evening, you take up the *huatou* I previously suggested and keep it present—excellent, excellent! Having resolved your mind in this way, you should take awakening as your standard. If [you do so] yourself...
A sense of despondency arises; that is to say, one’s faculties and nature are deemed inferior and base, and one seeks further for a point of entry.

This is precisely like asking for the location of Chang’an while standing inside the Han-yuan Palace—it is simply a matter of where it is. At the very moment of intense alertness (*tisi*), who is it that can know those faculties and nature are inferior and base?
Furthermore, who is it that seeks a point of entry? And who is it, O Miaoxi, that you do not spare your verbal karma to explain clearly for the sake of this layman?
It is simply this Wang Yanzhang; there is no second, only this one Wang Yanzhang.
Where else could one find someone who can call forth [the mind] and recognize that their root-nature is base and inferior, yet still seeks a point of entry?
All those who come from the depths [of such conceptualization] should be known as but shadows of Wang Yanzhang; they have nothing to do with the actual Wang Yanzhang himself.
If he were truly Wang Yanzhang, his fundamental nature would certainly not be so base and inferior, nor would he seek a point of entry.
He would simply trust in his own master, and there would be no need for all this fuss and agitation. Long ago, there was a monk...
He asked Yangshan, "In the Chan school’s sudden enlightenment, what is the ultimate meaning of entering the gate? Yangshan replied, "This meaning is extremely difficult.
If one belongs to the lineage of the Patriarchs with superior faculties and supreme wisdom, they may attain a thousand awakenings upon hearing it once and achieve the Great Totality (Mahādhāraṇī).
Such individuals of superior capacity are rare to find. As for those with dull faculties and inferior wisdom, this is why the ancient masters said: 'If you do not settle in dhyāna and stillness...'"

When one reaches this point, one must inevitably be left utterly bewildered. A monk asked, "Apart from this 'extraordinary' realm, is there any other expedient means by which a student may gain entry?
Deshan said, "'Something else' or 'nothing else'—these only cause your mind to be unsettled. I shall now ask you: where are you from?
The monk replied, "A man from Youzhou. Deshan said, "Do you ever think of that place? The monk replied, "I do."

[Zhaozhou] reflected. Yunmen said, "In that place, there are towers, pavilions, groves, and gardens, with people and horses crowding together. Reflect back upon what you were reflecting on: do those many things still exist?
[Zhaozhou] said, "When I arrived here, I did not see anything at all. Yunmen said, "Your understanding is still within the realm of objects;
this is the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), but it is not yet the stage of the person (*pudgala-bhūmi*). Miaoxi remarked, "I have already been too overbearing with my grandmotherly heart."
One must add another footnote here: the person in question is none other than Wang Yanzhang. His state of faith consists in recognizing his own inferior root-nature and seeking a point of entry.
When you are in the midst of intensely scrutinizing the *huatou*, reflect back upon that which is performing the scrutiny—is it still Wang Yanzhang?
At this juncture, there is not even time for a hair’s breadth of hesitation; if you pause to reflect or allow your mental activity to cease, you will miss the mark.
Then one is deluded by shadows. Please exert yourself with vigor; do not be negligent, do not be negligent! (In reply to Wang Yanzhang) I have previously received your instructions.
My spiritual faculties are dull and obtuse, yet though I strive diligently in my practice, I have still not attained the means for transcendent awakening.
Some time ago, while I was at Shuangjing, I answered the questions posed by Fu Jishen; they were exactly the same as this present inquiry.

One who is able to recognize their own dullness and ignorance is, in truth, certainly not dull or ignorant. Where else would one seek transcendental awakening? This is the Way that gentlemen and scholars should study.
One must nevertheless borrow the state of dullness and obscurity to enter. If you cling to this dullness and say, "I have no share in this," then you will be seized by the demon of dullness.
This is because your habitual views and understandings—largely driven by a mind seeking realization—stand before you as obstacles.
Therefore, one's own correct knowledge and vision cannot manifest before oneself. This hindrance does not come from without, nor is it a separate entity;
it is simply the very master who is capable of knowing, yet is dull and obscured.
Thus, Master Ruiyan would constantly call out from within his quarters, "Master! and then respond himself, "Yes! Stay alert! and then respond again.
"Understood. At another time, on a later day, do not allow yourself to be deceived. Furthermore, you should yourself say, "Understood, understood.
Fortunately, there have been such precedents since ancient times. Let us heedfully reflect upon this: what is it? It is precisely this very act of reflection.
It is not anyone else; it is simply this one who is aware of his own dullness.
This one who is aware of his own dullness is also not anyone else; he is Li Baowen’s own original spirit (*mìngmèng yuánchén*).
This is merely Miaoxi’s expedient means of administering medicine according to the illness, intended only to briefly point out for the Layman the path for returning home to sit in peace.
If you were to simply identify the words of death as being truly one's own life-root and primal source (*mìngběn yuánchén*), then you would be recognizing the spirit as the self;
this would be utterly devoid of connection to the truth. Therefore, Master Changsha said: "The student of the Way does not recognize the Real."
This is solely because from the beginning one has been deluded regarding the conscious spirit; it has been the root of birth and death for immeasurable eons.
Fools call this the "original person. What was previously described as "entering through dullness and ignorance" refers to this very thing.
However, simply observe that which is able to perceive such dullness and ignorance—after all, what is it? Look right here; there is no need to seek a transcendental awakening. Observe this.
Look! Suddenly, one bursts into laughter and departs. Beyond this, there is nothing more to be said.

(In response to Li Maojia) When scholars and officials study the Way, those of sharp faculties miss it, while those of dull faculties find it difficult to enter. If they find it difficult to enter, they naturally become discouraged;
if they miss it, they will undoubtedly give rise to slander. If you wish to settle upon the truth, simply take that which is "missing" and shift it to the place where it is "difficult to enter."

Instead, take that which is difficult to enter and shift it to the point where one has already missed the mark; naturally, you will become settled and cease to harbor the notion that there is anything difficult to enter or anything missed.
Once you have attained such realization, it is well to let go of yourself entirely right here. When you let go:
Nor should you adopt the principle of "letting go. As the ancient masters said: "To let loose [the mind] is to remain forever like a dazed idiot;
there is another who naturally has one who loves him" (addressed to Chen Cizhong). Lethargy and agitation were condemned by the former sages.
When sitting in stillness, as soon as you perceive these two ailments manifesting, simply raise the phrase: "The dog has no Buddha-nature. These two ailments...

Do not strive to exert force to cast them aside; let it be naturally settled and still right now. As days pass and months deepen, when you first perceive that effort has been relieved, this is precisely where power is gained.
Furthermore, there is no need to perform the practice of "stillness overcoming" (stopping the mind); this very state is itself the practice.
(Reply to Fu Jishen) Your esteemed brother, Lord Baohue, initially had never known the matter of "managing and forgetting. I believe...
He touches his nose with his hand. Although he has not yet fully discerned the heterodox and the orthodox of all quarters, his fundamental basis is firm and solid;
thus, no poisonous heterodoxy can invade him, and the state of "forgetting the mind" (wànghuái) is maintained within it.

If one were to exclusively maintain this state of forgetting the mind, the resolve for liberation from birth and death would not be broken, yet the demons of the aggregates (yīnmó) would find their opportunity, inevitably causing one to partition empty space into two separate realms. Regarding this place:

In stillness, one experiences immeasurable joy; amidst clamor, one experiences immeasurable suffering. To attain the equilibrium of suffering and joy, simply do not give rise to a mind that seeks to manage or control them.
Let the mind be forgotten and set aside. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, leave it to be vast and open.
Should old habits suddenly flash forth, do not apply the mind to suppress them; rather, right at the point where they flash forth, look into the *huatou*.
"Does a dog have Buddha-nature? No. At this very moment, it is like a single speck of snow upon a red-hot furnace.
Only those with eyes that discern and hands that act with intimacy can leap up and seize it at once; only then will they know what Lanrong meant when he said:

"Precisely when the mind is applied, precisely there is no application of mind. To speak circuitously of names and forms is wearisome; to speak directly of non-existence is redundant. Non-mind is precisely..."
Just as it is used, its constant use is precisely non-existence. Now I speak of the state of no-mind; it is not different from having a mind. This is not a deceptive word.
(In response to Zhu Yan-chong) Your instruction states: "When responding to conditions and engaging with diverse objects, one never fails to be within the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, amidst the movements and gestures of daily life, one uses the koan 'The dog has no Buddha-nature' to shatter emotional attachments."
Dust. If you apply yourself with such effort, I fear you will not yet attain awakening. I ask that you look beneath your own heels:

from what source do these differentiated realms arise? Amidst the movements and turns of daily life, how can you use the phrase "the dog has no Buddha-nature" to shatter the dust of emotional attachments?
And who is it that knows how to shatter this dust of attachment? It is the Buddha.
Is it not said: "Sentient beings are inverted; deluded regarding themselves, they pursue external objects"? Objects fundamentally have no self-nature;

those who are deluded regarding themselves simply pursue them themselves. Boundaries fundamentally have no differentiation; those who are deluded regarding themselves simply differentiate them themselves.

Since one daily encounters differentiated boundaries while yet remaining within the Buddha-dharma—and since one is already within the Buddha-dharma—then these are not differentiated boundaries. Since...
Within the realm of differentiation, it is no longer the Buddha-dharma. Picking up one thing and putting down another—when will there ever be an end to this?
When the butcher Guang'e, at the assembly of Nirvāṇa, cast down his butcher’s blade, he became a Buddha on the spot.
How could there have been so much tedious and prolix talk? In the midst of daily life, when responding to conditions, as soon as you perceive yourself entering the realm of differentiation, simply...
Focus solely on the point of distinction: take up the saying, "The dog has no Buddha-nature. Do not conceive of it as a refutation;
do not conceive of it as an object of the emotions; do not conceive of it as a distinction; do not conceive of it as the Buddha-dharma.
Simply look at the saying, "The dog has no Buddha-nature," and simply bring up the word "no. Furthermore, do not harbor the intention to attain enlightenment; if you harbor [such an intention]...

When the mind and its like awaken, then there are distinctions among objects, distinctions among the Buddha-dharma, distinctions among the sensory dusts of the passions, and distinctions regarding the saying "the dog has no Buddha-nature.
There are distinctions between states of interruption and states of non-interruption;
there are distinctions between states where the body and mind are not at peace due to being deluded by the sensory dusts of the passions. One must be able to know these many distinctions.
There are also distinctions between these various approaches. If you wish to eliminate this illness, simply look at the single word "Mu" (No).
Just look at the broad-faced butcher who, casting down his cleaver, said, "I am counted among the thousand Buddhas. Is this real or is it false?
If you engage in deliberations over its reality or falsity, you will once again fall into the realm of conceptual differentiation. It is better to settle the matter with a single stroke.
One must not dwell on what follows or reflect upon what precedes. To dwell on what follows or reflect upon what precedes is to create further distinctions.
Xuan Sha said: "This matter cannot be constrained; it is where the paths of thought and reason are cut off. It is not produced by adornment, but is fundamentally true and pure.

Whether in movement, speech, or laughter, it is clearly manifest everywhere, lacking nothing at all. People of the present age do not awaken to this underlying principle, and thus they recklessly involve themselves [in conceptualization]."

Matters involve the dust of the world; everywhere there is defilement and attachment, and at every turn there are fetters. Even if one attains awakening, the sensory realms remain chaotic and names and forms are unreal.
Should one then intend to settle the mind and withdraw thoughts, to gather phenomena back into emptiness, or close the eyes and hide the pupils—whenever a thought arises, it follows suit.

To repeatedly break and shatter [thoughts], and to immediately suppress them as soon as subtle thoughts arise—such a view is precisely that of an externalist who has fallen into nihilism, a dead man whose soul has not yet dispersed. It is a state of dark obscurity, devoid of awareness or knowledge;
it is like stuffing one's ears to steal a bell, merely deceiving oneself. The various letters you have sent from left and right are entirely the maladies condemned by Xuansha.
One must not fail to realize that "silent illumination" and "heretical Chan" are bottomless pits that bury people alive. When raising a koan, do not employ any of these many clever maneuvers;
simply ensure there is no interruption while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and likewise amidst joy, anger, sorrow, or pleasure.

Do not give rise to discrimination. Whether lifting it up or putting it down, looking at it or looking away, when you realize there is no logical path and no flavor, and your mind becomes feverish and stifled—this is precisely where you should let go of body and life. Remember this, remember this!
Do not let your resolve falter upon encountering such a state; such a state is the very message of becoming a Buddha or an Ancestor.
Furthermore, the current generation of false teachers of silent illumination (mozhao) takes mere wordlessness and speechlessness as the ultimate standard.
They call this the matter beyond the time of Wei-yin, and they also call it the matter prior to the empty kalpa. They do not believe in the gate of awakening;
they regard awakening as a deception, as the "second head," as expedient language, and as mere words for guiding others.
Such people as these deceive others and deceive themselves; they lead others astray and lead themselves astray. This must not remain unknown.
Within the four modes of daily conduct (*catur-īryāpatha*), when one encounters various differentiated states and realizes a sense of effortlessness, that is precisely where one gains strength.

Where one gains strength, there is ultimate effortlessness. If one employs even a hair’s breadth of conscious exertion to support oneself, it is certainly a heterodox teaching and not the Buddha-dharma.

This is the Dharma. Simply cultivate a long-term resolve and engage with the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan until you reach the precipice—climbing it and descending it again and again until the mind has nowhere to go.
Suddenly, it is like waking from a dream, like a lotus flower blooming, like seeing the sun after parting the clouds.
When you reach such a state, it will naturally become one seamless whole. Simply, in the midst of the sevenfold chaos of daily life, look only at this word "Mu.
Do not concern yourself with whether there is awakening or penetration. The Buddhas of the three periods of time were merely people of no affairs;
the patriarchs of successive generations were likewise merely people of no affairs. As an ancient worthy said: "Simply penetrate through to the matter."
There is no such thing. One sees forms and hears sounds without being deaf. Furthermore, an ancient worthy said: "The foolish person eliminates objects but does not eliminate the mind;
the wise person eliminates the mind but does not eliminate objects. When one is without mind in all places, then the various differentiated realms of experience will naturally cease to exist.
Nowadays, most scholars are of an impatient temperament; they wish immediately to understand Zen, yet regarding the scriptural teachings...
Furthermore, regarding the Master’s words and phrases, you attempt to grasp their measure and insist on explaining them with clarity.

Little do you realize that the very point where clarity is sought is precisely the matter where there is no clarity. If you can penetrate this word "Mu," then whether it is clear or not clear will not require asking others.
When the old man instructs scholars and officials to let themselves become dull, this is exactly that principle. Be dull!
Being ranked as the provincial champion is not a bad thing either; I fear only that one will end up "dragging a white ear"—a smile [at this].

(In response to Director Zong. To know one is deluded yet fail to awaken is a great error. To persist in delusion while waiting for awakening is an even greater error. Why? Because one is deluded due to a lack of awareness (*abodha*).
To persist in delusion while waiting for awakening is to be unaware within unawareness, and deluded within delusion. One must resolutely break through these two layers.
Barrier. I ask you to let it go all at once. If you cannot let it go, then whether in delusion or awakening, until the end of the future, how can there ever be rest?
(Shown to Huang Boceng). It is further said: When studying this Way and one has not yet found the point of entry, one feels that it is a thousandfold difficult and ten-thousandfold hard.
Upon hearing a master cite a phrase, one finds it even more difficult to comprehend. This is because one is still grasping for realization and seeking a place of rest.

The mind does not cease; on the contrary, it becomes an obstacle to itself. Only when this mind momentarily subsides does one realize that [enlightenment] is neither difficult nor easy, and that it cannot be transmitted by a teacher.

If you wish to attain enlightenment by using the mind to wait for it, or to wait for its cessation, you may practice from your current station until Maitreya descends to be born in this world, yet you will still be unable to attain enlightenment, nor will you be able to achieve cessation. It will only turn [into further delusion].
He became even more bewildered. Master Píngtián said, "The divine light is not obscured; it is a magnificent legacy for all ages. Having entered this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.
Furthermore, an ancient worthy said, "This matter cannot be sought with a mind of intentional effort, nor can it be attained through a mind of non-existence.
It cannot be constructed through words and language, nor can it be communicated through silent stillness. This is the foremost [teaching]."

Entering the mud and entering the water—these are the words of an old woman. Often, those who practice Chan merely recite them over and over, failing to examine carefully what kind of principle they embody.

If one possesses true backbone, as soon as these words are raised, they will immediately take up the Diamond King’s Precious Sword and sever this fourfold tangle of vines in a single stroke; thus, the path of birth and death—
It is also cut off. The path of both ordinary people and sages is cut off. Calculation and deliberation are cut off. Gain and loss, right and wrong, are also cut off.
Beneath the feet of the person present, it is pure and naked, bare and clear, with nothing to grasp. Is this not joyful? Is this not refreshing?
Have you not seen how, in the past, when Master Guankui first visited Linji, as soon as Linji saw him coming, he immediately brought down his rope?
Zhuang climbed onto the bed and seized him by the chest. Guankxi immediately said, "Understood, understood. Jue knew that he had already attained thorough penetration;

he then pushed him out and offered no further words or phrases with which to deliberate with him. At such a moment, how could Guankxi have been able to respond through any calculation or deliberation?
Fortunately, there were such precedents in the past, yet nowadays people do not take them as a matter of concern. Only...

This is because of a coarse mind. When Guankui was first [beginning his practice], if there had been even a single point of mind waiting for enlightenment, waiting for realization, or waiting for rest, let alone saying he would have been captured and awakened—his hands and feet would have been bound.
Even if he were dragged around the four quarters of the world, he could not have attained awakening, nor could he have found rest. (Answered to Zeng Tianyou. Your instruction has arrived. Early.

For years you have known your faith and inclination toward this Way; yet in your later years, you have been obstructed by intellectual understanding (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*), and there has not yet been a single point of awakening or entry.
You wish to know the expedient means for embodying the Way day and night. Having received your utmost sincerity, I dare not keep it from you;

I shall provide a few words of "entanglement" (*gēténg*) based on my own experience as a conclusion. This very seeking for awakening and entry is itself the intellectual understanding that obstructs the Way. Is there anything else?
What kind of intellectual understanding acts as an obstacle for you? Ultimately, what do you call "intellectual understanding"? From where does it come? And who is it that is being obstructed?
In this single sentence alone, there are three inversions: first, to say that one is obstructed by intellectual understanding;
second, to say that one has not yet awakened and willingly remains a deluded person; and third, to remain further within that delusion.

To set the mind upon awaiting enlightenment is one [error]. These three inversions are themselves the very root of birth and death. You must simply ensure that not a single thought arises and that the inverted mind is severed;
only then will you know that there is no delusion to be destroyed, no enlightenment to be awaited, and no intellectual understanding to be obstructed.
It is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself. After a long time, this will become natural; do not harbor such views.

It is so. However, if one looks at the mind that is capable of knowing and understanding, can it still be obstructed? Within that mind capable of knowing and understanding, are there not all these various modes?

Since ancient times, those of great wisdom have never failed to take knowledge and understanding as their companions and to take knowledge and understanding as their expedient means; within knowledge and understanding, they practice equanimity.
Compassion performs all the works of the Buddhas upon the basis of cognitive understanding; it is like a dragon obtaining water or a tiger relying on a mountain.
One never regards this as a source of affliction, simply because one recognizes the point of origin of that cognitive understanding.

Once the point of origin is recognized, this very cognitive understanding becomes the site of liberation and the place for transcending birth and death. Since it is the site of liberation, [it is the means of] emergence...
Regarding the realm of birth and death, one knows its bottom and understands its bottom; its very substance is quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).

Since that which is known and understood is already quiescent extinction, the knower who knows and understands cannot but be quiescent extinction. Bodhi, nirvāṇa, true thusness (*tathatā*), and buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) cannot but be quiescent extinction.
What further thing could there be to obstruct? Where else could one seek awakening and entry? (Answered by Fù Jìshēn). Dingguang.
Master Miaodao asked Yunmen, "Regarding this mind and this nature, how do delusion and awakening, or turning away and turning toward, function?
I beg you to point out the essential point. Yunmen remained silent for a long while and did not answer. Miaodao asked again.
Yunmen smiled and said, "If one speaks of the essential point, it cannot be pointed out to others. If it could be pointed out, it would not be the essential point. Miaodao—

[The monk] asked, "Is there not some skillful means to lead students toward [enlightenment]? Yunmen said, "If we speak of skillful means, then the mind has neither delusion nor awakening, and the nature has neither orientation nor aversion.
It is only because people establish views of delusion and awakening and cling to interpretations of orientation and aversion that they wish to clarify this mind and see this nature;
yet this mind and this nature immediately follow along with their inversions and become confused, flowing into erroneous paths."
Therefore, one fails to distinguish between Buddha and Mara, and cannot differentiate the heterodox from the orthodox.

This is because one does not understand that this nature and this mind are like a dream or an illusion, yet falsely establishes two kinds of conventional designations, taking their orientation toward or away from, and their delusion or awakening, as real, and recognizing this mind and this nature as true.
Little do they realize that whether real or unreal, false or non-false, mundane or supramundane—all these are but provisional designations.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known. To act upon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing [is to miss it]."
This constitutes seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is not the seeking of the Dharma. Furthermore, an ancient worthy said:
"If you take your own self and your own mind as the ultimate, there will inevitably be other things and other people to serve as counteragents. Moreover, the Buddha said to Pūrṇa:

"You [mistakenly] treat the emptiness of form and form itself as mutually displacing and mutually usurping within the Tathāgatagarbha; thus the Tathāgatagarbha follows along as form and emptiness, pervading everywhere."
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, I unite my wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor arising—with the Tathāgata-garbha;
yet the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm. This Tathāgata-garbha is precisely this mind and this nature.

However, the Buddha provisionally pointed to the mutual overturning and mutual usurping of form and emptiness as being "not so," while taking this wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor arising—as "so. These two sections [are thus].
These are words of medicine, intended to treat the two maladies of delusion and awakening; they are not the fixed intent of the Buddha.
They are merely spoken to refute those who cling to the mind-nature as being a real entity that either turns toward or away from delusion and awakening. As the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha said:
"All three periods of time are merely verbal expressions. Among all dharmas, there is no basis within verbal expressions. All words...

It is said: "Among all dharmas, there is likewise no place of reliance. If one’s views on delusion and awakening are extinguished and the opposition between turning toward and turning away is severed, then this mind will be as clear and bright as the shining sun, and this nature will be as vast and expansive as empty space.

It will emit light from beneath one's own feet, shaking the earth and illuminating the ten directions. Those who behold this light will all realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). When it reaches such a time..."
Spontaneously, this mind and this nature silently accord with one another. Only then does one know that originally there was no delusion, and now there is fundamentally no enlightenment.
Enlightenment is itself delusion; delusion is itself enlightenment. Facing is itself turning away; turning away is itself facing.
Nature is itself mind; mind is itself nature. Buddha is itself Mara; Mara is itself Buddha. This single path is pure and equal, wherein there is neither equality nor inequality. All...
This is the constant nature of my own mind; it does not depend on any external methods. Since it is already thus, I speak these words out of necessity, yet you must not take them as literal truth.

If you take them as literal truth, you fail to recognize the skillful means and fixate upon dead words, thereby further increasing delusion and wandering in confusion without end. At this point, there is no place for you.
Regarding the place where the mind is applied, it is better to recognize such matters for what they are, set them aside, and then turn your head to look.
There is Mazu’s “Mind is Buddha” and “Neither mind nor Buddha”; there is “Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing”;
there is Zhaozhou’s “The cypress tree in the courtyard”; there is Yunmen’s “Mount Sumeru”; there is Dayu’s “Sawing apart a hammer with a saw”; and there is Venerable Yan Yang.
"A clod of earth. Mo-wang of Fenzhou. Jizhi pointing his finger up. What principle is this ultimately?
This is the skillful means (*upāya*) of Yunmen. Miaodao, contemplate this (addressed to the practitioner Miaodao).
This very state of being in a hurry is itself the news of the thirtieth day of the twelfth month. What is the Buddha? A dried piece of dung. If you do not penetrate this point..."
"What is different about the thirtieth day of the twelfth month? (Answer to Lü Lónglǐ). Your instruction states: "One can perform Buddhist rites yet not understand Chan language;
as for being able or unable, there is neither distinction nor sameness. One should simply know that that which is able to perform rites is itself Chan language.
To understand Chan language yet be unable to perform Buddhist rites is like a person sitting at the bottom of water crying out for thirst, or sitting inside a basket of rice crying out for hunger.
What difference is there between hunger and [the state of realization]? You should know that the words of Chan are themselves the Buddha-work, and the Buddha-work is itself the words of Chan.

To be able to practice and to be able to understand depends on the person, not on the Dharma. (Answered to Fan Maoshi) To shoulder this great matter of causal conditions, one must possess a resolute will.
If one is half-believing and half-doubting, then there is no connection at all. An ancient worthy said: "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire; when you encounter..."
The smoke must not yet cease; one must wait until the appearance of the Venus star before returning home at last.
If you wish to know the place where one finally arrives, it is the same for both one’s own realm and another’s realm. (Shown to Li Xianchen) It is also said:

Master Zhaozhou remarked, "In my twelve periods of the day, except for the two times of rice gruel and meals, these are instances of distracted mental activity. At other times, there is no place for distracted mental activity."
This is the true place of practice for this old monk. Do not interpret it through the lens of Buddha-dharma, Chan, or the Way;
impermanence is swift. The matter of birth and death is great. Within the realm of sentient beings, those who follow the course of birth and death are as numerous as hemp or millet.
Having cleared away one layer after another, they arrive yet again. If you do not take these two characters, "birth and death," and pin them upon yourself—

If you apply the antidote only at the tip of your nose, you will wait until the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, when your hands are flustered and your feet are in turmoil—like a crab falling into boiling water—and by then it will be too late to know regret.

If you wish for a direct approach, please cut it off right now (addressing Vice-Director Nie). To study this Way, one must possess resolute faith; when encountering circumstances of adversity or favor, [one must remain steadfast].
When the mind is unshakable, it truly enters the stage of progression. The Buddha said: "Faith can eternally extinguish the root of afflictions;

faith can single-mindedly direct one toward the merits of the Buddha; faith is unattached to sense objects; and by remaining far removed from all difficulties, one attains the state free from difficulty.
It is further said: "Faith can transcend the paths of all māras and reveal the unsurpassed path of liberation. These are the teachings as described above.

There are clear scriptural texts. How could the Buddha deceive people? If one is half-illuminated and half-obscured, half-believing and half-disbelieving, then whenever encountering circumstances or conditions, doubt will arise in the mind.
This is because the mind remains attached to objects within the sensory realm, unable to attain certainty and freedom from doubt regarding this Path.
Thus, the root of afflictions is not extinguished, and one remains far removed from the transcendence of all difficulties. These "difficulties" consist in the lack of certainty.

Faith. One is disturbed by the demon of one's own shadows. If one can, for a single thought-moment, realize that conditioned arising is non-arising, then without departing from this very thought, one immediately transcends the path of demons. What is called the "path of demons" is nothing other than this:
it is to obscure this mind and, outside of this mind, falsely give rise to various discriminatory views; thus, this mind follows after those discriminatory deluded thoughts.

Because of this cyclic wandering, one achieves the realm of Māra. If one can, from the very bottom, believe that this mind is definitively and originally a Buddha, and suddenly forget all views, then this very path of Māra is precisely the path for the person to transcend birth and death and attain Bodhi.

(Shown to Deng Zili) As for those of the Daoist school, they rely entirely on deluded thoughts and mental conceptions—such as the "essence of the sun" and the "flower of the moon," swallowing mists and ingesting vital breaths.
If one can still preserve the physical form and remain in the world, unassailed by cold or heat, how much more so when this mind and these thoughts are entirely centered within Prajñā?
The former sages spoke clearly on this: it is like the *tāma* insect, which can settle anywhere except upon a flame.
The minds of sentient beings are likewise; they can take objects of perception everywhere, yet alone cannot [settle]...

Resting upon Prajñā, if you do not retreat from your original resolve in every thought-moment, take this very mind-consciousness of yours—which has been directed toward worldly defilements—and bring it back to rest upon Prajñā.

Although you may not achieve complete penetration in this life, at the time of death you will certainly not be dragged away by evil karma to fall into the evil realms. When you emerge in your next birth, you will follow me in this life.
The power of the vow is firmly established within Prajñā; its manifestation and realization are the definitive matter, leaving no room for doubt.
(Answered to Zeng Tianyou) When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, neither affection nor love can be of any use;

neither power nor influence can be of any use; neither wealth nor treasures can be of any use; neither temperament nor character can be of any use; and neither official rank nor position can be of any use.

Attachment! Even when one possesses wealth and honor, one must remain unattached. When the light of the eyes falls to the ground [at death], only the two paths of habitual good and evil will manifest before one.
If one has committed much evil and little good, one will drift away following the power of evil karma.
If one has performed much good and little evil, one will be born among humans or devas within a family of the ten wholesome actions, following the power of virtuous karma.

Once you have realized that both these paths belong to the realm of illusion, you must then give rise to a mind of courageous, diligent, and firm non-retrogression, resolutely intending to transcend emotions and leave behind views, thereby penetrating through and escaping birth and death.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month, neither the path of good nor the path of evil shall be able to seize or bind you. (He pointed toward the residence of the Governor of Deng.)

Since arriving in the city, I have donned my robes, eaten my meals, and held my grandchildren; everything remains as it was before. Now, I am deceased.
My feelings of attachment and stagnation no longer give rise to thoughts of the extraordinary, and my long-standing habitual obstructions have also somewhat diminished.

Reciting these words three times, I was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; this is indeed the verification of studying the Buddha. Were it not for one of superlative capacity, such a thing would not occur.
If one were to achieve a hundredfold completion and a thousandfold resolution within a single smile, one would still be unable to know that our house possesses an untransmitted marvel.
Were it otherwise, the two dharma-gates of "doubt" and "anger" would remain indestructible until the end of the future;
even if the great void became the entrance to Yunmen’s gate, and all grasses, trees, tiles, and stones emitted radiance to assist in explaining the principle, it would still not be so.
What can be done? Only now do I believe that this matter of karmic conditions cannot be transmitted nor learned;

it must be personally realized and personally awakened to, personally accepted and personally stilled, before one finally reaches the end. You have now, with a single laugh, suddenly cast away all that was gained. What more is there to say?
The Yellow-Faced Old Man said: "Do not grasp at the words spoken by sentient beings, nor at any conditioned, illusory phenomena.
Although one does not rely on the path of speech, one likewise does not cling to wordlessness.

What you have written in your letter has already cast off the sentiment of stagnation and does not give rise to thoughts of something extraordinary; it accords in secret with what the Yellow-Faced Old Man has said.
That which is spoken by this speaker is called the Buddha’s teaching; that which deviates from what this speaker says is the teaching of Pāpīyān.

In the past, I made a great vow: "I would rather take this body to undergo the sufferings of hell on behalf of all sentient beings than ever use this mouth to treat the Buddha-dharma as a matter of personal favor, thereby blinding the eyes of all people. Since you have now arrived at such a field...

Dizang said, "I know for myself that this matter was not obtained from another; let us simply continue as before. There is no need to further inquire whether the Great Dharma is clear or not, or whether one's capacity is hindered or unimpeded.
If you entertain such thoughts, then you will not be continuing as before. After the summer retreat had concluded, he received [the transmission].
Only then may you emerge; this would greatly satisfy the sick monk’s intent. If you continue to wander restlessly in pursuit amidst such heat and turmoil, it will not be appropriate.
Yesterday, seeing your extreme joy, I did not dare to break the matter to you, fearing that my words might cause you offense.
Now that joy has been established, I venture to point this out: this matter is extremely difficult; one must give rise to a sense of shame before it can be attained.
Often those of sharp faculties and superior wisdom acquire it without expending effort, whereupon they develop a complacent attitude and fail to practice.
They are frequently carried away by immediate circumstances and cannot maintain mastery over themselves. As days and months pass, [the delusion deepens].
Deluded and failing to return, the power of the Way cannot overcome the power of karma; Māra finds his opportunity and takes possession of you through meditative concentration.
Even at the moment of death, you will find no strength. Take to heart my words from the other day: "In principle, there is sudden awakening, and through awakening, all is simultaneously dissolved;
yet in practice, things are not suddenly eliminated, but are exhausted through a gradual process. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must by no means—
Forget it. As for the various other distinct sayings of the ancients, none of them can be taken as real, yet neither can they be taken as false.
If you practice until you are thoroughly matured, you will naturally and silently accord with your own original mind;

there is no need to seek anything else extraordinary or marvelous. (Below this, the accounts of the three masters’ encounters—Baizhang meeting Mazu, Gushan meeting Xuefeng, and Huiming on Mount Dayu meeting the Sixth Patriarch—are provided in detail.)
Regarding the "Chapter on the Three Masters," by means of the three causal conditions involving the three venerable elders, Master Gong was relieved within a single laugh.
As for how superior or inferior this is, please judge for yourself. Is there any other extraordinary principle here? If there were another, it would be as if he had not been relieved at all.
Simply know how to become a Buddha; do not worry that the Buddha does not understand your speech. This has been so since ancient times.

The practitioner of the Way, having already attained sufficiency within themselves, extends their surplus to respond to circumstances and engage with others. They are like a bright mirror set upon its stand or a luminous pearl held in the palm;
when a Hu comes, it reflects the Hu; when a Han comes, it reflects the Han. This is not a matter of deliberate effort. If there were deliberate effort, [it would be artificial].
In that case, there would be a substantial dharma being handed over to a person. You wish for the Great Dharma to be clearly manifest and respond to capacities without obstruction;

however, simply continue as you have been. There is no need to consult others; in time, they will nod their heads of themselves. The words I addressed to you face-to-face upon my departure—please inscribe them by your seat.
Beyond this, there is nothing further to say. Even if there were something more to say, in your case, it would all become mere superfluous talk. A tangle of vines.

"Too much. Let us set this matter aside. (This was the reply to Li Hanlao. Li again sent a letter stating: "I, Bing, have recently received your instructions and have fully grasped their profound meaning. There are three things I have personally verified:

first, regarding matters of favor or adversity, I respond according to conditions without retaining anything in my breast; second, my long-standing habitual tendencies, though thick, naturally diminish without the need for deliberate suppression; third, ancient kōans which I previously found utterly bewildering now occasionally flash before me. As for the remark in your previous letter that 'the Great Dharma is not yet clear,' I suspect you feared I might be content with a small attainment; I shall expand and fulfill it—how could I seek any further superior understanding? The Master then replied in another letter: "After your letter..."

My admiration for you increases ever further. I have not known whether, since our last meeting, you have been following conditions with ease and relaxation, acting according to your will with mastery; whether, amidst the four modes of deportment, you are not overcome by the dust and toil of worldly affairs; whether, in the two states of waking and sleeping, you have attained oneness; whether, in your ordinary dwelling, there is no more wandering or striving;

and whether, regarding the mind of birth and death, it no longer continues as a stream. Simply exhaust all mundane sentiments, and apart from this, there is no separate "sage's understanding. Since you have already laughed once and opened the true eye, all traces of conceptual news have suddenly vanished.

Whether one has gained strength or not is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known only by oneself. Nevertheless, in the midst of daily life, you should rely on what the Old Man of Yellow Face (the Buddha) said: "Carve away its fundamental nature, eliminate its auxiliary causes, and contravene its manifest karma. This is the man who has finished the matter; it is the true expedient within the absence of expedients, where there is neither cultivation nor realization.

True cultivation and realization within non-acceptance and non-rejection is itself true acceptance and rejection. An ancient worthy said: "When skin and flesh have fallen away entirely, there remains only the one true reality. It is also like sandalwood: when its many branches and twigs have all fallen away, only the true sandalwood remains. This is the ultimate point of "contravening manifest karma, eliminating auxiliary causes, and gouging out the fundamental nature. You should consider this:

such talk, from the perspective of one who has already settled the matter, is much like a fan made of wax in the middle of winter; yet fearing that the climate in the South may be unpredictable, it cannot be dispensed with. (A smile. The Master also wrote in a letter to Jiang Shaoming:

"I am deeply pleased, deeply pleased, that you have been visiting and conversing with the Senior Censor these past few days. This gentleman has brought his restless seeking to rest; he has reached the state where the path of words is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished."

These are distinct paths. To catch a glimpse of the ancient masters’ hands and feet is not to be ensnared by their skillful means or their words and letters. Seeing him thus, I have never spoken a single word to him; I feared only to weary him.

I wait until he comes of his own accord to speak with me, only then do I join him in a close, intimate investigation, brow to brow. It does not end merely like this. If a student of the Way does not cease his restless pursuit, even if he were to investigate with me brow to brow, what benefit would there be?
He would simply be a fool running outside the gate. (The Councilor Han is old. On this day of steaming heat, I wonder how you are faring in your leisure.
Tranquil and expansive, acting with natural ease, are you untroubled by the various māras? Within the four modes of daily conduct, are you one with the koan "Does a dog have Buddha-nature"?
Regarding the two extremes of movement and stillness, can you remain free from discrimination?
Are dream and waking merged? Do principle and phenomenon accord? Are mind and objects both as they truly are? As Old Pang said: "The mind is as the object..."
It is thus: neither real nor unreal, neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it a sage or a holy one—it is an ordinary person who has thoroughly understood the matter.
If you can truly become such an ordinary person who has thoroughly understood the matter, then Śākyamuni and Bodhidharma are nothing but lumps of clay;
the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are nothing but the rattling sound of a hot bowl. Since you have already [realized] this—
Within this single gate, to have self-confidence free from doubt is no small matter.
One must let the familiar become unfamiliar and let the unfamiliar become familiar; only then will one correspond even slightly with this matter.
It often happens that gentlemen frequently attain a moment of sudden awakening within what is not as they intend, yet lose it entirely within what is as they intend. This must not be overlooked.
Let the Master know: while you are amidst favorable circumstances, you must constantly keep in mind the seasons of unfavorable ones;

you must never forget this for even a moment. If you obtain the root, do not worry about the branches; if you know only how to become a Buddha, do not worry that the Buddha will not understand your speech.
This one point is easy to attain but difficult to maintain; you must never neglect it. You must ensure that the beginning is upright and the end is upright, expanding [this practice] throughout.

And fill [the self] with it. Only then does one extend what remains from oneself to reach others. (In response to Liu Yanxiu) Formerly, Yang Wengong Dainan met Master Guanghui Lian at the age of thirty. He cast off that which was obstructing his chest.

From that time onward, whether in the court or in the countryside, he maintained a single course of conduct from beginning to end; he was not moved by fame or office, nor was he led astray by wealth or status.
This is not because he intentionally disregards fame, achievement, wealth, or honor; rather, it is because such is the nature of the Way and the Dharma.
Zhaozhou said, "While others are driven by the twelve periods of the day, I am the one who drives the twelve periods. This is what this old man meant.
This is not done by force; it is because the Dharma is thus. Generally speaking, studying and practicing the Way are one and the same.

Yet nowadays, students often take benevolence, righteousness, ritual, wisdom, and sincerity as their "study," while taking the investigation of things, loyalty, and reciprocity—such as the principle of being "unified by one"—as the "Way.
They merely engage in this like those who guess riddles, or like a group of blind men feeling an elephant, each grasping a different part.

He speaks of heterodox views. Does not the Śākya [Buddha] say: "To use the conceptualizing mind to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow;
when faced with the critical juncture of birth-and-death and fortune-or-disaster, it will prove utterly ineffective.
This is precisely because of this. Yangzi said: "The purpose of the student is to cultivate their nature (*xing*); nature is itself the Way (*Dao*). And the Yellow-Faced Old Man [the Buddha] said:

One’s nature accomplishes the unsurpassed path. Guifeng said: "To perform deeds that accord with principle is the awakened mind; to perform deeds that do not accord with principle is the deluded and chaotic mind.
