Only those who find peace and happiness are truly people. Take Master Zhengen, for instance; his handling of past and present cases was not inferior to that of Xuedou.
Yet, as the teachings have been transmitted through later generations, they have instead become mere verbal sophistry. Small-minded practitioners do nothing but ask: "How did the Ancients respond?
"What words did Zhenru use? "What words did Yangqi use? You have no business meddling in such idle matters.

To cure an illness, one does not rely on medicine carried by a donkey. If the medicine is administered in accordance with the specific ailment, even a single blade of grass picked up from the base of a hedge can cure the disease.
What need is there to speak of cinnabar, *achyranthes*, *ginseng*, and *atractylodes*?
One day the Master said, "In my place, there is no Zen that advances day by day. He then snapped his fingers once and said, "If you understand this..."

He then dismissed the assembly and said: "Nowadays, there is a certain class of masters who, when guiding others, allow them to enter the room three or five times without being able to clarify their understanding.
Instead, they tell the student to speak of their realization, and further ask, 'Tell me, what is your view?
When the student says, 'My view cannot be expressed,' the master replies, 'If you cannot express it, how can I see what you have realized? If things were left at that..."
Mozhi asked, "How do you instruct others? When Daquan went to visit Ciming, Ciming said, "A single cloud spans the mouth of the valley;
from where does the traveler come? Daquan said, "What fire burns at night? It has burned out the graves of the ancients. Ciming said, [and Daquan replied: "..."
"Wait, let me say more. Nanquan then made a tiger's roar. Baoming struck him with his sitting mat. Nanquan pushed Baoming onto the meditation platform.
Baoming then made a tiger's roar. Nanquan said, "I have seen eighty-four spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), but only you have succeeded in carrying on the Linji tradition.
Look at these few lines of question and answer; where is the seeing?"
Elsewhere it is said: "It must be like this before one can succeed. This mountain monk waits for people with sincere intent; they must possess the proper disposition before they can succeed.
This is the 'one leap directly entering the stage of the Tathāgata. In Zen practice, one must have a direct mind, direct conduct, direct thoughts, and direct speech.
Because the mind and speech are direct, throughout the stages from beginning to end, there will forever be no trace of crookedness."—The Patriarch.
The Master came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha.

A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? Yunmen said, "A dried piece of excrement. To hesitate or engage in deliberation is already to have gone astray; how much more so to resort to empty fabrications!
These days, many of you brothers rely on intellectual views and emotional interpretations, insisting on citing idle words and long-winded talk when answering here. This is very much like...
Holding a priceless *maṇi* jewel in your hand, when someone asks you what it is, you drop it and instead pick up a clod of earth—how utterly foolish!
If you investigate in such a manner, you will not attain realization even in a "donkey-year.
Here, I have no dharma to give people; I simply settle the case according to the facts. It is just like taking a piece of lapis lazuli...
"Bring the jar. "How would you protect it? "The moment I see it, I shall break it for you.
You brought the mani-jewel again, and I took it away once more. Seeing you come in such a manner, I cut off both your hands.
Therefore, Master Linji said: "When encountering a Buddha, kill the Buddha; when encountering a Patriarch, kill the Patriarch; when encountering an Arhat, kill the Arhat."
Arhat, tell me this: since you are called a "good friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*), why would you need to kill someone?
Look at what kind of principle this is! Nowadays, you brothers who practice the Way do not realize where this fault lies;
it is simply because you wish to clarify it. For instance, it is not permissible to act thus, nor is it permissible not to act thus.
"Neither 'thus' nor 'not thus' is acceptable. What is it? Can you clarify it by offering a single turning word?

Yongming could not do so. The ancients were exceedingly direct. It is because you are unwilling to act in such directness that, precisely because it is so utterly clear, what you have attained is delayed. The Master said, "In my life, I have been fond of scolding people."
While reading the *Xuansha Yulu*, I was greatly delighted by his examination of Lingyun, where he said: "How perfectly true! How perfectly true!
Yet I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate. This may be described as standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.
Later, after speaking with Lingyun, Xuansha said: "Only now, at last, are you truly through. Then, however, he acted as if he were urinating and defecating upon him. [He] then asked Yuan...
"How did you awaken? Yuanwu asked. Yuanwu laughed and said, "In the future, things will turn out this way; even I cannot understand it.

He then went down and returned to his quarters, where he finally realized that Xuansha had been acting quite strangely. He then recounted the incident to Yuanwu. Yuanwu laughed and said, "I am glad you have come to know this.
Huitang said, "Nowadays, at most monasteries, there are many who lack this kind of medicine. The Master said: [This concludes the record.]
One must take care that outsiders do not hear these coarse words. For a Bodhisattva, seeing the Buddha-nature with the eyes means it must be seen with the eyes;
this is the universal teaching.
Qian Ji-yi requested a general discourse. The Master said: "The Dharma cannot be seen, heard, sensed, or known.

If one proceeds by means of seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, then that is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is not the seeking of the Dharma. Since it lies outside of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, what then can be called 'the Dharma'?
Reaching this point, it is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself. Unless one realizes it for oneself..."
Only upon awakening can one truly see this. If one is a person who has actually realized and awakened, then by lifting up even a single hair-tip, they will understand the entire world at once.

Nowadays, not only among Zen practitioners, but even among the scholar-officials—those who are clever, sharp-witted, and have read extensively to the limits of all books—each and every one suffers from two kinds of illnesses. If they do not apply their minds, it is forgetfulness; if they do apply their minds, it is attachment.
To harbor [thoughts] is to fall into the ghost cave beneath Black Mountain; in the teachings, this is called *styāna* (sloth).
To fixate the mind is for the consciousness to fly about in confusion; one thought follows after another, the preceding thought not yet ceased as the succeeding one continues.
In the teachings, this is called *auddhatya* (restlessness). One does not know that beneath the feet of every person there exists a great segment of reality that is neither sinking nor restless.
This great causal nexus of events is like the sky universally covering all, or like the earth universally supporting all. Before the world existed, this great causal nexus already existed;
even when the world is destroyed, this great causal nexus does not waver by so much as a single hair’s breadth.
Often, scholars and officials are prone to agitation, and nowadays in various quarters there is a certain kind of "silent illumination" heresy.

Chan. Seeing that gentlemen and officials were obstructed by worldly defilements (*rajas*) and their minds were not at peace, [the masters] would simply instruct them to become like cold ashes or withered wood, to become a single strip of white silk, to become an incense burner in an ancient temple, or to become a chilly, stagnant pool—using these to bring people to rest.
Do you think they can truly find rest through this? Little do you realize that this "monkey" will not...
How can one find rest when death is imminent? How can one find rest when that which comes as the vanguard and goes as the rearguard does not die?

This wind was extremely prevalent in the Fujian region in years past. When Miaoxi first entered Min to dwell in a hermitage at the beginning of the Shaoxing era, he forcefully refuted it, calling it a severing of the Buddha’s life-force, stating that even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, they could not grant repentance for such an act. He—
Among them was a scholar named Zheng Shangming. He was extremely intelligent;
he understood the Buddhist scriptures and he understood the Daoist canon, while his mastery of Confucianism was naturally a given. One day, holding a piece of incense, he came into Miaoxi’s quarters.
His anger was palpable, and his voice and expression were both stern as he said, "I have a piece of incense that has not yet been burned.
I wish to discuss one matter with the Master. For instance, remaining silent and speechless is the foremost place of rest within the Dharma-gate.
Yet the Master has dismissed it with reckless derision; thus, I suspect that the Master has not reached this stage. Therefore—
I do not believe you. Consider, for instance, when Śākyamuni was in the kingdom of Magadha during the three weeks following his enlightenment;

he closed his room and remained silent. Was this not the Buddha’s silence? Furthermore, in the city of Vaiśālī, thirty-two bodhisattvas each spoke on the Dharma-gate of non-duality, until finally Vimalakīrti had no words. Mañjuśrī praised him as excellent. Was this not the work of a bodhisattva?
Silence. Subhūti sat in meditative seclusion within a mountain cave; he spoke not and said nothing. Is this not the silence of a śrāvaka?
When Śakra, Lord of Devas, saw Subhūti sitting in meditative seclusion within the cave, he rained down flowers as an offering; yet he too spoke not.
Is this not the silence of an ordinary person? When Bodhidharma traveled through Liang and Wei, he sat coldly at Shaolin for nine years.
"Is it not the case that the Patriarch remained silent? When Luzu saw a monk, he simply faced the wall; is this not the silence of a Master?
Why, then, do you, O Monk, so forcefully reject 'silent illumination' (mozhao), deeming it heterodox and wrong?
Miaoxi said: "Shangming, you have asked well of me as well. Wait while I explain it to you. If what I say does not work, then I shall burn one [of my fingers]."
Burn incense. Pay me three prostrations. If what I say is put into practice, then you may receive my incense and prostrations;
I shall not speak of the words of Old Śākyamuni or the former worthies to you. I will speak right here in your own room.
This is what is called "borrowing a mother-in-law’s shawl to bow for New Year. He then asked, "Have you ever read the *Zhuangzi*?
[The monk] replied, "Why would I not have read it? Miaoxi said, "The *Zhuangzi* says: 'If words are sufficient, one may speak all day long and exhaust the Way;

if words are insufficient, one may speak all day long and exhaust only phenomena. The ultimate limit of the Way and phenomena cannot be carried by either speech or silence. It is neither speech nor..."
Silence. There is a limit to what can be expressed through meaning. I have never looked at Guo Xiang’s commentary, nor the commentaries of various other schools;
I have merely relied on my own fabrications to explain this silence of yours.
Have you not seen how one day Confucius was greatly startled and exclaimed, "Zhan, my Way is unified by a single thread"? Zengzi replied, "Yes. You commoners, as soon as you hear this—
This single word "Vow" (唯)—and yet you come here to speak such harsh words! You say that this "Vow" shares the same root as heaven and earth and is one body with the myriad things;
that it elevates the ruler above Yao and Shun, establishes families and nations, and produces generals and ministers;
and even when laying hands and feet in death, nothing emerges beyond this "Vow. You are fortunate indeed to have no connection with it! Little do you realize that this Way—
In principle, what the Master said was sufficient; what Zengzi said was also sufficient. His disciples did not understand, however, and asked, "What does this mean?
Seeing that they could not grasp it, Zengzi answered from a secondary perspective, saying that the Way of the Master cannot be without words;
thus he said, "The Way of the Master is simply loyalty and reciprocity."
In short, at the ultimate limit of the Way and all phenomena, it does not reside in speech, nor does it reside in silence.

Speech cannot carry it; silence cannot carry it either. What you have said does not even accord with the intent of Zhuangzi, let alone accord with the intent of Śākyamuni, Laozi, and Master Bodhidharma. You must understand that Zhuangzi was not...
To say that silence does not convey meaning—is there any limit to what can be expressed? This is precisely what the Great Master Yunmen did when he held up his fan and said:
"The fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra.
A carp from the Eastern Sea is struck with a single blow, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin. If you can understand this speech of Yunmen, it is the same as what Zhuangzi spoke.
"Dì! (Bottom! What did Zengzi say? What did Confucius say? They are one and the same. The monk then remained silent.
Miaoxi said, "Although you do not speak, your mind has not yet been subdued. It is clear that the ancients certainly did not sit in silence.
When you just now cited Śākyamuni’s 'closing the room' and Vimalakīrti’s silence, look at the seat that existed back then!"
The Master called him Dharma Master Zhao and said to him: "Bring forth that which is beyond words and speech, and explain it to people!
Śākyamuni closed his chamber in Magadha; Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī; Subhūti proclaimed 'non-speaking' to manifest the Way;
and when Śakra and Brahmā ceased their listening, flowers rained down. In all these cases, the Principle was governed by the divine, and thus the mouth remained silent."

"How can it be said that there is no eloquence? It is that which eloquence cannot express. This principle suddenly collides with the divine; one is unconsciously brought to a point where speech is impossible.
Although there is no speaking, its resonance is like thunder. Therefore it is said: "How can it be said that there is no eloquence?
It is simply that which eloquence cannot express. At this point, all the worldly cleverness and rhetorical skill have no place to apply themselves.
It cannot be attained. Only when one reaches such a state is it truly the place where one lets go of the body and abandons life.
Such a realm must be personally realized and awakened to by the individual themselves. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The palaces of the Tathāgata are boundless;
those who have spontaneously awakened dwell within them. This is the Great Dharma of Liberation of all the sages of antiquity.
The Gate is boundless and immeasurable; it is without gain and without loss, without silence and without speech, without going and without coming.
It is thus in every particle of dust, thus in every buddha-field, thus in every thought-moment, and thus in every phenomenon.

It is only because the faculties and natures of sentient beings are narrow and inferior that they fail to reach the realm of the sages of the Three Teachings, and thus distinguish between "that" and "this. Little do they realize that the realm is as vast and great as this.
It is said that one has gone toward the black mountain down into a ghost cave, sitting there in silence;

therefore, the former sages condemned it as a deep pit of liberation—a place to be feared. When viewed with the divine eye of the path of spiritual powers, it is but a mountain of knives and trees of swords.
"Sitting amidst the boiling cauldrons and furnace coals is all the same," said the Master of the Seat (Zuozhu).
"Even those who do not linger in the state of silence—let alone the guests under the Gate of the Patriarchs—say that as soon as one opens the mouth, one falls into 'this age' (jinti).
For now, let us rejoice that there is no connection [between words and reality]. Shangming bowed unconsciously. Miaoxi said, 'Although you have bowed, there is still more to come. At evening..."
He entered the room, and I asked him, "How old are you this year? He replied, "Sixty-four. I asked again, "Where did you come from sixty-four years ago?
He was unable to open his mouth. I took my bamboo staff and struck him on the back, sending him out.
The next day he came into the room again and said, "Sixty-four years ago, I had not yet even been born. As it was, [I struck him again].
Master He, in turn, asked Yang, "From where have you come? Miaoxi said, "Sixty-four years ago, you could not have originally been at Zheng’s house in Fuzhou.
As for this present, vivid, solitary clarity that hears the Dharma and expounds the Dharma—before it was born, where exactly did it reside? Yang said, "I do not know. Miaoxi said, "If you..."
If you do not realize this, it is truly a great birth. Now, in this life, the limit is but one hundred years.
After those hundred years, even if you wish to fly out beyond the three-thousandfold world system, you must still enter a coffin before you can do so. At that time—
The four elements and five aggregates dissolve all at once. There are eyes that do not see objects; there are ears that do not hear sounds.
There is a lump of flesh—a mind—whose discernment no longer functions. There is a body that feels no pain even when burned by fire or cut by a blade.
At this point, where does that which is vividly and solitary luminous go? He replied, "Even Ang does not know. Miaoxi said:
Since you do not know this, it is truly a great matter of death. Therefore it is said: "Impermanence is swift; the matter of birth and death is great. This is precisely that principle.
At this point, one cannot employ cleverness, nor can one rely on memorization. Let me ask you further:
throughout your life you have produced so much of the "zhi-hu-ye-ze" (the various literary flourishes); on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, which single word will you use to confront it?
Regarding his birth and death, one must first know clearly the point where life comes from and where death goes; only then can it be attained. If one does not know this, one is a fool.
Only when the other person’s mind is thus subdued can one then rescue them; one must not remain stuck in a state of wordlessness and silence.

If you are willing to apply yourself to practice here, (he replied to Zeng Tianyou, saying: "Old Pang said: 'I only wish that you would empty all that exists; by no means should you reify what does not exist. If you can only master these two sentences,")

The task of a lifetime’s study is finished. Nowadays, there is a certain class of shaven-headed outsiders who, their own eyes being dim, merely instruct others to "rest" and "cease" in a state of frantic desperation. If one rests and ceases in such a manner, even when a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, one will still not attain rest; it only serves to make the mind increasingly confused and distressed.

Furthermore, they teach people to "follow conditions," "maintain control," or to practice "forgetting emotions" through silent illumination—shining and shining, carrying and carrying. This only increases confusion and distress without end, utterly failing to grasp the expedient means of the Patriarchs and misleading people.

It causes people to live and die in vain all along, further teaching them not to manage any affairs, but simply to "rest" like that. When these wandering thoughts cease upon resting, at such a time, it is not a state of dark oblivion.

"Non-knowing" is simply being alert and lucid; those of this sort are even more poisonous and harmful, for they blind people's eyes. Again he said: "To tell people to 'manage and maintain' [the mind] is to produce an understanding based on guarding the present mirror-like awareness.

To tell people to 'forcefully rest' or 'cease' is to produce an understanding based on guarding a state of forgetfulness and empty stillness. When resting until there is neither awareness nor knowing, one becomes like earth, wood, tiles, or stones—at such a time, it is not a state of dark, unconscious ignorance, yet it is to produce an understanding by mistakenly taking a provisional teaching meant to loosen bonds as the ultimate truth.

To tell people to 'follow conditions while looking after' and 'not let unwholesome thoughts arise' is to produce an understanding by clinging to the intellectual consciousness of the skull. To tell people to simply 'let go and remain expansive, allowing things to be as they are,' [is likewise a trap]."

Do not concern yourself with the arising of thoughts or the movement of the mind. Thoughts arise and cease; they have no inherent substance from the beginning. If you grasp at them as real, the mind of birth and death arises. This [grasping] is yet another case of those who take the preservation of the "natural body" as the ultimate Dharma and thereby give rise to intellectual understanding.

The various ailments mentioned above are not the fault of the student; they all stem from blind-eyed masters who have given erroneous instructions. In response to Liu Yanxiu, he said: "On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, how will you settle the account? You must not wait until your eyes are about to fall out before saying to the Old Man of Yama:

'Wait a moment while I clarify my spirit and steady my thoughts; then I shall go to meet you. In response to Zhang Anguo, he said: "Some sit in the dark ghost-cave of wordlessness and speechlessness, closing their brows and shutting their mouths."

The eye is called that which lies beyond the limit of majestic sound (*vīra-ghoṣa*); it is the news of the time before one’s parents were born. It is also called "silently and constantly illuminating," which is what is meant by being a practitioner of Chan. Those of such a sort do not seek wondrous enlightenment;

they regard enlightenment as falling into the "second head," they regard enlightenment as deceiving and frightening people, and they regard enlightenment as something to be established. Since they themselves do not understand enlightenment, they do not believe that there is such a thing as enlightenment. Miaoxi once said to the assembly of monks: "In the world, even in the various crafts and arts, if there is no point of awakening, one cannot attain their subtlety;

how much more so when one wishes to escape birth and death? He replied to Rong Maoshu, saying: "There is a certain type of person who proclaims false doctrines as the teachings of a patriarch. They say to students: 'Simply keep to stillness. Yet they do not know what it is that keeps, nor what it is that is still."

People, however, say that the state of stillness is the fundamental basis, yet they do not believe in awakening, claiming that awakening is merely a branch or a leaf. Furthermore, they cite a monk’s question to Yangshan: "In these times, is awakening still necessary? Yangshan replied, "As for awakening, it is not non-existent."

Alas, it falls into the second head. One must not speak of dreams before a fool; they would take them as the realization of a substantial dharma, claiming that "awakening" is the second head. Little do they realize that Yaoshan had words of his own to warn students, which were truly piercing:

"To investigate the ultimate principle and take awakening as the standard—where would such a statement even fit? One must not allow Yaoshan to be suspected of misleading later generations by causing them to fall into the second head. Huang De-yong requested a general discourse. (De-yong was Huang Duānfú.

Duānfú had previously entreated Wú Yuánzhào to compose a formal invitation to request that a branch of the Yangqi lineage be established at his family hermitage to open the Dharma there. The Master sent Míguāng to respond to this request.)

At that time, Duānfú passed away. Deyòng and his brothers requested the Master to deliver a general discourse. Deyòng and his brothers went specifically to Dāngān, where they provided funds to prepare offerings and commissioned this mountain monk to deliver a general discourse to proclaim the fundamental tenets (*zongzhì*) in order to repay the grace bestowed by all the sages.
But what do you call the "fundamental tenets"? And how are they to be proclaimed? The state of the Buddha-dharma in recent times is lamentable; false teachers preach the Dharma like...

As numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each established its own school traditions and devised its own extraordinary methods; by twisting and fabricating these doctrines at every turn, they misled successive generations in numbers beyond count.
Among those who practice Chan meditation, there are none who possess the eye that discerns the Dharma, while among those who act as teachers, it is said their Dharma-eye is not clear.

It came to pass in this manner. Initially, Yunmen did not know Yuanzhao. Later, while he was in Jiangxi, he saw Yuanzhao’s colophon to his transcription of the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in which Yuanzhao stated that he had attained a point of realization within that chapter and no longer doubted the tongues of the teachers of the world.
At that time, Yunmen already grasped the essential point and spoke to his brothers, saying: "This man is merely..."
He has merely realized that there is no Brahma-conduct; he has already had his face broken by a false teacher.
If Yunju had seen him, he would have spared no effort to save him. Now that they have met at Changle, he comes to inquire and seek entry into the inner chamber.
He immediately took the point where [the monk] had attained realization and cut it off with two phrases, saying:
"What you have realized is what Yongjia called 'vast emptiness that negates cause and effect'—a state of chaotic indifference that invites calamity.

He then further cited for him a passage from the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* as a mistaken proof, saying: "In the body there is nothing to grasp; in cultivation there is nothing to cling to; in the Dharma there is nothing..."
That which abides has already ceased in the past; it has not yet arrived in the future; and in the present, it is empty and quiescent.
There is no agent of action, nor is there any recipient of retribution. This world does not shift, and that world does not change. Within this, what dharma is called the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
From where does the holy life (brahmacarya) come? To whom does it belong? What is its essence? By whom is it produced? Is it existent or non-existent?
Is it form (rūpa) or non-form? Is it feeling (vedanā) or non-feeling? Is it perception (saṃjñā) or non-perception?
Is it mental formations (saṃskāra) or non-formation? Is it consciousness (vijñāna) or non-consciousness? Thus one contemplates the holy life.

Because dharmas are unattainable. If one relies on this to cite proof—namely, that there is no Brahma-conduct, and that [the absence of] Brahma-conduct is the true Brahma-conduct—then this is to slander the Great Prajñāpāramitā;
one will enter hell as swiftly as an arrow shot. To speak further for you:

nowadays, various groups of heterodox teachers in all quarters each claim for themselves to have attained unsurpassed Bodhi, each preaching divergent doctrines to deceive the Hu and mock the Han, using ancient...
Regarding the causes and conditions for people entering the Way, they falsely engage in speculative interpretation.

Some take the long period of silence—neither speaking nor saying anything—to be an event from before the empty kalpa (*śūnyakalpa*), teaching people to "cease" and "rest," and to rest until they are like earth, wood, tiles, or stones.
Yet, fearing that others will say they are sitting beneath the Black Mountain in a ghost cave, they subsequently cite the Patriarchs.

The scriptural evidence states: "Because it is always known with perfect clarity, words cannot reach it. When one comes to rest so that one is like earth, wood, tiles, or stones, this is not a state of dark ignorance;
rather, it is a state of being vividly alert and clearly discerning throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
From time to time, maintain this; simply practice in this manner, and after a long while, you will naturally accord with your original mind.

Some take the shedding of emotional dust and the non-establishment of fixed patterns as their primary approach, claiming that as soon as an ancient master’s *gong'an* is raised, it is already understood.
Or, when a teacher asks, "It is not the mind, not the Buddha, not a thing—how do you understand this? they respond accordingly.
He would then say, "The Master is quite alert," or "Where has the Master come from?
or "One must not add a point to what is already sharp on an arrowhead," or "How many people have you deceived? Or he would repeat it once more, saying, "It is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.
Whenever he was asked about the kōans of the ancients, he always responded at the very moment the case was raised.
Accept this. Realize it at the point where a stone is struck and sparks fly, or like a flash of lightning. As soon as the case is raised, you must realize it.
Whatever questions are asked, do not accept them; this is called being unencumbered and free, attaining great bliss.

Some take "the three realms are but mind" and "all phenomena are but consciousness" as their primary principle, citing various points of similarity with ancient masters as proof, relying on what the eyes see.

Hearing with the ears is the place where one gains power. Among all points of entry, there has never been one where awakening occurred without seeing an object, nor has there ever been one where awakening occurred without hearing a sound.

Whenever there is a formal arrangement or imitation of the ancients' similar examples, and someone asks a question, one simply adheres strictly to the point of the questioner's inquiry and answers; this is called "attaining the Unborn beneath the words. This is precisely [the way].
It is like the people of Fuzhou who spin hemp together; it is called "dense and subtle," yet it does not fall into the dust of emotional attachments.

For example, when a monk asked an ancient worthy, "How can one escape from the three realms? he replied, "Bring me the three realms and I will deliver you. Or he said, "What do you call the 'three realms'?
Or he said, "If you understand the point of this monk's question, escaping the three realms is not difficult. It is just like this.
A monk asked Fayan, "What is a single drop of water from the Cao River source? He replied, "It is a single drop of water from the Cao River source.
Huichao consulted the Master, asking, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "You are Huichao.
Citing such examples as proof, it is both entirely so and entirely not so. Furthermore, as discussed, when Yaoshan addressed the assembly at night, he said, "I have..."
"One phrase: wait until the hornless ox gives birth to a calf, and then I shall tell you. A monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "The hornless ox has already given birth to a calf;
it is simply that you, Master, have not spoken. Yaoshan said, "Bring a lamp here. The monk then returned to the assembly.
Later, Fading (Fadeng) came forth and said, "Tell me, is the one born a bull or a cow? He provided his own response: "They are twins.
When this was discussed, it was also interpreted as being in accord with the realization of non-arising upon hearing the words. Yaoshan said, "I have a phrase;
wait until the hornless ox gives birth to a child, and that shall be the end of the matter. Therefore, this monk understood and departed.
"Come here! The ox has already given birth. From this point on, the Master said nothing more; he was simply so dense and subtle that not even a trace of his sharp edge was revealed.
Fading Dengwei asked, "Tell me, was it a cow or a bull that gave birth? He then provided a substitute answer himself, saying, "It was twins.
This too should be understood as a realization of non-arising right beneath the words. [Dengwei] remarked, "He himself asked whether it was a bull or a cow."
He himself then provided his own answer, saying, "It is born as twins; there is not even a hair’s breadth more. Even the Buddha-eye cannot see it.
Take such words and understand them as a definitive breakthrough—without revealing a sharp edge and without expending effort.
It is like an ancient who pointed to a slab of stone and asked a student, "Is this slab of stone inside the mind or outside the mind? The student replied, "It is..."
"Within the mind. An ancient worthy said, "What such desperate urgency do you have? You are placing a slab of stone within your mind.

The assembly discussed this, saying, "It was not appropriate to answer him in terms of 'inside' and 'outside. Had he answered in terms of inside and outside, there would have been a deficiency or a redundancy in the Dharma.
Another spoke these words: "A truly fine slab of stone! Or: "Painfully receive this one question. Or: "What do you call 'one'?"
"A flat stone. Cheng said, "Yes, yes. Some say it was in front of the Dharma Hall; some say he thanked the Master for his instruction;
some say, "Does the Abbot still know shame? or "You have frustrated me to death. Whenever answering such questions, he would simply encompass them with a single phrase;
this is called "dense and subtle" and "not wandering astray. Such a style of insight is very common in the monastic communities.

Or it may be said that all verbal expressions are entirely irrelevant. Whenever one attempts to awaken [to the truth], one first stares wide-eyed, like a small child suffering from a convulsion, as if seeing gods and ghosts.
One merely seeks to grasp the meaning at this point of staring brows and bulging eyes. Furthermore, they mistakenly cite the words of ancient masters as evidence, saying:
"If you do not look back when the word is raised, you are already mistaken; to deliberate and reflect upon it is to miss the mark."
When awakening occurs in any kalpa, it must necessarily be triggered by looking with the eyes; it is simply a matter of being alerted once by the words and phrases of the ancients.
To call this "not being within the words and phrases" refers to examples such as the cypress tree, the washing of the alms bowl, or the three catties of hemp.
Once you have passed through one of these, you can set aside the rest like turning over a tally, and no further effort will be required. It is like this.
This "striking fire from stone" and "flashing lightning"—it merely adds a furrowed brow and a glare.
Each of you also claims to have grasped the very nose of the Patriarch; do not slander these ancients.
For instance, consider the case where a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the phrase that penetrates the Dharmakāya? Yunmen replied, "Hide yourself within the Big Dipper. How do you understand this?
The student stares wide-eyed and says, "Hiding one's body within the Big Dipper. Sometimes the teacher uses this as a provisional means to suppress him;
the student then cries out several times, "Hiding one's body within the Big Dipper! Hiding one's body within the Big Dipper!
Thinking that he has gained a firm grip and mastery, remaining unswayed by change, the teacher cannot bring himself to strike him down, and thus labels this state "reality."

[The Master] raised his head and only then asked, "What is the meaning of this? He then uttered these words: "Even the Buddha-eye cannot see it. Or he said: "Lift your head and look beyond the heavens.
Or, when asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? he replied: "The cypress tree in the courtyard. He then uttered these words:
"One branch points south, one branch points north. Or he said: "He is the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet he does not follow them."
It withers in the four seasons. All of the above lies within the realm of raising the eyebrows and staring with bulging eyes.

Only then do they offer a "concluding word" (he-tou yu) as something marvelous. You fools, you must not think that Zen exists when one raises the eyebrows and stares with bulging eyes, and does not exist when one does not;
nor must you think that Zen exists when one is being alerted (ti-si), and does not exist when one is not.
This is Chan. When some people hear Yunmen speak in this way, they misunderstand it further, saying:
"It is the same whether one is alerting the mind or not; there are no two different kinds. Those who think in such a way are truly beyond salvation.
Others do not understand at all; as soon as the Dharma is mentioned or the place of awakening is discussed, they become frantic, which is yet another error.
Citing the words of an ancient, it is said: "Fundamentally, there is no person who is deluded or awakened; one simply needs to realize it this very day.

Generally speaking, the causal conditions provided by the ancients are called "establishing expedient means" (*upāya*) or "institutionalization. The true essence, however, lies precisely in the place where there is no deliberation regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Whenever there is a question and answer, respond to each one with complete sincerity and reality. In the ordinary state of non-action, heaven is heaven and earth is earth.
This is the ground; the pillar is wood; the vajra is clay sculpture. When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. What else is there?
Have you not seen Master Zhenjing say: "Do not take 'nothingness' as your understanding; nothingness will weary the human heart.
Those who have often been poisoned by this "nothingness" instead regard these words as erroneous. Or perhaps, seeing the ancients...
A *gong'an* is a point where one cannot engage through rational deliberation; it requires a single turn of words that is entirely beyond conceptual reach, responding to every contingency.
This is called "mysterious and wondrous," also called "not entering the path of meaning," and also called "penetrating liberation in accordance with the occasion.
For example, when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "The myriad dharmas return to One; to what does the One return? Zhaozhou replied, "I am in Qingzhou."
[The Master] made a single cotton shirt weighing seven *jin*. Many people have mistakenly deliberated on this, saying: "This monk posed a most extraordinary question;
had it not been for Zhaozhou’s own way of being in the world, [the Master] would have been unable to deal with it."

It is said that "the myriad dharmas return to the One. Yet this One has nowhere further to which it may return; if there were a place for it to return, then there would be a substantial dharma. This is why Zhaozhou recognized it as such.
In his wondrous application of the occasion, he responded to every inquiry by saying: "In Qingzhou, I made a garment of plain cotton cloth;
it weighed seven *jin*. How truly extraordinary! Some have deliberated on this, saying: "The myriad dharmas return to the One; the One..."
"To what do you return? If there is nowhere to return, one falls into emptiness. Thus, Zhaozhou said, "When I was in Qingzhou, I made a cotton shirt that weighed seven *jin*.
This turning word of Zhaozhou is truly extraordinary; it does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence.
His answer is most wondrous. Some might say that Yunmen spoke in this way merely because he feared people would become attached.
Attachment. If one does not cling, this is the essential heart-instruction of the Patriarchs. It simply requires that one does not cling to this matter, remaining free and at ease.
It is not a place established apart from reality; wherever one stands is itself reality. What else is there?
Or, if someone asks, "Before your parents were born, what was your original face? one simply says, "Attendant, there is no one here to answer."
"Venerable Master, you take this karmic consciousness as your original life-spirit (*bǐngmìng yuánchén*). Those of such a sort are all merely deluded madmen wandering on the periphery.

Furthermore, there is another class who, knowing for themselves that their 'eye of the Way' is not clear and that they cannot gain the trust of others in their Chan, have no means to instruct students.
Having never studied the teachings since their youth, they now go about seeking a quick sale from the masters of the Abhidharma."
Having caught a stray word or half-phrase, they use fox-like charms to delude the ignorant. Master Linji said:
"There is a certain class of blind shavelings who, within the scriptures, take liberties with the meaning to concoct phrases and doctrines.
It is like taking a lump of excrement into one's mouth and then spitting it out onto another; it is truly intolerable. When Yuanzhao first heard this spoken, his mind...
Although he harbored doubts within, his mouth was quite stubborn; he even sneered at me as I sat among the mountain monks.

That evening, when he came into my room, I questioned him only on the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature, and he could not escape it. Only then did he come to know that practicing Chan requires awakening.
I stayed in Changle for ten days. Twenty times I entered the hall and displayed every skill I possessed, yet I could not achieve anything;
only then did I begin to feel anxious. I told the mountain monk in truth: "There is no need to display your skills.
You must simply 'crack' and 'break through'—only then can you confront birth and death. What end is there to displaying skills? Furthermore, I told him: "No..."
"You must hurry; you cannot attain realization in this life, but you shall do so in a future life. He then believed this and took his leave.
After more than ten days had passed, he suddenly sent a letter along with ten verses on ancient cases (*gū*), all concerning the karmic causes and conditions that had arisen within my own quarters.
In the letter, he wrote: "While on the road to Yanping, I suddenly attained a profound realization. I truly dare not deceive myself."
Only then can one believe that this matter is not obtained from others. One of those verses says: "It is not the mind, it is not the Buddha, it is not an object;
throughout the body is a single string of golden chain-bones. Zhaozhou met the old Nanquan and was able to say, 'In Zhenzhou they grow radishes.
I, this mountain monk, find this most puzzling. At that time, Shiguang Chan asked, "According to this verse, does it suffice?"
"Is there birth and death, or not? Yunmen turned toward the corridor and said, "As for whether one has attained it or not, go and ask Yuanzhao.
He then cited a letter from Chan Master Guang, which said: "When the Scholar meets you, he will find you exactly as the Master described. The assembly, tell me: what do you say?
What could one say? *Ei!* This would leave the whole world in doubt. Let those with the eye of discernment distinguish it for themselves.
Nowadays, those who practice Zen do not inquire whether they can or cannot resolve the matter of birth and death; they seek only swift efficacy and desire merely to "understand" Zen.
Not a single one among them fails to speak of principles. When you, the donor and the administrators, see their fondness for discoursing on principles, you consequently...
He showed him an irrational cause and condition to look at. A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? Yunmen said, "A dried piece of excrement.

Fearing that he might interpret this through intellectual reasoning, Yunmen first told him: "One must not say that the Way is in excrement and urine; the Way is in weeds and chaff; the Way is in tiles and pebbles.
One must not say 'clarifying the mind through form' or 'revealing the principle by attaching to objects. One must not say..."
Every place is real; every speck of dust is entirely of the nature of the original person. When he looked at these words, he could not bring himself to let them go.
He exerted all his strength to contemplate them, yet in the end, he could not penetrate them. Suddenly one day, he realized that this matter cannot be understood through intellectual reasoning.
He then said, "I have attained an awakening," and proceeded to compose several verses to present his realization.

The first says: "The Great Void is vast and empty; one forcibly gives it a name. Even if this were for Sengyou to paint, he could not do so. What need is there to seek its source or ask for its definitive point?
There is not a single dharma that can correspond to the mind. It further says: "Once you have arrived home, why speak further of the journey? When spring comes, the myriad trees naturally flourish.
If you encounter a superior stream and are asked about it, tell them the sun’s orb rises from the eastern side of Fusang."
It is further said: "Once the antelope has passed, the pursuit is severed; the wondrous secret is transmitted in vain at Shaolin. Idly I pluck a single tune on the stringless lute;
the clear breeze and bright moon are my two companions. It is also said: "Casting off one's hands over the precipice is truly not in vain;
when root and dust are suddenly exhausted, nothing remains. Only then does one know that the Buddha-dharma is not much; to seek it outwardly is but to become increasingly estranged."
The mountain monk said, "To compose a verse is well; to explain the principles is also fine. However, this only takes one further from the Way.
The other was not satisfied and composed another verse, saying: "One must strictly avoid discussing the mysterious or explaining the subtle;
how can one possibly follow after sounds or pursue forms? To sweep away even this single fragment—everyone here lacks true insight. Furthermore, he sent a letter saying, "Look!"

This talk is such that it directly leads to the severing of words upon awakening to the Way; where the movements of the mind cease, there is no word that can be spoken and no principle that can be extended.
One does not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of a mind for cultivation or study. One knows nothing and understands nothing; one does not engage in thought, nor enter the paths of logic.
It is simply peace and bliss. The mountain monk further says: This is a principle that transcends the ordinary. If...

This is the "dry dung-spatula" koan. When one speaks with such penetration, it is like sawing through a weightstone, or the "three catties of hemp," or "the dog has no Buddha-nature," or "sucking the waters of the West River dry in a single gulp," or "it is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing."
The phrases "there is a sentence" and "there is no sentence," like a vine leaning against a tree, and the saying "this very mind is Buddha"—all such expressions can be explained in this way.
Yet, since they cannot be understood merely in this manner, one must attain awakening (*satori*). Through awakening, all things are of one family;

without awakening, there are ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences. To err by a hair's breadth is to lose the mark by a thousand miles. You must be extremely careful. Let people say what they will: "Clouds..."
"It was improper for me to wait at the gate for a donor. However, my heart bears no grudge against others, and my face shows no color of shame.

When he saw that I, a mountain monk, spoke to him with such utmost sincerity, he finally realized that the Buddha-dharma has no partiality toward human relations; thus, he came to believe it. Once he believed, I simply instructed him to contemplate:
'What is the Buddha? It is a dried turd. This too was merely to cause him to break through like a bird’s cry and sever through like a sudden snap."
Because Qu served as an official, he donated his wealth to establish a hermitage and set aside estates to provide for the assembly, even to the point of making offerings to the mountain monks;
yet he took this to be the ultimate goal. If that were the case, then all the destitute people throughout the world would have no further opportunity to practice Chan.

Not only would this cause one to lose the "eye" of a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) that distinguishes between people, but it would also mislead others for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes—this is no small matter.
This summer, there were several more monks who refused to apply themselves to practice in a way that saves effort;
they merely busied themselves in a frantic manner, coming to present their own views and compose verses on ancient cases (gong'an). Yunmen said to them, "This is not the principle."
[The Master] immediately said, "I have seized him and will not let him go. I shall ask you this: have you yourself yet been able to let go?
Zhaozhou said, "In other places, it is difficult to see but easy to recognize; here with me, it is easy to see but difficult to recognize. Yunmen usually asked his students:
"If you call it a bamboo stick, you commit the error of 'contact'; if you do not call it a bamboo stick, you commit the error of 'aversion. You may not [fall into either]."
As for speech, one cannot remain without speaking; there are ten people for every five pairs. Their eyes are covered in rheum and grime.

Even if there were those who, claiming to be clever, presented their own intellectual insights, they could at most manage to utter the word "understood" with all their might. Some would snatch the bamboo staff from one's hand; others would simply shake out their sleeves and depart.
Beyond these, perverse interpretations are beyond counting. Not a single one among them has even a drop of blood beneath the skin. Ancient [masters].
Deyun, this matter is like an eighty-year-old man entering the examination hall; it is no child’s play.
If it were something that could be contrived or fabricated, one could have fabricated a thousand, ten thousand, even millions of such cases.

Since it cannot be contrived, you must awaken to it first. Beyond this, there is no other principle. Even if you truly possess a place of awakening, the master will deliberately say it is not so. Furthermore—
The karmic cause and effect involved here is no small matter. Today, on account of this vegetarian feast and its celebratory praise, I bring it forth for the great assembly.
It was because Yuanzhao that Huang Duangfu first came to know Yunmen; it was also because Yuanzhao that Guang Chan went to reside at his hermitage.

That Duangfu’s two sons today have prepared this feast and invited this mountain monk to deliver a general discourse is likewise due to Yuanzhao. This entire performance by Yunmen was made possible by him.
A tangle. It is also because of Yuan Zhao. Since it is thus, tell me: what is the ultimate matter regarding Yuan Zhao? After a long silence, he said:
"Wait until he comes to Yunmen in person during the winter; at that time, I shall reveal it to you all. He struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
The Lady of Qin requested a general discourse. (The lady was Ji Shi Fazhen, the mother of Zhang Wei Gong Xu. She had lived as a widow since her youth and secluded herself.)

While living amidst worldly splendor, she maintained a vegetarian diet and engaged in ritual recitations. The Master sent Chan Master Xian to visit Duke Wei. The Duke subsequently requested that Xian instruct his wife. The lady asked, "How does the Abbot of Jingshan usually guide people?

Xian then recounted the Master’s teachings on the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan and the "cane" koan, as well as the instructions not to seek realization at the moment the words are uttered. He further advised her to temporarily suspend her recitations and focus exclusively on contemplating the koan;

once the head of the koan is penetrated, even ritual recitations become sublime function. The lady then came to have deep faith. One day, she suddenly attained sudden enlightenment. She then related the circumstances of her realization and presented several verses to the Master. One of the verses says: "Every day I read the scriptures, Like meeting an old acquaintance. Do not say there are frequent obstacles; A single utterance—"

"A new turn! The Master saw this and approved it. On the occasion of the birthday of Lady Ji of the Qin State, he requested the Master to deliver a general discourse (*pūsè*). At the beginning of the chapter, there is a dialogue; the narrative details are not recorded here. "Today is the birthday of Lady Ji of the Qin State.
Yesterday, Chan Master Qian came up and told me, 'Venerable Sir, please explain the illnesses of Chan in detail.
He further requested that I establish the conditions for the Prajñā-pāramitā for the sake of Lady Qin and the great assembly. I said to him, 'What illness of Chan is there to be explained?'"
Zen has never suffered from headaches, nor has it suffered from foot pain, nor deafness, nor dimness of sight.

It is only those who practice Zen who suffer these distinctions: they attain distinctions in their realization, distinctions in their application of mind, and distinctions in their reliance upon teachers.
Because of these distinctions, they are said to have "illness"; it is not that Zen itself possesses illness.
It is an illness. What is the Buddha? "The very mind is the Buddha. What illness is there in that? Does a dog have Buddha-nature? "No. What illness is there in that?
To call it a bamboo stick is to encounter resistance; not to call it a bamboo stick is to turn one's back on it.
"What illness do you have? What is the Buddha? "Three catties of hemp. "What illness do you have? What is the Buddha? "A dried piece of excrement. "What illness do you have?
You have not yet penetrated it. As soon as you employ intellectual reasoning in an attempt to penetrate it, you are already thousands of miles away and there is no connection.
If you intend to fix your mind upon it or intend to contemplate it, you must instead realize it at the very moment it is raised."
Briefly stated: to realize the moment of the "flashing lightning at the strike of a stone" is precisely where the illness lies; even worldly physicians fold their hands in helplessness.
Yet, ultimately, this has nothing to do with the matter of Chan. Zhaozhou said: "If you wish to be a disciple of the Empty King, do not let the illness of the mind be the most difficult to cure.
I recall Śāriputra asking the girl Candrottarā: "Which vehicle are you currently practicing?"
[Is it] for practicing the Śrāvaka-yāna? For practicing the Pratyekabuddha-yāna? Or for practicing the Mahāyāna? The girl Candrottarā replied:
"Śāriputra, since you have asked which vehicle I practice, I shall now ask you in turn. Śāriputra, I pray that you will answer me as you please:
Is the Dharma realized by you, Śāriputra, for the sake of practicing the Śrāvaka-yāna, or for practicing..."
"The Pratyekabuddhayāna is for the practice of the Mahāyāna. Śāriputra said, "No, Noble Daughter of the Moon. Why is that?
For those dharmas are without differentiation and without verbal expression; they are neither distinct nor one, nor are they many.
The Noble Daughter of the Moon said, "Śāriputra, for this reason one should not differentiate between the single characteristic and the diverse characteristics of all dharmas."
There is no distinct characteristic; among all characteristics, there is nothing upon which one can dwell. The Master said: "Śāriputra asked thus, and Candrottarā answered thus.
Tell me, how does this differ from the Dharma realized by the Great Lady of the State of Qin?
Is there anyone who can judge this? Come forward and judge it! If not, then for now, let us remain within the tangle of words."
To realize [the truth]. Thus it is said: "Those who study must investigate the living word; do not investigate the dead word.
If you can realize it under the living word, you will never forget it for eons. If you realize it under the dead word, you will not even be able to save yourself.
All of you, every day as you come and go, drink tea and soup in the quarters, carry salt and flour to the farm, or walk through the Sangha Hall—[this is the living word].
Yi. Picking vegetables beneath the long corridor, carrying arrows in the back garden, pushing the millstone beneath the millhouse—at such a time, even the Buddha-eye cannot see you.
Tell me, is this a dead word, a living word, or a word that is neither dead nor alive?
Try to determine it for yourself. Even if you manage to determine it, you still cannot escape being within these three phrases. Is this not so?
A monk saw Master Nanquan and asked, "The statement that 'this very mind is Buddha' cannot be accepted, and the statement that 'neither this mind nor Buddha' cannot be accepted either.
What is your meaning, Master? Nanquan said, "You simply believe that 'this very mind is Buddha' and that is enough. Why speak further of what can or cannot be attained?
It is just like when you, Venerable Sir, have finished eating and walk from the east corridor to the west corridor—you cannot [say you did not do it]."
This is a general inquiry into whether one has attained [realization] or not. If you can recognize Nanquan here, you will no longer be driven by the three phrases;

instead, you will be able to employ them. Once you can employ the three phrases, only then will you see with the same eye as Nanquan, hear with the same ear, smell with the same nose, taste with the same tongue, touch with the same body, and think with the same mind.

Reflect upon this: there is no difference whatsoever. It is simply because you grasp at the medicine as being the illness; the old ailment has not yet been removed, and the new ailment has already arisen.
You have instead allowed yourself to be driven about by the "dead word" and the "live word," falling into seven ups and eight downs. You take that place where the ancients cut straight through—
For now, this winding path has been cleared. But what was that direct shortcut taken by the ancients?
Let me cite one or two cases for you. For instance, Nanquan said: "If you lead the ox eastward toward the stream, it will inevitably eat the king’s water and grass;
if you lead the ox westward toward the stream, it will inevitably eat the king’s water and grass. It is better to accept things as they are."
A mere trifle? Not at all. How many have wrongly adjudicated this koan! What is the principle of "taking a little"?
It is simply saying: "Put on your clothes and eat your food. What difficulty is there in that?
To make a living following after donkeys and horses—do not slander Nanquan so easily! Since you have misunderstood this, you have also misunderstood that which is fixed.
Huangbo said, "All of you here are nothing but fellows who eat dregs of wine. Traveling on pilgrimage like this, how could you have reached this day?
Do you know that within the Great Tang Empire there are no Zen masters? At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "But what about those in various quarters who guide disciples and lead assemblies?
Huangbo replied, "I do not say there are no Zen masters; I simply say there are no teachers. This—

This very *huatou* (critical phrase) is a source of calamity. Let alone those who have not yet attained awakening, even if one were to attain it thoroughly from beginning to end, if the Great Dharma is not understood, one still fails to see Huangbo. Consider this:
when Huangbo said, "I do not say there is no Chan; I only say there is no teacher," how will you understand this? Among the assembly, they deliberate and say that everyone [possesses] their own...
Above all, who is not a great man? How could one possibly rely on a teacher’s transmission? To consume wine dregs is simply to gnaw at words;

yet words are but the dregs left over by the ancients. Be glad that there is no connection here. If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
Have you not seen how Guishan raised this story and asked Yangshan, "What was Huangbo’s intention?"
"How is it? Yangshan said, "The king of geese selects milk; he has never been of the class of ducks. Guishan said, "This is indeed difficult to discern.
But as for Guishan and Yangshan’s question and answer like this, how would you deliberate upon it?
To reach this point, one must be a person of true caliber. Since you do not understand this, you will surely take up 'the cypress tree in front of the courtyard' or 'three pounds of flax.'"

"A dried piece of dung," "sawing through an iron weight," and so forth—all are nothing but dregs and chaff. Having already misunderstood this point, you will certainly misunderstand again when it comes to Dongshan’s question to Chan-shouzuo:
"The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space; responding to things and manifesting forms is like the moon in water.
How do you explain the principle of this 'responding'? Chan replied, "It is like a donkey looking down a well. Dongshan—

Yun said, "As for the Way, you have gone too far in speaking of it; you have only managed to express eighty percent of it. Xian asked, "How about you, Master? Shan replied, "It is like a well looking at a donkey.
Various quarters of the monastic community have discussed this, saying that "like a donkey looking at a well" leaves traces, whereas "like a well looking at a donkey" is traceless.
They further call this "the extinction of emotion and the wiping away of traces," yet they should rejoice that this has nothing to do with it; after all, it is not this.
This is the principle. Since you have misunderstood this, you must also have misunderstood what Master Nanyue said:
"It is like an ox pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, one may strike the cart; one may also strike the ox. When Mazu heard this being cited, he attained great enlightenment.
Nowadays, those among the Chan community understand it to mean that the ox represents the mind and the cart represents the Dharma; they simply clarify the mind, [but neglect the Dharma].
This is self-evident. It is simply like striking the ox; the cart moves of its own accord. For now, let us rejoice that there is no further involvement.
If it were otherwise, Mazu would not have attained enlightenment even in a "donkey-year.

This old fellow initially thought that Buddhahood could be accomplished by sitting and that Chan could be realized by sitting. He sat and waited for a long time, until Master Nanyue realized his delusion.
The Master was thus taking a brick and polishing it before the other’s hermitage. Mazu asked, "Reverend, what are you doing by polishing this brick?

Nanyue replied, "I am polishing it to make a mirror. Mazu said, "How can polishing a brick produce a mirror? Nanyue said, "If polishing a brick cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha?
Mazu was shaken by these words; his mind grew feverish with anxiety, and he immediately asked:
How is this so? Right here, the nose-string has already been grasped by the hands of Master Nanyue.
Therefore it is said: "If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season.
Master Nanyue, knowing that the time had arrived, said to him: "Are you practicing seated meditation, or are you practicing sitting as a Buddha? If you practice..."
Dhyāna. Dhyāna is neither sitting nor lying down. If you study sitting as the Buddha, the Buddha is not a fixed form. Within the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject.
If you sit as the Buddha, that is precisely killing the Buddha. If you cling to the form of sitting, you do not penetrate its principle.
It is like suddenly confiscating all the family assets of another, yet further demanding that they pay tribute, leaving them with no way out; only then will they finally consent.
He relinquished his life, seeking the place of death. Once his life had been relinquished, he was able to ask: "How should one apply the mind?
This is precisely in accord with the signless samādhi. Nanyue said: "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground is like planting seeds below; I shall explain the essentials of the Dharma."
"It is like that heavenly rain; because the conditions have converged, you shall see the Way. He asked again, "The Way has no form or appearance; how can it be seen?
Nanyue said, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way; so too is it with the signless samādhi. The Patriarch asked, "Is there arising and ceasing?
Nanyue said, "If one were to see the Way through arising and ceasing, or gathering and dispersing—"
"No, it is not so. At this, Mazu was completely relieved of his doubts. As the saying goes: "If one does not enter the tiger's den, one shall not obtain the tiger's cub.
If, after awakening, one does not encounter a true person, ten out of ten will have five pairs of misconceptions; they will certainly be unable to benefit others.
Do you wish to recognize those who awaken and then encounter a true person? Mazu himself is the very model. Mazu.
