In a meticulous manner, you should understand this well. If you understand it in such a way, would that not be taking an object for the mind?

Since it is already your own mind, why must you go about recognizing something else as it? Furthermore, there is another kind who takes the Three Mysteries of Linji and the Three Statements of Yunmen, explaining them phrase by phrase, and categorizing the words and phrases of the patriarchs from the *Chuan Deng Lu* and *Guang Deng Lu* according to their respective schools.
When a single mote of dust just arises, the entire great earth is fully contained within it. From a single hair-tip lion, ten billion hair-tip lions manifest.
The entire great earth is this very gate of liberation; the entire great earth is the single eye of the śramaṇa.
If a person recognizes their own mind, there is not an inch of soil in the great earth. Mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness—all are the wondrous luminosity.
The category of things within the True Mind is assigned as the "Mystery within the Body.

This is the phrase that "encases and covers heaven and earth," exemplified by the three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves, the sawing of a weight-stone, and the centipede swallowing a tiger amidst the flames.

When Mañjuśrī gave rise to views of Buddha and views of Dharma, he was banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains. "The East Mountain walks upon the water" and "hiding one's body within the Northern Dipper"—these are all ordinary words.
When one cannot find a point for commentary or explanation, it is said: "A mosquito trying to bite an iron ox; you have no place to set your teeth.

Instances such as these are called the "mystery within the phrase" (zhongzhong xuan) or the "phrase that cuts off all streams" (jueduan zhongliu ju). It is like treading upon a scale-weight: hard as iron.
"Tread through and break your straw sandals and walk barefoot. When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep. The mountains are mountains, the waters are waters.
When walking, simply walk; when sitting, simply sit. A large month has thirty days, a small month has twenty-nine.

Instances such as these are called "the mystery within mysteries" and are known as "phrases that follow the waves and drift with the current. Have you not seen how the Venerable Fenyang composed this verse?
"The three mysteries and three essentials are difficult to distinguish; when one attains the meaning, forgetting the words, the Way is easy to approach.
One phrase, luminously clear, encompasses all phenomena; on the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh. This old man has clearly pointed out for you the very marrow of Linji;
yet [some] come to provide word-by-word commentaries, claiming that "the three mysteries and three essentials are difficult to distinguish" is a general verse. To attain the meaning...

"When the mind forgets and the Way is easily approached" is the mystery within the essence (*ti-chung-hsüan*). "A single phrase, luminously encompassing the myriad phenomena" is the mystery within the phrase (*chü-chung-hsüan*).
"On the ninth day of the Double-Ninth Festival, the chrysanthemums are fresh" is the mystery within the mystery (*hsüan-chung-hsüan*).

These were the words of former masters who bore great fame and reputation and possessed genuine realization; yet, because the Great Dharma was not yet fully clarified, they lacked a formal lineage and fabricated their own teachings, thus leading the masses astray.
The eye is born. As for the rest—those who peddle and trade—they need not even be mentioned. I imagine the Elder of Fenyang would still not be willing to nod his head.
I tell you clearly: "The Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are difficult to distinguish; when one attains the meaning and forgets the words, the Way is easy to approach.
A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena; on the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh. Having spoken thus, he further—
To attach a handle to a bowl—do not say that you possess a great name, great eloquence, and great wisdom;
even if it were the Great Master Bodhidharma himself who came forth and acted in such a manner, he would rightly be seized and buried alive, lest he corrupt the sons and daughters of others.
One blind man leading a multitude of blind men—when questioned on the Three Essentials, one is unable to provide an exegesis.
Thus, he brought together: Deshan’s bowl-carrying; Yantou’s “last word”; Nanquan’s killing of the cat; Baizhang’s wild fox; Guizong’s cutting of the snake; Daisu’s slash-and-burn;
Zhaozhou’s examination of the old woman and his examination of the hermitage master; Muzhou’s carrying of the wooden board; Chancellor Chen Cao’s examination of the monk;
Xuefeng’s “I dare say you, elder brother, have not yet reached the end”; and Dongshan’s saying, “That is so.”
"Ta Sha Dao could only speak it eighty percent. Bodhidharma’s departure to the West with his single shoe—cases such as these are all called the 'final word.
Then [the text] cites Lu Pu, who said: 'The final phrase reaches the secure barrier; it blocks the vital ford, allowing passage neither to the mundane nor to the sagely.
Though the world may rejoice in its abundance, I alone do not consent. This is what is called 'I'."
The Dharma King has mastery over the Dharma. No matter how much you scholars may exert your supernatural powers or display your skills, I shall simply hold fast and not permit it;
you call this a "secure barrier. You wait until the moment of appointing a monk to a monastery, where it is transmitted from ear to ear in a secret chamber.
Such practices as these destroy the true cause for oneself and instead propagate demonic teachings. Furthermore, there is another kind [of person]:

Regarding the Way: there are cases such as Nanquan’s beheading of the cat, Baizhang and the wild fox, Guizong’s beheading of the snake, Daisuī’s slash-and-burn farming, and Zhaozhou’s interrogations of the old woman and the hermitage master;
these are called the "establishing of the school's tradition. In reality, there was never such a thing;
they were merely intended to entice and guide students. Furthermore, there is another type that takes the interplay of the "partial" and the "correct" as its core principle, such as Dongshan.
While crossing a stream with Yunju, Dongshan asked, "How deep is the water? Yunju replied, "It is not wet. Dongshan said, "A coarse fellow.
Yunju then asked him in turn, "How deep is the water? Dongshan replied, "It is not dry. This means that while water avoids being called "wet," he [Yunju] spoke of "wet" right in its face.
To be unable to shift or turn back [the meaning] is called being a "coarse person. Yunju, however, said "not wet," which is to touch upon a taboo name without being able to shift it.
Dongshan said "not dry"; this is having words within words. What is meant by "having words"? "Not dry" is what is meant by "no words.
"Not dry" is it; "not dry" is precisely "wet. This is a living word; it can shift and turn back, and thus does not touch upon a taboo.
This is because it conceals [the ultimate reality]. Furthermore, one uses black and white circles to represent the forms of the five positions (*wuwei*).

A completely black circle represents that which is beyond the limit of *Viyūha* (the limit of sound), prior to the birth of parents, before the empty eon (*kṣaya-kalpa*), and when the primordial chaos had not yet differentiated;

this is called the "Correct Position" (*zhengwei*). A circle that is two parts black and one part white represents "The Partial within the Correct" (*zhengzhongpian*), wherein one returns to the realm of whiteness to speak of blackness.
Furthermore, one must not come into contact with black characters; to touch a black character is to encounter a taboo. To further cite a verse by Dongshan: "The Centeredness within Deviation:
'Before the moon becomes bright at the beginning of the third watch. This means that one can exercise mutual interpenetration (*huīhù*); thus, he speaks only of the 'third watch.'"

The third watch is dark; the first watch is dark; before the moon becomes bright is dark. One does not simply say "dark," but rather specifies "the third watch, the first watch, and before the moon becomes bright.

This is a skillful way of shifting the perspective so as not to touch upon what is taboo. By using a circle divided into two parts white and one part black, it represents "being centered within the partial.
Thus, one comes to speak of the white portion from the standpoint of the dark portion, yet without violating the essential message of the white portion.
It is said: "Correctness within partiality. An old woman at dawn encounters an ancient mirror. He does not speak of "brightness" or "white," but rather speaks of "dawn" and the "ancient mirror.
This is because he is able to employ *huì* (reciprocal avoidance/interchange). By using the characters for "dawn" and "ancient mirror," he avoids the tabooed words.
For "dawn" is the light within darkness, and the "ancient mirror" is likewise the light within darkness. As for the old woman, her head is white; yet instead of saying "white," he says...
"His wife. The "white" (the mundane) is already contained therein, for he is able to interweave and transform the word "white. Furthermore, regarding the verse on "Coming from the Center," it says:

"Coming from the Center—there is no path within the midst, yet it is separated from dust and grime. Some say "exiting from dust and grime," meaning that whenever there are words or phrases, they are all sung forth from the midst of the non-existent, thereby spontaneously encompassing the wondrous realization. There is nothing that does not come from the position of the Center. Or...

Whether bright or dark, whether arriving or reaching, all are wondrously embraced by the penetrating essence. In every single rank, these five matters are fully present, neither lacking nor redundant, like the five fingers on a hand.
"Simultaneous arrival" (*jiānzhōng zhì*) means arriving while simultaneously encompassing black and white, and simultaneously encompassing the partial and the orthodox.

What is meant by "arriving"? It is like a person returning home who reaches their private dwelling even before arriving at the main gate; this refers to being on the road [yet already having arrived].

Regarding matters concerning people, one can also employ skillful interchanges; the subtlety lies in being prior to the essence. This is called "reaching within the simultaneous" (*jiānzhōngdào*), meaning that one takes the preceding four positions, all of which are subtle, and brings them back to the primary position.
This is termed "settling the account and returning to sit amidst the coals," which likewise describes the dark realm.
Yet he reverses the black characters; instead of saying "black," he speaks of "charcoal. Furthermore, some say that Caoshan stated:

"The 'correct position' (zhengwei) is the realm of emptiness (*ākāśadhātu*), where there is absolutely nothing. The 'partial position' (pi'anwei) is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), wherein there are all manner of diverse myriad phenomena.
'Reaching both simultaneously' means abandoning phenomena to enter principle. 'Coming from within the correct' means turning away from principle to attend to..."

Regarding the matter of being "simultaneously encompassing": this refers to responding to all conditions in a hidden manner, not following along with the various realms of existence (*bhava*). It is neither defiled nor pure; it is without correctness and without partiality.
Therefore, it is called the "Vast and Mysterious Essential Path" and the "Unattached True Doctrine. The former masters have inferred that this single stage is the most wondrous and the most profound.
One must carefully examine and clearly discern its essential nature. Furthermore, it is said that each of the five stages consists of a three-character phrase.
The partial and the correct, the upper and the lower, revolve and intermingle without transgressing the center; the center is the position of correctness (*zhengwei*).
Whether speaking of principle or phenomena, the teachings have clear textual evidence. Is the Way of the direct pointing transmitted outside the teachings truly like this?
If it is indeed like this, what an excellent Cao Shan he was! Furthermore, he cites Fushan’s "True Praise of Dayang": "A black dog with feet of burnished silver."

The self-commentary states: "In this statement of the ultimate position (*zhengwei*), there is a partial position (*piānwei*). 'The black dog' is the ultimate position; 'the decaying silver hooves' is the partial position.
'A white elephant ridden by a Kunlun man'—the self-commentary states: 'In this statement of the partial position, there is the ultimate position.
Thus, there is non-obstruction between these two. The self-commentary states: 'This statement does not fall into the two extremes of existence and non-existence. Therefore, Dongshan said: 'Not...'"
"Who would dare to harmonize with the falling of existence and non-existence? A wooden horse neighs amidst the fire. (The Master added his own note: "This is 'Miaojie' (Wondrous Clasp).

Although it is indeed wondrously clashing, it is a proclamation of the Way through the void and the profound. When one speaks such words, one must require you to burn the crown of your head and cauterize your arms to make a vow, so that they may not be transmitted recklessly;
only then shall they be entrusted to you. This is also called the 'Final Phrase. Having finished speaking, the Master snapped his fingers.
Zhizhuo said: "This is a fine kind of 'concealing the colors' Chan. If one has even a single drop of blood under the skin, would they still be willing to eat such food?
Let me ask you: on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, when the four elements are about to disperse, will that which you have memorized and learned in the past be able to adapt?
When it must adapt, will you still be applying conscious effort? At such a time..."
At such a time, when the mind and consciousness have already grown dim, how can one turn back or evade?

Since it is impossible to turn back or evade, one will certainly crash into the womb of a donkey or the belly of a horse, receiving retribution according to one's karma. At that moment, even if one wished to touch upon the taboo and act as a coarse person, it would be impossible.
How much less could one oppose the cycle of birth and death? Furthermore, there is a discussion regarding Dongshan’s address to the assembly, which says:

"When facing [the situation], what is it like? When responding, what is it like? When functioning, what is it like? When functioning together, what is it like? When functioning beyond functioning, what is it like?
At that time, a monk asked, "What is 'facing'? Dongshan replied, "When eating, what is it like? As it is said:
"What is 'serving'? He said, "When one is turning one's back [to it], how is it? "What is 'merit'? He said, "When one has laid down the hoe, how is it?
"What is 'shared merit'? He said, "One does not perceive form. "What is 'merit of merit'? He said, "It is not shared.
"How is it when one is heading toward it? This refers to inclining toward this matter. He replied, "When one is eating a meal, how is it? This refers to this very matter.
When eating rice, there is no merit that can be interrupted. How do you attend to it? "To attend" means to serve.
It is like a person attending upon their elders: first they pay respect, and then they serve.

What was previously established as merit is such that the moment one directs oneself toward it, the sense of attendance arises. He replied: "How do you attend when turning your back? This refers to this matter.
There is no interruption. It is the same whether one is "facing" [the moment] or "turning away" from it; "turning away" is precisely the meaning of "facing.
Indeed, both facing and turning away are meritorious achievements. What is the function of this achievement? The achievement is simply activity. He asked:
"When you have set down the hoe, what then? Holding the hoe is activity; setting down the hoe is non-activity. This is the intention of Dongshan.
That is to say: both utility and non-utility are meritorious achievements. This also carries the meaning of being without interruption. As for "acting together with merit," how is this?
It means that the Dharma and the object oppose one another. The answer is: one cannot obtain form; thus, the Dharma and the object cannot become a single form.
At the very moment of actual application, this manifests the state of non-utility. Non-utility is itself utility. If it were made into a single form, then—

These ten [phrases] constitute "dead words. The fundamental principle of Dongshan’s school is that speech must avoid being "tenly complete" (i.e., definitive or final). Thus it is said, "one must not perceive color"—this is a "living word.
When it comes to "functioning within function," what is it? It means that both phenomena and their objects are empty;

this is called "the great liberation of non-existence. Therefore it is said, "not shared. This means there is no dharma with which one can share. The meaning of "not shared" is entirely contained within the realm of meritorious achievement (*guoxun*).
This is precisely what is meant by the non-obstruction of phenomena within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Before you there is no "I," and before me there is no "you.
Thus, Jia Shan said: "In this place there is no old monk; before one's eyes there is no disciple. Such is his teaching.
All proceed toward serving and attending [the Master]. Within the four modes of deportment during daily life, there is nothing that does not encompass both the mundane and the supramundane;
this is called the "Five Stages of Merit. You say, "Does the meaning of those ancients truly lie in this?
If it were merely like this, what would be so extraordinary? It would simply be a tangle of oral transmission and mental instruction. Since it is not thus, then—
What was the ultimate intention of the ancients? Miaoxi shall provide you with a commentary, so that those from all quarters may examine it.
Have you not seen Fenyang say: "The face and features are present; feel free to choose. Thus, Vimalakīrti said:
"One should eliminate only the illness, but not the dharma. Furthermore, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: "If you listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind, this Dharma..."
It is also a matter of conditions. Although the single words and half-sentences of the ancients were expressions of compassion, they all fell into error before one had even defecated.
Such things as the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, the Four Kinds of Discernment, and the Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality are likewise this same principle.
When Miaoxi speaks thus, it is not to disparage the various quarters; rather, he wishes for those within the school to distinguish between the black and the white.
Furthermore, there is another kind [of realization]. It does not reside in words; it does not reside in the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients;
it does not reside in the nature of mind; it does not reside in the mysterious and wondrous; nor does it reside on the side of existence or non-existence, gain or loss.
It is like fire: it burns as soon as it is touched. It does not stand apart from reality to establish its location; where it stands is itself reality. To take it up with a trusting hand—this is it.
Come! Transcending the present and surpassing the past—sentence after sentence comes and goes, yet at the end there is one extra sentence; this is what it means to "gain the advantage.
Those like this are merely playing with a mass of deluded karmic consciousness. They claim there is no cause and effect, no retribution, no human beings, and no Buddhas.
They say that drinking wine and eating meat do not obstruct Bodhi, and that committing theft and adultery are likewise no hindrance.
This obstructs Prajñā. Such as these are precisely "the worms within the lion's body," devouring the very flesh of the lion's body.
This is what Yongjia meant when he said: "To recklessly embrace emptiness and deny cause and effect; to roam wildly and carelessly, inviting calamity and disaster."
There is a way of discussing the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients called the "craft of needlework," or the "Chan of the young gentlemen.
For instance, when discussing the words regarding the woman emerging from samādhi, it is said: "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas;
why was he unable to bring the woman out of her samādhi? It is replied: "Mañjuśrī had no affinity with the woman; it was Wǎngmíng who [had that affinity]. This is the first [point].
Regarding the Bodhisattva Ding (Earth): why was she able to emerge from the woman’s samādhi? It is said that she had an affinity with the woman. The response given was: "The enemy has its head;
the debt has its owner. Furthermore, they deliberated: "Mañjuśrī was not free of intention, and therefore he could not emerge.
Wuming was without intention, and therefore she was able to emerge. The response given was: "Where there is intentional application, error is formed; where there is no..."
When one seeks it with the mind, it remains as elusive as ever. Furthermore, there are those who deliberate: "Why was Mañjuśrī unable to emerge from the woman's samādhi?
The handle of the ladle was in the woman's hand. Why, then, was Wangming able to emerge? This is like a worm gnawing through wood.
Others say it is like using the wind to fan a fire. Still others say, "What can be done about the woman? The most extreme of these erroneous interpretations even go so far as to compose...
He assumes the posture of entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), then again the posture of emerging from it. He gives a push, snaps his fingers once, and cries out "Heaven!

several times. "I humbly pray that you will still partake [of this offering]. Beholding such gestures as the sweeping of the sleeves with a cold eye, one is filled with mortification. Furthermore, Bāzhuo said:
"You have a staff; I give you a staff. You have no staff; I snatch away your staff.
He deliberated, saying: "If you are such a person, I shall speak these words to you—this is called 'giving you a staff.
If you are not such a person, I shall pluck out your eyes right before your face."
This is called "snatching away your staff. The response given is: "Appointing to office according to one's talent. It is also said: "Watching the tower, one strikes the tower.
Furthermore, there are those who deliberate, saying: "There is giving and taking; there is seizing and releasing. Such understandings among students are as numerous as hemp or millet.
As stated above, all of these are merely oral transmissions and heart-to-heart instructions—exposed, tangled vines struck from a printing block.
"Come! To cast it out from a mold is not only to slander yourself, but also to slander the ancients of old.
This is the 'sea-shell' Chan learned by those in various quarters. Do you all, venerable sirs, believe this? Have you not heard it said: 'When compassion descends, there is the Dharma;
where there is no Dharma, compassion does not descend'? Grasp the meaning at the tip of the hook; do not fixate on the zero point of the scale. Thus I say:
This is the Zen of the sea oyster: as soon as it opens its mouth, its heart, liver, and five viscera are revealed; all rare treasures are right before one’s face.
When it closes its mouth, where can one find even a crack? This is not a matter of forced effort; the Dharma is simply thus. Venerable elders, time is precious.
Each of you, while your physical strength and vigor remain, must exert yourselves with fierce spirit to realize it. Do not—
To love others is extraordinary; yet this extraordinariness deceives and misleads people.

With poisonous defilements within their consciousness, they will not find strength even at a later time, nor will they be able to transcend death at the moment of dying. What more can be said of opposing birth and death?
Worldly ignorance and afflictions are, in fact, limited in scope; if one discerns them in a single thought-moment, they are extinguished in their very substance.

Ignoble knowledge and ignoble views regarding the objects of the mind (dharmas) and afflictions are limitless; they can obstruct the eye of the Path and cause your consciousness to ceaselessly wander day and night.
You slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, thereby creating karma for the hells. Thus, even though these may be virtuous causes, they instead bring about evil fruits.
Only those who are truly wise men of great character can recognize this for what it is and remain undisturbed by it.
Have you not heard the words of Master Yunmen? "He brings the entire universe at once and places it upon the lashes of your eyes.
When you hear such a statement, I do not expect any of you to impulsively come forward and give this old monk a slap; rather, please proceed with caution.
Examine it slowly and thoroughly: does it exist or not? What kind of principle is this?
Even if you were to understand it here, in the school of the patch-robed monks, you would deserve to have your legs broken with a mallet.
If you are a person of substance, upon hearing where an old master has appeared in the world, you should spit right in his face to defile my ears and eyes. If you are not such a person—
This person has both hands and feet; as soon as they hear someone raise a point, they immediately take it upon themselves—this already falls into the secondary mechanism.
Furthermore, have you not seen the words of Master Luoshan: "The Gate of Mystery has no dharma; it establishes no regulations. If you wish to seek it out, look before the sound. O sons of the Buddha:
the true mind is not fixed, and true wisdom is boundless. If I were to let loose these two flaps of skin...
From this day forth until the end of the future, it shall continue in an unbroken succession like a linked chain, without borrowing the power of others.
This is the portion belonging to every person; it is the matter each possesses in full. One cannot add a single thing to it, nor can one subtract a single thing from it.
When Buddhas and Patriarchs attain it, they call it the Dharma-gate of Great Liberation; when sentient beings lose it—
This is called worldly toil and affliction. Yet, gain has never been gained, and loss has never been lost; for gain and loss reside in the person, not in the Dharma.
The Patriarch said: "The ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear.
A difference of a hair’s breadth, and heaven and earth are as far apart. If you wish to see what lies before you, do not maintain compliance.
[The Master] said, "No. Every one of you Chan practitioners can recite it; have you ever applied even a fraction of your attention to understanding its meaning?
The Patriarch established this name and called it the 'Inscription on Faith' (Xinxin Ming) solely so that all people might believe in this vast, quiescent, and wondrous mind."
It is certain that it cannot be obtained from others; therefore, there is a saying in between: "If the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
Without fault, there are no dharmas; with non-arising, there is no mind. When the capacity [of the mind] follows the object and ceases, the object pursues the capacity and sinks.

The object arises through the capacity, and the capacity arises through the object. It is further said: "The essence of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult. It is also said: "To grasp it is to lose the measure; it must..."
Entering onto a wrong path—let it be as it is naturally. In its essence, there is neither going nor staying. You need only believe in this Dharma of the single mind;
it is neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned. Then you may well let go of body and life right here. If you cannot let go, it is because your faculties are dull.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, do not mistakenly blame this old man. It is hot; I have stood for a long time. (He gave a shout.)

The Master struck the seat and descended (proceeding to the general discourse at Xuefeng). It is said: "Nowadays, how many people in all quarters have misconstrued this! When those of the lineage have not yet attained clear vision, they come forward to pose a question. Yet the blind fellows on the meditation platform simply respond with conventional, clichéd phrases, saying:

'He helped him across the waters of the broken bridge; he accompanied him back to the village of the bright moon. One phrase comes, one phrase goes; they say, 'I have answered with the profound, I have answered with the wondrous.

Students do not recognize good from bad; they tuck it into their bags and carry it about. Wherever they find a fit, they come back and demand certification. If the master does not find it fitting, they harbor such unqualified and impure things in their chests, treating good people with contempt and creating the karma for hell."—Also, the Counselor Qian.

Please explain this universally. Some say: "These various heads of schools—whether of the Yunmen, Linji, Caodong, Fayan, or Guiyang lineages—if the Great Dharma is not clearly understood, each will merely honor their own school, follow their own teacher, revere their own father, and cherish their own son.

They merely manage to understand the 'essence' (zongzhi), yet it is neither fervent nor vital. When I was among the assembly, I once requested instruction from a venerable elder. This elder spoke of the Chan gate’s teaching that "within words there is no word, and within no-word there is a word.

He cited a proof for me, saying: "Within words there is no word: 'When you meet a dead snake on the road, do not strike it; carry it home in a bottomless basket. This is called 'within words there is no word. It is also called 'within no-word there is a word.'"

“Speech. How is it that there is no speech within speech? “When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it down. How is it that there is speech within no-speech? “Carry it home in a bottomless basket. This single phrase possesses both of these meanings. “When you encounter a dead snake on the road, do not strike it down” is speech within no-speech;

“Carry it home in a bottomless basket” is no-speech within speech. It means that since it is already a dead snake, there is no further need to strike it down. Furthermore, he asked: “How is it that there is difference within sameness? “The egret standing in the snow is not of the same color.

How is it that there is sameness within difference? “The bright moon among the reeds is not like him. When I speak thus, you may understand it immediately, but what does that accomplish? Such people as this— (Note: The final sentence is left untranslated here as it appears to be a fragment or a concluding rhetorical aside.)

Do not study the Great Dharma as if after the light has already dawned; once you have raised even a single thread or a hair’s breadth, you will understand everything all at once. Furthermore, he said to Huang Boceng: "In ancient times, as soon as a student entered the gate, the Master would immediately strike with a staff or shout. This was done only for fear that the student might be unable to take it up, lest they become impatient.

How much less would one engage in tedious and repetitive talk—discussing phenomena, principles, mysteries, or subtleties—like a needle searching for a horsehair in a haystack? In recent years, this Way has declined. Those who occupy high seats to act as teachers of men do nothing but use the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients to offer praise or censure, or transmit them in secret chambers.

Those who claim to practice the Way of Chan either take silence and wordlessness to be the affairs of beyond Vipaśyin Buddha, prior to the empty kalpa; or they take what is seen by the eye and heard by the ear, along with the raising of awareness and the urging of mindfulness, to be the Way of Chan."

To act with reckless abandon, like sparks struck from stone or flashes of lightning—claiming that upon being raised, one immediately understands and thereby negating everything—is not the way for those who take up the Way of Chan. Since such things are not it, what then is the point of true realization?

If there were a point of true realization, how would it differ from these? Those with the eye [of wisdom] know it the moment it is raised. The above are all words of warning that point out and condemn erroneous understandings. Furthermore, they are the most urgent exhortations. (No more of this insatiable, entangling verbiage.)
The Chan Master Miaoguang Jiaozhong was a man of destiny from Quanzhou. Initially he relied upon Yuanwu, and subsequently he visited Foxin.

Having already paid his respects to the Master [Juefan Huihong], the Master asked him, "Recite one or two instances of what you have attained while with Foxin, and let me see. Miaoguang then cited an instance where Foxin had taken up a staff.
The "Puhua Gong'an" states: When asked, "The Buddha-mind is not like this; what is it like when one does not come in such a way at all?

[Puhua] struck him across the back, saying, "Let him manifest his body throughout the entire world. The Master asked, "What is your intention? Guang said, "I do not approve of his adding a footnote at the end.
The Master said, "This is precisely taking a sickness for the Dharma. Guang remained resolute and did not believe him.
"Is it to your satisfaction? The Master said, "You must simply examine and contemplate it for yourself. Guāng ultimately did not believe this was so.
After ten days had passed, he suddenly recalled Hǎiyìn’s remark: "The sound of thunder is vast, yet there are no raindrops at all. He felt a sudden, unobstructed clarity.

He hurried to inform the Master, who then questioned him regarding the cases of Dào zhě meeting Lángyá and Xuánshā’s statement that [Dào zhě] had not yet reached full penetration. Once Guāng had responded, the Master said:
Although you have advanced one step, you still do not know where to rest. It is like a man cutting down a tree: if he strikes a single blow at the root, the life-force of the tree is severed.
If you strike at the branches instead, can you possibly sever the life-force? Nowadays, those everywhere who discourse on Chan in such a vast clamor all possess this same kind of insight;
what benefit does it bring to the matter at hand? As for the direct transmission of Yangqi, there are only three or four people.
Having said this, Huiguang departed in indignation. The following day, the Master asked him, "Have you returned to your doubts? Huiguang replied, "There is nothing to be doubted.

The Master said, "As for the ancients when they met one another, they already knew whether a person was empty or substantial even before a word was spoken; yet others would hear their words and [know the same]."

He immediately discerned [Guang’s] depth and shallowness. "What is the principle behind this? Guang asked, trembling with awe. The Master directed him to investigate the "phrase with words" and the "phrase without words.
When the Master passed by Yunmen Hermitage, Guang attended him on the journey. One day he asked, "I have reached this point, yet I cannot attain thorough penetration.
Where does my illness lie? The Master said, "Your illness is most peculiar; even the world's physicians fold their hands in helplessness. Why? Because others can die, but you cannot."
"Alive! You are now alive; you have never died. To reach the ground of great peace and bliss, you must die once.
Because of this, Guang became even more doubtful. Later, when he entered the room, the Master asked: "The congee is finished; the bowls have been washed."
"Set aside the medicinal taboos and bring me a single phrase. Guang said, "Torn asunder. The Master roared with a shout of awe and said, "Are you speaking of Chan again?
At that, Guang attained great enlightenment. The Master beat the drum and addressed the assembly, saying, "The tortoise's hair—Shide laughs heartily."

With a single blow, ten thousand layers of locks are opened; the joy and fulfillment of a lifetime are realized this very day. Who would say that a thousand miles have deceived me here? Guang also presented a verse, saying:
"A single pressure brings forth a roar like a thunderclap at the opportune moment; it startles Mount Sumeru and causes the Northern Dipper to hide within."
The vast waves surge boundlessly, their crests reaching to the heavens. Having grasped the nostrils, one loses the mouth.

Chan Master Dingxu of Xichan Monastery in Fuzhou was a youth who had passed the civil service examinations. At the age of twenty-five, he happened to read the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa* (Yijiao jing) and suddenly exclaimed, "How nearly have I been misled by the scholar’s cap!
He wished to leave the household life, but his mother opposed him, citing that the wedding ceremony was imminent. Dingxu replied, "The peach blossoms are red and the apricot trees are pink."

At one time, he entrusted [the Dharma] to the spring breeze; with green bamboos and yellow flowers, they became his eternal companions on the Way. Eventually, following Baoshou, he took pleasure in becoming a bhikṣu.
Carrying a single staff through Lake and Xiang, he visited renowned masters everywhere. He built a hermitage at the summit of Qiang Peak and did not descend the mountain for three years.
Later, Fuxin invited him out to lead the assembly at Dachen. Once, he asked a student: "That which is right before you—"
"Mind is itself Buddha" is the causal condition [for this teaching]. At that time, Master [Zhaozhou] was staying at the Yangyu Hermitage.

Master Guang was on friendly terms with Master Xu, so he said to him, "The hermitage master’s methods are different from those of other quarters; you should come for a brief visit. Xu did not respond. Guang used a stratagem to compel him to go.
It happened that the Master was then conducting a private interview with the assembly. Xu joined the ranks of the assembly, and the Master asked him about the saying, "Mind is itself Buddha."
"How do you understand this? [Fengxue] was asked to provide a response. The Master rebuked him, saying, "With such a level of understanding, how dare you act as a teacher to others?
He then beat the drum for a public discourse, exposing all the points upon which [Fengxue] had placed his lifelong reliance and dismissing them all as erroneous interpretations.

Fengxue reflected on his own delusions and confusion; tears flowed down his cheeks as he thought silently to himself, "Since what I have attained is not correct, then that which the Patriarch from the West transmitted..."
"What is the essential fruit [of this]? One day, the Master asked him, "When there is no letting out from within and no letting in from without—just at such a time as this, what is it?
As Xu was about to open his mouth, the Master took up his bamboo staff and struck him repeatedly across the spine.
Xu attained great enlightenment and cried out in a stern voice, "The Master has already given too much! The Master struck him once more. Xu bowed, and the Master smiled.
He said, "Today I finally know that I have not deceived you. He sealed this with a verse. Chan Master Tanyi of Yuyuan and Chan Master Zunpu of Yuyang both studied together under Yuanwu.
They each claimed to have no further doubts. Tanyi went into the world at Xiangyun in Fuzhou, where Zunpu served as his assistant;
the Dharma assembly there was quite flourishing. When the Master entered Min, he realized that Tanyi’s realization was not yet stable and feared...
He was misleading the assembly. He sent a letter ordering [Yi] to come. Yi hesitated. The Master gave a small-scale discourse (*xiaocan*) and severely rebuked his error.

Yi then broke his summer retreat to come and see him. The Master questioned him regarding his realization, saying: "With such a view as yours, how can you dare claim to be a successor to the Elder Yuanwu?
Yi returned home and subsequently withdrew from the monastery. Together with Pu, he relied upon the Master's seat. One day, the Master asked Pu: "Sansheng Xing..."
"Whether he manifested [himself] or did not manifest himself; whether he spoke as a person or did not speak as a person—tell me, do these two old fellows have a way to emerge, or not?
Xuepo struck the Master’s knee with his fist. The Master said, "This punch of yours—is it to vent the spirit of Xinghua, or is it to vent the spirit of Sansheng?
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! As Xuepo hesitated, the Master struck him across the back with his staff.

"Strike! he said. "Furthermore, you must not forget this one blow. On another day, while listening to another monk enter the room for private interview, the Master asked that monk, "When Deshan saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately strike him.
When Linji saw a monk enter the gate, he would immediately shout at him. When Xuefeng saw a monk enter the gate, he would say, 'What is this? When Muzhou saw a monk enter the gate, he would say—"
"I grant you thirty blows for presenting this public case (gong'an). Do these four old fellows have any way of benefiting others? A monk said, "They do. The Master said, "Stop!
The monk hesitated, and the Master immediately shouted and sent him out. Upon hearing this, Pu suddenly attained realization. One day Yi entered the inner chamber;
the Master asked, "I want someone who does not know Chan to serve as National Teacher. Yi said, "I will do it."

"You have attained the status of National Teacher," the Master said, and he drove him out with a shout. After a long while, the Master said to him, "Xiangyan’s place of awakening was not at the point where the bamboo struck;
Jushi’s place of awakening was not on his fingertip. Yiyi also attained realization.
Chan Master Daqian of Kshan first relied upon Yuanwu. Later, having followed his teacher to dwell in a hermitage in Quannan, when the teacher took charge of Mount Jing, he [Daqian] was ordered...
Xian traveled to Changsha to deliver a letter to the Layman Ziyuan. Xian said to himself, "I have practiced Chan for twenty years without reaching a point of entry.
To undertake this journey again would merely waste more time and years; I intend not to go.
A friend named Zongyuan rebuked him, saying, "It is not that you cannot practice Chan while on the road. Go! I will go with you. Xian did not [dissent].
Having received [the instructions], he set out on his journey. On the road, he wept and said to Yuan, "I have practiced Chan, yet I have gained no real strength from it.

Now, as I travel hurriedly along this road, how can I achieve resonance with the truth? Yuan replied, "You need only take that which you have studied under various masters, that which you have awakened to, and that which Yuanwu and Miaoxi have explained for you—you must not concern yourself with any of these at all. While on the road..."
"As for matters that can be substituted, I will substitute for you entirely. There are only five things for which I cannot substitute;
these you must attend to yourself. Xuefeng asked, "What are these five things? Yuanwu said, "Wearing clothes, eating food, defecating and urinating, and carrying a corpse along the road.
At these words, Xuefeng attained realization. When Xuefeng returned home after delivering a letter, the Master was at the midpoint of the mountain.

From the pavilion, he looked out and said, "This fellow has changed his very bones. When Xuefeng heard this, he remarked, "In the way an old man examines people, I am surely not surpassed by Śākyamuni.
(Xuefeng once addressed the assembly, saying: "Time passes easily; you must practice diligently. There is no other practice; simply let go and that is it.

Take everything within the mind-consciousness and let it go all at once. This is the truly direct and decisive practice. If there were any other practice, it would all be nothing but wandering outside in folly and madness. I usually say: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must certainly... )

"It is so. Seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing—these are certainly not it. Thinking and discriminating—these are certainly not it. Speech, questioning, and answering—these are certainly not it. Try cutting off these four paths and look. If you do not cut them off, you will certainly not awaken; if you do cut them off, [you will].

A monk asked Zhaozhou, 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, 'No. 'What is the Buddha? Yunmen said, 'A dried piece of dung. You may take it for granted that you will burst into a great laugh. Master Ying Zhongwen highly praised these words.
Chan Master Wuben of Jianfu had long relied upon the Master [Zhaozhou] without receiving his seal of approval. Consequently, he wished to depart.
The Master said to him, "You need only focus your mind on investigation. If you have any realization, I shall recognize it even before you open your mouth.

Later, when Wenben entered the inner quarters, the Master said to him, "Attendant Wenben has been practicing Chan for many years, yet day after day he says nothing but 'I do not understand. Wenben retorted, 'You little devil, even before you were born...'"

"I have already had my teeth pulled three times at the Temple of Mount Huo. You should know this well! From this point on, I shall redouble my resolve to investigate the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature.
One night, when the third watch was approaching, while he was leaning against a pillar in the hall and drifting off to sleep, the word "Mu" (無) involuntarily escaped his lips.
Suddenly, he attained sudden enlightenment. Three days later, the Master returned from the prefectural city. [The disciple] went to meet him...
As soon as his feet had crossed the threshold of the master’s chamber, before he had even uttered a word, the Master suddenly said, "Old Barbarian, this time you have finally reached the very end.
Ben went to seek out Guoqian Gong at his hermitage in Jianyang. At that moment, Guoqian was citing the case of the Five-Perfected Immortal from Baoning’s verse:
"For immeasurable kalpas one has never awakened; how can one reach within it without moving? Do not—
It is said that the Buddha-dharma has no "offspring. Qiu Tan [Zongmi] asked most earnestly about this single penetration.
Xian replied, "I love his way because it does not move into the midst of things. Since it does not move, how can it reach there? Observe how the ancients attained it.
To casually bring this forth naturally strikes at the person's itchy spot. Bencheng said, "For what reason do you say, 'Most painful, Gautama, that one passage'?
Xuefeng Qian said, "Before you were even born, I had already thrice lost my teeth in the temple of Mount Huo.
Thereupon, they looked at each other and laughed heartily. The benefit of such mutual polishing among friends is truly like a seal [impressing its mark].
The seal of the covenant was without discrepancy; reaching the point of mutual understanding, they laughed heartily.

This could cause future generations to long for his dignified bearing. (Tang Zhongshe Wenruo considered himself to have made some progress on the Way. Whenever he heard monks speak of the Master’s realization prior to his formal instruction, he did not believe it. When the Master returned from Mei, Tang encountered him by chance at a boat station.

Upon seeing him, the Master said, "Are you not the descendant of Zixi? Tang replied, "I am his grandson. The Master said, "Your grandfather was at Wujin’s residence for a very long time. It seems you possess a principle of self-attainment without a teacher, yet you have not yet realized the direct path.")

The bamboo whisk remained in the hands of Shanzhu; Tang bowed his head in deep sighing and offered incense with reverence. They then traveled together by boat to E-zhu, where they earnestly sought instruction.

As for Chan Master Fozhao Deguang of Yuwang Monastery: he initially relied upon Chan Master Guanghua Ji. One day, while entering the inner quarters for instruction, Ji asked, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, and it is not an object—what is it?
Deguang was at a loss and consequently fell into doubt. He did not sleep all night. The following day, he went to...
The Abbot requested further instruction, saying: "Yesterday, I was graced by the Master’s question: 'It is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor any thing; what, after all, is it?
I hope the Master will compassionately grant me guidance. Ji-zhen gave a shout of defiance.
"This novice monk further demands that I provide a sub-commentary for you. Seizing his staff, the Master struck him across the spine and drove him out. At this, Guang attained awakening.

Having visited various renowned masters, he ultimately could not bring himself to accept their teachings. Later, when the Master was presiding over Yuyang Monastery and Guang was attending the Dharma seat, the Master asked Guang from within his quarters:
"To call it a bamboo stick is to encounter resistance; not to call it a bamboo stick is to turn one's back on it."
He was not permitted to speak, nor was he permitted to remain silent. As Guang prepared to respond, the Master struck him with his staff. At that moment, Guang attained great enlightenment;

everything he had previously acquired crumbled like falling tiles and melted away like ice. Chan Master Zuoyuan of Nengren Monastery on Mount Yan first visited Xuefeng Yicun and Focin Cai, both of whom had already verified his realization.
Later, while residing at Yunmen Hermitage under the Master, he was sitting in meditation one night when he saw a monk.
"Trimming the lamp, one finally attains thorough realization. There is a verse that says: "Trimming the lamp reveals this fire;
It shatters the ignorance of kalpas. Returning to the hall, I bump into the Holy Monk; I nearly let him slip past me face-to-face. What is it that does not slip away?
For fifteen years, it has been extraordinary; As before, it remains only this. The Master presented him with a verse, saying: "At the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff..."

The body is liberated; rising as before, one is once again alert. Eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty, there is nothing at all to do—what need is there to discuss whether one is the person of old or not?
Chan Master Shanzhi of Jiangshan first visited the Master beneath Huiganyan Peak.
One day, the Master asked him, "Where are you from, Senior Monk? Zhizhi replied, "I am a man from Anzhou. The Master said, "I have heard that you..."
Anzhou asked, "Do you know how to wrestle? Zhi immediately assumed a wrestling stance. The Master said, "When people from Hunan eat fish, why does someone from Hubei get a bone stuck in their throat?
Zhi performed a somersault and left. The Master said, "Who would have known that within cold ashes there was a single bean ready to burst?
The Chan Master Wuzhuo Miaozong of Zishou Nunnery in Pingjiang, whose secular surname was Su, was a former Chancellor.
She was the granddaughter of Gong Song and was about thirty years of age when she severed her worldly ties to travel and study under renowned masters.

Having already established firm right faith, she followed the Master to Mount Jingshan and joined him for the summer retreat. Upon hearing the Master ascend the hall and cite the dialogue between Yaoshan and Shitou regarding Mazu, she attained sudden and complete enlightenment.
When the Master descended from his seat, Feng Jichuan followed him to the abbot’s quarters and said, "I..."
"I have understood the public case (gong'an) that the Master just cited. The Master asked, "How do you understand it, Layman?
Chuan said, "To say 'it is so' is not permissible. *Suru svāhā*. To say 'it is not so' is also not permissible. *Siri svāhā*.
To say both 'it is so' and 'it is not so' is likewise not permissible. *Surusiri svāhā*. The Master related this to the assembly.
Zong said, "I once saw Guo Xiang’s commentary on the *Zhuangzi*, and those who understand it say that it is actually the *Zhuangzi* commenting on Guo Xiang.
When the Master saw that Zong’s words were unconventional, he brought up the story of Yantou and the old woman to question him. Zong replied with a verse:

"A single-leaf skiff floats upon the vast and boundless; Paddling and rowing, it strikes a note apart from the *gong* and *shang*. Clouds, mountains, water, and moon are all cast aside, Winning only..."
"Zhuang Zhou’s dream of being a butterfly has long since ended. The Master retired. [The monk] was suspicious that what he had realized was not yet genuine.
Later, when he passed through Wuxi, [Dahui] invited him onto his boat and asked: "A woman gave birth to seven sons; six did not meet with a true connoisseur.
This one alone was not even worth keeping, so she cast him into the water. Dahui, the Great Wisdom Teacher, said: "If a practitioner understands this, how do they understand it?"

Miaozong said, "Meeting. Zongtong said, "All that has been offered above is entirely based on reality. Daquan was greatly startled. One day, while the Master was hanging up his robe, Zongtong entered the room.
The Master asked, "The ancients did not leave the abbot's quarters; why then did they go to the manor to eat oil-cakes?
Zongtong said, "If you, Master, would let Miaozong pass, then I would dare to communicate a message. The Master said, "I..."
"I let you pass. Try to say something. They both replied, "Miaozong also lets the Master pass. The Master said, "What about the oil-cake?

Miaozong gave a shout and departed. The Layman Zhang Jiucheng, the Minister Wugou, before he had passed the imperial examinations, admired the learning of Yang Wen-gong and Lü Weizhong. He visited Baoyin Ming and asked him about entering the Way.

The essential point is this: clarify that this matter requires nothing less than never abandoning it from moment to moment. After a long time of such cultivation, when the proper season arrives, one will naturally realize and enter [enlightenment].
He then brought up the story of the "Cypress Tree" to have him reflect upon it constantly. For a long time, the Master had no realization and took his leave to visit Chan Master Qing of Shanquan.
The Master asked, "Is it true that everyone has a share in this matter, and each person can achieve its perfect fulfillment? Chan Master Qing replied:
However, the Duke said, "Why is it that I have no point of entry? Qing took a string of prayer beads from his sleeve and showed them to him, asking, "Whose are these?
The Duke looked up and down, unable to respond. Qing then put them back in his sleeve and said, "If they are yours, take them;
as soon as you engage in discursive thought, they are not yours. The Duke was struck with awe. Not long after, he stayed at the residence of the Su family.
One night, while using the toilet, he was precisely contemplating the koan of the "cypress tree. Upon hearing the sound of a frog, he attained sudden enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying:
"A single cry from a frog on a spring moonlit night Shatters heaven and earth; all share one family. At such a moment as this, who can understand?

At the head of the ridge, the feet ache—there is Xuan Sha. (*Chanlin Leiju* states: When the Master visited Duke Hu Wen-ding and asked about the way of cultivating oneself and governing the mind, Duke Hu said: "You need only read [the classics] thoroughly...")

Mencius categorized the various instances where he spoke of benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*) together as one. One day, while using the toilet, he was reflecting on how the mind of compassion is the "sprout" of benevolence. Suddenly, hearing the croaking of frogs, he attained a sudden realization. Unconsciously, he raised the question: "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

and replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. He could not help but laugh loudly; sweat poured down his body. He then composed a verse, which is recorded here for its uniqueness. At dawn, he went to visit the Dharma Seal, Master Yigong. Their exchange of words was deeply harmonious.
It happened to be the anniversary of the master's private memorial service, so they gathered at Mingjing Hermitage to offer sustenance to the traveling monks. The presiding monk, Weishang, had just—
When [Zhaozhou] saw him, he extended his hand. The Master (Gong) immediately shouted. Yunshang struck the Master on the cheek.
The Master stepped forward, and Yunshang said, "How can you, Registrar Zhang, slander the Great Prajñā? The Master replied, "My realization is simply like this; what about you, Master?
Yunshang brought up the story of Mazu ascending the hall and Baizhang rolling up his mat to challenge him. Before he had finished speaking, the Master pushed over the table.
The boy, Shang, cried out, "Teacher Zhang, the Registrar, has killed someone! The Master sprang up and asked a monk standing nearby, "And what about you? The monk was at a loss for words.
The Master struck him and looked back at Shang, saying, "If the ancestors do not settle their affairs, the calamity falls upon their descendants.

Shang laughed heartily. The Master presented a verse, saying: "The circumstances of rolling up the mat are truly marvelous; When heard by those in all quarters, they all knit their brows. The Terrace..."

With a single step, he overturned the board and scattered the stars; this straightforward man has never been deceived. In the *Guichou* year of the Xiangxing era, having topped the civil service examinations, he went again to visit Chang at Dong’an.
Chang said, "Fushan Yuanjian said: 'Even if you were able to enter the chamber of Fenyang, only then would you reach the gate of Fushan;
yet you have still not seen the old monk. What do you say to this? The Master rebuked his attendant monk, saying: [He then struck him.]
"Why do you not respond? The monk was at a loss. The Master struck the monk with his palm and said, "Indeed, there are no dragons in a toad's den.
One day, the Master visited Chief Seat Gui. As soon as they met, Gui asked, "I have heard that you, Scholar, found an entry point through the croaking of frogs;
is this true? The Master replied, "Where did you get such news? Gui said, "It is already manifest."
[Case: What is the meaning of "Hui"? Gong said in a stern voice, "The fire has broken out! Gui looked around at the monks nearby.
Gong said, "It has already burned down to your heels. Gui said, "I thought you had some special skill; it turns out you were only here all along."
On another day, while they were sitting together around a brazier according to their usual custom, Huigui suddenly picked up a fire-tongs and said, "You must not call this a fire-tongs;
after all, what do you call it? Master Gong then snatched the fire-tongs away, kicked over the soup kettle, and walked out.
Later, when the *Record of Essential Sayings* (Yuyao) of Master Dong of Mount Jing reached Master Gong, he read it and sighed, saying, "Now I know there are people in the ancestral gate."
"I regret that we did not meet once before. Upon arriving at Mount Jing on the day of Gengshen, he discussed "investigating things" (gewu) with Mr. Feng Jichuan and several others for a time.
The Master said, "You gentlemen know only of 'investigating things,' but you do not know of 'things being investigated' (wugé).

The gentlemen were utterly bewildered. The Master laughed heartily. They asked, "Can the Master explain this to us? The Master replied, "Have you not seen it recorded in a minor history? There was a man of the Tang dynasty who..."
Regarding An Lushan’s plot to rebel: that man had previously served as the Governor of Langzhou, and a portrait of him was there.

When Emperor Minghuang reached Shu, he saw it and grew angry; he ordered an attendant to strike the head off with a sword. At that time, the Governor of Langzhou was in Shaanxi, yet the head suddenly fell to the ground.
The Master (Zhao Gong) immediately grasped the subtle meaning and inscribed on the wall of the "Immovable Hall": "Zishao [examines] things through their patterns; Tanhui [sees] things as they are."
[The Master] said, "To understand 'one thread running through all,' it is like two five-hundred-pence pieces. The Master approved of this. On another day, he asked:

"Since you, my predecessor, have already attained realization, why do you still concern yourself with Linji’s Four Kinds of Critical Examination? What is the point of such discussion? The Master replied:

"Your current view may allow you to enter the Buddha-dharma, but it will not allow you to enter the realm of Māra. How could one possibly bypass the process of critical examination? He continued, "You..."
He then raised the question of "subduing and conforming" to Linji. Upon reaching the point where both the person and the environment are seized away, he could not help but feel joyful.
The Master said, "I am not like that. He asked, "What is your intention, Master? The Master replied, "Breaking down the city of Caizhou and killing Wu Yuanyuan.
At these words, he attained great mastery. He once said, "Whenever I hear what the Elder of Mount Jing has brought up..."

As for causes and conditions: it is like a thousand doors and ten thousand gates that open without even a single step being taken; or like being joined in carriages and seated side by side as one ascends the heights of a high mountain;
or like walking slowly and steadily as one enters the depths of deep water—this is not within the flow of ordinary experience.
"No one knows where the two of us have ended up. That I have settled this final great matter is truly due to the presence of the Elder.

I dare not let this incense-offering fall short of my debt to him. In the year of Xinyou, the Duke entered a period of mourning for his father. While passing through Mount Jing, he provided a meal for the monastics.

The person holding the reins of power claimed that the Duke had discussed matters of state administration with the Master; consequently, the Master was exiled to Hengyang. When the Duke’s term of mourning concluded, [the Master] was further relocated.
In the spring of the *bingzi* year, [Master] Nán'ān was released and allowed to return home. While traveling through Xīngǎn, he happened upon the Master, who had arrived there by chance.

They met and engaged in an intense discussion regarding the fundamental tenets (*zongzhì*), never once mentioning past events. At that time, Gōng’s nephew, Qiān Xiàn, was present in attendance. Gōng ordered his nephew to bow to the Master.
Xiàn said, "I have never bowed to monks. Gōng said, "Try to question him. Xiàn then cited the "Mandate of Heaven" from the *Zhōngyōng*.

"This is what is called 'nature. Following nature is what is called the 'Way. Cultivating the Way is what is called 'instruction. With this, he questioned him. The Master said, "If ordinary people do not know where their own life-destinies and primal sources fall, how can they further drag good people into the fire-pit? He [Hui]xian asked, "Can my teacher pierce through this for me, as the sages and worthies did? The Master said: [The Master replied: "I am capable of piercing through it for you. He [Hui]xian asked: "What is it that you call the 'life-destiny and primal source'? The Master said: "It is simply your own original face. He [Hui]xian asked: "How can one see it? The Master said: "When you have not yet opened your eyes, what do you see? He [Hui]xian said: "I see nothing at all. The Master said: "This is precisely your original face. When you open your eyes, you see mountains, rivers, the great earth, and myriad phenomena; when you close your eyes, you see darkness. This seeing of darkness is your original face. If you do not recognize it, you will wander through birth and death for countless kalpas. He [Hui]xian said: "I understand. The Master said: "Do you understand? He [Hui]xian said: "I do not understand. The Master said: "If you do not understand, how can you say you understand? If you say you understand, how can you say you do not understand? Understanding and not understanding are both delusions. Only by transcending both understanding and non-understanding can you see your original face. He [Hui]xian said: "I understand. He said: "What Heaven mandates is called nature; this is the Pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Following one's nature is called the Way;

this is the Perfectly Full Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Cultivating the Way is called teaching; this is the thousand-billion Transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). He looked at Official Gong and said: "When you prostrate, what excuse do you have?
Official Gong and the Daoist of Sanchuan discussed how one need not worry about thoughts arising, only that one fears awakening late. Official Gong then offered this verse:
It is said: "Thought is the son of the thief; awakening is the chief of the thieves. Once the chief of the thieves is struck down and killed, where can the sons of thieves go?
Upon this majestic great highway, I alone travel it. From south of Yue to north of Yan, from Liaodong to Longxi—letting go of the hand, one arrives immediately;

what need for worry or doubt? The divine sword rests upon the mountain; its edge is cold and its light is chilling. Goblins, *kui*, and *wangliang* spirits dare not dare to interfere. This is called the True."

Regarding "Awakening" (jue): during the Qin dynasty, [the character was written as] 轢. Master Jiang said: "To speak of awakening and to speak of mindfulness is to turn one's back and make it face forward; there is neither mindfulness nor awakening."
Where do you search? Who is it that arises? Who is it that awakens? When the doors and windows are flung wide open, the great void is vast and expansive.
Casting off your hands and walking forward without looking back at others—when was the carriage of the Qin dynasty ever made? You have since set your mind upon the six perfections.

He made no plans for his descendants. Consequently, he took the *Avataṃsaka* as his spiritual mentor (*kalyāṇamitra*) and provided two daily meals for it, using the food to sustain the monastic community.
He also once made offerings to the Sixteen Great Devas, and the tea cups for all their positions were filled with milk. The Duke composed a verse, saying:
"I prostrate to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha of the ten directions; I prostrate to all the deities who protect the Dharma. I now make offerings to these three..."

O Treasure Heaven, it is like a single drop in the ocean or a single hair on a cow; what wondrous art could possibly move you? Allow me to explain this for you by means of the conceptual mind (*manovijñāna*).
My mind and that of the Buddha and the heavens are no different. When even a single speck of dust arises, the great earth is divided from it.

If that dust were to vanish, awareness would become perfectly pure and clear; therefore, the Buddhas and the heavens descend to appear. If I wish to make offerings to the Buddha, the Buddha immediately manifests. If I wish...
When making offerings to the devas, the devas also appear. If a son of the Buddha should give rise to doubt, one might ask: "From where does this milk come?
Doubt is itself a particle of dust, and that dust is itself doubt; in the end, it is not at all like the Buddhas and devas. I shall now sweep away your doubts for you.
It is like pouring hot water on snow or fire melting ice. You now have a slight trace of doubt and delusion; the hawk has already flown off to the kingdom of Silla.
The Layman Li Bing, whose courtesy name was Hanlao and who served as a State Councilor, had long been intoxicated with the Way of the Patriarchs.

When he heard that the Master had categorized "silent illumination" as heterodox Chan, his heart was filled with doubt and anger. He went to the Master’s quarters to observe and listen, arriving just as the Master was addressing the assembly and citing the case of Zhaozhou.
Regarding the story of the Cypress Tree at Zhaozhou, he offered this turning phrase: "The cypress tree in the courtyard—today I raise it up once more.
To break through Zhaozhou’s barrier, one needlessly seeks out words. He then asked the assembly: "Since you have already broken through Zhaozhou’s barrier, why do you still needlessly seek out words?
After a long silence, he said: "At first I only spoke of the length of the thatch; it was only after burning it that I realized..."

Realizing that the ground was uneven, the Master suddenly attained enlightenment and said to his teacher, "Had it not been for your final words, Teacher, I would have nearly missed this lifetime" (the letter he later sent to the Master seeking further instruction is recorded above). As the Master’s illness approached its end, he sent a verse to Chan Master Miaoguang Jiaozhong, saying:
In years past, you once crossed the ferry of peril; you deeply relied upon the Dharma-power of Yunmen.

Now that your spirit and clarity have somewhat returned, how could you fail to repay your teacher’s kindness? Master Guang replied: "Sitting steadily on the Huchang chair, you have already reached the ford.
Where else would you seek the Gate of Non-duality? When the eight sufferings arise, the entire body is revealed; who knows who can repay such profound kindness?"
Tu received his retribution; after he finished reading [the scriptures], he passed away. Amidst such a great transformation of birth and death, he remained unperturbed and unchanged.
His statement that the spirit returns to its origin can be seen as reflecting his usual state.

Master Luel attained enlightenment at the age of thirty-seven. He lived in a hermitage for over ten years before becoming the abbot of Jingshan, where the prosperity of his Dharma assembly was preeminent in its time.
Later, because he disagreed with the official Xing Zishao, he was demoted to Hengyang.
He served for ten years. He then moved to Mei Yang for five more years; Mei was a region plagued by miasmic pestilence and unfit for human habitation, yet monks flocked there in ceaseless succession.
He returned to lead Yuwang for two years and again led Jingshan for four years. He retired to live in seclusion at the Bright Moon Hall (Mingyue Tang) for three years.
On the twelfth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Longxing era (the Guiwei year), he manifested illness.
On the fourteenth day, a large star fell behind his quarters; it emitted a stream of light and a sound.

On the ninth day of the eighth month, he exhorted the fourfold assembly, saying, "I shall depart tomorrow. At the fifth watch, he personally wrote his final testament and a letter to the Layman of Purple Rock (Jiyuan).
When the attendant monk Liao Xian requested a verse, the Master said in a stern voice, "If there is no verse, I shall not die."
He took up his brush and said, "In life it is thus; in death it is thus. Whether there is a verse or not, what does it matter? What a fuss! He then cast down his brush and passed away.
His secular age was seventy-five, and he had spent fifty-eight summer retreats in the monastic community. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa beside the Bright Moon Hall (Mingyuetang).

His recorded sayings consist of eighty fascicles and circulate alongside the Tripitaka (the Chronological Biography states they are sixty fascicles; this includes the correspondence recorded in the biography).
Regarding the titles of the *Fayu pushi* (General Discourses on the Dharma), many are currently incomplete in the extant editions of the Tripitaka. It is unknown who abridged these three volumes.

The *Xudeng lu* states that nine individuals—Nuxi, Sishan, Yue, Miguang, Wuben, Shoujing, Daoyuan, Daoqian, and Zunpu—who received the Dharma from their masters, all attained vast realization before their teachers passed away; yet their recorded sayings (*yulu*) are not seen in their entirety in the world today.

Furthermore, their most eminent disciples also died young, not being permitted to propagate the Dharma for long or serve as celestial and human eyes for the world. How lamentable is the Dharma of the Final Age!

Jiá (gǔ qiè; pronounced jiǎ): the two sides of the face. Chéng (zhí zhēn qiè; pronounced chéng): beautiful jade. Huì (gǔ wài qiè; pronounced huài): to cut. Guǎ (same as guāi). Nián (yú zhàn).
Qiè (pronounced nián; name of a fish): *bó* (pronounced bó; a horse with a variegated, non-uniform color). Zī (pronounced zī; diligence). Kù (pronounced kū;
extreme exhaustion from labor). Rù (pronounced rù; damp heat). Mì (pronounced mèi; enigmatic speech). Zì (pronounced zì; a female ox). Tí (pronounced tí; a weed).

Bài (pronounced bài; a grass resembling rice). Pí (pronounced dàn [entering tone]; the skin is thin and loose). Chī (pronounced chī; congealed eye-secretion). Xiá (pronounced xiá; cunning). Jiào (a cellar).
